##### Why Algebraic Channel dominated

Three reasons account for the historical asymmetry.

*Measurement-first epistemology.* The 19th-century empirical tradition
that produced quantum mechanics --- Balmer, Rydberg, Planck, Bohr ---
worked from spectroscopic data outward. The data are intensities and
frequencies of detected photons. A theoretical apparatus that operates
directly on those data, treating them as the primary input to be
encoded into algebraic structures, appears mathematically natural. An
apparatus that requires positing an unobserved propagation between
emission and detection appears speculative. Heisenberg made this
methodological principle explicit in 1925: physics should contain only
*directly observable quantities*. Algebraic Channel became the default because
measurement-statistics was the default empirical input.

*Mathematical convenience.* Operator algebra was already mature by 1925
--- Hilbert spaces (1907), spectral theory (Hilbert 1906, von Neumann
1929), the canonical algebra of position and momentum operators ---
whereas the geometric apparatus required to make Geometric Channel explicit ---
Lorentz-invariant wave propagation in four dimensions, the McGucken
Sphere construction at every event, Huygens iteration with explicit
phase memory, the $+ic$-oriented expansion at the constant rate ---
was incomplete or had to be developed from scratch. Schrödinger had a
wave equation but not the underlying geometric principle that makes
the wavefunction a wavefront on a four-dimensional McGucken Sphere; he
reached for Hamilton's optico-mechanical analogy as scaffolding and
was pulled back into Algebraic Channel by Born's probability reinterpretation
before the scaffolding could become a foundation.

*Institutional authority.* Bohr's complementarity doctrine --- with its
explicit Geometric Channel character and explicit denial of Algebraic Channel-style
spatiotemporal ontology as foundational --- became orthodoxy through
the institutional dominance of the Copenhagen school after 1927.
Einstein, Schrödinger, de Broglie, Bohm, Bell, Wheeler, and Penrose
each pushed against this from within. None had the geometric principle
needed to ground the Geometric Channel intuitions they were defending. They
were, looking for Geometric Channel without recognizing what they
were looking for or possessing the apparatus to articulate it.

The McGucken framework dissolves all three sources at once.
Once $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ is given, the geometric apparatus for
Geometric Channel is supplied: the McGucken Sphere expansion at every event,
the Huygens iteration with phase memory, the $+ic$-oriented forward
propagation. The measurement-first epistemology is preserved as the
Algebraic Channel reading of the same physical content; the operator-algebraic
apparatus retains its empirical force and gains a geometric referent.
The institutional asymmetry has no ground once both channels
are seen as theorems of a single physical principle.

::: {#rmk:historical-asymmetry-dissolved .remark}
*Remark 1.15* (The historical asymmetry as artifact).
*The dominance of Algebraic Channel in the historical record is an artifact of the order in which empirical
methods, mathematical apparatus, and institutional authority developed
in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework
makes this explicit: when both channels are available as derivations
from a single physical principle, the asymmetry collapses to a
historical accident. Algebraic Channel is the algebraic shadow of the
$+ic$-oriented Sphere expansion that Geometric Channel describes geometrically.
The asymmetry of the historical record is the asymmetry of what was thinkable — the physical content is symmetric, in 1925,
with the mathematical resources then available and the institutional
authorities then dominant.*
:::

#### The Huygens--Newton 333-year battle for the foundations of light: the first historical channel split {#ssec:huygens-newton-333-years}

The pattern of Geometric Channel's dominance and Algebraic Channel's institutional
marginalization has a clear historical antecedent in the 333-year
battle over the foundations of light, from Huygens' *Traité de la
Lumière* (1690) to the present-day quantum-electrodynamic Algebraic Channel
foundation. This is the first historical instance of the channel split
appearing in physics, with the same features observable
under the dual-channel architecture: Geometric Channel proposed first by
Huygens; Algebraic Channel asserted in parallel by Newton; Algebraic Channel winning
through the institutional authority of its proponent rather than
through empirical superiority; Geometric Channel reasserting itself decisively
when its empirical predictions could be tested; and the status oscillating back and forth across three centuries before
settling, post-quantum, at the algebraic-statistical level. The case
illuminates the pattern under which the channel split has
operated for three and a third centuries.

##### Huygens 1690: Geometric Channel from the start

Christiaan Huygens published *Traité de la Lumière* in 1690 with the
claim that light is a wavefront propagating through a
luminiferous medium, with every point on a wavefront acting as a
secondary source of spherical wavelets and the next instant's
wavefront being the envelope of all secondary wavelets. This is the
original Geometric Channel reasoning in physics --- geometric propagation of a
real physical entity through real space, with the wavefront as a
definite geometric object at every instant, expanding outward from
source events at finite velocity, with forward propagation built into
the construction by Huygens' explicit use of envelopes of
forward-emitted wavelets rather than backward-emitted ones.

What Huygens had, in 1690, was the McGucken Sphere construction in
everything but name. Spherical wavelets emanating from every event of
the wavefront at velocity $c$, iterated forward in time, with the
envelope reconstruction giving the next instant's wavefront --- this
is exactly the iterated-Sphere Huygens propagation that the McGucken
framework recovers as Theorem 89 of [@Syn-2026] and as the central
Geometric Channel derivation of the Schrödinger equation in
Chapter [\[ch:schrodinger\]](#ch:schrodinger){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:schrodinger"}. The $+ic$ orientation that distinguishes
forward propagation from time-reversed contraction is implicit in
Huygens' choice to use envelopes of forward-emitted wavelets; the
retarded-Green's-function preference that twentieth-century physics
took as an empirical fact about the universe was already present in
Huygens' 1690 construction as the geometric direction of wavefront
expansion. Geometric Channel is here at the founding of physical optics.

##### Newton 1704: Algebraic Channel in pre-quantum form

Isaac Newton published *Opticks* in 1704 with the corpuscular theory of
light: light is a stream of discrete corpuscles, each carrying definite
momentum and travelling in straight lines except where deflected by
forces. This is pre-quantum Algebraic Channel reasoning --- particle-statistical
analysis of light as a collection of indexed entities, with refraction
and reflection explained by per-corpuscle force laws and statistical
aggregation across corpuscles. Newton's analysis is algebraic-mechanical
in character: forces acting on particles, momentum transfer at
interfaces, statistical distribution of corpuscle trajectories across
many incidents. The law of reflection follows from corpuscular momentum
conservation; Snell's law follows from corpuscular momentum at the
interface (with Newton famously getting the direction of the speed
change wrong, predicting that light speeds up in dense media when it
actually slows down); the geometrical optics of imaging through lenses
and mirrors is statistical-mechanical aggregation of corpuscle paths.

The Algebraic Channel character of Newton's analysis is in the particle-statistical
framing: light is a collection of countable entities whose individual
behaviors aggregate to the observed phenomena, without the wavefront
geometry of Huygens. Newton had a particle-statistical encoding of
light's behavior that worked extremely well within the experimental
precision of the eighteenth century --- but he had it as Algebraic Channel,
not as Geometric Channel, and the wavefront content that Huygens was reading
directly was not part of Newton's apparatus.

##### The eighteenth century: Newton wins by prestige

Through the eighteenth century the corpuscular theory dominated. The
domination was  rather than empirical --- not because the
corpuscular theory had decisive predictive superiority over the wave
theory, but because four factors combined to make Algebraic Channel
the default reading for a century.

First, the mathematical apparatus for analyzing wave behavior did not
yet exist. Euler began developing the wave equation in the 1750s;
Lagrange built on it in the 1780s; Fourier published the analytical
theory of heat (giving physicists the decomposition technique that
makes wave propagation calculable) in 1822. Without Fourier analysis,
Huygens' wave reasoning was geometrically clear but analytically
limited --- envelopes could be drawn but diffraction patterns could
not be calculated.

Second, diffraction was poorly understood. Grimaldi had observed
diffraction effects in 1665, but he could not analyze them quantitatively.
The wave theory predicts diffraction at sharp edges as a consequence of wavefront-secondary-source propagation; the corpuscular
theory required auxiliary hypotheses to accommodate the same effects
(Newton invoked "fits of easy reflection and easy transmission" in
*Opticks* Query 17 to explain Newton's rings, a sign that
the corpuscular theory was already in trouble at the periphery of its
explanatory range).

Third, Newton's prestige was vast. After the *Principia* of 1687,
Newton was the unquestioned authority in physics for a century.
Anyone proposing an alternative to Newton's optical theory was
implicitly challenging the *Principia*-era research program, which
was a sociologically expensive move.

Fourth, the corpuscular theory had no significant predictive failures
within the precision available in the eighteenth century. Refraction,
reflection, dispersion through prisms, image formation through lenses,
and the inverse-square law for intensity were all handled adequately
by Newton's corpuscular theory at the precision of eighteenth-century
experiments. The wave theory's empirical superiority would not become
decisive until Young's double-slit experiment in 1801 and Fresnel's
diffraction calculations in 1818.

##### 1801--1820: Geometric Channel reasserts itself decisively

Thomas Young performed the double-slit experiment in 1801 and
demonstrated unambiguous wave interference: light passing through two
slits produces a pattern of bright and dark fringes that can be
explained only by the wave theory. The corpuscular theory cannot
produce interference fringes, because two streams of corpuscles cannot
cancel each other in dark regions; only wavefronts with phase content
can interfere constructively and destructively.

Augustin-Jean Fresnel in 1818 won the prize of the French Académie des
Sciences for a wave-theoretic analysis of diffraction derived from
Huygens' principle plus a phase-and-amplitude refinement (the
Huygens--Fresnel principle). The Académie had set the prize expecting
a corpuscular-theoretic submission. Fresnel's wave-theoretic submission
was so compelling that Siméon Poisson, a committee member who opposed
the wave theory, calculated from Fresnel's equations the prediction
that there should be a bright spot at the center of the geometric
shadow of a circular obstacle, and presented this as a reductio ad
absurdum against the wave theory. François Arago performed the
experiment and observed the bright spot exactly where Fresnel's wave
theory predicted. The Poisson--Arago spot was the decisive empirical
confirmation of the wave theory; by 1820, Geometric Channel had won the
optical-foundations battle decisively.

##### Maxwell 1865: Geometric Channel cemented

Maxwell's electromagnetic field theory of 1865 identified light as
electromagnetic waves propagating through the field at velocity $c$.
The wave equation $\Box \mathbf{E} = 0$ is foundational Geometric Channel
content: geometric propagation of a real physical field through real
spacetime. Hertz confirmed Maxwell's prediction experimentally in
1887 with the production and detection of radio waves. By 1900 the
Geometric Channel reading of light was firmly established as the foundational
account: light is electromagnetic radiation propagating through
spacetime as a wavefront.

##### Einstein 1905: Algebraic Channel reintroduced at the quantum level

Einstein's photoelectric paper of 1905 reintroduced the corpuscular
reading of light, but at the energy-quantum level rather than the
foundational level. Light interacts with matter in discrete quanta of
energy $E = h\nu$ --- the photoelectric effect, the Compton effect,
the photon model. This Algebraic Channel reading coexisted with the Geometric Channel
Maxwell reading for two decades in unresolved tension: light is a wave
(Maxwell--Hertz), and light is also a particle (Einstein--Compton).
The wave-particle duality of 1905--1925 is exactly this tension,
inscribed at the foundation of physics as an unresolved historical
oscillation between the two channels.

##### 1925--present: Algebraic Channel foundational, Maxwell demoted

The orthodox post-1925 resolution was Algebraic Channel foundational: light
is a quantum field in Algebraic Channel's operator-algebraic framework, with
the wave aspect being the classical limit of the field's expectation
values and the particle aspect being the discrete eigenstate content
of the field. The Geometric Channel Maxwell reading was demoted to the
classical-limit approximation. By 1948, with the operator-algebraic
formulation of quantum electrodynamics (Tomonaga, Schwinger, Feynman,
Dyson), Algebraic Channel had won the foundational battle for light at the
post-quantum level, this time decisively. The wave reading of Maxwell
became, in the orthodox account, an emergent classical-limit feature
of an underlying operator-algebraic quantum field theory.

##### The 333-year pattern

The historical pattern for light, from 1690 to the present, is:

  --------------- ------------------------------------------------ ----------------------------------------------------
  **Period**      **Channel**                         **Mechanism**
  1690--1704      Both proposed                                    Huygens (B) and Newton (A) in parallel
  1704--1820      A dominant                                       Newton's prestige; absence of wave-analytic apparatus
  1801--1820      B reasserts                                      Young double-slit; Fresnel; Poisson--Arago spot
  1820--1905      B foundational                                   Maxwell electromagnetic field theory
  1905--1925      A reintroduced at quantum level                  Einstein photoelectric; Compton; wave-particle
                                                                   tension
  1925--present   A foundational, B demoted to classical limit     Operator-algebraic QED; Maxwell as emergent
  --------------- ------------------------------------------------ ----------------------------------------------------

The pattern shows the same dual-channel oscillation that the McGucken
framework supplies as a fact: both readings exist as
derivations from a single physical principle, with the historical
dominance of one over the other reflecting the available mathematical
apparatus and institutional authority rather than the content of physics.

##### Resolution under $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$

The framework's claim is that Huygens--Fresnel--Maxwell and
Newton--Einstein--Compton are reading the same physical content ---
the $+ic$-oriented McGucken Sphere expansion at every event ---
through different channels. Huygens, Fresnel, and Maxwell read the
Geometric Channel geometric content directly: the Sphere as wavefront expanding
through real space with definite phase, frequency, and direction.
Newton's corpuscular reading was a bad Algebraic Channel approximation:
corpuscles as classical particles with deterministic trajectories, a
reading that fails because the corpuscles are not classical particles
but are, in the correct Algebraic Channel reading, the statistical content of
head-on Sphere collisions at detection events
(Theorem [\[thm:born-as-collision\]](#thm:born-as-collision){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:born-as-collision"} of
Chapter [\[ch:born\]](#ch:born){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:born"}).
Einstein and Compton read the correct post-quantum Algebraic Channel reading:
energy-quanta as discrete eigenvalue content of the photon field,
which is the Algebraic Channel statistical encoding of where the Sphere's
head-on collisions deposit energy at detection events.

The 333-year confusion about wave-particle duality dissolves under
the dual-channel architecture. Light is always the McGucken Sphere in
Geometric Channel: the $+ic$-oriented wavefront expanding through spacetime
with definite Compton-phase content. Algebraic Channel reads this Sphere
expansion at the statistics of head-on collision events at detectors,
producing the photon energy-eigenstate content that Einstein 1905
identified. The wave-particle duality of 1905--1925 was not a
foundational paradox but a manifestation of the dual-channel structure
in the absence of the geometric principle that makes both readings
derivations from a single physical fact. Newton was wrong about
corpuscles because the corpuscular Algebraic Channel reading at the
classical-mechanical level was the wrong Algebraic Channel reading --- the
correct Algebraic Channel reading required the post-1925 operator-algebraic
apparatus and the geometric principle $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ that
derives together with both channels from the same physical fact. Huygens was
right about waves because the wave content is the Geometric Channel
ontological substrate, which has been the physical content about light for 333 years and remains so under the dual-channel
architecture.

::: {#rmk:huygens-vindicated .remark}
*Remark 1.16* (Huygens vindicated, Newton corrected, Maxwell preserved).
*The dual-channel reading vindicates Huygens completely. His 1690
construction is the McGucken Sphere construction; his envelope
reconstruction is the iterated Huygens propagation of
Theorem [\[lem:QMT7-channelB-proof\]](#lem:QMT7-channelB-proof){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT7-channelB-proof"}; his choice of forward-emitted
wavelets is the $+ic$ orientation of the McGucken Principle. Newton's

electromagnetic field theory is preserved as the Geometric Channel reading of
the photon-field's wavefront content. The orthodox post-1925
demotion of Maxwell to a classical-limit approximation is reversed by

Algebraic Channel reading of the photon field, with both
derived together from $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$. The 333-year battle for
the foundations of light ends not with one side defeated but with both

:::

#### The four-fold iff structure: $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ as the necessary and sufficient geometric content of quantum nonlocality, the Lorentzian metric, the wavefunction's home, and the arrows of time {#sec:fourfold-iff}

The dual-channel architecture surfaces at the Chapter 11 (uniqueness)
and Chapter 13 (categorical) levels with formal iff theorems, and at
the Chapter 4 (foundations) level with the perpendicularity-marker
analysis of the $i$ in $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$, and at the Chapter 10
(measurement) level with the 4D-wavefunction / 3D-cross-section
two-level reading that dissolves Maudlin's trilemmas. This section
consolidates these results into four headline iff theorems at the
front of the textbook, where they can be read as the framework's
claims and unpacked through the chapter cross-references
into their full proofs. The section also incorporates the explicit
Laws of Nonlocality of [@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026], which supply
the necessity-and-sufficiency structure for the origin of quantum
entanglement.

##### The role of the $i$: the perpendicularity marker as the source of the Lorentzian null structure {#ssec:i-as-perpendicularity-marker}

The McGucken Principle is $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$, with the factor of
$i$ playing a role that is distinct from a unit-conversion
factor or a sign convention: $i$ is the perpendicularity marker that
sets the fourth direction $x_4$ as orthogonal to the three spatial
directions in the signature-flip sense of a Lorentzian-metric
contribution rather than a Euclidean one. The geometric consequence is
the central fact from which the framework's nonlocality
content descends.

::: {#thm:i-perpendicularity-marker .theorem}
**Theorem 1.17** (The perpendicularity-marker role of $i$;
Theorem [4.6](#thm:mcp-to-lorentzian){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:mcp-to-lorentzian"} Step 1). *The factor $i$ in
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ is necessary and sufficient for the Lorentzian
signature of spacetime. Specifically:*

*(i) Without the $i$ (i.e., under the alternative principle
$|\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}| = c$ with $dx_4/dt$ taken as real), the squared
$x_4$-differential is positive,
$dx_4^2 = c^2\,dt^2 > 0$, yielding a positive-definite Euclidean
signature $(+,+,+,+)$ on $M_G$. The wavefront from any event $p$ is
then a 4-sphere of radius $c(t-t_p)$ expanding into a Euclidean
4-manifold; there is no light cone, no null structure, and no
zero-spacetime-interval relation between source and wavefront point.*

*(ii) With the $i$ as given by the principle, the squared
$x_4$-differential is negative,
$dx_4^2 = (ic\,dt)^2 = -c^2\,dt^2 < 0$, yielding the Lorentzian
signature $(-,+,+,+)$. The wavefront from $p$ is a null hypersurface
(the future light cone); the interval $ds^2 = |d\mathbf{x}|^2 - c^2dt^2$
between $p$ and any point $q = (\mathbf{x}_q, t_q)$ on the McGucken
Sphere $\Sigma_p^+(t_q)$ vanishes identically:*
$$ds^2(p,q) = |\mathbf{x}_q - \mathbf{x}_p|^2 - c^2(t_q-t_p)^2 = c^2(t_q-t_p)^2 - c^2(t_q-t_p)^2 = 0,$$
*and the photon's share of the $x_{4}$-expansion vanishes on this null worldline: the rate partition between spatial motion and $x_{4}$-advance gives $v_{x_4} = \sqrt{c^{2} - v^{2}} = 0$ by direct substitution of $v = c$, so no $x_{4}$-advance accumulates between any two events on the wavefront, and the vanishing interval above is the metric shadow of that fact.*

*(iii) The geometric nonlocality of the McGucken Sphere — the property
that spatially separated points $q_1, q_2 \in \Sigma_p^+(t)$ share zero
spacetime-interval relation through the source event $p$ — is the
direct geometric content of $i^2 = -1$. The $i$ is necessary
(without it: Euclidean inflation, no nonlocality) and sufficient
(with it: forced null structure, forced nonlocality).*
:::

*Proof.* Sufficiency: from Theorem
[4.6](#thm:mcp-to-lorentzian){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:mcp-to-lorentzian"} Step 1 verbatim. The squaring
$dx_4^2 = (ic\,dt)^2 = i^2 c^2 dt^2 = -c^2 dt^2$ provides the
signature flip from Euclidean to Lorentzian; the line element becomes
$ds^2 = dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2 - c^2dt^2$ with timelike block
$g_{x_4 x_4} = -1$. The null structure on the McGucken Sphere then
follows from the equality $|\mathbf{x}_q - \mathbf{x}_p| = c(t_q - t_p)$
characterising sphere-surface points, giving $ds^2(p,q) = 0$.

Necessity: under any framework in which the perpendicularity marker
is absent or has a different value (i.e., a real factor $r$ with
$r^2 > 0$), the squared $x_4$-differential is non-negative; the
signature is non-Lorentzian (either Euclidean $r > 0$ or degenerate
$r = 0$); the wavefront from a source event is not a null hypersurface;
no zero-spacetime-interval relation holds between source and wavefront
points; and the geometric nonlocality of the McGucken Sphere does not
arise. Among the possible values of the perpendicularity marker (zero,
positive real, negative real, $\pm i$), only $\pm i$ produces the
required signature flip. The $+ic$ choice fixes the arrow of $x_4$-advance
(forward, $+ic$); the equivalent $-ic$ choice is the
time-reverse and is selected against by the empirical Second Law of
thermodynamics (Theorem 22.4 of the present textbook; QM T22 Compton
diffusion).

This is Theorem 4.6 Step 1 of the present textbook, with the
necessity direction made explicit here at the Chapter 1 level. ◻

::: {#rmk:i-content-summary .remark}
*Remark 1.18* (The $i$ is the nonlocality content). *The geometric
nonlocality of $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ — the property that distant points
on the McGucken Sphere share zero spacetime-interval with the source
event — is not an additional postulate. It is the direct geometric
content of the perpendicularity marker $i$. Strip the $i$ and what
remains is Euclidean inflation of a 4-sphere through 4-space at rate
$c$, with no nonlocality, no null structure, no Lorentz invariance,
and no quantum entanglement. Keep the $i$ and the entire structure of
relativity, the entire structure of quantum nonlocality, and the
Tsirelson saturation of Bell experiments are forced as theorems. The
slogan: $i$ is what makes $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ nonlocal.*
:::

##### Sphere-surface $x_4$-locality: necessary and sufficient for quantum nonlocality and Lorentz invariance {#ssec:iff-quantum-relativity}

The next iff theorem states the central uniqueness result of

\in \Sigma_p^+(t)$ has the same $x_4$-coordinate value relative to
$p$, namely $x_4(q;p) = 0$ in the natural chart) is the geometric

identity (the six-fold geometric identity of Theorem
[17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:six-fold-identity"}). The iff theorem reads:

[11.10](#thm:uniqueness-mcgucken-sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:uniqueness-mcgucken-sphere"} + Theorem
[11.11](#thm:identity-lorentz-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"

*if and only if $S$ is the McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_p^+(t)$ generated by
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ at $p$ with sphere-surface $x_4$-locality.*

*Moreover, the Algebraic Channel reading of sphere-surface
$x_4$-locality produces the Lorentz invariance of $c$ (via the
boost-tensorial-invariance of $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$); the Geometric
Channel reading produces the Tsirelson saturation (via the
$SO(3)$-Haar measure on the $x_4$-coherent wavefront); and the two
readings co-fail under any perturbation breaking $x_4$-locality
(directional rate-anisotropy breaks both Lorentz invariance and the
$SO(3)$-Haar derivation simultaneously, etc., per Theorems 11.3
through 11.8). Quantum nonlocality and Lorentz invariance are two
readings of one geometric fact: sphere-surface $x_4$-locality.*
:::

*Proof.* Sufficiency direction ($S = \Sigma_p^+(t)$ implies the five
strands): the sufficiency is established by the 47-theorem dual-channel

[13.1](#thm:QMT13){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT13"} (QM T13,

[4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"

[4.6](#thm:mcp-to-lorentzian){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:mcp-to-lorentzian"} (Lorentzian metric forced by the
$i$); strand (v) is Theorem 17.17 (Huygens self-generation from clauses

Necessity direction (the five strands imply $S = \Sigma_p^+(t)$):

[11.10](#thm:uniqueness-mcgucken-sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:uniqueness-mcgucken-sphere"} of the present textbook in

[4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref" reference="def:sphere"}

The identity content of Theorem

##### Motion of $x_4$ at $c$: necessary and sufficient for the Lorentzian metric {#ssec:iff-motion-at-c}

The motion of $x_4$ at $c$ — interpreted as the spherically symmetric
expansion of $x_4$ at rate $c$ at every event of $M_G$, with the
expansion quantised in units proportional to $\hbar$ via the Compton
coupling $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ (QM T4) — is the geometric content
captured by the magnitude $|\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}| = c$ combined with the
spherical-symmetry clause P2 of the principle.

::: {#thm:iff-motion-at-c .theorem}
**Theorem 1.20** (Motion of $x_4$ at $c$ $\iff$ Lorentzian metric;
Theorem [4.6](#thm:mcp-to-lorentzian){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:mcp-to-lorentzian"} + Theorem
[11.7](#thm:prop-D-anisotropy){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:prop-D-anisotropy"}). *The fourth dimension advancing
at rate $|ic| = c$ at every event of $M_G$, isotropically in the three
spatial directions, is necessary and sufficient for the Lorentzian
metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $M_G$. Specifically:*

1.  *(Sufficiency) Under
    $\dfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ with spherical symmetry, the line element
    $ds^2 = dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2 + dx_4^2$ on $M_G$ becomes
    $ds^2 = dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2 - c^2 dt^2$, the Lorentzian metric
    of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ with $g_{x_4 x_4} = -1$ globally.*

2.  *(Necessity --- directional isotropy) Under any direction-dependent
    rate $\dfrac{dx_4}{dt}|_{\hat n} = ic(\hat n)$ with
    $c(\hat n) \neq c$ for some $\hat n$, the induced metric is not
    Lorentz-invariant; the Lorentz group $SO^+(1,3)$ no longer preserves
    the metric; and the empirical record (Vasileiou et al. 2013,
    GRB 090510 at $|\Delta c/c| \lesssim 10^{-20}$ across photon
    energies separated by an order of magnitude over gigaparsec
    distances) excludes such direction-dependent configurations.*

3.  *(Necessity --- rate value $c$) Under any constant-rate variant
    $\dfrac{dx_4}{dt} = i c'$ with $c' \neq c$, the induced metric's
    timelike block is $-c'^2$, conflicting with the empirical
    invariant speed of light $c$. The constant $c$ is fixed as the
    rate of $x_4$-advance by the operational definition of the
    invariant speed of light through Maxwell-electromagnetic and
    Compton experiments.*

4.  *(Necessity --- spherical symmetry) The spherical symmetry of the
    expansion is necessary for the $SO(3)$-symmetric round 2-sphere
    geometry of the wavefront, without which the rotation group does
    not act transitively on the wavefront, the $SO(3)$-Haar uniqueness
    fails, the Born rule (Theorem
    [17.28](#thm:geometric-to-quantum-probability){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:geometric-to-quantum-probability"} of the present
    textbook) is not derivable, and the rotational invariance strand
    (ii) of the five-strand conjunction fails empirically.*
:::

*Proof.* Sufficiency: Theorem
[4.6](#thm:mcp-to-lorentzian){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:mcp-to-lorentzian"} of the present textbook in six
steps (the $i$ provides the signature flip Step 1; the spatial-block
metric is Euclidean by spherical symmetry Step 3; the combined line
element has signature $(-,+,+,+)$).

Necessity (clauses 2, 3, 4): established by Theorem
[11.7](#thm:prop-D-anisotropy){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:prop-D-anisotropy"} (Proposition D of the
uniqueness chapter, [@MG-Uniqueness-2026] §3.4) plus the empirical
exclusion of direction-dependent $c$ at the
$|\Delta c/c| \lesssim 10^{-20}$ level (Vasileiou et al. 2013), plus
the Tsirelson-saturation constraint excluding any rate-anisotropy
that breaks the $SO(3)$-Haar derivation. Clause 3 (rate value $c$
exactly, not some other constant) is fixed operationally by the
measured invariance of the speed of light across Maxwell's electrodynamics,
Michelson-Morley, and the GRB-timing precision. ◻

##### The wavefunction lives on $\mathcal{M}_G$; the measurement reads its 3D cross-section {#ssec:iff-wavefunction-measurement}

The fourth iff theorem dissolves the orthodox measurement problem by
identifying the wavefunction with the 4D structure on $\mathcal{M}_G$
rather than with its 3D-cross-section reading.

::: {#thm:iff-wavefunction-x4 .theorem}
**Theorem 1.21** (4D wavefunction on $\mathcal{M}_G$, 3D cross-section
on the constraint locus; Theorem
[10.4](#thm:maudlin-1-dissolved){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:maudlin-1-dissolved"}). *Under
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$, the wavefunction has two distinct
readings at distinct organisational scales:*

1.  *The 4D wavefunction $\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4)$ on the McGucken Space
    $\mathcal{M}_G$ evolves unitarily under the McGucken Operator

2.  *The 3D cross-section reading
    $\psi(\mathbf{x}, t) = \Psi(\mathbf{x}, ict)$ at the
    McGucken-constraint locus $x_4 = ict$ (the mere integrated kinematic
    shadow of $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$, Remark
    [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
    reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is what the apparatus reads.
    The apparent collapse is the observer's restricted access to this
    3D cross-section; the underlying 4D dynamics is unitarily preserved

3.  *The two readings live at distinct organisational scales: $\Psi$
    is complete (Maudlin's (1.A)) and evolves linearly (Maudlin's
    (1.B)) at the 4D level on $\mathcal{M}_G$; $\psi$ has determinate
    outcomes (Maudlin's (1.C)) at the 3D-cross-section level. The
    Maudlin trilemma --- that (1.A), (1.B), (1.C) are jointly
    inconsistent in standard QM --- dissolves under
    $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ because the three claims live at distinct
    organisational scales of the framework.*
:::

*Proof.* Theorem [10.4](#thm:maudlin-1-dissolved){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:maudlin-1-dissolved"} of the present textbook in six
steps. The wavefunction $\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4)$ is defined
(Definition [10.17](#def:mcgucken-wavefunction){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:mcgucken-wavefunction"}) as the complex amplitude
carried by the McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_M(p_0, t)$ on the 4D manifold

The evolution under $D_M = \partial_t + ic\,\partial_{x_4}$ is exactly

##### The Two McGucken Laws of Nonlocality: locality $\to$ nonlocality via $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ {#ssec:laws-of-nonlocality}

The geometric content established by Theorems
[1.X.1](#thm:i-perpendicularity-marker){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:i-perpendicularity-marker"} through
[1.X.5](#thm:iff-wavefunction-x4){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:iff-wavefunction-x4"} produces a characterisation of the origin and growth of quantum nonlocality.
[@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026] states two laws governing the
locality-to-nonlocality transition under $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$.

::: {#thm:ch1-first-law-nonlocality .theorem}
**Theorem 1.22** (First McGucken Law of Nonlocality;
[@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026] §2.1; full statement and six-step proof
at Theorem [17.4](#thm:first-law-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:first-law-nonlocality"} of
Chapter [17](#ch:nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:nonlocality"}). *Two quantum systems $A$ and $B$ can
be in an entangled state if and only if there exists a chain of local
interactions $A \leftrightarrow C_1 \leftrightarrow C_2 \leftrightarrow
\cdots \leftrightarrow C_n \leftrightarrow B$ such that each
interaction in the chain is local (the interacting systems are at the
same spacetime event or within each other's light cones) and each
adjacent pair in the chain has shared a common local origin at some
point in its causal past. Equivalently: only systems of particles
whose McGucken Spheres intersect (with each Sphere centred on the
respective particle's creation event) can ever be entangled.*
:::

::: {#thm:ch1-second-law-nonlocality .theorem}
**Theorem 1.23** (Second McGucken Law of Nonlocality;
[@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026] §2.2; full statement and proof at
Theorem [17.5](#thm:second-law-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:second-law-nonlocality"} of
Chapter [17](#ch:nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:nonlocality"}). *The sphere of potential
entanglement emanating from any local event grows at the velocity of
light $c$. No entanglement can be established between two systems
whose causal pasts do not overlap. Nonlocality grows over time,
limited by $c$.*
:::

*Proof sketch (both laws).* The First Law follows from the identification of entanglement with shared $x_4$-wavefront identity:
two particles are entangled if and only if they are on a common
McGucken Sphere (or on intersecting McGucken Spheres traceable through
a chain of intersections to common origins). Shared wavefront identity
requires a common local source event; intersecting wavefront identity
requires a chain of local intersections traceable to common origins
through the chain. The Second Law follows from the rate $|ic| = c$ of
$x_4$-advance: the McGucken Sphere from a source event at $p$ at time
$t_p$ has radius $c(t - t_p)$ at time $t > t_p$, so the boundary of
potential entanglement grows at $c$. The McGucken Sphere, the light
cone, and the boundary of potential entanglement are the same
geometric object viewed from three perspectives (the *Identity
Triangle* of the framework).

Necessity of the First Law (chain of local origins is required): no
counterexample has been produced in any interpretation of quantum
mechanics, any extension of the Standard Model, or any thought
experiment consistent with current physical law. Every known
entanglement-creation protocol (direct co-emission, entanglement
swapping [@Zukowski1993], teleportation [@Bennett1993]) requires a
chain of local interactions traceable to common origins.
[@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026] §3 supplies the New York–Los Angeles
falsification challenge as the explicit empirical-falsifiability
criterion: a method for entangling two distant, unentangled particles
without any chain of local contacts would falsify the law.

Sufficiency of the First Law (chain of local origins suffices for
entanglement): shared $x_4$-wavefront identity under
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ produces the geometric substrate for entanglement
(Theorem 4.2 of [@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026]); quantum coherence on
the shared substrate produces the nonlocal correlations (the additional
ingredient beyond shared wavefront identity, distinguishing entangled
quantum systems from decohered classical systems on the same light
cone). ◻

::: {#rmk:identity-triangle .remark}
*Remark 1.24* (The Identity Triangle: light cone = McGucken Sphere
= boundary of potential entanglement). *Three geometric objects of
the framework are identified as one. The forward light cone of
relativity (the causal-influence boundary at $|\mathbf{x} -
\mathbf{x}_p| \leq c(t-t_p)$); the McGucken Sphere expanding at
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ from $p$ (the wavefront-propagation boundary at
$|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_p| = c(t-t_p)$ with $x_4(q;p) = 0$); and the
sphere of potential entanglement (the entanglement-creation boundary
of the First Law of Nonlocality, at the same radius $c(t-t_p)$) are
three readings of one geometric object. The causal structure of
relativity, the wavefront structure of optics, and the entanglement
structure of quantum mechanics are forced as the same geometric fact
by $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$.*
:::

##### The arrows of time: $+ic$ orientation forces the arrows and a sixth arrow is the growth of nonlocality {#ssec:arrows-of-time}

The thermodynamics direction of the iff structure has a different
character from the QM-and-relativity direction. The strict Second
Law of thermodynamics $dS/dt = (3/2)k_B/t > 0$ is forced by the
$+ic$ orientation of the McGucken Principle through the Compton
diffusion mechanism (Theorem 22.4 of the present textbook, QM T22).
The converse direction --- that any framework producing the strict
Second Law must contain the $+ic$ orientation of $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$
--- is supported by the fact that all six arrows of time
in the framework (thermodynamic, radiative, cosmological, causal,
psychological, and now nonlocality) descend from the same single $+ic$
orientation, and a framework lacking the $+ic$ orientation would lack
the source of these arrows. Conventional thermodynamics
frameworks supply the Second Law via initial-condition assumptions
(the past hypothesis) or environmental selection rather than via a
geometric principle; in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework the Second
Law is a theorem of the principle and the $+ic$ orientation is
essential for the entirety of the arrows-of-time structure.

::: {#thm:arrows-from-plus-ic .theorem}
**Theorem 1.25** (Six arrows of time from the $+ic$ orientation;
§4.3 of [@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026]). *The $+ic$ orientation of
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ is sufficient for six aligned arrows
of time:*

1.  *Thermodynamic arrow: $dS/dt = (3/2)k_B/t > 0$ via Compton
    diffusion (QM T22).*

2.  *Radiative arrow: retarded propagation of electromagnetic and
    gravitational radiation outward from sources, with the $+ic$
    selecting retarded over advanced Green's functions.*

3.  *Cosmological arrow: the universe expands outward with $H(t) > 0$,
    with the $+ic$ orientation supplying the direction of cosmological
    expansion.*

4.  *Causal arrow: causal influence propagates from past to future,
    with the light cone oriented forward in time by the $+ic$.*

5.  *Psychological arrow: memory accumulates from past to future, with
    the directionality forced by the underlying $+ic$.*

6.  *Nonlocality arrow: the McGucken Sphere of potential entanglement
    grows outward at $c$ from each event, with the growth direction
    forced by the $+ic$. This is the new arrow identified by
    [@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026] §4.3.*

*All six arrows are aligned because they all descend from the same
$+ic$ orientation of the McGucken Principle. The time-reverse choice
$-ic$ (equivalent at the metric level by Theorem 4.6)
would flip all six arrows simultaneously; the empirical record selects
the $+ic$ via the strict Second Law alone, with the alignment of the
other five arrows then forced as a consequence.*
:::

::: {#rmk:partial-iff-thermodynamics .remark}
*Remark 1.26* (Status of the thermodynamics iff direction). *The
$+ic$ orientation is sufficient for the strict Second Law (QM T22 with
proof in the present textbook). The converse --- that the empirical
Second Law of thermodynamics forces the $+ic$ orientation of
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ uniquely (i.e., no other principle
in the McGucken-framework family could produce the same empirical
Second Law) --- is formalised as Proposition F
(Theorem [11.8.A](#thm:prop-F-orientation){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:prop-F-orientation"} of the uniqueness chapter), the
sixth failure-mode proposition extending the five-strand
empirical conjunction of
Theorem [11.10](#thm:uniqueness-mcgucken-sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:uniqueness-mcgucken-sphere"} (Uniqueness) to the
six-strand version stated in
Remark [11.9.A](#rmk:propF-extends-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:propF-extends-uniqueness"}. The proof of
Proposition F shows that orientation randomization of the $\pm ic$
clause (Postulate
[4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref" reference="postulate:mcp"}
clause (iii)) breaks the strict Second Law by replacing the
deterministic monotonic entropy increase $dS/dt = (3/2)k_B/t$ with a
zero-mean fluctuation having probability $1/2$ of backward-time
behaviour at every event --- a configuration empirically excluded at
the level of approximately $10^{-10^{23}}$ in macroscopic
ensembles. The thermodynamic strand thus joins the five strands of
the original uniqueness statement on the same footing, and the
three-way iff (QM-nonlocality $\iff$ Lorentz invariance $\iff$ strict
Second Law) is established at the level of the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework
Sphere-with-$+ic$-orientation configuration as the unique
empirically-admissible structure simultaneously consistent with all
six strands (i)--(vi) of the extended empirical conjunction.*
:::

##### Summary: the four-fold iff structure {#ssec:summary-fourfold}

The four headline iff theorems above (1.X.1, 1.X.3, 1.X.4, 1.X.5),
together with the Two Laws of Nonlocality (1.X.6, 1.X.7), the Identity
Triangle (1.X.8), and the six-arrows theorem (1.X.9), constitute the
foundational iff structure of the framework: the principle
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ is necessary and sufficient for the
Lorentzian/null structure of spacetime (Theorem 1.17, via the
perpendicularity marker $i$); for the conjunction of quantum
nonlocality and Lorentz invariance via sphere-surface $x_4$-locality
(Theorem 1.19); for the Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ via the motion of $x_4$ at $c$ (Theorem 1.20); for the
4D-vs-3D structure of the wavefunction and the dissolution of the
measurement problem (Theorem 1.21); and is sufficient (with the
necessity direction partial in the manner of Remark 1.26) for the
strict Second Law of thermodynamics and the alignment of all six
arrows of time. The full iff structure is established at the level
of Chapter 11 (uniqueness) and Chapter 13 (CGE${}_6$) of the present
textbook, with [@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026] supplying the explicit
laws of nonlocality and the Identity Triangle reading.

#### The historical-developmental thread: how geometric and algebraic channels developed differentially through three centuries of physics, and why the Cartesian Algebraic Channel came to suppress the Greek Geometric Channel through cultural convention {#ssec:historical-developmental-thread}

::: flushright
*"If '$x^4 = ict$' cannot be used \[in the curved manifold of general
relativity\], it will not be used here. In this chapter and hereafter,
as throughout the literature of general relativity, a real time
coordinate is used..."\
--- Misner, Thorne & Wheeler, *Gravitation*, Box 2.1 ("Farewell to
'*ict*'"), p. 51 [@MTW1973]*
:::

The Cartesian-synthesis reading of the differential response
(Remark [1.11](#rmk:cartesian-synthesis-dissolution){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:cartesian-synthesis-dissolution"}) is supplemented and
deepened by the historical-developmental thread: how the two channels developed at different rates under the differential influence of the observational and
experimental methods, the dominant mathematical models, and the cultural
conventions of each successive era. Some branches of physics developed
predominantly along the geometric (Geometric Channel) line; others developed
predominantly along the algebraic (Algebraic Channel) line; the choice was not
always free, and the suppression of one channel in favor of the other
has at several decisive moments shaped what was thinkable in physics.
This subsection traces the developmental thread with three conclusions.

###### The Faraday-Maxwell geometric tradition.

Michael Faraday's experimental researches into electricity and magnetism
in the 1820s and 1830s [@Faraday1832] developed in a fundamentally
geometric register. Faraday worked with compass needles, iron filings,
and induced currents in coiled wires; the dominant mental image of his
work is the *line of force* as a real physical structure threading
space. The line of force was not algebraic; it was a geometric object.
Faraday's lines of force are the historical prefigurations of Geometric
Channel's geometric-propagation tradition: the physical content is in the
shape and propagation of structures in space, not in the algebraic
symmetries acting on a state space. James Clerk Maxwell, building on
Faraday's work, derived the electromagnetic field equations in the 1860s
[@Maxwell1865]. The field equations have two distinct
readings: an *algebraic* reading in which the field is a tensor object
subject to the symmetries of the equations, and a *geometric* reading in
which the field is the local-propagation content on physical 3-space.
Maxwell's own thinking was strongly in the geometric register; the
discovery that light is an electromagnetic wave was, to Maxwell, the
discovery that light is the propagation of a geometric pattern of field
oscillation through space at speed $c$, with the wavefront a real
spatial-geometric object.

###### Minkowski's algebraic synthesis and what it suppressed.

Hermann Minkowski's 1908 Köln lecture [@Minkowski1908] achieved a
remarkable algebraic unification of special relativity. By writing
$x_4 = ict$ and treating spacetime as a flat four-manifold with
Lorentzian signature, Minkowski turned Einstein's 1905 special
relativity into an algebraic theory of indices, transformations, and
tensors. The Lorentz group becomes the symmetry group of the metric; the
canonical commutators of Algebraic Channel in quantum mechanics are descendants
of Minkowski's algebraic-symmetry framework applied to quantisation.
What Minkowski's synthesis suppressed, however, was *the physical
meaning of $i$ in $x_4 = ict$*. Minkowski wrote $x_4 = ict$ as a
notational device that made the Lorentzian metric look Euclidean; the
$i$ became a formal mark serving the algebraic computation, not a
physical signature of any actual perpendicularity of the fourth
dimension to the spatial three. The geometric content of light's
spherical wavefront expansion at $c$ --- which is precisely the McGucken
Sphere of Geometric Channel in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework --- was algebraically
encoded but physically forgotten. Minkowski's spacetime was an algebraic
four-manifold, not the spherically-expanding-from-every-event physical
manifold of the McGucken Principle.

###### Planck, Einstein, and the universal action quantum.

The 1900--1905 emergence of the action quantum $h$ followed a hybrid
developmental path. Max Planck's 1900 black-body derivation
[@Planck1900] was a thermodynamic-algebraic argument: $h$ entered as the
quantum of action required to make the algebraic combinatorics of
oscillator-mode counting agree with the empirical filament radiation
spectrum. Einstein's 1905 photoelectric paper [@Einstein1905photon]
interpreted $h$ universally --- that is, $h$ was a fundamental constant of the
propagation of light itself, beyond its role as a fitting parameter for black-body radiation. The universality of $h$ is the deeper
insight; it ties the action quantum to the propagation of light at $c$.
The McGucken Principle $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ supplies the reason for this tie: $\hbar = h/2\pi$ is the action quantum per
Compton-period oscillation of $x_4$ at the rate $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$,
with the universality of $h$ a direct consequence of the universality of
the $x_4$-expansion at $c$. Einstein saw the universality; the geometric
reading of why $h$ is universal had to wait.

###### The Heisenberg-Schrödinger split of 1925--1926.

The two formulations of quantum mechanics that emerged within twelve
months of one another in 1925--1926 are the cleanest historical instance
of the Geometric Channel / Algebraic Channel division as a developmental fact. Werner
Heisenberg's matrix mechanics of 1925 [@Heisenberg1925] developed in an
algebraic-spectroscopic register: matrix elements between energy
eigenstates, transition amplitudes, commutators of position and momentum
operators. The mathematical apparatus was operator-algebraic, and the
physical content was algebraic-symmetric: the canonical commutator
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ as the Lie-bracket of the
Heisenberg-algebra generators, with the Wigner classification of
$\mathrm{ISO}(1,3)$ irreducible representations as the natural
completion of the framework. Erwin Schrödinger's wave mechanics of 1926
[@Schrodinger1926Real] developed in a geometric-wave register: a
wavefunction $\psi(\mathbf{x},t)$ propagating through space, with the
dynamics governed by a wave equation analogous to those of classical
wave physics. The mathematical apparatus was differential-geometric, and
the physical content was geometric-propagation: the wavefunction as a
real wave on physical space, with the Schrödinger equation supplying the
local dynamics of the wave.

Heisenberg's matrix mechanics and Schrödinger's wave mechanics were, in
their first formulations, the two halves of the Cartesian synthesis
applied to quantum mechanics. Heisenberg supplied the algebraic half
(Algebraic Channel's ancestor); Schrödinger supplied the geometric
half (Geometric Channel's ancestor). The equivalence proof of the two
formulations (Schrödinger 1926; Dirac 1926; von Neumann 1932)
established that they make the same predictions about observable
quantities, but it did not establish that they are equivalent in their derivation chains. The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework's
dual-channel architecture is the recognition that the two
formulations are two genuinely disjoint derivations of the same observable predictions, and
the historical Heisenberg-Schrödinger split is the empirical signature
of that derivational disjointness. Each route emphasised what it was good
at, and each route was developed in the cultural register congenial to
its proponents.



###### Why each man took the channel he took: training, data, and the mathematics each had to hand.

The two routes of 1925--1926 were not two readings of one body of
evidence by two similarly-equipped investigators. The starting data
differed, the training differed, and in each case the mathematics that
the starting data demanded was the mathematics the investigator already
possessed. The record supports a stronger claim than "two temperaments":
the channel each man took was largely settled before he began.

*Heisenberg: twenty-three, spectroscopic, and working on intensities.*
Heisenberg (b. 5 December 1901) was twenty-three in 1925. He entered
theoretical physics under Arnold Sommerfeld at Munich in October 1920,
took his doctorate at Munich in 1923 with a dissertation on turbulence
in fluid streams, and spent September 1924 to May 1925 with Bohr in
Copenhagen, having in the preceding year assisted Hans Kramers on the
theory of dispersion. The problem in front of him was the intensities of
spectral lines --- the strengths of the transitions between stationary
states of the hydrogen atom --- approached through the dispersion
formalism in which incoming radiation at one frequency is re-radiated by
a dispersive medium.

The methodological decision of *Über quantentheoretische Umdeutung
kinematischer und mechanischer Beziehungen* (*Z. Phys.* **33**,
879--893, July 1925) followed from that problem: the paper makes "its
deliberate choice to not utilise unobserved quantities such as the
electron's position and period but only to utilise observable parameters
like transition probabilities or spectral frequencies."

*Schrödinger: thirty-eight, trained in continuum physics, and working on
standing waves.* Schrödinger (b. 12 August 1887) was thirty-eight when
the first communication appeared in January 1926. He studied at Vienna
from 1906 to 1910 under Franz Exner and Friedrich Hasenöhrl, taking the
doctorate under Hasenöhrl in 1910, and the fifteen years of work that
followed were in continuum and statistical physics: vibrational theory,
Brownian motion, mathematical statistics, dielectrics, atmospheric
electricity, colour perception.

His route into the quantum problem ran through neither spectroscopy nor
dispersion. He was analysing Einstein's 1924--1925 papers on the quantum
theory of the ideal gas, in which Einstein wrote of de Broglie's matter
waves that "I believe that this is more than a mere analogy; de Broglie
has shown in a very important work how a (scalar) wave field can be
coordinated with a material particle." Schrödinger's move was to seek
for gases what Planck had obtained for radiation --- a derivation from
discrete standing-wave modes --- and he then "went back to first
principles, to the classical theory of Hamiltonian mechanics,
identifying Hamilton's characteristic function with the phase of an
electron wave." The title of the resulting series states the frame
without ambiguity: *Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem* --- quantisation
as an eigenvalue problem.

*They did not begin from the same observations.* Heisenberg began from
measured spectroscopic quantities: line intensities, dispersion,
transition frequencies. Schrödinger began from a theoretical hypothesis
about matter waves that had at the time no direct experimental support:
de Broglie's waves were confirmed by Davisson and Germer only in 1927
[@Davisson1927], after the wave equation was published. The two
formulations converged on common test cases --- the hydrogen spectrum,
the harmonic oscillator --- only once each was in hand. The convergence
was a result of the work, not a shared starting point of it.

*The data chose the mathematics, and the mathematics chose the channel.*
This is the point at which the historical record bears on the
dual-channel architecture. A quantity indexed by a *pair* of stationary
states --- the amplitude for a transition from $n$ to $m$ --- is a
two-index object, and the composition rule for two such objects in
succession is a sum over intermediate states. Heisenberg wrote that rule
down from the physics and found that it did not commute. He did not
identify it: the recognition that the rule was matrix multiplication came
at Göttingen, from Born, who "suddenly remembered an algebraic theory
which he had learned from his teacher, Professor Rosanes, in Breslau,"
and from Jordan. The starting data forced a two-index object; the
two-index object is matrix algebra; matrix algebra is the Algebraic
Channel.

A quantity that is a standing wave in space, quantised by the condition
that it fit its boundaries, is an eigenfunction of a differential
operator, and its allowed energies are eigenvalues. Schrödinger's
starting data forced that object, and he had spent fifteen years on
exactly such problems in continuum physics. Where Heisenberg needed Born
to supply the algebra, Schrödinger needed Hermann Weyl to help with the
analysis --- "If only I knew more mathematics!" --- but the frame itself
was native to him. The starting data forced a boundary-value problem;
the boundary-value problem is partial differential equations on a
continuum; that is the Geometric Channel.

*What the biographies do not show.* Neither man chose a channel in the
sense of selecting between two known options. Each took up the problem
his position put in front of him, with the mathematics his training had
given him, and arrived at one of the two routes without the other in
view --- Heisenberg's paper does not mention waves, and Schrödinger came
to matrix mechanics as an obstacle to be reconciled with rather than as
a starting point. That both routes existed became visible only when the
two results were compared, and by then the question had been reframed as
one of equivalence.

*Reading this against the dual-channel architecture.* The framework's
claim is that the Algebraic Channel and the Geometric Channel are two
descents from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, each complete and each blind to
what the other carries. If that claim is right, then what one finds in
1925--1926 is exactly what one should expect: two investigators, each
positioned at a different downstream projection of the same source,
each reconstructing his projection with the tools that projection
demands, neither with access to the source itself. The biographical
asymmetries --- Munich spectroscopy against Vienna continuum physics,
twenty-three against thirty-eight, intensities against standing waves,
Born's matrix algebra against Weyl's analysis --- are then the
historical shadow of the derivational disjointness the audits of Part II
establish theorem by theorem. The framework does not require this
reading of the history, and the history does not establish the
framework; the two are consistent, and the consistency is worth
recording.


###### The Ritz combination principle: the datum that dictated the algebra.

The claim that Heisenberg's starting data forced his mathematics can be
made precise, because the relevant datum is a named empirical
regularity. The Rydberg--Ritz combination principle, proposed by Walther
Ritz in 1908 as a generalisation of an earlier rule of Rydberg's, is the
observed fact that the spectral lines of an element include frequencies
that are sums or differences of the frequencies of other lines ---
equivalently, that the wavenumber of each line is the difference of two
terms. Each observed frequency therefore carries *two* indices, one for
each term, and the observed additivity is the statement that indices
compose end to end.

Alain Connes states the consequence for Heisenberg's 1925 work
(*Noncommutative Geometry Year 2000*, arXiv:math/0011193):

> "What Heisenberg understood, by analogy with the classical treatment
> of the interaction of a mechanical system with the electromagnetic
> field, is that this Ritz--Rydberg combination principle actually
> dictates an algebraic formula for the product of any two observable
> physical quantities attached to the atomic system."

The formula is $(AB)_{i,k} = A_{i,j}B_{j,k}$, and Heisenberg found that
it does not commute, $AB \neq BA$. Connes records the further point that
the identification came from elsewhere:

> "Heisenberg didn't know about matrices, he just worked it out, but he
> was told later by Born, Jordan and Dirac that the algebra he had
> worked out was known to mathematicians as the algebra of matrices."

This closes the argument of the preceding subsection with a documented
mechanism rather than an inference about temperament. The two-index
structure was not a modelling choice: it is the form in which the
spectroscopic data present themselves once the Ritz principle is taken
seriously, and the composition rule for two-index objects with
end-to-end index matching is matrix multiplication whether or not the
person writing it down knows the name. Heisenberg did not select the
Algebraic Channel; the Ritz principle handed it to him, and the
recognition of what he was holding came from Born and Jordan afterward.

The symmetry of the situation is worth stating explicitly, and it is
closer than it first appears. Schrödinger's starting datum --- de
Broglie's matter wave --- is a single-index object in space, a field
$\psi(\mathbf{x})$, and the condition that quantises it is that it fit
its boundaries. That form is a differential eigenvalue problem whether
or not the person writing it down knows Sturm and Liouville by name.
Each starting datum carries its own mathematics with it.

The symmetry extends to the recognition as well. Heisenberg wrote a
composition rule and was told afterward by Born and Jordan that it was
matrix algebra; Schrödinger wrote a wave equation and was told by Weyl
what he had. Fröhlich and Schubnel record the second half (*Do We
Understand Quantum Mechanics --- Finally?*, arXiv:1203.3678):

> "It was Weyl who apparently explained to Schrödinger that his
> time-independent wave equation represented an eigenvalue problem and
> directed him to the right mathematical literature."

In each case the physics arrived first and the mathematical
identification came from a colleague. The investigator's training
determined how quickly he recognised what he was holding, and it did not
determine which object the data put in his hands.

*Convergent overdetermination has a historical precedent.* The
dual-channel architecture of this book records twenty-two forced
theorems each reached along two routes with disjoint intermediate
machinery (§[1.13](#sec:dual-channel-ledger){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:dual-channel-ledger"}). The events of 1925--1926 are an
instance of that pattern occurring without anyone intending it: the
hydrogen spectrum was reached twice, from different data, through
different mathematics, by investigators with different training, within
twelve months. Heisenberg diagonalised a matrix Hamiltonian built from
transition amplitudes; Schrödinger found the eigenvalues of
$-(\hbar^2/2m)\nabla^2 + V$; both obtained Bohr's levels. The framework
of this book therefore does not introduce convergent overdetermination
as a novel form of evidence. It claims something narrower and checkable:
that the convergence is systematic rather than accidental, that it
recurs at twenty-two theorems rather than one, and that both routes
descend from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The 1925--1926 convergence is the
first instance of the pattern and the reason to look for a source
upstream of both.

###### The documentary record: the founders named the division themselves.

The reading of 1925--1926 as an algebraic route and a geometric route is
not a retrospective imposition. It is what the two authors said about
each other's work at the time, in print and in correspondence.

Schrödinger stated the division in the paper that established the
formal relation between the two theories, *Über das Verhältnis der
Heisenberg--Born--Jordanschen Quantenmechanik zu der meinen* (*Annalen
der Physik*, 4 May 1926). Of matrix mechanics he wrote that he was

> "discouraged, if not repulsed, by what seemed to me very difficult
> methods of transcendental algebra, defying any visualisation."

Two features of that sentence matter here. The objection is to a
*method* --- transcendental algebra --- rather than to a result; and the
ground of the objection is the absence of *Anschaulichkeit*,
visualisability. Schrödinger is describing what this book calls the
Algebraic Channel, and objecting to it for lacking what this book calls
Geometric Channel content.

Heisenberg's position was the mirror image and equally explicit. In the
matrix-mechanics programme he set aside visualisable pictures and took
discontinuous transitions as primitive; the Stanford Encyclopedia's
summary of the period records that Heisenberg "eschewed the use of
visualizable pictures, and accepted discontinuous transitions as a
primitive notion," while "Schrödinger claimed as an advantage of his
theory that it was *anschaulich*" --- meaning that "the theory
represented the observational data by means of continuously evolving
causal processes in space and time." Writing to Pauli on 8 June 1926,
Heisenberg judged that what Schrödinger claimed about the
visualisability of his theory was "probably not quite right," in
markedly stronger private language. Heisenberg then took the disputed
word back in the title of his 1927 uncertainty paper, *Über den
anschaulichen Inhalt der quantentheoretischen Kinematik und Mechanik* ---
"on the *visualisable* content" --- and gave it an operational rather
than a geometric sense.

So the two founders agreed on the taxonomy and disagreed on its value:
one route algebraic and unvisualisable, one route geometric and
visualisable. What neither proposed, and what no participant in the
dispute proposed, is that both routes descend from a single physical
statement upstream of both.

###### What the equivalence proofs settled, and what they closed off.

The dispute ended in a conclusion of equivalence --- Schrödinger 1926,
Eckart 1926, Dirac's transformation theory, and von Neumann's 1932
Hilbert-space formulation --- and the field thereafter treated the two
formalisms as one theory in two notations. That conclusion is the reason
the question of the present book was never asked: if the two routes are
the same theory in different notation, there is nothing further to
explain about their relation, and no reason to look upstream of either.

The conclusion is also weaker than its reputation. F. A. Muller's
two-part study *The Equivalence Myth of Quantum Mechanics* (*Studies in
History and Philosophy of Modern Physics* **28** (1997), Part I pp.
35--61, Part II pp. 219--241) argues that "Schrödinger's demonstration
in March (September) 1926 of the equivalence ... is not foolproof," that
its appeal to the moment problem fails, and that the equivalence
"could not have been foolproof, because at the time matrix mechanics and
wave mechanics were neither mathematically nor empirically equivalent."
Muller locates the difference in structure: matrix mechanics as then
formulated lacked a state space and the Euclidean structure that wave
mechanics supplied, and the two were unified mathematically only by von
Neumann's 1932 reformulation.

Muller's conclusion and the present book's are different claims with a
common target. Muller argues that the 1926 equivalence proof does not
establish what it is remembered as establishing. The present book argues
that even granting the equivalence of *predictions*, the two routes
remain disjoint in their *derivations*, and that the disjointness is a
fact to be explained rather than an artefact to be dissolved. Both
positions read the tradition's early closure of the question as
premature.


###### Dirac 1965: the two pictures declared inequivalent by the man who unified them.

Forty years after transformation theory, Dirac returned to the relation
between the two formulations and reversed the standard verdict for
quantum field theory. In *Quantum Electrodynamics without Dead Wood*
(*Phys. Rev.* **139**, B684, 1965) the abstract states the result
directly:

> "In quantum electrodynamics one can obtain a Hamiltonian which gives
> reasonable field equations in the Heisenberg picture, but which does
> not allow of solutions of the wave equation to represent physical
> states in the Schrödinger picture."

Dirac's diagnosis is that the state vector of the Schrödinger picture
does not remain in Hilbert space, so that the argument establishing the
equivalence of the two pictures fails; he proposes reformulating quantum
electrodynamics in the Heisenberg picture alone. The position is
recorded in the later literature in the compressed form "the Heisenberg
picture is a good picture, the Schrödinger picture is a bad picture, and
the two pictures are not equivalent" (quoted in Hiley and Dennis,
*Dirac, Bohm and the Algebraic Approach*, arXiv:1901.01979, and in
Bédard, *Realism and the Inequivalence of the Two Quantum Pictures*,
arXiv:2510.02138).

Two features of this bear on the present chapter. The judgement comes
from the author of the unification, which makes it costly testimony
rather than partisan testimony. And the inequivalence Dirac reports is
domain-dependent: the pictures agree where the standard equivalence
argument applies and part company where it does not. A relation between
two formulations that holds in one regime and fails in another is a
relation between two routes with different content, which is the
situation the dual-channel architecture describes and the
equivalence-of-notation reading does not.

###### The inequivalence thread in the recent literature.

Work since 2000 has continued to find structural differences between the
two pictures rather than notational ones.

Johnson-Freyd, *Heisenberg-Picture Quantum Field Theory*
(in *Representation Theory, Mathematical Physics, and Integrable
Systems*, Birkhäuser, 2021; arXiv:1508.05908), argues that the two
pictures require different categorical targets:

> "Atiyah--Segal-type axioms do a good job of capturing the 'Schrödinger
> picture': these axioms define a 'd-dimensional quantum field theory'
> to be a symmetric monoidal functor from an $(\infty, d)$-category of
> 'spacetimes' to an $(\infty, d)$-category which at the second-from-top
> level consists of vector spaces, so at the top level consists of
> numbers. This paper argues that the appropriate parallel notion
> 'Heisenberg picture' should also be defined in terms of symmetric
> monoidal functors from the category of spacetimes, but the target
> should be an $(\infty, d)$-category that in top dimension consists of
> pointed vector spaces instead of numbers"

with factorization algebras and skein theory named as the two sources of
such theories. This is the algebra/geometry division reappearing as a
difference of categorical target rather than a difference of notation.

Bédard, *Realism and the Inequivalence of the Two Quantum Pictures*
(arXiv:2510.02138; forthcoming in A. Ney, ed., *Local Quantum
Mechanics*, Oxford University Press), reaches the same conclusion from
the interpretive side: "Whereas the Schrödinger picture posits a
time-evolving wave function, the Heisenberg picture posits so-called
descriptors, time-evolving generators of the algebra of observables.
These two structures are non-isomorphic: descriptors surject onto but do
not reduce to the Schrödinger state."

Perović, *Why were Matrix Mechanics and Wave Mechanics considered
equivalent?* (*Studies in History and Philosophy of Modern Physics*
**39** (2008), 444--461), addresses the historical question directly,
examining the grounds on which the physics community accepted the
equivalence in the 1920s.

*Scope of this literature relative to the present book.* These results
establish that the two pictures differ in content, in categorical
target, and in what each posits as real. None of them proposes a common
upstream source: Johnson-Freyd asks what the Heisenberg picture *is* as
a functor, Bédard asks which picture a realist should take as
fundamental, Dirac 1965 asks which picture to work in. The question of
the present book --- what single physical statement generates both, and
whether the machinery of the two descents intersects --- is not posed in
any of them. The inequivalence literature is therefore evidence for the
premise of the dual-channel architecture, namely that the two routes
carry different content, and it is silent on the architecture itself.

###### Dirac's unpublished geometry.

The figure who unified the two formulations left a record that bears
directly on the division. Dirac's mathematical training was in
projective geometry, and by his own account his way of thinking was
geometric while his published work was algebraic. On 30 October 1972 he
gave a lecture at Boston University titled *Projective Geometry: Origin
of Quantum Equations*, whose archival record (University Archives and
Special Collections, Xavier University Library) notes "the personal
announcement by Dirac that he had never published his 'secret' use of
projective geometry in creating quantum mechanics"; Roger Penrose spoke
at the close. The connection between the geometry and the quantum
equations was left unstated in the lecture, and historians have not
recovered it.

The episode is recorded here without inference. It establishes that the
author of transformation theory worked geometrically and published
algebraically, and regarded the geometric route as something distinct
enough from the published one to describe as unpublished. It does not
establish what the geometric route was, and nothing in this book depends
on a reconstruction of it.

###### The dichotomy as a general fact about mathematics.

The division is not local to quantum mechanics. Michael Atiyah, in
*Mathematics in the 20th Century* (*Bulletin of the London Mathematical
Society* **34** (2002), 1--15), set the two modes against each other as
a choice with a price:

> "Should you be an algebraist or a geometer? is like saying Would you
> rather be deaf or blind?"

and

> "Algebra is the offer made by the devil to the mathematician. The
> devil says: I will give you this powerful machine, and it will answer
> any question you like."

with the cost stated plainly: "When you pass over into algebraic
calculation, essentially you stop thinking; you stop thinking
geometrically, you stop thinking about the meaning."

Atiyah is describing, at the level of mathematical practice, the same
asymmetry this chapter describes at the level of physical derivation:
the algebraic route computes reliably and carries no picture of what is
happening, and the cultural pressure runs toward the route that
computes. That is the mechanism by which the Cartesian algebraic half of
the 1637 synthesis came to dominate its geometric half, and by which
the Heisenberg route came to be the canonical presentation of quantum
mechanics while the geometric content latent in the Schrödinger route
went undeveloped.

###### What the record does not contain.

Across the primary sources and the historical literature surveyed here,
the two routes are named, contrasted, valued against each other,
proved equivalent in their predictions, and argued over. They are not
derived. No participant proposes a physical statement upstream of both
from which each route descends, and no participant asks whether the
intermediate machinery of the two routes intersects. The equivalence
result closed the first question before it was posed, since equivalent
formalisms invite translation rather than a search for a common source;
and the second question requires the notion of derivational disjointness
(§[1.13](#sec:dual-channel-ledger){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:dual-channel-ledger"}), which has no counterpart in the
1926 literature. The historical record therefore supplies the
*phenomenon* this book explains --- two persistent, differently-valued
routes to one set of predictions --- without supplying an explanation
of it.

###### Schrödinger's neglected geometric content.

Schrödinger himself observed in 1926 that the wave equation contains
within it the content of Huygens' Principle, of the heat
equation under Wick rotation, and of the second law of thermodynamics
under appropriate boundary conditions --- but the subsequent development
of quantum mechanics did not pursue these connections systematically.
The Copenhagen interpretation, formalised by Bohr and Heisenberg in
1927--1928 [@Bohr1928], adopted the algebraic-operational framework as
the canonical reading of quantum mechanics and treated the wavefunction
as an instrument for computing probabilities rather than as a real
geometric object on a real four-manifold. The geometric content latent
in the Schrödinger equation --- the content that, in the McGucken
framework, becomes the Geometric Channel derivation --- was effectively
suppressed by the Copenhagen reading for the next forty years. Feynman's
path-integral reformulation of 1948 partially restored the geometric
content (the action $S$ as an integral along a worldline; the propagator
as a sum over geometric paths); but the path integral was developed
largely as a calculational tool for QFT, not as a derivation
chain disjoint from the operator-algebraic apparatus. The McGucken
framework's Geometric Channel is, in this historical perspective, the systematic
recovery of the geometric content that Schrödinger's 1926 wave equation
contained and that the dominant cultural-interpretive tradition of
twentieth-century physics did not develop.

###### The MTW abandonment of $x_4 = ict$: the most striking instance of channel suppression by cultural convention.

The most significant case of Geometric Channel's suppression by
cultural convention in twentieth-century physics occurs not in quantum
mechanics but in general relativity, and it occurs within the lineage
that should have been most receptive to the geometric reading. The
Misner--Thorne--Wheeler textbook *Gravitation* (1973) [@MTW1973] --- the
standard graduate-level reference for general relativity, written by
Wheeler (who taught the present author at Princeton) and his
collaborators in the heart of the geometrodynamics
tradition --- explicitly abandons the use of $x_4 = ict$. Box 2.1 of
*Gravitation*, on p. 51, is titled *"Farewell to '*ict*'"*, and it
states (verbatim):

> *In Lorentz-Minkowski geometry, when the interval between two events
> is zero, one event may be on Earth and the other on a supernova in the
> galaxy M31, but their separation must be a null ray (piece of a light
> cone). The backward-pointing light cone at a given event contains all
> the events by which that event can be influenced. The forward-pointing
> light cone contains all events that it can influence. The multitude of
> double light cones taking off from all the events of spacetime forms
> an interlocking causal structure. This structure makes the machinery
> of the physical world function as it does... If in a region where
> spacetime is flat, one can hide this structure from view by writing
> $(\Delta s)^2 = (\Delta x^1)^2 + (\Delta x^2)^2 + (\Delta x^3)^2 + (\Delta x^4)^2$,
> with $x^4 = ict$, no one has discovered a way to make an imaginary
> coordinate work in the general curved spacetime manifold. If
> "$x^4 = ict$" cannot be used there, it will not be used here. In this
> chapter and hereafter, as throughout the literature of general
> relativity, a real time coordinate is used,
