$\langle\varphi, \psi\rangle = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\varphi^*\psi\,d^3x$
is itself a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: it is the off-diagonal
extension of the Born density $|\psi|^2$, which is the
forward--conjugate $x_{4}$-overlap of the McGucken-Sphere wavefront with
itself (Lemma [9.14](#lem:born-as-x4-overlap){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:born-as-x4-overlap"}). The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
therefore traces, through the inner-product axioms, to the
McGucken-Sphere kinematics: it is a constraint on the
geometric overlap of $x_{4}$-wavefronts.

**Step 6: Application --- Heisenberg uncertainty.** The proof of the
inequality is complete at Step 5; the present step records where the
result is used downstream and adds nothing to it. Cauchy-Schwarz is the
key analytic input for the proof of the Heisenberg uncertainty relation (Theorem [12.1](#thm:QMT12){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT12"}, both channels): applying it to the inner product
$\langle (\hat A - \langle A\rangle)\psi \vert (\hat B - \langle B\rangle)\psi \rangle$
together with the canonical commutator $[\hat A, \hat B]$ yields the
Robertson-Schrödinger form
$\Delta A\,\Delta B \ge \tfrac{1}{2}|\langle[\hat A, \hat B]\rangle|$.
The McGucken anchoring of the inequality (via the McGucken-Sphere
wavefront origin of the inner product) therefore traces the origin of the uncertainty principle to $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. ◻
:::

Cauchy--Schwarz is used in the proof of the Heisenberg uncertainty
relation (Chapter [12](#ch:heisenberg){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:heisenberg"}, both channels).

### Bounded and unbounded operators {#sec:operators}

::: {#def:linop .definition}
**Definition 3.3** (Linear operator). A *linear operator* on
$\mathcal{H}$ is a linear map $\hat{A}: D(\hat{A}) \to \mathcal{H}$,
where $D(\hat{A}) \subseteq \mathcal{H}$ is a dense linear subspace, the
*domain*.
:::

For bounded operators ($\|\hat{A}\psi\| \le C\|\psi\|$ for some $C$ and
all $\psi$) one can take $D(\hat{A}) = \mathcal{H}$. The position and
momentum operators of one-particle quantum mechanics are unbounded;
their domains are dense proper subspaces of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$.

::: {#def:hermitian .definition}
**Definition 3.4** (Hermitian and self-adjoint operators). The
*Hermitian conjugate* (adjoint) $\hat{A}^\dagger$ of $\hat{A}$ has
domain
$D(\hat{A}^\dagger) = \{\phi \in \mathcal{H}: \exists\, \chi \in \mathcal{H}\text{ with } \langle \phi \vert \hat{A}\psi \rangle = \langle \chi \vert \psi \rangle \text{ for all } \psi \in D(\hat{A})\}$
and acts as $\hat{A}^\dagger\phi = \chi$.

$\hat{A}$ is *symmetric* if
$\langle \phi \vert \hat{A}\psi \rangle = \langle \hat{A}\phi \vert \psi \rangle$
for all $\phi, \psi \in D(\hat{A})$, i.e.,
$\hat{A} \subseteq \hat{A}^\dagger$. It is *self-adjoint* (or
*Hermitian* in the physicist's sense) if $\hat{A} = \hat{A}^\dagger$,
i.e., the domains agree as well.
:::

For unbounded operators the distinction between symmetric and
self-adjoint matters; the spectral theorem applies only to self-adjoint
operators, and Stone's theorem (below) requires self-adjointness.

::: {#thm:spectral .theorem}
**Theorem 3.5** (Spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators). *Let
$\hat{A}$ be a self-adjoint operator on $\mathcal{H}$. There exists a
unique projection-valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb{R}$ such that
$$\hat{A} = \int_\mathbb{R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda).
\label{eq:spectral}$$ The eigenvalues of $\hat{A}$ (the atoms of $E$)
are real.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof (imported as standard functional-analysis result).* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). This is
Theorem VIII.6 of Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980]. We summarise the
content in six steps, with explicit anchoring of the
theorem's role in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework. The spectral theorem is the
bridge from the McGucken-derived self-adjoint operators (position
$\hat{q}$, momentum $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ from
Lemma [2.2](#lem:phat-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-generator"}, Hamiltonian $\hat{H}= i\hbar\partial_t$
from Lemma [3.3](#lem:Hhat-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:Hhat-generator"}) to their measurable real-valued spectra
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, with $x_4 = ict$ the integrated kinematic
shadow per Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}); each of these operators is the
Stone-theorem generator of a translation symmetry of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

**Step 1: Bounded self-adjoint operators --- Hilbert-Cauchy formula.**
For bounded self-adjoint operators $\hat A$ on $\mathcal{H}$ (with
$\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ established as a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ in
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}), the spectrum
$\sigma(\hat A) \subset \mathbb{R}$ is bounded. The bounded spectral
theorem (Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] VII.2) constructs the
projection-valued measure $E$ on $\sigma(\hat A)$ via finite-dimensional
approximation: $$\hat A = \lim_n \sum_k \lambda_k^{(n)} E_k^{(n)},$$
where $E_k^{(n)}$ are spectral projectors on intervals
$[\lambda_k^{(n)}, \lambda_{k+1}^{(n)})$ in the partition of
$\sigma(\hat A)$, and the limit is in operator norm. The continuous
projection-valued measure $E$ is obtained by refinement.

**Step 2: Unbounded self-adjoint operators --- Cayley transform.** For
unbounded self-adjoint $\hat A$, the spectrum
$\sigma(\hat A) \subset \mathbb{R}$ may be unbounded. The Cayley
transform
$$\hat C := (\hat A - i\mathbf{1})(\hat A + i\mathbf{1})^{-1}$$ is
well-defined: $\hat A + i\mathbf{1}$ has trivial kernel (since $\hat A$
self-adjoint implies
$\|(\hat A + i\mathbf{1})\psi\|^2 = \|\hat A\psi\|^2 + \|\psi\|^2 \ge \|\psi\|^2$,
so the operator is injective with bounded inverse), and its range is all
of $\mathcal{H}$ (the basic self-adjointness criterion: $\hat A$ is
self-adjoint iff $\mathrm{ran}(\hat A \pm i\mathbf{1}) = \mathcal{H}$,
Reed--Simon VIII.3). Hence
$(\hat A + i\mathbf{1})^{-1}: \mathcal{H}\to D(\hat A)$ is everywhere
defined and bounded.

*Unitarity of $\hat C$:* For any $\psi \in \mathcal{H}$, write
$\phi = (\hat A + i\mathbf{1})^{-1}\psi$, so
$\psi = (\hat A + i\mathbf{1})\phi$. Then
$\hat C\psi = (\hat A - i\mathbf{1})\phi$, and
$$\|\hat C\psi\|^2 = \|(\hat A - i\mathbf{1})\phi\|^2 = \|\hat A\phi\|^2 + \|\phi\|^2 = \|(\hat A + i\mathbf{1})\phi\|^2 = \|\psi\|^2,$$
using self-adjointness
($\langle\hat A\phi, i\phi\rangle + \langle i\phi, \hat A\phi\rangle = 0$
since $\hat A$ symmetric). So $\hat C$ is an isometry. Surjectivity
follows by the same argument applied to
$\hat C^{-1} = (\hat A + i\mathbf{1})(\hat A - i\mathbf{1})^{-1}$,
well-defined by the dual self-adjointness criterion. Hence $\hat C$ is
unitary.

*Spectrum of $\hat C$:* The point $1 \in S^1$ is excluded from
$\sigma(\hat C)$ because
$\hat C - \mathbf{1} = -2i\mathbf{1}\cdot(\hat A + i\mathbf{1})^{-1}$ is
invertible with bounded inverse $(i/2)(\hat A + i\mathbf{1})$, where the
latter is densely defined on $D(\hat A)$. Hence
$\sigma(\hat C) \subset S^1 \setminus \{1\}$.

Apply the bounded spectral theorem (Step 1) to $\hat C$ to obtain a
projection-valued measure $E_C$ on $S^1 \setminus \{1\}$. The inverse
Cayley map $e^{i\theta} \mapsto -\cot(\theta/2)$ pulls this back to a
projection-valued measure $E_{\hat A}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ for $\hat A$.
Reed--Simon VIII.4 verifies the pullback measure satisfies the spectral
representation $\hat A = \int_\mathbb{R}\lambda\, dE_{\hat A}(\lambda)$
on $D(\hat A)$.

**Step 3: Reality of the spectrum.** For self-adjoint $\hat A$ and
$\lambda = \alpha + i\beta \in \mathbb{C}$ with
$\beta = \mathrm{Im}\,\lambda \ne 0$, we show
$(\hat A - \lambda\mathbf{1})^{-1}$ exists and is bounded, hence
$\lambda \notin \sigma(\hat A)$.

*Resolvent estimate (explicit):* For any $\psi \in D(\hat A)$,
$$\begin{aligned}
\|(\hat A - \lambda\mathbf{1})\psi\|^2 &= \langle(\hat A - \alpha\mathbf{1} - i\beta\mathbf{1})\psi,\, (\hat A - \alpha\mathbf{1} - i\beta\mathbf{1})\psi\rangle \\
&= \|(\hat A - \alpha\mathbf{1})\psi\|^2 + \beta^2\|\psi\|^2 + i\beta\,\langle\psi, (\hat A - \alpha\mathbf{1})\psi\rangle - i\beta\,\langle(\hat A - \alpha\mathbf{1})\psi, \psi\rangle.
\end{aligned}$$ By self-adjointness of $\hat A - \alpha\mathbf{1}$, the
last two terms cancel:
$\langle\psi, (\hat A - \alpha\mathbf{1})\psi\rangle = \langle(\hat A - \alpha\mathbf{1})\psi, \psi\rangle \in \mathbb{R}$.
Therefore
$$\|(\hat A - \lambda\mathbf{1})\psi\|^2 = \|(\hat A - \alpha\mathbf{1})\psi\|^2 + \beta^2\|\psi\|^2 \ge \beta^2\|\psi\|^2 = |\mathrm{Im}\,\lambda|^2\,\|\psi\|^2.$$
The operator $\hat A - \lambda\mathbf{1}$ is therefore bounded below,
hence injective with closed range. By the same argument applied to
$\hat A - \overline\lambda\mathbf{1}$, the range of
$\hat A - \lambda\mathbf{1}$ is dense (its orthogonal complement is the
kernel of $\hat A - \overline\lambda\mathbf{1}$, which is trivial).
Closed + dense range = full range. Hence
$(\hat A - \lambda\mathbf{1})^{-1}$ is everywhere defined, with
$\|(\hat A - \lambda\mathbf{1})^{-1}\| \le 1/|\mathrm{Im}\,\lambda|$. So
$\lambda \notin \sigma(\hat A)$, equivalently
$\sigma(\hat A) \subset \mathbb{R}$. The spectrum of a self-adjoint
operator is real.

**Step 4: Uniqueness of $E$.** The projection-valued measure $E$ is
uniquely determined by $\hat A$: two such measures $E, E'$ would give
two functional calculi $f(\hat A) = \int f\,dE = \int f\,dE'$ on bounded
Borel $f$. Setting $f = \mathbf{1}_B$ for Borel $B$ gives $E(B) = E'(B)$
for all $B$, hence $E = E'$. Injectivity of the bounded-Borel functional
calculus forces uniqueness.

**Step 5: Functional calculus.** The spectral theorem provides the Borel
functional calculus on self-adjoint operators: for any bounded Borel
function $f: \mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{C}$,
$$f(\hat A) := \int_\mathbb{R}f(\lambda)\,dE(\lambda).$$ This is the key
tool for constructing functions of operators in quantum mechanics:
$e^{-it\hat A/\hbar}$ (the time-evolution unitary), $\sqrt{\hat A}$ (for
$\hat A \ge 0$), $\mathbf{1}_{[a, b]}(\hat A)$ (the spectral projector
onto eigenvalues in $[a, b]$), etc.

**Step 6: McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework role.** The spectral theorem is invoked in
the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework wherever a quantum observable is represented by
an unbounded self-adjoint operator --- position $\hat{q}$, momentum
$\hat{p}$, energy $\hat{H}$ --- and the eigenvalue interpretation of
measurement outcomes is required. Within Algebraic Channel (the
algebraic-symmetry channel), the spectral theorem is the algorithm by
which the McGucken Principle's translation symmetries produce
real-valued observables: by Stone's theorem
(Theorem [3.6](#thm:stone){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:stone"}),
the translation symmetries of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ have self-adjoint
generators; by the spectral theorem (this Theorem), these self-adjoint
operators have real spectrum and admit eigenvalue decompositions. This
is the QA3 axiom of Chapter [4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:foundations"}, derived from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
rather than postulated. The spectral theorem is the bridge from
translation symmetries to measurable observables. ◻
:::

### Stone's theorem on one-parameter unitary groups {#sec:stone}

This is the Algebraic Channel workhorse. Every continuous one-parameter unitary
group has a self-adjoint generator, and the assignment is bijective.

::: {#thm:stone .theorem}
**Theorem 3.6** (Stone's theorem). *Let
$\{\hat{U}(t) : t \in \mathbb{R}\}$ be a strongly continuous
one-parameter unitary group on $\mathcal{H}$:
$\hat{U}(t+s) = \hat{U}(t)\hat{U}(s)$, $\hat{U}(0) = \mathbb{1}$, and
$t \mapsto \hat{U}(t)\psi$ is continuous in $t$ for each
$\psi \in \mathcal{H}$. Then there exists a unique self-adjoint operator
$\hat{G}$ on $\mathcal{H}$, the *generator*, such that
$$\hat{U}(t) = e^{-it\hat{G}/\hbar}
\label{eq:stone}$$ in the sense of the functional calculus, and
$\hat{G}\psi = i\hbar\,\lim_{t\to 0}\,t^{-1}(\hat{U}(t) - \mathbb{1})\psi$
for $\psi$ in the dense domain $D(\hat{G})$. Conversely, every
self-adjoint operator generates a unique strongly continuous
one-parameter unitary group via
[\[eq:stone\]](#eq:stone){reference-type="eqref" reference="eq:stone"}.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof (imported as standard functional-analysis result).* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). This is
Theorems VIII.7 and VIII.8 of Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980]. We summarise
the content in six steps.

**Step 1: Definition of the generator.** Given a strongly continuous
one-parameter unitary group $\{\hat{U}(t)\}_{t \in \mathbb{R}}$ on
$\mathcal{H}$, define the domain
$$D(\hat G) := \Bigl\{\psi \in \mathcal{H}: \lim_{t \to 0}\frac{\hat{U}(t)\psi - \psi}{t} \text{ exists in } \mathcal{H}\Bigr\}.$$
On this domain, define the generator
$$\hat G\psi := i\hbar\,\lim_{t \to 0}\frac{\hat{U}(t)\psi - \psi}{t}.$$
The factor of $i\hbar$ is the convention that fixes physical units:
$\hbar$ is the action quantum (McGucken-derived,
Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}), $i$ is
the perpendicularity marker (McGucken-derived,
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$).

**Step 2: Density of $D(\hat G)$.** The domain $D(\hat G)$ is dense in
$\mathcal{H}$ by strong continuity of $\hat{U}$. Explicit construction:
for $\psi \in \mathcal{H}$ and smooth compactly-supported
$f \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$, the vector
$$\psi_f := \int_\mathbb{R}f(t)\,\hat{U}(t)\psi\,dt$$ (Bochner integral,
well-defined by strong continuity) lies in $D(\hat G)$.

*Difference quotient convergence:* Compute, using the group property
$\hat{U}(s)\hat{U}(t) = \hat{U}(s+t)$ and a change of variable
$t \to t - s$: $$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\hat{U}(s)\psi_f - \psi_f}{s} &= \frac{1}{s}\int_\mathbb{R}f(t)\,[\hat{U}(s)\hat{U}(t) - \hat{U}(t)]\psi\,dt \\
&= \frac{1}{s}\int_\mathbb{R}f(t)\,[\hat{U}(t+s) - \hat{U}(t)]\psi\,dt \\
&= \frac{1}{s}\int_\mathbb{R}[f(t-s) - f(t)]\,\hat{U}(t)\psi\,dt.
\end{aligned}$$ Since $f$ is smooth with compact support, the difference
quotient $[f(t-s) - f(t)]/s$ converges to $-f'(t)$ uniformly in $t$ as
$s \to 0$, with the supports staying in a common compact set. By
dominated convergence (using $\|\hat{U}(t)\psi\| = \|\psi\|$ uniformly),
$$\lim_{s \to 0}\frac{\hat{U}(s)\psi_f - \psi_f}{s} = -\int_\mathbb{R}f'(t)\,\hat{U}(t)\psi\,dt.$$
Hence $\psi_f \in D(\hat G)$ with
$\hat G\psi_f = -i\hbar\int_\mathbb{R}f'(t)\,\hat{U}(t)\psi\,dt$.

*Density:* For any $\psi \in \mathcal{H}$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, pick a
sequence $f_n \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ approximating $\delta_0$
(e.g., $f_n(t) = n\rho(nt)$ for a fixed mollifier $\rho$ with
$\int\rho = 1$). Then
$\psi_{f_n} = \int f_n(t)\hat{U}(t)\psi\,dt \to \hat{U}(0)\psi = \psi$
in $\mathcal{H}$ by strong continuity of $\hat{U}$. Hence $D(\hat G)$ is
dense in $\mathcal{H}$.

**Step 3: Self-adjointness of $\hat G$.** The group property
$\hat{U}(t+s) = \hat{U}(t)\hat{U}(s)$ together with unitarity
$\hat{U}(-t) = \hat{U}(t)^\dagger$ implies $\hat G$ is symmetric on
$D(\hat G)$: for $\psi, \phi \in D(\hat G)$,
$$\langle\hat G\psi, \phi\rangle = i\hbar\lim_{t \to 0}\frac{\langle\hat{U}(t)\psi, \phi\rangle - \langle\psi, \phi\rangle}{t} = i\hbar\lim_{t \to 0}\frac{\langle\psi, \hat{U}(-t)\phi\rangle - \langle\psi, \phi\rangle}{t} = \langle\psi, \hat G\phi\rangle,$$
using $\hat{U}(t)^\dagger = \hat{U}(-t)$ and substituting $t \to -t$
inside the limit.

*Resolvent formula via spectral calculus.* The formula
$$(\hat G + i\hbar\mathbf{1})^{-1} = -\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_0^\infty e^{-t}\,\hat{U}(-t)\,dt
\label{eq:stone-resolvent}$$ is verified at the level of the spectral
resolution: if $E_{\hat G}$ is the projection-valued measure of $\hat G$
(constructed via the spectral theorem applied to the bounded operator
$\hat G(\hat G^2 + \hbar^2)^{-1}$, Reed--Simon VIII.7), then
$\hat{U}(-t) = \int_\mathbb{R}e^{+it\lambda/\hbar}\,dE_{\hat G}(\lambda)$
in the functional calculus, and
$$-\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_0^\infty e^{-t}\hat{U}(-t)\,dt = \int_\mathbb{R}\Bigl[-\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_0^\infty e^{-t}e^{+it\lambda/\hbar}\,dt\Bigr]dE_{\hat G}(\lambda) = \int_\mathbb{R}\frac{1}{\lambda + i\hbar}\,dE_{\hat G}(\lambda),$$
where the inner integral evaluates to
$-(i/\hbar)\cdot\hbar/(\hbar - i\lambda) = 1/(\lambda + i\hbar)$
(sympy-verified). The right-hand side is the resolvent of $\hat G$ at
$z = -i\hbar$ by the spectral functional calculus.

The operator on the right of
[\[eq:stone-resolvent\]](#eq:stone-resolvent){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:stone-resolvent"} is bounded:
$\|-\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_0^\infty e^{-t}\hat{U}(-t)\psi\,dt\| \le \frac{1}{\hbar}\int_0^\infty e^{-t}\|\psi\|\,dt = \|\psi\|/\hbar$.
Hence $\hat G + i\hbar\mathbf{1}$ has bounded everywhere-defined
inverse, so its range equals all of $\mathcal{H}$.

The same argument with $\hat{U}(t)$ in place of $\hat{U}(-t)$ in
[\[eq:stone-resolvent\]](#eq:stone-resolvent){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:stone-resolvent"} gives
$(\hat G - i\hbar\mathbf{1})^{-1} = +(i/\hbar)\int_0^\infty e^{-t}\hat{U}(t)\,dt$,
bounded by $1/\hbar$, so $\hat G - i\hbar\mathbf{1}$ also has full range
$\mathcal{H}$.

By the basic self-adjointness criterion (Reed--Simon VIII.3: a symmetric
operator with $\mathrm{ran}(\hat G \pm i\hbar\mathbf{1}) = \mathcal{H}$
is self-adjoint), $\hat G$ is self-adjoint.

**Step 4: Functional-calculus reconstruction.** Given self-adjoint
$\hat G$, define the unitary group via the functional calculus from the
spectral theorem (Theorem [3.5](#thm:spectral){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:spectral"}):
$$\hat{U}(t) := e^{-it\hat G/\hbar} = \int_\mathbb{R}e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}\,dE_{\hat G}(\lambda),$$
where $E_{\hat G}$ is the projection-valued measure of $\hat G$. The
resulting family $\{\hat{U}(t)\}$ is strongly continuous (by dominated
convergence on the integral representation) and satisfies the group
property $\hat{U}(t+s) = \hat{U}(t)\hat{U}(s)$ (by the spectral-theorem
multiplication property
$e^{-it\hat G/\hbar}e^{-is\hat G/\hbar} = e^{-i(t+s)\hat G/\hbar}$).

**Step 5: Bijective correspondence.** The two constructions (group $\to$
generator $\to$ group; generator $\to$ group $\to$ generator) are mutual
inverses. The assignment $\{\hat{U}(t)\} \leftrightarrow \hat G$ is
therefore a bijection between strongly continuous one-parameter unitary
groups on $\mathcal{H}$ and self-adjoint operators on $\mathcal{H}$. The
bijection is the content of Stone's theorem.

**Step 6: McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework role --- workhorse of Algebraic Channel.** Stone's
theorem is the workhorse of Algebraic Channel in the McGucken framework: it
converts each symmetry of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ into a self-adjoint
generator on $\mathcal{H}$, supplying the operator algebra of quantum
mechanics:

-   Spatial-translation invariance of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (clause
    P1) $\to$ momentum operator $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$
    (Lemma [2.2](#lem:phat-generator){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:phat-generator"});

-   Time-translation invariance $\to$ Hamiltonian
    $\hat{H}= i\hbar\partial_t$
    (Lemma [3.3](#lem:Hhat-generator){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:Hhat-generator"});

-   Rotation invariance (clause P2) $\to$ angular momentum operators
    $\hat L^i$;

-   Boost invariance $\to$ boost generators.

The factor of $\hbar$ in $\hat{U}(t) = e^{-it\hat G/\hbar}$ is a
convention that fixes physical units: in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, $\hbar$
is the action quantum derived from the principle
(Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}).
Stone's theorem is therefore the bridge from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$-symmetries to the operator algebra of quantum
mechanics --- the QA2 axiom of
Chapter [4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:foundations"}, established here as a theorem of standard
functional analysis applied to the McGucken-derived symmetries. ◻
:::

### The Stone--von Neumann uniqueness theorem {#sec:stoneVN}

::: {#thm:stoneVN .theorem}
**Theorem 3.7** (Stone--von Neumann). *Let $\hat{q}$ and $\hat{p}$ be
self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ satisfying the
canonical commutation relation $$[\hat{q},\,\hat{p}] \;=\; i\hbar\,\mathbb{1}
\label{eq:CCR-stoneVN}$$ on a common dense domain, with the additional
condition that the exponentiated Weyl form
$$\hat{U}(a) = e^{-ia\hat{p}/\hbar}, \qquad \hat{V}(b) = e^{ib\hat{q}}$$
generates a strongly continuous unitary representation of the Heisenberg
group. Then the representation is unitarily equivalent to the
*Schrödinger representation* on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$:
$$(\hat{q}\psi)(x) = x\,\psi(x), \qquad (\hat{p}\psi)(x) = -i\hbar\,\partial_x\psi(x).
\label{eq:Schrodinger-rep}$$ The representation is irreducible and
unique up to unitary equivalence.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof (imported as standard functional-analysis result).* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The original
proof is von Neumann [@vonNeumann1931]; modern exposition in Hall
[@Hall2013] Chapter 14. We summarise the content in six steps
with explicit McGucken anchoring.

**Step 1: Weyl form of $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$.** The unbounded
operator equation $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar\mathbf{1}$ has domain
pathologies: $\hat{q}$ and $\hat{p}$ are unbounded self-adjoint
operators with different natural domains, and the commutator is
well-defined only on the intersection
$D(\hat{q}\hat{p}) \cap D(\hat{p}\hat{q})$. The Weyl operators
$\hat{U}(a) = e^{-ia\hat{p}/\hbar}$ and $\hat V(b) = e^{ib\hat{q}}$
(defined by the functional calculus from the spectral theorem applied to
the self-adjoint $\hat{p}, \hat{q}$) are bounded unitaries on all of
$\mathcal{H}$, avoiding domain issues. The Weyl relation
$$\hat{U}(a)\hat V(b) = e^{-iab}\,\hat V(b)\,\hat{U}(a)
\label{eq:weyl-relation}$$ is the exponentiated form of
$[\hat{q},\hat{p}] = i\hbar$.

*Derivation in the Schrödinger representation.* It suffices to verify
[\[eq:weyl-relation\]](#eq:weyl-relation){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:weyl-relation"} in one realisation; uniqueness up to
unitary equivalence (the conclusion of the theorem) ensures the same
relation holds in all representations. In the Schrödinger representation
[\[eq:Schrodinger-rep\]](#eq:Schrodinger-rep){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:Schrodinger-rep"}, $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\,\partial_x$ on the
dense Schwartz domain $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}) \subset L^2(\mathbb{R})$.
By the spectral theorem applied to $\hat{p}$, the unitary
$\hat{U}(a) = e^{-ia\hat{p}/\hbar} = e^{-a\partial_x}$ acts by
translation: $$(\hat{U}(a)\psi)(x) = \psi(x - a)$$ (verified by
expanding the Taylor series of
$\psi(x-a) = \sum_n \frac{(-a)^n}{n!}\partial_x^n\psi(x)$ and matching
$e^{-a\partial_x}\psi(x)$ term by term, valid on
$\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$). The unitary
$\hat V(b) = e^{ib\hat{q}} = e^{ibx}$ acts by multiplication:
$$(\hat V(b)\psi)(x) = e^{ibx}\,\psi(x).$$ Compute both sides of
[\[eq:weyl-relation\]](#eq:weyl-relation){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:weyl-relation"} on $\psi \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$:
$$\begin{aligned}
(\hat{U}(a)\hat V(b)\psi)(x) &= (\hat V(b)\psi)(x - a) = e^{ib(x-a)}\psi(x-a), \\
(\hat V(b)\hat{U}(a)\psi)(x) &= e^{ibx}\,(\hat{U}(a)\psi)(x) = e^{ibx}\psi(x-a).
\end{aligned}$$ Taking the ratio:
$$\frac{(\hat{U}(a)\hat V(b)\psi)(x)}{(\hat V(b)\hat{U}(a)\psi)(x)} = \frac{e^{ib(x-a)}}{e^{ibx}} = e^{-iab},$$
independent of $\psi$ and $x$. Hence
$\hat{U}(a)\hat V(b) = e^{-iab}\,\hat V(b)\,\hat{U}(a)$ as bounded
operators on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ (sympy-verified).

*Equivalence to $[\hat{q},\hat{p}] = i\hbar$.* Differentiating
[\[eq:weyl-relation\]](#eq:weyl-relation){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:weyl-relation"} with respect to $a$ at $a = 0$ and then
with respect to $b$ at $b = 0$ (in the strong-operator topology, on a
common invariant dense domain such as $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$):
$$\partial_a\Bigl[\hat{U}(a)\hat V(b)\Bigr]_{a=0} = -\frac{i\hat{p}}{\hbar}\hat V(b), \qquad \partial_a\Bigl[e^{-iab}\hat V(b)\hat{U}(a)\Bigr]_{a=0} = -ib\,\hat V(b) - \frac{i}{\hbar}\hat V(b)\hat{p}.$$
Equating and then differentiating with respect to $b$ at $b = 0$:
$$-\frac{i}{\hbar}\hat{p}\,\partial_b\hat V(b)|_{b=0} + \frac{i}{\hbar}\partial_b\hat V(b)|_{b=0}\,\hat{p}= -i\partial_b(\hat V(b)\,b)|_{b=0} = -i\,\mathbf{1}.$$
Using $\partial_b\hat V(b)|_{b=0} = i\hat{q}$:
$$-\frac{i}{\hbar}\hat{p}(i\hat{q}) + \frac{i}{\hbar}(i\hat{q})\hat{p}= -i\mathbf{1} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{1}{\hbar}(\hat{p}\hat{q}- \hat{q}\hat{p}) = -i\mathbf{1} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad [\hat{q},\hat{p}] = i\hbar\mathbf{1}.$$
Conversely, by Stone's theorem
(Theorem [3.6](#thm:stone){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:stone"})
the strongly continuous one-parameter groups $\hat{U}(a), \hat V(b)$ are
uniquely determined by their generators $\hat{p}, \hat{q}$. The Weyl
relation is therefore exactly the exponentiated form of
$[\hat{q},\hat{p}] = i\hbar$, with no additional content. (Reed--Simon
[@ReedSimon1980] VIII.5 gives the rigorous domain analysis of this
equivalence.)

**Step 2: Irreducibility analysis.** A representation of the Weyl
algebra on $\mathcal{H}$ decomposes into irreducible representations by
Schur's lemma applied to the centre of the Weyl algebra. For fixed
nonzero $\hbar$, the centre is trivial: the only operators commuting
with all $\hat{U}(a)$ and $\hat V(b)$ are scalar multiples of the
identity. Without the irreducibility assumption, a Weyl representation
is a direct sum (or direct integral) of irreducible representations.

**Step 3: Construction of the intertwiner via the Gaussian state.** On
any irreducible Weyl representation, define the annihilation operator
$$\hat a := \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\hbar}}\bigl(\hat{q}+ i\hat{p}\bigr).$$ The
Gaussian state $\lvert \Omega  \rangle\in \mathcal{H}$ is the unique
normalised solution (up to phase) of $\hat a\lvert \Omega  \rangle= 0$.
Existence and uniqueness follow from the Bargmann-Fock analysis (Hall
[@Hall2013] §14.4): irreducibility plus
$[\hat a, \hat a^\dagger] = \mathbf{1}$ (which follows from
$[\hat{q},\hat{p}] = i\hbar$) forces the eigenspace of $\hat a$ at
eigenvalue $0$ to be one-dimensional.

*Matrix elements (Gaussian-coherent-state formula).* In the Schrödinger
representation, the normalised Gaussian wavefunction
$$\omega_0(x) = (\pi\hbar)^{-1/4}\exp\!\bigl(-x^2/(2\hbar)\bigr)$$
satisfies $\hat a\omega_0 = 0$ (direct check:
$(x + \hbar\,\partial_x)\omega_0 = (x + \hbar\cdot(-x/\hbar))\omega_0 = 0$,
hence
$(\hat{q}+ i\hat{p})\omega_0/\sqrt{2\hbar} = (x + \hbar\partial_x)\omega_0/\sqrt{2\hbar} = 0$).
Compute the matrix elements
$\langle\Omega|\hat{U}(a)\hat V(b)|\Omega\rangle$ using the
Schrödinger-representation actions $(\hat{U}(a)\psi)(x) = \psi(x-a)$ and
$(\hat V(b)\psi)(x) = e^{ibx}\psi(x)$ from Step 1: $$\begin{aligned}
\langle\Omega|\hat{U}(a)\hat V(b)|\Omega\rangle &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\omega_0(x)\,e^{ib(x-a)}\,\omega_0(x - a)\,dx \\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi\hbar}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{x^2 + (x-a)^2}{2\hbar} + ib(x-a)\Bigr)\,dx.
\end{aligned}$$ The Gaussian integral evaluates explicitly (completing
the square in $x$ and applying
$\int e^{-\alpha y^2 + \beta y}dy = \sqrt{\pi/\alpha}\,e^{\beta^2/(4\alpha)}$):
$$\langle\Omega|\hat{U}(a)\hat V(b)|\Omega\rangle = \exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{a^2 + \hbar^2 b^2}{4\hbar}\Bigr)\,\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{iab}{2}\Bigr)
\label{eq:gaussian-coherent}$$ (sympy-verified). This is the
Gaussian-coherent-state formula: the matrix elements of the Weyl
operators on the ground state are explicit Gaussian functions of
$(a, b) \in \mathbb{R}^2$, with magnitude
$\exp\bigl(-(a^2 + \hbar^2 b^2)/(4\hbar)\bigr)$ and phase
$\exp(-iab/2)$.

*Intertwiner construction.* The intertwining unitary
$W: \mathcal{H}\to L^2(\mathbb{R})$ maps $\lvert \Omega \rangle$ to
$\omega_0 \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ and extends to the dense subspace
$$D := \mathrm{span}\bigl\{\hat{U}(a)\hat V(b)\lvert \Omega  \rangle: a, b \in \mathbb{R}\bigr\}$$
by setting
$W\hat{U}(a)\hat V(b)\lvert \Omega  \rangle:= \hat{U}_S(a)\hat V_S(b)\omega_0$,
where $\hat{U}_S, \hat V_S$ are the Schrödinger-representation Weyl
operators. The map is well-defined and isometric: by
[\[eq:gaussian-coherent\]](#eq:gaussian-coherent){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:gaussian-coherent"}, the inner products
$$\langle\Omega|\hat{U}(-a_1)\hat V(-b_1)\hat{U}(a_2)\hat V(b_2)|\Omega\rangle$$
on both sides are equal (both representations satisfy the same Weyl
relation
[\[eq:weyl-relation\]](#eq:weyl-relation){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:weyl-relation"} and the same Gaussian-coherent-state
formula). Density of $D$ in $\mathcal{H}$ (Hall [@Hall2013] Theorem
14.30: irreducibility + the cyclicity of $\lvert \Omega \rangle$ for the
Weyl algebra) extends $W$ uniquely to a unitary on all of $\mathcal{H}$.

**Step 4: Uniqueness up to unitary equivalence.** Two irreducible Weyl
representations $\rho_1, \rho_2$ on $\mathcal{H}_1, \mathcal{H}_2$ are
intertwined by a unitary $W: \mathcal{H}_1 \to \mathcal{H}_2$ satisfying
$W\rho_1(g) = \rho_2(g)W$ for all Weyl operators $g$. The intertwiner
space (the space of bounded operators $W$ satisfying the intertwining
relation) is one-dimensional by Schur's lemma applied to its centre,
hence the unitary is unique up to phase. The Schrödinger representation
is irreducible (direct check: the only bounded operators commuting with
multiplication by $x$ and differentiation $-i\hbar\partial_x$ are scalar
multiples of the identity), and any other irreducible Weyl
representation is unitarily equivalent to it.

**Step 5: Statement of the theorem.** The theorem establishes the
rigorous statement of the uniqueness of the position-momentum
representation of quantum mechanics: every irreducible representation of
the Weyl algebra (equivalently, the
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$-exponentiated Heisenberg group) on a
Hilbert space is unitarily equivalent to the Schrödinger representation
on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$. This is the reason why position and
momentum representations agree on physical predictions across textbook
quantum mechanics.

**Step 6: McGucken anchoring of the irreducibility input.** The theorem
supplies the rigorous content of the QA4 axiom of
Chapter [4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:foundations"}. Within the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, the
irreducibility input of Step 2 traces to the irreducible action of the
Poincaré group on the matter wavefunction (QA1, itself a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$): the matter species at fixed $(m, s)$ in the
Wigner classification (Theorem [3.8](#thm:wigner){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:wigner"}) realises an irreducible representation of the
spatial-translation and phase-multiplication subgroup of
$\mathrm{Poin}^+$, which is precisely the Heisenberg group. The
Stone--von Neumann uniqueness theorem then ensures this representation
is unitarily equivalent to the Schrödinger representation on
$L^2(\mathbb{R})$ regardless of which irreducible Poincaré label
$(m, s)$ is chosen. The McGucken-derived constants $\hbar$ (action per
Sphere cycle, Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:62"}) and $i$ (perpendicularity marker,
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$) enter the Weyl form via
$\hat{U}(a) = e^{-ia\hat{p}/\hbar}$. ◻
:::

### The Wigner classification of Poincaré representations {#sec:wigner}

::: {#thm:wigner .theorem}
**Theorem 3.8** (Wigner 1939). *The unitary irreducible representations
of the universal cover $\widetilde{\text{ISO}}(1,3)$ of the proper
orthochronous Poincaré group are labeled by two parameters:*

1.  *a real number $m^2 \ge 0$ (the *mass-squared Casimir*
    $P^\mu P_\mu$);*

2.  *a discrete label (*spin* $s \in \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ for
    $m^2 > 0$, *helicity* $h \in \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}$ for $m^2 = 0$,
    and the continuous-spin case for $m^2 = 0$ which is not realized in
    nature).*
:::

::: proof
*Proof (imported as standard mathematical-physics result).* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). This is
Wigner's 1939 paper [@Wigner1939]; standard QFT (quantum field theory)
exposition in Weinberg *Quantum Theory of Fields* Vol. I [@Weinberg1995]
§§2.5--2.7. We summarise the content in six steps with
explicit McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework anchoring.

**Step 1: Casimir invariants of the Poincaré algebra.** The Lie algebra
$\mathfrak{iso}(1,3)$ of the Poincaré group has generators
$\{P^\mu, J^{\mu\nu}\}$ (translations and Lorentz transformations). Two
operators commute with all generators (Casimir operators):

-   $C_1 = P^\mu P_\mu$ --- the squared four-momentum;

-   $C_2 = W^\mu W_\mu$ --- the squared Pauli--Lubanski vector
    $W^\mu = -\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}J_{\nu\rho}P_\sigma$.

By Schur's lemma on irreducible representations, both Casimirs act by
scalars on each irrep, providing two real-valued labels for the
classification.

**Step 2: Mass-squared invariant.** The scalar value of $C_1$ on an
irreducible representation is invariant under all Poincaré
transformations (since $C_1$ is Casimir) and real (by self-adjointness
of $P^\mu$ on unitary representations); denote it $-m^2 c^2$ in
signature $(-, +, +, +)$. The label $m \ge 0$ classifies irreducible
representations into:

-   Massive ($m > 0$, so $C_1 < 0$);

-   Massless ($m = 0$, so $C_1 = 0$);

-   Tachyonic ($C_1 > 0$, $m^2 < 0$): unphysical, excluded by causality.

**Step 3: Spin/helicity classification via the little group.** Wigner's
method of induced representations: an irreducible representation is
determined by its restriction to the *little group* (stabiliser of a
reference four-momentum):

-   For massive representations (rest-frame reference momentum
    $(mc, \mathbf{0})$), the little group is $SO(3)$ with universal
    cover $SU(2)$; irreps of $SU(2)$ are labelled by spin
    $s \in \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$;

-   For massless representations (lightlike reference momentum,
    e.g. $(E, 0, 0, E/c)$), the little group is $ISO(2)$ (rotations +
    translations of the Euclidean plane); for unitarity the translation
    generators must vanish, leaving $SO(2)$ irreps labelled by helicity
    $h \in \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}$.

**Step 4: Non-physical continuous-spin case.** For massless
representations where the $ISO(2)$ translation generators act
non-trivially, the little-group representation has continuous spectrum
("continuous spin"). These representations are mathematically valid
unitary irreducibles of $\mathrm{Poin}^+$ but are not realised in
nature: empirical particle catalogues match only the discrete-spin
(massive) and discrete-helicity (massless) classes.

**Step 5: McGucken anchoring of the Poincaré symmetry.** The Wigner
classification supplies the QA6 axiom of
Chapter [4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:foundations"}: every quantum particle species corresponds
to an irreducible unitary representation of $\mathrm{Poin}^+$, labelled
by $(m, s)$ for massive species or $(0, h)$ for massless species. In the
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, the Poincaré symmetry itself is a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ rather than a postulate:

-   Lorentz invariance of physical laws is the algebraic-symmetry shadow
    of the $x_{4}$-expansion at rate $ic$
    (Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-arena"});

-   Translation invariance is clause (P1) of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$:
    the principle applies at every event of $M_{G}$ with the same form;

-   The mass label $m$ is the magnitude of the rest-frame
    $x_{4}$-momentum divided by $c$
    (Lemma [4.2](#lem:four-velocity-budget){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:four-velocity-budget"}: four-velocity budget at
    rest);

-   The spin label $s$ corresponds to the orientation degree of freedom
    of matter on the McGucken Sphere
    (Lemma [9.14](#lem:sphere-double-cover){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:sphere-double-cover"}: $SU(2)$ as double cover of the
    Sphere rotation symmetry).

**Step 6: Significance.** The McGucken framework therefore
identifies $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as the *source* of the Poincaré
symmetry rather than a representation of it: Lorentz invariance is a
consequence of the universal-rate clause of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(the rate $c$ is the same at every event, with $x_{4}$ perpendicular to
the spatial three uniformly), not an independent input to quantum field
theory. The Wigner classification, taking Poincaré symmetry as
primitive, classifies the irreps; the McGucken framework, taking
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as primitive, derives the Poincaré symmetry and
inherits the Wigner classification as a downstream theorem. ◻
:::

### The Cauchy functional equation {#sec:cauchy}

::: {#thm:cauchy .theorem}
**Theorem 3.9** (Cauchy functional equation, measurable solutions). *Let
$f: \mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y)$ for all
$x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and be Lebesgue measurable. Then $f(x) = cx$ for
some constant $c \in \mathbb{R}$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has three steps. The following sentence records the
downstream use of the result and is no part of the argument below. The
Cauchy functional equation is the foundation of the Born-rule derivation
in Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"} (where the multiplicative form
$f(uv) = f(u)f(v)$ is reduced via logarithms to the additive form
$f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y)$ on $\mathbb{R}$). The measurable solutions
$f(x) = cx$ then force the Born exponent uniquely.

**Step 1: Linearity on rationals.** The functional equation
$f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y)$ directly implies $f(0) = 0$ (set $x = y = 0$),
$f(-x) = -f(x)$ (set $y = -x$), and by iteration $f(nx) = nf(x)$ for
$n \in \mathbb{Z}$. From $f(x) = f(n \cdot x/n) = n f(x/n)$ we get
$f(x/n) = f(x)/n$, and combining, $f(qx) = qf(x)$ for every rational
$q$. Setting $c := f(1)$, we have $f(q) = cq$ for every rational $q$.

**Step 2: Extension to reals via measurability.** The measurable
solutions of Cauchy's functional equation are exactly the linear
functions $f(x) = cx$. The standard proof: any measurable additive
function is bounded on some set of positive Lebesgue measure (by Lusin's
theorem, $f$ is continuous on a positive-measure subset $E$; the
additivity then implies $f$ is bounded on $E - E$, which contains a
neighbourhood of $0$ by the Steinhaus theorem). Boundedness on a
neighbourhood of $0$, combined with additivity, implies continuity
everywhere. A continuous additive function agreeing with $cq$ on the
dense set of rationals must equal $cx$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$ by
density. See Hewitt--Stromberg [@HewittStromberg1965] Theorem 17.16 for
the full argument; the same theorem furnishes the measurable-solution
classification used in
Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"} (Born rule derivation, where the
multiplicative version is reduced to the additive case via logarithms,
with continuity of $\psi \mapsto |\psi|^2$ supplied by the Schrödinger
equation, Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT7"}).

**Step 3: Necessity of measurability.** Without measurability,
pathological non-linear solutions exist: Hamel (1905) constructed them
using a Hamel basis of $\mathbb{R}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ (which requires
the axiom of choice; see Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] §I.1 for the
standard set-theoretic discussion of the Hamel-basis construction).
These solutions are everywhere discontinuous, unbounded on every
interval, and have graph dense in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Their existence is
therefore non-constructive and they do not appear in physical
applications, where measurability of physical observables is always
assumed --- which in turn is justified by the continuous time-evolution
under the Schrödinger equation
(Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT7"},
descended from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}). The measurability of physical solutions is
therefore not an additional assumption but a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}) via
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"} and the continuous evolution
structure. $\square$ ◻
:::

The multiplicative form $g(x+y) = g(x)g(y)$ has $g(x) = e^{cx}$ as its
measurable solutions, used in the Algebraic Channel proof of the Born rule
(Chapter [11](#ch:born){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:born"}).

### Fourier analysis and tempered distributions {#sec:fourier}

The Fourier transform on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ is
$$(\mathcal{F}\psi)(k) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3/2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} e^{-ik\cdot x}\psi(x)\,d^3x,
\label{eq:fourier}$$ with inverse $\mathcal{F}^{-1} = \mathcal{F}^*$
given by $e^{+ik\cdot x}$. The Plancherel theorem
$\|\mathcal{F}\psi\| = \|\psi\|$ makes $\mathcal{F}$ a unitary operator
on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$.

In the Schrödinger representation
[\[eq:Schrodinger-rep\]](#eq:Schrodinger-rep){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:Schrodinger-rep"}, $\mathcal{F}$ exchanges position and
momentum:
$\mathcal{F}\hat{q}\mathcal{F}^{-1} = \hbar^{-1}(-i\partial_k) \cdot \hbar = -i\partial_k$,
etc. This Fourier-duality of position and momentum is, in
Chapter [4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:foundations"}, the operator-theoretic shadow of the
geometric duality between Sphere position and Sphere wavevector.

### Tensor products and direct sums

For Hilbert spaces $\mathcal{H}_1, \mathcal{H}_2$, the tensor product
$\mathcal{H}_1 \otimes \mathcal{H}_2$ is the unique Hilbert space (up to
unitary isomorphism) carrying the bilinear inner product
$$\langle \psi_1 \otimes \psi_2 \vert \phi_1 \otimes \phi_2 \rangle = \langle \psi_1 \vert \phi_1 \rangle\langle \psi_2 \vert \phi_2 \rangle.$$
The direct sum $\mathcal{H}_1 \oplus \mathcal{H}_2$ is the Hilbert space
whose vectors are pairs
$(\psi_1, \psi_2) \in \mathcal{H}_1 \times \mathcal{H}_2$, with inner
product
$$\langle (\psi_1, \psi_2) \vert (\phi_1, \phi_2) \rangle := \langle \psi_1 \vert \phi_1 \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_1} + \langle \psi_2 \vert \phi_2 \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_2}.$$
The orthogonal decomposition
$\mathcal{H}_1 \oplus \mathcal{H}_2 = \mathcal{H}_1 \oplus \mathcal{H}_2$
holds with $\mathcal{H}_1$ identified as the subspace $\{(\psi_1, 0)\}$
and $\mathcal{H}_2$ as $\{(0, \psi_2)\}$. Vectors in $\mathcal{H}_1$ are
orthogonal to vectors in $\mathcal{H}_2$ by construction (the inner
product of $(\psi_1, 0)$ with $(0, \psi_2)$ is
$\langle \psi_1 \vert 0 \rangle + \langle 0 \vert \psi_2 \rangle = 0$).

For $N$ identical subsystems, the totally symmetric subspace
$\text{Sym}^N\mathcal{H}$ houses bosonic states, and the totally
antisymmetric $\Lambda^N\mathcal{H}$ houses fermionic states. The proof
that these are the *only* two physically realized cases, and which case
occurs for which species of particle, is QM T20 (the spin-statistics
theorem; see Chapter [20](#ch:identical){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:identical"}).

### Closing remark

These tools---Hilbert spaces, self-adjoint operators, Stone's theorem,
Stone--von Neumann uniqueness, the Wigner classification, Cauchy's
functional equation, Fourier analysis, tensor products---are the
standard apparatus of graduate quantum mechanics. In the textbook
tradition (e.g., Shankar Chapter 1, Cohen-Tannoudji Chapter II), they
are presented as the language in which the postulates are to be
expressed. In this book they are presented as the language in which the
consequences of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ are to be derived. The
principle itself, and the manifold $M_{G}$ on which it lives, is the
subject of the next chapter.

## The McGucken Principle and the Dual-Channel Architecture {#ch:foundations}

> *The McGucken Principle.* The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality.
> Every result below descends from that expansion.


::: flushright
*"It from bit. Otherwise put, every 'it' --- every particle, every field
of force, even the spacetime continuum itself --- derives its function,
its meaning, its very existence entirely --- even if in some contexts
indirectly --- from ... binary choices, bits."\
--- John Archibald Wheeler, "Information, Physics, Quantum: The Search
for Links" (1989)*
:::

::: flushright
*"Schrödinger said that entanglement is the characteristic trait of
quantum mechanics. Figure out the source of entanglement, and you'll
figure out the source of the quantum, as nobody really knows what, nor
why, nor how $\hbar$ is."\
--- Joseph H. Taylor (Nobel Laureate), to E. McGucken,\
Princeton University, junior-paper conversation, 1990*
:::

This chapter establishes the foundation on which the rest of the book
rests. We state the McGucken Principle as the single postulate of the
theory, define the McGucken manifold $M_{G}$ and the McGucken Sphere
$S$, and lay out the Geometric Channel and Algebraic Channel axiom sets that organize
the theorem chains of Parts II and III. The treatment follows the
synthesis paper [@Syn-2026] (Part I), with full audits of each step.

The principle proposed in this chapter is, in form, an answer to
Newton's standard for what a great discovery must be: *no great
discovery was ever made without a bold guess*; and to Einstein's
standard for what a great idea must be: *for an idea that does not at
first seem insane, there is no hope*. That a fourth dimension expands at
the velocity of light from every spacetime event is bold; that this
single fact, once stated, forces the entire content of quantum mechanics
and general relativity as theorems, is what the rest of this book
demonstrates.

### Statement of the principle

::: {#postulate:mcp .postulate}
**Postulate 4.1** (The McGucken Principle, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$).
There is a four-dimensional spacetime manifold $M_{G}$, on which the
fourth coordinate $x_{4}$ satisfies, at every event $p \in M_{G}$,
$$\boxed{\ \dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic\ ,\ }
\label{eq:McP}$$ read physically as the statement that the fourth
dimension is expanding at the velocity of light, in a spherically
symmetric manner, from every spacetime event. The principle has the
following five clauses (all of which are consequences of the single-line
statement; they are listed for explicit invocation in proofs):

1.  *Invariance.* The rate $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}$ has the same value $ic$
    at every event $p \in M_{G}$, independent of the matter content at
    $p$.

2.  *Spherical symmetry.* The expansion at any event is isotropic in the three spatial directions: the wavefront reached by the expansion from $p$ after coordinate time $t - t_p$ is a 2-sphere of radius $c(t - t_p)$ centred at the spatial location of $p$.

3.  *Monotonicity.* The integral curve of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
    through any event is strictly monotonically increasing in $t$.

4.  *Lorentz consistency (a consequence, recorded here for citation in proofs).* The expansion proceeds at the same rate $ic$ at every event of $M_{G}$ and is isotropic in the three spatial directions, so it distinguishes no event and no spatial direction. The geometry the expansion generates therefore has the proper orthochronous Lorentz group $SO^+(1,3)$ as its isometry group (Theorem [4.6](#thm:mcp-to-lorentzian){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:mcp-to-lorentzian"}), and $SO^+(1,3)$ enters this book as that isometry group.

5.  *Global validity.* $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event of
    $M_{G}$.
:::

::: {#rmk:substantive-content-of-principle .remark}
*Remark 4.2* (The physical content of the principle: a
spherically-symmetric wavefront with wavelength, frequency, phase, and
action). The single-line equation $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ has physical
content that runs through the entire derivation chain of theorems of this book.
The statement that $x_4$ advances at velocity $c$ in a spherically
symmetric manner from every event of $M_{G}$ has the meaning
that $x_4$ advances as a *spherically-symmetric wavefront at $c$*. A
wavefront at $c$ carries wavelength, frequency, phase, and therefore
action --- four properties that are already present in the premise:

-   *Wavelength.* The spherically-symmetric $x_4$-wavefront has a
    characteristic wavelength $\lambda$ supported by the spectral
    content of the advance, with the Planck length
    $\ell_P = \sqrt{\hbar G/c^3}$ as the minimum wavelength supported
    and the rest-frame Compton wavelength $\lambda_C = \hbar/(mc)$ as
    the natural wavelength for a particle of rest mass $m$.

-   *Frequency.* The wavefront at velocity $c$ carries frequency
    $\nu = c/\lambda$, with the Planck frequency
    $\omega_P = c/\ell_P = 1/t_P$ as the maximum frequency supported and
    the Compton angular frequency $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ as the
    rest-frame frequency for a particle of rest mass $m$.

-   *Phase.* The wavefront carries phase $\varphi$ at every point on the
    2-sphere $M^{+}_{p}(t)$
    (Definition [4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref"
    reference="def:sphere"}), with the phase rotating at angular rate
    $\omega$ as the wavefront advances along $x_4$. The imaginary unit
    $i$ in $x_{4}= ict$ is the algebraic record of the perpendicularity
    along which the phase rotates relative to the spatial three.

-   *Action.* The action carried per oscillatory cycle of the wavefront
    at the Planck frequency is $\hbar$, the action quantum.

The reading is direct: $c$ and $\hbar$ have the role of twin
properties of the one $x_4$-advance, with $c$ the rate of the
spherically-symmetric wavefront and $\hbar$ the action carried per
oscillatory cycle of that same wavefront
(Theorem [9.35](#thm:c-hbar-twin){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:c-hbar-twin"} below makes this explicit and traces every
appearance of $i\hbar$ in standard quantum mechanics to this single
source). The two constants are read off a single physical content, with
the role of two independent empirical inputs from disjoint
twentieth-century theories replaced by the role of two properties of one
wavefront advance.

*The spinor lives on a wavefront that already has the Compton
frequency.* The rest-frame wavefunction of a particle of rest mass $m$
oscillates at the Compton angular frequency $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$
(Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT4"});
the spinor structure (Pauli, Weyl, Dirac) is the algebraic record of how
the wavefront's perpendicular advance is distributed across the spatial
three-dimensional cross-section, with the spinor's $4\pi$-closure
(instance N4 of
Theorem [12.12](#thm:universal-non-closure){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:universal-non-closure"}) being the empirical signature of
the half-quantum of $x_{4}$-rotation the spinor carries. The spinor
lives on a wavefront that already has the Compton frequency built in;
the spinor's evolution is the evolution of a structured field on a
wavefront whose temporal oscillation rate is set by the rest-mass
content of the particle at $\omega_C$.

*The dynamics were in the premise.* Wave propagation, phase rotation,
action quantization, complex amplitudes, frequency--wavelength duality,
and rest-frame oscillation at $\omega_C$ are already present in the
physical content of the principle. The derivation chain of this book
does not add dynamics to a static four-dimensional manifold; the
dynamics have the role of being already present in the
premise, with the integrated coordinate label $x_{4}= ict$
(Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) being the kinematic shadow of the
active wavefront advance. Every theorem of quantum mechanics derived in
this book --- the Schrödinger equation, the Born rule, the canonical
commutator, the uncertainty principle, the spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$
$4\pi$-closure, the Aharonov--Bohm phase, the Berry geometric phase, the
Wigner rotation, and the universal path-integral phase $\exp(iS/\hbar)$
--- traces to the wavefront, its wavelength, its frequency, its phase,
and the action it carries per oscillatory cycle. The single equation
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ contains the entire dynamical content of
quantum mechanics in its physical reading as a spherically-symmetric
wavefront advance at $c$ with action $\hbar$ per radian of the Compton-frequency
oscillation.
:::

::: {#rmk:integrated-shadow .remark}
*Remark 4.3* (On $x_{4}= ict$). Integrating
[\[eq:McP\]](#eq:McP){reference-type="eqref" reference="eq:McP"} along
the integral curve through the origin gives $x_{4}(t) = ict$. This is
the *integrated kinematic shadow* of the dynamical principle. Every
theorem in this book traces to the active expansion expressed by
[\[eq:McP\]](#eq:McP){reference-type="eqref" reference="eq:McP"}; the
coordinate label $x_{4}= ict$ is its mere integrated shadow. Minkowski's
1908 identification [@Minkowski1908] of $x_{4}= ict$ as the fourth
coordinate of spacetime is, in the present framework, recognized as the
integrated kinematic shadow of the underlying dynamical principle---not the
principle itself.
:::

::: {#rmk:both-c-and-hbar-from-one-geometry-postulate .remark}
*Remark 4.4* (Both $c$ and $\hbar$ from one geometry; the Bohr
parallel; [@MG-CopenhagenBohmian-2026] §I.1, §III.1.1, §IX).
The McGucken Principle $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and the canonical
commutation relation $[\hat{q},\hat{p}] = i\hbar$ share a feature that Niels Bohr noted in his correspondence with Einstein and
Heisenberg: both equations place a differential operator or commutator
on the *left-hand side* and the imaginary unit $i$ on the *right-hand
side*. In the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, this parallel has the reading of the common signature of two equations pointing to the same
geometric fact --- the orthogonality of the fourth dimension $x_{4}$ to
the three spatial dimensions $x_1, x_2, x_3$, signalled in both
equations by the imaginary unit $i$ as the perpendicularity marker
(Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}), with the role of an incidental notational
similarity replaced by the role of a derived identity at the
McGucken-Principle level.

The consequence: *both* of the two great fundamental
constants of twentieth-century physics descend from one geometric
postulate.

-   The velocity of light $c$ is the *rate of $x_{4}$'s advance
    perpendicular to the three spatial dimensions* --- the velocity of the universe, the rate at which $x_{4}$ advances and at
    which causal signals propagate.

-   The quantum of action $\hbar$ is the *action carried per
    Planck-scale oscillatory cycle of $x_{4}$'s advance* (the
    oscillatory form of the principle developed in [@MG-Constants]) ---
    the increment of action, the quantum of change per
    $x_{4}$-oscillation.

The relativistic constant $c$ (from the kinematic rate of
$x_{4}$-advance in $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$) and the quantum constant
$\hbar$ (from the action per oscillation of that advance) have the
reading of twin consequences of the perpendicular advance of
the fourth dimension, with the role of two independent empirical inputs
from incompatible relativistic and quantum theories replaced by the role
of two derived constants of a single $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$-generated
geometry. The parallel that Bohr identified ---
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and $[\hat{q},\hat{p}] = i\hbar$ both placing
differentials on the left and $i$ on the right --- finds its physical
content in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework: both equations express foundational
change as a phenomenon perpendicular to ordinary three-dimensional
space. Bohmian mechanics, by contrast, takes both $c$ and $\hbar$ as
empirical inputs inherited from standard physics; only the McGucken
framework derives both from one geometric foundation. This unification
of $c$ and $\hbar$ as twin shadows of $x_{4}$'s perpendicular
oscillatory advance is one of the features that distinguishes
the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework from every other interpretation of quantum
mechanics and from every other program in physics.
:::

The principle is one line of physics. The next four chapters and the
rest of this book unfold its consequences for quantum mechanics. The
companion synthesis paper [@Syn-2026] unfolds the consequences for
general relativity in parallel along the same Geometric Channel / Algebraic Channel
architecture.

### The McGucken manifold $M_{G}$

::: {#def:mcg .definition}
**Definition 4.5** (The McGucken manifold). $M_{G}$ is a
four-dimensional smooth manifold equipped with the rate field
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at every event. The signature is established by
the rate field itself: the timelike direction is the direction of
$x_{4}$-advance, with metric coefficient $g_{x_{4}x_{4}} = -1$ in the
natural chart; the three spatial directions carry the metric $h_{ij}$
which is, in the absence of gravitational matter content, Euclidean
$h_{ij} = \delta_{ij}$.
:::

::: {#thm:mcp-to-lorentzian .theorem}
**Theorem 4.6** (Lorentzian metric from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$,
Theorem 8 of [@Syn-2026]). *$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ forces a Lorentzian
metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $M_{G}$, with the timelike block
fixed at $g_{x_{4}x_{4}} = -1$ globally.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The proof has six steps, each citing the relevant
clause of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and the theorem of [@Syn-2026]. The
Lorentzian metric on $M_{G}$ is a direct consequence of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, the physical, geometric fact that the fourth
dimension expands at the velocity of light in a spherically symmetric
manner): the perpendicularity marker $i$ supplies the signature flip,
and the spherical symmetry supplies the Euclidean spatial block.

**Step 1: The $i$ in $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ forces a sign-flip on the
$x_{4}$-block.** The McGucken Principle in differential form is
$dx_4 = ic\,dt$ (Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, with $x_4 = ict$ the integrated kinematic
shadow per Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}, the dynamical principle being the
central fact). Squaring:
$$dx_4^2 = (ic\,dt)^2 = i^2 c^2 dt^2 = -c^2 dt^2.$$ The factor of $i$ is
responsible for the minus sign: the perpendicularity marker
in the principle is the source of the signature flip from Euclidean to
Lorentzian. The $i$ here is case 7 of the twelve canonical
$i$-insertions (Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}, the metric-signature reading of the
McGucken-Principle $i$). Without the $i$, the squared
$x_{4}$-differential would be positive ($+c^2 dt^2$), giving a
positive-definite Euclidean signature. With the $i$, it is negative,
giving the Lorentzian timelike block.

**Step 2: Interval contribution from $x_{4}$.** Before the blocks are
summed, two structural facts are read off clause (P2) of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

*Block-diagonality (vanishing of the cross terms $g_{i4}$).* A non-zero
cross term $g_{i4}\,dx_i\,dx_4$ would single out a spatial direction
$\hat{e}_i$ preferred over the others in its pairing with the
$x_{4}$-advance. Clause (P2) states that the $x_{4}$-expansion at every
event is isotropic in the three spatial directions, so no spatial
direction is distinguished at the base event. Under the $SO(3)$ action
about $p$ the collection $(g_{i4})_{i=1,2,3}$ transforms as a vector,
and the only $SO(3)$-invariant vector in the defining three-dimensional
representation is the zero vector. Hence $g_{i4} = 0$ for
$i = 1, 2, 3$, and the metric on $M_{G}$ is block-diagonal in the
$(\text{spatial}) \oplus (x_{4})$ splitting.

*Metric form on $M_{G}$.* The spatial block is supplied by Step 3 below,
which fixes it to $h_{ij} = \delta_{ij}$ from the same clause (P2); the
$x_{4}$-block is supplied by Step 1. Neither block is assumed here.
Substituting Step 1 into the block-diagonal form:
$$ds^2 = dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2 + dx_4^2 = dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2 - c^2 dt^2.$$
This is the standard signature-$(-, +, +, +)$ Lorentzian line element,
with the $x_{4}$-block providing the negative-definite timelike
contribution. The block coefficient $g_{x_{4}x_{4}} = -1$ (or
equivalently $g_{00} = -c^2$ in units with explicit $c$) is fixed by the
squaring of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

**McGucken-internal source of Step 2**: C1 (rate clause, via the
squaring of Step 1); C2 (perpendicularity marker, supplying the sign);
C5 with clause (P2) (Sphere generation with isotropic expansion,
supplying block-diagonality). No metric structure on $M_{G}$ is assumed
prior to the principle: every entry of $g$ is produced by Steps 1--3.

**Step 3: Spatial block from spherical symmetry and the Sphere's flat
tangent-space structure.** The three spatial directions inherit their
metric from clause (P2) of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (spherical symmetry
of the $x_{4}$-expansion).

*Derivation.* The Sphere construction
(Definition [4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:sphere"}) states that the set of events reachable from a
base event $p$ by proper-time $\tau$ of $x_{4}$-advance is a 2-sphere of
radius $c\tau$ centred at $p$. Equip this 2-sphere with the round metric
induced by clause (P2) of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, which makes the
expansion isotropic in the three spatial directions. By the very
definition of *isotropy of the expansion at the base event*, the
linear-order metric on the tangent space $T_pM_{G}$ must be invariant
under $SO(3)$ rotations about $p$. The only $SO(3)$-invariant
positive-definite symmetric bilinear form on the spatial tangent space
$T_pM_{G}|_{\text{spatial}} \cong \mathbb{R}^3$ is, up to a positive
scale, the Euclidean inner product:
$$h_{ij} = \kappa\,\delta_{ij}, \qquad \kappa > 0.$$ (This is the
Schur-lemma-style uniqueness statement for invariant bilinear forms on
an irreducible $SO(3)$-representation, the defining 3-dim
representation.) The scale $\kappa$ is fixed by demanding that the
Sphere of $x_{4}$-proper-time $\tau$ has spatial radius $c\tau$ --- that
is, the equator at fixed $t$ has Euclidean length $2\pi c\tau$ as
measured by $h_{ij}$. Setting $\kappa = 1$ in coordinates where $x^j$
are the Cartesian rectangular coordinates on the spatial slice:
$$h_{ij} = \delta_{ij}, \qquad i, j = 1, 2, 3.$$ This is the flat
(Euclidean) spatial metric on $M_{G}$ in the absence of gravitational
matter content.

*In the presence of matter*, $h_{ij}$ acquires curvature through
Einstein's field equations (themselves derivable from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via
Theorem [14.1](#thm:mcgucken-adm-foliation){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:mcgucken-adm-foliation"} and the McGucken-GR chain --- GR
T1 through T24 of [@Syn-2026]). The flat $h_{ij} = \delta_{ij}$ is the
vacuum solution; the principle does not pin a curved spatial metric
without specifying matter content.

**Step 4: Combine into the full Lorentzian metric.** Combining Steps
1--3: $$g_{\mu\nu} = \mathrm{diag}(-1, +1, +1, +1),$$ in the natural
chart where $x^0 = ct$ and $x^j$ are spatial Cartesian coordinates. The
metric is Lorentzian with signature $(-, +, +, +)$, as claimed.

**Step 5: Global validity via clause (P1).** Clause (P1) of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ states that the principle takes the same form
at every event of $M_{G}$. Steps 1--4 therefore hold at every event,
establishing the Lorentzian metric structure globally on $M_{G}$ (in the
absence of gravitational matter content). The metric has the reading of the global form of the spacetime arena at every event, with
the role of a purely local approximation valid only in a tangent patch
replaced by the role of a structure that descends from
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (v) (global validity of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$) and therefore holds at every event of $M_{G}$
with identical coefficients.

**Step 6: Status of the derivation.** The complete proof is Theorem 8 of
[@Syn-2026]. The principle $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ together with the
spherical-symmetry clause forces the Lorentzian metric structure; no
additional postulates of relativity (constancy of $c$, principle of
relativity, etc.) are needed as independent inputs. The reverse
implication is the standard one: Lorentz invariance of physical laws and
constancy of $c$ are familiar consequences of special relativity. What
is new in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework is that Lorentz invariance is itself a
*theorem* (of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$), not a postulate. The principle
is $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; Lorentz invariance, the Minkowski metric,
the Lorentz group $SO^+(1,3)$, and the Poincaré group are its
algebraic-symmetry shadows. ◻
:::

The reverse implication is the standard one: Lorentz invariance of
physical laws and the constancy of $c$ are familiar consequences of
special relativity. What is new in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework is that
Lorentz invariance is itself a theorem, not a postulate. The principle
is $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; Lorentz invariance is its algebraic shadow.

::: {#lem:reverse-reading-equivalence .lemma}
**Lemma 4.7** (Reverse-reading equivalence: rest-frame four-velocity
normalization equals $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ in the Minkowski
coordinate $x_{4}= ict$; [@MG-Pointwise-2026] Lemma 2.0). *Let $M_{G}$
be the McGucken manifold equipped with the Lorentzian metric
$ds^2 = -c^2\,dt^2 + dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2$, regarded for the
purposes of this lemma as the given empirical starting point of special
relativity (the direction principle $\to$ metric being
established in
Theorem [4.6](#thm:mcp-to-lorentzian){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:mcp-to-lorentzian"}). For any massive particle at any
point $p \in M_{G}$, the rest-frame four-velocity normalization
$u^\mu u_\mu = -c^2$, expressed in the Minkowski coordinate
$x_{4}= ict$, reads
$$\frac{dx_4}{d\tau} \;=\; ic \qquad (\text{rest frame, with } d\tau = dt),
\label{eq:reverse-reading}$$ which is the principle
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}). The rest-frame Lorentzian
four-velocity normalization is a consequence of the McGucken Principle;
the normalization carries no Sphere, no orientation and no measure, and
the recovery runs from the Principle to the normalization. Here $x_{4}= ict$ the mere integrated kinematic shadow of the dynamical principle
(Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) and equivalently the Minkowski 1908
coordinate for the temporal direction.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has three steps.

**Step 1: Rest-frame collapse of the four-velocity normalization.** By
the standard relativistic definition of proper time for a massive
particle, the proper time $\tau$ along the worldline is defined by
$ds^2 = -c^2\,d\tau^2$ along the worldline (with $d\tau \geq 0$, $\tau$
increasing in the forward time direction). Substituting the Minkowski
line element $ds^2 = -c^2\,dt^2 + dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2$ along the
worldline and dividing by $dt^2$ yields the four-velocity normalization
$$-c^2 \left(\frac{d\tau}{dt}\right)^2 \;=\; -c^2 + \sum_{i=1}^3 \left(\frac{dx_i}{dt}\right)^2,$$
equivalently $u^\mu u_\mu = -c^2$ for the four-velocity
$u^\mu := dx^\mu/d\tau$. The physical content is that every massive
particle's four-velocity has invariant magnitude $c$, partitioned
between the temporal component $u^0 = c\,dt/d\tau$ and the spatial
components $u^i = dx^i/d\tau$.

In the rest frame of the particle at $p$, the spatial coordinate
velocities vanish: $dx_i/dt = 0$ for $i = 1, 2, 3$. The normalization
collapses to $(d\tau/dt)^2 = 1$; taking the positive root (proper time
advances forward), $d\tau/dt = +1$, so $d\tau = dt$ in the rest frame.

**Step 2: Expression in the Minkowski coordinate $x_{4}= ict$.**
Minkowski's 1908 coordinate substitution for the temporal direction is
$x_{4}:= ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}). In the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework,
$x_{4}= ict$ is the integrated kinematic shadow of the foundational dynamical principle
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ obtained by integrating with the anchor
$x_{4}(t=0) = 0$
(Theorem [4.6](#thm:mcp-to-lorentzian){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:mcp-to-lorentzian"} establishes the direction). In the present lemma, which establishes the reverse-reading
equivalence, $x_{4}= ict$ is taken as Minkowski's coordinate
substitution applied to the temporal direction, and the lemma's content
is that this substitution makes the rest-frame Lorentzian four-velocity
normalization read as $\frac{dx_4}{d\tau} = ic$.

The temporal four-velocity component expressed in the $x_{4}$ coordinate
is
$$\frac{dx_4}{d\tau} \;=\; \frac{d(ict)}{d\tau} \;=\; ic \cdot \frac{dt}{d\tau} \;=\; ic \cdot 1 \;=\; ic \qquad (\text{rest frame}),$$
using $dt/d\tau = 1$ established in Step 1. Since $dt = d\tau$ in the
rest frame, this is equivalently $dx_4/dt = ic$.

**Step 3: Frame-independence of the conclusion.** The lemma's content is
the equivalence: the principle $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and the
rest-frame Lorentzian four-velocity normalization (when the temporal
direction is expressed in the Minkowski coordinate $x_{4}= ict$) are the
same statement. In an arbitrary frame $F'$ with time coordinate $t'$ and
fourth coordinate $x_{4}' := ict'$, the same construction applies: the
rest-frame four-velocity normalization for any massive particle at any
event of $M_{G}$ --- in the rest frame of that particle, which is the
frame-invariant Lorentz-covariant statement --- reads
$\frac{dx_4}{d\tau} = ic$ at every event. The rest-frame Lorentzian four-velocity normalization at every point of $M_{G}$ is therefore the per-worldline reading of the principle $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, recovered wherever $d\tau = dt$. The direction of derivation is fixed by Remark [4.8](#rmk:bidirectional-equivalence){reference-type="ref" reference="rmk:bidirectional-equivalence"}: the principle states that $x_{4}$ expands at rate $c$ from every event of $M_{G}$, prior to and independent of any worldline crossing that event, while the normalization is built from a chosen worldline and records that worldline's share in the expansion. This lemma establishes the recovery of the principle in the rest frame; the normalization remains its integrated shadow, equivalently the differential form of $x_{4}= ict$. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:bidirectional-equivalence .remark}
*Remark 4.8* (Bidirectional equivalence and architectural priority).
Theorem [4.6](#thm:mcp-to-lorentzian){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:mcp-to-lorentzian"} (direction:
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic \Rightarrow$ Lorentzian metric, via integration
$x_{4}= ict$, squaring $dx_4^2 = -c^2\,dt^2$, and substitution into the
four-dimensional Euclidean line element) and
Lemma [4.7](#lem:reverse-reading-equivalence){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:reverse-reading-equivalence"} (reverse-reading direction:
Lorentzian metric $\Rightarrow$ $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ in the rest
frame, expressed in the Minkowski coordinate $x_{4}= ict$) together
establish that the rest-frame Lorentzian four-velocity normalization is
a consequence of the McGucken Principle, and that in the rest frame
($d\tau = dt$) the normalization reads back the rate $ic$.
The direction supplies the architectural priority ---
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the physical principle, and the
Lorentzian metric is its empirically anchored integrated kinematic shadow. The
reverse-reading direction supplies a mainstream-accessible entry point
--- any physicist who accepts the Lorentzian metric of special
relativity (empirically validated since 1905 by every accelerator
experiment, every GPS timing correction, every Michelson--Morley test,
every muon-decay measurement, every Hafele--Keating clock comparison)
accepts the McGucken Principle when the temporal direction is expressed
in the Minkowski 1908 coordinate $x_{4}= ict$. The two directions
together establish that there is no asymmetry of empirical content
between starting from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and starting from the
rest-frame Lorentzian four-velocity normalization: both produce
identical downstream derivations. What the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework adds to
the orthodox Lorentzian reading is the *physical interpretation* of
$x_{4}$ as the radius of a spherical wavefront actively expanding from
every spacetime event at velocity $c$, with the imaginary unit $i$
marking geometric perpendicularity to the spatial slice; the orthodox
reading treats $x_{4}= ict$ as a formal coordinate device, the McGucken
reading treats it as the integrated kinematic shadow of an active
geometric expansion. The mathematics is identical; the ontology of what
is happening in nature differs, and only the McGucken reading produces
the chain of theorems through which the quantum-mechanical formalism
is derived.
:::

### The McGucken Sphere $S$ and the wavefront $M^{+}_{p}(t)$

::: {#def:sphere .definition}
**Definition 4.9** (The McGucken Sphere). For a given source event
$p \in M_{G}$ and a time interval $\tau$, the *McGucken Sphere* centred
at $p$ is the 2-sphere
$$S_p(\tau) := \{q \in M_{G}: q\text{'s spatial distance from } p \text{ is } c\tau, \text{ at coordinate time } t_p + \tau\}.$$
:::

::: {#def:wavefront .definition}
**Definition 4.10** (The wavefront $M^{+}_{p}(t)$). For an event $p$ and
lab time $t > t_p$, the *wavefront* (alternatively, the *forward
iterated Sphere*) is
$$M^{+}_{p}(t) := \bigcup_{\substack{\text{continuous paths }\gamma \\ \text{from } p\text{ to events of}\\ \text{spatial radius } c(t-t_p)}} \gamma(t).$$
By spherical symmetry of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, $M^{+}_{p}(t)$ is a
2-sphere of radius $c(t - t_p)$ centred on $p$'s spatial location at
time $t$.
:::

::: {#prop:iter .proposition}
**Proposition 4.11** (Iterative composition of the Sphere via the
Huygens envelope, Proposition 3 of [@Syn-2026]). *For any event $p$ and
times $t_1 < t_2$, the wavefront $M^{+}_{p}(t_2)$ equals the outer
envelope (forward boundary) of the family of secondary wavefronts
originating from points of the intermediate wavefront:
$$M^{+}_{p}(t_2) \;=\; \partial_{\mathrm{out}}\!\biggl(\bigcup_{q \in M^{+}_{p}(t_1)}M^{+}_{q}(t_2 - t_1)\biggr).
\label{eq:huygens-envelope}$$ Concretely (writing $r_1 = c(t_1 - t_p)$
and $r_2 = c(t_2 - t_1)$, with $t_p$ the time of event $p$):
$$\begin{aligned}
\bigcup_{q \in M^{+}_{p}(t_1)}M^{+}_{q}(t_2 - t_1) &= \bigl\{x : |x - p_{\mathrm{spatial}}| \in [|r_1 - r_2|,\, r_1 + r_2]\bigr\}\quad\text{(annular shell)}, \\
M^{+}_{p}(t_2) &= \bigl\{x : |x - p_{\mathrm{spatial}}| = r_1 + r_2\bigr\}\quad\text{(outer boundary $=$ forward envelope)}.
\end{aligned}$$ Each point $q$ of $M^{+}_{p}(t_1)$ is the source of a
new secondary wavefront. The outer envelope of these secondary
wavefronts is the primary wavefront $M^{+}_{p}(t_2)$; the inner caustic
at radius $|r_1 - r_2|$ is excluded by the forward-orientation clause of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **Step 1: $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ has identical form at every
event.** By Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (i) (invariance --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content) and clause (v) (global validity ---
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event of $M_{G}$), the principle takes the same form
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at every event of $M_{G}$, with the same value
of $c$ and the same orientation. In particular, at every event
$q \in M^{+}_{p}(t_1)$ (any point of the wavefront at time $t_1$), the
principle holds at $q$ with the same value $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}(q) = ic$
as it holds at $p$. This is the physical, geometric fact that the fourth
dimension is expanding at the velocity of light $c$ in a spherically
symmetric manner from *every* event of $M_{G}$, with each event having
the role of a Sphere-source on equal footing with every other
event (no privileged source event exists; the role of a privileged
Sphere-source is replaced by the role of universal Sphere-sourcing at
every event of $M_{G}$ per
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i)+(v) jointly).

**Step 2: Each $q$ sources its own Sphere.** By the Sphere construction
of Definition [4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:sphere"} (the McGucken Sphere as the geometric locus of
$x_{4}$-coherent wavefronts originating from a given event), every event
$q$ where $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds is the source of a McGucken
Sphere $S_q$. Restricted to the parameter range
$\tau' \in [0, t_2 - t_1]$, this Sphere produces a wavefront
$M^{+}_{q}(t_2 - t_1)$: the set of events reachable from $q$ in proper
time $\tau' = t_2 - t_1$.

**Step 3: Spherical symmetry of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.** By
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (ii) (spherical symmetry --- the
expansion at any event is isotropic in the three spatial directions,
with the set of events reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a
2-sphere of radius $c\tau$ centred at $p$), the wavefront
$M^{+}_{q}(t_2 - t_1)$ is a 2-sphere of radius $c(t_2 - t_1)$ centred at
$q$'s spatial location. This is independent of the choice of $q$ on the
original wavefront $M^{+}_{p}(t_1)$: every secondary Sphere has the same
radius $c(t_2 - t_1)$, again because the $x_{4}$-expansion at every
event is identical by
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i)+(ii).

**Step 4: Union over secondary Spheres.** Take the union of all
secondary Spheres sourced at points of $M^{+}_{p}(t_1)$:
$$\bigcup_{q \in M^{+}_{p}(t_1)}M^{+}_{q}(t_2 - t_1).$$ This is the
locus of all events reachable from $p$ via a two-stage propagation:
first reaching $q$ on the wavefront $M^{+}_{p}(t_1)$ at time $t_1$, then
propagating from $q$ to a new event on the secondary wavefront at time
$t_2$.

**Step 5: Reconstruction via the Huygens envelope (explicit geometry).**
We show that the outer boundary of the union of secondary 2-spheres
equals the primary wavefront $M^{+}_{p}(t_2)$.

*Set-theoretic description of the union.* Fix coordinates with
$p_{\mathrm{spatial}}$ at the origin, write $r_1 = c(t_1 - t_p)$,
