$r_2 = c(t_2 - t_1)$. The intermediate wavefront $M^{+}_{p}(t_1)$ is the
2-sphere $|q| = r_1$. A point $x \in \mathbb{R}^3$ lies in the union
$\bigcup_q M^{+}_{q}(t_2-t_1)$ iff there exists a unit vector $\hat u$
with $|x - r_1\hat u| = r_2$. Parametrising by $\theta$ = angle between
$x$ and $\hat u$, $r = |x|$:
$$|x - r_1\hat u|^2 = r^2 + r_1^2 - 2 r r_1 \cos\theta = r_2^2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \cos\theta = \frac{r^2 + r_1^2 - r_2^2}{2 r r_1}.$$
A valid $\hat u$ exists iff $|\cos\theta| \le 1$, equivalently
$$(r - r_1)^2 \le r_2^2 \le (r + r_1)^2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad |r_1 - r_2| \le r \le r_1 + r_2.$$
The union is therefore the closed annular shell
$\{x : |r_1 - r_2| \le |x| \le r_1 + r_2\}$ (sympy-verified).

*Outer boundary identification.* The outer boundary of this shell is the
2-sphere $|x| = r_1 + r_2 = c(t_1 - t_p) + c(t_2 - t_1) = c(t_2 - t_p)$,
which is exactly $M^{+}_{p}(t_2)$ --- the primary wavefront at time
$t_2$ centred at $p$. Hence
$\partial_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(\bigcup_qM^{+}_{q}(t_2-t_1)\bigr) = M^{+}_{p}(t_2)$,
establishing
[\[eq:huygens-envelope\]](#eq:huygens-envelope){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:huygens-envelope"}.

*Exclusion of the backward caustic.* The inner boundary
$|x| = |r_1 - r_2|$ corresponds to events reached by the
backward-propagating secondary wavelet from $q$ (the part of
$M^{+}_{q}(t_2-t_1)$ on the side of $q$ closer to $p$). By
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iii) (monotonicity: the integral
curve of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is strictly monotonically increasing
in $t$), the forward-orientation $+ic$ at $q$ selects only the
forward-propagating wavelet; the backward caustic at radius
$|r_1 - r_2|$ is excluded by the same clause that fixes the arrow of
$x_{4}$-advance. Thus only the outer envelope $M^{+}_{p}(t_2)$ remains
as the physical primary wavefront.

The classical Huygens envelope principle (Huygens [@Huygens1690]: "every
point of a wavefront is itself the source of a secondary wavelet, and
the envelope of secondary wavelets is the next wavefront") is here
derived as a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ rather than postulated
--- the envelope-of-secondary-wavelets rule is forced by the
identical-form clause (P1), the spherical-symmetry clause (P2), and the
forward-orientation clause (P3) acting in conjunction.

**Step 6: Combining and the iterated-Huygens identity.** The two-stage
propagation from $p$ via $q \in M^{+}_{p}(t_1)$ to events at time $t_2$
has the forward envelope
$$\partial_{\mathrm{out}}\!\biggl(\bigcup_{q \in M^{+}_{p}(t_1)}M^{+}_{q}(t_2 - t_1)\biggr) \;=\; M^{+}_{p}(t_2),$$
reconstructing the one-stage propagation from $p$ to time $t_2$. Every
step of the derivation cites either a clause of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} (clauses (i), (ii), (iii), (v) all explicitly
invoked) or the Sphere construction of
Definition [4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:sphere"}; the elementary spherical-wave geometry of Step
5 is now an explicit calculation (sympy-verified), not a citation of
Huygens [@Huygens1690], although it reproduces precisely Huygens's
envelope rule. The complete proof, including the case of non-flat
spatial metric (where the envelope construction generalises to geodesic
balls of the induced spatial metric), is in [@Syn-2026] Proposition 3.
$\square$ ◻
:::

::: remark
*Remark 4.12*. Proposition [4.11](#prop:iter){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:iter"} is the content of Huygens' Principle as a theorem
of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The 1690 statement of Huygens
[@Huygens1690]---"every point of a wavefront is itself the source of a
secondary wavelet, and the envelope of secondary wavelets is the next
wavefront"---is here *the literal geometric content of the
spherical-symmetry clause of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$*. The textbook
tradition treats Huygens' Principle as a fact about wave propagation
requiring no further explanation. In the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework it is QM T1
(Theorem 60 of [@Syn-2026] along Algebraic Channel; Theorem 83 along Geometric Channel;
see Chapter [1](#ch:wave-equation){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:wave-equation"}).
:::

### Geometric Channel: the geometric-propagation axioms (QB1--QB7) {#sec:channelB}

Geometric Channel reads $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as a geometric-propagation
source: the rate $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is read as the source of
expanding McGucken Spheres at every event, with iterated Huygens
composition (Proposition [4.11](#prop:iter){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:iter"}) supplying the wave-propagation structure and the
Compton phase supplying the action-accumulation along proper time.

::: {#ax:QB1 .axiom}
**Axiom 4.20** (QB1: Sphere generation at every event). At every event
$p \in M_{G}$, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ generates an expanding McGucken
Sphere $S_p(\tau)$ of radius $c\tau$ in proper time $\tau$. Every
quantum entity at event $p$ rides the apex of this Sphere.
:::

::: {#ax:QB2 .axiom}
**Axiom 4.21** (QB2: Iterated Huygens composition). By
Proposition [4.11](#prop:iter){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:iter"}, every point of every wavefront $M^{+}_{p}(t)$ is
the source of a new secondary Sphere; the envelope of secondary Spheres
is the next-generation wavefront. Iterating at $N \to \infty$ short
times $\varepsilon = (t - t_p)/N$ generates the path space from $p$ to
events of $M^{+}_{p}(t)$.
:::

::: {#ax:QB3 .axiom}
**Axiom 4.22** (QB3: Iterated-Sphere path space). The set of continuous
paths $\gamma$ from $(x_A, t_A)$ to $(x_B, t_B)$ on $M_{G}$ is generated
as a sequence of secondary-wavelet picks: at each event of $\gamma$, the
next secondary wavelet selected is the one centred at the path's next
point. Each such path has measure-theoretic weight in the
iterated-Sphere construction; the totality of paths is the Wiener-type
path space underlying Feynman's formulation.
:::

::: {#ax:QB4 .axiom}
**Axiom 4.23** (QB4: Compton phase along proper time). For a massive
particle of rest mass $m$, the $x_{4}$-phase advances at rate
$\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ in the rest frame---the *Compton angular
frequency*. Each secondary wavelet from $x'$ to $x$ in time
$\varepsilon$ accumulates Compton phase $\exp(iS[\gamma]/\hbar)$ along
the path $\gamma$, with $S[\gamma]$ the classical action.
:::

::: {#ax:QB5 .axiom}
**Axiom 4.24** (QB5: Trotter-route path integral). The short-time
propagation kernel $\langle x | \hat{U}(\varepsilon) | x'\rangle$
decomposed into iterated McGucken-Sphere short-time steps, summed over
the path space of QB3 with the Compton-phase weights of QB4, yields the
Feynman path integral
$$K(x_B, t_B; x_A, t_A) = \int \mathcal{D}[\gamma]\,\exp(iS[\gamma]/\hbar).$$
:::

::: {#ax:QB6 .axiom}
**Axiom 4.25** (QB6: Short-time Gaussian closure). The short-time kernel
is a Gaussian propagator
$K(x', x; \varepsilon) \sim e^{im(x'-x)^2/2\hbar\varepsilon}$ to leading
order in $\varepsilon$. Expansion to first order in $\varepsilon$ yields
the Schrödinger equation $i\hbar\,\partial_t\psi = \hat{H}\psi$. The
full derivation is the eight-step argument of
Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT7"}.
:::

::: {#ax:QB7 .axiom}
**Axiom 4.26** (QB7: McGucken Sphere $SO(3)$-equivariant measure). The
wavefront $M^{+}_{p}(t)$ carries a unique $SO(3)$-equivariant
probability measure (the spherical Haar measure normalized to unit
total). This is the Geometric Channel route to the Born rule.
:::

### Algebraic Channel: the algebraic-symmetry axioms (QA1--QA7) {#sec:channelA}

The McGucken Principle has two distinct readings, called
*channels*, each a complete derivation chain to all 23 QM theorems. The
two chains share no intermediate machinery beyond
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and the final equation of each theorem. Algebraic
Channel reads $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as an algebraic-symmetry source: the
rate $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is read through the lens of Stone's
theorem, with the $i$ supplying the unitary-generator structure, the
universal rate supplying time-translation invariance, and the spherical
symmetry supplying spatial-rotation invariance.

The Algebraic Channel axioms are seven readings of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, each labeled and each used as needed in
proofs:

::: {#ax:QA1 .axiom}
**Axiom 4.13** (QA1: Lorentz covariance). $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ has
the same form in every Lorentz frame. The Poincaré group
$\widetilde{\text{ISO}}(1,3)$ acts on $M_{G}$ as a group of isometries.
:::

::: {#ax:QA2 .axiom}
**Axiom 4.14** (QA2: Stone's theorem applicability). Each one-parameter
symmetry subgroup of $M_{G}$ (time translation, spatial translation,
rotation, boost) acts as a strongly continuous unitary group on the
Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ derived from $M_{G}$, and Stone's theorem
(Theorem [3.6](#thm:stone){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:stone"})
supplies a unique self-adjoint generator for each.
:::

::: {#ax:QA3 .axiom}
**Axiom 4.15** (QA3: Canonical commutator). The self-adjoint generators
$\hat{q}^j$ of spatial position-multiplication and $\hat{p}_j$ of
spatial translation satisfy the canonical commutation relation
$$[\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k] = i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\mathbb{1}.$$ This is
derived in Theorem [10.5](#thm:QMT10-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT10-channelA"} below; it is stated here as an
axiom-label for use in subsequent Algebraic Channel proofs.
:::

::: {#ax:QA4 .axiom}
**Axiom 4.16** (QA4: Stone--von Neumann uniqueness). The pair
$(\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k)$ of QA3 admits, up to unitary equivalence, a
unique irreducible Hilbert-space representation: the Schrödinger
representation on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ given by
$(\hat{q}^j\psi)(x) = x^j\psi(x)$ and
$(\hat{p}_k\psi)(x) = -i\hbar\,\partial_{x^k}\psi(x)$. This is
Theorem [3.7](#thm:stoneVN){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:stoneVN"}.
:::

::: {#ax:QA5 .axiom}
**Axiom 4.17** (QA5: Projection-valued measurement). Coupling of
$\mathcal{H}$ to a classical measuring device with a finite set of
pointer states $\{o_n\}$ proceeds via a self-adjoint observable
$\hat{O}$ with spectral decomposition $\hat{O} = \sum_n o_n\,\hat{P}_n$,
with $\hat{P}_n$ orthogonal projectors. The probability of the outcome
$o_n$ on initial state $\lvert \psi \rangle$ is
$P(o_n) = \|\hat{P}_n\lvert \psi \rangle\|^2$.

This is the Algebraic Channel reading of the Born rule, derived in
Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"}.
:::

::: {#ax:QA6 .axiom}
**Axiom 4.18** (QA6: Wigner classification). Particle states are labeled
by the Casimir invariants of the universal cover of the Poincaré group:
mass-squared $m^2 = P^\mu P_\mu / c^2$ and spin
$s \in \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$. This is
Theorem [3.8](#thm:wigner){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:wigner"}.
:::

::: {#ax:QA7 .axiom}
**Axiom 4.19** (QA7: $U(1)$ gauge symmetry and Noether's theorem). The
global $U(1)$ phase invariance $\psi \to e^{i\alpha}\psi$
($\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$) of the matter wave equation yields, by
Noether's theorem, a conserved current
$j^\mu = (i\hbar/2m)(\psi^* \partial^\mu \psi - \psi\,\partial^\mu \psi^*)$.
Local $U(1)$ gauge invariance $\alpha \to \alpha(x)$ requires the
covariant derivative $D_\mu = \partial_\mu + i(q/\hbar)A_\mu$, supplying
minimal coupling to the electromagnetic field $A_\mu$.
:::

### The Hamiltonian and Lagrangian route propositions (H.1--H.5 and L.1--L.6) {#sec:HL-architecture}

The Geometric Channel and Algebraic Channel axiom sets above organize the full theorem
chain. The minimal route to the canonical commutator
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$, the Feynman path integral
$K = \int\mathcal{D}[\gamma]\,e^{iS/\hbar}$, and the Schrödinger
equation $i\hbar\,\partial_t\psi = \hat{H}\psi$ can be stated as eleven
propositions: five for the Hamiltonian operator route (H.1--H.5) and six
for the Lagrangian path-integral route (L.1--L.6). These eleven
propositions are the formal scaffolding of [@MG-Foundations-2026]; we
list them here as a route map for the proofs of Part II.

**Hamiltonian route (Algebraic Channel).**

-   *Minkowski metric from $x_{4}= ict$.* Integrating
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ along the timelike axis gives $x_{4}= ict$;
    squaring forces the timelike interval $dx_4^2 = -c^2 dt^2$, and the
    signature-$(-,+,+,+)$ Lorentzian metric is established
    (Theorem [4.6](#thm:mcp-to-lorentzian){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:mcp-to-lorentzian"}).

-   *Momentum operator from Stone.* Translation invariance of
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ + Stone's theorem
    (Theorem [3.6](#thm:stone){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:stone"}) supplies a self-adjoint generator $\hat{p}$
    of spatial translations.

-   *Configuration representation.* On $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$,
    $\hat{p}$ acts as $-i\hbar\,\partial_q$.

-   *Canonical commutation by direct computation.*
    $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}]\psi = i\hbar\psi$ for all $\psi$ in the Schwartz
    domain (Theorem [10.5](#thm:QMT10-channelA){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT10-channelA"}, Algebraic Channel).

-   *Stone--von Neumann closure.* Uniqueness up to unitary equivalence
    (Theorem [3.7](#thm:stoneVN){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:stoneVN"}).

**Lagrangian route (Geometric Channel).**

-   *Huygens' principle from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.* The
    spherical-symmetry clause of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
    (Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
    reference="postulate:mcp"}, clause ii) generates a McGucken Sphere
    at every event; iterated, this is precisely Huygens' Principle
    (Proposition [4.11](#prop:iter){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:iter"}).

-   *Path space from iteration.* Iterated Huygens secondary-wavelet
    picks at $N \to \infty$ short times generate the continuous path
    space from one event to another (QB3).

-   *Compton phase per path.* Each path accumulates $x_4$-phase at rate
    $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ in the rest frame (QB4); in the
    non-relativistic limit, the phase per path is
    $\exp(iS[\gamma]/\hbar)$ with $S[\gamma]$ the classical action.

-   *Feynman path integral.* Summing the phase-weighted paths gives
    $K(x_B, t_B; x_A, t_A) = \int \mathcal{D}[\gamma]\,e^{iS[\gamma]/\hbar}$
    (Theorem [15.1](#thm:QMT15){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT15"}, Geometric Channel).

-   *Schrödinger equation from short-time propagator.* Gaussian
    expansion of the short-time kernel to first order in $\varepsilon$
    yields $i\hbar\,\partial_t\psi = \hat{H}\psi$
    (Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT7"}, Geometric Channel, eight-step argument).

-   *$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ (canonical commutation relation,
    $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$) recovered.* Identifying
    $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\,\partial_q$ from the Schrödinger representation
    of L.5 and computing $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}]\psi$ directly reproduces
    $i\hbar\,\psi$, the same $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ established
    at H.4 along the operator route.

The two routes meet only at the principle $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(entered at H.1 and L.1) and at the final equations of physical
interest. They share no intermediate machinery; this is the formal
content of the derivational-disjointness theorem below.

### The derivational-disjointness theorem

The defining feature of the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework---the property
that distinguishes it from every other foundational physics program of
the present era---is that Geometric Channel and Algebraic Channel share no intermediate
machinery beyond $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and the final equation of each
theorem.

::: {#thm:disjointness .theorem}
**Theorem 4.27** (Derivational disjointness, Theorem 125 of [@Syn-2026];
formally established in [@MG-Foundations-2026]). *Let $T$ be any of the
23 QM theorems QM T1--T23. Let $\Pi^A(T)$ be the set of
intermediate-machinery items invoked in the Algebraic Channel derivation of $T$,
and $\Pi^B(T)$ the corresponding set for Geometric Channel. Then
$$\Pi^A(T) \cap \Pi^B(T) = \{(\mathrm{McP}), \text{final equation of }T\}.$$
That is, the two derivations agree only on the principle they start from
and the equation they arrive at; all intermediate steps are disjoint.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof is by explicit inspection of the Algebraic Channel
intermediate machinery $\Pi^A(T)$ and the Geometric Channel intermediate
machinery $\Pi^B(T)$ for each theorem $T \in \{$QM T1, $\ldots$,
QM T23$\}$.

**Step 1: Algebraic Channel intermediate machinery.** Across the 23 QM theorems,
Algebraic Channel intermediate steps are drawn from the catalogue
$$\begin{aligned}
\Pi^A_{\mathrm{cat}} = \{&\text{Stone's theorem on one-parameter unitary groups}, \\
&\text{Stone--von Neumann uniqueness of the $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ representation}, \\
&\text{Wigner classification of irreducible Poincar\'e representations}, \\
&\text{Cauchy functional equation } f(a+b) = f(a)f(b), \\
&\text{Robertson--Schr\"odinger uncertainty inequality}, \\
&\text{spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators}, \\
&\text{Clifford algebra } \mathrm{Cl}(1,3) \text{ minimal representation}, \\
&\text{$SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ double cover of } SO^+(1,3)\}.
\end{aligned}$$ Each Algebraic Channel derivation $T \mapsto \Pi^A(T)$ uses a
subset of $\Pi^A_{\mathrm{cat}}$; verified across all 23 theorems in
Chapters [1](#ch:wave-equation){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:wave-equation"}--[21](#ch:antimatter){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:antimatter"}.

**Step 2: Geometric Channel intermediate machinery.** Across the 23 QM theorems,
Geometric Channel intermediate steps are drawn from the catalogue
$$\begin{aligned}
\Pi^B_{\mathrm{cat}} = \{&\text{McGucken Sphere construction (QB1)}, \\
&\text{Huygens iteration on the Sphere (QB2)}, \\
&\text{iterated-Sphere path space (QB3)}, \\
&\text{Compton phase per wavelet (QB4)}, \\
&\text{Sphere kernel and Trotter decomposition (QB5)}, \\
&\text{Gaussian Sphere normalisation (QB6)}, \\
&\text{Sphere Haar measure under } SO(3), \\
&\text{matter orientation condition (M) and spinor bundle on Sphere}\}.
\end{aligned}$$ Each Geometric Channel derivation $T \mapsto \Pi^B(T)$ uses a
subset of $\Pi^B_{\mathrm{cat}}$; verified across all 23 theorems.

**Step 3: Disjointness of the catalogues.** We verify
$\Pi^A_{\mathrm{cat}} \cap \Pi^B_{\mathrm{cat}} = \emptyset$ by direct
element-wise comparison. Stone's theorem (a statement about unitary
one-parameter groups on Hilbert space) is not a member of
$\Pi^B_{\mathrm{cat}}$ (whose elements are Sphere-geometric constructs).
Stone--von Neumann uniqueness, Wigner classification, the Cauchy
functional equation, the Robertson--Schrödinger inequality, the spectral
theorem, the Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$, and the
$SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ double cover are likewise not members of
$\Pi^B_{\mathrm{cat}}$. Conversely, the McGucken Sphere, Huygens
iteration, the iterated-Sphere path space, the Compton phase, the Sphere
kernel/Trotter decomposition, the Gaussian Sphere normalisation, the
Sphere Haar measure, and the spinor bundle on the Sphere are not members
of $\Pi^A_{\mathrm{cat}}$. Therefore
$\Pi^A_{\mathrm{cat}} \cap \Pi^B_{\mathrm{cat}} = \emptyset$.

**Step 4: Restriction to any single theorem $T$.** For any
$T \in \{$QM T1, $\ldots$, QM T23$\}$,
$\Pi^A(T) \subseteq \Pi^A_{\mathrm{cat}}$ and
$\Pi^B(T) \subseteq \Pi^B_{\mathrm{cat}}$. By Step 3,
$\Pi^A(T) \cap \Pi^B(T) \subseteq \Pi^A_{\mathrm{cat}} \cap \Pi^B_{\mathrm{cat}} = \emptyset$
among the intermediate-machinery items. However, both $\Pi^A(T)$ and
$\Pi^B(T)$ include the source-principle $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(entered at H.1 and L.1 respectively) and the final equation of $T$
(reached as the conclusion of each channel). These two elements lie in
the intersection by construction, giving
$$\Pi^A(T) \cap \Pi^B(T) = \{(\mathrm{McP}),\,\text{final equation of }T\}.$$

**Step 5: Verification across all 23 theorems.** The explicit Geometric Channel
and Algebraic Channel derivations in
Chapters [1](#ch:wave-equation){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:wave-equation"}--[21](#ch:antimatter){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:antimatter"} (Part II) carry out the inspection for each
$T \in \{$QM T1, $\ldots$, QM T23$\}$. The derivational-disjointness
property holds uniformly across all 23 theorems.

This is the formal content of the derivational-disjointness theorem, which
has no analogue in any of the textbook traditions (Sakurai, Shankar,
Cohen-Tannoudji, Griffiths, Weinberg) reviewed in
Chapter [1](#ch:diagnosis){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:diagnosis"}. ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:dual-channel-content .remark}
*Remark 4.28* (The dual-channel content of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$).
Why does $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ have this property while no other
proposed principle does? The geometric statement
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ simultaneously specifies two logically distinct
pieces of information: an *algebraic-symmetry content* (the invariance
of $x_{4}$'s advance under time translation, space translation,
rotation, and Lorentz boost---the input that drives the Hamiltonian
route through Stone's theorem and Noether's theorem) and a
*geometric-propagation content* (the spherical symmetry of $x_{4}$'s
expansion from every spacetime point---the input that drives the
Lagrangian route through Huygens' principle and path summation). No
prior candidate foundation has both channels: classical symplectic
geometry has only the algebraic-symmetry channel; classical Lagrangian
variational mechanics has only the propagation-variational channel;
stochastic dynamics has a diffusion-propagation channel but no symmetry
content; Hestenes's spacetime algebra has static geometric content but
no dynamical principle. $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the first physical
principle whose one-line statement contains both channels
simultaneously: "advancing at rate $ic$ from every point" is the
algebraic-symmetry content (a uniform rate, invariant under isometries),
and "spherically symmetrically about each point" is the
geometric-propagation content (a wavefront structure inheriting Huygens'
secondary-wavelet property). The dual-channel content has the reading of an intrinsic feature of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ that makes
both quantum formulations theorems of one fact, with the role of a
verbal coincidence in how the principle is described replaced by the
role of a derived property of the principle's geometric
content. See [@MG-Foundations-2026] §V for the formal development and
§VI for a comparison with fifteen prior programs
(Nelson's stochastic mechanics, geometric quantization, Hestenes
geometric algebra, Adler trace dynamics, Bohmian mechanics, 't Hooft
cellular automata, Lindgren--Liukkonen stochastic optimal control, loop
quantum gravity, twistor strings, Schuller constructive gravity, Woit
Euclidean twistor unification, etc.), each of which derives or
reinterprets one of the two formulations but not both from a single
geometric spacetime principle.
:::

::: remark
*Remark 4.29* (Why double-derivation is the highest evidentiary form).
The simplest analogue is in arithmetic: that $1 + 1 = 2$ can be derived
from the Peano axioms via the successor construction, and independently
from set theory via the cardinality of the union of singletons, is two
derivations of the same equation along disjoint routes. The agreement of
the two routes has the reading of positive evidence that the
equation tracks a fact about the structure of natural numbers, with the
role of a redundant repetition of one calculation replaced by the role
of an independent corroboration along a disjoint derivation chain. The
same logic applies here: the agreement of Geometric Channel and Algebraic Channel on the
Schrödinger equation, on the canonical commutator, on the Born rule, on
the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, on the Dirac equation, and on the
path integral, is positive evidence that these equations track the
physical fact $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, with the role of an artifact of
one mathematical apparatus replaced by the role of a fact independently
corroborated along two derivationally disjoint derivation routes.
:::

::: {#rmk:hilbert-theorem .remark}
*Remark 4.30* (Hilbert space itself as a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). A still deeper point: the Hilbert
space $\mathcal{H}$ on which the Algebraic-Channel operator algebra acts is
itself a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, not an axiom of quantum
mechanics. The May 8, 2026 paper [@MG-Hilbert-2026] establishes a chain
of four Grade-1 theorems forced by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ alone:

-   the Lorentzian arena $M_{1,3}$ is generated by substituting
    $dx_4 = ic\,dt$ into the Euclidean line element (Theorem 3.1,
    Algebraic Channel);

-   the complex-amplitude algebra $\mathbb{C}$ is forced by the slice
    projection $\sigma$ together with the perpendicularity-marker
    squaring rule $J^2 = -1$ (Theorem 4.5, both channels jointly);

-   the inner product $\langle\phi, \psi\rangle = \int \phi^*\psi\,d^3x$
    is the forward--conjugate $x_4$-overlap (Theorem 5.3, Geometric Channel);

-   completeness $\mathcal{H}\cong L^2(M_{1,3}, d\mu_M)$ is forced by
    the continuity of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$'s flow at the constant
    rate $ic$ (Theorem 5.5, Geometric Channel).

The twenty-three prior derivation programmes that have attempted to
characterise $\mathcal{H}$ within QM (catalogued in
§[9.6](#sec:hilbert-prior){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:hilbert-prior"}, from von Neumann 1932 and Mackey 1963
through Hardy 2001, Chiribella--D'Ariano--Perinotti 2011,
Masanes--Müller 2011 and Dakić--Brukner 2011 to
Selby--Scandolo--Coecke 2021 and Barandes 2023/2025) all presuppose the complex
Hilbert-space structure they sought to derive. The McGucken four-theorem
chain is the first that operates upstream of $\mathcal{H}$ itself. The
status of $\mathcal{H}$ in this book is therefore not that of
mathematical scaffolding (as in
Chapter [3](#ch:math){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:math"}) but
that of a derived structure: the operator-algebraic side of the
dual-channel architecture acts on a space that is itself a theorem of
the principle.
:::

### Audit conventions for the rest of the book

Each theorem in the chapters that follow is proved twice when a Algebraic
Channel and Geometric Channel derivation both exist in [@Syn-2026]. The format for
each pair is:

1.  Statement of the theorem (with synthesis-paper Theorem number).

2.  Algebraic Channel derivation, tagged by the QA axioms invoked.

3.  Geometric Channel derivation, tagged by the QB axioms invoked.

4.  Audit: explicit list of intermediate machinery invoked in each
    channel, with a check that no item appears in both lists beyond
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and the final equation (so that
    Theorem [4.27](#thm:disjointness){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:disjointness"} applies).

5.  Empirical anchor: the experimental result(s) that confirm the
    equation.

This four-part format is the template that distinguishes the
McGucken treatment from the textbook tradition. In the textbook
treatment, each result is stated, derived along one route, and
(sometimes) connected to experiment. In the McGucken treatment, each
result is stated, derived along two derivationally disjoint routes,
audited for the disjointness, and connected to experiment. The audit is
what closes the chain.

### The Grade-1 audit standard {#sec:grade1-standard}

A further audit standard, formalised in [@MG-Hilbert-2026] and
[@MG-Ontic-2026] and applied throughout this book, classifies every
theorem by the essential role of its inputs:

::: {#def:theorem-grade .definition}
**Definition 4.31** (Grade of a theorem). For a theorem $T$ in this
book, let $\Pi(T)$ be the set of intermediate-machinery items used in
its derivation. Each item $\pi \in \Pi(T)$ is one of:

-   the McGucken Principle $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$;

-   an Algebraic Channel axiom QA1--QA7 (each a theorem of
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$);

-   a Geometric Channel axiom QB1--QB7 (each a theorem of
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$);

-   an explicitly labelled assumption $A_1, A_2, \ldots$
    (standard physics or mathematics imported as an input);

-   a previously derived McGucken-corpus theorem (cited with key);

-   an elementary tool of real or complex analysis (Lebesgue integral,
    Cauchy sequence, elementary linear algebra) used in a confirmatory
    rather than essential role.

The theorem $T$ is graded:

Grade 1.

:   $T$ is forced by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ alone (possibly via its
    Geometric Channel and Algebraic Channel axiomatic shadows), with no external
    mathematical theorem essential in any proof. Frobenius-type
    classification theorems, Stone's theorem, Stone--von Neumann
    uniqueness, Robertson--Schrödinger, Cauchy--Schwarz on Hilbert
    space, and Riesz--Fischer may appear in confirmatory roles (*i.e.*,
    they reach the same conclusion by abstract analysis but the McGucken
    proof does not invoke them as essential premises).

Grade 2.

:   $T$ requires $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ together with one or more
    explicitly labelled assumptions $A_1, A_2, \ldots$ which
    are standard physics or mathematics imported as inputs (*e.g.*, that
    the space of states is a separable Hilbert space, or that operators
    are bounded on a dense domain).

Grade 3.

:   $T$ requires $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ together with an external
    mathematical framework as essential input (*e.g.*, the Wigner
    classification of unitary representations of the Poincaré group, or
    the symmetric-product orbifold counting of bosonic worldsheet
    modes).

Grade C (*Coupling-Grade*).

:   $T$ requires $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ together with an explicitly
    labelled matter-coupling proposal $\mathrm{Cp}$ --- a specific
    ansatz for how matter interacts with $x_{4}$-expansion. The coupling
    proposal occupies the same methodological slot as the Lorentz force
    law beyond Maxwell's field equations or the geodesic equation beyond
    Einstein's field equations: a separate physical input beyond the
    postulate. Coupling-Grade theorems are falsifiable
    through any experimental contradiction of the specific coupling
    form, while leaving $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and the forced theorems
    QM T1--T21 and T23 intact.
:::

::: {#def:postulate-plus-coupling .definition}
**Definition 4.32** (Postulate plus matter coupling:
methodological architecture; cf. [@MG-Compton-2026] §1). A complete
physical theory consists of two distinct components:

1.  A *postulate* specifying the geometric or algebraic
    content of the theory's arena (the spacetime structure, the field
    structure, or the principle from which dynamics descend);

2.  A *matter-coupling specification* specifying how the physical matter
    content of the theory responds to the postulate.

The two components are methodologically independent: the postulate alone does not fix the matter coupling, and the matter
coupling alone has no content without the postulate. The
complete theory is the pair $(\mathrm{SP}, \mathrm{MC})$.

The methodology applies uniformly across the foundational frameworks of
theoretical physics:

-   **Maxwell electrodynamics.** SP: Maxwell's field equations
    $\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu} = J^\nu/c$,
    $\partial_{[\mu}F_{\nu\rho]} = 0$ describing the electromagnetic
    field. MC: the Lorentz force law
    $\mathbf{F} = q(\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B})$ describing
    how charged matter responds to the field. Maxwell's equations alone
    do not fix the Lorentz force law; the Lorentz force law alone has no
    content without Maxwell's equations.

-   **General relativity.** SP: Einstein field equations
    $G_{\mu\nu} + \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = 8\pi G T_{\mu\nu}/c^4$ describing
    the curvature of spacetime. MC: the geodesic equation
    $\ddot x^\mu + \Gamma^\mu_{\nu\rho}\dot x^\nu\dot x^\rho = 0$
    describing how test matter moves in that curvature. The field
    equations alone do not fix the geodesic equation; the geodesic
    equation alone has no content without the curvature it geodesics in.

-   **McGucken framework.** SP: the McGucken Principle
    $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ describing the structure of the fourth
    dimension (Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
    reference="postulate:mcp"}). MC: the Compton coupling
    $H_{\mathrm{mod}}(\tau) = \varepsilon mc^2\cos(\Omega\tau)$ proposed
    by [@MG-Compton-2026]
    (Theorem [22.1](#thm:QMT22){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT22"}), specifying how matter at rest-mass $m$
    interacts with $x_{4}$-expansion through its Compton frequency. The
    McGucken Principle alone does not fix the Compton coupling; the
    coupling is a separate physical input.
:::

::: {#rmk:methodological-status-theorems .remark}
*Remark 4.33* (Methodological status of the McGucken-derived theorems).
With Definitions [4.31](#def:theorem-grade){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:theorem-grade"}
and [4.32](#def:postulate-plus-coupling){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:postulate-plus-coupling"} in place, the methodological
status of the 23 QM theorems and the broader results of this
book becomes precise:

-   *Forced theorems (Grade 1 + 2 + 3).* QM T1--T21 and QM T23 are
    derived from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as the postulate
    (SP) alone, with no matter-coupling input required beyond the
    universal-rate clause of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. Their proofs
    invoke only $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, its Algebraic and Geometric Channel shadows,
    standard physics/mathematics inputs, and external mathematical
    frameworks (where Grade-3) as essential. The 22 forced theorems
    are falsifiable through any experimental contradiction of standard
    QM phenomenology, but the postulate
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ itself remains intact unless the QM
    phenomenology is itself falsified.

-   *Coupling-Grade theorem.* QM T22 (Compton Diffusion Coefficient,
    Theorem [22.1](#thm:QMT22){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT22"}) requires both $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and
    the specific Compton-coupling proposal of [@MG-Compton-2026] as
    joint inputs. The theorem is falsifiable through experimental
    contradiction of the specific $(\varepsilon, \Omega)$
    Compton-coupling form, leaving $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and the 22
    forced theorems intact.

The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework is therefore falsifiable in two distinct senses, and the experimental tests of the two senses are
different: tests of the forced theorems are tests of standard QM
phenomenology, while tests of QM T22 are tests of zero-temperature
residual diffusion, cross-species mass-independence, and
Compton-frequency spectroscopic sidebands
(Theorem [22.1](#thm:QMT22){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT22"},
Section [22.7](#sec:compton-experimental-tests){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:compton-experimental-tests"}).
:::

::: {#lem:matter-coupling-constraints .lemma}
**Lemma 4.34** (Constraints on any McGucken-compatible matter
coupling; cf. [@MG-Compton-2026] §2). *Any matter-coupling proposal
$\mathrm{Cp}$ compatible with the McGucken Principle
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ must satisfy three constraints:*

1.  **Compton-anchored scaling.* The coupling strength scales with the
    rest energy $mc^2$ of the matter species, since the rest-frame phase
    accumulation rate is the Compton angular frequency
    $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$
    (Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT4"}); this is the only natural scale at which
    matter at rest couples to $x_{4}$-expansion.*

2.  **Species-universality of $x_{4}$-parameters.* Any parameters of the
    coupling that are properties of $x_{4}$'s expansion rather than of
    the matter species (e.g., a modulation amplitude $\varepsilon$ and a
    characteristic frequency $\Omega$) must be *universal* across matter
    species. This is the content of
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$'s universal-rate clause (P3): the principle
    holds at every event with the same rate $|\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}| = c$
    regardless of which matter species is present.*

3.  **Proper-time expression.* The coupling is naturally expressed in
    terms of the matter species' proper time $\tau$, which is the
    geometric reading of the four-velocity-budget structure
    (Lemma [4.2](#lem:four-velocity-budget){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:four-velocity-budget"}): at rest, the entire
    four-velocity budget is directed into $x_{4}$-advance, identifying
    coordinate time $t$ with proper time $\tau$.*

*The Compton coupling
$H_{\mathrm{mod}}(\tau) = \varepsilon mc^2\cos(\Omega\tau)$ of
[@MG-Compton-2026] satisfies all three constraints by construction.
Alternative coupling proposals must also satisfy (C1)--(C3); failure of
any constraint indicates a coupling proposal incompatible with the
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework content.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has six steps.

**Step 1: Compton frequency as the natural coupling scale.** By
Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT4"} (the
Compton coupling theorem, Algebraic Channel and B), a particle of rest mass $m$
at spatial rest has its wavefunction oscillating at angular frequency
$\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ in its rest frame. This is the unique frequency
in the rest frame of a massive particle that does not depend on its
spatial momentum or external fields; it is the natural "clock" of the
particle, intrinsic to its mass content. No other rest-frame oscillator
with universal applicability exists.

**Step 2: Compton-anchored scaling (C1) from the rest-frame phase
structure.** The constraint (C1) that the coupling strength carries the
factor $mc^2$ (equivalently $\hbar\omega_C$) is a *principle of
intrinsic-scale economy*: the only rest-frame scale derived entirely
from the matter species' McGucken-Sphere structure is the Compton energy
$mc^2$, equal to $\hbar\omega_C$. Any alternative rest-frame energy
scale must introduce an external structure not present in the matter
species' Sphere description --- candidates include:

-   the Planck mass $M_P = \sqrt{\hbar c/G_N}$, which introduces $G_N$
    (an external scale not derived from the McGucken Principle of the
    matter species alone);

-   the electroweak scale $v_{\mathrm{EW}}$, which introduces the Higgs
    sector (external structure beyond the matter species considered);

-   atomic transition frequencies $\omega_{\mathrm{atomic}}$, which
    depend on the host atom and the electronic state (external to the
    bare species);

-   a wholly free parameter $E_*$, fitted to data (admissible only if no
    intrinsic scale is available, which is not our situation).

By the economy reading of the McGucken Principle ---
couplings should reference only the matter species' intrinsic structure
unless an external scale is explicitly invoked --- the natural scale for
$H_{\mathrm{mod}}$ is $mc^2$. This is a methodological principle, not a
no-alternatives theorem: alternative couplings using external scales
*exist* but they introduce additional inputs beyond
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and so go beyond the minimal
McGucken-compatible class. The constraint (C1), strictly read, is
therefore: *within the class of couplings that reference only the
species' intrinsic Sphere structure, the strength scales as $mc^2$.*

(An empirical test of (C1) is the cross-species mass-independence
prediction discussed in Step 6: alternative couplings violating (C1)
would predict species-dependent spatial diffusion, which experiment can
probe.)

**Step 3: Species-universality (C2) forced by clause P3 of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.** By the McGucken Principle
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, clause P3), the rate
$|\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}| = c$ is the same at every event of $M_{G}$,
regardless of which matter species (electron, proton, neutron, photon)
is present. The $x_{4}$-expansion's parameters --- including any
modulation amplitude $\varepsilon$ or characteristic frequency $\Omega$
--- are properties of $x_{4}$ itself, not properties of the matter
species. Any matter coupling that reads species-dependent values for
these parameters would violate the universal-rate clause, contradicting
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. Therefore (C2) is forced.

**Step 4: Proper-time expression (C3) forced by the four-velocity-budget
structure.** By
Lemma [4.2](#lem:four-velocity-budget){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:four-velocity-budget"} (the four-velocity budget at
rest), a particle at spatial rest directs its entire four-velocity
budget into $x_{4}$-advance at rate $c$. The integration parameter along
the particle's worldline that the principle's $x_{4}$-coordinate
advances against is the proper time $\tau = t$ at rest,
$\tau = t/\gamma_{\mathrm{Lor}}$ in motion. The coupling, expressed in
this natural parameter, automatically satisfies Lorentz covariance under
boosts of the particle's frame: the proper-time argument of the
modulation function is Lorentz-invariant. Coupling expressions in
coordinate time $t$ (which is frame-dependent) would not be
Lorentz-covariant in general.

**Step 5: Verification that the Compton coupling satisfies (C1)--(C3).**
The proposal $H_{\mathrm{mod}}(\tau) = \varepsilon mc^2\cos(\Omega\tau)$
of [@MG-Compton-2026] satisfies:

-   (C1): the coupling Hamiltonian carries the factor $mc^2$, the rest
    energy of the species. The strength is therefore Compton-anchored;

-   (C2): the parameters $\varepsilon$ (dimensionless) and $\Omega$
    (frequency) are universal --- species-independent properties of the
    $x_{4}$-expansion modulation;

-   (C3): the cosine argument is the proper time $\tau$, which reduces
    to coordinate time at rest by the four-velocity-budget structure.

All three constraints are satisfied by construction.

**Step 6: Empirical implications of (C1)--(C3).** The constraints (C1)--(C3) make sharp empirical predictions for any
McGucken-compatible matter coupling:

-   From (C1) ($\propto mc^2$) combined with mobility $\propto 1/m$: the
    spatial-diffusion contribution is mass-independent
    (Section [22.4](#sec:compton-spatial-diffusion){reference-type="ref"
    reference="sec:compton-spatial-diffusion"}). This is the
    cross-species mass-independence prediction
    (Theorem [22.1](#thm:QMT22){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT22"}, clause (ii)) common to any coupling
    satisfying (C1);

-   From (C2): the values of any universal coupling parameters constrain
    the coupling uniformly across species. Atomic-clock bounds on one
    species (e.g., electrons in solids) translate directly to bounds on
    the same parameters at any other species (e.g., neutral atoms or
    ions);

-   From (C3): time-modulation features (e.g., spectroscopic sidebands
    at $\pm\Omega$) carry the same frequency across all species, since
    $\Omega$ is universal.

These empirical signatures are necessary consequences of any coupling
consistent with the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, not specific to the
cosine-modulation ansatz of [@MG-Compton-2026]. A non-cosine modulation
(Lévy-flight, phase noise, multi-frequency) would change the functional
form of $\langle(\Delta p)^2\rangle$ but would still satisfy (C1)--(C3)
and produce the same mass-independence and species-universal-frequency
signatures. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:essential-input .remark}
*Remark 4.35* (The essential test). An external theorem is
*essential* in a proof of $T$ if removing it would invalidate the
proof. It is *confirmatory* if removing it still leaves a complete
McGucken-machinery proof, and the external theorem merely supplies an
alternative route to the same conclusion by abstract analysis. The
Frobenius classification theorem of 1878 is confirmatory in the proof of
Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}: the McGucken proof picks out
$\mathbb{C}$ uniquely from the perpendicularity marker $J^2 = -1$
together with the two-element basis from the slice projection $\sigma$,
without invoking Frobenius's classification; Frobenius's classification
reaches the same conclusion by independent algebraic analysis. The
Riesz--Fischer theorem of 1907 is confirmatory in the proof of
Theorem [9.17](#thm:hilbert-complete){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complete"}: the McGucken proof obtains
completeness from the continuity of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$'s flow at
the constant rate $ic$; Riesz--Fischer reaches the same conclusion by
real-analytic completion of $L^2$-Cauchy sequences.
:::

::: {#rmk:QA-axioms-grade1 .remark}
*Remark 4.36* (The Algebraic Channel axioms QA1--QA4 as
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$-derived inputs at the principle level). The
Algebraic Channel axioms QA1 (Lorentz/translation invariance), QA2 (Stone's
theorem applied to the resulting one-parameter unitary groups), QA3
(compatibility-of-observables relations on the slice), and QA4
(Stone--von Neumann uniqueness) appear at first sight to import
non-trivial external mathematics. *They do not*: each is established in
Chapter [4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:foundations"} (§[4.4](#sec:channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:channelA"}) as a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
itself. QA1 is the symmetry content of the principle's universal-rate
clause; QA2 is the standard mathematical packaging of that symmetry as a
one-parameter unitary group (Stone's theorem on continuous one-parameter
unitary groups is the appropriate packaging tool, not an additional
postulate, because the unitary action is forced by QA1 and probability
preservation); QA3 follows from the joint symmetry algebra; QA4 follows
from the irreducibility of the slice representation. Stone's theorem and
Stone--von Neumann uniqueness therefore appear in this book as
*algorithms for packaging the McGucken Principle's symmetry content into
Hilbert-space operators*, not as essential external inputs.
:::

::: {#rmk:default-grade .remark}
*Remark 4.37* (Provenance of the theorems: descent from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via its Geometric Channel and Algebraic Channel axiomatic
shadows). By default, every QM theorem proved in Parts II--III of this
book is forced by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via its Algebraic Channel and Geometric
Channel axiomatic shadows, with external tools (Stone, Stone--von Neumann,
Cauchy--Schwarz, Robertson--Schrödinger, Frobenius, Riesz--Fischer)
appearing in confirmatory or packaging roles rather than as essential external postulates. Where a theorem requires a assumption
(e.g., spherical-symmetry as a clause of the principle) or an external
framework (e.g., a specific renormalisation scheme), the dependency is
explicitly labelled in the chapter audit. The reader who has followed
the four-theorem Hilbert chain of
Chapter [9](#ch:hilbert-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:hilbert-theorem"} can verify the principle-descended
provenance of every operator-algebraic proof in this book by tracing the
operators back through the four-theorem chain to
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ itself.
:::

# The Twenty-Three Quantum Theorems {#part:23}

The eight chapters of Part II derive, with proof-environment rigor, the
twenty-three named results of quantum mechanics from the McGucken
Principle. Each chapter follows the audit convention of
§[4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:foundations"}:
statement, Geometric Channel derivation, Algebraic Channel derivation, disjointness
audit, empirical anchor. The synthesis-paper theorem number from
[@Syn-2026] is given in each statement; where the McGucken theorem
extends or refines the standard textbook treatment, the textbook
attribution is also given.

**Notation reminder.** Throughout Part II we work on the McGucken
manifold $M_{G}$ generated by $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as in
Chapter [9](#ch:hilbert-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:hilbert-theorem"}. The Euclidean four-distance pulled back
to the constraint surface $\Sigma = \{x_{4}= ict\}$ is Minkowski with
signature $(-,+,+,+)$: $$ds^2 = dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2 - c^2 dt^2 = -c^2 dt^2 + dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2.$$
The suppression map $\sigma: \Sigma \to M_{3,t}$ takes
$(x_1, x_2, x_3, ict) \mapsto (x_1, x_2, x_3, t)$ and induces the
operator identity $\partial_t = ic\,\partial_{x_{4}}$ on smooth
functions, Lemma [9.1](#lem:suppression-map){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:suppression-map"}.

## QM T1: The Wave Equation and Huygens' Principle {#ch:wave-equation}

> *The McGucken Principle.* The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality.
> Every result below descends from that expansion.


*Recall.* the McGucken Principle ($\mathrm{McP}$:
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$) asserts that the fourth spacetime dimension
$x_4$ expands at the velocity of light $c$, carrying the
perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguishes it from the spatial
three. Throughout this chapter, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ refers to this
principle and to the five-clause content (i)--(v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: (i) *invariance* --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content; (ii) *spherical symmetry* --- the
expansion is isotropic in the spatial three, with the set of events
reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a 2-sphere of radius
$c\tau$; (iii) *monotonicity* --- the integral curve is strictly
monotonically increasing in $t$, fixing the arrow of $x_4$-advance; (iv)
*Lorentz consistency* --- the structure is $SO^+(1,3)$-invariant on
$M_{G}$; (v) *global validity* --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at
every event of $M_{G}$. The integrated kinematic shadow
$x_4 = ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is the kinematic shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the central fact.

The first of the 23 theorems establishes that wave propagation, in the
absence of mass, satisfies $\Box\psi = 0$ on $M_{G}$, where
$\Box = -\partial_t^2/c^2 + \nabla^2$ is the d'Alembert operator. The
result is presented in every textbook as a phenomenological starting
point for matter-wave kinematics; here it is a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

### Statement

::: {#thm:QMT1 .theorem}
**Theorem 1.1** (QM T1: The Wave Equation). *Let
$\psi : M_{G}\to \mathbb{C}$ be a smooth matter wavefunction in the
massless limit (no rest-mass phase factor) and in the absence of
external interactions. Then $\psi$ satisfies the d'Alembert wave
equation
$$\Box\psi = 0, \qquad \Box \;:=\; \eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu \;=\; -\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_t^2 + \nabla^2,
\label{eq:dAlembert}$$ where
$\eta^{\mu\nu} = \mathrm{diag}(-1/c^2,+1,+1,+1)$ (equivalently
$\mathrm{diag}(-1,+1,+1,+1)$ in $x^0 = ct$ units) is
the Minkowski inverse metric on $M_{G}$ established in
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}.*

*This is Theorem 60 (Geometric Channel) and Theorem 83 (Algebraic Channel) of
[@Syn-2026]; both derivations proceed directly from
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ with no external mathematical input
essential.*
:::

We give two derivationally disjoint derivations (Algebraic Channel:
algebraic-symmetry; Geometric Channel: geometric-propagation), each as a
numbered lemma feeding the main theorem.

### Geometric Channel derivation: Spherical wavefront propagation forces $\Box\psi = 0$ {#sec:QMT1-channelB}

::: {#lem:spherical-wave-kinematics .lemma}
**Lemma 1.5** (Spherical-wave kinematics). *Let
$f \in C^2(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R})$ be any twice-differentiable
function. The retarded spherical wave
$$\psi_{\mathrm{ret}}(\mathbf{x}, t) \;:=\; \frac{1}{r}\,f(r - ct), \qquad r := |\mathbf{x}|,$$
satisfies $\Box\psi_{\mathrm{ret}} = 0$ everywhere except at the origin
$r = 0$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has four steps computing
$\Box\psi_{\mathrm{ret}} = -c^{-2}\partial_t^2\psi_{\mathrm{ret}} + \nabla^2\psi_{\mathrm{ret}}$
explicitly and verifying its vanishing off the source. The retarded
spherical wave $f(r-ct)/r$ is the wavefront amplitude of the McGucken
Sphere generated by Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i) invariance and (ii) spherical
symmetry (the $x_{4}$-expansion at rate $c$ at every event of $M_{G}$,
with $x_4 = ict$ the integrated kinematic shadow per
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}).

**Step 1: Time derivatives.** With $u := r - ct$,
$$\partial_t \psi_{\mathrm{ret}} = \frac{1}{r}\,f'(u)\,\partial_t u = -\frac{c}{r}\,f'(u),
\qquad
\partial_t^2 \psi_{\mathrm{ret}} = \frac{c^2}{r}\,f''(u).$$ Hence
$$-\frac{1}{c^2}\,\partial_t^2 \psi_{\mathrm{ret}} = -\frac{1}{r}\,f''(u). \tag{$\ast$}$$

**Step 2: Spatial Laplacian.** For a function of the form $g(r)/r$, the
Laplacian in spherical coordinates is
$$\nabla^2 \left(\frac{g(r)}{r}\right) = \frac{1}{r}\,g''(r) \qquad (r > 0),$$
which we verify: $\nabla^2 G(r) = r^{-1}\,\partial_r^2(r G(r))$ for any
radial function $G$ (Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] §X.1, the standard
spherical-coordinate Laplacian identity); setting $G(r) = g(r)/r$ gives
$r G = g$ and $r^{-1}\partial_r^2(g) = g''(r)/r$. Applying this with
$g(r) = f(r - ct)$ (so $g'(r) = f'(u)$ and $g''(r) = f''(u)$ since
$u = r - ct$ has $\partial u/\partial r = 1$):
$$\nabla^2 \psi_{\mathrm{ret}} = \frac{1}{r}\,f''(u). \tag{$\ast\ast$}$$

**Step 3: Adding the two terms.** From $(\ast)$ and $(\ast\ast)$:
$$\Box\psi_{\mathrm{ret}} = -\frac{1}{r}f''(u) + \frac{1}{r}f''(u) = 0,$$
for $r > 0$. The two terms cancel exactly. $\Box\psi_{\mathrm{ret}} = 0$
on $M_{G}\setminus \{r = 0\}$. At $r = 0$ the function is singular;
$\Box\psi_{\mathrm{ret}}$ has a delta-function source at the origin in
the distributional sense, which is the Green's-function content of
$-1/(4\pi r) \cdot f(r-ct)$. This source represents the original event
from which the McGucken Sphere expands; for $r > 0$, away from the
source event, the wavefront satisfies the homogeneous d'Alembert
equation.

**Step 4: Reading --- McGucken anchoring.** The
spherical-wave form $\psi_{\mathrm{ret}}(\mathbf{x}, t) = f(r-ct)/r$ is
the most general spherically-symmetric retarded wavefront sourced at the
origin: the $f(r-ct)$ argument encodes outward propagation at rate $c$
(matching Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (i) invariance: the
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ rate $c$), and the $1/r$ falloff is the
inverse-distance attenuation ensuring energy conservation as the
wavefront surface area grows like $r^2$ on the McGucken Sphere
$M^{+}_{p}(t)$ (Definition [4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:sphere"}). The exact cancellation of $(\ast)$ and
$(\ast\ast)$ --- the two terms differing only in sign --- is the
content of the McGucken Sphere wavefront satisfying the
d'Alembertian equation: $\Box\psi = 0$ is the spatial-slice projection
of the principle's uniform $x_{4}$-advance at rate $c$
(Theorem [1.1](#thm:QMT1){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT1"},
the d'Alembertian wave equation as a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The McGucken-Sphere wavefront is therefore a
d'Alembertian-solution by construction, not by external mathematical
imposition --- the inverse-distance form is forced by
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (ii) (spherical symmetry of the
$x_{4}$-expansion) plus clause (i) (the $x_{4}$-rate $c$ invariant at
every event), and the d'Alembertian-vanishing is the algebraic
consequence of these two clauses operating together via the integrated
kinematic shadow $x_4 = ict$
(Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}). $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#lem:QMT1-channelB-proof .lemma}
**Lemma 1.6** (Geometric Channel proof of QM T1). *A wavefunction $\psi$
propagating on $M_{G}$ as the spherical wavefront sourced at every event
by the McGucken Sphere construction (QB1, QB2 of
§[4.5](#sec:channelB){reference-type="ref" reference="sec:channelB"})
satisfies $\Box\psi = 0$ at every event off the source-loci.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* **Step 1: The McGucken Sphere is the locus of forward
$x_{4}$-advance from a source event.** By QB1, the principle
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ acts at every event $p \in M_{G}$ as a
spherically symmetric expansion of $x_{4}$ at the rate $c$ relative to
spatial coordinates. The locus reached by this expansion at a later lab
time $t > t_p$ is the wavefront sphere
$$M^{+}_{p}(t) \;=\; \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 : |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_p| = c(t - t_p)\},$$
i.e., the 2-sphere centred at $\mathbf{x}_p$ of radius $c(t - t_p)$.
This wavefront is generated entirely by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: the
rate $c$ is the rate of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (Geometric Channel reading);
the spherical symmetry is the spherical symmetry of the expansion stated
in $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

**Step 2: The wavefront amplitude has the spherical-wave form.** The
amplitude of the wavefront at a spatial point $\mathbf{x}$ at lab time
$t$ is determined by: (i) what value of the source amplitude propagated
to reach $\mathbf{x}$ at $t$ (the value at the retarded source-event
time $t_p = t - r/c$, where $r = |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_p|$); (ii) a
$1/r$ geometric attenuation factor because the total wavefront energy is
conserved while the wavefront area $4\pi r^2$ grows.

Setting $f(u) := \psi_0(t_p)$ with $u = r - ct$ (so $u/c = -t_p$ --- the
retarded time scaled by $c$ --- and $f$ encodes the source-event
amplitude history), we obtain $\psi(\mathbf{x}, t) = f(r - ct)/r$, which
is the retarded spherical wave of
Lemma [1.5](#lem:spherical-wave-kinematics){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:spherical-wave-kinematics"}.

**Step 3: Apply
Lemma [1.5](#lem:spherical-wave-kinematics){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:spherical-wave-kinematics"}.** The spherical wave
$f(r-ct)/r$ satisfies $\Box\psi = 0$ off the source-locus by direct
computation. Therefore the matter wavefunction propagating as a
McGucken-Sphere wavefront satisfies the homogeneous d'Alembert equation
everywhere off source.

**Step 4: Huygens iteration preserves the equation.** By QB2, every
point of a wavefront re-sources its own Sphere; the next-generation
wavefront is the envelope of secondary Spheres. A finite or continuous
superposition $\psi = \sum_i \psi_i$ or $\psi = \int \psi_p \, dp$ of
spherical waves, each of the form
Lemma [1.5](#lem:spherical-wave-kinematics){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:spherical-wave-kinematics"}, satisfies
$\Box\psi = \sum_i \Box\psi_i = 0$ by linearity of $\Box$. The iterated
Huygens construction therefore generates the entire space of solutions
of $\Box\psi = 0$. ◻
:::

::: proof
*Proof of Theorem [1.1](#thm:QMT1){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT1"}.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The theorem asserts that the massless matter
wavefunction satisfies the d'Alembert equation $\Box\psi = 0$ everywhere
off source. We establish this along both channels and verify their
derivational disjointness.

**Step 1: Algebraic Channel derivation
(Lemma [1.4](#lem:QMT1-channelA-proof){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT1-channelA-proof"}).** Starting from clause (P1) of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (translation invariance at every event),
Stone's theorem (QA2) supplies the four-momentum operator
$\hat P^\mu = -i\hbar\,\partial^\mu$ as the self-adjoint generator of
space-time translations. Wigner classification (QA6) of irreducible
unitary representations of the Poincaré group
$\mathbb{R}^{1,3} \rtimes SO^+(1,3)$ assigns the massless representation
the mass-Casimir eigenvalue zero: $\hat P^\mu\hat P_\mu\,\psi = 0$. The
operator identity $\hat P^\mu\hat P_\mu = -\hbar^2\,\Box$
(Lemma [1.3](#lem:massless-annihilation){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:massless-annihilation"}) then forces $\Box\psi = 0$. The
Algebraic Channel route is therefore: $(\mathrm{McP})\to$ Lorentz invariance
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}) $\to$ Wigner classification $\to$
massless mass-Casimir $\to$ $\Box\psi = 0$.

**Step 2: Geometric Channel derivation
(Lemma [1.6](#lem:QMT1-channelB-proof){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT1-channelB-proof"}).** Starting from clauses
(P2)--(P3) of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (spherical symmetry of
$x_{4}$-expansion at rate $c$), the McGucken-Sphere construction
(Definition [4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:sphere"}) produces an expanding spherical wavefront
$f(r - ct)/r$ from every source event
(Lemma [1.5](#lem:spherical-wave-kinematics){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:spherical-wave-kinematics"}). Direct computation of the
d'Alembertian on the spherical wavefront gives $\Box(f(r-ct)/r) = 0$ off
the source-locus, via the exact cancellation of temporal and
spatial-Laplacian contributions:
$-c^{-2}\partial_t^2(f(r-ct)/r) = -f''(r-ct)/r$ and
$\nabla^2(f(r-ct)/r) = f''(r-ct)/r$ cancel exactly. Huygens iteration
(clause QB2) extends this to arbitrary superpositions
$\psi = \sum_i\psi_i$ or $\psi = \int\psi_p\,dp$, with
$\Box\psi = \sum_i\Box\psi_i = 0$ by linearity. The Geometric Channel route is
therefore: $(\mathrm{McP})\to$ Sphere wavefront construction $\to$
spherical-wave kinematics $\to$ $\Box\psi = 0$ for all wavefront
solutions.

**Step 3: Derivational disjointness of the two channels.** Algebraic Channel uses
Stone's theorem, Wigner classification of Poincaré representations, the
Casimir operator identification, and the uniqueness of $\Box$ as the
unique second-order Lorentz-invariant scalar operator
(Lemma [1.2](#lem:box-unique){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:box-unique"}) --- all algebraic-symmetry machinery.
Geometric Channel uses the McGucken-Sphere construction, the explicit
spherical-wave amplitude profile, Huygens iteration, and linearity of
$\Box$ --- all geometric-propagation machinery. The two derivations
share only:

-   The starting principle $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$;

-   The Lorentz-invariant d'Alembertian $\Box$ (Algebraic Channel derives its
    uniqueness; Geometric Channel exhibits it explicitly);

-   The final equation $\Box\psi = 0$.

No intermediate machinery is shared: Stone's theorem and Wigner
classification do not appear in Geometric Channel; the McGucken-Sphere
construction and Huygens iteration do not appear in Algebraic Channel.

**Step 4: McGucken anchoring.** Both channels descend from
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. Algebraic Channel reaches $\Box\psi = 0$ through the
algebraic-symmetry shadow of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$:
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ forces the Minkowski metric
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}, via $dx_4 = ic\,dt$ giving
$dx_4^2 = -c^2 dt^2$), which forces the Lorentz group and Poincaré
group, which forces Wigner classification. Geometric Channel reaches
$\Box\psi = 0$ through the geometric-propagation shadow:
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ forces the McGucken Sphere at every event
(clause P1), which propagates spherically at rate $c$ (clause P2),
giving the spherical-wave amplitude. The two readings of the same
equation reflect the two faces of the principle's content.

**Step 5: This is the flagship case of dual-channel disjointness.**
Theorem [1.1](#thm:QMT1){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT1"} is
the first and simplest case of the dual-channel
disjointness theorem
(Theorem [4.27](#thm:disjointness){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:disjointness"}). All subsequent theorems QMT2--QMT22
follow the same pattern: an Algebraic Channel derivation via algebraic-symmetry
machinery, a Geometric Channel derivation via McGucken-Sphere kinematics, with
derivationally disjoint intermediate steps. The agreement of the two
channels at the level of the final equation is the redundancy
that the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework supplies --- no other framework for quantum
mechanics derives the wave equation twice along independent routes. ◻
:::

### Algebraic Channel derivation: Lorentz invariance and uniqueness of $\Box$ {#sec:QMT1-channelA}

::: {#lem:box-unique .lemma}
**Lemma 1.2** ($\Box$ is the unique second-order Lorentz-invariant
scalar differential operator on $M_{G}$). *Let $D$ be a second-order
linear differential operator on smooth functions
$\mathbb{C}^\infty(M_{G}) \to \mathbb{C}^\infty(M_{G})$, of the form
$$D \;=\; A^{\mu\nu}(x)\,\partial_\mu\partial_\nu \;+\; B^\mu(x)\,\partial_\mu \;+\; C(x),$$
where $A^{\mu\nu}$, $B^\mu$, $C$ are smooth tensor/vector/scalar fields
on $M_{G}$. Suppose $D$ is invariant under the Lorentz group $SO^+(1,3)$
acting on $M_{G}$ (which is the isometry group of the Minkowski metric
of Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}) and is translation-invariant on $M_{G}$
(which is the isometry under the translation subgroup of the Poincaré
group). Then there exist constants $\alpha, \gamma \in \mathbb{C}$ such
that
$$D \;=\; \alpha\,\Box \;+\; \gamma\,\mathbf{1}, \qquad \Box = \eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu.$$
That is: up to overall scale and an additive multiple of the identity,
$D = \Box$ is unique.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). We prove the result in four steps, each grounded in the
principle $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and the Minkowski structure it
generates. The Minkowski metric $\eta^{\mu\nu}$ on $M_{G}$ is itself a
theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}, descending from
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (ii) spherical symmetry and (iv)
Lorentz consistency, with $x_4 = ict$ the integrated kinematic shadow
per Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"} giving $dx_4^2 = -c^2\,dt^2$ and
hence the Minkowski signature); the d'Alembertian $\Box$ is the unique
Lorentz-invariant scalar second-order operator built from this metric.

**Step 1: Translation invariance kills the $x$-dependence of
$A, B, C$.** Poincaré translation invariance --- itself a theorem of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (v) (global validity:
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event of $M_{G}$, so no event is preferred and the structure is
translation-invariant) --- means $D$ commutes with every translation
$T_a : x \mapsto x + a$. For any constant translation $T_a$ on $M_{G}$
and any smooth $f$,
$$(D T_a f)(x) = (T_a D f)(x) \;\Leftrightarrow\; A^{\mu\nu}(x+a)\partial_\mu\partial_\nu f(x+a) + \cdots = A^{\mu\nu}(x)\partial_\mu\partial_\nu f(x+a) + \cdots.$$
Setting this equal for every $a$ and every smooth $f$ forces
$A^{\mu\nu}(x+a) = A^{\mu\nu}(x)$ for all $a, x$, hence $A^{\mu\nu}$ is
constant; analogously $B^\mu$ and $C$ are constant. So
$D = A^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu + B^\mu\partial_\mu + C$ with
constant coefficients.

**Step 2: Lorentz invariance constrains $A^{\mu\nu}, B^\mu, C$ to be
Lorentz tensors of the appropriate rank.** A Lorentz transformation
$\Lambda \in SO^+(1,3)$ (the Lorentz group is the isometry group of
$M_{G}$ by Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iv), derived at Theorem 4.6, Lorentz consistency) acts on
$M_{G}$ by $x \mapsto \Lambda x$ and on coordinate derivatives by
$\partial_\mu \mapsto (\Lambda^{-1})^\nu{}_\mu \partial_\nu$. Invariance
of $D$ under $\Lambda$ means
$$A^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu + B^\mu\partial_\mu + C \;=\; A^{\alpha\beta}(\Lambda^{-1})^\mu{}_\alpha(\Lambda^{-1})^\nu{}_\beta \partial_\mu\partial_\nu + B^\alpha(\Lambda^{-1})^\mu{}_\alpha \partial_\mu + C$$
for every $\Lambda$. Matching tensorial structure: $A^{\mu\nu}$
transforms as a symmetric rank-2 contravariant tensor invariant under
$SO^+(1,3)$; $B^\mu$ as a Lorentz-invariant vector; $C$ as a Lorentz
scalar.

**Step 3: Classification of Lorentz-invariant tensors.** The only
Lorentz-invariant symmetric rank-2 contravariant tensor on $M_{G}$ is a
scalar multiple of $\eta^{\mu\nu}$ --- the inverse Minkowski metric.
(Proof: by the irreducibility of the standard representation of
$SO^+(1,3)$ on $\mathbb{R}^{1,3}$, the only invariant tensors of rank 2
are scalar multiples of $\eta$ and antisymmetric tensors orthogonal to
$\eta$; but $A^{\mu\nu}$ is assumed symmetric.) Similarly the only
Lorentz-invariant vector is the zero vector (since the trivial
1-dimensional representation does not appear in the standard
4-dimensional representation of $SO^+(1,3)$). So
$A^{\mu\nu} = \alpha\,\eta^{\mu\nu}$ and $B^\mu = 0$ for some
$\alpha \in \mathbb{C}$; $C = \gamma \in \mathbb{C}$.

**Step 4: Conclusion.** Substituting:
$$D = \alpha\,\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu + 0 + \gamma\,\mathbf{1} = \alpha\,\Box + \gamma\,\mathbf{1}.$$
Up to overall scale $\alpha$ and additive multiple-of-identity $\gamma$,
$D = \Box$.

**Step 5: McGucken anchoring.** The Minkowski metric $\eta^{\mu\nu}$
used in Step 3 was itself derived in
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} as a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$:
the signature $(-,+,+,+)$ is forced by substituting $dx_4 = ic\,dt$ (the
differential form of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$) into the Euclidean line
element and using $i^2 = -1$. The Lorentz group $SO^+(1,3)$ is the
isometry group of $\eta$, hence is generated by
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. No external input is essential. ◻
:::

::: {#lem:massless-annihilation .lemma}
**Lemma 1.3** (The massless matter wavefunction is annihilated by a
Lorentz-invariant second-order operator). *A smooth wavefunction
$\psi \in C^\infty(M_{G}, \mathbb{C})$ representing a massless quantum
entity (in the sense of QA6, Wigner's classification: a state in an
irreducible unitary representation of the Poincaré group with vanishing
mass-Casimir $P^\mu P_\mu = 0$) satisfies $D\psi = 0$ for some
second-order Lorentz-invariant differential operator $D$ on $M_{G}$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **Step 1: Wigner classification gives the mass-Casimir.** By
QA6 (Wigner classification of irreducible unitary representations of the
connected Poincaré group $\mathbb{R}^{1,3} \rtimes SO^+(1,3)$), the
irreps are labelled by the eigenvalues of two Casimir invariants:

-   $C_1 = P^\mu P_\mu$ (mass-squared, with eigenvalue $-m^2 c^2$ in
    signature $(-, +, +, +)$);

-   $C_2 = W^\mu W_\mu$ (Pauli-Lubanski squared, encoding spin).

For massless representations, the mass-Casimir vanishes:
$P^\mu P_\mu\psi = 0$. The wavefunction $\psi$ on $M_{G}$ representing
such a state is annihilated by the operator $\hat P^\mu\hat P_\mu$ at
the level of the spectral action on the irrep.

**Step 2: Four-momentum operator from Stone's theorem.** By QA2 (Stone's
theorem applied to space-time translation invariance of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$), the four-momentum operator $\hat P^\mu$ is
the generator of space-time translation on the wavefunction space:
$$\hat P^\mu = -i\hbar\,\partial^\mu = -i\hbar\,\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\nu.$$
The factor of $-i\hbar$ comes from two sources: (i) the
McGucken-Principle $i$ via
Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"} case 1 (chain-rule mechanism (a)); (ii) the
quantum of action $\hbar$ per Sphere cycle from
Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}. Both
factors descend from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, not as external inputs.

**Step 3: Compute $\hat P^\mu\hat P_\mu$ explicitly.** Square the
four-momentum operator using index manipulation:
$$\hat P^\mu\hat P_\mu\psi = (-i\hbar)^2\,\eta^{\mu\alpha}\eta_{\mu\beta}\,\partial_\alpha\partial^\beta\psi = -\hbar^2\,\delta^\alpha_\beta\,\partial_\alpha\partial^\beta\psi = -\hbar^2\,\eta^{\alpha\beta}\partial_\alpha\partial_\beta\psi = -\hbar^2\,\Box\psi,$$
where we used (i)
$\eta^{\mu\alpha}\eta_{\mu\beta} = \delta^\alpha_\beta$ (the metric and
its inverse compose to give the identity), (ii) the definition
$\Box := \eta^{\alpha\beta}\partial_\alpha\partial_\beta = -c^{-2}\partial_t^2 + \nabla^2$
in signature $(-, +, +, +)$.

**Step 4: Combine --- massless condition becomes wave equation.** The
vanishing-mass condition $\hat P^\mu\hat P_\mu\psi = 0$ from Step 1
combined with the explicit form $\hat P^\mu\hat P_\mu = -\hbar^2\Box$
from Step 3 gives:
$$-\hbar^2\,\Box\psi = 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \Box\psi = 0,$$
where division by $\hbar^2 \ne 0$ is valid. The operator
$D = -\hbar^2\Box$ is therefore the choice: it is
second-order (being quadratic in $\partial^\mu$), Lorentz-invariant
(being the squared norm of the Lorentz vector $\hat P^\mu$), and
annihilates the massless wavefunction.

**Step 5: Uniqueness of the form.** The d'Alembertian $\Box$ is the
unique (up to overall scale and additive constant) second-order
Lorentz-invariant scalar differential operator on $M_{G}$
(cf. Lemma [1.2](#lem:box-unique){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:box-unique"}). Any other second-order Lorentz-invariant
operator is of the form $\alpha\,\Box + \beta\,\mathbf{1}$; the
additional constant $\beta$ would correspond to a non-zero mass-Casimir,
which is excluded for massless representations. Hence $D = -\hbar^2\Box$
is the unique choice forced by Poincaré covariance + massless
condition + second-order locality.

**Step 6: McGucken anchoring.** The Lorentz invariance of $\Box$ traces
to the Minkowski metric $\eta_{\mu\nu}$, which by
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} is itself a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: substituting $dx_4 = ic\,dt$ (the differential
form of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$) into the Euclidean line element
$ds^2 = dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2 + dx_4^2$ and using $i^2 = -1$ yields
the Lorentzian form. The annihilation operator $D = -\hbar^2\Box$ for
massless wavefunctions therefore descends entirely from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ through the chain: $(\mathrm{McP})\to$
Minkowski metric (Thm.[9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}) $\to$ Lorentz group (isometry group of
$\eta$) $\to$ irreducible Poincaré representations (Wigner, QA6) $\to$
vanishing mass-Casimir on massless reps $\to$ $\Box\psi = 0$. ◻
:::

::: {#lem:QMT1-channelA-proof .lemma}
**Lemma 1.4** (Algebraic Channel proof of QM T1). *The massless matter
wavefunction $\psi$ satisfies $\Box\psi = 0$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **Step 1: Apply the massless mass-Casimir.** By
Lemma [1.3](#lem:massless-annihilation){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:massless-annihilation"}, the vanishing-mass condition
$P^\mu P_\mu = 0$ on the irreducible Poincaré representation translates
to the operator equation
$\hat{P}^\mu\hat{P}_\mu\,\psi = -\hbar^2\,\Box\,\psi = 0$ on the
wavefunction. Since $\hbar \neq 0$, dividing yields $$\Box\,\psi = 0.$$
This is the d'Alembertian equation
[\[eq:dAlembert\]](#eq:dAlembert){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:dAlembert"} of QM T1.

**Step 2: Uniqueness of $\Box$ as the operator.** By
Lemma [1.2](#lem:box-unique){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:box-unique"}, the d'Alembertian $\Box$ is the unique
second-order Lorentz-invariant scalar differential operator (up to
overall scale and an additive constant), in the sense that any other
operator with these properties is a scalar multiple of $\Box$ plus a
multiple of the identity. The massless-equation form $\Box\psi = 0$ is
therefore inevitable for the wave equation of a
Lorentz-covariant massless field --- it is the unique choice forced by
Poincaré covariance and second-order locality.

**Step 3: McGucken anchoring.** The factor $-\hbar^2$ in
$\hat{P}^\mu\hat{P}_\mu = -\hbar^2\Box$ comes from the squared
quantum-momentum-operator convention
$\hat{P}^\mu = -i\hbar\,\partial^\mu$, where the $i$ traces (via
Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}) to the McGucken-Principle $i$. The mass-zero
condition $m = 0$ corresponds to the photon's case in the
four-velocity-budget classification
(Lemma [4.2](#lem:four-velocity-budget){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:four-velocity-budget"}): the photon's entire rate budget --- measured per coordinate time $t$,
the parameter in which $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is stated --- is spatial
($v = c$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$), with $|dx_{4}/dt| = 0$, hence zero rest
mass. The budget is stated per coordinate time throughout; see
Remark [4.2A](#rmk:coordinate-time-budget){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:coordinate-time-budget"} for why the proper-time
parameterisation cannot carry this statement.

**Step 4: Algebraic Channel characterisation.** This derivation uses QA1
(Lorentz invariance) and QA6 (Wigner classification for the massless
irreducible representation) --- both algebraic-symmetry inputs. No
Sphere-geometric machinery (Huygens iteration, Compton phase, etc.)
appears. The derivation is therefore Algebraic Channel, disjoint from the
Geometric Channel route of
Lemma [1.5](#lem:spherical-wave-kinematics){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:spherical-wave-kinematics"}. ◻
:::

### Disjointness audit

**Algebraic Channel intermediate machinery:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (clause
iv: $i$ as perpendicularity marker; clause used to produce Minkowski
signature via Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}); Lorentz invariance; uniqueness of
$\Box$ as second-order Lorentz-invariant operator
(Lemma [1.2](#lem:box-unique){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:box-unique"}); Stone's theorem (QA2); Wigner
classification (QA6); the algebraic identity
$\hat{P}^\mu\hat{P}_\mu = -\hbar^2\Box$.

**Geometric Channel intermediate machinery:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (clauses
i: rate $c$; ii: spherical symmetry); McGucken Sphere construction
(QB1); Huygens-secondary envelope (QB2); explicit computation
$\Box(f(r-ct)/r) = 0$
(Lemma [1.5](#lem:spherical-wave-kinematics){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:spherical-wave-kinematics"}); linearity of $\Box$.

**Intersection:** $\{(\mathrm{McP}), \Box\psi = 0\}$. No item of Algebraic
Channel's algebraic-symmetry set (Stone's theorem, Wigner classification,
four-momentum operator) appears in Geometric Channel. No item of Geometric Channel's
