single Sphere has both an apex and a wavefront --- all
geometric-propagation machinery. The intermediate machinery is disjoint:

-   Fourier transform and Plancherel theorem appear in Algebraic Channel, not in
    Geometric Channel;

-   McGucken-Sphere apex/wavefront duality appears in Geometric Channel, not in
    Algebraic Channel.

The two channels share only $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and the conclusion
(both readings forced).

**Step 4: Parallel between channels.** The Algebraic Channel
Hilbert-space duality and the Geometric Channel Sphere apex/wavefront duality
correspond term by term: the position eigenbasis of $\mathcal{H}$ is the
Algebraic Channel image of the Sphere's apex reading; the momentum eigenbasis is
the Algebraic Channel image of the Sphere's wavefront reading. The Fourier
conjugacy on $\mathcal{H}$ is the algebraic shadow of the geometric
apex/wavefront duality on the McGucken Sphere.

**Step 5: Resolution of the textbook duality paradox.** The textbook
framing of wave-particle duality treats the wave and particle pictures
as alternative ontological categories whose simultaneous applicability
is paradoxical (\"how can the electron be both a wave and a
particle?\"). The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework dissolves the paradox: both
readings are forced features of a single underlying object --- the
McGucken Sphere --- with the \"duality\" being the fact that
a Sphere has both an apex and a wavefront. Neither reading is
fundamental; both are inevitable. The empirical signature of duality ---
interference patterns in the double-slit experiment with localised
detector clicks --- is the simultaneous manifestation of both readings
at different stages of the experiment: wavefront propagation between
source and detector (W reading), apex registration at the detector (P
reading).

**Step 6: Physical content.** The dual readings are universal across
quantum systems: photons (Sphere apex at emission point, wavefront
propagating at $c$), electrons (massive Sphere with rest-mass
Compton-phase oscillation, wavefront in the de Broglie wave reading),
atoms (composite Sphere with internal structure, wavefront in
matter-wave interferometry), and molecules (now empirically confirmed up
to fullerenes, $C_{60}$, in Arndt et al.'s 1999 experiments). The
McGucken framework derives the duality as a theorem of
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ along both algebraic and geometric channels. ◻
:::

### Algebraic Channel derivation: Position and momentum eigenbases as Fourier-conjugate decompositions {#sec:QMT6-channelA}

::: {#lem:position-localized .lemma}
**Lemma 6.2** (Position eigenstates are localised at single spatial
points). *For any $\mathbf{x}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^3$, the (improper)
position eigenstate $\lvert \mathbf{x}_0 \rangle$ in the Schrödinger
representation $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ is the Dirac
distribution
$\psi_{\mathbf{x}_0}(\mathbf{x}) = \delta^3(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0)$,
satisfying
$\hat{q}\,\lvert \mathbf{x}_0 \rangle = \mathbf{x}_0\,\lvert \mathbf{x}_0 \rangle$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **Step 1: $\hat{q}$ as multiplication by $\mathbf{x}$.** On the
Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3x)$ derived in
Theorem [9.17](#thm:hilbert-complete){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complete"} of
Chapter [9](#ch:hilbert-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:hilbert-theorem"} from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (the
spatial slice $\mathbb{R}^3$ inherits the standard Lebesgue measure
$d^3x$ from the McGucken-derived Minkowski metric, restricted to the
time slice), the position operator
$\hat{q}= (\hat{q}^1, \hat{q}^2, \hat{q}^3)$ acts as multiplication by
the coordinate functions $\mathbf{x} = (x^1, x^2, x^3)$:
$$(\hat{q}^j \psi)(\mathbf{x}) := x^j\,\psi(\mathbf{x}).$$ This is the
only self-adjoint extension on the Schwartz domain that satisfies
$[\hat{q}^j, \hat{q}^k] = 0$ and acts as multiplication on smooth
compactly supported test functions; uniqueness follows from von
Neumann's spectral theorem applied to a triple of commuting self-adjoint
operators with spectrum $\mathbb{R}^3$ (provided in Reed--Simon
[@ReedSimon1980] Theorem VIII.5).

**Step 2: Eigenvalue equation.** An eigenstate of $\hat{q}^j$ with
eigenvalue $x_0^j$ is a generalised function $\psi_{\mathbf{x}_0}$
satisfying
$$(x^j - x_0^j)\,\psi_{\mathbf{x}_0}(\mathbf{x}) = 0 \quad \text{for every } j = 1, 2, 3.$$
The only distribution on $\mathbb{R}^3$ supported at the single point
$\mathbf{x}_0$ is (a scalar multiple of) the Dirac delta
$\delta^3(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0)$; normalising to
$\langle \mathbf{x}_0 | \mathbf{x}_0'\rangle = \delta^3(\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{x}_0')$
fixes the scale.

**Step 3: Localization interpretation.** The Dirac delta has support
$\{\mathbf{x}_0\}$, a single point in $\mathbb{R}^3$. A measurement
projecting the wavefunction onto $\lvert \mathbf{x}_0 \rangle$ registers
the particle as localised at $\mathbf{x}_0$. This is the (P) reading:
*particle as localised event at the Sphere apex's spatial
cross-section*. ◻
:::

::: {#lem:momentum-planewave .lemma}
**Lemma 6.3** (Momentum eigenstates are plane waves of definite spatial
wavevector). *For any $\mathbf{p}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^3$, the (improper)
momentum eigenstate $\lvert \mathbf{p}_0 \rangle$ in the Schrödinger
representation is the plane wave
$\psi_{\mathbf{p}_0}(\mathbf{x}) = (2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\,e^{i\mathbf{p}_0\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}$,
satisfying
$\hat{p}\,\lvert \mathbf{p}_0 \rangle = \mathbf{p}_0\,\lvert \mathbf{p}_0 \rangle$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has six steps establishing the plane-wave
form of momentum eigenstates and their McGucken-Sphere wavefront
interpretation.

**Step 1: Momentum operator $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ from Stone's
theorem.** By Lemma [2.2](#lem:phat-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-generator"} of
Chapter [2](#ch:de-broglie){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:de-broglie"}, the momentum operator $\hat{p}$ on
$\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ acts as $$\hat{p}= -i\hbar\,\nabla,$$
derived as the self-adjoint generator of the spatial-translation unitary
group $\hat{U}(\mathbf{a}) = e^{-i\mathbf{a}\cdot\hat{p}/\hbar}$ via
Stone's theorem (QA2) applied to the spatial-translation invariance of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (QA1).

**Step 2: Eigenvalue equation for $\hat{p}$.** An (improper) eigenstate
$\psi_{\mathbf{p}_0}$ of $\hat{p}$ with eigenvalue
$\mathbf{p}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ satisfies
$$-i\hbar\,\nabla\psi_{\mathbf{p}_0}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{p}_0\,\psi_{\mathbf{p}_0}(\mathbf{x}).$$
Component-wise, this reads
$$-i\hbar\,\partial_{x^j}\psi_{\mathbf{p}_0}(\mathbf{x}) = p_0^j\,\psi_{\mathbf{p}_0}(\mathbf{x}), \quad j = 1, 2, 3.$$
Rearranging:
$\partial_{x^j}\psi_{\mathbf{p}_0} = (ip_0^j/\hbar)\psi_{\mathbf{p}_0}$.
This is a first-order linear ODE in each spatial direction.

**Step 3: Solve the ODE.** The general smooth solution to the system of
three coupled ODEs is, up to overall scale,
$$\psi_{\mathbf{p}_0}(\mathbf{x}) = C\,\exp\!\left(\frac{i\mathbf{p}_0\cdot\mathbf{x}}{\hbar}\right),$$
with $C \in \mathbb{C}$ a normalisation constant. The exponent is the
dot product of the eigenvalue vector $\mathbf{p}_0$ with the position
vector $\mathbf{x}$, divided by $\hbar$. The factor of $i$ in the
exponent comes from the $-i\hbar$ in $\hat{p}$ cancelled by the implicit
$i$ from the eigenvalue equation; the origin of the $i$ is
the McGucken-Principle perpendicularity marker
(Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"} case 1).

**Step 4: Normalisation by Dirac-delta orthogonality.** The
improper-basis normalisation
$$\langle\mathbf{p}_0|\mathbf{p}_0'\rangle = \delta^3(\mathbf{p}_0 - \mathbf{p}_0')$$
fixes the constant $C$. Explicitly,
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}|C|^2\,e^{-i\mathbf{p}_0\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}\,e^{i\mathbf{p}_0'\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}\,d^3\mathbf{x} = |C|^2\,(2\pi\hbar)^3\,\delta^3(\mathbf{p}_0 - \mathbf{p}_0'),$$
using the Fourier representation
$\int e^{i(\mathbf{p}'-\mathbf{p})\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}d^3\mathbf{x} = (2\pi\hbar)^3\,\delta^3(\mathbf{p}' - \mathbf{p})$.
Setting this equal to $\delta^3(\mathbf{p}_0 - \mathbf{p}_0')$ gives
$|C|^2 = (2\pi\hbar)^{-3}$, so $C = (2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}$ (real positive
convention).

**Step 5: Momentum eigenstate is a plane wave.** The result is
$$\psi_{\mathbf{p}_0}(\mathbf{x}) = (2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\,\exp\!\left(\frac{i\mathbf{p}_0\cdot\mathbf{x}}{\hbar}\right),$$
a plane wave with definite spatial wavevector
$\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{p}_0/\hbar$ (de Broglie relation,
Theorem [2.1](#thm:QMT2){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT2"}).
The plane wave has constant amplitude $(2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}$ across
$\mathbb{R}^3$ and oscillates with spatial frequency
$|\mathbf{k}| = |\mathbf{p}_0|/\hbar$.

**Step 6: Wavefront interpretation as McGucken-Sphere far-field limit.**
The plane wave
$\psi_{\mathbf{p}_0}(\mathbf{x}) \propto e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}}$
is the local-plane-wave limit of the McGucken-Sphere wavefront
$\psi(\mathbf{x}, t) = f(r - ct)/r$ in the far-field regime
(Lemma [2.5](#lem:plane-wave-limit){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:plane-wave-limit"}). The momentum eigenstate is therefore
the geometric wave-character of the McGucken Sphere --- an
extended-amplitude oscillation across all of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with
definite spatial wavevector. This is the (W) reading: particle as
extended wave on the Sphere wavefront, the geometric content of the
principle's $x_{4}$-expansion at the wavefront cross-section. Together
with the (P) reading (position eigenstates as localised events at the
Sphere apex, Lemma [6.2](#lem:position-localized){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:position-localized"}), the momentum eigenstates supply
the second of the two Fourier-conjugate readings of the McGucken-Sphere
wavefunction (Lemma [6.5](#lem:QMT6-channelA-proof){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT6-channelA-proof"}). ◻
:::

::: {#lem:fourier-conjugate .lemma}
**Lemma 6.4** (Fourier conjugacy of position and momentum bases). *The
position and momentum eigenbases on $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ are
related by the Fourier transform:
$$\langle\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{p}\rangle = (2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\,e^{i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar},$$
and any wavefunction admits both expansions
$$\psi = \int d^3x\,\psi(\mathbf{x})\,\lvert \mathbf{x} \rangle = \int d^3p\,\tilde\psi(\mathbf{p})\,\lvert \mathbf{p} \rangle,$$
with
$\tilde\psi(\mathbf{p}) = \langle\mathbf{p}|\psi\rangle = (2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\int d^3x\,e^{-i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}\,\psi(\mathbf{x})$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **Step 1: Position-momentum overlap.** By
Lemma [6.2](#lem:position-localized){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:position-localized"} the position eigenstates are
$\lvert \mathbf{x} \rangle = \delta^3(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x})$
(improper basis on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$); by
Lemma [6.3](#lem:momentum-planewave){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:momentum-planewave"} the momentum eigenstates are plane
waves
$\langle\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{p}\rangle = (2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\,e^{i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{y}/\hbar}$.
The overlap is
$$\langle\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{p}\rangle = \int d^3y\,\delta^3(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x})\,(2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\,e^{i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{y}/\hbar} = (2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\,e^{i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}.$$

**Step 2: Plancherel theorem on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$.** The Plancherel
theorem (Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Theorem IX.1) states that the
Fourier transform
$$(\mathcal{F}\psi)(\mathbf{p}) := (2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}d^3x\,e^{-i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}\,\psi(\mathbf{x})$$
is a unitary isomorphism
$\mathcal{F}: L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3x) \to L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3p)$.
Unitarity gives $\|\mathcal{F}\psi\|_{L^2(d^3p)} = \|\psi\|_{L^2(d^3x)}$
for every $\psi$, and the inverse is the inverse Fourier transform with
$+i$ in the exponent. The factor $(2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}$ is the standard
convention that makes $\mathcal{F}$ unitary on $L^2$.

**Step 3: Eigenbases of conjugate operators.** The position operator
$\hat{q}$ acts as multiplication by $\mathbf{x}$ on
$L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3x)$, with improper eigenbasis
$\{\lvert \mathbf{x} \rangle\}_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3}$. The
momentum operator $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ becomes, in the
Fourier-conjugate $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3p)$ representation,
multiplication by $\mathbf{p}$, with improper eigenbasis
$\{\lvert \mathbf{p} \rangle\}_{\mathbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^3}$. The Fourier
transform is the unitary intertwiner between the two representations.

**Step 4: Two expansions of the same vector.** Every
$\psi \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ admits the position-space expansion
$\psi = \int d^3x\,\psi(\mathbf{x})\,\lvert \mathbf{x} \rangle$ and the
momentum-space expansion
$\psi = \int d^3p\,\tilde\psi(\mathbf{p})\,\lvert \mathbf{p} \rangle$
with
$\tilde\psi(\mathbf{p}) = (\mathcal{F}\psi)(\mathbf{p}) = \langle\mathbf{p}|\psi\rangle$.
The two expansions are related by the Fourier transform; both represent
the same Hilbert-space vector.

**Step 5: McGucken anchoring.** The complex exponential
$e^{i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}$ carries the McGucken-Principle
$i$ via Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"} case (a) (chain-rule mechanism). The Fourier
conjugacy is the spatial-slice expression of the principle's
wave-particle dual nature: position-eigenstates are localised apexes
(P-reading), momentum-eigenstates are extended plane waves (W-reading)
--- both readings of the same McGucken-Sphere wavefunction
(cf. Lemma [6.6](#lem:sphere-apex-wavefront){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:sphere-apex-wavefront"}). ◻
:::

::: {#lem:QMT6-channelA-proof .lemma}
**Lemma 6.5** (Algebraic Channel proof of QM T6). *A quantum entity carries simultaneously the wave reading and the particle reading of its wavefunction, as two Fourier-conjugate expansions of a single
Hilbert-space vector $\psi \in \mathcal{H}$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has six steps establishing the
wave-particle duality as the Fourier-conjugacy of complete eigenbases on
a single Hilbert space.

**Step 1: Position eigenbasis (P reading).** By
Lemma [6.2](#lem:position-localized){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:position-localized"}, the position eigenstates
$\{\lvert \mathbf{x} \rangle\}_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3}$ form an
improper basis of $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$. Each
$\lvert \mathbf{x} \rangle$ corresponds to a sharply-localised event at
spatial point $\mathbf{x}$: the wavefunction is concentrated at one
point with zero spatial extent. This is the particle (P) reading:
localised registration of a discrete event.

**Step 2: Momentum eigenbasis (W reading).** By
Lemma [6.3](#lem:momentum-planewave){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:momentum-planewave"}, the momentum eigenstates
$\{\lvert \mathbf{p} \rangle\}_{\mathbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^3}$ form an
improper basis of $\mathcal{H}$. Each $\lvert \mathbf{p} \rangle$
corresponds to an extended plane wave
$e^{i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}$ of constant amplitude across
$\mathbb{R}^3$ with definite spatial wavevector
$\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{p}/\hbar$. This is the wave (W) reading:
extended-amplitude oscillation with definite wavelength.

**Step 3: Both bases are complete on the same $\mathcal{H}$.** By
Lemma [6.4](#lem:fourier-conjugate){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:fourier-conjugate"}, both the position and momentum
eigenbases are complete on the same Hilbert space
$\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$. Every wavefunction
$\psi \in \mathcal{H}$ admits two equivalent expansions:
$$\psi = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} d^3\mathbf{x}\,\psi(\mathbf{x})\,\lvert \mathbf{x} \rangle \quad\text{(P expansion)}; \qquad \psi = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} d^3\mathbf{p}\,\tilde\psi(\mathbf{p})\,\lvert \mathbf{p} \rangle \quad\text{(W expansion)}.$$
The two expansions are related by the unitary Fourier transform:
$\tilde\psi(\mathbf{p}) = (\mathcal{F}\psi)(\mathbf{p}) = (2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\int e^{-i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}\psi(\mathbf{x})\,d^3\mathbf{x}$.

**Step 4: Same Hilbert-space vector, two decompositions.** The crucial
fact is that the P and W expansions have the reading of two decompositions of *the same* Hilbert-space vector
$\psi \in \mathcal{H}$, with the role of two distinct objects replaced
by the role of two basis-decompositions of one underlying state. The
wave-particle duality has the reading of a duality between
two complete decompositions of one underlying quantum state, with the
role of a duality between two different physical entities replaced by
the role of a representation-choice between two Fourier-conjugate
complete bases. The \"duality\" disappears at the level of the abstract
Hilbert-space vector and reappears at the level of representation
choice.

**Step 5: Parallel to the McGucken Sphere.** This
Hilbert-space duality has a direct geometric parallel: the McGucken
Sphere $S_p$ at source event $p$ has the apex reading (P,
sharply-localised source event at $p$) and the wavefront reading (W,
extended 2-sphere $M^{+}_{p}(t)$ at lab time $t$) simultaneously
(Lemma [6.6](#lem:sphere-apex-wavefront){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:sphere-apex-wavefront"}). The position eigenbasis of
$\mathcal{H}$ is the Algebraic Channel image of the Sphere's apex reading; the
momentum eigenbasis is the Algebraic Channel image of the Sphere's wavefront
reading. Both readings are forced by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at the
source event $p$.

**Step 6: Algebraic Channel characterisation.** The derivation uses
Hilbert-space tensor structure
(Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}), the spectral theorem
(Theorem [3.5](#thm:spectral){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:spectral"}) for $\hat{q}$ and $\hat{p}$, and the
Plancherel theorem (Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Theorem IX.1) on
$L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$. All ingredients are algebraic-symmetry machinery;
no Sphere-geometric machinery (Huygens iteration, Compton phase,
geometric apex/wavefront duality) is invoked. The proof is Algebraic Channel,
derivationally disjoint from the Geometric Channel Sphere apex/wavefront route of
Lemma [6.7](#lem:QMT6-channelB-proof){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT6-channelB-proof"}.

**McGucken anchoring.** The dual basis structure
$\mathcal{H}= \overline{\mathrm{span}}\{\lvert \mathbf{x} \rangle\} = \overline{\mathrm{span}}\{\lvert \mathbf{p} \rangle\}$
is the Algebraic Channel shadow of the McGucken Sphere's geometric duality. The
textbook framing of wave-particle duality as a paradox ("how can the
electron be both a wave and a particle?") treats P and W as alternative
ontological categories; the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework shows they are two
complete representations of one Hilbert-space vector, which is itself a
theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. ◻
:::

### Resolving the classic experiments

The duality resolution removes the apparent paradoxes of the
quantum experiments:

-   **Double-slit.** Each electron sources a McGucken Sphere whose
    wavefront passes through both slits. The interference pattern is the
    wavefront's amplitude distribution on the screen (W); the detection
    events at the screen are sharp registrations (P). Both are correct
    readings of the Sphere ---
    Lemma [6.6](#lem:sphere-apex-wavefront){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:sphere-apex-wavefront"}.

-   **Delayed-choice (Wheeler).** The Sphere's wavefront extends across
    the experimental region regardless of when the observer chooses to
    register. The choice does not change the past; it selects which
    reading --- W or P --- to extract from the Sphere at the moment of
    measurement.

-   **Quantum eraser.** Erasing the which-path information restores the
    W reading; the wavefront amplitudes were always there. The
    which-path measurement merely projected to the P reading, and
    erasure unprojects.

A formal treatment of each experiment is given in
[@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026] (the six-fold geometric identity of the
wavefront), reproduced in
Chapter [17](#ch:nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:nonlocality"}.

### Disjointness audit

**Geometric Channel:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, McGucken Sphere construction
(QB1), apex/wavefront geometric duality
(Lemma [6.6](#lem:sphere-apex-wavefront){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:sphere-apex-wavefront"}), Sphere geometry.

**Algebraic Channel:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, Stone's theorem (QA2) applied
to spatial translation
(Lemma [2.2](#lem:phat-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-generator"}), position and momentum eigenbases as
Fourier-conjugate decompositions
(Lemmas [6.2](#lem:position-localized){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:position-localized"}--[6.4](#lem:fourier-conjugate){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:fourier-conjugate"}), Plancherel theorem.

**Intersection:**
$\{(\mathrm{McP}), \text{wave--particle duality holds}\}$. No item of
Algebraic Channel's Fourier/Plancherel set appears in Geometric Channel; no item of
Geometric Channel's Sphere-geometric set appears in Algebraic Channel. *Disjointness
verified.*

### Empirical anchor

Double-slit experiments with light (Young 1801), electrons
(Davisson--Germer 1927 [@Davisson1927], Jönsson 1961), neutrons
(Zeilinger et al. 1988), atoms, and molecules up to
$\sim 25\,\text{kDa}$ (Fein et al. 2019 [@Fein2019]). Delayed-choice
variants (Hellmuth, Walther et al. 1987; Jacques et al. 2007). Quantum
eraser (Walborn et al. 2002).

### The three-part ontology and the dissolution of wave--particle duality {#sec:three-part-ontology}

::: {#thm:three-part-ontology .theorem}
**Theorem 6.8** (Three-part ontology of quantum entities under
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; [@MG-deBroglie-2026] §VI.1). *A quantum entity
in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework consists of three aspects, all of
which are theorems of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$:*

1.  **The McGucken Sphere.* The 3D spatial cross-section of $x_{4}$'s
    spherical expansion from the emission event
    $p_0 = (\mathbf{x}_0, t_0)$ at any later time $t > t_0$ is a
    2-sphere of radius $c(t - t_0)$ in the 3D spatial slice. For photons
    (null worldline), the entity's 3D amplitude support is *on* this
    sphere; for massive particles (timelike worldline), the entity's
    amplitude support is *inside* the forward light cone of $p_0$, since
    the particle's 3D velocity is $< c$. The sphere is a physical
    geometric object: the surface of $x_{4}$'s expansion in 3D, as
    established by clauses (i)--(iii) of
    Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
    reference="postulate:mcp"}.*

2.  **The oscillatory amplitude on the sphere.* The McGucken-Sphere
    wavefront carries a complex amplitude $\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)$ with
    phase $e^{iS/\hbar}$, where $S$ is the classical action along the
    worldline from emission $p_0$ to the point $(\mathbf{x}, t)$ on the
    sphere (Theorem [15.1](#thm:QMT15){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT15"}, the path-integral theorem). The amplitude
    oscillates at the frequency $\omega$ appropriate to the emission
    process: $\omega = ck$ for photons (null wavefront,
    Theorem [2.1](#thm:QMT2){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT2"}), $\omega = \gamma\omega_C$ for massive
    particles in the boosted frame
    (Theorem [2.7](#thm:phase-group-velocity-geometric){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:phase-group-velocity-geometric"}, Step 2). The
    amplitude has the reading of a physical oscillation phase
    and magnitude of $x_{4}$ at each 3D point on the sphere, with the
    role of a purely calculational amplitude replaced by the role of a
    geometric content of the $x_{4}$-advance under
    Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
    reference="postulate:mcp"}.*

3.  **The localisation event.* When the McGucken Sphere interacts with a
    3D measurement apparatus, the sphere-wide amplitude is reduced to a
    single 3D point --- the localisation event at which the measurement
    registers. The probability density of the localisation event at
    position $\mathbf{x}$ is the Born density
    (Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"})
    $$P(\mathbf{x}) \;=\; |\psi(\mathbf{x})|^2,$$ which is the squared
    amplitude on the sphere at that point. The localisation is the 3D-cross-section projection of the sphere-wide oscillatory structure onto a single 3D
    detection point, with the probability distribution fixed by
    $|\psi|^2$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The proof has four steps establishing each aspect
from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

**Step 1: (O1) from clauses (i)--(iii) of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.**
The McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ at event $p_0$ and later time $t$
is the set of 3D-spatial points reachable from $p_0$ in the proper time
$\tau = t - t_0$ by $x_{4}$-advance at the McGucken rate $c$. By clause
(i) of Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} (invariance), the rate is $c$ at every event;
by clause (ii) (spherical symmetry), the set of reachable points at
proper time $\tau$ is a 2-sphere of radius $c\tau$ centered at $p_0$; by
clause (iii) (monotonicity), the sphere advances forward in $t$. Thus
$$M^{+}_{p_0}(t) \;=\; \bigl\{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 : |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0| = c(t - t_0)\bigr\},$$
a physical 2-sphere in the 3D slice. For photons on the null geodesic,
the amplitude support is the full 2-sphere; for massive particles on
timelike worldlines (3D velocity $< c$), the amplitude support is
restricted to the closed 3-ball of radius $c(t - t_0)$ inside the
forward light cone.

**Step 2: (O2) from the path-integral theorem.** By
Theorem [15.1](#thm:QMT15){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT15"}
(Feynman path integral, derived along Geometric Channel from Huygens-iterated
McGucken-Sphere wavefronts), the wavefunction at $(\mathbf{x}, t)$ is
the sum over all worldlines from $p_0$ to $(\mathbf{x}, t)$ of the phase
factor $e^{iS[\gamma]/\hbar}$:
$$\psi(\mathbf{x}, t) \;=\; \int_{\gamma: p_0 \to (\mathbf{x}, t)} e^{iS[\gamma]/\hbar}\,\mathcal{D}[\gamma],$$
where $S[\gamma]$ is the classical action along path $\gamma$ and the
integration is over all paths (the Feynman path-integral measure
$\mathcal{D}[\gamma]$). The phase rate $S/\hbar$ accumulates as
$\omega t$ in the temporal direction (with $\omega = E/\hbar$,
Theorem [3.1](#thm:QMT3){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT3"}) and
as $\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}$ in the spatial direction (with
$\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{p}/\hbar$,
Theorem [2.1](#thm:QMT2){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT2"}),
giving the local plane-wave form
$e^{i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x} - \omega t)}$ on the Sphere wavefront
(Lemma [2.5](#lem:plane-wave-limit){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:plane-wave-limit"}). The amplitude is the geometric
content of $x_{4}$'s oscillatory advance: each point on the McGucken
Sphere carries the integrated phase from $p_0$, and the oscillation at
$\omega$ is the physical advance of $x_{4}$ at the Compton-coupling rate
(Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT4"}).

**Step 3: (O3) from the Born rule.** By
Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"} (Born rule, derived along Geometric Channel from
$SO(3)$-Haar measure on the McGucken-Sphere wavefront), the probability
density for localisation at $\mathbf{x}$ is $|\psi(\mathbf{x})|^2$. The
localisation event itself is the 3D-cross-section projection of the 4D
wavefunction $\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_{4})$ at the McGucken-constraint locus
$x_{4}= ict$ onto the 3D spatial slice at the detection time
(Theorem [19.1](#thm:QMT19){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT19"},
Measurement). The probability that the projection lands at $\mathbf{x}$
is fixed by the squared amplitude.

**Step 4: Single geometric process.** The three aspects (O1)--(O3) have
the reading of three moments of one geometric
process: $x_{4}$'s spherical expansion from $p_0$ at rate $c$ (O1)
carries an oscillatory amplitude (O2) which, upon 3D-cross-section
interaction with a measurement apparatus, produces a localisation event
(O3), with the role of three independent objects replaced by the role of
three temporal/moments of a single
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$-generated process. The sphere, the amplitude,
and the localisation are the pre-measurement, mid-measurement, and
post-measurement aspects of the same geometric advance. They share a
single source event $p_0$, a single $x_{4}$-expansion rate $c$, and a
single $\hbar$-per-cycle action unit. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#thm:duality-dissolved .theorem}
**Theorem 6.9** (Wave--particle duality dissolved as
pre-/post-localisation aspects of the McGucken Sphere;
[@MG-deBroglie-2026] §VI.2). *Under the three-part ontology of
Theorem [6.8](#thm:three-part-ontology){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:three-part-ontology"}, the "wave" of wave--particle
duality has the reading of the McGucken Sphere with its
oscillatory amplitude --- aspects (O1) + (O2) of
Theorem [6.8](#thm:three-part-ontology){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:three-part-ontology"}; the "particle" has the reading of the localisation event --- aspect (O3). The wave and the
particle have the role of the pre-localisation and post-localisation
aspects of one geometric process: $x_{4}$'s expansion at $c$ from the
source event, with $\hbar$-per-cycle action quantization, projected onto
a 3D detection point by measurement, with the role of two distinct
mysteriously-coexisting entities replaced by the role of two temporal
aspects of a single $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$-generated process.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The proof has five steps. The wave--particle duality of
standard QM is dissolved by recognising that $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, the physical, geometric fact that the fourth
dimension expands at the velocity of light in a spherically symmetric
manner, with $x_4 = ict$ as the integrated kinematic shadow per
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) supplies both the extended-wave
aspect (the McGucken Sphere wavefront generated by $x_{4}$-expansion at
every event, per Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (ii) spherical symmetry) and the
localised-particle aspect (the 3D-cross-section projection of the Sphere
amplitude at the McGucken-constraint locus, with Born statistics by
Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"}).

**Step 1: "Wave" as (O1) + (O2).** What appears in matter-wave
interferometry as the "matter wave" --- the spatial wavefunction
$\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)$ whose phase coherence produces double-slit
interference, Davisson--Germer electron diffraction, and the matter-wave
interference patterns of cold-atom and molecular interferometry --- is,
in the three-part ontology, the McGucken Sphere with its oscillatory
amplitude. The wave is physically extended over the 3D-spatial slice
(the 2-sphere $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ for photons; the 3-ball interior for
massive particles), with the local plane-wave structure
$e^{i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x} - \omega t)}$ produced by the Sphere's
local oscillation at the appropriate frequency
(Lemma [2.5](#lem:plane-wave-limit){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:plane-wave-limit"}). The wavefront is generated by
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (ii) (spherical symmetry of the
$x_{4}$-expansion: the set of events reachable from a source $p_0$ in
proper time $\tau$ is a 2-sphere of radius $c\tau$), with the Compton
frequency $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ supplying the matter-wave oscillation
rate (Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT4"}).

**Step 2: "Particle" as (O3).** What appears in matter-wave
interferometry as the "particle" --- the discrete, pointlike, localised
detection events that build up the matter-wave interference pattern
statistically --- has the reading of the localisation event
of (O3). Before measurement, the entity has the reading of
the full extended McGucken Sphere amplitude, with the role of a
pre-measurement pointlike particle replaced by the role of an extended
wavefront amplitude. The localisation occurs at the moment of
3D-cross-section interaction with the detector, with the probability
distribution $|\psi|^2$ (Born rule).

**Step 3: No tension between (1) and (2).** The wave aspect (extended
McGucken Sphere amplitude) and the particle aspect (localised 3D
detection) are not in tension because they describe *different temporal
phases* of the same process. Before measurement: extended Sphere
amplitude (wave). At measurement: 3D-cross-section projection to a
localisation event (particle). The "duality" of standard quantum
mechanics, which treats the wave as an abstract amplitude $\psi$ without
specified physical referent and the particle as a point mass without
geometric mechanism, is dissolved by identifying the wave with the
physical McGucken Sphere and the particle with its 3D-cross-section
projection.

**Step 4: All matter-wave experiments confirm both aspects.** Every
matter-wave experiment from Young 1801 (light) through Davisson--Germer
1927 (electrons) to Fein et al. 2019 (molecules up to $\sim 25$ kDa)
confirms both aspects simultaneously:

-   The *wave* aspect produces the interference pattern across the
    screen: the McGucken Sphere amplitude with phase
    $e^{i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x} - \omega t)}$ is extended over the
    screen surface and interferes coherently between the two slit paths;

-   The *particle* aspect produces the localised detection events: each
    detection is a single 3D-cross-section projection, with probability
    density $|\psi|^2$ summed over the two slit paths.

The interference pattern is the statistical accumulation of many
localisation events with probabilities fixed by the squared amplitude.

**Step 5: No paradox.** The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework account dissolves what
was historically presented as a paradox: matter is *not*
sometimes-a-wave and sometimes-a-particle in alternation, with
measurement choosing one or the other; matter is the McGucken Sphere
with oscillatory amplitude (wave) whose 3D-cross-section interaction
with a detector produces the localisation event (particle). Both aspects
are physically real, both are consequences of the same geometric
principle $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, and the apparent "duality" is the
fact that one geometric object has two distinguishable
observational signatures: the extended wave (in coherent propagation
between measurements) and the localised detection (at measurement).
$\square$ ◻
:::

### Double-slit, delayed-choice, and quantum-eraser experiments inside a single McGucken Sphere {#sec:double-slit-eraser-unified}

The three-part ontology of
Theorem [6.8](#thm:three-part-ontology){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:three-part-ontology"} dissolves not only wave--particle
duality but also the apparent paradoxes of the three classic
interpretational puzzles --- the double-slit experiment, Wheeler's
delayed-choice experiment, and the quantum-eraser experiment. All three
take place within the confines of one McGucken Sphere centered on the
emission event [@MG-deBroglie-2026] §VI.3; the apparent paradoxes
dissolve once the full 4D geometry is recognized.

::: {#prop:double-slit-as-mcgucken-sphere .proposition}
**Proposition 6.10** (Double-slit interference as McGucken-Sphere
amplitude propagation; [@MG-deBroglie-2026] §VI.3.1). *A double-slit
experiment is the propagation of a single McGucken Sphere
$M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ from a source event $p_0$ through both slits to the
detection screen, with the interference pattern at the screen arising
from the coherent superposition of the two Huygens-secondary-wavefront
amplitudes from the two slits.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* **Step 1: One emission, one McGucken Sphere.** The particle
(photon, electron, neutron, atom, molecule) is emitted at a single event
$p_0$. By Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, $x_{4}$ expands spherically from $p_0$ at
rate $c$, producing a single McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$. The
wavefront at any later time $t$ is the 2-sphere of radius $c(t - t_0)$
centered at $\mathbf{x}_0$ (or its 3-ball interior for massive
particles).

**Step 2: Huygens' Principle at the barrier.** When the McGucken Sphere
wavefront encounters the barrier with two slits at locations
$\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2$, the principle of Huygens
(Theorem [1.1](#thm:QMT1){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT1"},
Geometric Channel) applies: each point on the wavefront where the barrier is
open acts as a secondary source of new spherical wavelets. The two slits
are the only open regions; they become the two secondary sources, and
from each a new McGucken Sphere expands into the region beyond the
barrier:
$$M^{+}_{p_0}(t) \;\longrightarrow\; M^{+}_{(\mathbf{a}_1, t_1)}(t) \;+\; M^{+}_{(\mathbf{a}_2, t_1)}(t),$$
where $t_1$ is the time the wavefront reached the slits.

**Step 3: Coherent superposition at the screen.** At any point
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{screen}}$ on the detection screen, the amplitude is
the sum of the path-integral phase contributions from the two secondary
spheres:
$$\psi(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{screen}}, t) \;=\; A_1 e^{iS_1/\hbar} + A_2 e^{iS_2/\hbar},$$
where $S_1, S_2$ are the classical actions along the two paths
($p_0 \to \mathbf{a}_1 \to \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{screen}}$ and
$p_0 \to \mathbf{a}_2 \to \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{screen}}$) and $A_1, A_2$
are slowly-varying amplitudes. The phase $e^{iS/\hbar}$ on each path is
the integrated Sphere phase along the path, with the imaginary unit $i$
in the exponent being the same $i$ as in $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via
Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"} case 2 (the $x_{4}$-perpendicularity marker
carried into the propagator phase via the Compton-frequency phase
mechanism of Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT4"}). The Born density $|\psi|^2$
(Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"}) has the interference cross-term:
$$|\psi|^2 \;=\; |A_1|^2 + |A_2|^2 + 2|A_1||A_2|\cos\bigl((S_1 - S_2)/\hbar\bigr),$$
producing constructive (bright fringes) and destructive (dark fringes)
interference as $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{screen}}$ varies.

**Step 4: "Both slits at once" as McGucken-Sphere geometry.** The
classical paradox --- "how can a single particle pass through both
slits?" --- dissolves: the entity has the reading of an
extended McGucken Sphere amplitude, physically distributed across the
wavefront and therefore present at both slits simultaneously, with the
role of a pointlike particle that must choose one slit replaced by the
role of a spatially-extended wavefront that intersects both open slits.
The presence of the wavefront at both slits has the reading
of a geometric fact about the McGucken-Sphere wavefront's spatial extent
in 3D, with the role of a particle-level choice between two slits
replaced by the role of a geometric intersection of the wavefront with
both open slits. The two Huygens-secondary spheres are launched from
both slits by the action of the extended wavefront on the barrier, with
no division of any pointlike particle required. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#prop:delayed-choice-as-mcgucken-sphere .proposition}
**Proposition 6.11** (Wheeler delayed-choice experiment: no
retrocausality, only McGucken-Sphere geometry; [@MG-deBroglie-2026]
§VI.3.2). *In Wheeler's delayed-choice experiment, no past behaviour of
the particle is changed by future measurement choice. The entire
experiment --- emission, slit passage, delayed measurement choice,
detection --- takes place within a single McGucken Sphere, and what 3D observers describe as "the past" is separated from the detection event by zero accumulated $x_{4}$-advance along the Sphere's null wavefront.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The proof has five steps. The delayed-choice paradox dissolves
under $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, the physical, geometric fact that the fourth
dimension expands at the velocity of light in a spherically symmetric
manner): the photon's null worldline collapses all events on a single
McGucken Sphere to zero proper-time separation
(Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT4"},
with $x_4 = ict$ the integrated kinematic shadow per
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}), eliminating any invariant temporal ordering between "slit passage" and "measurement choice": no $x_{4}$-advance accumulates between them along the wavefront.

**Step 1: Wheeler's apparent paradox.** Wheeler's 1978 thought
experiment (experimentally realized by Jacques et al., *Science*
**315**, 966 (2007)) asks: what if the decision to observe "which path"
or "interference" is made after the particle has already passed through
the slits? Naively, this would mean the particle's past behaviour
(wave-like or particle-like) is determined by a future measurement
choice --- an apparent retroactive influence.

**Step 2: No past behaviour changes.** In the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, the
past behaviour of the particle is not changed by the future measurement
choice. The McGucken Sphere amplitude propagates through both slits at
$t_1$ (the slit-passage time) regardless of what happens later, by
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (ii) (spherical symmetry of the
$x_{4}$-expansion: the wavefront propagates isotropically from every
event independent of any later measurement choice). The amplitude
carries the full Huygens-iterated structure of
Proposition [6.10](#prop:double-slit-as-mcgucken-sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:double-slit-as-mcgucken-sphere"} between $t_1$ and the
detection time $t_d$, with the propagation governed by
Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT7"}
(Schrödinger equation as a deterministic linear evolution).

**Step 3: The measurement choice selects which aspect is revealed.** The
measurement choice at $t_d$ determines which aspect of the
McGucken-Sphere geometry is revealed at the detection point, not which
aspect existed before the choice:

-   If the detector is configured to observe interference (no which-path
    information), the two Huygens-secondary amplitudes contribute
    coherently to the propagator at the detection point and fringes
    appear;

-   If the detector is configured to observe which-path information (a
    screen-side instrument that distinguishes paths), the two amplitudes
    carry distinguishable $x_{4}$-phases that cannot interfere and no
    fringes appear.

In both cases, the McGucken Sphere amplitude was present at both slits
throughout; only the readout differs.

**Step 4: The photon's share of the expansion is zero, so no $x_{4}$-advance accumulates.** The Sphere expands at $c$ from the emission event by Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref" reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i)--(ii), and the partition of any worldline's rate between spatial motion and $x_{4}$-advance gives the photon's share by direct substitution of $v = c$: $v_{x_4} = \sqrt{c^{2} - v^{2}} = 0$. The accumulated $x_{4}$-advance $X_{4} = \int ic\,d\tau$ is therefore constant along the photon's worldline, and the emission event, the slit-passage events, the delayed-choice event, and the detection event all sit at the same $X_{4}$. No invariant temporal ordering separates "passing through the slits" from "choosing the measurement." The apparent paradox of delayed choice arises from imposing a 3D-observer temporal ordering on a 4D geometric process whose events carry no invariant order.

**Step 5: No retrocausality.** What appears to a 3D observer as "the
past behavior of the particle was determined by a future measurement
choice" is, in the full 4D geometry, the trivial statement that the same
McGucken Sphere amplitude is read differently by different measurement
configurations. No information propagates backward in time; no past
event is changed by a future event. The McGucken Sphere has the same
amplitude structure regardless of what measurement is later performed;
only the projection of the amplitude onto the detector differs.
$\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#prop:quantum-eraser-as-mcgucken-sphere .proposition}
**Proposition 6.12** (Quantum-eraser experiment: erasure on a shared
McGucken Sphere, not retroactive determination; [@MG-deBroglie-2026]
§VI.3.3). *In a quantum-eraser experiment with entangled photon pairs,
no future choice (to erase or not erase which-path information)
retroactively changes whether interference occurred in the past. The
entangled photon pairs share a common McGucken Sphere (since they were
created at the same local event), and the erasure changes which paths on
the shared sphere are allowed to interfere at the detection point, not
what happened in the past.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* **Step 1: Common creation event $\Rightarrow$ shared McGucken
Sphere.** Entangled photon pairs produced by spontaneous parametric
down-conversion (SPDC) at a nonlinear crystal are created at the same
local event $p_0$. By
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, both photons share the McGucken Sphere
$M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ centered on $p_0$. The "signal" photon and the "idler"
photon are both on the same $x_{4}$-wavefront; they share the Sphere's
geometric identity as a single null-hypersurface cross-section. This is
the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework content of the Bell-correlation source in
entangled-pair experiments
(Theorem [18.1](#thm:QMT18){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT18"}).

**Step 2: Erasure as path-distinguishability operation on the shared
Sphere.** In the Scully--Drühl quantum-eraser setup (Phys. Rev. A
**25**, 2208 (1982); Kim et al. Phys. Rev. Lett. **84**, 1 (2000)),
which-path information is first obtained via the idler photon and then
"erased" by measuring the idler in a complementary basis. In the
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, the which-path information is encoded in
distinguishable $x_{4}$-phases on the shared McGucken Sphere; the
erasure operation projects the idler photon onto a basis in which the
two slit-path phases become indistinguishable, restoring coherence
between them on the shared Sphere.

**Step 3: No retroactive change of past.** The McGucken Sphere amplitude
structure does not change as a function of the future erasure choice.
What changes is whether the two paths on the sphere are distinguishable
or indistinguishable at the joint detection event:

-   Before erasure (which-path information available): the two paths
    carry distinguishable $x_{4}$-phases on the shared Sphere; the joint
    amplitude $\psi_{\mathrm{signal}} \otimes \psi_{\mathrm{idler}}$ is
    a product structure with no coherent superposition; no interference;

-   After erasure (idler measured in complementary basis): the
    idler-side projection makes the two paths indistinguishable on the
    shared Sphere; the joint amplitude becomes a coherent superposition;
    interference restored in the conditioned subset.

The Sphere itself did not change; the projection onto the joint
detection event did.

**Step 4: Zero $x_{4}$-advance resolution.** As in the delayed-choice case
(Proposition [6.11](#prop:delayed-choice-as-mcgucken-sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:delayed-choice-as-mcgucken-sphere"}), no $x_{4}$-advance accumulates between the creation event $p_0$, the signal photon's detection, and the idler photon's measurement at the eraser: all three sit at the same $X_{4}$ on the shared Sphere and carry no invariant order in the full 4D geometry. The erasure
does not change the past; it selects which projection of the shared
Sphere is registered at the joint detection event. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:photon-frame-unifying .remark}
*Remark 6.13* (The photon-frame as the unifying insight). All three
experiments --- double-slit, delayed-choice, quantum-eraser --- take
place within McGucken Spheres, and all three apparent paradoxes
(simultaneous passage through both slits, retroactive determination of
past behaviour, retroactive erasure of which-path information) dissolve
by the same geometric fact: *along the null worldline the photon rides on the McGucken Sphere, no $x_{4}$-advance accumulates between any two events on the sphere*. What a 3D observer describes as "the past" in a quantum eraser experiment is separated from the present by zero $x_{4}$-advance; what is described as a great spatial separation is no separation
at all. The paradoxes live in the 3D projection; in the 4D geometry,
there are no paradoxes.
:::

## QM T7: The Schrödinger Equation {#ch:schrodinger}

> *The McGucken Principle.* The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality.
> Every result below descends from that expansion.


*Recall.* the McGucken Principle ($\mathrm{McP}$:
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$) asserts that the fourth spacetime dimension
$x_4$ expands at the velocity of light $c$, carrying the
perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguishes it from the spatial
three. Throughout this chapter, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ refers to this
principle and to the five-clause content (i)--(v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: (i) *invariance* --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content; (ii) *spherical symmetry* --- the
expansion is isotropic in the spatial three, with the set of events
reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a 2-sphere of radius
$c\tau$; (iii) *monotonicity* --- the integral curve is strictly
monotonically increasing in $t$, fixing the arrow of $x_4$-advance; (iv)
*Lorentz consistency* --- the structure is $SO^+(1,3)$-invariant on
$M_{G}$; (v) *global validity* --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at
every event of $M_{G}$. The integrated kinematic shadow
$x_4 = ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is the kinematic shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the central fact.

This chapter contains the central derivation of the McGucken treatment
of quantum mechanics. The Schrödinger equation, postulated in Sakurai
[@Sakurai2020], Shankar [@Shankar1994], Cohen-Tannoudji [@CT2019],
Weinberg [@Weinberg2015], and inserted by analogy in Griffiths
[@Griffiths2018], is here a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. We give
two derivationally disjoint derivations: a six-step Algebraic Channel proof via
Stone's theorem on the time-evolution unitary group, and an eight-step
Geometric Channel proof of Huygens propagation on the McGucken Sphere. Each step
is a formally stated lemma with a self-contained proof.

### Statement

::: {#thm:QMT7 .theorem}
**Theorem 7.1** (QM T7: Schrödinger Equation). *The non-relativistic
matter wavefunction $\psi(\mathbf{x}, t) : M_{G}\to \mathbb{C}$ of a
particle of mass $m$ in an external scalar potential $V(\mathbf{x})$
satisfies
$$i\hbar\,\partial_t\psi(\mathbf{x}, t) \;=\; \hat{H}\,\psi(\mathbf{x}, t), \qquad \hat{H}\;=\; -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2 + V(\mathbf{x}).
\label{eq:Schrodinger}$$ This is Theorem 66 (Geometric Channel) and Theorem 89
(Algebraic Channel) of [@Syn-2026].*
:::

### The Hamilton route as Geometric Channel heuristic: how Schrödinger reached the equation in 1926 {#sec:QMT7-hamilton-route}

The two derivationally disjoint derivations below recover Theorem
[7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT7"} along Algebraic
Channel and Geometric Channel routes from $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$. The historical record
of how the equation was first reached, by Erwin Schrödinger in
1926, is illuminating because it exhibits the same dual-channel
structure in nascent form, with Schrödinger employing Geometric Channel
reasoning as the heuristic route to an equation that was then
absorbed into Algebraic Channel within a year of its publication.

Schrödinger's route in 1926 began with a piece of mathematical physics
that had been sitting in the literature for ninety years without being
read as a principle. William Rowan Hamilton in the 1830s
had observed that the principle of least action in mechanics and
Fermat's principle in optics share a common mathematical structure:
both extremize an integral along paths, with the optical case
extremizing the optical path length and the mechanical case extremizing
the action. Hamilton showed further that the Hamilton--Jacobi equation
of mechanics --- a first-order partial differential equation for the
action $S(\mathbf{x}, t)$ as a function of position and time --- has
the same mathematical structure as the eikonal equation of geometrical
optics, which is the short-wavelength limit of a wave equation. The
eikonal equation describes ray paths as gradients of a phase function
in the limit where the wavelength is small compared to the geometric
features of the medium; the rays are the trajectories along which the
wavefronts propagate in the geometrical-optics limit. Hamilton's
analogy: classical mechanical trajectories are formally the rays of an
underlying wave theory, and the Hamilton--Jacobi equation is the
eikonal limit of that wave theory.

What Hamilton did not have, in the 1830s, was a wave theory of matter
of which the classical trajectories would be the rays. Hamilton's
analogy was understood as a formal mathematical equivalence between
two pieces of classical physics --- mechanics and geometrical optics
--- without empirical force as a claim about the actual nature of
matter. It sat in the literature for ninety years as a mathematical
curiosity.

Louis de Broglie in 1924 supplied the missing piece. His doctoral
thesis proposed that matter has wave character with wavelength
$\lambda = h/p$, where $p$ is the momentum and $h$ is Planck's
constant. The proposal was made on dimensional and grounds
--- light has both wave and particle character with $\lambda = h/p$
(via $p = h\nu/c = h/\lambda$); matter should have the same dual
character by analogy --- and Davisson and Germer would confirm it
experimentally in 1927 by electron diffraction off a nickel crystal.
With de Broglie's matter waves in hand, Hamilton's analogy became
physically substantive: if matter has wave character, then the
Hamilton--Jacobi equation might be the eikonal limit not of an
analogical wave theory but of an actual wave equation for matter.

Schrödinger took this idea seriously as a principle.
Through late 1925 and the first months of 1926 he asked the question
that would yield his equation: what wave equation has the
Hamilton--Jacobi equation as its short-wavelength limit and de
Broglie's matter waves as its plane-wave solutions? The construction
proceeds in three steps. First, write down a plane-wave ansatz
$\psi = A \exp(i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x} - \omega t))$ with
$\hbar \mathbf{k} = \mathbf{p}$ and $\hbar\omega = E$ (the de Broglie
relations). Second, require that the wave equation should, in the
short-wavelength limit, reduce to the classical Hamilton--Jacobi
equation $\partial_t S + \frac{(\nabla S)^2}{2m} + V = 0$, with
$S = \hbar \mathrm{phase}$ identified as the action up to a factor of
$\hbar$. Third, take the simplest linear differential operator whose
plane-wave solutions satisfy the dispersion relation
$\hbar\omega = (\hbar k)^2/(2m) + V$. The answer is
$i\hbar\,\partial_t\psi = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2\psi + V\psi$ ---
the Schrödinger equation.

Schrödinger's heuristic route is Geometric Channel reasoning throughout.
Hamilton's optico-mechanical analogy frames classical mechanics as a
short-wavelength limit of a wave-propagation theory in real space, with
classical trajectories as rays of an underlying wavefront propagation
--- precisely the Geometric Channel picture. de Broglie's matter waves supply
the wave-character of matter as an explicit wavefront structure in real
space, with wavelength $\lambda = h/p$ as a definite geometric
feature. The wave equation sought is the equation governing the
propagation of a real physical wave in spacetime, with classical
mechanics emerging as the eikonal limit. Schrödinger's intended reading
of $\psi$ in 1926 was Geometric Channel throughout: $\psi$ was a real physical
wave, the eigenfunctions were definite spatial structures of the
electron, and the wave equation governed the propagation of a real
physical entity in real space.

The institutional fate of Schrödinger's Geometric Channel reading was decided
within months. Max Born in June 1926 [@Born1926] reinterpreted
$|\psi|^2$ as the probability density for finding the electron at
position $\mathbf{x}$, demoting $\psi$ itself from a real physical wave
to a calculational amplitude on configuration space whose role is to
generate measurement statistics. Niels Bohr in 1927 elevated Born's
probabilistic reading to the principle of complementarity:
$\psi$ is to be read as an algebraic object whose role is to encode what can be said about
measurement outcomes. Werner Heisenberg incorporated Schrödinger's
equation into the matrix-mechanics framework by showing the formal
equivalence of the two formulations [@Heisenberg1926-Equivalence],
relocating the equation from Schrödinger's intended Geometric Channel
ontology into Heisenberg's Algebraic Channel operator-algebraic framework.

By the end of 1927, the Geometric Channel scaffolding that had carried
Schrödinger to his equation --- Hamilton's optico-mechanical analogy,
de Broglie's matter waves, the eikonal limit of a wave equation,
$\psi$ as a real physical wave --- had been removed, with the equation
itself reabsorbed into Algebraic Channel as a piece of operator-algebraic
machinery whose physical content was to be read through the projection
postulate and the Born rule rather than through the wave-propagation
geometry. Schrödinger objected to this reinterpretation publicly and
in correspondence throughout the remainder of his career, insisting
that his equation had been derived as a description of a real physical
wave and that the Algebraic Channel reading had stripped it of its intended
content. The orthodox tradition treated his objection as
philosophical rather than derivational --- a personal preference for a
different interpretation of an empirically settled formalism.

The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework supplies, retrospectively, the missing
foundational piece that would have justified Schrödinger's intended
Geometric Channel reading and prevented the absorption into Algebraic Channel. The
piece is the geometric principle $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ that supplies
the McGucken Sphere as the wavefront on which $\psi$ has its physical
referent. With the principle in hand, Schrödinger's wavefunction
acquires the geometric content he intended: $\psi$ is the algebraic
encoding, through the suppression map $\sigma$, of a wavefront on the
McGucken Sphere $\Sphere_p^+$ expanding at $+ic$ from the source event
$p$. The Geometric Channel derivation below
(§[\[sec:QMT7-channelB\]](#sec:QMT7-channelB){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:QMT7-channelB"}) makes the construction explicit by
deriving the Schrödinger equation as the first-order expansion of the
short-time iterated McGucken-Sphere Huygens propagator. The Hamilton
route that Schrödinger employed as heuristic in 1926 becomes, in the
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, an authentic Geometric Channel derivation: the iterated
Huygens propagation on the Sphere is the wave equation whose eikonal
limit is the Hamilton--Jacobi equation and whose plane-wave solutions
are the de Broglie matter waves. The historical Geometric Channel route was
not wrong; it was incomplete. The completion is $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$,
and the completion supplies, ninety years after Hamilton and one
hundred years after Schrödinger, the principle that
justifies the Geometric Channel reading of the equation as a description of
a real physical wave on the McGucken Sphere.

::: {#rmk:schrodinger-vindicated .remark}
*Remark 7.A* (Schrödinger's intended reading vindicated). *The Geometric
Channel derivation of the Schrödinger equation below recovers Schrödinger's
intended reading without compromise. The wavefunction
$\psi$ has its physical referent as wavefront content on the McGucken
Sphere expanding at $+ic$ from a source event. The Algebraic Channel
operator-algebraic apparatus reaches the same equation by Stone's
theorem applied to time-translation invariance, with the same
mathematical content but a different physical referent. The
equivalence of the two routes is the derivational-disjointness theorem;
the equivalence of the two readings as derivations from
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt}=ic$ is the dual-channel content of QM T7. Born's
probabilistic reading is preserved as the Algebraic Channel reading of
$|\psi|^2$ as detection statistics; Schrödinger's wave reading is
preserved as the Geometric Channel reading of $\psi$ as the algebraic encoding
of the Sphere wavefront. The seventy-year contest between Born and
Schrödinger over the physical content of $\psi$ dissolves into a
integration in which both readings hold simultaneously as
derivations from a single physical principle.*
:::

### Geometric Channel derivation: Iterated McGucken-Sphere Huygens propagation {#sec:QMT7-channelB}

This is the central Geometric Channel derivation: the Schrödinger equation as
the first-order $\varepsilon$-expansion of the short-time iterated
McGucken-Sphere propagator. We follow Theorem 89 of [@Syn-2026] in seven
explicit lemmas.

::: {#lem:sphere-and-huygens .lemma}
**Lemma 7.7** (Sphere generation and Huygens secondary wavelets). *At
each event $p = (\mathbf{x}_0, t_0)$ along the worldline of a matter
particle, the McGucken Sphere of radius $c\varepsilon$ expands
isotropically at $c$ during proper-time interval $\varepsilon$. Each
point of the wavefront at $t_0 + \varepsilon$ is itself a
Huygens-secondary source emitting an outgoing Sphere of radius
$c\varepsilon'$ during the next proper-time interval $\varepsilon'$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **Step 1: Sphere generation at $p$ (QB1).** By
Definition [4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:sphere"} of
Chapter [4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:foundations"}, the McGucken Principle
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at event $p = (\mathbf{x}_0, t_0)$ initiates
the spherically symmetric $x_{4}$-expansion at rate $c$ sourced at $p$.
The spatial trace of this expansion at the slightly advanced lab time
$t_0 + \varepsilon$ (for small proper-time interval $\varepsilon > 0$)
is the set of points reached by propagation at rate $c$ from
$\mathbf{x}_0$ in time $\varepsilon$:
$$M^{+}_{p}(t_0 + \varepsilon) = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 : |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0| = c\varepsilon\},$$
which is a 2-sphere of radius $c\varepsilon$ centred at $\mathbf{x}_0$.
This is the McGucken-Sphere wavefront at the short time $\varepsilon$
after the source event.

**Step 2: $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ applies at every event (P1).** By
clause (P1) of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, the principle takes the same
form at every event of $M_{G}$. In particular, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
holds at every point $q \in M^{+}_{p}(t_0 + \varepsilon)$ on the
wavefront with the same value $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}(q) = ic$ as at the
original source event $p$. Each such $q$ is therefore a source from
which the principle generates a new McGucken Sphere $S_q$.

**Step 3: Secondary Sphere from each wavefront point.** Applying
Definition [4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:sphere"} at $q$ produces a secondary McGucken Sphere
$S_q$ with apex at $q$. After a further proper-time interval
$\varepsilon'$, the wavefront of $S_q$ is
$$M^{+}_{q}((t_0 + \varepsilon) + \varepsilon') = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 : |\mathbf{x} - q| = c\varepsilon'\},$$
a 2-sphere of radius $c\varepsilon'$ centred at $q$. This is the
secondary Huygens wavelet from the wavefront point $q$.

**Step 4: Huygens envelope reconstructs the next-generation wavefront.**
By Proposition [4.11](#prop:iter){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:iter"} (Iterative composition of the Sphere, established
as a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$), the union of secondary
spheres
$$\bigcup_{q \in M^{+}_{p}(t_0 + \varepsilon)}M^{+}_{q}((t_0 + \varepsilon) + \varepsilon')$$
has as its outer envelope the 2-sphere of radius
$c(\varepsilon + \varepsilon')$ centred at $\mathbf{x}_0$ --- exactly
$M^{+}_{p}(t_0 + \varepsilon + \varepsilon')$. The next-generation
wavefront is reconstructed from the secondary wavelets; this is Huygens'
principle applied to $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

**Step 5: Iteration generates the path space.** Iterating the Huygens
construction $N$ times with time-steps
$\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2, \ldots, \varepsilon_N$ produces a network
of $N$-stage descents from the original source event. Each stage chooses
a secondary source from the current wavefront; the collection of all
such $N$-stage paths is the iterated-Sphere path space. In the limit
$N \to \infty$, $\max_n\varepsilon_n \to 0$ with fixed total time
$\sum_n\varepsilon_n = t - t_0$, the path space becomes the Feynman
path-integral space --- the configuration space for the path-integral
formulation of quantum mechanics (QB3, axiomatised in
Chapter [4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:foundations"}).

**Step 6: Geometric Channel characterisation.** The derivation uses only
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (clauses P1: principle applies at every event;
P2: rate $ic$ at every event; P3: spherical symmetry of
$x_{4}$-expansion) and the Sphere construction
(Definition [4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:sphere"}). No Stone's theorem, no spectral theorem, no
abstract Hilbert-space machinery is invoked; the entire structure is
geometric, descending from the principle at every event. The result is
Geometric Channel --- the geometric-propagation channel that this Lemma
initiates and that flows downstream to the Schrödinger equation
derivation in
Lemma [7.12](#lem:QMT7-channelB-proof){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT7-channelB-proof"}.

**McGucken anchoring.** The two ingredients in Huygens-Sphere
propagation are (i) the rate $c$ (forced by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$),
and (ii) the principle's applicability at every event (clause P1). Both
are direct content of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; neither is an external
geometric input. Huygens' principle, traditionally treated as a
phenomenological rule for wave propagation, is here a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. ◻
:::

::: {#lem:compton-phase-wavelet .lemma}
**Lemma 7.8** (Compton phase per Huygens wavelet). *For a
non-relativistic particle of mass $m$ in a potential $V$, each
Huygens-secondary wavelet from $\mathbf{x}'$ to $\mathbf{x}$ in proper
time $\varepsilon$ accumulates a quantum-mechanical phase
$$\Delta\theta = \frac{S[\gamma]}{\hbar}, \quad S[\gamma] = \frac{m(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')^2}{2\varepsilon} - V\!\left(\tfrac{\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{x}'}{2}\right)\varepsilon,$$
where $S[\gamma]$ is the classical action of the straight-line path
$\gamma$ from $\mathbf{x}'$ to $\mathbf{x}$ in time $\varepsilon$
(midpoint rule for the potential).*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has four steps: (1) compute the classical action of
the straight-line path; (2) derive the rest-frame Compton-phase rule
from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; (3) Lorentz-boost the rest-frame rule to
the moving frame, obtaining the general action-to-phase rule
$\Delta\theta = S[\gamma]/\hbar$; (4) trace every constant to its
McGucken origin.

**Step 1: Action of the classical straight-line path.** The
non-relativistic Lagrangian of a particle of mass $m$ in a scalar
potential $V$ is $L = \tfrac{1}{2}m\dot{\mathbf{x}}^2 - V(\mathbf{x})$.
The straight-line path from $\mathbf{x}'$ to $\mathbf{x}$ in proper-time
interval $\varepsilon$ is
$\gamma(\tau) = \mathbf{x}' + (\tau/\varepsilon)(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')$
for $\tau \in [0, \varepsilon]$, with constant velocity
$\dot\gamma = (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')/\varepsilon$. The action along
$\gamma$ is
$$S[\gamma] \;=\; \int_0^\varepsilon L\bigl(\gamma(\tau), \dot\gamma(\tau)\bigr)\,d\tau \;=\; \int_0^\varepsilon\!\Bigl[\,\tfrac{m}{2}\Bigl(\frac{\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)^{\!2} \,-\, V\bigl(\gamma(\tau)\bigr)\,\Bigr]\,d\tau.$$
The first integrand is constant in $\tau$, giving
$\frac{m(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}')^2}{2\varepsilon^2}\cdot\varepsilon = \frac{m(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}')^2}{2\varepsilon}$.
The second integrand is approximated for short $\varepsilon$ by the
midpoint value $V\!\bigl(\tfrac{\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{x}'}{2}\bigr)$ to
leading order (midpoint rule; the error is $O(\varepsilon^2)$ for
$V \in C^2$):
$$\int_0^\varepsilon V\bigl(\gamma(\tau)\bigr)\,d\tau \;=\; V\!\Bigl(\tfrac{\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{x}'}{2}\Bigr)\,\varepsilon + O(\varepsilon^3).$$
Therefore
$$S[\gamma] \;=\; \frac{m(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')^2}{2\varepsilon} \;-\; V\!\Bigl(\tfrac{\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{x}'}{2}\Bigr)\,\varepsilon \;+\; O(\varepsilon^3).$$
This is the explicit action; no McGucken machinery is invoked at this
step, only the classical Lagrangian and elementary calculus.

**Step 2: Rest-frame Compton-phase rule from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.**
In the rest frame of the particle, $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at the
source event generates a uniform $x_{4}$-advance at rate $ic$. By
Theorem [5.1](#thm:QMT5){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT5"}
(rest-mass phase factor), the rest-frame matter wavefunction carries the
Compton-frequency oscillation
$$\psi_{\mathrm{rest}}(\tau) \;=\; \psi_0\,\exp\!\bigl(-i\,\omega_C\,\tau\bigr), \qquad \omega_C \;=\; \frac{mc^2}{\hbar},$$
along proper time $\tau$, where $\omega_C$ is the Compton angular
frequency derived directly from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as follows. The
McGucken Sphere at the source event $p$ expands at rate $c$ in the
perpendicular $x_{4}$-direction; the integrated $x_{4}$-advance over
proper time $\tau$ is $x_4(\tau) = x_4(0) + ic\tau$, of magnitude
$|x_4(\tau) - x_4(0)| = c\tau$. The rest-mass relation $E_0 = mc^2$ at
the source event (the four-velocity budget at rest is entirely in
$x_{4}$, $u^4_{\mathrm{rest}} = ic$, giving $E_0 = mc \cdot c = mc^2$ by
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}) combined with the action quantum per
cycle $\hbar$ (Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:62"}) gives the Compton angular frequency
$$\omega_C \;=\; \frac{E_0}{\hbar} \;=\; \frac{mc^2}{\hbar},$$ which is
the rate of $x_{4}$-oscillation phase accumulation per unit proper time.

The action along the rest-frame worldline from $\tau = 0$ to
$\tau = \varepsilon$ is $S_{\mathrm{rest}} = -mc^2\,\varepsilon$ (the
rest-frame Lagrangian for a free particle is
$L_{\mathrm{rest}} = -mc^2$, the negative rest energy times unit proper
time; this is the standard relativistic free-particle Lagrangian, which
descends from the rest-mass energy $E_0 = mc^2$ via Legendre
transformation). The rest-frame phase is
$$-\omega_C\,\varepsilon \;=\; -\frac{mc^2\,\varepsilon}{\hbar} \;=\; \frac{S_{\mathrm{rest}}}{\hbar}.$$
The rest-frame action-to-phase rule
$\Delta\theta_{\mathrm{rest}} = S_{\mathrm{rest}}/\hbar$ is established
directly from McGucken machinery (the Compton frequency from
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at the source event, the action quantum from
the McGucken Sphere cycle).

**Step 3: General action-to-phase rule from Lorentz invariance on
$M_{G}$.** The Minkowski metric on $M_{G}$ descends from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} (substitution $dx_4 = ic\,dt$ into the
Euclidean four-distance). Lorentz transformations
$\Lambda \in SO^+(1,3)$ preserve the Minkowski line element
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iv), Lorentz consistency); they act
on four-vectors by linear transformation and on four-velocities $u^\mu$,
four-momenta $P^\mu$, and the classical action $S$ as Lorentz scalars
(the action $S = \int L\,d\tau$ is a Lorentz scalar by construction,
since $L$ is a scalar function of the four-velocity and $d\tau$ is
proper-time-Lorentz-scalar).

The wavefunction phase $\theta(p) = \arg\psi(p)$ at an event
$p \in M_{G}$ is also a Lorentz scalar (the phase is gauge-independent
and frame-independent; only the modulus $|\psi|$ depends on the boost
weight). The proportionality between $\theta$ and $S$ established in the
rest frame (Step 2) --- namely
$\Delta\theta_{\mathrm{rest}} = S_{\mathrm{rest}}/\hbar$ --- therefore
extends to every Lorentz frame by Lorentz invariance:
$$\Delta\theta(p \to q) \;=\; \frac{S[\gamma_{p \to q}]}{\hbar},$$ where
$\gamma_{p \to q}$ is the (classical) worldline from event $p$ to event
$q$ and $S[\gamma]$ is the action along this worldline computed using
the frame-appropriate Lagrangian. This is the general action-to-phase
rule.

Applied to the non-relativistic limit at short proper time $\varepsilon$
with the Lagrangian $L = \tfrac{m}{2}\dot{\mathbf{x}}^2 - V(\mathbf{x})$
(Step 1), the wavelet from $\mathbf{x}'$ to $\mathbf{x}$ accumulates
phase
$$\Delta\theta \;=\; \frac{S[\gamma]}{\hbar} \;=\; \frac{1}{\hbar}\!\Bigl[\,\frac{m(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')^2}{2\varepsilon} - V\!\Bigl(\tfrac{\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{x}'}{2}\Bigr)\,\varepsilon\,\Bigr] + O(\varepsilon^2),$$
which is the conclusion stated in the Lemma.

**Step 4: McGucken anchoring of every constant.** The exponent
$iS/\hbar$ has its constants traced to $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as
follows.

-   The $i$ is the perpendicularity marker of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.
    By Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}, $x_4 = ict$ is the integrated kinematic shadow of the dynamical principle, with the $i$ marking the perpendicularity of $x_4$
    to the spatial three. By Theorem 42 of [@MG-Ontic-2026], every $i$
    in the matter wavefunction is the suppression-map image of this
    single $i$ via one of three mechanisms (chain-rule,
    signature-change, contour-integration); the $i$ in $e^{iS/\hbar}$ is
    the chain-rule (case (a)) image via the rest-frame Compton phase
    $-i\omega_C\tau = -imc^2\tau/\hbar$ (Step 2), Lorentz-boosted to the
    moving frame (Step 3). The exponent's $i$ is therefore the same $i$
    as in $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

-   The $\hbar$ is the action quantum per McGucken-Sphere cycle
    (Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}).
    The McGucken Sphere at the source event oscillates at the Compton
    frequency $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ derived from
    $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; one full cycle of the Sphere corresponds
    to $\tau = 2\pi/\omega_C = 2\pi\hbar/(mc^2)$, with action
    $|S_{\mathrm{cycle}}| = mc^2 \cdot 2\pi\hbar/(mc^2) = 2\pi\hbar$, or
    one quantum of action $\hbar$ per radian of cycle. Thus $\hbar$ is
    McGucken-derived.

-   The action $S[\gamma]$ is the classical Lagrangian integral along
    the worldline; it is a Lorentz scalar on $M_{G}$, which is itself
    the McGucken-Principle-derived arena
    (Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}).

All three constants in $e^{iS/\hbar}$ are theorems of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, not external inputs. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#lem:short-time-kernel .lemma}
**Lemma 7.9** (Short-time kernel from Huygens summation). *The
short-time propagation kernel
$K(\mathbf{x}, t + \varepsilon; \mathbf{x}', t)$ --- i.e., the amplitude
that a particle at $(\mathbf{x}', t)$ propagates to
$(\mathbf{x}, t + \varepsilon)$ --- equals
$$K(\mathbf{x}, t + \varepsilon; \mathbf{x}', t) = \mathcal{N}_\varepsilon\,\exp\!\left[\frac{i}{\hbar}\left(\frac{m(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')^2}{2\varepsilon} - V\!\left(\tfrac{\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{x}'}{2}\right)\varepsilon\right)\right],
\label{eq:shorttime-kernel}$$ where $\mathcal{N}_\varepsilon$ is a
normalization to be fixed in
Lemma [7.10](#lem:gaussian-normalization){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:gaussian-normalization"}.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has five steps: (1) construct the iterated-Huygens
path-integral form from
Lemmas [7.7](#lem:sphere-and-huygens){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:sphere-and-huygens"}
and [7.8](#lem:compton-phase-wavelet){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:compton-phase-wavelet"}; (2) localise to the
stationary-phase neighbourhood of the classical path; (3) substitute the
classical action; (4) trace the prefactor and exponent's $i$ to the
McGucken-Principle perpendicularity marker; (5) defer the normalisation
to Lemma [7.10](#lem:gaussian-normalization){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:gaussian-normalization"}.

**Step 1: Path-integral form from iterated McGucken-Sphere Huygens
propagation.** By
Lemma [7.7](#lem:sphere-and-huygens){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:sphere-and-huygens"}, the McGucken Sphere expands at rate
$c$ from each event of $M_{G}$ (clause (i) and (ii) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}), with each wavefront point serving as a
Huygens-secondary source for the next iteration (clause (v), global
validity of the principle). Iterating $N$ times with proper-time steps
$\varepsilon_n$ (with $\sum_n \varepsilon_n = \varepsilon$, the total
interval), the propagator from $(\mathbf{x}', t)$ to
$(\mathbf{x}, t+\varepsilon)$ decomposes into a sum over $N$-stage paths
$\gamma_N$ from $\mathbf{x}'$ to $\mathbf{x}$ via $N-1$ intermediate
Sphere-wavefront points
$\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{N-1}$. By
Lemma [7.8](#lem:compton-phase-wavelet){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:compton-phase-wavelet"}, each wavelet from
$\mathbf{x}_{n}$ to $\mathbf{x}_{n+1}$ in time $\varepsilon_n$ carries
phase $\exp(iS_n/\hbar)$ with
$S_n = m(\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n)^2/(2\varepsilon_n) - V(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_n)\varepsilon_n$
(midpoint $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_n = (\mathbf{x}_n + \mathbf{x}_{n+1})/2$).
The total phase along the $N$-stage path is the sum
