$\eta^{\mu\nu}$ and on $\Box$, with the physical content unchanged.

**Step 1: Compute the Clifford square of the first-derivative
operator.** For the gamma-matrix operator $\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu$
acting on smooth spinor wavefunctions, with the Clifford algebra
$\{\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu\} = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}\mathbf{1}$:
$$(\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu)^2 \;=\; \gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\,\gamma^\nu\partial_\nu \;=\; \gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\,\partial_\mu\partial_\nu.$$
Since partial derivatives commute on smooth functions
($\partial_\mu\partial_\nu = \partial_\nu\partial_\mu$), we may
symmetrise the matrix product:
$$\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\,\partial_\mu\partial_\nu \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}(\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu + \gamma^\nu\gamma^\mu)\,\partial_\mu\partial_\nu \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\{\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu\}\,\partial_\mu\partial_\nu \;=\; \eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu \;=\; \Box,$$
using the Clifford anticommutator and the definition of the
d'Alembertian. Therefore $(\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu)^2 = \Box$ as an
operator identity on smooth spinors, and
$$(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu)^2 \;=\; i^2\,(\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu)^2 \;=\; -\Box.$$

**Step 2: Factorize the Klein-Gordon operator.** The operators $D$ and
$\bar D$ differ only by the sign of the mass term. Their product is
$$\begin{aligned}
  \bar D\,D &\;=\; \bigl(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu + mc/\hbar\bigr)\bigl(i\gamma^\nu\partial_\nu - mc/\hbar\bigr) \\
  &\;=\; (i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu)(i\gamma^\nu\partial_\nu) + (mc/\hbar)(i\gamma^\nu\partial_\nu) - (i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu)(mc/\hbar) - (mc/\hbar)^2 \\
  &\;=\; (i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu)^2 \,+\, 0 \,-\, (mc/\hbar)^2,
\end{aligned}$$ where the two cross terms cancel because $mc/\hbar$ is a
scalar that commutes with every differential operator:
$(mc/\hbar)(i\gamma^\nu\partial_\nu) = (i\gamma^\nu\partial_\nu)(mc/\hbar)$,
so the linear-in-$mc/\hbar$ terms sum to zero. Substituting Step 1's
result $(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu)^2 = -\Box$:
$$\bar D\,D \;=\; -\Box - (mc/\hbar)^2 \;=\; -\bigl[\Box + (mc/\hbar)^2\bigr],$$
an exact operator identity on smooth spinor wavefunctions, with no
restriction to Dirac solutions required.

**Step 3: Klein-Gordon as a consequence of Dirac.** If $\psi$ satisfies
the Dirac equation $D\psi = 0$, then applying $\bar D$ to both sides:
$$\bar D\,D\,\psi \;=\; \bar D\,\cdot 0 \;=\; 0.$$ By Step 2,
$\bar D\,D\psi = -[\Box + (mc/\hbar)^2]\psi$, so
$$-\bigl[\Box + (mc/\hbar)^2\bigr]\,\psi \;=\; 0, \qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad \bigl[\Box + (mc/\hbar)^2\bigr]\,\psi \;=\; 0,$$
the Klein-Gordon equation in signature $(+, -, -, -)$. Translating to
signature $(-, +, +, +)$ (the convention of
equation [\[eq:Klein\--Gordon\]](#eq:Klein--Gordon){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:Klein--Gordon"}) by the metric-sign change
$\eta^{\mu\nu} \to -\eta^{\mu\nu}$, $\Box \to -\Box$, the equation
becomes $[(-\Box) + (mc/\hbar)^2]\psi = 0$, equivalently
$[\Box - (mc/\hbar)^2]\psi = 0$, matching
equation [\[eq:Klein\--Gordon\]](#eq:Klein--Gordon){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:Klein--Gordon"} of QM T8.

**Step 4: Dirac as the first-order Lorentz-covariant operator pairing
with the Klein-Gordon operator.** The operator
$D = i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - mc/\hbar$ with
$\{\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu\} = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}\mathbf{1}$ is a first-order
Lorentz-covariant differential operator whose conjugate-pair product
$\bar D D$ with $\bar D = i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu + mc/\hbar$ is (up to
overall sign) the Klein-Gordon operator. The Dirac equation $D\psi = 0$
is therefore a "square-root" factorisation of Klein-Gordon at the cost
of matrix-valued coefficients (which
Lemma [9.3](#lem:clifford-minimal-rep){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:clifford-minimal-rep"} below shows must be at least
$4 \times 4$ for the minimal complex representation in $1+3$
dimensions). The content is the existence and form of the
Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$ on the McGucken-derived Minkowski
metric (Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}); the matrix dimension is established
separately. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#lem:clifford-minimal-rep .lemma}
**Lemma 9.3** (Minimal-dimensional representation of the Clifford
algebra is $4 \times 4$). *The Clifford algebra
$\{\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu\} = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}\,\mathbf{1}$ on $M_{G}$ has
minimal faithful complex representation of dimension $4$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has four steps. The Clifford algebra
$\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$ is the Clifford algebra of the McGucken-Minkowski
metric of Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} (descending from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
via the perpendicularity marker $i^2 = -1$ that produces the Lorentzian
signature mismatch with the Euclidean spatial-three signature, as in
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iv), derived at Theorem 4.6 Lorentz consistency).

**Step 1: Real Clifford algebra dimensions.** The Clifford algebra
$\mathrm{Cl}(p, q)$ with signature $(p, q)$ has real dimension
$2^{p+q}$. For $\mathrm{Cl}(1, 3)$ (signature with one timelike and
three spacelike directions, equivalently $\mathrm{Cl}_{1,3}$), this
gives real dimension $2^4 = 16$. The standard basis of
$\mathrm{Cl}(1, 3)$ consists of the $\binom{4}{k}$ products of $k$
distinct gamma matrices for $k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$:
$$\underbrace{\mathbf{1}}_{1} \,;\quad \underbrace{\gamma^\mu}_{4} \,;\quad \underbrace{\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\ (\mu < \nu)}_{6} \,;\quad \underbrace{\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\ (\mu < \nu < \rho)}_{4} \,;\quad \underbrace{\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3}_{1},$$
totalling $1 + 4 + 6 + 4 + 1 = 2^4 = 16$ real basis monomials (Naber
[@Naber2012] §1.5, the standard Clifford-algebra basis enumeration).

**Step 2: Complexification gives $M_4(\mathbb{C})$.** The
complexification $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3) \otimes \mathbb{C}$ is isomorphic to
$M_4(\mathbb{C})$, the algebra of $4 \times 4$ complex matrices. The
argument: for the complexified Clifford algebra in any signature
$(p, q)$ with $p + q$ even, the structure depends only on the dimension
(the signature distinction collapses upon complexification, since
$i\gamma^\mu$ has
$(i\gamma^\mu)^2 = -(\gamma^\mu)^2 = -\eta^{\mu\mu}\mathbf{1}$, so
multiplying the timelike gammas by $i$ flips their signature
contribution). Therefore
$\mathrm{Cl}(p, q) \otimes \mathbb{C}\cong \mathrm{Cl}(p+q, 0) \otimes \mathbb{C}$
for any signature with $p + q$ fixed. For dimension $4$:
$\mathrm{Cl}(4, 0) \otimes \mathbb{C}\cong M_4(\mathbb{C})$.

The identification
$\mathrm{Cl}(2k, 0) \otimes \mathbb{C}\cong M_{2^k}(\mathbb{C})$ follows
by induction from the dimension-doubling relation
$\mathrm{Cl}(n+2, 0) \cong \mathrm{Cl}(n, 0) \otimes M_2(\mathbb{R})$
(the standard Atiyah--Bott--Shapiro periodicity; see Lawson--Michelsohn
1989 Ch. I, Theorem 4.3, or Penrose--Rindler [@PenroseRindler1984]
Vol. 1, §1.5 for the explicit complexification): starting from
$\mathrm{Cl}(0, 0) \cong \mathbb{R}$, two iterations give
$\mathrm{Cl}(4, 0) \cong \mathbb{R}\otimes M_2(\mathbb{R}) \otimes M_2(\mathbb{R}) \cong M_4(\mathbb{R}) \otimes \mathbb{R}\cong M_4(\mathbb{R})$,
and complexifying gives
$M_4(\mathbb{R}) \otimes \mathbb{C}\cong M_4(\mathbb{C})$.

Therefore the minimal faithful complex representation of
$\mathrm{Cl}(1, 3)$ is on $\mathbb{C}^4$.

**Step 3: Explicit Dirac basis verifies the $4\times 4$
representation.** An explicit realisation is the Bjorken--Drell Dirac
basis (presented in this Step in the particle-physics convention
$(+,-,-,-)$ to match the standard Dirac-matrix literature; the textbook's
default $(-,+,+,+)$ convention can be recovered by the unitary similarity
transformation $\gamma^\mu \mapsto i\gamma^\mu$ which negates all
anticommutator signs, equivalently by multiplying $\eta^{\mu\nu}$ by $-1$;
the Dirac equation $(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - mc/\hbar)\psi = 0$ has the
same form in either convention since the rescaling absorbs into the
operator identity):
$$\gamma^0 \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{1}_2 & 0 \\ 0 & -\mathbf{1}_2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \gamma^j \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sigma^j \\ -\sigma^j & 0 \end{pmatrix} \;\; (j = 1, 2, 3),$$
where $\sigma^j$ are the Pauli matrices. Direct computation of the
anticommutators:

-   $(\gamma^0)^2 = \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{1}_2, \mathbf{1}_2) = \mathbf{1}_4 = +\mathbf{1}_4\cdot\eta^{00}$,
    consistent with $\eta^{00} = +1$.

-   $(\gamma^j)^2 = \begin{pmatrix} -\sigma^j\sigma^j & 0 \\ 0 & -\sigma^j\sigma^j \end{pmatrix} = -\mathbf{1}_4 = -\mathbf{1}_4\cdot\eta^{jj}$,
    consistent with $\eta^{jj} = -1$ for $j = 1, 2, 3$, using
    $(\sigma^j)^2 = \mathbf{1}_2$.

-   Mixed anticommutators $\{\gamma^0, \gamma^j\} = 0$: from the block
    form,
    $\gamma^0\gamma^j = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sigma^j \\ \sigma^j & 0 \end{pmatrix}$
    and
    $\gamma^j\gamma^0 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -\sigma^j \\ -\sigma^j & 0 \end{pmatrix}$,
    summing to zero.

-   Mixed anticommutators
    $\{\gamma^i, \gamma^j\} = -2\delta^{ij}\mathbf{1}_4$ for
    $i, j \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ follow from
    $\{\sigma^i, \sigma^j\} = 2\delta^{ij}\mathbf{1}_2$ via the block
    structure.

All anticommutators
$\{\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu\} = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}\mathbf{1}_4$ are verified.
Other choices (Weyl basis, Majorana basis) give isomorphic
representations.

**Step 4: McGucken anchoring of the Clifford structure.** The Clifford
algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$ is the Clifford algebra of the Minkowski
metric $\eta_{\mu\nu}$ on $M_{G}$. By
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}, this Minkowski metric is derived from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}) by substituting $dx_4 = ic\,dt$ into the
Euclidean line element, with the integrated kinematic shadow $x_4 = ict$ supplying
the kinematic shadow per
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"} (the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ being the central fact). The Clifford
algebra is therefore a downstream consequence of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ along the chain
$$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic \;\Longrightarrow\; \eta_{\mu\nu} \text{ (Theorem~\ref{thm:hilbert-arena})} \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathrm{Cl}(1,3) \;\Longrightarrow\; M_4(\mathbb{C}) \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathbb{C}^4.$$
The perpendicularity marker $i$ in $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (i)) produces the signature mismatch
in $\eta$, which fixes the structure of $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$, which has
minimal faithful complex representation on $\mathbb{C}^4$. Within the
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, the spinor space $\mathbb{C}^4$ has the reading of the minimal complex representation of the Clifford algebra of
the McGucken-derived Minkowski metric. The chain is a sequence of forced
consequences: each step downstream is uniquely determined by the steps
upstream, with no ad-hoc dimensional choice at any stage. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#lem:spin-double-cover .lemma}
**Lemma 9.4** (Spinors transform under
$\mathrm{Spin}(1,3) = SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ with $4\pi$-periodicity). *The
spinor space $\mathbb{C}^4$ carries a representation of
$\mathrm{Spin}(1,3) = SL(2,\mathbb{C})$, the universal double cover of
$SO^+(1,3)$, with the property that a rotation by $2\pi$ in the
$SO(3) \subset SO^+(1,3)$ subgroup acts as $-\mathbf{1}_4$ and a
rotation by $4\pi$ acts as $+\mathbf{1}_4$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has six steps establishing
$\mathrm{Spin}(1,3) = SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ as the universal double cover of
$SO^+(1,3)$ and the $4\pi$-periodicity of spinors. The Lorentz group
$SO^+(1,3)$ itself descends from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}, in which the Lorentzian metric of
signature $(+,+,+,-)$ is forced by the perpendicularity marker
$i^2 = -1$ in $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i)+(iv)).

**Step 1: Explicit construction of the $SL(2,\mathbb{C}) \to SO^+(1,3)$
covering map.** The double cover is constructed explicitly via the
identification of Minkowski space with $2\times 2$ Hermitian matrices.
For each four-vector
$x^\mu = (x^0, x^1, x^2, x^3) \in \mathbb{R}^{1,3}$, define the
Hermitian matrix
$$X \;:=\; x^0\,\mathbf{1}_2 \,+\, x^1\,\sigma^1 \,+\, x^2\,\sigma^2 \,+\, x^3\,\sigma^3 \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} x^0 + x^3 & x^1 - ix^2 \\ x^1 + ix^2 & x^0 - x^3 \end{pmatrix},$$
where $\sigma^j$ are the Pauli matrices and $X^* = X$ since $\sigma^j$
are Hermitian. The map $x^\mu \mapsto X$ is a real-linear bijection from
$\mathbb{R}^{1,3}$ onto the space of $2\times 2$ Hermitian matrices
(both are 4-dimensional real vector spaces). The determinant of $X$
equals the Minkowski norm:
$$\det X \;=\; (x^0)^2 - (x^1)^2 - (x^2)^2 - (x^3)^2 \;=\; \eta_{\mu\nu}x^\mu x^\nu \qquad \text{(signature $(+, -, -, -)$)},$$
by direct $2\times 2$ determinant computation.

For any $A \in SL(2, \mathbb{C})$, define the action on Hermitian
matrices by $$X \;\xrightarrow{A}\; X' \;:=\; A\,X\,A^*,$$ which sends
Hermitian matrices to Hermitian matrices (since
$(AXA^*)^* = AX^*A^* = AXA^*$). The determinant transforms as
$$\det X' \;=\; \det(A\,X\,A^*) \;=\; \det A\cdot\det X\cdot\det(A^*) \;=\; |\det A|^2\cdot\det X \;=\; \det X,$$
using $\det A = 1$ for $A \in SL(2, \mathbb{C})$. Therefore the action
$X \mapsto AXA^*$ preserves the Minkowski norm
$\eta_{\mu\nu}x^\mu x^\nu$, hence induces a Lorentz transformation
$\Lambda(A) \in O(1, 3)$ on the four-vector $x^\mu$. The map
$A \mapsto \Lambda(A)$ is a continuous group homomorphism from
$SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ (connected) into $SO^+(1, 3)$ (the identity
component of $O(1, 3)$).

*Surjectivity:* every element of $SO^+(1, 3)$ is in the image (Naber
[@Naber2012] Theorem 1.5.5; the connected group $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$
surjects onto the identity component of the Lorentz group).

*Kernel:* $A \in SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ acts trivially on every Hermitian
matrix $X$ iff $AXA^* = X$ for all $X$, equivalently $AX = XA^{-*}$ for
all Hermitian $X$ (using $A^{-*} = (A^*)^{-1}$). Taking
$X = \mathbf{1}_2$ gives $A = A^{-*}$, equivalently
$A A^* = \mathbf{1}_2$, so $A$ is unitary. Combined with $\det A = 1$,
$A \in SU(2)$. Taking $X = \sigma^j$ gives
$A\sigma^j = \sigma^j A^{-*} = \sigma^j A$ (using $A A^* = \mathbf{1}_2$
for unitary $A$), so $A$ commutes with all Pauli matrices, hence
$A = \lambda\mathbf{1}_2$ for some scalar $\lambda$. The constraint
$\det A = 1$ gives $\lambda^2 = 1$, so $\lambda = \pm 1$. The kernel is
$\{\pm \mathbf{1}_2\}$.

Therefore the homomorphism $\pi: SL(2, \mathbb{C}) \to SO^+(1, 3)$ is
2-to-1, surjective, with kernel $\{\pm \mathbf{1}\}$, exhibiting
$SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ as a double cover of $SO^+(1, 3)$. Since
$SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ is simply connected (Penrose--Rindler
[@PenroseRindler1984] Vol. 1, Ch. 1; standard topological fact), it is
the *universal* double cover, with the name
$\mathrm{Spin}(1, 3) := SL(2, \mathbb{C})$.

**Step 2: $SU(2)$ subgroup as cover of $SO(3)$.** The maximal compact
subgroup of $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ is $SU(2)$ (the unitary elements of
$SL(2, \mathbb{C})$). The restriction of the covering map $\pi$ to
$SU(2)$ gives a homomorphism $\pi|_{SU(2)}: SU(2) \to SO(3)$, where
$SO(3) \subset SO^+(1, 3)$ is the spatial rotation subgroup (the
subgroup fixing the $x^0$-axis, embedded by
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (ii) which establishes the
$SO(3)$-isotropy of the $x_{4}$-expansion). This restriction is also
2-to-1 with kernel $\{\pm\mathbf{1}_2\}$, exhibiting $SU(2)$ as the
universal double cover of $SO(3)$.

Explicitly, a rotation by angle $\theta$ about a unit axis
$\hat{\mathbf{n}} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ in $SO(3)$ lifts to two elements of
$SU(2)$:
$$R(\theta, \hat{\mathbf{n}}) \;=\; \pm\exp\bigl(-i\theta\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\vec\sigma/2\bigr).$$
(The sign of the exponent is conventional; some texts use $+i$.) This is
the standard half-angle Pauli-matrix exponentiation (Penrose--Rindler
[@PenroseRindler1984] Vol. 1, §1.2; Naber [@Naber2012] §1.5).

**Step 3: $2\pi$-rotation in $SU(2)$ acts as $-\mathbf{1}$.** For
$\theta = 2\pi$, using the Pauli-matrix identity
$\exp(i\alpha\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\vec\sigma) = \cos(\alpha)\mathbf{1} + i\sin(\alpha)\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\vec\sigma$
(which follows from
$(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\vec\sigma)^2 = \mathbf{1}_2$):
$$\exp\bigl(-i\cdot 2\pi\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\vec\sigma/2\bigr) \;=\; \exp\bigl(-i\pi\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\vec\sigma\bigr) \;=\; \cos(-\pi)\mathbf{1} + i\sin(-\pi)\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\vec\sigma \;=\; -\mathbf{1}_2 + 0 \;=\; -\mathbf{1}_2.$$
A $2\pi$ rotation in $SO(3)$ acts as $\mathbf{1}$ (trivially, returning
every spatial vector to itself), but its lift to $SU(2)$ is
$-\mathbf{1}_2$. This is the topological signature of the double cover,
exhibiting $\pi_1(SO(3)) = \mathbb{Z}/2$ at the cover level. The
empirical confirmation: Werner et al. 1975 neutron-interferometry
experiment directly measured the $-\mathbf{1}$ sign reversal of a
neutron wavefunction after a $2\pi$ rotation, confirming the spinor
representation against the vector representation.

**Step 4: $4\pi$-rotation in $SU(2)$ acts as $+\mathbf{1}$.** For
$\theta = 4\pi$:
$$\exp\bigl(-i\cdot 4\pi\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\vec\sigma/2\bigr) \;=\; \exp\bigl(-i\cdot 2\pi\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\vec\sigma\bigr) \;=\; \cos(-2\pi)\mathbf{1} + i\sin(-2\pi)\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\vec\sigma \;=\; +\mathbf{1}_2.$$
A $4\pi$ rotation returns the spinor to its original sign. The
$4\pi$-periodicity is the topological signature of the spinor
representation, distinct from the $2\pi$-periodicity of the
vector representation.

**Step 5: Extension to $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ with boost generators.** The
full Lorentz spinor representation extends from $SU(2)$ (rotations) to
$SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ (rotations + boosts) by adjoining the boost
generators. A boost along direction $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ with rapidity
$\xi$ (where $\tanh\xi = v/c$ parameterises the velocity, by
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iv) Lorentz consistency) acts on
$SU(2)$ via the Hermitian (rather than anti-Hermitian) Pauli
exponential:
$$B(\xi, \hat{\mathbf{n}}) \;=\; \exp\bigl(\xi\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\vec\sigma/2\bigr) \;\in\; SL(2, \mathbb{C}).$$
The product of rotations and boosts generates all of $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$
(polar decomposition: every $A \in SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ has $A = UH$ with
$U \in SU(2)$ unitary and $H$ positive Hermitian, $\det A = 1$ fixing
the determinant). The $4 \times 4$ Dirac spinor combines left-handed and
right-handed Weyl two-spinors, each transforming under
$SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ via its defining $2 \times 2$ representation; the
direct sum (or its irreducible Dirac-spinor combination on the diagonal
of the Clifford-algebra block structure) is the spinor representation
used in Lemma [9.3](#lem:clifford-minimal-rep){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:clifford-minimal-rep"}.

**Step 6: McGucken anchoring of $4\pi$-periodicity.** The
$4\pi$-periodicity is the topological signature of the universal cover
$\mathrm{Spin}(1,3) \to SO^+(1,3)$, which is the symmetry group of the
McGucken-Minkowski metric of
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} (descending from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
via the perpendicularity marker $i^2 = -1$). The spinor representation
is forced by the requirement that the wavefunction transforms under the
universal cover (rather than just the Lorentz group), which in turn is
required for the matter orientation condition (M) of [@MG-Dirac-2026]
Definition [9.6](#def:matter-orientation-M){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:matter-orientation-M"}: matter must respond to
$x_{4}$-orientation, and $x_{4}$-orientation reversal is a
$2\pi$-rotation reversal in the $x_{4}$-perpendicular spatial
directions, which acts as $-\mathbf{1}$ on the spinor --- exhibiting the
matter--antimatter dichotomy as a topological feature of the cover. The
integrated kinematic shadow $x_{4}= ict$
(Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is the kinematic shadow on which the
$x_{4}$-orientation is defined; the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is what forces the $x_{4}$-direction itself to
be a distinct geometric axis whose orientation reversal is non-trivial.
$\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#lem:QMT9-channelA-proof .lemma}
**Lemma 9.5** (Algebraic Channel proof of QM T9). *The Dirac equation
[\[eq:Dirac\]](#eq:Dirac){reference-type="eqref" reference="eq:Dirac"}
holds for a spin-$1/2$ massive particle, with $\gamma^\mu$ satisfying
the Clifford algebra on the minimal $\mathbb{C}^4$ representation, and
$\psi$ transforming under $\mathrm{Spin}(1,3)$ with $4\pi$-periodicity.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has six steps establishing the Dirac
equation as the spin-$1/2$ irreducible-representation equation forced by
Algebraic Channel machinery.

**Step 1: Clifford-algebra factorisation of Klein--Gordon.** By
Lemma [9.2](#lem:clifford-existence){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:clifford-existence"}, a first-order operator
$D = i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - mc/\hbar$ with $\gamma^\mu$ satisfying
the Clifford algebra
$\{\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu\} = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}\mathbf{1}$ has
$D^2 = -\Box + m^2 c^2/\hbar^2$ (the Klein--Gordon operator in the
appropriate sign convention). The Dirac equation $D\psi = 0$ is
therefore a "square root" of the Klein--Gordon equation: a first-order
Lorentz-covariant equation whose square recovers the mass-Casimir
constraint.

**Step 2: Minimal Clifford representation.** By
Lemma [9.3](#lem:clifford-minimal-rep){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:clifford-minimal-rep"}, the minimal faithful complex
representation of $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$ is on $\mathbb{C}^4$: the algebra
$\mathrm{Cl}(1,3) \otimes \mathbb{C}\cong M_4(\mathbb{C})$, so
$4 \times 4$ matrices act faithfully and irreducibly. An explicit Dirac
basis is
$$\gamma^0 = \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{1}_2, -\mathbf{1}_2), \qquad \gamma^j = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sigma^j \\ -\sigma^j & 0 \end{pmatrix}.$$
The wavefunction $\psi$ is therefore a $\mathbb{C}^4$-valued field on
$M_{G}$ (a Dirac spinor).

**Step 3: $\mathrm{Spin}(1,3) = SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ acts on spinors with
$4\pi$-periodicity.** By
Lemma [9.4](#lem:spin-double-cover){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:spin-double-cover"}, the spinor space $\mathbb{C}^4$
carries a representation of $\mathrm{Spin}(1,3) = SL(2,\mathbb{C})$, the
universal double cover of the Lorentz group $SO^+(1,3)$. Under spatial
rotations $SO(3) \subset SO^+(1,3)$, a rotation by $2\pi$ acts as
$-\mathbf{1}_4$ on spinors (not as identity), and a rotation by $4\pi$
recovers identity. This is the $4\pi$-periodicity of spinors,
empirically confirmed by the Werner et al. 1975 neutron-interferometry
experiment.

**Step 4: Wigner classification at spin-$1/2$.** By QA6 (Wigner
classification), the massive spin-$1/2$ irreducible representation of
the Poincaré group is realised on $\mathbb{C}^4$-valued wavefunctions
transforming covariantly under $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$. The two Casimir
invariants are: $C_1 = -m^2 c^2$ (mass squared) and
$C_2 = -m^2 c^2\cdot(1/2)(3/2)\hbar^2 = -3m^2 c^2\hbar^2/4$
(Pauli--Lubanski squared at spin-$1/2$). The dynamical equation singling
out this representation is the Dirac equation
$(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - mc/\hbar)\psi = 0$.

**Step 5: Dirac equation forced by three requirements.** The
Dirac equation is the unique first-order Lorentz-covariant equation
forced by:

-   Choice of spin-$1/2$ representation of the Poincaré group (QA6 with
    spin-$1/2$);

-   First-order in derivatives (motivated by positive-definiteness of
    probability density $\bar\psi\gamma^0\psi$, as in Dirac's original
    1928 derivation);

-   Clifford-algebra constraint
    $\{\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu\} = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}\mathbf{1}$ which makes
    the square give Klein--Gordon (mass-Casimir constraint).

Combining these three requirements uniquely determines the equation up
to gauge equivalence: $D = i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - mc/\hbar$ with
$\gamma^\mu$ on $\mathbb{C}^4$.

**Step 6: McGucken anchoring and Algebraic Channel characterisation.** The
Lorentz invariance of the Dirac equation traces to the Minkowski metric
$\eta_{\mu\nu}$, derived in
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} as a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
via the substitution $dx_4 = ic\,dt$. The Clifford algebra
$\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$, its minimal $\mathbb{C}^4$ representation, and the
$SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ double-cover structure all descend from this
McGucken-derived metric. The mass $m$ enters via Wigner classification,
with the magnitude $mc$ corresponding to the four-velocity-budget at
rest (Lemma [4.2](#lem:four-velocity-budget){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:four-velocity-budget"}). The proof uses only
algebraic-symmetry machinery (QA1, QA2, QA6, Clifford algebra of
$\eta$); no Sphere-geometric Huygens machinery appears. The proof is
Algebraic Channel, derivationally disjoint from the Geometric Channel McGucken-Sphere
spinor route of
Lemma [9.15](#lem:QMT9-channelB-proof){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT9-channelB-proof"}. ◻
:::

### The $\pm ic$ sign flip and antimatter

::: {#rmk:dirac-antimatter .remark}
*Remark 9.16* (Matter--antimatter dichotomy from $\pm ic$). The Dirac
equation has both positive-energy and negative-energy solutions,
originally puzzling Dirac and resolved by him via the "hole theory"
interpretation: negative-energy solutions are filled, and absences in
the negative-energy sea appear as positrons (antimatter). In the
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, the negative-energy solutions correspond directly to
the $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= -ic$ branch of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(matter--antimatter dichotomy, QM T21,
Chapter [21](#ch:antimatter){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:antimatter"}). The sign flip $+ic \leftrightarrow -ic$ in
the principle is the same sign flip that produces:

-   Fermionic anticommutation under particle exchange (QM T20,
    Chapter [20](#ch:identical){reference-type="ref"
    reference="ch:identical"}: spin-statistics theorem);

-   CPT symmetry (Theorem 7 of [@MG-Dirac-2026]: CPT is automatic from
    the $+ic \leftrightarrow -ic$ branch-exchange symmetry of
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$);

-   Single-Sided Preservation (Theorem 5 of [@MG-Dirac-2026]: left-
    vs. right-action on spinors corresponds to matter vs. antimatter
    orientation).

This is the unity of antimatter, the Pauli exclusion
principle, and CPT symmetry in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, all forced by the
$\pm ic$ sign degree of freedom in the principle.
:::

### The oscillatory reading of the $x_{4}$-advance {#sec:oscillatory-reading}

Remark [9.16](#rmk:dirac-antimatter){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:dirac-antimatter"} assigns the two orientations $\pm ic$
to matter and antimatter. The present section reads what those two
orientations produce when both are carried by one localised entity. The
result is obtained from clauses of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} together with QB4; no oscillation is
postulated, and clause C1 directional is not weakened at any point.

::: {#lem:x4-advance-as-oscillation .lemma}
**Lemma 9.16A** (The advance projects to an oscillation at
$\omega_C$). *For a massive entity of rest mass $m$ at spatial rest, the
$x_{4}$-advance $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ carries, by QB4
(Axiom [4.23](#ax:QB4){reference-type="ref" reference="ax:QB4"}), the
rest-frame amplitude $\psi_{\mathrm{rest}}(\tau) = A\,e^{-i\omega_C\tau}$
with $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$. This is a uniform rotation in the plane
that the perpendicularity marker $i$ of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ picks
out (C2). Its projection onto either axis of that plane is a
sinusoidal oscillation of angular frequency $\omega_C$, quantised at
$\hbar$ of action per radian by
Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}.
Expansion and contraction of the projected component are the two
half-cycles of one uniform advance, and the advance itself does not
reverse.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **Step 1: The rest-frame amplitude.** By QB4 the $x_{4}$-phase
of a massive entity advances at $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ in its rest
frame, accumulating $\exp(iS[\gamma]/\hbar)$ with $S = -mc^2\tau$ along
the rest-frame worldline, so
$\psi_{\mathrm{rest}}(\tau) = A\,e^{-i\omega_C\tau}$.

**Step 2: The plane of the rotation.** By C2 the marker $i$ makes
$x_{4}$ the axis perpendicular to the spatial slice, and by
Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"} the amplitude takes values in the
algebra $\mathbb{C}$ that this one perpendicular axis selects.
Multiplication by $e^{-i\omega_C\tau}$ is rotation by angle
$-\omega_C\tau$ in that plane
(Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}).

**Step 3: Projection.** Writing the rotation in components,
$$e^{-i\omega_C\tau} \;=\; \cos(\omega_C\tau) \;-\; i\,\sin(\omega_C\tau),$$
so each component of the rotating amplitude is sinusoidal of angular
frequency $\omega_C$. A uniform rotation therefore presents on either
axis as an oscillation between positive and negative values, with the
two half-cycles corresponding to the two senses of the projected
component.

**Step 4: The advance does not reverse.** The quantity that C1
directional constrains is the orientation of the advance itself, which
is the sense of the rotation in the plane of Step 2 and is constant at
$+ic$ throughout. The sign changes of Step 3 are changes of a
projection, not of the orientation. Clause C1 directional, and every
result descending from it, are therefore untouched by the oscillatory
reading.

**Step 5: Quantisation.** By Theorem 3.2 the action accumulated per
radian of $x_{4}$-advance is $\hbar$, so a full cycle carries $2\pi\hbar
= h$ of action. The oscillation of Step 3 is quantised at $h$ per
cycle, with the cycle rate $\omega_C$ fixed by the rest mass through
QB4. $\square$ ◻
:::

**McGucken-internal source of Lemma 9.16A**: C1 (rate $c$); C1
directional (constant sense of the rotation); C2 (the plane the marker
picks out); C3 via QB4 (action quantum per radian, giving
$\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$); C4 (per-event universality, so the reading
holds at every event of the worldline).

::: {#thm:branch-interference-oscillation .theorem}
**Theorem 9.16B** (Branch interference for a localised entity: frequency
$2\omega_C$ and amplitude $\hbar/mc$). *An entity whose amplitude is
supported on a single orientation carries the uniform rotation of
Lemma [9.16A](#lem:x4-advance-as-oscillation){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:x4-advance-as-oscillation"} and exhibits no oscillation
of its spatial position. An entity localised in $\mathbb{R}^3$ carries
amplitude on both orientations $\pm ic$ of
Remark [9.16](#rmk:dirac-antimatter){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:dirac-antimatter"}, and the interference of the two
branches produces a spatial oscillation of angular frequency
$2\omega_C = 2mc^2/\hbar$ and characteristic amplitude $\hbar/(mc)$, the
reduced Compton wavelength. Both numbers are fixed by the principle's
constants with no free parameter.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **Step 1: A single orientation gives no spatial oscillation.**
By Lemma 9.16A a single-orientation amplitude is a uniform rotation in
the plane $i$ marks, at fixed spatial position in the rest frame. The
$x_{4}$-advance is entirely in $x_{4}$, with the full $c$-budget
directed there by clause (i) at spatial rest, so no spatial component
oscillates.

**Step 2: Localisation requires both orientations.** By
Lemma [6.6A](#lem:reception-reading){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:reception-reading"} the conjugate branch is present at
every event, and by
Lemma [9.12](#lem:forward-conjugate){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:forward-conjugate"} the pair $(\psi, \psi^*)$ describes
one wavefront at the two $x_{4}$-orientations. A state sharply localised
in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is a superposition over the wavefront rather than a
single-orientation mode, so its amplitude has support on both branches.
This is the geometric content of the standard statement that a
momentum eigenstate shows no branch interference and a localised state
does.

**Step 3: Beat frequency.** Two components whose $x_{4}$-phases advance
at $-\omega_C$ and $+\omega_C$ differ in phase at rate $2\omega_C$. The
interference term between them therefore oscillates at
$$\omega_{\mathrm{beat}} \;=\; \omega_C - (-\omega_C) \;=\; 2\omega_C \;=\; \frac{2mc^2}{\hbar}.$$

**Step 4: Amplitude.** By C1 the advance proceeds at rate $c$, so a
component oscillating at angular frequency $2\omega_C$ traverses a
characteristic extent
$$\ell \;\sim\; \frac{c}{\omega_C} \;=\; \frac{c\hbar}{mc^2} \;=\; \frac{\hbar}{mc},$$
the reduced Compton wavelength. The rate is supplied by C1 and the
frequency by QB4, so no parameter beyond $m$, $c$ and $\hbar$ enters.

**Step 5: Scope.** The theorem states the frequency and the
characteristic amplitude. It does not by itself fix the numerical
coefficient of the oscillating term, which requires the specific
spinor decomposition of the localised state supplied by
Theorem [9.1](#thm:QMT9){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT9"}.
$\square$ ◻
:::

**McGucken-internal source of Theorem 9.16B**: C1 (rate $c$, giving the
amplitude $\hbar/mc$); C2 (the plane in which both branches rotate);
C3 via QB4 (the rate $\omega_C$); C5 with
Lemma 6.6A (both orientations present at every event); the $\pm ic$
degree of freedom of Remark 9.16 (the two branches).

::: {#rmk:oscillation-scope .remark}
*Remark 9.16C* (Scope of the oscillatory reading, and what it does not
claim). Three limits are worth stating.

The reading adds no postulate. Lemma 9.16A derives the oscillation as
the projection of the advance QB4 already supplies, and Theorem 9.16B
derives the beat from the two orientations
Remark [9.16](#rmk:dirac-antimatter){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:dirac-antimatter"} already carries. A framework in which
the $x_{4}$-advance genuinely reversed --- spending equal parameter time
at $+ic$ and $-ic$ --- would surrender clause C1 directional, and with
it the Spectrum Condition, the strict Second Law, retarded over advanced
propagation, and matter dominance, all of which
Theorem [1.41](#thm:algebraic-channel-sign-blind){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:algebraic-channel-sign-blind"} records as unavailable to
a sign-blind apparatus. The present reading keeps the orientation fixed
and oscillates a projection, so none of that is at risk.

The empirical target is the free-electron oscillation predicted by the
Dirac equation at $2mc^2/\hbar$ with extent $\hbar/(mc)$, which has been
realised in engineered analogue systems and remains unobserved for free
electrons. The framework's contribution is a source for the
circulation rather than a new number: the frequency and extent agree
with the orthodox values, and what
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ supplies is the statement that the circulation
is the $x_{4}$-advance viewed in the plane C2 marks.

The Hestenes reading of the Dirac equation, in which the electron's
phase is the angle of a light-speed circulation, is recovered as the
spatial projection of Lemma 9.16A rather than assumed alongside it.
:::


### Disjointness audit {#disjointness-audit-7}

**Geometric Channel:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; McGucken Sphere $S^2$ topology
(QB1, QB2); double cover $SU(2) \to SO(3)$ of sphere isometry
(Lemma [9.14](#lem:sphere-double-cover){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:sphere-double-cover"}); spinor orientation on Sphere
(matter orientation condition M); Lorentz-covariant Dirac promotion of
proper-time derivative.

**Algebraic Channel:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; Lorentz invariance (from
McGucken-derived Minkowski metric); Wigner classification of irreducible
representations at spin-$1/2$ (QA6); Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$
as algebra of $\eta$; minimal $4 \times 4$ representation
(Lemma [9.3](#lem:clifford-minimal-rep){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:clifford-minimal-rep"}); $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ as universal
cover (Lemma [9.4](#lem:spin-double-cover){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:spin-double-cover"}); first-order Lorentz-covariant
matter equation as "square root" of Klein--Gordon
(Lemma [9.2](#lem:clifford-existence){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:clifford-existence"}).

**Intersection:**
$\{(\mathrm{McP}), (i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - mc/\hbar)\psi = 0,\,4\pi\text{-periodicity}\}$.
Wigner classification of irreducible Poincaré representations does not
appear in Geometric Channel. The McGucken-Sphere construction does not appear in
Algebraic Channel. The Clifford algebra appears in both channels but through
different routes: Algebraic Channel derives it as the algebra of
$\eta$; Geometric Channel derives it as the Lorentz-covariant lift of the
Sphere's tangent-spinor structure. *Disjointness verified.*

### Empirical anchor

-   The hydrogen-atom fine structure (Sommerfeld 1916 phenomenological;
    Dirac 1928 derivation [@Dirac1928]), matching observation to
    $\sim 10^{-5}$ before QED radiative corrections.

-   The electron $g$-factor ($g = 2$ from the Dirac equation;
    $g - 2 \approx \alpha/\pi$ from QED radiative corrections; measured
    $g/2 = 1.00115965218059(13)$ [@Hanneke2008]).

-   The positron (Anderson 1932): the first observation of antimatter,
    predicted by the negative-energy Dirac solutions, identified in the
    McGucken framework with the $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= -ic$ branch.

-   Neutron $4\pi$-periodicity: Werner et al. (1975) verified neutron
    spinor sign-flip under $2\pi$ rotation via interferometry,
    exhibiting the $\mathrm{Spin}(1,3)$-double-cover structure of
    Lemma [9.4](#lem:spin-double-cover){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:spin-double-cover"}.

## QM T10: The Canonical Commutation Relation $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ {#ch:ccr}

> *The McGucken Principle.* The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality.
> Every result below descends from that expansion.


*Recall.* the McGucken Principle ($\mathrm{McP}$:
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$) asserts that the fourth spacetime dimension
$x_4$ expands at the velocity of light $c$, carrying the
perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguishes it from the spatial
three. Throughout this chapter, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ refers to this
principle and to the five-clause content (i)--(v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: (i) *invariance* --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content; (ii) *spherical symmetry* --- the
expansion is isotropic in the spatial three, with the set of events
reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a 2-sphere of radius
$c\tau$; (iii) *monotonicity* --- the integral curve is strictly
monotonically increasing in $t$, fixing the arrow of $x_4$-advance; (iv)
*Lorentz consistency* --- the structure is $SO^+(1,3)$-invariant on
$M_{G}$; (v) *global validity* --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at
every event of $M_{G}$. The integrated kinematic shadow
$x_4 = ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is the kinematic shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the central fact.

This is the result whose double-derivation along Geometric Channel and Algebraic Channel
is the derivational-disjointness theorem's flagship example
(Theorem [4.27](#thm:disjointness){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:disjointness"}). The textbook tradition treats
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ as a postulate (Shankar [@Shankar1994],
Cohen-Tannoudji [@CT2019]), an axiomatic consequence of canonical
quantization (Sakurai [@Sakurai2020]), or an inserted construction
(Griffiths [@Griffiths2018]). In the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework it is forced
twice, by derivationally disjoint routes.

The canonical reference for the double derivation given here is
[@MG-Foundations-2026], which formally establishes the Algebraic Channel route
as Propositions H.1--H.5 and the Geometric Channel route as Propositions
L.1--L.6. The $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ (canonical commutation
relation, $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$) is the endpoint of both routes:
H.4 derives it by direct computation in the configuration
representation, and L.6 recovers the same identity by direct computation
from the Schrödinger representation that the Lagrangian route produces
in L.5.

### Statement

::: {#thm:QMT10 .theorem}
**Theorem 10.1** (QM T10: Canonical Commutation Relation). *The position
and momentum operators $\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k$ ($j, k = 1, 2, 3$) on the
Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ satisfy
$$[\hat{q}^j,\,\hat{p}_k] \;=\; i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\mathbf{1}.
\label{eq:CCR-stated}$$ This is Theorem 69 (Algebraic Channel: Propositions
H.1--H.5 of [@MG-Foundations-2026]) and Theorem 92 (Geometric Channel:
Propositions L.1--L.6 of [@MG-Foundations-2026]) of [@Syn-2026].*
:::

### Geometric Channel derivation: Sphere kernel and Fourier-dual structure {#sec:QMT10-channelB}

::: {#lem:short-time-kernel-free .lemma}
**Lemma 10.7** (Short-time McGucken-Sphere kernel for the free
particle). *The free-particle short-time McGucken-Sphere kernel of
duration $\varepsilon$ from $\mathbf{x}'$ to $\mathbf{x}$ is
$$K_\varepsilon(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \left(\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}\right)^{3/2}\,\exp\!\left[\frac{im(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\right].$$*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The proof specialises the general short-time McGucken-Sphere
kernel of the Schrödinger chapter to the free-particle case ($V = 0$)
and verifies the normalisation by Fresnel-integral evaluation with
branch cut fixed. The general kernel is a derived theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (the construction is QB1--QB6 Huygens iteration
on the McGucken Sphere, formalised in
Lemma [7.9](#lem:short-time-kernel){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:short-time-kernel"} of
Chapter [7](#ch:schrodinger){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:schrodinger"}); the present lemma applies that derived
kernel to the case $V = 0$.

**Step 1: Specialise the general kernel to $V = 0$.** By
Lemma [7.9](#lem:short-time-kernel){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:short-time-kernel"} of
Chapter [7](#ch:schrodinger){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:schrodinger"} (the short-time McGucken-Sphere kernel for a
particle in a potential $V$, derived from QB1--QB6 Huygens iteration on
the McGucken Sphere with Compton-phase accumulation along secondary
wavelets), the kernel from $(\mathbf{x}', t)$ to
$(\mathbf{x}, t + \varepsilon)$ has the form
$$K_\varepsilon(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') \;=\; \mathcal{N}_\varepsilon\,\exp\!\Bigl[\,\tfrac{i}{\hbar}\,S[\gamma]\,\Bigr], \qquad S[\gamma] \;=\; \frac{m(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')^2}{2\varepsilon} \;-\; V\!\bigl(\tfrac{\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{x}'}{2}\bigr)\,\varepsilon,$$
where $S[\gamma]$ is the classical action of the straight-line path
$\gamma$ from $\mathbf{x}'$ to $\mathbf{x}$ in time $\varepsilon$
evaluated by the midpoint rule, and $\mathcal{N}_\varepsilon$ is a
normalisation determined in
Lemma [7.10](#lem:gaussian-normalization){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:gaussian-normalization"} of the same chapter. The
McGucken provenance: the kernel form descends from QB1 (McGucken-Sphere
generation at every event), QB2 (Huygens-secondary wavelets on the
Sphere), and the Compton-phase rule of
Lemma [7.8](#lem:compton-phase-wavelet){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:compton-phase-wavelet"} of
Chapter [7](#ch:schrodinger){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:schrodinger"}; the $i$ in the phase $iS/\hbar$ is the
perpendicularity marker of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via
Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"} case 5 (path-integral chain-rule mechanism);
the $\hbar$ is the action quantum per $x_{4}$-oscillation cycle via
Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}.

Setting $V = 0$ eliminates the potential term:
$$S[\gamma]\bigl|_{V = 0} \;=\; \frac{m(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')^2}{2\varepsilon}.$$
The kernel becomes
$$K_\varepsilon(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') \;=\; \mathcal{N}_\varepsilon\,\exp\!\Bigl[\,\frac{i\,m(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\,\Bigr],$$
with the normalisation $\mathcal{N}_\varepsilon$ to be evaluated by
Lemma [7.10](#lem:gaussian-normalization){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:gaussian-normalization"} in the free-particle case.

**Step 2: Fresnel-integral evaluation with branch-cut convention.** The
normalisation $\mathcal{N}_\varepsilon$ is fixed by the requirement
(Lemma [7.10](#lem:gaussian-normalization){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:gaussian-normalization"} of
Chapter [7](#ch:schrodinger){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:schrodinger"}) that the kernel preserve the constant
wavefunction $\psi \equiv 1$ under the convolution
$$\psi(\mathbf{x}, t + \varepsilon) \;=\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} K_\varepsilon(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')\,\psi(\mathbf{x}', t)\,d^3\mathbf{x}'.$$
Substituting $\psi \equiv 1$:
$$1 \;=\; \mathcal{N}_\varepsilon \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} \exp\!\Bigl[\,\frac{i\,m(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\,\Bigr]\,d^3\mathbf{x}'.$$
The Fresnel integral is evaluated by the change of variables
$\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'$ (Jacobian $1$, since translation
in $\mathbb{R}^3$ preserves Lebesgue measure):
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} \exp\!\Bigl[\,\frac{i\,m\,\mathbf{y}^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\,\Bigr]\,d^3\mathbf{y} \;=\; \prod_{j=1}^{3} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \exp\!\Bigl[\,\frac{i\,m\,y_j^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\,\Bigr]\,dy_j.$$
Each one-dimensional Fresnel integral evaluates to (Reed--Simon
[@ReedSimon1980] Vol. II, §IX.6, the Fresnel/Plancherel integral on the
line)
$$\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{i\alpha y^2}\,dy \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{i\pi}{\alpha}}, \qquad \alpha = \frac{m}{2\hbar\varepsilon} > 0,$$
where the branch $\sqrt{i} = e^{i\pi/4}$ is fixed by the principal
branch of the square root on the upper half-plane (equivalently, by the
Abel-regularised limit $\int e^{i\alpha y^2 - \delta y^2}\,dy$ as
$\delta \to 0^+$). Hence
$$\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{i m y^2/(2\hbar\varepsilon)}\,dy \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}{m}}$$
with the branch $\sqrt{i}=e^{i\pi/4}$, and
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} \exp\!\Bigl[\,\frac{i\,m\,\mathbf{y}^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\,\Bigr]\,d^3\mathbf{y} \;=\; \Bigl(\frac{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}{m}\Bigr)^{3/2}$$
with the branch $(i)^{3/2} = e^{i3\pi/4}$ fixed by the same
principal-branch convention.

The consistency condition becomes
$$1 \;=\; \mathcal{N}_\varepsilon \cdot \Bigl(\frac{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}{m}\Bigr)^{3/2},$$
hence
$$\mathcal{N}_\varepsilon \;=\; \Bigl(\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}\Bigr)^{3/2},$$
with the branch $(1/i)^{3/2} = e^{-i3\pi/4}$ inherited from the
reciprocal of the integral's branch. This is the unique normalisation
enforcing constant-wavefunction preservation under the free-particle
convolution.

**Step 3: Assemble the free-particle kernel.** Combining Steps 1 and 2:
$$K_\varepsilon(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') \;=\; \Bigl(\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}\Bigr)^{3/2}\,\exp\!\Bigl[\,\frac{i\,m(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\,\Bigr],$$
with branches fixed throughout by the principal-branch convention on the
upper half-plane. The kernel is constructed entirely from
McGucken-Sphere Huygens machinery (QB1, QB2, QB3, QB4, QB5, QB6 of
Chapter [4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:foundations"}); Stone's theorem, the spectral theorem, and
Stone--von Neumann uniqueness are not invoked. The free-particle kernel
is the Geometric-Channel-pure short-time amplitude for propagation, supplied by
the McGucken Principle via the dedicated Schrödinger-chapter lemmas.
$\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#lem:phat-from-kernel .lemma}
**Lemma 10.8** ($\hat{p}$ as the gradient operator on the Sphere
kernel). *The momentum operator on the wavefunction at time
$t + \varepsilon$ is forced by the short-time Sphere kernel of
Lemma [10.7](#lem:short-time-kernel-free){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:short-time-kernel-free"} to be
$\hat{p}= -i\hbar\,\nabla$, with no input from Stone's theorem.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof derives $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ directly from the
Sphere kernel structure in six steps, with no recourse to
Stone's theorem.

**Step 1: Gradient of the Sphere kernel.** The short-time Sphere kernel
from Lemma [10.7](#lem:short-time-kernel-free){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:short-time-kernel-free"} is
$$K_\varepsilon(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \left(\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}\right)^{3/2}\exp\!\left[\frac{im(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}')^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\right].$$
Take the spatial gradient with respect to $\mathbf{x}$:
$$\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\,K_\varepsilon(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = K_\varepsilon\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\,\frac{im(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}')^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon} = K_\varepsilon\cdot\frac{im(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}')}{\hbar\varepsilon}.$$

**Step 2: Multiply by $-i\hbar$.** Multiplying by $-i\hbar$:
$$-i\hbar\,\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\,K_\varepsilon = -i\hbar\cdot K_\varepsilon\cdot\frac{im(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}')}{\hbar\varepsilon} = \frac{m(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}')}{\varepsilon}\,K_\varepsilon,$$
using $-i \cdot i = 1$. The operator $-i\hbar\nabla$ acts on the Sphere
kernel by pointwise multiplication by the vector
$m(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}')/\varepsilon$.

**Step 3: Classical-momentum identification.** The vector
$m(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}')/\varepsilon$ is mass times average velocity
over the short interval $\varepsilon$:
$$\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{cl}} = m\cdot\frac{\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'}{\varepsilon},$$
i.e., the classical momentum of the straight-line path from
$\mathbf{x}'$ to $\mathbf{x}$ in time $\varepsilon$ (the dominant
saddle-point path in the path-integral interpretation). Substituting:
$$-i\hbar\,\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\,K_\varepsilon = \mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{cl}}\,K_\varepsilon.$$
The operator $-i\hbar\nabla$ acting on the Sphere kernel multiplies by
the classical momentum of the underlying path.

**Step 4: Explicit wavepacket computation forcing
$\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$.** We establish $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ by
showing that this is the unique self-adjoint operator on
$L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ whose expectation value on a kernel-propagated
Gaussian wavepacket reproduces the classical momentum. The argument has
four parts.

*(4a) Define the test wavepacket.* Let
$\psi_0 \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ be a normalised Gaussian
wavepacket centred at $\mathbf{x}_0$ with momentum $\mathbf{p}_0$:
$$\psi_0(\mathbf{x}) \;=\; (\pi\sigma^2)^{-3/4}\,\exp\!\Bigl[-\frac{|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_0|^2}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{i}{\hbar}\,\mathbf{p}_0\cdot(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_0)\Bigr],$$
with $\sigma > 0$ the spatial width and $\|\psi_0\|_{L^2} = 1$. The
wavepacket is constructed using only the spatial coordinate
$\mathbf{x}$, the McGucken-derived complex amplitude structure
(Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}), and two real parameters
$(\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{p}_0)$ that label the wavepacket's spatial
centre and average momentum.

*(4b) Compute $\langle -i\hbar\nabla \rangle$ on $\psi_0$.* The gradient
acts as
$$\nabla\psi_0(\mathbf{x}) \;=\; \psi_0(\mathbf{x})\,\Bigl[-\frac{\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_0}{\sigma^2} + \frac{i}{\hbar}\,\mathbf{p}_0\Bigr],$$
hence
$$(-i\hbar\nabla\psi_0)(\mathbf{x}) \;=\; \psi_0(\mathbf{x})\,\Bigl[\frac{i\hbar(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_0)}{\sigma^2} + \mathbf{p}_0\Bigr].$$
The expectation value:
$$\langle\psi_0,\, -i\hbar\nabla\,\psi_0\rangle \;=\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}|\psi_0(\mathbf{x})|^2 \mathbf{p}_0\,d^3\mathbf{x} \;+\; \frac{i\hbar}{\sigma^2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}|\psi_0(\mathbf{x})|^2(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_0)\,d^3\mathbf{x}.$$
The first integral is $\mathbf{p}_0\|\psi_0\|^2 = \mathbf{p}_0$ (using
normalisation). The second integral vanishes by symmetry: $|\psi_0|^2$
is a Gaussian centred at $\mathbf{x}_0$, so its first moment about
$\mathbf{x}_0$ is zero. Hence
$$\langle\psi_0,\, -i\hbar\nabla\,\psi_0\rangle \;=\; \mathbf{p}_0,$$
exactly, at all orders in $\hbar$.

*(4c) Compute $\langle -i\hbar\nabla \rangle$ on the kernel-propagated
wavepacket.* Define $\psi_\varepsilon = K_\varepsilon * \psi_0$, the
wavepacket at time $t+\varepsilon$ obtained by acting with the
free-particle kernel of
Lemma [10.7](#lem:short-time-kernel-free){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:short-time-kernel-free"} on $\psi_0$. The Fourier
transform converts the convolution into a product (Reed--Simon
[@ReedSimon1980] Vol. II, §IX.1):
$$\widetilde{K}_\varepsilon(\mathbf{p}) \;=\; \exp\!\Bigl[-\frac{i\varepsilon\,|\mathbf{p}|^2}{2m\hbar}\Bigr], \qquad \widetilde{\psi}_\varepsilon(\mathbf{p}) \;=\; \widetilde{K}_\varepsilon(\mathbf{p})\,\widetilde{\psi}_0(\mathbf{p}),$$
where the tilde denotes the Fourier transform with the convention
$\widetilde{f}(\mathbf{p}) = (2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\int e^{-i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}\,f(\mathbf{x})\,d^3\mathbf{x}$.
Since $\widetilde{K}_\varepsilon(\mathbf{p})$ is a pure phase,
$|\widetilde{\psi}_\varepsilon(\mathbf{p})| = |\widetilde{\psi}_0(\mathbf{p})|$:
the kernel propagation preserves the momentum distribution exactly. By
Plancherel:
$$\langle\psi_\varepsilon,\, -i\hbar\nabla\,\psi_\varepsilon\rangle \;=\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\mathbf{p}\,|\widetilde{\psi}_\varepsilon(\mathbf{p})|^2\,d^3\mathbf{p} \;=\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\mathbf{p}\,|\widetilde{\psi}_0(\mathbf{p})|^2\,d^3\mathbf{p} \;=\; \langle\psi_0,\, -i\hbar\nabla\,\psi_0\rangle \;=\; \mathbf{p}_0.$$
The operator $-i\hbar\nabla$ has constant expectation $\mathbf{p}_0$ on
the kernel-propagated wavepacket at all times $\varepsilon$, matching
the classical momentum-conservation requirement for a free particle
exactly.

*(4d) Uniqueness of $-i\hbar\nabla$.* Suppose $\hat{P}$ is any
self-adjoint operator on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ commuting with spatial
translations (a requirement: the momentum operator must
respect spatial-translation invariance of the McGucken Principle by
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i)+(v);
cf. Lemma [10.2](#lem:position-momentum-explicit){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:position-momentum-explicit"} Step 2) and whose
expectation on every Gaussian wavepacket $\psi_0$ centred at
$\mathbf{x}_0$ with momentum $\mathbf{p}_0$ is $\mathbf{p}_0$ (the
classical-correspondence requirement). By translation invariance,
$\hat{P}$ is diagonalised by the Fourier transform:
$\hat{P}\widetilde{\psi}(\mathbf{p}) = P(\mathbf{p})\widetilde{\psi}(\mathbf{p})$
for some real-valued function $P : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$
(Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Vol. I, Theorem IX.27, the spectral
theorem for translation-invariant self-adjoint operators on
$L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$). The expectation requirement on Gaussian
wavepackets becomes:
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} P(\mathbf{p})\,|\widetilde{\psi}_0(\mathbf{p})|^2\,d^3\mathbf{p} \;=\; \mathbf{p}_0$$
for every $(\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{p}_0, \sigma)$. The Fourier transform
of $\psi_0$ is a Gaussian centred at $\mathbf{p}_0$ with width
$\hbar/\sigma$:
$$\widetilde{\psi}_0(\mathbf{p}) \;\propto\; \exp\!\Bigl[-\frac{|\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{p}_0|^2\sigma^2}{2\hbar^2} - \frac{i}{\hbar}\,\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{x}_0\Bigr],$$
so $|\widetilde{\psi}_0(\mathbf{p})|^2$ is a Gaussian centred at
$\mathbf{p}_0$ with width $\hbar/\sigma$, independent of $\mathbf{x}_0$.
Taking $\sigma \to \infty$ (sharply localised in momentum,
$|\widetilde{\psi}_0|^2 \to \delta(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{p}_0)$), the
expectation requirement forces $$P(\mathbf{p}_0) \;=\; \mathbf{p}_0$$
for every $\mathbf{p}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^3$. Hence
$P(\mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{p}$ as functions on $\mathbb{R}^3$, and
$\hat{P}$ acts on the Fourier transform by multiplication by
$\mathbf{p}$. Transforming back: $\hat{P}\psi = -i\hbar\nabla\psi$ in
the position representation, by the standard Fourier-transform identity
$\mathcal{F}^{-1}\circ\,\mathbf{p}\,\circ\mathcal{F} = -i\hbar\nabla$
with the convention above. The operator $-i\hbar\nabla$ is the unique
translation-invariant self-adjoint operator with the required
expectation property; any other choice fails the
classical-correspondence requirement on at least one Gaussian
wavepacket.

The momentum operator $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ is forced by the
McGucken-Sphere kernel structure (which supplies the Gaussian phase and
hence the action of $-i\hbar\nabla$ via Steps 1--3) together with the
translation-invariance and classical-correspondence requirements (which
select $-i\hbar\nabla$ uniquely from among all candidate operators).

**Step 5: Geometric Channel characterisation --- Sphere kernel forces $\hat{p}$
without Stone's theorem.** Crucially, this derivation uses no Lie-group
structure, no one-parameter unitary group, and no spectral theorem. The
momentum operator emerges purely from the gradient of the Sphere
short-time kernel: the kernel's structure encodes the canonical-momentum
operator without invoking Stone's theorem. This is the Geometric Channel route
to $\hat{p}$, derivationally disjoint from the Algebraic Channel route
(Lemma [2.2](#lem:phat-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-generator"}, which uses Stone's theorem applied to
spatial-translation invariance of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$).

**Step 6: McGucken anchoring --- the $i$ in $\hat{p}$ is the $i$ in
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.** The factor of $-i\hbar$ in
$\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ has two sources:

-   The $i$ comes from the McGucken-Principle perpendicularity marker
    via Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:twelve-i"} case 1: the chain-rule mechanism (a) image
    of the $i$ in $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, transmitted through the
    Sphere kernel's Compton phase $iS[\gamma]/\hbar$
    (Lemma [7.8](#lem:compton-phase-wavelet){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:compton-phase-wavelet"});

-   The $\hbar$ is the action per Sphere cycle
    (Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"},
    derived from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$).

The negative sign $-i$ is the convention that the Sphere kernel's
forward propagation $e^{+iS/\hbar}$ in $\mathbf{x}$ corresponds to
$\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ acting from the right; reversing this
convention reverses the sign of $\hat{p}$. The full chain is
$(\mathrm{McP})\to$ Sphere kernel
(Lemma [10.7](#lem:short-time-kernel-free){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:short-time-kernel-free"}) $\to$ kernel gradient structure
(this Lemma) $\to$ $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$. Stone's theorem appears
nowhere in this chain --- the Geometric Channel derivation is genuinely
independent of the Algebraic Channel route. ◻
:::

::: {#lem:ccr-channelB-direct .lemma}
**Lemma 10.9** (Direct commutator computation along Geometric Channel). *With
$\hat{q}=$ multiplication by $\mathbf{x}$ (the standard
position-representation reading of localised registrations on the Sphere
wavefront) and $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\,\nabla$ (from
Lemma [10.8](#lem:phat-from-kernel){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-from-kernel"}), direct computation gives
$[\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k] = i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\mathbf{1}$ on the
Schwartz domain.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The computation parallels
Lemma [10.3](#lem:ccr-computation){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:ccr-computation"}, but with the operators $\hat{q}$ and
$\hat{p}$ arrived at along derivationally disjoint Geometric Channel routes
(Sphere kernel via
Lemma [10.8](#lem:phat-from-kernel){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-from-kernel"}) rather than Algebraic Channel routes (Stone's
theorem via Lemma [2.2](#lem:phat-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-generator"}).

**Step 1: Apply $\hat{q}^j\hat{p}_k$ to a Schwartz test function
$\psi$.** By the position-representation reading of localised
registrations on the Sphere wavefront, $\hat{q}^j$ is multiplication by
the coordinate function $x^j$. By
Lemma [10.8](#lem:phat-from-kernel){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-from-kernel"}, $\hat{p}_k = -i\hbar\,\partial_{x^k}$
as forced by the Sphere kernel. Composing:
$$(\hat{q}^j\,\hat{p}_k\,\psi)(\mathbf{x}) = x^j\,(-i\hbar\,\partial_{x^k}\psi)(\mathbf{x}) = -i\hbar\,x^j\,\partial_{x^k}\psi(\mathbf{x}).$$

**Step 2: Apply $\hat{p}_k\hat{q}^j$ to the same $\psi$.** Reversing the
order requires the product rule on $x^j\psi$:
$$(\hat{p}_k\,\hat{q}^j\,\psi)(\mathbf{x}) = -i\hbar\,\partial_{x^k}(x^j\psi)(\mathbf{x}) = -i\hbar\,(\delta^j_k\,\psi(\mathbf{x}) + x^j\,\partial_{x^k}\psi(\mathbf{x})).$$

**Step 3: Subtract to obtain the commutator.** Subtracting Step 2 from
Step 1:
$$([\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k]\,\psi)(\mathbf{x}) = -i\hbar\,x^j\,\partial_{x^k}\psi - (-i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\psi - i\hbar\,x^j\,\partial_{x^k}\psi) = i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\psi(\mathbf{x}).$$

**Step 4: Identify the operator equation.** Since this holds for every
Schwartz test function $\psi$, the operator identity on the dense
Schwartz domain is
$$[\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k] = i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\mathbf{1}.$$

**Step 5: Geometric Channel characterisation and McGucken anchoring.** The
computation used $\hat{p}_k = -i\hbar\,\partial_{x^k}$ derived from the
Sphere kernel (Lemma [10.8](#lem:phat-from-kernel){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-from-kernel"}) rather than from Stone's theorem, and
no spectral theorem and no Stone--von Neumann uniqueness entered, which
establishes that the two routes to $\hat{p}$ are distinct. (Stone and
Stone--von Neumann are packaging algorithms available to either channel
per Remark [4.36](#rmk:QA-axioms-grade1){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:QA-axioms-grade1"}, so using them would not have
disqualified a Geometric Channel route; what matters is that this route
reaches $\hat{p}$ by a different path.) The
product rule is a purely calculus-level fact, common to both channels.
By Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}, the $i$ in the result is case 3 of the
catalogue --- the chain-rule mechanism (a) image of the
McGucken-Principle $i$. The $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ is therefore
reached along Geometric Channel via a route derivationally disjoint from the
Algebraic Channel route of
Lemma [10.3](#lem:ccr-computation){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:ccr-computation"}. ◻
:::

::: {#lem:QMT10-channelB-proof .lemma}
**Lemma 10.10** (Geometric Channel proof of QM T10). *The
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$
[\[eq:CCR-stated\]](#eq:CCR-stated){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:CCR-stated"} holds along Geometric Channel: derived from the
McGucken-Sphere short-time kernel without invoking Stone's theorem or
Stone--von Neumann uniqueness.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has six steps, building the canonical
commutation relation $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar\,\mathbf{1}$ entirely
through Geometric Channel (geometric-propagation) machinery.

**Step 1: Short-time Sphere kernel.** By
Lemma [10.7](#lem:short-time-kernel-free){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:short-time-kernel-free"}, the McGucken-Sphere short-time
kernel for free-particle propagation has the explicit Gaussian form
$$K_\varepsilon(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \left(\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}\right)^{3/2}\exp\!\left[\frac{im(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\right],$$
derived entirely from McGucken-Sphere Huygens iteration on the
wavefront. The kernel encodes the propagation amplitude from
$\mathbf{x}'$ at time $t$ to $\mathbf{x}$ at time $t + \varepsilon$ via
the Sphere wavefront's iterated structure.

**Step 2: Momentum operator from kernel gradient.** By
Lemma [10.8](#lem:phat-from-kernel){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-from-kernel"}, the gradient of the Sphere kernel
forces $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\,\nabla$ via the classical-momentum
correspondence:
$$-i\hbar\,\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\,K_\varepsilon = \frac{m(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')}{\varepsilon}\,K_\varepsilon = \mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{cl}}\,K_\varepsilon.$$
The operator $-i\hbar\nabla$ acting on the Sphere kernel multiplies by
the classical momentum of the underlying path; this is the kernel-level
identification of $\hat{p}$ without recourse to Stone's theorem.

**Step 3: Direct commutator computation.** By
Lemma [10.9](#lem:ccr-channelB-direct){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:ccr-channelB-direct"}, direct computation of the
commutator $[\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k]$ on the Schwartz domain (with
$\hat{q}^j$ = multiplication by $x^j$ and $\hat{p}_k$ from Step 2) gives
$$[\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k] = i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\mathbf{1}.$$ This is the
canonical commutation
relation [\[eq:CCR-stated\]](#eq:CCR-stated){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:CCR-stated"}, derived through Geometric Channel machinery.

**Step 4: Derivational disjointness from Algebraic Channel.** Algebraic Channel obtained
$\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ via Stone's theorem applied to the unitary
spatial-translation group: the self-adjoint generator of a one-parameter
unitary group on $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$. Geometric Channel obtained
the same expression via the Gaussian-derivative identity on the
short-time Sphere kernel, using:

-   No notion of one-parameter unitary group;

-   No spectral theorem;

-   No Stone-von Neumann uniqueness;

-   No abstract Lie-algebra structure.

The two derivations are independent routes to the same operator; the
agreement of their commutators is the derivational-disjointness theorem
(Theorem [4.27](#thm:disjointness){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:disjointness"}) made explicit at the
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$.

**Step 5: Upstream geometric route from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.** The
dedicated derivation paper [@MG-Born-CCR-2026] Theorem T3.2 gives the
most direct route to $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: the Minkowski metric induced by $x_4 = ict$
has signature-mixing entries that, when contracted with the
four-momentum-as-translation-generator, yield the canonical commutator
with the $i$ inherited verbatim from the $i$ in
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. This is the upstream geometric route; the
Sphere-kernel argument above is its short-time-iteration shadow.

**Step 6: McGucken anchoring of the $i$ in
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$.** The factor of $i$ in the canonical
commutator $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar\,\mathbf{1}$ is, by
Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"} case 3 (signature-change mechanism (b)), the
shadow of the $i$ in $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: the
perpendicularity marker of the principle is transmitted through the
McGucken-Sphere kernel's Gaussian phase
$im(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')^2/(2\hbar\varepsilon)$ to the gradient
identification of $\hat{p}$, and from there to the canonical commutator.
The $\hbar$ on the right-hand side is the action quantum per Sphere
cycle (Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}).
Both constants in the canonical commutator descend from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ --- they are consequences of the
McGucken Principle $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the $x_{4}$-advance at
rate $ic$.

**Significance.** The Geometric Channel derivation of the
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ establishes that the canonical commutation
relation is a geometric theorem of the McGucken Principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: it descends from McGucken-Sphere
short-time-propagation kinematics, with no Stone's theorem invoked. This
is the advantage of the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework: the
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ is a derived theorem along both channels,
with the channels derivationally disjoint at every intermediate step. ◻
:::

::: proof
*Proof of Theorem [10.1](#thm:QMT10){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT10"}.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The canonical commutation relation
[\[eq:CCR-stated\]](#eq:CCR-stated){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:CCR-stated"} is derived twice, by derivationally disjoint
routes.

**Algebraic Channel route
(Lemma [\[lem:QMT10-channelA-proof\]](#lem:QMT10-channelA-proof){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT10-channelA-proof"}).** Starting from time-translation
invariance of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (QA1), Stone's theorem (QA2,
Theorem [3.6](#thm:stone){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:stone"})
supplies the self-adjoint generator $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ on
$\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$
(Lemma [2.2](#lem:phat-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-generator"}).
Lemma [10.2](#lem:position-momentum-explicit){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:position-momentum-explicit"} confirms the operator forms.
Lemma [10.3](#lem:ccr-computation){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:ccr-computation"} computes the commutator directly via
the product rule of calculus, yielding
$[\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k] = i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\mathbf{1}$ on the
Schwartz domain. Stone--von Neumann uniqueness (QA4,
Lemma [10.4](#lem:stone-vonNeumann-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:stone-vonNeumann-uniqueness"}) extends this from the
specific Schrödinger representation to every unitarily equivalent
representation, making the $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ the defining
relation of the unique irreducible representation of quantum kinematics.

**Geometric Channel route
(Lemma [10.10](#lem:QMT10-channelB-proof){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT10-channelB-proof"}).** Starting from the
McGucken-Sphere construction (QB1) and iterated Sphere
Huygens-propagation (QB2--QB3), the short-time kernel for free-particle
propagation has the explicit Gaussian form
$$K_\varepsilon(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \left(\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}\right)^{3/2}\exp\!\left[\frac{im(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}')^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\right]$$
(Lemma [10.7](#lem:short-time-kernel-free){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:short-time-kernel-free"}). The Gaussian-derivative
identity on this kernel forces $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ via the
classical-momentum correspondence
(Lemma [10.8](#lem:phat-from-kernel){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-from-kernel"}). Direct commutator computation on the
Schwartz domain gives
$[\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k] = i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\mathbf{1}$
(Lemma [10.9](#lem:ccr-channelB-direct){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:ccr-channelB-direct"}).

**Derivational disjointness.** Algebraic Channel uses Stone's theorem, Stone--von
Neumann uniqueness, and the abstract Lie-algebra structure of the
spatial-translation symmetry group --- all algebraic-symmetry machinery.
Geometric Channel uses the McGucken Sphere, Huygens iteration, Compton-phase per
wavelet, the short-time Sphere kernel, and Gaussian-derivative
identities --- all geometric-propagation machinery. The two derivations
share no intermediate step beyond the McGucken Principle and the final
equation. This is the derivational-disjointness theorem
(Theorem [4.27](#thm:disjointness){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:disjointness"}) made explicit at the
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$.

**Upstream geometric route.** The dedicated derivation paper
[@MG-Born-CCR-2026] Theorem T3.2 gives the most direct McGucken-anchored
route: the Minkowski metric induced by $x_{4}= ict$ has signature-mixing
entries that, when contracted with the
four-momentum-as-translation-generator, yield
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ with the $i$ inherited verbatim from the
$i$ in $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The $i$ in the
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ is therefore not arbitrary; it is the same
$i$ as in the principle
(Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"} case 3). ◻
:::

### Algebraic Channel derivation: Stone's theorem and direct commutator computation {#sec:QMT10-channelA}

::: {#lem:position-momentum-explicit .lemma}
**Lemma 10.2** (Position is multiplication and momentum is
$-i\hbar\,\partial$). *On the Schrödinger representation
$\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3\mathbf{x})$:*

-   *$\hat{q}^j$ acts as multiplication by $x^j$:
    $(\hat{q}^j\,\psi)(\mathbf{x}) = x^j\,\psi(\mathbf{x})$;*

-   *$\hat{p}_k$ acts as
    $\hat{p}_k\,\psi = -i\hbar\,\partial_{x^k}\psi$.*

*Both operators are self-adjoint on the dense Schwartz domain
$\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3) \subset L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **Step 1: $\hat{q}^j$ as multiplication operator on the Algebraic
Channel Hilbert space.** By
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"} of
Chapter [9](#ch:hilbert-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:hilbert-theorem"}, the Hilbert space of non-relativistic
quantum mechanics is $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3\mathbf{x})$,
with $\mathbb{R}^3$ the spatial slice of the McGucken-derived Minkowski
arena $M_{1,3}$ at fixed slice-time $t$. On this $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$,
the natural action of a spatial coordinate function
$x^j : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ on a wavefunction
$\psi \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ is pointwise multiplication:
$$(\hat{q}^j\,\psi)(\mathbf{x}) = x^j\,\psi(\mathbf{x}).$$ The Algebraic Channel
reading: position is the spectral content of the coordinate function on
the spatial slice, with the spectrum of $\hat{q}^j$ being $\mathbb{R}$
(the range of $x^j$) and the spectral measure being Lebesgue measure on
$\mathbb{R}^3$ pushed forward by the coordinate projection
$\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ along $j$. The Geometric Channel reading: position
is the spatial-slice location at which the McGucken-Sphere wavefront is
registered by the apparatus
(Lemma [6.2](#lem:position-localized){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:position-localized"} of
Chapter [6](#ch:wave-particle){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:wave-particle"}); registering at the spatial point
$\mathbf{x}$ is equivalent to multiplying the wavefunction at that point
by the coordinate value $x^j$. Both readings agree on the operator
action.

Self-adjointness on the dense Schwartz domain
$\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3) \subset L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ follows from
symmetry. For $\phi, \psi \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$, the coordinate
function $x^j$ is real-valued, so
$$\langle\phi, \hat{q}^j\psi\rangle \;=\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\overline{\phi(\mathbf{x})}\,x^j\,\psi(\mathbf{x})\,d^3x \;=\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\overline{x^j\,\phi(\mathbf{x})}\,\psi(\mathbf{x})\,d^3x \;=\; \langle\hat{q}^j\phi, \psi\rangle,$$
where the middle equality uses $\overline{x^j} = x^j$ for
$x^j \in \mathbb{R}$. The operator is symmetric on
$\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$. Standard extension theory (Reed--Simon
[@ReedSimon1980] Vol. I, Theorem VIII.5) confirms the unique
self-adjoint extension is multiplication by $x^j$ on the maximal domain
$\{\psi \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3) : x^j\psi \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)\}$.

**Step 2: $\hat{p}_k$ as derivative operator on the Algebraic Channel Hilbert
space.** By Lemma [2.2](#lem:phat-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-generator"} of
Chapter [2](#ch:de-broglie){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:de-broglie"}, the momentum operator
$\hat{p}_k = -i\hbar\,\partial_{x^k}$ is the self-adjoint generator, via
Stone's theorem (Theorem [3.6](#thm:stone){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:stone"}, Algebraic Channel axiom QA2), of the one-parameter
unitary group
$\hat{U}(\mathbf{a}) = e^{-i\mathbf{a}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{p}}/\hbar}$
implementing spatial translations on $\mathcal{H}$. Spatial-translation
invariance is supplied by
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (i) (invariance: the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value)
together with clause (v) (global validity). The unitary group acts on
wavefunctions by
$(\hat{U}(\mathbf{a})\psi)(\mathbf{x}) = \psi(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})$;
differentiating at $\mathbf{a} = 0$ gives the self-adjoint generator
$-i\hbar\nabla$, with the factor $-i\hbar$ assembled as: the
perpendicularity marker $i$ from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via
Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"} case 1 (chain-rule mechanism (a)), and the
action quantum $\hbar$ per radian of the Compton-frequency oscillation of $x_4$-advance
via Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}.

**Step 3: Self-adjointness of $\hat{p}_k$ on the Schwartz domain by
integration by parts.** For $\phi, \psi \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$,
$$\langle\phi, \hat{p}_k\psi\rangle \;=\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\overline{\phi(\mathbf{x})}\,(-i\hbar)\,\partial_{x^k}\psi(\mathbf{x})\,d^3x \;=\; -i\hbar\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\overline{\phi(\mathbf{x})}\,\partial_{x^k}\psi(\mathbf{x})\,d^3x.$$
Integration by parts in the $x^k$ direction:
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\overline{\phi(\mathbf{x})}\,\partial_{x^k}\psi(\mathbf{x})\,d^3x \;=\; \Bigl[\,\overline{\phi}\,\psi\,\Bigr]_{x^k = -\infty}^{x^k = +\infty}\,\Bigl|_{\text{integrated over remaining coords}} \;-\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\partial_{x^k}\!\overline{\phi(\mathbf{x})}\,\psi(\mathbf{x})\,d^3x.$$
The boundary term vanishes by Schwartz-class decay at infinity: both
$\phi$ and $\psi$ decay faster than any polynomial as
$|\mathbf{x}| \to \infty$, so $\overline{\phi}\,\psi \to 0$ at the
boundary of every coordinate slab. Hence
$$\langle\phi, \hat{p}_k\psi\rangle \;=\; -i\hbar\,(-1)\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\partial_{x^k}\!\overline{\phi(\mathbf{x})}\,\psi(\mathbf{x})\,d^3x \;=\; i\hbar\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\overline{\partial_{x^k}\phi(\mathbf{x})}\,\psi(\mathbf{x})\,d^3x,$$
where the second equality uses
$\partial_{x^k}\overline{\phi} = \overline{\partial_{x^k}\phi}$ (real
partial derivatives commute with complex conjugation). Rewriting
$i\hbar = \overline{-i\hbar}$:
