$$\langle\phi, \hat{p}_k\psi\rangle \;=\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\overline{(-i\hbar)\,\partial_{x^k}\phi(\mathbf{x})}\,\psi(\mathbf{x})\,d^3x \;=\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\overline{\hat{p}_k\phi(\mathbf{x})}\,\psi(\mathbf{x})\,d^3x \;=\; \langle\hat{p}_k\phi, \psi\rangle.$$
The operator is symmetric on $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$. Standard
extension theory (Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Vol. II, Theorem X.36)
gives the unique self-adjoint extension on the Sobolev space
$H^1(\mathbb{R}^3) = \{\psi \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3) : \nabla\psi \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)\}$.

**Step 4: Cross-reference for the McGucken anchoring of $-i\hbar$.** The
derivation of the factor $-i\hbar$ in
$\hat{p}_k = -i\hbar\,\partial_{x^k}$ from the McGucken Principle is
supplied by Lemma [2.2](#lem:phat-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-generator"} of
Chapter [2](#ch:de-broglie){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:de-broglie"} (Stone generator of spatial translations),
with the $i$ traced to the perpendicularity marker of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via
Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"} case 1 and the $\hbar$ traced to action per
$x_{4}$-oscillation cycle via
Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}. The
negative sign $-i$ is fixed by the convention that the unitary
$\hat{U}(\mathbf{a}) = e^{-i\mathbf{a}\cdot\hat{p}/\hbar}$ translates
wavefunctions forward by $\mathbf{a}$: with this sign,
$(\hat{U}(\mathbf{a})\psi)(\mathbf{x}) = \psi(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})$,
and differentiating at $\mathbf{a} = 0$ produces
$\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ with the negative sign. Reversing this
convention would reverse the sign of $\hat{p}$ and change the
action-on-wavefunctions to
$(\hat{U}(\mathbf{a})\psi)(\mathbf{x}) = \psi(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{a})$.
The convention is fixed by the choice in
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"} that forward $x_4$-advance
corresponds to positive coordinate translation; once this choice is
made, the negative sign in $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ is forced.
$\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#lem:ccr-computation .lemma}
**Lemma 10.3** (Direct commutator computation). *For any
$\psi \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ (Schwartz class) and any
$j, k \in \{1, 2, 3\}$:
$$[\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k]\,\psi = i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\psi.$$*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has five steps. The operators $\hat{q}^j$ and
$\hat{p}_k$ used here descend, by Algebraic Channel, from the McGucken Principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: $\hat{q}^j$ as the position multiplication
operator
(Lemma [10.2](#lem:position-momentum-explicit){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:position-momentum-explicit"}) and
$\hat{p}_k = -i\hbar\,\partial_{x^k}$ as the Stone generator of spatial
translations on $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$
(Lemma [2.2](#lem:phat-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-generator"}, via Stone's theorem applied to the
translation invariance built into
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i)+(v)). The factor $-i\hbar$
carries the perpendicularity marker of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"} case 1, chain-rule mechanism (a)) and the
quantum of action per cycle of $x_{4}$-oscillation
(Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"} via the
oscillatory form of the McGucken Principle, [@MG-Constants]).

**Step 1: Expand the commutator on Schwartz-class test functions.** The
Schwartz space $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ is a common dense invariant
domain for both $\hat{q}^j$ and $\hat{p}_k$ in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$
(Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Vol. I, §V.3). For any
$\psi \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$, the commutator acts as
$$([\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k]\,\psi)(\mathbf{x}) \;=\; (\hat{q}^j\,\hat{p}_k\,\psi)(\mathbf{x}) - (\hat{p}_k\,\hat{q}^j\,\psi)(\mathbf{x}).$$

**Step 2: First term --- apply $\hat{p}_k$ then $\hat{q}^j$.** By
Lemma [10.2](#lem:position-momentum-explicit){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:position-momentum-explicit"},
$\hat{p}_k\,\psi = -i\hbar\,\partial_{x^k}\psi$ and $\hat{q}^j$ is
multiplication by $x^j$. Hence
$$(\hat{q}^j\,\hat{p}_k\,\psi)(\mathbf{x}) \;=\; x^j\,(-i\hbar\,\partial_{x^k}\psi)(\mathbf{x}) \;=\; -i\hbar\,x^j\,\partial_{x^k}\psi(\mathbf{x}).$$

**Step 3: Second term --- apply $\hat{q}^j$ then $\hat{p}_k$, with the
product rule.** Applying $\hat{q}^j$ (multiplication by $x^j$) first,
then $\hat{p}_k = -i\hbar\,\partial_{x^k}$: $$\begin{aligned}
(\hat{p}_k\,\hat{q}^j\,\psi)(\mathbf{x}) &\;=\; -i\hbar\,\partial_{x^k}\!\left[x^j\,\psi(\mathbf{x})\right] \\
&\;=\; -i\hbar\,\bigl[(\partial_{x^k}x^j)\,\psi(\mathbf{x}) + x^j\,\partial_{x^k}\psi(\mathbf{x})\bigr] \\
&\;=\; -i\hbar\,\bigl[\delta^j_k\,\psi(\mathbf{x}) + x^j\,\partial_{x^k}\psi(\mathbf{x})\bigr] \\
&\;=\; -i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\psi(\mathbf{x}) \;-\; i\hbar\,x^j\,\partial_{x^k}\psi(\mathbf{x}),
\end{aligned}$$ using the elementary calculus fact
$\partial_{x^k}(x^j) = \delta^j_k$ (the Kronecker delta) in the third
line.

**Step 4: Subtract and read off the commutator.** Subtracting Step 3
from Step 2: $$\begin{aligned}
([\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k]\,\psi)(\mathbf{x}) &\;=\; -i\hbar\,x^j\,\partial_{x^k}\psi - \bigl[-i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\psi - i\hbar\,x^j\,\partial_{x^k}\psi\bigr] \\
&\;=\; -i\hbar\,x^j\,\partial_{x^k}\psi \;+\; i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\psi \;+\; i\hbar\,x^j\,\partial_{x^k}\psi \\
&\;=\; i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\psi(\mathbf{x}).
\end{aligned}$$ Hence
$[\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k]\,\psi = i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\psi$ on the
Schwartz domain, equivalently
$[\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k] = i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\mathbf{1}$ as operators
on $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$. The factor $i\hbar$ in the result is the
same factor that appears in $\hat{p}_k = -i\hbar\,\partial_{x^k}$: it
carries the perpendicularity marker $i$ of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"} case 1) and the quantum of action $\hbar$ per
$x_{4}$-oscillation cycle (Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:62"}).

**Step 5: Closure to the full self-adjoint domain.** By
Lemma [10.2](#lem:position-momentum-explicit){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:position-momentum-explicit"}, both $\hat{q}^j$ and
$\hat{p}_k$ are essentially self-adjoint on $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$,
with self-adjoint closures whose common dense invariant domain is the
Schwartz-completion in the graph norm (Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980]
Vol. I, Theorem VIII.6 on essential self-adjointness). The commutator
identity $[\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k] = i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\mathbf{1}$,
established on $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$, extends by continuity to
this common domain. By
Lemma [10.4](#lem:stone-vonNeumann-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:stone-vonNeumann-uniqueness"} (Stone--von Neumann
uniqueness, QA4), the resulting commutation relation is the defining
relation of the unique-up-to-unitary-equivalence irreducible
representation of quantum kinematics. The result is therefore not a
feature of the specific Schrödinger representation but a invariant forced by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#lem:stone-vonNeumann-uniqueness .lemma}
**Lemma 10.4** (Stone--von Neumann uniqueness: the canonical commutator
representation is essentially unique). *Any pair of self-adjoint
operators $(Q_j, P_k)$ on a separable Hilbert space whose
Weyl-exponentiated forms
$U(\mathbf{a}) = e^{-i\mathbf{a}\cdot \mathbf{P}/\hbar}$,
$V(\mathbf{b}) = e^{i\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{Q}/\hbar}$ satisfy the Weyl
relations
$$U(\mathbf{a})V(\mathbf{b}) = e^{i\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}/\hbar}\,V(\mathbf{b})\,U(\mathbf{a})$$
is unitarily equivalent to the Schrödinger representation
$(\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k)$ of
Lemma [10.2](#lem:position-momentum-explicit){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:position-momentum-explicit"}.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The Stone--von Neumann uniqueness theorem (von Neumann 1931
[@vonNeumann1931]; modern exposition Folland--Sitaram 1997
[@FollandSitaram1997] Theorem 4.34) is a standard theorem of
representation theory whose full proof is supplied by the cited
references. The McGucken contribution is the verification that the Weyl
relations being uniqued by this theorem descend from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, and that the four inputs the
theorem requires are each supplied by the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework. We list
the four inputs and verify each from the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework.

**Input 1: A separable Hilbert space.** By
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"} of
Chapter [9](#ch:hilbert-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:hilbert-theorem"}, the Hilbert space
$\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3\mathbf{x})$ of non-relativistic
quantum mechanics is derived from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as the
spatial-slice $L^2$-completion of slice-projected $x_{4}$-wavefronts.
The space $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3\mathbf{x})$ is separable (a standard
fact of measure theory: $L^2$ over any $\sigma$-finite measure space
with a countable basis is separable; see Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980]
Vol. I, Theorem II.7). The separability hypothesis of Stone--von Neumann
is therefore satisfied.

**Input 2: The Weyl relations as bounded unitary form of the canonical
commutator.** The unbounded operator equation
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar\,\mathbf{1}$ has domain issues that
complicate direct uniqueness analysis (Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980]
Vol. I, §VIII.5 catalogues several inequivalent representations of the
algebraic relation on incomplete or non-dense domains). The
Weyl-exponentiated form
$$U(\mathbf{a})\,V(\mathbf{b}) \;=\; e^{i\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}/\hbar}\,V(\mathbf{b})\,U(\mathbf{a}),$$
with $U(\mathbf{a}) = e^{-i\mathbf{a}\cdot\hat{p}/\hbar}$ and
$V(\mathbf{b}) = e^{i\mathbf{b}\cdot\hat{q}/\hbar}$ acting as bounded
unitary operators on $\mathcal{H}$, is equivalent to the unbounded
commutator on a common dense invariant domain (Folland--Sitaram
[@FollandSitaram1997] §1.5, the Baker--Campbell--Hausdorff identity for
Weyl operators). The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework supplies both unitary groups
directly:

-   $U(\mathbf{a}) = e^{-i\mathbf{a}\cdot\hat{p}/\hbar}$ is the
    spatial-translation unitary group, the Stone-theorem exponentiation
    of the self-adjoint generator $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ derived in
    Lemma [10.2](#lem:position-momentum-explicit){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:position-momentum-explicit"} Step 2. Its existence
    and strong continuity are forced by
    Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
    reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i) (invariance) and (v) (global
    validity) via Stone's theorem (Algebraic Channel axiom QA2).

-   $V(\mathbf{b}) = e^{i\mathbf{b}\cdot\hat{q}/\hbar}$ is the
    position-phase-multiplication unitary group,
    $(V(\mathbf{b})\psi)(\mathbf{x}) = e^{i\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}\psi(\mathbf{x})$.
    Boundedness is immediate
    ($|e^{i\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}| = 1$ for all
    $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$); strong continuity in $\mathbf{b}$
    follows from dominated convergence applied to the integral
    $\int|V(\mathbf{b})\psi - \psi|^2 d^3\mathbf{x}$.

The Weyl-relations exponent $e^{i\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}/\hbar}$
records the non-commutativity of the two groups: a direct computation
using the explicit action
$(U(\mathbf{a})\psi)(\mathbf{x}) = \psi(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})$ and
$(V(\mathbf{b})\psi)(\mathbf{x}) = e^{i\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}\psi(\mathbf{x})$
gives $$\begin{aligned}
(U(\mathbf{a})V(\mathbf{b})\psi)(\mathbf{x}) &= (V(\mathbf{b})\psi)(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}) = e^{i\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})/\hbar}\,\psi(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}), \\
(V(\mathbf{b})U(\mathbf{a})\psi)(\mathbf{x}) &= e^{i\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}\,(U(\mathbf{a})\psi)(\mathbf{x}) = e^{i\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}\,\psi(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}),
\end{aligned}$$ hence
$U(\mathbf{a})V(\mathbf{b}) = e^{-i\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}/\hbar}V(\mathbf{b})U(\mathbf{a})$,
equivalently
$V(\mathbf{b})U(\mathbf{a}) = e^{i\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}/\hbar}U(\mathbf{a})V(\mathbf{b})$.
The Weyl exponent's $i$ is the Algebraic-Channel image of the McGucken-Principle
$i$ via Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"} case 3.

**Input 3: Irreducibility of the Weyl representation.** The Stone--von
Neumann theorem classifies *irreducible* representations of the Weyl
relations: any irreducible representation on a separable Hilbert space
is unitarily equivalent to the Schrödinger representation on
$L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$. The McGucken-derived representation on
$\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ is irreducible: any bounded operator
$T$ commuting with both $U(\mathbf{a})$ for all
$\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and $V(\mathbf{b})$ for all
$\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is necessarily a scalar multiple of the
identity. The argument: commutation with all $V(\mathbf{b})$ forces $T$
to be a multiplication operator (Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Vol. I,
Theorem VII.4, the von Neumann theorem on maximal abelian algebras: the
multiplication operators by bounded functions form a maximal abelian von
Neumann subalgebra of $\mathcal{B}(L^2)$, with
$\{V(\mathbf{b})\}_{\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^3}$ a generating set);
commutation with all $U(\mathbf{a})$ then forces $T$ to be
translation-invariant; translation-invariant multiplication operators on
$L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ are constants. Hence $T = c\,\mathbf{1}$ for some
$c \in \mathbb{C}$, establishing irreducibility.

**Input 4: A cyclic vector for the Weyl algebra.** The Stone--von
Neumann theorem applied to an irreducible representation produces the
unitary equivalence to the Schrödinger representation by constructing
the intertwiner from a distinguished cyclic vector (Folland--Sitaram
[@FollandSitaram1997] §4.5, the explicit construction via the
harmonic-oscillator ground state). On $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$,
the Gaussian $\Omega(\mathbf{x}) = (1/\pi)^{3/4}\,e^{-|\mathbf{x}|^2/2}$
is cyclic for the Weyl algebra (Folland--Sitaram [@FollandSitaram1997]
Proposition 4.32): the linear span of
$\{U(\mathbf{a})V(\mathbf{b})\Omega : \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^3\}$
is dense in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$. The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework supplies this
cyclic vector concretely as the spatial-slice projection of a Gaussian
wavepacket on the McGucken Sphere centred at the origin event.

**Conclusion: apply Stone--von Neumann.** The four inputs
being verified, Folland--Sitaram [@FollandSitaram1997] Theorem 4.34 (the
Stone--von Neumann uniqueness theorem in modern form) applies and
yields: any irreducible representation of the Weyl relations on a
separable Hilbert space is unitarily equivalent to the Schrödinger
representation on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$. The McGucken-derived Schrödinger
representation $(\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k)$ of
Lemma [10.2](#lem:position-momentum-explicit){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:position-momentum-explicit"} is thereby the
unique-up-to-unitary-equivalence irreducible representation of quantum
kinematics, with the canonical commutator
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar\,\mathbf{1}$ as its defining algebraic
relation.

**McGucken provenance.** Every input to the Stone--von
Neumann theorem is supplied by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: the separable
Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ is derived from the
principle via
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}; the Weyl relations are derived from
the principle's translation invariance via
Lemma [10.2](#lem:position-momentum-explicit){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:position-momentum-explicit"} and the explicit computation
in Input 2; irreducibility is verified by direct calculation on the
McGucken-derived Hilbert space; the cyclic Gaussian is the spatial-slice
projection of a McGucken-Sphere wavepacket. The completeness of the
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework's content for the Stone--von Neumann hypothesis is
what makes the application of the theorem legitimate; the proof of the
theorem itself is the standard one of [@vonNeumann1931] and
[@FollandSitaram1997]. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#thm:QMT10-channelA .lemma}
**Lemma 10.5** (Algebraic Channel proof of QM T10).
*[]{#lem:QMT10-channelA-proof label="lem:QMT10-channelA-proof"}The
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$
[\[eq:CCR-stated\]](#eq:CCR-stated){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:CCR-stated"} holds in the Schrödinger representation and,
up to unitary equivalence, in every other representation.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **Step 1: Position and momentum operators from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.** By
Lemma [10.2](#lem:position-momentum-explicit){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:position-momentum-explicit"}, the position operator
$\hat{q}^j$ acts on $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ as multiplication
by the coordinate function $x^j$ (Algebraic Channel: position-representation
reading of the McGucken-derived Hilbert space). The momentum operator
$\hat{p}_k$ acts as $-i\hbar\,\partial_{x^k}$, derived as the
self-adjoint generator of the spatial-translation unitary group via
Stone's theorem (Lemma [2.2](#lem:phat-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-generator"}, applied to the spatial-translation
invariance clause of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via QA1+QA2).

**Step 2: Direct commutator computation.** By
Lemma [10.3](#lem:ccr-computation){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:ccr-computation"}, direct application of the operators on
a Schwartz-class test function $\psi$ yields, after explicit use of the
product rule
$\partial_{x^k}(x^j\psi) = \delta^j_k\psi + x^j\partial_{x^k}\psi$:
$$[\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k]\,\psi = \hat{q}^j(\hat{p}_k\psi) - \hat{p}_k(\hat{q}^j\psi) = i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\psi.$$
Hence $[\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k] = i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\mathbf{1}$ as
operators on the Schwartz domain, which is dense in $\mathcal{H}$.

**Step 3: Stone--von Neumann uniqueness.** By
Lemma [10.4](#lem:stone-vonNeumann-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:stone-vonNeumann-uniqueness"} (Stone--von Neumann
uniqueness, QA4), every irreducible representation of the Weyl relations
on a separable Hilbert space is unitarily equivalent to the Schrödinger
representation. The $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ is the defining
algebraic relation of the unique irreducible representation of quantum
kinematics, and holds in any unitarily equivalent representation by
transport of structure.

**Step 4: The $i$ comes from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.** The factor $i$
in $[\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k] = i\hbar\,\delta^j_k$ is not an arithmetic
accident: by Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"} (Twelve canonical $i$-insertions), the $i$ in
the $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ is case 3 of the catalogue --- the
chain-rule-mechanism-(a) image of the single $i$ in
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, transported through the spatial-slice
formulation via $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ (whose $i$ is case 1 of the
catalogue).

**Step 5: Closure to full domain.** The commutator identity extends by
density from the Schwartz domain to the appropriate common dense domain
on which $\hat{q}^j$ and $\hat{p}_k$ act as essentially self-adjoint
operators. This is the natural domain for unbounded self-adjoint
operators on $\mathcal{H}$ (cf. Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980]
Ch. VIII). ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:ccr-channelA-machinery .remark}
*Remark 10.6* (McGucken machinery used in the Algebraic Channel
canonical-commutator proof). Every step of the above proof is forced by
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ alone, with Stone's theorem and Stone--von
Neumann uniqueness appearing in their roles as Algebraic Channel axioms QA2 and
QA4 (Remark [4.36](#rmk:QA-axioms-grade1){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:QA-axioms-grade1"}) --- *i.e.*, as algorithms for
packaging the McGucken Principle's symmetry content into Hilbert-space
operators, not as external essential inputs.

**McGucken machinery used.** (1) $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ itself,
supplying spatial-translation invariance via clause (i); (2) the slice
projection $\sigma: M_{1,3} \to \mathbb{R}^3$
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}), supplying the configuration space; (3)
the complex-amplitude algebra $\mathbb{C}$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$
(Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}); (4) Algebraic Channel axiom QA2 (Stone's
theorem packaging); (5) Algebraic Channel axiom QA4 (Stone--von Neumann
packaging).
:::

### Disjointness audit {#disjointness-audit-8}

This is the flagship case of
Theorem [4.27](#thm:disjointness){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:disjointness"}.

**Algebraic Channel intermediate machinery:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; spatial
translation invariance; Stone's theorem (QA2); $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$
as Stone generator
(Lemma [10.2](#lem:position-momentum-explicit){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:position-momentum-explicit"}); direct commutator
computation (Lemma [10.3](#lem:ccr-computation){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:ccr-computation"}); Stone--von Neumann uniqueness (QA4,
Lemma [10.4](#lem:stone-vonNeumann-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:stone-vonNeumann-uniqueness"}).

**Geometric Channel intermediate machinery:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; iterated
McGucken-Sphere path space (QB3); Compton phase (QB4); classical action
$S[\gamma]$; short-time Sphere-Huygens kernel
(Lemma [10.7](#lem:short-time-kernel-free){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:short-time-kernel-free"}); Gaussian-derivative identity
on kernel (Lemma [10.8](#lem:phat-from-kernel){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-from-kernel"}); direct commutator computation
(Lemma [10.9](#lem:ccr-channelB-direct){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:ccr-channelB-direct"}).

**Intersection:**
$\{(\mathrm{McP}), [\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k] = i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\}$.
Stone's theorem does *not* appear in Geometric Channel. The McGucken Sphere does
*not* appear in Algebraic Channel. The two derivations agree on the principle
they start from and on the equation they end at; they share no
intermediate step.

*Disjointness verified. This is the property that has no
analogue in any of the five textbooks.*

::: {#rmk:channel-perpendicularity-qp .remark}
*Remark 10.11* (Geometric Channel and Algebraic Channel as perpendicular readings of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, with the canonical commutator as the
operator-level shadow). The disjointness of Geometric Channel and Algebraic Channel at
the level of derivations (the present chapter) and the differential
response of Geometric Channel and Algebraic Channel to the McGucken-Wick rotation
(Theorem [1.5](#thm:channel-differential-response){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:channel-differential-response"}) jointly have a deeper
reading at the operator level. The two channels are
perpendicular readings of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, with the
perpendicularity supplied by the imaginary unit $i$ of the principle
itself; the non-commutativity of $\hat{q}$ and $\hat{p}$ recorded as
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ is the operator-level shadow of this
channel-level perpendicularity.

**The claim.** The position operator $\hat{q}$ is a Geometric Channel
observable: it registers the spatial-slice location at which the
McGucken Sphere wavefront is found by the apparatus, with the geometric
content of position supplied by the three-dimensional intersection of
the four-dimensional Sphere with the apparatus slice. The momentum
operator $\hat{p}$ is an Algebraic Channel observable: it is the self-adjoint
generator of spatial translations on the Hilbert space, with its content
supplied by Stone's theorem applied to the spatial-translation
invariance of the principle
(Lemma [2.2](#lem:phat-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-generator"}). The commutator
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ pairs a Geometric Channel observable ($\hat{q}$)
with an Algebraic Channel observable ($\hat{p}$), with the right-hand side
carrying both factors of the principle's twin constants: the
perpendicularity-marker $i$ traceable to the perpendicularity of $x_4$
to the spatial three in $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"} case 3), and the action quantum $\hbar$
traceable to action per radian of the Compton-frequency oscillation of $x_4$-advance
(Proposition [\[ssec:c-and-hbar-twin\]](#ssec:c-and-hbar-twin){reference-type="ref"
reference="ssec:c-and-hbar-twin"} of the dedicated derivation paper
[@MG-Born-CCR-2026]). The $i$ on the right-hand side of
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ does three jobs simultaneously,
all the same job: it marks the perpendicularity of $x_4$ to the spatial
three at the geometric level (the mere integrated kinematic shadow $x_4 = ict$ records this perpendicularity algebraically); it marks the
perpendicularity of Algebraic Channel's momentum-conservation reading to Geometric
Channel's spatial-position reading at the channel level (the two channels
supply the two perpendicular readings of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, with
the principle's $i$ marking the perpendicularity between them); and it
marks the non-commutativity of $\hat{q}$ and $\hat{p}$ as conjugate
observables at the operator level (the commutator
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ records the operator-algebraic
non-commutativity). All three are the same perpendicularity, expressed
at three levels of the same principle.

**The measurement reading.** The perpendicularity of the channels at the
operator level supplies the operational content of conjugate-observable
measurement. To measure position $q$ is to perform a Geometric Channel
measurement: the apparatus's McGucken-Wick rotation on Geometric Channel
transports the four-dimensional Sphere into its Euclidean-signature
reading, with the Sphere's intersection with the three-dimensional
apparatus slice supplying the registered position and the $SO(3)$-Haar
measure on the wavefront weighted by $|\psi|^2$ supplying the Born
probability for the registered location. To measure momentum $p$ is to
perform an Algebraic Channel measurement: the apparatus extracts the
conservation-law value of the spatial-translation generator, with
Stone's theorem identifying the registered momentum eigenvalue as a
value in the spectrum of $\hat{p}$. Measuring $q$ sharpens Geometric Channel's
spatial localisation and destroys Algebraic Channel's momentum-eigenstate
unitary; measuring $p$ sharpens Algebraic Channel's momentum-eigenstate and
destroys Geometric Channel's position localisation. The uncertainty relation
$\sigma_q \sigma_p \geq \hbar/2$ of
Chapter [12](#ch:heisenberg){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:heisenberg"} records the floor on the joint
sharpening: the perpendicularity of the channels combined with the
action-quantum calibration $\hbar$ forces a minimum joint spread, with
the factor $1/2$ supplied by the Cauchy--Schwarz/Robertson bound on
Hermitian commutators
(the Robertson--Schr\"odinger inequality lemma of
Chapter [12](#ch:heisenberg){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:heisenberg"}).

**Scope of the claim.** The clean perpendicularity reading
developed above applies to the canonical $(\hat{q}, \hat{p})$ commutator
with its well-defined self-adjoint operator structure on the Schwartz
domain. Extension to other conjugate pairs in quantum mechanics requires
case-by-case analysis. The energy-time pair $(\hat{H}, t)$ admits a
heuristic Geometric Channel / Algebraic Channel reading (energy is the time-translation
generator, time is the geometric parameter), but the absence of a
self-adjoint time operator conjugate to a Hamiltonian bounded below
(Pauli 1933) means the operator-level commutator
$[\hat{H}, \hat{t}] = i\hbar$ does not hold as a clean identity; the
relation is Fourier conjugacy at the parameter level, not operator
non-commutativity. The angular momentum-azimuth pair
$(\hat{L}_z, \hat{\varphi})$ has the analogous angle-operator domain
problem ($\varphi$ multivalued with period $2\pi$, no clean self-adjoint
operator on $L^2(S^1)$; Carruthers--Nieto 1968 worked out the domain
corrections). The number-phase pair $(\hat{N}, \hat{\varphi})$ has the
Susskind--Glogower 1964 obstruction (no self-adjoint phase operator
conjugate to a number operator bounded below; the polar decomposition
yields exponential phase operators that are not self-adjoint; the
Pegg--Barnett 1989 phase operator recovers commutator structure only in
a truncated-state-space limit). The Geometric Channel / Algebraic Channel
perpendicularity reading is therefore clean at
$(\hat{q}, \hat{p})$ specifically; whether it extends to the other
canonical pairs depends on whether their operator structure carries the
analogy, and the technical obstructions in the three other pairs are
well-known features of the operator theory that block direct extension.
The cleanly novel result is the $(\hat{q}, \hat{p})$ case,
with its $i$ as the perpendicularity-marker of the channels.
:::

### Empirical anchor

The $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ is the operator-theoretic content of
the Heisenberg uncertainty principle
(Chapter [12](#ch:heisenberg){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:heisenberg"}), confirmed in every uncertainty-relation
measurement: single-slit electron diffraction (Davisson--Germer 1927),
squeezed-light measurements (Wu et al. 1986 [@Wu1986]), trapped-ion
ground-state cooling (Wineland 2012 Nobel [@Wineland2003]), and so on.
The $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$'s universality across all measurement
species --- it is the same $\hbar$ regardless of the particle --- is the
cross-species mass-independence diagnostic of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

## QM T11: The Born Rule $P = |\psi|^2$ {#ch:born}

> *The McGucken Principle.* The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality.
> Every result below descends from that expansion.


*Recall.* the McGucken Principle ($\mathrm{McP}$:
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$) asserts that the fourth spacetime dimension
$x_4$ expands at the velocity of light $c$, carrying the
perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguishes it from the spatial
three. Throughout this chapter, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ refers to this
principle and to the five-clause content (i)--(v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: (i) *invariance* --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content; (ii) *spherical symmetry* --- the
expansion is isotropic in the spatial three, with the set of events
reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a 2-sphere of radius
$c\tau$; (iii) *monotonicity* --- the integral curve is strictly
monotonically increasing in $t$, fixing the arrow of $x_4$-advance; (iv)
*Lorentz consistency* --- the structure is $SO^+(1,3)$-invariant on
$M_{G}$; (v) *global validity* --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at
every event of $M_{G}$. The integrated kinematic shadow
$x_4 = ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is the kinematic shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the central fact.

This is the result Weinberg [@Weinberg2015] singles out as the deepest
foundational problem of the textbook tradition: "Where does the Born
rule come from?" In the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, it is forced twice---once
from the Cauchy functional equation on Algebraic Channel, and once from the
$SO(3)$-Haar measure on the McGucken Sphere on Geometric Channel.

### Statement

::: {#thm:QMT11-channelA .theorem}
**Theorem 11.1** (QM T11: Born Rule, = Theorem 70 (Algebraic Channel) and
Theorem 93 (Geometric Channel) of [@Syn-2026]). *For a normalized state
$\psi \in \mathcal{H}$, the probability of detecting the particle at
spatial position $x$ in a measurement at coordinate time $t$ is
$$P(x, t) = |\psi(x, t)|^2.
\label{eq:Born}$$*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* We give the Algebraic Channel proof in full and reference the disjoint
Geometric Channel proof below. The Algebraic Channel route derives
[\[eq:Born\]](#eq:Born){reference-type="eqref" reference="eq:Born"} from
four requirements, each a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the proof
has six explicit steps. The Born rule descends from the physical,
geometric fact that the fourth dimension is expanding at the velocity of
light $c$ in a spherically symmetric manner
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, with $x_4 = ict$ the integrated kinematic
shadow per Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}): the spherical symmetry of the
$x_{4}$-expansion forces the $SO(3)$-Haar measure on the McGucken Sphere
wavefront, and the perpendicularity marker $i$ in
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ forces $\psi$ to be complex, with $|\psi|^2$
then the unique real, non-negative, phase-invariant scalar.

**Step 1: Real-valuedness (R1).** A probability density is real-valued
--- operationally, frequencies of detection events on the 3D spatial
slice (Theorem [19.1](#thm:QMT19){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT19"}) are real numbers. Hence $P(x)$ is real-valued.

**Step 2: Non-negativity (R2).** $P(x) \ge 0$ for all $x$, by the same
operational origin as R1.

**Step 3: Global $U(1)$ phase invariance (R3).** By
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (i) (invariance --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds with the same magnitude at every event
independent of overall phase) and
Theorem [16.1](#thm:QMT16){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT16"}
(gauge invariance, with the global $U(1)$ a consequence of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the integrated $x_4 = ict$ entering the
matter wavefunction only through $\exp(\text{linear in }x_4)$), the
global transformation $\psi(x) \to e^{i\alpha}\psi(x)$ leaves
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ unchanged. Hence $P(x)$ depends on $\psi$ only
through $|\psi(x)|$.

**Step 4: Composition under independent products (R4) and the
multiplicative Cauchy equation.** For two independent subsystems with
$\Psi(x_1, x_2) = \psi_1(x_1)\psi_2(x_2)$, the joint probability
factors: $P_{12}(x_1, x_2) = P_1(x_1)P_2(x_2)$. By R1--R3,
$P(x) = f(|\psi(x)|)$ for some
$f: \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$. Substituting into the
factorization and using $|\psi_1\psi_2| = |\psi_1|\cdot|\psi_2|$:
$$f(uv) = f(u)\,f(v) \quad \text{for all } u, v \ge 0.$$ *Boundary value
at $u = 0$.* Setting $v = 0$: $f(0) = f(0)f(v) = f(0)f(0) = f(0)^2$,
hence $f(0) \in \{0, 1\}$. The case $f(0) = 1$ would assign nonzero
probability density to the point where $\psi$ vanishes, contradicting
R2's operational origin (where $\psi = 0$ no detection events occur).
Hence $f(0) = 0$. *Multiplicative non-degeneracy on $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$.*
If $f(u_0) = 0$ for some $u_0 > 0$, then for every $v > 0$,
$f(u_0 v) = f(u_0)f(v) = 0$, so $f \equiv 0$ on
$u_0\mathbb{R}_{>0} = \mathbb{R}_{>0}$, giving the degenerate solution
$P \equiv 0$ everywhere. Excluding this degenerate case (which
corresponds to the null wavefunction $\psi \equiv 0$), $f > 0$ on
$\mathbb{R}_{>0}$. *Logarithmic substitution.* For $u, v > 0$ with
$f(u), f(v) > 0$, take logarithms: setting $g(\log u) := \log f(u)$, the
multiplicative equation becomes the additive Cauchy equation
$g(s+t) = g(s) + g(t)$ on $\mathbb{R}$. Smoothness of
$\psi \mapsto P(\psi)$ under the continuous time-evolution of
Schrödinger (Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT7"}) forces $f$, and hence $g$, to be continuous,
hence Lebesgue-measurable. By
Theorem [3.9](#thm:cauchy){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:cauchy"}
(Hewitt--Stromberg [@HewittStromberg1965] Theorem 17.16), the only
measurable solutions of the additive Cauchy equation are linear:
$g(s) = c\,s$ for some constant $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Therefore
$f(u) = u^c$ on $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$, and $f(|\psi|) = |\psi|^c$ on the
support of $\psi$, with the $f(0) = 0$ boundary value extending the
formula to $|\psi| = 0$ by continuity (for $c > 0$).

**Step 5: Pinning $c = 2$ by the continuity equation.** The Schrödinger
equation (Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT7"}) supplies the continuity equation
$\partial_t|\psi|^2 + \nabla\cdot\mathbf{j} = 0$ with quadratic current
$\mathbf{j} = (i\hbar/2m)(\psi\nabla\psi^* - \psi^*\nabla\psi)$. We
verify by direct computation, then derive uniqueness of $c = 2$ by an
explicit divergence-decomposition argument.

*Verification of the continuity equation.* Schrödinger reads
$i\hbar\,\partial_t\psi = \hat{H}\psi$, hence
$\partial_t\psi = -(i/\hbar)\hat{H}\psi$. The conjugate, using
self-adjointness of $\hat{H}$ on real-valued $V$, is
$\partial_t\psi^* = +(i/\hbar)\hat{H}\psi^*$. Then
$$\partial_t|\psi|^2 \;=\; \psi^*\,\partial_t\psi + \psi\,\partial_t\psi^* \;=\; -\tfrac{i}{\hbar}\psi^*\hat{H}\psi + \tfrac{i}{\hbar}\psi\hat{H}\psi^* \;=\; -\tfrac{i}{\hbar}\bigl[\psi^*\hat{H}\psi - \psi\hat{H}\psi^*\bigr].$$
Substituting $\hat{H}= -(\hbar^2/2m)\nabla^2 + V$ with
$V \in \mathbb{R}$:
$$\psi^*\hat{H}\psi - \psi\hat{H}\psi^* \;=\; -\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\bigl[\psi^*\nabla^2\psi - \psi\nabla^2\psi^*\bigr] + V\bigl[\psi^*\psi - \psi\psi^*\bigr] \;=\; -\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\,\nabla\!\cdot\!\bigl[\psi^*\nabla\psi - \psi\nabla\psi^*\bigr],$$
using $V\psi^*\psi - V\psi\psi^* = 0$ and the Leibniz identity
$\psi^*\nabla^2\psi - \psi\nabla^2\psi^* = \nabla\cdot(\psi^*\nabla\psi - \psi\nabla\psi^*)$.
Therefore
$$\partial_t|\psi|^2 \;=\; -\tfrac{i}{\hbar}\cdot\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\Bigr)\,\nabla\!\cdot\!\bigl[\psi^*\nabla\psi - \psi\nabla\psi^*\bigr] \;=\; \tfrac{i\hbar}{2m}\,\nabla\!\cdot\!\bigl[\psi^*\nabla\psi - \psi\nabla\psi^*\bigr].$$
Hence $\partial_t|\psi|^2 + \nabla\cdot\mathbf{j} = 0$ with
$\mathbf{j} = -\tfrac{i\hbar}{2m}(\psi^*\nabla\psi - \psi\nabla\psi^*) = \tfrac{i\hbar}{2m}(\psi\nabla\psi^* - \psi^*\nabla\psi)$.
The current $\mathbf{j}$ is bilinear in
$(\psi, \nabla\psi^*) \cup (\psi^*, \nabla\psi)$: each term is a local
algebraic product of $\psi$ or $\psi^*$ with a first-order spatial
derivative of the conjugate field. No higher-derivative or non-bilinear
terms appear.

*Uniqueness of $c = 2$ by divergence decomposition.* Consider
$P^{(c)}(\mathbf{x}, t) = |\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)|^c$ for $c > 0$. We ask:
for which $c$ does $P^{(c)}$ satisfy a continuity equation
$\partial_t P^{(c)} + \nabla\cdot \mathbf{J}^{(c)} = 0$ with
$\mathbf{J}^{(c)}$ a local current bilinear in $(\psi, \psi^*)$ and
their first-order spatial derivatives, with $V$-independence of
$\mathbf{J}^{(c)}$ (so the current depends only on $\psi$ and not on the
external potential)?

By the chain rule, $|\psi|^c = (|\psi|^2)^{c/2}$, so
$$\partial_t P^{(c)} \;=\; \frac{c}{2}\,(|\psi|^2)^{c/2 - 1}\,\partial_t|\psi|^2 \;=\; \frac{c}{2}\,|\psi|^{c-2}\,\partial_t|\psi|^2 \;=\; -\frac{c}{2}\,|\psi|^{c-2}\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{j},$$
using the verified continuity equation for $|\psi|^2$. Decompose the
right-hand side by the product rule for the divergence:
$$|\psi|^{c-2}\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{j} \;=\; \nabla\cdot\bigl(|\psi|^{c-2}\,\mathbf{j}\bigr) \;-\; \bigl(\nabla|\psi|^{c-2}\bigr)\cdot\mathbf{j}.$$
The first term is a local divergence; it admits the form
$\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}^{(c)}$ with
$\mathbf{J}^{(c)} = (c/2)|\psi|^{c-2}\,\mathbf{j}$. The second term,
$(\nabla|\psi|^{c-2})\cdot\mathbf{j}$, is not in general a divergence:
its value is
$$\bigl(\nabla|\psi|^{c-2}\bigr)\cdot\mathbf{j} \;=\; (c-2)\,|\psi|^{c-4}\,(\nabla|\psi|^2)/2\cdot\mathbf{j} \;=\; \frac{c-2}{2}\,|\psi|^{c-4}\,(\nabla|\psi|^2)\cdot\mathbf{j}.$$
For $c = 2$, the prefactor $(c-2)/2 = 0$ and the second term vanishes
identically, leaving $\partial_t P^{(2)} = -\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}^{(2)}$
with $\mathbf{J}^{(2)} = \mathbf{j}$ --- a continuity equation in the
required form. For $c \neq 2$, the second term
$\tfrac{c-2}{2}|\psi|^{c-4}(\nabla|\psi|^2)\cdot\mathbf{j}$ is not in
general a divergence and not zero on generic wavefunctions; to absorb it
into the divergence on the LHS would require introducing an additional
non-bilinear or higher-derivative current, contradicting the requirement
that $\mathbf{J}^{(c)}$ be bilinear in first derivatives. Therefore
$c = 2$ is the unique exponent for which $P^{(c)} = |\psi|^c$ satisfies
a continuity equation with a local bilinear current built from
$\psi, \psi^*, \nabla\psi, \nabla\psi^*$ and depending only on $\psi$
(not on $V$).

**Step 6: Normalization and McGucken anchoring.** With $c = 2$,
$\int|\psi|^2\,d^3x = 1$ is the standard $L^2$-normalization, consistent
with $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ from
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"} (Hilbert space as a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). Therefore $P(x) = |\psi(x)|^2$, which is
[\[eq:Born\]](#eq:Born){reference-type="eqref" reference="eq:Born"}. The
complex character of $\psi$ that makes $|\psi|^2$ non-trivial is itself
a consequence of the perpendicularity marker $i$ in
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}); the $i$ in the continuity-equation
current $\mathbf{j}$ is case 2 of
Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}, the chain-rule image of the
McGucken-Principle $i$.

**Geometric Channel.** The disjoint Geometric Channel derivation appears in
§[11.3](#ssec:T11-channelB){reference-type="ref"
reference="ssec:T11-channelB"} below: it derives $P = |\psi|^2$ from the
$SO(3)$-Haar measure on the McGucken Sphere wavefront $M^{+}_{p}(t)$
(forced by Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (ii), spherical symmetry of the
$x_{4}$-expansion) combined with $U(1)$-equivariance of the probability
density and continuity-equation conservation under Schrödinger
evolution. The Geometric Channel route does not invoke the Cauchy functional
equation; the Algebraic Channel route does not invoke the Haar measure. The two
are derivationally disjoint and agree. $\square$ ◻
:::

### Geometric Channel derivation (QB7 --- $SO(3)$-Haar measure on McGucken Sphere) {#ssec:T11-channelB}

::: channelb
*Geometric Channel Derivation 11.4* (Born rule from $SO(3)$-equivariant
probability density on the wavefront). **Step B-1 (Wavefront and
section).** By QB1+QB2, the wavefront $M^{+}_{p}(t)$ at coordinate time
$t > t_p$ is the McGucken-Sphere image of the source event $p$. The
matter wavefunction $\psi$ is, in the Geometric Channel reading, a section of a
complex $U(1)$-line bundle $E \to M^{+}_{p}(t)$: at each point
$x \in M^{+}_{p}(t)$, $\psi(x) \in E_x \cong \mathbb{C}$, with the gauge
group $U(1)$ acting on each fiber by
$\psi(x) \to e^{i\alpha(x)}\psi(x)$.

**Step B-2 ($SO(3)$-Haar measure on the wavefront, QB7).** By the
spherical-symmetry clause (ii) of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$,
$M^{+}_{p}(t)$ is a 2-sphere; the rotation group $SO(3)$ acts
transitively on it. By the Haar theorem (Hewitt--Ross, *Abstract
Harmonic Analysis*, Theorem 15.5), there exists a *unique* (up to
overall normalization) measure on the 2-sphere invariant under the
transitive $SO(3)$-action: the spherical Haar measure
$d\Omega = \sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi$. Normalizing to unit total mass:
$$\int_{M^{+}_{p}(t)} d\Omega_{\text{normalised}} = 1.$$ This is the
unique $SO(3)$-equivariant probability measure on the bare wavefront
2-sphere.

**Step B-3 (Imprint of the wavefunction's amplitude).** The bare Haar
measure $d\Omega$ corresponds to a uniform wavefunction
$|\psi|^2 = \text{const}$. For a generic $\psi$, the amplitude
$|\psi(x)|^2$ is non-uniform; the physical probability measure on
$M^{+}_{p}(t)$ must therefore be of the form
$$d\mu(x) = \rho[\psi(x), \psi^*(x)]\,d\Omega(x)
\label{eq:wavefront-density}$$ for some density $\rho$ on $M^{+}_{p}(t)$
depending on the wavefunction.

**Step B-4 ($U(1)$-equivariance pins the polynomial form of $\rho$).**
The density $\rho$ must be invariant under the local $U(1)$ phase action
$\psi \to e^{i\alpha(x)}\psi$ (the same gauge freedom that supplies the
connection in QM T16, Chapter [16](#ch:gauge){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:gauge"}). Smoothness of $\rho$ under continuous
time-evolution by the Schrödinger equation
(Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT7"})
requires $\rho$ to be a polynomial in $(\psi, \psi^*)$ to leading order
in $|\psi|$ (higher-derivative dependence is excluded by locality at
$x$).

*Polynomial $U(1)$-invariant theory.* The polynomial algebra
$\mathbb{C}[\psi, \psi^*]$ carries the $U(1)$-action
$(\psi, \psi^*) \mapsto (e^{i\alpha}\psi, e^{-i\alpha}\psi^*)$. A
monomial $\psi^m(\psi^*)^n$ transforms by the phase $e^{i(m-n)\alpha}$;
it is $U(1)$-invariant if and only if $m = n$. Hence the algebra of
$U(1)$-invariant polynomials in $(\psi, \psi^*)$ is generated by the
single invariant $\psi\psi^* = |\psi|^2$ (classical invariant theory of
the diagonal $U(1)$-action; see Weyl, *The Classical Groups*, Theorem
II.A on the first fundamental theorem for $U(1)$). The most general
$U(1)$-invariant polynomial density therefore takes the form
$$\rho = \rho_0 + \rho_1\,|\psi|^2 + \rho_2\,|\psi|^4 + \cdots + \rho_K\,|\psi|^{2K}$$
for some $K < \infty$ and constants $\rho_n \in \mathbb{C}$. Reality of
$\rho$ (R1 of Algebraic Channel) forces each $\rho_n \in \mathbb{R}$;
non-negativity (R2) constrains the $\rho_n$ further. The operational
requirement that $\rho \to 0$ where $\psi \to 0$ (no detection
probability at points where the wavefunction vanishes) forces
$\rho_0 = 0$, since the $|\psi|^{2n}$ terms with $n \ge 1$ all vanish at
$\psi = 0$ but $\rho_0$ does not.

*Divergence-decomposition exclusion of higher powers.* For $k \ge 2$, we
ask: does $|\psi|^{2k}$ admit a local continuity equation
$\partial_t|\psi|^{2k} + \nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}^{(2k)} = 0$ with
$\mathbf{J}^{(2k)}$ bilinear in first derivatives of $(\psi, \psi^*)$
and independent of the external potential $V$? By the chain rule applied
to the Schrödinger continuity equation
[\[eq:continuity\]](#eq:continuity){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:continuity"} for $|\psi|^2$:
$$\partial_t|\psi|^{2k} \;=\; k\,|\psi|^{2(k-1)}\,\partial_t|\psi|^2 \;=\; -k\,|\psi|^{2(k-1)}\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{j}.$$
Decompose by the product rule for the divergence:
$$|\psi|^{2(k-1)}\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{j} \;=\; \nabla\cdot\bigl(|\psi|^{2(k-1)}\,\mathbf{j}\bigr) \;-\; \bigl(\nabla|\psi|^{2(k-1)}\bigr)\cdot\mathbf{j}.$$
The first term admits the form $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}^{(2k)}$ with
$\mathbf{J}^{(2k)} = k\,|\psi|^{2(k-1)}\,\mathbf{j}$. The second term
equals
$$\bigl(\nabla|\psi|^{2(k-1)}\bigr)\cdot\mathbf{j} \;=\; (k-1)\,|\psi|^{2(k-2)}\,(\nabla|\psi|^2)\cdot\mathbf{j},$$
which for $k \geq 2$ has coefficient $(k-1) \geq 1$ and is non-vanishing
on generic wavefunctions. Therefore $|\psi|^{2k}$ for $k \geq 2$ does
not satisfy a continuity equation with a local bilinear $V$-independent
current; only $k = 1$ admits the required form (with $(k-1) = 0$).

*Conclusion.* Combining the polynomial-invariant theorem ($\rho$ is a
polynomial in $|\psi|^2$), the boundary condition ($\rho_0 = 0$), and
the divergence-decomposition argument (only $|\psi|^2$ admits the
required continuity equation), the density reduces to
$$\rho = \rho_1\,|\psi|^2,$$ with the constant $\rho_1$ fixed in
Step B-5.

**Step B-5 (Normalization).** Demand $\int_{M^{+}_{p}(t)} d\mu = 1$ for
normalized $\psi$ (i.e., $\int |\psi|^2 d^3x = 1$). This forces
$\rho_1 = 1$ in spatial-volume coordinates, yielding
$$d\mu(x) = |\psi(x)|^2\,d^3 x.$$

The probability of detecting the particle at $x \in M^{+}_{p}(t)$ is
therefore $|\psi(x)|^2\,d^3 x$, exactly the Born rule. ◻

**Upstream geometric route.** The dedicated derivation paper
[@MG-Born-CCR-2026], Theorem T4.2, gives the upstream geometric content
of the Born rule: the Minkowski metric induced by $x_{4}= ict$ is rank
2, so the $x_{4}$-flux density is bilinear in $(\psi, \psi^*)$; phase
invariance, reality, non-negativity, and normalization then fix the
density to be $|\psi|^2$. The Geometric Channel derivation above is the
McGucken-Sphere $SO(3)$-Haar-measure realization of the same upstream
geometric fact; the explicit signature-rank argument supplies the deeper
reason that the density is the squared modulus rather than
the bare modulus.

**The Born density as $x_4$-overlap diagonal.** The geometric content of
the Born rule is further refined by Theorem 5.3 of [@MG-Hilbert-2026]:
the inner product $\langle\phi, \psi\rangle = \int \phi^*\psi\,d^3 x$ is
the integrated forward--conjugate $x_4$-overlap of two
oppositely-oriented Sphere expansions on a spatial slice. The Born
probability density at $x$ is the *diagonal* of this overlap with
$\phi = \psi$: $$\rho(x) = (\psi^*\,\psi)(x) = |\psi(x)|^2,$$ the
pointwise pairing of the forward $x_4$-advance with the conjugate
$x_4$-advance at the spatial event $x$. The squared modulus has two
equivalent readings: the $U(1)$-equivariant bilinear density
characterised in Steps B-1 through B-5 above, and the pointwise diagonal
of the integrated $x_4$-overlap structure that defines the Hilbert-space
inner product. The Born rule and the Hilbert-space inner product share a
single underlying construction: they are the diagonal and integrated
readings of the same forward--conjugate $x_4$-overlap.
:::

### Algebraic Channel derivation (QA5 plus Cauchy functional equation)

::: channela
*Algebraic Channel Derivation 11.2* (Born rule from four requirements). We derive [\[eq:Born\]](#eq:Born){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:Born"} from four requirements, each itself a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$:

**Requirement (R1) --- Real-valuedness.** A probability density is a
real-valued function. The wavefunction
$\psi: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{C}$ is complex; the probability density
$P(x)$ must be a real-valued function built from $\psi(x)$ and
$\psi^*(x)$.

*Audit.* R1 follows from the operational fact that probabilities are
frequencies of detection events on the 3D spatial slice
(Theorem [19.1](#thm:QMT19){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT19"},
Algebraic Channel reading) and frequencies are real numbers.

**Requirement (R2) --- Non-negativity.** $P(x) \ge 0$ for all $x$.
*Audit:* same operational origin as R1.

**Requirement (R3) --- Global $U(1)$ phase invariance.** By the
universal-rate clause QA1 of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds with the same
magnitude $c$ at every event, independent of an overall phase choice.
Hence the global transformation $\psi(x) \to e^{i\alpha}\psi(x)$ with
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ constant leaves $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
unchanged. Probabilities, as observables, must therefore be invariant
under this global phase: $P(x)$ depends on $\psi$ only through
$|\psi(x)|$, not through $\arg \psi(x)$.

*Audit.* This is the formal expression of QA7's global $U(1)$ symmetry,
derived without reference to the gauge-field machinery of QA7's
local-promotion extension.

**Requirement (R4) --- Composition under independent product states.**
Consider two physically independent one-particle subsystems on disjoint
regions of space, with wavefunctions $\psi_1(x_1), \psi_2(x_2)$. The
composition rule for independent subsystems is the tensor product
(Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] §II.4); on configuration space, the joint
wavefunction is the product $$\Psi(x_1, x_2) = \psi_1(x_1)\,\psi_2(x_2).
\label{eq:independent-product}$$ The joint detection probability
density, being the frequency of joint detection events, must factor
under independence: $$P_{12}(x_1, x_2) = P_1(x_1)\,P_2(x_2).
\label{eq:probability-factors}$$

*Audit.* Independence here is the operational condition that the two
subsystems are not entangled and not interacting;
[\[eq:independent-product\]](#eq:independent-product){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:independent-product"} is the standard tensor-product
structure for non-entangled subsystems (which precedes the Born rule in
the derivation order: tensor-product Hilbert space structure follows
from QA1+QA4 Stone--von Neumann uniqueness applied to the joint
observable algebra, without invoking the probability density).

*Upstream geometric reading.* The bilinear form of the probability density in $(\psi, \psi^*)$ follows more directly from the rank-$2$ character of the McGucken-derived Minkowski metric: by
Lemma [9.13](#lem:bilinearity-rank2){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:bilinearity-rank2"} of
Chapter [9](#ch:hilbert-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:hilbert-theorem"}, the natural local density on the
spatial slice induced by a geometric pairing of $\psi$ with $\psi^*$
through the Minkowski metric is bilinear in
$(\psi(\mathbf{x}, t), \psi^*(\mathbf{x}, t))$, with higher-rank
alternatives (e.g., $|\psi|^4$) excluded by the rank-$2$ character of
$g_{\mu\nu}$. The R4-plus-Cauchy route of the present chapter and the
rank-$2$-metric route of
Lemma [9.13](#lem:bilinearity-rank2){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:bilinearity-rank2"} are two complementary derivations of
the same bilinear form: the operational route (R4 supplies
tensor-product independence, Cauchy supplies the
multiplicative-to-power-law step) and the geometric route (rank-$2$
contraction of one-forms). Both reach the bilinear ansatz; the present
chapter then pins the exponent $c = 2$ by the continuity-equation
argument of Step 5, while the rank-$2$-metric route reaches $|\psi|^2$
directly by identifying the bilinear contraction at the $0$-form level
as $\psi^*\psi$.

*Derivation.* By R1--R3, the density has the form $P(x) = f(|\psi(x)|)$
for some function $f: \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$. By
[\[eq:probability-factors\]](#eq:probability-factors){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:probability-factors"} applied to
[\[eq:independent-product\]](#eq:independent-product){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:independent-product"}:
$$f(|\psi_1(x_1)\psi_2(x_2)|) = f(|\psi_1(x_1)|)\,f(|\psi_2(x_2)|).$$
Since $|\psi_1\psi_2| = |\psi_1|\,|\psi_2|$, this reads
$$f(uv) = f(u)\,f(v) \qquad \text{for all } u, v \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}.
\label{eq:f-multiplicative}$$

**Solving
[\[eq:f-multiplicative\]](#eq:f-multiplicative){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:f-multiplicative"}.** The function
$f: \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ satisfies
$f(uv) = f(u)f(v)$ for all $u, v \ge 0$. We extract the content in three sub-steps.

*Boundary value at zero.* Setting $v = 0$ in $f(uv) = f(u)f(v)$ gives
$f(0) = f(u)f(0)$ for all $u \ge 0$, equivalently $f(0)[1 - f(u)] = 0$.
If $f(0) \ne 0$ then $f(u) \equiv 1$ for all $u \ge 0$, which violates
the operational requirement that $P \to 0$ as $|\psi| \to 0$ (no
probability where there is no wavefunction). Hence $f(0) = 0$.

*Non-degeneracy on $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$.* If $f(u_0) = 0$ for some
$u_0 > 0$, then for every $v > 0$, $f(u_0 v) = f(u_0)f(v) = 0$. The set
$u_0\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ equals $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$, so $f \equiv 0$ on
$\mathbb{R}_{>0}$, yielding the degenerate solution $P \equiv 0$
everywhere. Excluding this degenerate case (which corresponds to the
null wavefunction $\psi \equiv 0$), $f > 0$ on $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$.

*Logarithmic substitution.* For $u, v > 0$, take logarithms
(well-defined since $f(u), f(v) > 0$ by the previous sub-step). Set
$g(\log u) := \log f(u)$. Then
$g(\log u + \log v) = g(\log u) + g(\log v)$, i.e., $g$ satisfies the
additive Cauchy functional equation on $\mathbb{R}$.

The probability density is continuous in $\psi$ (it must depend smoothly
on the wavefunction; otherwise infinitesimal variations of $\psi$ would
produce discontinuous jumps in detection probabilities, contradicting
the smooth time-evolution of $\psi$ under
Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT7"}).
Hence $f$ is continuous, hence $g$ is continuous, hence
Lebesgue-measurable. By Theorem [3.9](#thm:cauchy){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:cauchy"} (Hewitt--Stromberg [@HewittStromberg1965]
Theorem 17.16), the only measurable solutions of Cauchy's equation are
linear: $g(u) = c\,u$ for some constant $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Therefore
$$\log f(|\psi|) = c\,\log|\psi| \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(|\psi|) = |\psi|^c \qquad \text{for } |\psi| > 0,$$
with the boundary value $f(0) = 0$ extending the formula to $|\psi| = 0$
continuously when $c > 0$.

**Pinning $c = 2$.** By R2, $f \ge 0$, hence $c \in \mathbb{R}$. We pin
$c$ by the unit-normalization requirement combined with the
time-evolution conservation law.

*Time-evolution conservation.* The Schrödinger equation
(Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT7"})
implies the continuity equation
$$\partial_t |\psi|^2 + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{j} = 0, \qquad \mathbf{j} = \frac{i\hbar}{2m}(\psi \nabla\psi^* - \psi^* \nabla\psi),
\label{eq:continuity}$$ verified by direct computation as follows.
Schrödinger reads $i\hbar\,\partial_t\psi = \hat{H}\psi$, hence
$\partial_t\psi = -(i/\hbar)\hat{H}\psi$. Self-adjointness of $\hat{H}$
(with $V \in \mathbb{R}$) gives the conjugate equation
$\partial_t\psi^* = +(i/\hbar)\hat{H}\psi^*$. Then
$$\partial_t |\psi|^2 \;=\; \psi^* \partial_t\psi + \psi \partial_t\psi^* \;=\; \psi^*(-i\hat{H}/\hbar)\psi + \psi(i\hat{H}/\hbar)\psi^* \;=\; -(i/\hbar)\bigl[\psi^*\hat{H}\psi - \psi\hat{H}\psi^*\bigr].$$
Substituting $\hat{H}= -(\hbar^2/2m)\nabla^2 + V$ with
$V \in \mathbb{R}$, the potential term cancels
($V\psi^*\psi - V\psi\psi^* = 0$) and the kinetic term gives, by the
Leibniz identity
$\psi^*\nabla^2\psi - \psi\nabla^2\psi^* = \nabla\cdot(\psi^*\nabla\psi - \psi\nabla\psi^*)$:
$$\psi^*\hat{H}\psi - \psi\hat{H}\psi^* \;=\; -(\hbar^2/2m)\,\nabla\cdot(\psi^*\nabla\psi - \psi\nabla\psi^*).$$
Hence
$\partial_t|\psi|^2 = (i\hbar/2m)\,\nabla\cdot(\psi^*\nabla\psi - \psi\nabla\psi^*)$,
which is $-\nabla\cdot\mathbf{j}$ with
$\mathbf{j} = (i\hbar/2m)(\psi\nabla\psi^* - \psi^*\nabla\psi)$. The
current $\mathbf{j}$ is bilinear in
$(\psi, \nabla\psi^*) \cup (\psi^*, \nabla\psi)$: each term is a local
algebraic product of $\psi$ or $\psi^*$ with a first-order spatial
derivative of the conjugate field, and $\mathbf{j}$ is independent of
the external potential $V$.

*Uniqueness of $c = 2$ by divergence decomposition.* Consider
$P^{(c)}(\mathbf{x}, t) = |\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)|^c$ for $c > 0$. We ask:
for which $c$ does $P^{(c)}$ satisfy a continuity equation
$\partial_t P^{(c)} + \nabla\cdot \mathbf{J}^{(c)} = 0$ with
$\mathbf{J}^{(c)}$ a local current bilinear in $(\psi, \psi^*)$ and
their first-order spatial derivatives, with $\mathbf{J}^{(c)}$
independent of the external potential $V$?

By the chain rule applied to $|\psi|^c = (|\psi|^2)^{c/2}$:
$$\partial_t P^{(c)} \;=\; \tfrac{c}{2}\,(|\psi|^2)^{c/2 - 1}\,\partial_t|\psi|^2 \;=\; \tfrac{c}{2}\,|\psi|^{c-2}\,\partial_t|\psi|^2 \;=\; -\tfrac{c}{2}\,|\psi|^{c-2}\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{j}.$$
Decompose the right-hand side by the product rule for the divergence:
$$|\psi|^{c-2}\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{j} \;=\; \nabla\cdot\bigl(|\psi|^{c-2}\,\mathbf{j}\bigr) \;-\; \bigl(\nabla|\psi|^{c-2}\bigr)\cdot\mathbf{j}.$$
The first term is a local divergence, admitting the form
$\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}^{(c)}$ with
$\mathbf{J}^{(c)} = (c/2)|\psi|^{c-2}\,\mathbf{j}$. The second term
equals
$$\bigl(\nabla|\psi|^{c-2}\bigr)\cdot\mathbf{j} \;=\; \tfrac{c-2}{2}\,|\psi|^{c-4}\,(\nabla|\psi|^2)\cdot\mathbf{j}.$$
For $c = 2$, the prefactor $(c-2)/2 = 0$ and the second term vanishes
identically, leaving $\partial_t P^{(2)} = -\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}^{(2)}$
with $\mathbf{J}^{(2)} = \mathbf{j}$ --- a continuity equation in the
required form. For $c \neq 2$, the second term
$\tfrac{c-2}{2}|\psi|^{c-4}(\nabla|\psi|^2)\cdot\mathbf{j}$ is not in
general a divergence and is non-vanishing on generic wavefunctions;
absorbing it would require introducing a non-bilinear or
higher-derivative current, contradicting the requirement that
$\mathbf{J}^{(c)}$ be bilinear in first derivatives. Therefore $c = 2$
is the unique exponent for which $P^{(c)} = |\psi|^c$ satisfies a
continuity equation with a local bilinear current built from
$\psi, \psi^*, \nabla\psi, \nabla\psi^*$ and independent of the external
potential $V$.

*Unit normalization.* With $c = 2$, $\int |\psi|^2\,d^3x = 1$ is the
standard $L^2$-normalization, consistent with
$\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$.

Therefore $$P(x) = |\psi(x)|^2,$$ exactly equation
[\[eq:Born\]](#eq:Born){reference-type="eqref" reference="eq:Born"}. ◻

*Why $c \ne 1$.* A frequent confusion is to write $P = |\psi|$ rather
than $|\psi|^2$. The above derivation forces $c = 2$ via the
continuity-equation requirement, not by aesthetic choice: $|\psi|^c$ for
$c \ne 2$ does not satisfy a quadratic-current continuity equation under
Schrödinger evolution. The Sinha--Couteau--Jennewein--Laflamme--Weihs
2010 three-slit experiment [@Sinha2010] ruled out $c \ne 2$ alternatives
to $\sim 10^{-3}$ in laboratory measurements.

The Algebraic Channel derivation uses (1) the Cauchy functional equation as the
algebraic content of independent-subsystem composition, (2) the
Schrödinger continuity equation as the dynamical pinning of $c = 2$, and
(3) unit normalization on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ as the final fixing of the
constant of proportionality.
:::

::: {#rmk:born-channelA-machinery .remark}
*Remark 11.3* (McGucken machinery used in the Algebraic Channel Born proof).
Every step of the proof above is forced by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
alone, with no external mathematical postulate essential.

**McGucken machinery used.** (1) $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via QA1's
universal-rate clause supplying global $U(1)$ phase invariance (R3); (2)
operational origin of probabilities as detection frequencies on the
spatial slice (R1, R2); (3) the McGucken-Sphere Hilbert space
$\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ as a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}), supplying the tensor-product
structure for R4 vian Algebraic Channel axiom QA4 (Stone--von Neumann); (4) the
Cauchy functional equation as elementary real analysis
(Hewitt--Stromberg [@HewittStromberg1965] Theorem 17.16, confirmatory);
(5) the McGucken-Schrödinger continuity equation
(Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT7"})
pinning $c = 2$.

**No external machinery is essential.** The Cauchy functional
equation appears only as the algebraic shape of R4 combined with R1--R3,
with its measurable solutions ($g(u) = cu$) being a fact of elementary
measure theory. The continuity-equation pinning of $c = 2$ is the
essential McGucken-machinery step.

**Confirmation.** Sinha--Couteau--Jennewein--Laflamme--Weihs 2010
[@Sinha2010] ruled out $c \ne 2$ alternatives experimentally to
$\sim 10^{-3}$; the empirical pinning of $c = 2$ confirms the
continuity-equation derivation above without supplying the reason for it.

**Upstream Geometric Channel route.** The same Born density $|\psi|^2$ is
derived as the unique $U(1)$-equivariant polynomial density on the
$SO(3)$-Haar measure of the McGucken Sphere (Geometric Channel below), which
itself descends from the rank-2 Minkowski metric (Theorem T4.2 of
[@MG-Born-CCR-2026]). The Geometric Channel route does not invoke the Cauchy
functional equation; the agreement of the two routes is the
disjointness-theorem instance for Born.
:::

### Exponent-2 overdetermination: the Metric Route and the Norm Route both force $|\psi|^2$ {#sec:born-exponent-2-overdetermination}

The Algebraic Channel proof of
Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"} pinned the exponent $c = 2$ in
$P = |\psi|^c$ via the continuity-equation argument (Step 5: only the
quadratic $|\psi|^2$ admits a local current bilinear in first derivatives
without external-potential dependence). The Geometric Channel
derivation (Geometric Channel Derivation 11.4) reached $P = |\psi|^2$ via
$SO(3)$-Haar measure with $U(1)$-equivariance forcing the polynomial
form to be a function of $|\psi|^2$. Both routes pin the exponent at
2. The present section establishes a third fact: the
exponent 2 is *overdetermined* by two derivationally disjoint
McGucken-internal routes that share no intermediate machinery between
the McGucken Principle and the conclusion. Both routes are internal to
the framework; both descend from $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$; neither
requires Jordan–von Neumann 1935 [@JordanVonNeumann1935] or
Lesovik 2014 [@Lesovik2014] as upstream input.

#### The McGucken-internal parallelogram identity {#sec:parallelogram-mcgucken-internal}

The parallelogram identity is the algebraic gateway between an
inner-product space's sesquilinear structure and its $L^2$-norm
structure. In the standard functional-analytic literature
([@JordanVonNeumann1935]) it appears as the *characterising* identity
for $L^2$: a normed space is a Hilbert space if and only if its norm
satisfies the parallelogram identity, with $L^2$ then the unique
$L^p$ space among $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ for which this holds. In the
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework the identity has a substantially shorter
derivation: it follows by a *direct two-line algebraic computation*
from the rank-2 sesquilinearity of the inner product established in
Lemma [9.13](#lem:bilinearity-rank2){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:bilinearity-rank2"}. No external functional analysis is
invoked; the identity is a McGucken-internal downstream consequence of
rank-2 sesquilinearity, which is itself a McGucken-internal
consequence of $(ic\,dt)^2 = -c^2\,dt^2$
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} Step 3).

::: {#lem:parallelogram-mcgucken-internal .lemma}
**Lemma 11.1A** (McGucken-internal parallelogram identity;
[@MG-Hilbert-2026] Lemma 7.6). *Let
$\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ be the rank-2 sesquilinear inner
product on the McGucken-derived Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ supplied
by Lemma [9.13](#lem:bilinearity-rank2){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:bilinearity-rank2"}. Let $\|\psi\|^2 := \langle \psi,
\psi \rangle$ denote the induced norm. Then for every
$x, y \in \mathcal{H}$,
$$\|x + y\|^2 + \|x - y\|^2 = 2(\|x\|^2 + \|y\|^2),$$
with the identity holding as a direct two-line algebraic consequence
of rank-2 sesquilinearity, internal to the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework and
independent of any external functional-analytic input.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof (two lines).* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). Expanding the left-hand side using
sesquilinearity (conjugate-linear in the first argument, linear in
the second; or the reverse — the convention is fixed in
Theorem [3.2](#thm:cauchy-schwarz){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:cauchy-schwarz"}):
$$\|x + y\|^2 = \langle x + y, x + y \rangle = \langle x, x \rangle + \langle x, y \rangle + \langle y, x \rangle + \langle y, y \rangle,$$
$$\|x - y\|^2 = \langle x - y, x - y \rangle = \langle x, x \rangle - \langle x, y \rangle - \langle y, x \rangle + \langle y, y \rangle.$$
Adding: the cross-terms $\pm \langle x, y \rangle$ and
$\pm \langle y, x \rangle$ cancel, leaving
$$\|x + y\|^2 + \|x - y\|^2 = 2\langle x, x \rangle + 2\langle y, y \rangle = 2(\|x\|^2 + \|y\|^2).$$
The cancellation of cross-terms is exactly the algebraic statement
that the pairing $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is rank-2 (degree
1 + 1 in $(x, y)$ with no higher-degree terms). For a rank-4 quartic
pairing (e.g., a hypothetical $\langle x, y \rangle^{(4)}$
quadrilinear in $(x, y, x^*, y^*)$) the cross-terms would not cancel
in this way and the parallelogram identity would fail. The
parallelogram identity is therefore the algebraic
witness-of-rank-2-ness of the inner product, derivable
McGucken-internally from
Lemma [9.13](#lem:bilinearity-rank2){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:bilinearity-rank2"} and ultimately from
$(ic\,dt)^2 = -c^2\,dt^2$ of
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} Step 3. ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:parallelogram-no-external-input .remark}
*Remark 11.1B* (Jordan–von Neumann 1935 as downstream consistency
check, not upstream input). The Jordan–von Neumann theorem
[@JordanVonNeumann1935] historically established that a normed space
admits an inner product if and only if its norm satisfies the
parallelogram identity, with the corollary that among $L^p$ spaces
only $L^2$ is a Hilbert space. In the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, this
theorem is *unnecessary as upstream input*: the inner product on
$\mathcal{H}$ is supplied directly by
Lemma [9.13](#lem:bilinearity-rank2){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:bilinearity-rank2"} from the rank-2 Minkowski metric,
and the parallelogram identity follows by
Lemma [11.1A](#lem:parallelogram-mcgucken-internal){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:parallelogram-mcgucken-internal"} as a
McGucken-internal downstream consequence. Jordan–von Neumann therefore
serves as a *downstream consistency check* — confirming that the
McGucken-derived parallelogram-identity structure on the
McGucken-derived $\mathcal{H}$ is consistent with general functional
analysis on $L^p$ spaces — rather than as a foundational selection
principle. The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework derives the $L^2$ character of
$\mathcal{H}$ internally; Jordan–von Neumann's historical theorem is
cited as the standard functional-analytic correlate but is not used as
upstream input to the chain of theorems.
:::

#### The Norm Route: $L^p$ non-conservation for $p \ne 2$ {#sec:norm-route-Lp}

The McGucken-derived Schrödinger evolution
(Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT7"}) preserves the $L^2$ norm exactly:
$$(d/dt) \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} |\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)|^2\, d^3 x = 0.$$
For $p \ne 2$ the $L^p$ norm of a normalized solution to the
Schrödinger equation is *not* in general preserved by the unitary
evolution. This is the content of the Norm Route: the only
exponent compatible with unitarity is $p = 2$.

::: {#prop:Lp-non-conservation .proposition}
**Proposition 11.1C** ($L^p$ non-conservation for $p \ne 2$;
[@MG-Hilbert-2026] §7.5 status note). *For a normalized 3D Gaussian
wavepacket $\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)$ solving the free Schrödinger
equation $i\hbar\,\partial_t \psi = -(\hbar^2/2m)\nabla^2 \psi$
with initial spatial width $\sigma_0$, the spatial width at large $t$
spreads as $\sigma(t) \sim \hbar t/(2m\sigma_0)$. The $L^p$ norm
$\|\psi_t\|_p = \left( \int |\psi_t(\mathbf{x})|^p d^3 x
\right)^{1/p}$ scales as*
$$\|\psi_t\|_p \;\sim\; \sigma(t)^{3(2-p)/(2p)} \;\sim\; t^{-3(p-2)/(2p)} \qquad (\text{large } t).$$
*Only the case $p = 2$ makes the exponent vanish, conserving the norm
exactly. For $p > 2$ the $L^p$ norm decays as a negative power of
$t$; for $p < 2$ the $L^p$ norm grows as a positive power of $t$.
Unitary evolution conserves the $L^p$ norm if and only if $p = 2$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). For the normalized 3D Gaussian wavepacket,
$$|\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)|^2 \;=\; (2\pi\sigma(t)^2)^{-3/2}\,\exp\!\left(-\tfrac{|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0|^2}{2\sigma(t)^2}\right),$$
so
$|\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)|^p \sim \sigma(t)^{-3p/2}\,\exp(-p|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0|^2/(2\sigma(t)^2))$
up to overall constants. The integral
$\int |\psi_t|^p d^3 x$ scales by Gaussian quadrature as
$\sigma(t)^{-3p/2} \cdot \sigma(t)^3 = \sigma(t)^{3(1 - p/2)} = \sigma(t)^{3(2 - p)/2}$.
Taking the $1/p$ root:
$\|\psi_t\|_p \sim \sigma(t)^{3(2 - p)/(2p)}$.

*Verification at $p = 2$:* exponent $3(2 - 2)/4 = 0$, so
$\|\psi_t\|_2 = \text{const}$ — the $L^2$ norm is conserved.

*Verification at $p = 4$:* exponent $3(2 - 4)/8 = -3/4$, so
$\|\psi_t\|_4 \sim \sigma(t)^{-3/4} \sim t^{-3/4}$ — the $L^4$
norm decays. The Aaronson-style quartic density
$|\psi|^4 / \sum_j |\psi_j|^4$ would therefore not be conserved by
the Schrödinger evolution; this excludes $|\psi|^4$ as a candidate
Born density (and rules out the Aaronson rank-4 quartic alternative
catalogued in §7.6 of [@MG-Hilbert-2026]).

*Verification at $p = 1$:* exponent $3(2 - 1)/2 = 3/2$, so
$\|\psi_t\|_1 \sim \sigma(t)^{3/2} \sim t^{3/2}$ — the $L^1$
norm grows. The $|\psi|$ candidate (with $c = 1$) would therefore not
be conserved either.

Only $p = 2$ vanishes the exponent. Since unitary evolution must
conserve the probability density's $L^p$ norm by probability
conservation, the exponent is forced to $p = 2$. ◻
:::

#### Statement of the exponent-2 overdetermination {#sec:exponent-2-overdetermination-thm}

::: {#thm:exponent-2-overdetermination .theorem}
**Theorem 11.1D** (Exponent-2 overdetermination via Metric Route and
Norm Route; [@MG-Hilbert-2026] §7.5 Theorem). *The exponent $c = 2$
in the Born rule $P = |\psi|^c$ is overdetermined by two
derivationally disjoint McGucken-internal routes:*

*(Metric Route, rank-2 metric route to bilinear density).*
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic \to$ Lorentzian metric on $M_{1,3}$
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}) $\to$ rank-2 character of
$\eta_{\mu\nu}$ $\to$ natural bilinear pairing on
$(\psi, \psi^*)$
(Lemma [9.13](#lem:bilinearity-rank2){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:bilinearity-rank2"}) $\to$ $P = |\psi|^2$
(Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"} Step 5: the continuity-equation
divergence-decomposition argument identifies the quadratic
$|\psi|^2$ as the unique density with bilinear current).

*(Norm Route, rank-2 sesquilinear inner product route to $L^2$-norm
structure, McGucken-internal).*
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic \to$ Lorentzian metric on $M_{1,3}$
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}) $\to$ rank-2 sesquilinear inner
product on $\mathcal{H}$
(Lemma [9.13](#lem:bilinearity-rank2){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:bilinearity-rank2"}) $\to$ parallelogram identity
by direct two-line algebra
(Lemma [11.1A](#lem:parallelogram-mcgucken-internal){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:parallelogram-mcgucken-internal"}) $\to$
$L^2$-norm structure on the McGucken-derived $\mathcal{H}$
(Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}) $\to$ $L^p$ non-conservation
for $p \ne 2$
(Proposition [11.1C](#prop:Lp-non-conservation){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:Lp-non-conservation"}) $\to$ $p = 2$ forced as the
unique exponent compatible with unitary evolution.

*Both routes start from $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$; both end at
$P = |\psi|^2$; they share only the upstream principle and the
rank-2 $\to$ sesquilinear chain
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} $\to$
Lemma [9.13](#lem:bilinearity-rank2){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:bilinearity-rank2"}) before diverging into derivationally
disjoint downstream machinery: Metric Route through density-degree
counting, Norm Route through norm structure and conservation.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$).

**Metric Route.** By
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} Step 3, the Lorentzian line element
$ds^2 = \eta_{\mu\nu}\,dx^\mu\,dx^\nu$ has signature $(-, +, +, +)$
produced by the substitution $dx_4 = ic\,dt$ (the differential form
of the McGucken Principle) into the four-dimensional Euclidean line
element. The metric $\eta_{\mu\nu}$ is rank 2: it pairs two vectors
and produces a scalar, bilinearly in both arguments. By
Lemma [9.13](#lem:bilinearity-rank2){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:bilinearity-rank2"}, the natural pairing on amplitudes
lifted from this rank-2 metric is the sesquilinear pairing
$(\psi, \psi^*) \mapsto \psi^* \psi$, bilinear in
$(\psi, \psi^*)$. By Step 5 of
Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"} (the divergence-decomposition
argument), the unique density bilinear in $(\psi, \psi^*)$ with a
local current depending only on first derivatives and independent of
the external potential is $|\psi|^2$. Hence $P = |\psi|^2$ via the
Metric Route, with the exponent 2 forced by the rank-2 character of
the Minkowski metric.

**Norm Route.** By
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}, the McGucken-derived Hilbert
space $\mathcal{H} \cong L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3 x)$ is the Cauchy
completion of the space of complex-valued square-integrable amplitudes
on the spatial slice, with the $L^2$ norm supplied by the inner
product induced by the geometric overlap of forward and conjugate
$x_4$-expansions. By
Lemma [11.1A](#lem:parallelogram-mcgucken-internal){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:parallelogram-mcgucken-internal"}, the parallelogram
identity
$\|x + y\|^2 + \|x - y\|^2 = 2(\|x\|^2 + \|y\|^2)$ holds as a
direct two-line algebraic consequence of rank-2 sesquilinearity. The
$L^2$-norm structure of $\mathcal{H}$ is therefore internal to the
framework. By
Proposition [11.1C](#prop:Lp-non-conservation){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:Lp-non-conservation"}, only $p = 2$ makes the $L^p$
norm conserved under the McGucken-derived unitary Schrödinger
evolution. Hence the probability density must have $p = 2$ exponent
to be conserved, and the Born rule is $P = |\psi|^2$ via the Norm
Route.

**Disjointness of routes.** The two routes share the upstream chain
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic \to$
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} $\to$
Lemma [9.13](#lem:bilinearity-rank2){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:bilinearity-rank2"} (rank-2 metric and rank-2
sesquilinear pairing). They diverge after this point:

- *Metric Route* uses the continuity-equation
  divergence-decomposition argument
  (Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
  reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"} Step 5) to identify the
  unique-density-with-bilinear-current — operating on density-degree
  counting.

- *Norm Route* uses the parallelogram identity
  (Lemma [11.1A](#lem:parallelogram-mcgucken-internal){reference-type="ref"
  reference="lem:parallelogram-mcgucken-internal"}) together with the
  $L^p$-non-conservation analysis
  (Proposition [11.1C](#prop:Lp-non-conservation){reference-type="ref"
  reference="prop:Lp-non-conservation"}) — operating on norm
  structure and unitarity conservation.

The two arguments share no downstream machinery. The convergence on
$P = |\psi|^2$ is therefore a convergent-overdetermination instance
of the kind catalogued in
§[1.10](#sec:remarkable-feature){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:remarkable-feature"}: the same conclusion
