reached through two routes sharing only the upstream principle, with
no shared intermediate machinery. ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:lesovik-jvn-status .remark}
*Remark 11.1E* (Lesovik 2014 and Jordan–von Neumann 1935 as downstream
consistency checks, not upstream input). The orthodox tradition has
two functional-analytic arguments that force the Born exponent on a
*given* Hilbert space:

*Lesovik 2014* [@Lesovik2014] derives the Born rule from unitarity by
the $L^p$ non-conservation argument
(Proposition [11.1C](#prop:Lp-non-conservation){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:Lp-non-conservation"} above is Lesovik's
result, with the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework derivation of the unitary
evolution itself in
Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT7"} and the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework derivation of the
Hilbert space in
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}). Lesovik presupposes the
Hilbert space and the unitary group; the McGucken framework derives
both from $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$.

*Jordan–von Neumann 1935* [@JordanVonNeumann1935] characterises the
parallelogram identity on a *given* $L^p$ space; the result is a
theorem about which Banach spaces admit inner products, with the
$L^p$ spaces themselves taken as input. In the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework
the parallelogram identity is internal
(Lemma [11.1A](#lem:parallelogram-mcgucken-internal){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:parallelogram-mcgucken-internal"}); Jordan–von Neumann
is a downstream consistency check confirming that the
McGucken-derived parallelogram-identity structure is consistent with
general functional analysis on $L^p$ spaces.

*Gleason 1957* [@Gleason1957] derives the form of the Born rule on a
*given* Hilbert space with the trace structure on the lattice of
subspaces already encoding the inner-product-derived bilinearity. The
present textbook's
Remark [10.14](#rmk:gleason-diagnostic){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:gleason-diagnostic"} establishes that the McGucken
derivation of Born is Gleason-independent: the Born rule follows from
McGucken-Sphere $SO(3)$-Haar structure without invoking the
non-contextuality lattice theorem.

In the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework all three arguments — Lesovik, Jordan–von
Neumann, Gleason — operate one level downstream of the chain of theorems: the
Hilbert space, the inner product, and the unitary group are all
theorems of $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$ before any of these
functional-analytic arguments are applied. The orthodox tradition's
arguments are therefore reinforcing consistency checks on the
McGucken-derived structure, not foundational selection principles
choosing the exponent.
:::

### The physical mechanism: Born rule as head-on $x_{4}$-collision of two McGucken Spheres {#sec:born-as-head-on-x4-collision}

The Algebraic Channel derivation (§ "Algebraic Channel derivation" above) and the
Geometric Channel derivation (§[11.3](#ssec:T11-channelB){reference-type="ref"
reference="ssec:T11-channelB"}) above establish $P = |\psi|^2$ as a
forced theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ along two disjoint routes. The present section supplies the underlying *physical
mechanism*: a concrete two-Sphere collision picture for the Born event,
in which the complex conjugate $\psi^*$ acquires explicit physical
meaning as the absorber's outgoing $x_{4}$-expansion as seen from the
emitter's frame, and the bilinear structure of $P = \psi^*\psi$ has the
role of a head-on $x_{4}$-collision rate between two oppositely-oriented
Sphere expansions sharing a spatial intersection point. The result
strengthens both Channel readings by supplying the physical interlocutor
for the conjugate factor that the formal arguments leave at the level of
$U(1)$-equivariance (Geometric Channel Step B-4) or unitarity (Algebraic Channel clause
R3).

::: {#thm:born-as-collision .theorem}
**Theorem 11.5** (Born rule as head-on $x_{4}$-collision of two McGucken
Spheres). *Let particle $A$ at emission event $E_A$ and particle $B$ at
emission event $E_B$ each generate a McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{E_A}(t)$
and $M^{+}_{E_B}(t')$ respectively, with each Sphere expanding at
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= +ic$ in the rest frame of its own source event
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i), (ii), (v) applied at $E_A$ and
at $E_B$). Let $P$ be a spatial point at which both Spheres arrive at
the same coordinate time --- i.e.,
$P \in M^{+}_{E_A}(t) \cap M^{+}_{E_B}(t')$. Then:*

1.  **Antiparallel $x_{4}$-orientation at $P$.* Along the shared spatial
    geodesic through $P$ on which the two Spheres meet head-on, the two
    outgoing $x_{4}$-directions are antiparallel:
    $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}|_A = +ic$ in $A$'s rest frame at $P$, and
    $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}|_B = -ic$ as seen in $A$'s rest frame at $P$
    (and conversely from $B$'s rest frame). The complex conjugate
    $\psi^*$ of the wavefunction has the role of the partner
    Sphere's outgoing $x_{4}$-expansion viewed from the observer's
    frame.*

2.  **$x_{4}$-momenergy cancellation at $P$.* Each Sphere carries
    $x_{4}$-momenergy density per unit volume proportional to $ic$ (the
    full four-velocity budget in the rest frame, by the four-velocity
    budget Lemma [4.2](#lem:four-velocity-budget){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:four-velocity-budget"}). At the head-on collision,
    the antiparallel $x_{4}$-momenergies cancel:
    $p_4^{\text{net}}(P) = 0$.*

3.  **Three-localization at $P$.* By conservation of total
    four-momenergy across the four dimensions of $M_{G}$, the
    $x_{4}$-momenergy cancelled in clause (C2) is transferred into the
    three spatial dimensions at $P$: both particles are knocked out of
    pure $x_{4}$-expansion and localized at the spatial event $P$. This
    is the detector click of measurement
    (Theorem [19.1](#thm:QMT19){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT19"}, QM T19).*

4.  **Bilinear collision rate.* The rate of head-on Sphere--Sphere
    collision events at $P$ is bilinear in the two incoming Sphere
    amplitudes at $P$. For a single emitter Sphere with amplitude
    $\psi(P, t)$ encountering a many-particle absorber (the detector,
    modelled as a dense ensemble of absorber Spheres each contributing
    an outgoing $x_{4}$-expansion in the absorber's rest frame), the
    collision rate at $P$ reduces to
    $$\text{rate}(P) \;\propto\; \psi^*(P, t)\,\psi(P, t) \;=\; |\psi(P, t)|^2,$$
    recovering the Born rule
    [\[eq:Born\]](#eq:Born){reference-type="eqref" reference="eq:Born"}
    as the rate of head-on $x_{4}$-collisions between the emitter's
    outgoing Sphere and the absorber's outgoing Sphere viewed from the
    emitter's frame.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The proof has six steps establishing the head-on
collision mechanism and its agreement with the bilinear $|\psi|^2$
density already derived in the Geometric Channel and Algebraic Channel routes above.

**Step 1: Two McGucken Spheres at $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= +ic$ in their
respective rest frames.** By
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (i) (invariance: the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value $ic$
independent of matter content) and clause (v) (global validity:
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event of $M_{G}$), both emission
events $E_A$ and $E_B$ source McGucken Spheres $M^{+}_{E_A}(t)$ and
$M^{+}_{E_B}(t')$ by Definition [4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:sphere"}. Each Sphere expands at the rate
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= +ic$ in the rest frame of its own source event,
with the $+$ sign forced by
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iii) (monotonicity: the integral
curve of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is strictly monotonically increasing
in $t$, fixing the forward orientation of $x_{4}$-advance at every
event). The two Spheres carry, respectively, the matter wavefunctions
$\psi_A$ and $\psi_B$ as amplitude profiles on their wavefronts
(Geometric Channel reading, Step B-3 of
§[11.3](#ssec:T11-channelB){reference-type="ref"
reference="ssec:T11-channelB"}); in the rest frame of each source event,
the wavefunction's phase advances at the Compton angular frequency
$\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ along $x_{4}$ by
Theorem [5.1](#thm:QMT5){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT5"}
(rest-mass phase).

**Step 2: Antiparallel $x_{4}$-orientation at the head-on collision
(clause C1).** Suppose $P$ is a spatial point at which both Spheres
arrive at the same coordinate time, lying on a shared spatial geodesic
along which the two Spheres meet head-on. Let $\hat n$ be the unit
spatial direction from $E_A$'s spatial projection toward $P$; then
$-\hat n$ is the unit direction from $E_B$'s spatial projection toward
$P$ (since the two Spheres meet head-on at $P$, their spatial sources
lie on opposite sides of $P$ along the geodesic). In the rest frame of
$A$, the outgoing $x_{4}$-direction at $P$ from Sphere $A$ is $+ic$
along $A$'s worldline tangent at $P$ (forward $x_{4}$-advance, Step 1).
In the same rest frame, Sphere $B$'s outgoing $x_{4}$-direction at $P$
is along $B$'s worldline tangent at $P$, which (with $B$'s spatial
projection on the opposite side of $P$ from $A$) points in the $-\hat n$
spatial direction; combined with $B$'s forward $x_{4}$-advance in $B$'s
own rest frame, the $x_{4}$-component of $B$'s outgoing worldline at $P$
*as seen in $A$'s rest frame* has the opposite sign convention relative
to $A$'s own forward direction at $P$. Formally: the relative
$x_{4}$-orientation between the two Spheres at $P$ is antiparallel,
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}|_A(P) = +ic$ and $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}|_B(P) = -ic$
*as both are reckoned in $A$'s rest frame*. By the frame-relational
symmetry of the construction, from $B$'s rest frame the situation
reverses: $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}|_B(P) = +ic$ and
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}|_A(P) = -ic$ as both are reckoned in $B$'s rest
frame. The complex conjugate of the wavefunction (the sign-reversal
$i \to -i$ in the perpendicularity marker,
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) has the reading of the
partner Sphere's outgoing $x_{4}$-expansion viewed from the observer's
frame, with the role of a formal algebraic operation on complex
amplitudes replaced by the role of a physical antiparallel
$x_{4}$-orientation between two Spheres meeting head-on at $P$. This
establishes clause (C1).

**Step 3: $x_{4}$-momenergy cancellation at $P$ (clause C2).** By
Lemma [4.2](#lem:four-velocity-budget){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:four-velocity-budget"} (the four-velocity budget at rest:
a particle at spatial rest directs its entire four-velocity budget into
$x_{4}$-advance at rate $c$), each particle's rest-frame four-momenergy
is concentrated in the $x_{4}$-component:
$$p_4 = mc \cdot (\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt})/|\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}| = mc \cdot i = imc \quad \text{(rest frame, } +ic \text{ orientation)},$$
with the imaginary unit $i$ marking the perpendicularity of $x_{4}$ to
the spatial three (Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}, case 1: the McGucken-Principle $i$ as the
perpendicularity marker of $x_{4}$). At the head-on collision event $P$,
the two Spheres' $x_{4}$-momenergies are antiparallel by Step 2:
$p_4^A(P) = +im_A c$ in $A$'s frame and $p_4^B(P) = -im_B c$ in $A$'s
frame (with the sign flip from the antiparallel orientation, and
$m_A, m_B$ the respective rest masses). The net $x_{4}$-momenergy at the
collision event is
$$p_4^{\text{net}}(P) \;=\; p_4^A(P) + p_4^B(P) \;=\; +i m_A c - i m_B c \;=\; i(m_A - m_B)c,$$
which for identical species ($m_A = m_B$) vanishes exactly:
$p_4^{\text{net}}(P) = 0$. For non-identical species, the cancellation
is partial; the relevant content of the head-on collision is that the
$x_{4}$-momenergies oppose each other and net to a value strictly
smaller in magnitude than the sum of magnitudes, with the loss of
$x_{4}$-momenergy then transferred to the spatial three by clause (C3)
below. This establishes clause (C2).

**Step 4: Three-localization at $P$ (clause C3).** By conservation of
total four-momenergy across the four dimensions of $M_{G}$ (Noether's
theorem applied to translation invariance of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at
every event, the algebraic-symmetry content of Algebraic Channel axiom QA1), the
four-momenergy lost from the $x_{4}$-component at the head-on collision
(Step 3) must appear in the three spatial components $p_1, p_2, p_3$ at
the same event $P$. The mechanism: prior to the collision, each
particle's four-velocity budget was concentrated in $x_{4}$-advance
(pure rest-frame propagation,
Lemma [4.2](#lem:four-velocity-budget){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:four-velocity-budget"}); at the collision event, with
$x_{4}$-momenergy cancelled, the conserved total four-momenergy is
redistributed into spatial momenergy with a definite spatial position
$P$. Both particles are thereby knocked out of pure $x_{4}$-expansion
and localized at the spatial event $P$. The transfer of momenergy from
$x_{4}$ into the spatial three has the geometric content of a *Wick
rotation of the particle out of $x_{4}$ into the spatial slice*: the
perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguished $x_{4}$ from the spatial
three in the pre-collision wavefunction
(Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}, complex amplitudes from
$x_{4}$-perpendicularity) is removed at the collision event, with the
particle's complex-amplitude wavefunction collapsing to a real spatial
position via the head-on cancellation of the two Spheres' $i$-marked
$x_{4}$-expansions. This is the detector click of measurement: collapse
has the reading of a head-on $x_{4}$-collision between the
particle's outgoing Sphere and the absorber's outgoing Sphere, with the
role of an independently-postulated measurement axiom (Process 1 of von
Neumann [@vonNeumann1932]) replaced by the role of a derived theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at the level of the two-Sphere intersection
event. This establishes clause (C3) and supplies the head-on-collision
picture for Theorem [19.1](#thm:QMT19){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT19"} (QM T19, measurement) and
Corollary [10.1](#cor:channel-asymmetry-measurement-problem){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor:channel-asymmetry-measurement-problem"} (the channel
asymmetry as the source of the orthodox-tradition measurement
problem).

**Step 5: Bilinear collision rate and reduction to $|\psi|^2$ (clause
C4).** The rate of head-on Sphere--Sphere collision events at the
spatial point $P$ is, by general probabilistic kinematics on the
wavefront, the product of the two incoming Sphere amplitudes at $P$. In
the standard collision-theory derivation (cross-section formalism,
Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] §XI.6 for the Lippmann--Schwinger
framework; Jackson *Classical Electrodynamics* §13.10 for the bilinear
cross-section structure), the rate of collision events at a target point
$P$ in a beam of incoming particles is bilinear in the beam amplitudes
(incoming $\psi_{\text{beam}}$) and the target amplitudes (outgoing
$\phi_{\text{target}}$):
$$\text{rate}(P) \;\propto\; \phi_{\text{target}}^*(P)\,\psi_{\text{beam}}(P).$$
In the present McGucken-Sphere head-on collision picture (Steps 1--4),
the bilinearity arises from the fact that a collision event
at $P$ requires both Spheres to arrive at $P$ with non-zero amplitude,
with the amplitude for joint arrival being the product of the individual
amplitudes
(Theorem [17.7](#thm:intersecting-spheres-transfer){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:intersecting-spheres-transfer"}, intersecting-Spheres
transfer: the joint amplitude at the intersection event is the product
of the individual Sphere amplitudes at that event).

For the canonical single-particle Born event (one emitter Sphere with
amplitude $\psi$, encountering a many-particle absorber acting as the
detector), the absorber is modelled as a dense ensemble of absorber
Spheres in their own rest frames. In the emitter's frame, each absorber
Sphere appears as an outgoing $x_{4}$-expansion at $-ic$ (by Step 2,
antiparallel orientation). The ensemble-averaged absorber amplitude at
the emitter's spatial point $P$ has the reading of the
conjugate of the emitter's own amplitude evaluated at $P$:
$$\langle\phi_{\text{absorber}}(P)\rangle_{\text{ensemble}} \;=\; \psi^*(P, t),$$
since (i) the absorber ensemble is dense and uniform around the emitter
(the detector is a macroscopic, homogeneous environment), (ii) each
absorber Sphere's outgoing $x_{4}$-expansion appears as $-ic$ in the
emitter's frame and thus contributes the conjugate phase, and (iii) the
macroscopic-detector limit makes the ensemble-averaged absorber
amplitude at $P$ proportional to the local emitter amplitude at $P$ (the
absorber's outgoing Sphere amplitude at $P$ tracks the emitter's
outgoing Sphere amplitude at $P$, since both Spheres meet at $P$ and the
absorber's contribution from a small neighborhood around $P$ is
dominated by the local matter density times the local emitter
amplitude). Substituting into the bilinear collision rate:
$$\text{rate}(P) \;\propto\; \psi^*(P, t)\,\psi(P, t) \;=\; |\psi(P, t)|^2,$$
which is the Born rule [\[eq:Born\]](#eq:Born){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:Born"}. This establishes clause (C4).

**Step 6: McGucken anchoring and agreement with Geometric and Algebraic Channels.** The
head-on $x_{4}$-collision mechanism descends from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}) at three distinct levels: (i) the
antiparallel $x_{4}$-orientation at the collision event (Step 2) is the
content of the perpendicularity marker $i$ in
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (clause (i) and
Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}), supplied with the role of a frame-relational
orientation between two Spheres; (ii) the $x_{4}$-momenergy cancellation
(Step 3) is the consequence of the four-velocity budget structure of the
rest-frame wavefunction
(Lemma [4.2](#lem:four-velocity-budget){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:four-velocity-budget"}, descending from clause (ii)
spherical symmetry and the integrated $x_4 = ict$ of
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}); (iii) the three-localization (Step
4) is the conservation-law content of clauses (i)+(v) applied to the
global translation invariance of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The
bilinearity of the collision rate (Step 5) reduces to the bilinear
density $\psi^*\psi$ in the single-particle-with-many-absorber limit,
agreeing with the Algebraic Channel derivation (Step 5 of the master proof: the
divergence-decomposition argument pinning $c = 2$) and the Geometric Channel
derivation (Step B-4 of §[11.3](#ssec:T11-channelB){reference-type="ref"
reference="ssec:T11-channelB"}: $U(1)$-equivariance forcing the
polynomial density to be $\rho \propto |\psi|^2$). The three derivations
are derivationally disjoint and pointwise agree on the Born density
$P(x) = |\psi(x)|^2$. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#cor:psi-star-as-absorber-sphere .corollary}
**Corollary 11.6** (The complex conjugate $\psi^*$ as the absorber's
outgoing $x_{4}$-expansion). *Under
Theorem [11.5](#thm:born-as-collision){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:born-as-collision"}, the complex conjugate $\psi^*$ of
the wavefunction has the explicit physical content of the absorber
Sphere's outgoing $x_{4}$-expansion as seen from the emitter's rest
frame. The Hilbert-space inner-product structure
$\langle\phi, \psi\rangle = \int \phi^*\psi\,d^3 x$ (Theorem 5.3 of
[@MG-Hilbert-2026]) is the integrated form of the head-on
$x_{4}$-collision rate between the bra-Sphere and the ket-Sphere, with
the integrand $\phi^*\psi$ at each spatial point $x$ being the local
collision rate at $x$ between the two Spheres meeting head-on. The Born
probability density $\rho(x) = (\psi^*\psi)(x) = |\psi(x)|^2$ is the
diagonal of this overlap with bra $=$ ket: the collision rate between
the emitter Sphere and its many-particle-absorber image (the conjugate
Sphere) at the same spatial point $x$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). By Step 2 of
Theorem [11.5](#thm:born-as-collision){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:born-as-collision"}, the absorber Sphere appears, from
the emitter's rest frame, as an outgoing $x_{4}$-expansion at $-ic$
rather than $+ic$ --- the sign reversal of the perpendicularity marker
$i \to -i$, which is by definition the complex-conjugation operation on
the wavefunction's amplitude (the wavefunction's $x_{4}$-phase has the
form $\exp(i\,x_{4}\text{-phase})$ for $+ic$ orientation, and
$\exp(-i\,x_{4}\text{-phase})$ for $-ic$ orientation, which is the
complex conjugate of the former). Therefore the absorber Sphere's
amplitude at $P$ has the reading of $\psi^*(P)$ in the
emitter's frame. By Step 5 of
Theorem [11.5](#thm:born-as-collision){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:born-as-collision"}, the collision rate at $P$ is
bilinear in the two amplitudes:
$\text{rate}(P) \propto \psi^*(P)\psi(P)$. Integrating over the spatial
slice gives the inner-product structure
$\langle\psi, \psi\rangle = \int |\psi|^2\,d^3 x$, identifying the
Hilbert-space inner product as the integrated head-on $x_{4}$-collision
rate between bra-Sphere and ket-Sphere. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:born-as-wick-rotation .remark}
*Remark 11.7* (Born event as a particle-scale Wick rotation;
large-ensemble emergence of thermodynamics). Each head-on
$x_{4}$-collision at a spatial event $P$ has the reading of a
Wick rotation of the colliding particles out of $x_{4}$ and into the
spatial three: the perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguished
$x_{4}$ from the spatial three in the pre-collision wavefunction
(Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}, complex amplitudes from
$x_{4}$-perpendicularity) is removed at the collision event, with the
post-collision particles localized at $P$ in the real spatial three.
This is the same content as the apparatus-performed Wick
rotation in the measurement chapter
(Corollary [10.1](#cor:channel-asymmetry-measurement-problem){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor:channel-asymmetry-measurement-problem"}); the Born
collision picture supplies the particle-scale mechanism behind the
apparatus-scale Wick rotation.

In a large ensemble of $N \sim 10^{23}$ particles, the head-on collision
rate per unit volume is on the order of $\sim N^2 \sigma v / V$ for
cross-section $\sigma$ and mean relative velocity $v$ in a volume $V$
--- typically $\sim 10^{10}$ collisions per second per molecule under
standard laboratory conditions, totalling $\sim 10^{33}$ Born events per
second in a macroscopic gas. Each Born event removes a small slice of
$x_{4}$-amplitude from the system's wavefunction by rotating two
particles into 3-localization. The accumulation of these collisional
Wick rotations over a macroscopic ensemble has the reading of
the emergence of thermodynamic behaviour from quantum mechanics: the
complex character of the quantum-mechanical wavefunction is
progressively reduced to real spatial-probability statistics by the
trillion-fold Wick rotation enacted by the collisions, with the role of
an independent passage from QM to thermodynamics replaced by the role of
a derived consequence of accumulated Born events at the
particle-collision level. This is the McGucken-Sphere mechanism behind
the well-known formal connection: under Wick rotation $t \to i\tau$, the
Schrödinger equation $i\hbar\partial_t\psi = \hat{H}\psi$ becomes the
heat equation $\hbar\partial_\tau\psi = -\hat{H}\psi$ (the diffusion
equation governing thermodynamic relaxation), with QM and statistical
mechanics interconverting through the same Wick rotation that the Born
collision performs at the particle level. The strict Second Law of
thermodynamics
(Theorem [22.4](#thm:compton-entropy){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:compton-entropy"} of
Chapter [22](#ch:compton-diffusion){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:compton-diffusion"}) has the reading of the
cumulative thermodynamic shadow of the trillions of head-on
$x_{4}$-collisions per second that the Born mechanism implements in any
macroscopic gas, descending ultimately from the forward orientation of
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= +ic$ at every event of $M_{G}$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iii), monotonicity).
:::

::: {#rmk:boost-measurement-x4-rotation .remark}
*Remark 11.8* (Boost and measurement as two readings of
$x_{4}$-rotation). A parallel between special relativity and
quantum mechanics emerges from the head-on collision mechanism. In
special relativity, a Lorentz boost has the reading of a
hyperbolic rotation in the $(x_{4}, x_j)$ plane: the boosted observer's
$x_{4}$-direction acquires a non-zero component along the spatial
direction $x_j$, with the boost magnitude controlled by the rapidity
$\eta$ via $\cosh\eta = \gamma$, $\sinh\eta = \beta\gamma$
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} of
Chapter [9](#ch:hilbert-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:hilbert-theorem"}, Lorentzian arena from
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). In quantum mechanics, a Born measurement
event has the reading of a head-on $x_{4}$-collision at a
spatial point: the particle's outgoing $x_{4}$-expansion is rotated out
of $x_{4}$ into the spatial three at the collision event, with the
rotation magnitude controlled by the relative angle between the
colliding Spheres' $x_{4}$-orientations (head-on, $\pi$, complete
cancellation; oblique, partial cancellation; parallel, no cancellation).
Both the relativistic boost and the quantum measurement have the
reading of rotations involving the $x_{4}$-direction, with
the role of two distinct rotational structures of different physical
theories replaced by the role of two channel-projections of the single
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: the Algebraic Channel reading (hyperbolic boost on the
algebraic-symmetry side) supplies the Lorentzian content of relativity,
and the Geometric Channel reading (head-on collision on the
geometric-propagation side) supplies the Born-rule content of quantum
mechanics. Both rotations affect the motion of the system: a boost
changes the four-velocity components; a collision changes the
four-momentum components by transferring $x_{4}$-momenergy into the
spatial three. The shared content has the reading of a single
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$-generated geometric primitive, with the
boost-vs-measurement contrast having the role of two channel-projections
of one underlying $x_{4}$-rotation phenomenon.
:::

::: {#rmk:collision-no-signaling .remark}
*Remark 11.9* (Compatibility with no-signaling). The head-on
$x_{4}$-collision mechanism is consistent with the McGucken No-Signaling
Theorem
(Theorem [17.32](#thm:mcgucken-no-signaling){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:mcgucken-no-signaling"} of
Chapter [17](#ch:nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:nonlocality"}). The collision event at $P$ is localised at
the apparatus's spatial position: no information about the collision is
transmitted superluminally across the spatial three. The Born-rule
statistics at $P$ depend only on the local amplitudes
$\psi(P), \psi^*(P)$ at $P$, with the role of a faster-than-light
information channel replaced by the role of local bilinear products of
amplitudes that arrived at $P$ along null worldlines from their
respective source events. The non-locality of quantum mechanics enters
only at the level of the emitter Sphere's global identity (the
wavefunction $\psi$ is non-zero at multiple spatial points, all sharing
the same $x_{4}$-coordinate by sphere-surface $x_{4}$-locality of
Theorem [11.10](#thm:uniqueness-mcgucken-sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:uniqueness-mcgucken-sphere"}), with the local collision
event preserving signal-locality through the bilinearity of the rate at
each spatial point separately.
:::

### Complex conjugation as McGucken-Sphere PT-symmetry through the source event {#sec:born-as-pt-symmetry-through-source}

The head-on $x_{4}$-collision mechanism of
§[11.4](#sec:born-as-head-on-x4-collision){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:born-as-head-on-x4-collision"} supplies the Born rule's
bilinear structure at detection events through two distinct McGucken
Spheres meeting at the registration point. The present section supplies
a complementary geometric reading specific to free propagation: the
wavefunction's complex-conjugation symmetry, and therefore the Born
rule's bilinearity in $(\psi, \psi^*)$, has a geometric source in the
PT-symmetry of a single McGucken Sphere through its source event. The
reading does not require an external absorber: the conjugate factor
$\psi^*$ is supplied by the McGucken Sphere's natural reflection
symmetry through $E$, with the geometric realization being the advanced
sector of the kernel that occupies the past light cone of $E$.

::: {#thm:born-as-pt-symmetry-through-source .theorem}
**Theorem 11.10** (Complex conjugation as McGucken-Sphere PT-symmetry
through the source event). *Let $E \in M_{1,3}$ be an emission event and
let $K_E: M_{1,3} \to \mathbb{C}$ be the McGucken-Sphere kernel
propagating outward from $E$ by the spherical-symmetry-and-velocity-$c$
expansion of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"},
Remark [4.2](#rmk:substantive-content-of-principle){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:substantive-content-of-principle"}). Define the
PT-reflection through $E$ by
$$\mathrm{PT}_E : M_{1,3} \to M_{1,3}, \qquad (x, t) \;\longmapsto\; (2x_E - x,\ 2t_E - t),$$
equivalently $(x - x_E,\ t - t_E) \longmapsto -(x - x_E,\ t - t_E)$.
Then:*

1.  *$\mathrm{PT}_E$ is the unique non-trivial spacetime symmetry of
    $M_{1,3}$ fixing $E$ that preserves both the spherical isotropy of
    the McGucken-Sphere expansion (Postulate clause (ii)) and the
    magnitude $|dx_4/dt| = c$ of the $x_{4}$-advance (Postulate clause
    (i)), while reversing the direction of $x_{4}$-advance through $E$.*

2.  *For any plane-wave component
    $\psi_k(x, t) = \exp\bigl(ik\cdot(x - x_E) - i\omega(k)(t - t_E)\bigr)$
    of the McGucken-Sphere kernel, with $k$ the spatial wavevector and
    $\omega(k)$ the dispersion relation appropriate to the kernel
    (relativistic Klein--Gordon, non-relativistic Schrödinger, or
    Dirac), the $\mathrm{PT}_E$-reflected value equals the
    complex-conjugate value exactly:
    $$\psi_k\bigl(\mathrm{PT}_E\cdot (x, t)\bigr) \;=\; \psi_k^*(x, t),$$
    holding identically on $M_{1,3}$ without any auxiliary assumption.*

3.  *The McGucken-Sphere kernel $K_E$, being a real-coefficient
    superposition of plane-wave components (the retarded Green's
    function of the dispersion relation in the standard normalization),
    satisfies the PT-symmetry relation at the kernel level:
    $$K_E\bigl(\mathrm{PT}_E\cdot (x, t)\bigr) \;=\; K_E^*(x, t),$$
    holding identically on $M_{1,3}$. Equivalently, the kernel's
    retarded sector $K_E^{(\mathrm{ret})}$ on the forward light cone of
    $E$ and the advanced sector $K_E^{(\mathrm{adv})}$ on the past light
    cone of $E$ are related by
    $K_E^{(\mathrm{adv})}(\mathrm{PT}_E\cdot \text{event}) = [K_E^{(\mathrm{ret})}(\text{event})]^*$.*

4.  *The Born density at any spatial-slice event $(P, t)$ for a free
    particle propagating from $E$ has the geometric reading
    $$\bigl|K_E(P, t)\bigr|^2 \;=\; K_E(P, t) \cdot K_E^*(P, t) \;=\; K_E(P, t) \cdot K_E\bigl(\mathrm{PT}_E\cdot (P, t)\bigr),$$
    with the right-hand form making the geometric content explicit: the
    Born density at $(P, t)$ is the product of the kernel's amplitude at
    $(P, t)$ with its amplitude at the $\mathrm{PT}_E$-reflected event
    $(2x_E - x_P,\ 2t_E - t)$. The bilinearity of the Born density in
    $(K_E, K_E^*)$ has the role of the algebraic shadow of the McGucken
    Sphere's PT-symmetry through the source event.*

5.  *For a free particle propagating from a known source event $E$ with
    no absorber present, the conjugate factor $K_E^*$ in the Born
    density is supplied by the McGucken Sphere's own PT-symmetry through
    $E$, with the geometric realization being the advanced sector of the
    kernel occupying the past light cone of $E$. This reading
    complements
    Theorem [11.5](#thm:born-as-collision){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:born-as-collision"} (the head-on $x_{4}$-collision
    reading, which applies at detection events where an absorber's
    sphere arrives at $P$) by supplying the free-propagation regime
    where no absorber is present.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). We verify each clause in turn.

**Step 1 (Clause (i)): uniqueness of $\mathrm{PT}_E$ as the
spherical-isotropy-and-velocity-preserving symmetry through $E$.**

The spacetime symmetries of $M_{1,3}$ fixing $E$ form the Lorentz group
with origin at $E$, equipped with the discrete extensions $P$ (spatial
parity, $(x, t) \mapsto (2x_E - x,\ t)$), $T$ (time reversal,
$(x, t) \mapsto (x,\ 2t_E - t)$), and their composition
$\mathrm{PT} = P \cdot T$. Among the discrete extensions, only those
that reverse the direction of $x_{4}$-advance through $E$ are
non-trivial candidates for the symmetry preserving $|dx_4/dt| = c$ while
reversing direction. There are three such candidates: $P$ alone, $T$
alone, and $\mathrm{PT}$.

Now $P$ alone reverses only the spatial direction of $x_{4}$-advance: at
events on the forward light cone of $E$ (where the $x_{4}$-advance
points in $+\hat n_P$ direction in the spatial slice), $P$ produces
events on the forward light cone of $E$ at the spatially-inverted
direction $-\hat n_P$. The temporal direction $+(t - t_E)$ is preserved,
so $P$ does not reverse the $x_{4}$-advance's temporal orientation. The
McGucken-Sphere structure under $P$ alone is preserved but with the
spatial orientation flipped; the temporal direction of the wavefront's
advance is unchanged. This is a symmetry of the spatial-slice structure
but does not reverse the $x_{4}$-advance.

Similarly, $T$ alone reverses only the temporal direction of
$x_{4}$-advance: at events on the forward light cone of $E$, $T$
produces events on the past light cone of $E$ at the same spatial
direction $+\hat n_P$. The spatial orientation is preserved; the
temporal orientation is flipped. The wavefront's spatial structure under
$T$ alone is preserved but with the temporal direction reversed.

Only $\mathrm{PT}_E = P \cdot T$ reverses both directions
simultaneously: events on the forward light cone of $E$ in direction
$+\hat n_P$ are mapped to events on the past light cone of $E$ in
direction $-\hat n_P$. The wavefront structure is preserved with both
spatial orientation and temporal orientation flipped. By
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (ii) (the spherical isotropy of the
expansion at every event of $M_{G}$), the McGucken-Sphere structure from
$E$ is invariant under the joint reflection $\mathrm{PT}_E$: a
spherically symmetric wavefront emitted at $E$ has spherical symmetry of
its full forward-and-past-light-cone structure through $E$, with the
PT-reflection through $E$ exchanging forward-and-past components while
preserving the spherical symmetry.

The uniqueness claim: among the discrete extensions, only
$\mathrm{PT}_E$ reverses both spatial and temporal directions of
$x_{4}$-advance while preserving the spherical isotropy at $E$. ✓

**Step 2 (Clause (ii)): the PT-symmetry equals complex conjugation for
plane-wave components.**

Let
$\psi_k(x, t) = \exp\bigl(ik\cdot(x - x_E) - i\omega(k)(t - t_E)\bigr)$.
Compute the value at the $\mathrm{PT}_E$-reflected event
$\mathrm{PT}_E\cdot (x, t) = (2x_E - x,\ 2t_E - t)$: $$\begin{aligned}
\psi_k\bigl(\mathrm{PT}_E\cdot (x, t)\bigr)
&= \exp\!\Bigl(ik\cdot\bigl((2x_E - x) - x_E\bigr) - i\omega(k)\bigl((2t_E - t) - t_E\bigr)\Bigr) \\
&= \exp\!\bigl(ik\cdot(x_E - x) - i\omega(k)(t_E - t)\bigr) \\
&= \exp\!\bigl(-ik\cdot(x - x_E) + i\omega(k)(t - t_E)\bigr) \\
&= \exp\!\Bigl(-\bigl[ik\cdot(x - x_E) - i\omega(k)(t - t_E)\bigr]\Bigr) \\
&= \bigl[\exp\!\bigl(ik\cdot(x - x_E) - i\omega(k)(t - t_E)\bigr)\bigr]^* \\
&= \psi_k^*(x, t).
\end{aligned}$$ The identity holds for every plane-wave component
without auxiliary assumption: no time-symmetry of the state, no
real-coefficient restriction, no choice of dispersion relation. The
chain of substitutions uses only that the argument $(x - x_E,\ t - t_E)$
enters linearly in the exponent and that $\mathrm{PT}_E$ reverses both
components by definition. ✓

**Step 3 (Clauses (iii)--(v)): extension to the kernel and the
Born-density reading.**

The McGucken-Sphere retarded kernel $K_E^{(\mathrm{ret})}$ is the
Green's function of the wave equation
$\bigl(\partial_t^2 - c^2\nabla^2 + m^2 c^4 / \hbar^2\bigr) K = 0$
(Klein--Gordon case; similar for Schrödinger and Dirac with
corresponding dispersion) supported on the closed forward light cone of
$E$, normalized to produce outward propagation from $E$ at velocity $c$.
By the standard Fourier representation,
$$K_E^{(\mathrm{ret})}(x, t) \;=\; \int \frac{d^3 k}{(2\pi)^3}\, G(k)\, \exp\!\bigl(ik\cdot(x - x_E) - i\omega(k)(t - t_E)\bigr)\,\theta(t - t_E),$$
with $G(k)$ a real-valued amplitude (e.g.,
$G(k) = \tfrac{1}{2\omega(k)}$ for the Klein--Gordon kernel) determined
by the dispersion relation $\omega(k)$. The real-valuedness of $G(k)$ is
a property of the Green's function in the standard normalization: the
kernel's Fourier-space amplitude is real (the only complex structure in
the kernel is in the plane-wave exponentials themselves).

Applying $\mathrm{PT}_E$ to the kernel's argument and invoking Step 2
component-wise: $$\begin{aligned}
K_E^{(\mathrm{ret})}\bigl(\mathrm{PT}_E\cdot (x, t)\bigr)
&= \int \frac{d^3 k}{(2\pi)^3}\, G(k)\, \psi_k\bigl(\mathrm{PT}_E\cdot (x, t)\bigr)\,\theta(2t_E - t - t_E) \\
&= \int \frac{d^3 k}{(2\pi)^3}\, G(k)\, \psi_k^*(x, t)\,\theta(t_E - t) \\
&= \bigl[K_E^{(\mathrm{ret})}(x, t)\bigr]^*\Bigg|_{\theta(t - t_E)\,\to\,\theta(t_E - t)} \\
&= K_E^{(\mathrm{adv})}(x, t)^*\Bigg|_{\text{kernel form}}.
\end{aligned}$$ The step from line 2 to line 3 uses that $G(k)$ is real
($G(k) = G^*(k)$), so the conjugation of the integrand affects only the
plane-wave exponential, with the result being the complex conjugate of
the kernel's value at $(x, t)$ --- except for the support: the retarded
kernel is supported on $t > t_E$ (forward light cone), while
$K_E^{(\mathrm{ret})}(\mathrm{PT}_E\cdot (x, t))$ is supported on
$t < t_E$ (past light cone). The latter is exactly the support of the
advanced kernel $K_E^{(\mathrm{adv})}$, which satisfies
$K_E^{(\mathrm{adv})}(x, t) = [K_E^{(\mathrm{ret})}(x, t)]^*$ on its
support by the standard retarded-advanced conjugation symmetry of
Green's functions.

Combining the support and conjugation observations: the PT-symmetry
through $E$ exchanges the retarded and advanced sectors of the kernel,
and on either sector it acts by complex conjugation. Identifying $K_E$
with the full kernel (sum of retarded and advanced sectors, or either
one extended trivially by the conjugation to the other), Clause (iii)
holds: $$K_E\bigl(\mathrm{PT}_E\cdot (x, t)\bigr) \;=\; K_E^*(x, t).$$

Clause (iv) then follows by substitution into the Born density: for a
spatial-slice event $(P, t)$ on the forward light cone of $E$,
$$\bigl|K_E(P, t)\bigr|^2 \;=\; K_E(P, t) \cdot K_E^*(P, t) \;=\; K_E(P, t) \cdot K_E\bigl(\mathrm{PT}_E\cdot (P, t)\bigr),$$
with the right-hand expression evaluating the kernel at the
$\mathrm{PT}_E$-reflected event $(2x_E - x_P,\ 2t_E - t)$ on the past
light cone of $E$. The bilinearity of the Born density in $(K_E, K_E^*)$
has the algebraic-shadow role of the McGucken Sphere's PT-symmetry
through $E$.

Clause (v) is the physical-interpretation consequence: for a free
particle (no absorber present), the conjugate factor in the Born density
is supplied by the McGucken Sphere's own PT-symmetry through $E$ via the
advanced sector. The reading is consistent with
Theorem [11.5](#thm:born-as-collision){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:born-as-collision"} (head-on $x_{4}$-collision at
detection events): the transition from free propagation to detection
corresponds to the appearance of the absorber's sphere taking over as
the physical source of the conjugate factor, with the kernel-level
PT-symmetry transitioning smoothly into the two-sphere collision reading
as the absorber becomes present at the registration point. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:pt-symmetry-vs-collision-and-chain .remark}
*Remark 11.11* (Three complementary geometric readings of the Born
rule). The Born rule's bilinearity in $(\psi, \psi^*)$ now has three distinct geometric readings within the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, each
illuminating a different physical context with the algebraic result
$P = |\psi|^2$ identical across all three:

-   *Chain of theorems-overlap reading*
    (Lemma [9.13](#lem:bilinearity-rank2){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:bilinearity-rank2"}, the rank-2 Minkowski-metric
    content of [@MG-Pointwise-2026] §7.4): the bilinearity of the inner
    product on $\mathcal{H}$ is inherited from the rank-2 character of
    the Lorentzian metric on $M_{1,3}$, which itself comes from
    $(ic)^2 = -c^2$ in $x_{4}= ict$. This is the most abstract reading
    and supplies the algebraic origin of the bilinearity at the chain of theorems
    level.

-   *Two-sphere head-on-collision reading*
    (Theorem [11.5](#thm:born-as-collision){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:born-as-collision"}, [@MG-Pointwise-2026] §7.7): the
    conjugate factor $\psi^*$ is the absorber's outgoing McGucken Sphere
    viewed from the emitter's frame, with the bilinear product
    $\psi^*\psi$ at the detection event $P$ being the head-on
    $x_{4}$-collision rate of two physically distinct spheres. This is
    the detection-event reading and supplies the concrete physical
    mechanism for the Born event at measurement.

-   *PT-symmetry-through-source reading*
    (Theorem [11.10](#thm:born-as-pt-symmetry-through-source){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:born-as-pt-symmetry-through-source"}, the present
    section): the conjugate factor $\psi^*$ at the kernel level is the
    McGucken Sphere's PT-reflection through its source event $E$, with
    the bilinear product $\psi^*\psi$ at any spatial-slice event being
    the product of the kernel's amplitude at that event with its
    amplitude at the PT-reflected event on the past light cone of $E$.
    This is the free-propagation reading and supplies the intrinsic
    geometric content of the conjugate factor in the absence of an
    absorber.

The three readings are complementary, each illuminating a different
physical situation. The overlap reading supplies the algebraic
origin of bilinearity (rank-2 metric forcing the structure); the
two-sphere reading supplies the detection-event mechanism (two spheres,
one collision); the PT-symmetry reading supplies the free-propagation
intrinsic content (one sphere, intrinsic reflection symmetry). The
transitions between physical regimes connect smoothly: a free particle
propagating from $E$ has its Born density supplied by the PT-symmetry
through $E$; the moment a detector interacts at $P$, the absorber's
sphere takes over as the source of the conjugate factor, and the
two-sphere reading applies, with the algebraic result $|\psi(P)|^2$
identical in both regimes.
:::

::: {#rmk:pt-symmetry-spinor-refinement .remark}
*Remark 11.12* (Spinor refinement: the Wigner antiunitary $T$ and the
$\sigma_y$ factor). For spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ wavefunctions, the standard
Wigner time-reversal operator acts antiunitarily as
$T\cdot\psi = -i\sigma_y\,\psi^*$ (with the global sign and $\sigma_y$
factor fixing the spinor-internal phase convention; one has $T^2 = -1$
by Kramers' theorem). The McGucken-Sphere PT-symmetry through $E$ for a
spinor wavefunction therefore carries the spin-internal $\sigma_y$
factor:
$$\psi_{\text{spinor}}\bigl(\mathrm{PT}_E\cdot \text{event}\bigr) \;=\; -i\sigma_y\,\psi_{\text{spinor}}^*(\text{event})$$
on the kernel level, with the $-i\sigma_y$ factor accounting for the
spinor's transformation under the spatial parity component of
$\mathrm{PT}_E$ (which exchanges left- and right-handed spinor
components via the $\sigma_y$ factor) and under the time-reversal
component (which complex-conjugates the spinor's phase). The $T^2 = -1$
Kramers signature is the algebraic record of the spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$
$4\pi$-closure (instance (N4) of
Theorem [12.12](#thm:universal-non-closure){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:universal-non-closure"} in
Chapter [12](#ch:heisenberg){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:heisenberg"}): the spinor's PT-symmetry has
Wigner-antiunitary structure, requiring a full $4\pi$ for closure of the
doubled PT-rotation. The consistency with the
physical-content reading
(Remark [4.2](#rmk:substantive-content-of-principle){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:substantive-content-of-principle"} of
Chapter [4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:foundations"}, "the spinor lives on a wavefront that
already has the Compton frequency"): the spinor's internal $\sigma_y$
structure under PT-symmetry through $E$ carries the same half-quantum
content as the spinor's external $4\pi$-closure under spatial rotations,
both being signatures of the McGucken-Sphere half-quantum of
$x_{4}$-rotation that the spinor carries.
:::

::: {#rmk:pt-symmetry-substantive-state-connection .remark}
*Remark 11.13* (Physical-state connection: $T = \mathrm{PT}_E$ joins the
framework's unifications). The McGucken Principle's physical
content
(Remark [4.2](#rmk:substantive-content-of-principle){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:substantive-content-of-principle"} of
Chapter [4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:foundations"}) is that $x_4$ advances as a
spherically-symmetric wavefront at $c$ from every event of $M_{G}$. A
spherically-symmetric wavefront emitted at $E$ admits a unique natural
reflection symmetry through $E$, which in 4D is precisely PT-symmetry.
Theorem [11.10](#thm:born-as-pt-symmetry-through-source){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:born-as-pt-symmetry-through-source"} reads off the
algebraic content of this natural geometric symmetry: the kernel
satisfies $K_E(\mathrm{PT}_E\cdot \text{event}) = K_E^*(\text{event})$
identically, with the Born density's bilinearity in $(K_E, K_E^*)$ being
the algebraic shadow of the wavefront's PT-symmetry through $E$. The
dynamics were in the premise
(Remark [4.2](#rmk:substantive-content-of-principle){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:substantive-content-of-principle"}): the wavefront's
natural reflection symmetry through $E$ generates complex conjugation as
an intrinsic geometric content of the McGucken-Sphere kernel.

The identification $T_{\mathcal{H}} = \mathrm{PT}_E$ --- the
Wigner antiunitary time-reversal operator $T$ acting on the Hilbert
space equals the spacetime PT-reflection through the source event $E$
--- joins the unifications already established in this
textbook. Each of the following identifications gives a Hilbert-space
algebraic operation a geometric realization at the spacetime level:

-   The imaginary unit $i$ in the canonical commutator
    $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ has its geometric realization as the
    perpendicularity marker for $x_{4}$'s orthogonality to $x_1 x_2 x_3$
    (Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}).

-   The action quantum $\hbar$ has its geometric realization as the
    action per radian of the Compton-frequency oscillation of $x_{4}$-advance
    (Theorem [9.35](#thm:c-hbar-twin){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:c-hbar-twin"}).

-   The complex-conjugation operator $\psi\mapsto\psi^*$ (equivalently,
    the Wigner antiunitary $T$) has its geometric realization as the
    McGucken-Sphere PT-reflection through the source event
    (Theorem [11.10](#thm:born-as-pt-symmetry-through-source){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:born-as-pt-symmetry-through-source"} above).

Three Hilbert-space algebraic operations --- multiplication by $i$,
multiplication by $\hbar$, and complex conjugation --- all have
geometric realizations at the McGucken-spacetime level, all descending
from the physical content of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as a
spherically-symmetric wavefront with wavelength, frequency, phase, and
action. The algebra of quantum mechanics has the role of the
function-space rendering of the active geometric content of the McGucken
Principle, with each algebraic operation acquiring its geometric meaning
from the principle's physical content.
:::

### Disjointness audit {#disjointness-audit-9}

**Geometric Channel:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, McGucken Sphere wavefront,
$SO(3)$ rotation group, Haar measure, $U(1)$-bundle structure, squared
modulus as unique equivariant density.

**Algebraic Channel:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, four requirements
(real-valuedness, non-negativity, phase invariance, smoothness), Cauchy
functional equation, unit normalization.

**Intersection:** $\{(\mathrm{McP}), P = |\psi|^2\}$. Cauchy functional
equation does *not* appear in Geometric Channel. Haar measure does *not* appear
in Algebraic Channel. *Disjointness verified.*

### Independence of the derivation from the Hilbert-space lattice tradition {#sec:born-independent-of-gleason}

The Algebraic Channel derivation (§ "Algebraic Channel derivation" above), the Geometric Channel
derivation (§[11.3](#ssec:T11-channelB){reference-type="ref"
reference="ssec:T11-channelB"} above), and the head-on $x_{4}$-collision
mechanism
(§[11.4](#sec:born-as-head-on-x4-collision){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:born-as-head-on-x4-collision"}) together establish
$P = |\psi|^2$ as a forced theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ through
three derivationally disjoint routes. None of the three routes presupposes
a Hilbert space, a non-contextuality axiom, a measure-theoretic argument
on the lattice of closed subspaces, a frequentist limit, a
decision-theoretic axiom, or an envariance, equivariance, or
branch-counting hypothesis. The four requirements R1--R4 of
the Algebraic Channel derivation descend directly from the principle: R1 reality
and R2 non-negativity from the operational character of probability as
the frequency of detection events on the spatial slice; R3 phase
invariance from the universal-rate clause of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}; and R4 bilinearity in $(\psi, \psi^*)$ from
the rank-2 character of the Minkowski metric induced by $x_{4}= ict$,
with the exponent 2 supplied directly by the rank-2 character without
recourse to any inside-Hilbert-space machinery.

This places the derivation upstream of the entire twentieth-century
tradition of Hilbert-space-internal Born-rule arguments, of which
Gleason's 1957 measure-theoretic argument [@Gleason1957] is the
canonical and most rigorous instance, and of which Deutsch--Wallace,
Zurek, and Farhi--Goldstone--Gutmann are the canonical
decision-theoretic, envariance, and frequentist successors. Each program
in that tradition presupposes the arena (a complex separable Hilbert
space) and imports one supplementary axiom (non-contextuality,
rationality, envariance, frequentist limit) sufficient to extract the
algebraic form of the rule from inside the arena. The McGucken
derivation supplies the arena as a downstream theorem
(Theorem [9.17](#thm:hilbert-complete){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complete"} of
Chapter [9](#ch:hilbert-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:hilbert-theorem"}, with the deeper identification $\mathcal{H}= L^2(M_{1,3}, \eta_{\mu\nu})$ of
Theorem [9.31](#thm:hilbert-minkowski-one-object){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-minkowski-one-object"}) and supplies the exponent
2 directly from the rank-2 character of the Minkowski metric, with no
supplementary axiom required.

::: {#rmk:gleason-diagnostic .remark}
*Remark 11.14* (Diagnostic: Gleason 1957 as a downstream
functional-analytic argument; [@MG-Pointwise-2026] §7.1.2, §7.5, §10.6).
Gleason's theorem [@Gleason1957] establishes that every countably
additive probability measure on the lattice of closed subspaces of a
separable complex Hilbert space of dimension $\geq 3$ takes the trace
form $\mu(P) = \mathrm{Tr}(\rho P)$ for some density operator $\rho$.
The theorem operates entirely inside an already-postulated Hilbert
space, with three black-box inputs: the lattice structure (closed
subspaces of $\mathcal{H}$); the complex field (the lattice lives on
$\mathbb{C}$, not on $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{H}$); and the
non-contextuality condition on the probability measure. The argument
extracts the algebraic form of the rule from these inputs but cannot
supply the inputs themselves. In the framework of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, each Gleason input is recovered as a
downstream theorem of the principle: the Hilbert space as the
function-space rendering $\mathcal{H}= L^2(M_{1,3}, \eta_{\mu\nu})$ of
the Minkowski manifold
(Theorem [9.31](#thm:hilbert-minkowski-one-object){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-minkowski-one-object"}); the complex field as the
algebraic record of $x_{4}$-perpendicularity inherited from $x_{4}= ict$
(Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}); the non-contextuality condition on
the probability measure as the operational shadow of the universal-rate
clause of the principle, the same fact that gives R3 phase invariance in
the derivation above. The McGucken derivation of $P = |\psi|^2$ from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ through R1--R4 is upstream of all three Gleason
inputs: the principle supplies the Hilbert space, the complex structure,
and the phase invariance simultaneously, with the exponent 2 supplied by
the rank-2 character of the Minkowski metric, the entire derivation
requiring no measure-theoretic argument on the lattice of closed
subspaces. The same observation applies to the other
canonical Hilbert-space-internal derivations --- Deutsch--Wallace
decision-theoretic, Zurek envariance, Hartle and
Farhi--Goldstone--Gutmann frequentist, Bohm--Valentini--Westman
quantum-equilibrium --- each of which presupposes a complex separable
Hilbert space and imports one further axiom whose physical origin
remains unexplained in the framework that imports it. The disposition of the McGucken derivation toward this tradition is one of
upstream sufficiency: the principle generates the arena and the rule
together, with the prior-tradition arguments reappearing as downstream
functional-analytic consistency checks whose inputs are themselves
McGucken theorems.
:::

### Empirical anchor

The Born rule is the operational interpretation of every quantum
mechanical experiment since 1926. The squared-modulus rule has been
tested to fractional precision $\sim 10^{-3}$ in three-slit experiments
(Sinha et al. 2010 [@Sinha2010]), excluding higher-order alternatives
such as $|\psi|^3$ or $|\psi|^4$ with high statistical significance. The
rule $P = |\psi|^2$ is one of the most precisely tested rules in
physics.

Weinberg's question "Where does the Born rule come from?"
[@Weinberg2015] is answered, in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, by the double
derivation above: it comes from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, twice.

## QM T12: The Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle {#ch:heisenberg}

> *The McGucken Principle.* The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality.
> Every result below descends from that expansion.


*Recall.* the McGucken Principle ($\mathrm{McP}$:
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$) asserts that the fourth spacetime dimension
$x_4$ expands at the velocity of light $c$, carrying the
perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguishes it from the spatial
three. Throughout this chapter, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ refers to this
principle and to the five-clause content (i)--(v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: (i) *invariance* --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content; (ii) *spherical symmetry* --- the
expansion is isotropic in the spatial three, with the set of events
reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a 2-sphere of radius
$c\tau$; (iii) *monotonicity* --- the integral curve is strictly
monotonically increasing in $t$, fixing the arrow of $x_4$-advance; (iv)
*Lorentz consistency* --- the structure is $SO^+(1,3)$-invariant on
$M_{G}$; (v) *global validity* --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at
every event of $M_{G}$. The integrated kinematic shadow
$x_4 = ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is the kinematic shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the central fact.

### Statement

::: {#thm:QMT12 .theorem}
**Theorem 12.1** (QM T12: Heisenberg uncertainty, = Theorem 71 (Algebraic
Channel) and Theorem 94 (Geometric Channel) of [@Syn-2026]). *For any normalized state
$\psi$ and any pair of self-adjoint operators $\hat{A}, \hat{B}$, the
standard deviations
$\Delta A = \sqrt{\langle\hat{A}^2\rangle - \langle\hat{A}\rangle^2}$
and $\Delta B$ satisfy the Robertson--Schrödinger inequality
$$\Delta A\,\Delta B \ge \tfrac{1}{2}|\langle[\hat{A}, \hat{B}]\rangle|.$$
In particular, for $\hat{A} = \hat{q}$, $\hat{B} = \hat{p}$, using
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$
(Theorem [10.5](#thm:QMT10-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT10-channelA"}),
$$\Delta q\,\Delta p \ge \frac{\hbar}{2}.
\label{eq:Heisenberg}$$*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). We prove the position-momentum case
[\[eq:Heisenberg\]](#eq:Heisenberg){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:Heisenberg"} along Algebraic Channel (Robertson--Cauchy--Schwarz
on the McGucken-derived canonical commutator) and Geometric Channel (Fourier
uncertainty principle on the McGucken-derived Hilbert space), then note
the general Robertson--Schrödinger refinement. Every constant in the
final inequality traces to $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via a named theorem.

**Algebraic Channel --- Robertson--Cauchy--Schwarz proof.** By QA3, the
canonical commutator is the McGucken-derived identity
$$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] \;=\; i\hbar\,\mathbf{1} \qquad \text{(Theorem~\ref{thm:QMT10-channelA})},$$
where the $i$ is the perpendicularity marker of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}, $x_4 = ict$ generates the Lorentzian
signature with $i$ marking the perpendicular fourth dimension) and
$\hbar$ is the action quantum per McGucken-Sphere cycle
(Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"},
derived from the Compton-frequency oscillation $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$
generated by $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at the source event). Define the
shifted self-adjoint operators
$$\delta\hat{q}\;:=\; \hat{q}- \langle\hat{q}\rangle\,\mathbf{1}, \qquad \delta\hat{p}\;:=\; \hat{p}- \langle\hat{p}\rangle\,\mathbf{1},$$
where $\langle\cdot\rangle = \langle\psi, \cdot\,\psi\rangle$ denotes
expectation in the normalized state $\psi$. Subtracting $c$-number
multiples of the identity preserves self-adjointness and the commutator:
$$[\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}] \;=\; [\hat{q}- \langle\hat{q}\rangle\mathbf{1},\, \hat{p}- \langle\hat{p}\rangle\mathbf{1}] \;=\; [\hat{q}, \hat{p}] \;=\; i\hbar\,\mathbf{1},$$
using that $\mathbf{1}$ commutes with every operator. The variances are
$$(\Delta q)^2 \;=\; \langle\delta\hat{q}^2\rangle \;=\; \langle\delta\hat{q}\,\psi,\,\delta\hat{q}\,\psi\rangle \;=\; \|\delta\hat{q}\,\psi\|^2,$$
using
$\langle\psi, \delta\hat{q}^2\,\psi\rangle = \langle\delta\hat{q}^*\,\psi, \delta\hat{q}\,\psi\rangle = \langle\delta\hat{q}\,\psi, \delta\hat{q}\,\psi\rangle$
from self-adjointness $\delta\hat{q}^* = \delta\hat{q}$. Similarly
$(\Delta p)^2 = \|\delta\hat{p}\,\psi\|^2$.

**Step 1: Cauchy--Schwarz on the McGucken-derived Hilbert space.** By
the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality on $\mathcal{H}$
(Theorem [3.2](#thm:cauchy-schwarz){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:cauchy-schwarz"}, proved in
Chapter [3](#ch:math){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:math"} by the
discriminant of the non-negative quadratic
$\|\,\delta\hat{q}\,\psi + t\,\delta\hat{p}\,\psi\,\|^2 \geq 0$ on
$t \in \mathbb{R}$), applied to the vectors
$\delta\hat{q}\,\psi, \delta\hat{p}\,\psi \in \mathcal{H}$:
$$|\langle\delta\hat{q}\,\psi,\, \delta\hat{p}\,\psi\rangle|^2 \;\leq\; \|\delta\hat{q}\,\psi\|^2 \cdot \|\delta\hat{p}\,\psi\|^2 \;=\; (\Delta q)^2\,(\Delta p)^2.$$
The Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ is itself a theorem
of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}), so the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality
applies on a McGucken-derived inner-product structure.

**Step 2: Decompose the inner product into symmetric (real) and
antisymmetric (imaginary) parts.** By the self-adjointness of
$\delta\hat{q}$:
$$\langle\delta\hat{q}\,\psi,\, \delta\hat{p}\,\psi\rangle \;=\; \langle\psi,\, \delta\hat{q}^*\,\delta\hat{p}\,\psi\rangle \;=\; \langle\psi,\, \delta\hat{q}\,\delta\hat{p}\,\psi\rangle,$$
since $\delta\hat{q}^* = \delta\hat{q}$. Decompose the operator product
$\delta\hat{q}\,\delta\hat{p}$ into its symmetric (anticommutator) and
antisymmetric (commutator) parts:
$$\delta\hat{q}\,\delta\hat{p}\;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\{\delta\hat{q},\, \delta\hat{p}\} \,+\, \tfrac{1}{2}[\delta\hat{q},\, \delta\hat{p}],$$
where $\{A, B\} := AB + BA$ is the anticommutator and
$[A, B] := AB - BA$ is the commutator. The two parts have opposite
Hermitian symmetry:
$\{\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}\}^* = \{\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}\}$
(self-adjoint, since $(AB + BA)^* = B^*A^* + A^*B^* = BA + AB$ when
$A, B$ are self-adjoint), while
$[\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}]^* = -[\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}]$
(anti-self-adjoint, since
$(AB - BA)^* = B^*A^* - A^*B^* = BA - AB = -[A,B]$).

The expectation value of a self-adjoint operator is real (since
$\langle\psi, A\psi\rangle = \langle A^*\psi, \psi\rangle = \langle A\psi, \psi\rangle = \overline{\langle\psi, A\psi\rangle}$,
hence $\langle A\rangle \in \mathbb{R}$); the expectation value of an
anti-self-adjoint operator is pure imaginary (since
$\langle\psi, B\psi\rangle = -\langle B^*\psi, \psi\rangle = -\overline{\langle\psi, B\psi\rangle}$,
hence $\langle B\rangle \in i\mathbb{R}$). Therefore
$$\langle\delta\hat{q}\,\delta\hat{p}\rangle \;=\; \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}\langle\{\delta\hat{q},\, \delta\hat{p}\}\rangle}_{\in\,\mathbb{R}\ \text{(symmetric part)}} \,+\, \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}\langle[\delta\hat{q},\, \delta\hat{p}]\rangle}_{\in\,i\mathbb{R}\ \text{(antisymmetric part)}}.$$
The antisymmetric part is computed from the McGucken-derived commutator:
$\tfrac{1}{2}\langle[\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}]\rangle = \tfrac{1}{2}\langle i\hbar\,\mathbf{1}\rangle = \tfrac{i\hbar}{2}\langle\mathbf{1}\rangle = \tfrac{i\hbar}{2}$
(using
$\langle\mathbf{1}\rangle = \langle\psi, \psi\rangle = \|\psi\|^2 = 1$
from the normalization).

**Step 3: Lower bound via $|z|^2 \ge (\Im z)^2$.** Write
$z := \langle\delta\hat{q}\,\psi, \delta\hat{p}\,\psi\rangle = a + i b$
with
$a = \tfrac{1}{2}\langle\{\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}\}\rangle \in \mathbb{R}$
and
$i b = \tfrac{1}{2}\langle[\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}]\rangle = i\hbar/2$,
so $b = \hbar/2 \in \mathbb{R}$. The squared modulus is
$$|z|^2 \;=\; a^2 + b^2 \;\geq\; b^2 \;=\; \Bigl(\frac{\hbar}{2}\Bigr)^{\!2},$$
since $a^2 \geq 0$. Equality $|z|^2 = b^2$ holds iff $a = 0$, i.e., iff
the symmetric covariance
$\tfrac{1}{2}\langle\{\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}\}\rangle$ vanishes.

**Step 4: Combine Steps 1 and 3.** From Step 1,
$|z|^2 \leq (\Delta q)^2(\Delta p)^2$; from Step 3,
$|z|^2 \geq (\hbar/2)^2$. Therefore
$$(\Delta q)^2(\Delta p)^2 \;\geq\; \Bigl(\frac{\hbar}{2}\Bigr)^{\!2}, \qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad \Delta q\,\Delta p \;\geq\; \frac{\hbar}{2}.$$
The lower bound is saturated by the Gaussian states for which the
Cauchy--Schwarz inequality becomes an equality and the symmetric
covariance vanishes --- the minimum-uncertainty wavepackets.

**Geometric Channel --- Fourier uncertainty.** The Geometric Channel derivation in
§[12.3](#ssec:T12-channelB){reference-type="ref"
reference="ssec:T12-channelB"} below proceeds purely by Fourier analysis
on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ (Cauchy--Schwarz plus integration by parts plus
Parseval), with no canonical-commutator input. The Fourier-uncertainty
inequality $\Delta x\,\Delta k \geq 1/2$ converts to
$\Delta x\,\Delta p \geq \hbar/2$ via de Broglie $p = \hbar k$
(Theorem [2.1](#thm:QMT2){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT2"},
derived from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ by the Compton-coupling argument).
The two channels are derivationally disjoint.

**General Robertson--Schrödinger.** For arbitrary self-adjoint
$\hat A, \hat B$ on $\mathcal{H}$ with
$\langle\hat A\rangle, \langle\hat B\rangle$ defined in the state
$\psi$, the same Cauchy--Schwarz + symmetric/antisymmetric decomposition
argument with $\delta\hat A := \hat A - \langle\hat A\rangle\mathbf{1}$,
$\delta\hat B := \hat B - \langle\hat B\rangle\mathbf{1}$ gives the
Robertson--Schrödinger inequality
$$(\Delta A)^2(\Delta B)^2 \;\geq\; \tfrac{1}{4}\,|\langle[\hat A,\hat B]\rangle|^2 \,+\, \tfrac{1}{4}\,|\langle\{\delta\hat A, \delta\hat B\}\rangle|^2,$$
since $|z|^2 = a^2 + b^2$ (not just $\geq b^2$), with
$a = \tfrac{1}{2}\langle\{\delta\hat A, \delta\hat B\}\rangle$ and
$b = \tfrac{1}{2i}\langle[\hat A,\hat B]\rangle$. Robertson's 1929
inequality
$\Delta A\,\Delta B \geq \tfrac{1}{2}|\langle[\hat A, \hat B]\rangle|$
retains only the antisymmetric part (the universal lower bound, the same
as Step 3 above); Schrödinger's 1930 refinement adds the symmetric part
for a tighter bound when the symmetric covariance is non-zero. In the
position--momentum case we used only the antisymmetric Robertson part,
which suffices for $\Delta q\,\Delta p \geq \hbar/2$ in any state.
$\square$ ◻
:::

### Geometric Channel derivation (QB3, QB4 --- Sphere wavevector vs. position width) {#ssec:T12-channelB}

::: channelb
*Geometric Channel Derivation 12.4* (Heisenberg from Fourier-conjugate widths on
the McGucken-Sphere wavefront). The Geometric Channel derivation proceeds in
five explicit steps, each anchored to $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via a
named theorem, using only Fourier analysis on the McGucken-derived
Hilbert space (no canonical-commutator input).

**Step B-1 (Wavefront as wavefunction support).** By QB1+QB2, the
wavefunction $\psi(\mathbf{x}, t) \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ is the
amplitude function on the iterated McGucken-Sphere wavefront
$M^{+}_{p}(t)$ at every event $p$ of the particle's worldline. Spherical
symmetry of the $x_{4}$-expansion (clause (ii) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}) supplies the $SO(3)$-invariant Haar measure
on the wavefront, which by
Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"} (Born rule) determines the
position-space probability density $|\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)|^2$. For a
normalized wavefunction ($\int|\psi|^2 d^3\mathbf{x} = 1$), the
position-space variance about the mean
$\langle\mathbf{x}\rangle = \int \mathbf{x}|\psi|^2 d^3\mathbf{x}$ is
$$(\Delta\mathbf{x})^2 \;:=\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}(\mathbf{x} - \langle\mathbf{x}\rangle)^2\,|\psi(\mathbf{x})|^2\,d^3\mathbf{x}.$$

**Step B-2 (Fourier-conjugate wavevector).** The Fourier transform on
$L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ with convention
$$\tilde\psi(\mathbf{k}) \;:=\; (2\pi)^{-3/2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}}\,\psi(\mathbf{x})\,d^3\mathbf{x}$$
is, by Plancherel's theorem (Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Vol. II,
Theorem IX.2), an isometry on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$, with
$\|\tilde\psi\|_{L^2} = \|\psi\|_{L^2}$. The Sphere-wavevector spread is
$$(\Delta\mathbf{k})^2 \;:=\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}(\mathbf{k} - \langle\mathbf{k}\rangle)^2\,|\tilde\psi(\mathbf{k})|^2\,d^3\mathbf{k}.$$
The McGucken-anchoring at this step: the Fourier transform is the
algebraic-symmetry expression of the spatial-translation invariance of
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (clauses (i), (v): the principle holds with the
same value at every spatial event, so spatial translation acts unitarily
on $\mathcal{H}$, and the spectral decomposition of the
spatial-translation generator $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ is precisely the
Fourier basis $e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}}$ with eigenvalue
$\hbar\mathbf{k}$).

**Step B-3 (Fourier-analytic uncertainty:
$\Delta x \cdot \Delta k \geq 1/2$).** It suffices to prove the
one-dimensional inequality $\Delta x\,\Delta k \geq 1/2$ for
$\psi \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ with $\|\psi\|_{L^2} = 1$ and zero means
$\langle x\rangle = \langle k\rangle = 0$ (achievable by translation in
position and modulation in momentum); the three-dimensional version
follows by applying the one-dimensional inequality to each axis. For
$\psi \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$ (Schwartz class; sufficient for the
calculus of integration by parts, with extension to $L^2$ by density):

*Sub-step B-3a: Cauchy--Schwarz on the Hilbert space.* By
Cauchy--Schwarz on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ applied to the vectors
$x\,\psi(x), \partial_x\psi(x) \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$:
$$\Bigl|\,\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} (x\,\psi(x))^*\,\partial_x\psi(x)\,dx\,\Bigr|^2 \;\leq\; \Bigl(\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}|x\,\psi|^2\,dx\Bigr)\cdot\Bigl(\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}|\partial_x\psi|^2\,dx\Bigr).$$
The first integral on the right is $(\Delta x)^2$ (with
$\langle x\rangle = 0$). The second integral, by Parseval on
$L^2(\mathbb{R})$ applied to $-i\partial_x\psi$ (whose Fourier transform
is $k\,\tilde\psi(k)$):
$$\int|\partial_x\psi|^2\,dx \;=\; \int|k\tilde\psi(k)|^2\,dk \;=\; \int k^2\,|\tilde\psi(k)|^2\,dk \;=\; (\Delta k)^2,$$
using $\langle k\rangle = 0$. Therefore
$$\Bigl|\,\int x\,\psi^*\,\partial_x\psi\,dx\,\Bigr|^2 \;\leq\; (\Delta x)^2(\Delta k)^2.$$

*Sub-step B-3b: Lower bound via the real part using integration by
parts.* The inner product $z := \int x\,\psi^*\,\partial_x\psi\,dx$ has
real and imaginary parts $z = \Re z + i\,\Im z$. To bound $|z|$ below,
we extract $\Re z$ via integration by parts. Compute the conjugate:
$$\bar z \;=\; \overline{\int x\,\psi^*\,\partial_x\psi\,dx} \;=\; \int x\,\psi\,\partial_x\psi^*\,dx,$$
since $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and complex conjugation interchanges
$\psi \leftrightarrow \psi^*$. Adding $z + \bar z = 2\Re z$:
$$2\Re z \;=\; \int x\,(\psi^*\,\partial_x\psi + \psi\,\partial_x\psi^*)\,dx \;=\; \int x\,\partial_x|\psi|^2\,dx,$$
using the product rule
$\partial_x|\psi|^2 = \partial_x(\psi^*\psi) = (\partial_x\psi^*)\,\psi + \psi^*\,(\partial_x\psi)$.
Integrate by parts on $\partial_x$ with the boundary term vanishing for
$\psi \in \mathcal{S}$ (since $|\psi|^2 \to 0$ as $|x| \to \infty$):
$$\int x\,\partial_x|\psi|^2\,dx \;=\; \bigl[x\,|\psi|^2\bigr]_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \,-\, \int (\partial_x x)\,|\psi|^2\,dx \;=\; 0 \,-\, \int |\psi|^2\,dx \;=\; -1,$$
using $\int|\psi|^2\,dx = \|\psi\|_{L^2}^2 = 1$ (normalization) and
$\partial_x x = 1$. Therefore $\Re z = -1/2$, and
$$|z|^2 \;=\; (\Re z)^2 + (\Im z)^2 \;\geq\; (\Re z)^2 \;=\; \Bigl(\frac{1}{2}\Bigr)^{\!2} \;=\; \frac{1}{4}.$$

*Sub-step B-3c: Combine.* From sub-step B-3a,
$|z|^2 \leq (\Delta x)^2(\Delta k)^2$; from sub-step B-3b,
$|z|^2 \geq 1/4$. Therefore
$$(\Delta x)^2(\Delta k)^2 \;\geq\; \frac{1}{4}, \qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad \Delta x \cdot \Delta k \;\geq\; \frac{1}{2}.$$
This is the Fourier-uncertainty inequality on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, derived
in four lines from Cauchy--Schwarz, Parseval, and integration by parts.
The three-dimensional analogue $\Delta x_j \cdot \Delta k_j \geq 1/2$
for each $j = 1, 2, 3$ follows by the same argument applied to each
axis. (Saturation occurs iff $\partial_x\psi = -\alpha x\,\psi$ for some
$\alpha > 0$, i.e., $\psi$ is a real Gaussian; this is the
Cauchy--Schwarz equality case.)

**Step B-4 (de Broglie conversion to $\Delta p$).** By
Theorem [2.1](#thm:QMT2){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT2"} (de
Broglie relation, Geometric Channel derivation), the McGucken-Sphere wavevector
$\mathbf{k}$ and the spatial momentum $\mathbf{p}$ of the particle are
related by $$\mathbf{p} \;=\; \hbar\,\mathbf{k},$$ where $\hbar$ is the
action quantum per Sphere cycle
(Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"},
derived from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at the source event via the
Compton-frequency $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$). The de Broglie relation in
turn descends from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: at the rest frame, the
Compton oscillation has wavevector $k_C = \omega_C/c = mc/\hbar$ along
$x_{4}$; Lorentz-boosting to the moving frame on $M_{G}$ (preserving the
Minkowski line element of
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}) converts the rest-frame
$x_{4}$-wavevector into a spatial wavevector
$\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{p}/\hbar$ in the boost direction. The conversion
preserves both the linearity and the factor $\hbar$.

The momentum spread is then
$\Delta\mathbf{p} = \hbar\,\Delta\mathbf{k}$, and substituting into the
Fourier-uncertainty inequality of Step B-3:
$$\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \;=\; \hbar \cdot \Delta x \cdot \Delta k \;\geq\; \frac{\hbar}{2}.$$

**Step B-5 (Geometric Channel characterisation).** The derivation uses three
inputs: (i) the McGucken-Sphere position-space wavefunction
structure (QB1+QB2, Step B-1); (ii) the Fourier transform on
$L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$, derived from spatial-translation invariance of
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (Step B-2); (iii) the de Broglie relation
$\mathbf{p} = \hbar\mathbf{k}$ from the Compton-frequency rest-frame
oscillation + Lorentz boost (Step B-4). The canonical commutator
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ does *not* appear in the derivation;
Stone's theorem does *not* appear; abstract operator-theoretic
Hilbert-space machinery beyond the Fourier transform does *not* appear.
The derivation is Geometric-Channel-pure, derivationally disjoint from the Algebraic
Channel route. Saturation $\Delta x\,\Delta p = \hbar/2$ holds for Gaussian
wavepackets; this is the geometric reading of the minimum-uncertainty
state as the optimally compact McGucken-Sphere wavefunction. $\square$
:::

### Algebraic Channel derivation (QA3 plus Cauchy--Schwarz on Hermitian operators)

::: channela
*Algebraic Channel Derivation 12.2* (Heisenberg from Cauchy--Schwarz on the
McGucken-derived canonical commutator). The Algebraic Channel derivation
proceeds in five explicit steps, each anchored to
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via a named theorem.

**Step CA-1: McGucken-derived inputs.** The proof uses three inputs, each a theorem of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$:

1.  The canonical commutator $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar\,\mathbf{1}$
    on $\mathcal{H}$
    (Theorem [10.5](#thm:QMT10-channelA){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT10-channelA"}, derived along Algebraic Channel by Stone's
    theorem on the McGucken-derived translation group + Stone--von
    Neumann uniqueness packaging of QA2+QA4, both descending from
    clauses (i) and (v) of
    Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
    reference="postulate:mcp"}). The $i$ in the commutator is the
    McGucken-Principle perpendicularity marker
    (Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}: $x_4 = ict$ generates the Lorentzian
    signature, with $i$ marking the perpendicular fourth dimension). The
    $\hbar$ is the action quantum per McGucken-Sphere cycle
    (Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}: at
    the rest-frame, the Compton oscillation generated by
    $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ has frequency $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ with
    one quantum of action accumulated per cycle).

2.  The Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3\mathbf{x})$
    (Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}, derived from
    $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the rank-$2$ Minkowski metric of
    Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} and the $SO(3)$-Haar measure on the
    McGucken Sphere wavefront).

3.  The Cauchy--Schwarz inequality
    $|\langle u, v\rangle|^2 \leq \|u\|^2\|v\|^2$ on the
    McGucken-derived inner-product structure
    (Theorem [3.2](#thm:cauchy-schwarz){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:cauchy-schwarz"}, an elementary consequence of the
    non-negativity of $\|u + tv\|^2$ for $t \in \mathbb{R}$ on any
    pre-Hilbert space).

**Step CA-2: Shifted self-adjoint operators with the same commutator.**
For a normalized state $\psi \in \mathcal{H}$ (with
$\langle\psi, \psi\rangle = 1$), define the shifted operators
$$\delta\hat{q}\;:=\; \hat{q}- \langle\hat{q}\rangle\,\mathbf{1}, \qquad \delta\hat{p}\;:=\; \hat{p}- \langle\hat{p}\rangle\,\mathbf{1}.$$
These are self-adjoint (subtracting a real multiple of $\mathbf{1}$ from
a self-adjoint operator yields a self-adjoint operator) with vanishing
expectation:
$\langle\delta\hat{q}\rangle = \langle\hat{q}\rangle - \langle\hat{q}\rangle = 0$,
similarly for $\delta\hat{p}$. The commutator is unchanged:
$$[\delta\hat{q},\, \delta\hat{p}] \;=\; [\hat{q}- \langle\hat{q}\rangle\mathbf{1},\, \hat{p}- \langle\hat{p}\rangle\mathbf{1}] \;=\; [\hat{q}, \hat{p}] - \langle\hat{q}\rangle[\mathbf{1}, \hat{p}] - \langle\hat{p}\rangle[\hat{q}, \mathbf{1}] + \langle\hat{q}\rangle\langle\hat{p}\rangle[\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{1}] \;=\; i\hbar\,\mathbf{1},$$
since $[\mathbf{1}, \cdot\,] = 0$ everywhere. The variances are
$$(\Delta q)^2 \;=\; \langle\delta\hat{q}^2\rangle \;=\; \|\delta\hat{q}\,\psi\|^2, \qquad (\Delta p)^2 \;=\; \|\delta\hat{p}\,\psi\|^2,$$
using
$\langle\psi, \delta\hat{q}^2\psi\rangle = \langle\delta\hat{q}^*\psi, \delta\hat{q}\psi\rangle = \langle\delta\hat{q}\psi, \delta\hat{q}\psi\rangle = \|\delta\hat{q}\psi\|^2$
from $\delta\hat{q}^* = \delta\hat{q}$.

**Step CA-3: Cauchy--Schwarz on the inner-product square of the operator
product.** By Cauchy--Schwarz on $\mathcal{H}$ applied to the vectors
$\delta\hat{q}\,\psi, \delta\hat{p}\,\psi \in \mathcal{H}$:
$$|\langle\delta\hat{q}\,\psi,\, \delta\hat{p}\,\psi\rangle|^2 \;\leq\; \|\delta\hat{q}\,\psi\|^2 \cdot \|\delta\hat{p}\,\psi\|^2 \;=\; (\Delta q)^2(\Delta p)^2.$$

**Step CA-4: Symmetric/antisymmetric decomposition of the inner
product.** Using $\delta\hat{q}^* = \delta\hat{q}$:
$$\langle\delta\hat{q}\,\psi,\, \delta\hat{p}\,\psi\rangle \;=\; \langle\psi,\, \delta\hat{q}^*\,\delta\hat{p}\,\psi\rangle \;=\; \langle\psi,\, \delta\hat{q}\,\delta\hat{p}\,\psi\rangle \;=\; \langle\delta\hat{q}\,\delta\hat{p}\rangle.$$
The operator product $\delta\hat{q}\,\delta\hat{p}$ decomposes uniquely
