into self-adjoint (symmetric/anticommutator) and anti-self-adjoint
(antisymmetric/commutator) parts:
$$\delta\hat{q}\,\delta\hat{p}\;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\{\delta\hat{q},\, \delta\hat{p}\} \,+\, \tfrac{1}{2}[\delta\hat{q},\, \delta\hat{p}],$$
with
$\{\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}\}^* = \{\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}\}$
self-adjoint and
$[\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}]^* = -[\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}]$
anti-self-adjoint (verified in Step 2 of the master proof of
Theorem [12.1](#thm:QMT12){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT12"}).
The expectation values are
$$\tfrac{1}{2}\langle\{\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}\}\rangle \;\in\; \mathbb{R}, \qquad \tfrac{1}{2}\langle[\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}]\rangle \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\langle i\hbar\,\mathbf{1}\rangle \;=\; \tfrac{i\hbar}{2}\,\langle\mathbf{1}\rangle \;=\; \tfrac{i\hbar}{2} \;\in\; i\mathbb{R},$$
using McGucken-derived
$[\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}] = i\hbar\,\mathbf{1}$ from Step CA-1 and
$\langle\mathbf{1}\rangle = \|\psi\|^2 = 1$ from normalization.

**Step CA-5: Lower bound via $|z|^2 \geq (\Im z)^2$.** Write
$z := \langle\delta\hat{q}\,\delta\hat{p}\rangle = a + ib$ with
$a = \tfrac{1}{2}\langle\{\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}\}\rangle \in \mathbb{R}$
and $ib = i\hbar/2$, i.e., $b = \hbar/2 \in \mathbb{R}$. The squared
modulus satisfies
$$|z|^2 \;=\; a^2 + b^2 \;\geq\; b^2 \;=\; \Bigl(\frac{\hbar}{2}\Bigr)^{\!2}.$$
Combining with the Cauchy--Schwarz upper bound of Step CA-3:
$$(\Delta q)^2(\Delta p)^2 \;\geq\; |z|^2 \;\geq\; \Bigl(\frac{\hbar}{2}\Bigr)^{\!2}, \qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad \Delta q\,\Delta p \;\geq\; \frac{\hbar}{2}.$$
Equality $\Delta q\,\Delta p = \hbar/2$ holds iff (a) the
Cauchy--Schwarz inequality is saturated, i.e.,
$\delta\hat{p}\,\psi = \lambda\,\delta\hat{q}\,\psi$ for some
$\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$, and (b) the symmetric covariance
$a = \tfrac{1}{2}\langle\{\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}\}\rangle$
vanishes. Both conditions hold simultaneously for the Gaussian
wavepacket states (the minimum-uncertainty states of the
harmonic-oscillator ground state and translated/rescaled Gaussians).
$\square$
:::

::: {#rmk:heisenberg-channelA-machinery .remark}
*Remark 12.3* (McGucken machinery used in the Algebraic Channel Heisenberg
proof). Every step of the proof above is forced by
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ alone, with no external postulate essential.

**McGucken machinery used.** (1) $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, via QA1+QA4
supplying the canonical commutator
(Theorem [10.5](#thm:QMT10-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT10-channelA"}, with Stone and Stone--von Neumann
appearing as packaging axioms QA2 and QA4 per
Remark [4.36](#rmk:QA-axioms-grade1){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:QA-axioms-grade1"}); (2) the McGucken Hilbert space
$\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3 x)$ as a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}); (3) the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality
on $\mathcal{H}$
(Theorem [3.2](#thm:cauchy-schwarz){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:cauchy-schwarz"}, proved in
Chapter [3](#ch:math){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:math"} by the
discriminant of the non-negative quadratic $\|\psi + t\phi\|^2 \ge 0$,
an elementary fact about non-negative real quadratics).

**No external machinery is essential.** The Robertson 1929 inequality
is not essential here: the four lines of the proof apply
Theorem [3.2](#thm:cauchy-schwarz){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:cauchy-schwarz"} directly on the McGucken-derived Hilbert
space, with the antisymmetric-part identity
$\tfrac{1}{2}\langle[\delta\hat{q}, \delta\hat{p}]\rangle = i\hbar/2$
being a direct algebraic consequence of the McGucken-derived
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$. Robertson's 1929 paper reaches the same
conclusion through the same Cauchy--Schwarz argument, supplying
historical precedence rather than essential mathematical input.

**Confirmation.** The textbook tradition (Sakurai [@Sakurai2020] §1.4,
Shankar [@Shankar1994] §9.2, Cohen-Tannoudji [@CT2019] Ch. III §D)
presents this proof essentially as we have done above; the McGucken
framework's added value is that every input to the proof is itself a
theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, with no postulate inserted.
:::

**Upstream geometric route.** The dedicated derivation paper
[@MG-Born-CCR-2026], Theorem T6.1, gives the upstream geometric content:
the uncertainty principle follows from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the
Robertson--Schrödinger inequality applied to the derived commutator on
the derived Hilbert space, with both the commutator and the Hilbert
space themselves theorems of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (T3.2 and T5.1 of
the same paper). The standard textbook derivation of Heisenberg from
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ via Cauchy--Schwarz is, in this reading,
the inner two steps of a three-step chain that begins at
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and has no postulate inserted along the way.

### Disjointness audit {#disjointness-audit-10}

**Geometric Channel:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, McGucken Sphere wavefront,
Fourier transform, Fourier-analytic uncertainty principle, de Broglie
$p = \hbar k$.

**Algebraic Channel:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, canonical commutator
(Theorem [10.5](#thm:QMT10-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT10-channelA"}), Cauchy--Schwarz inequality,
symmetric/antisymmetric operator decomposition.

**Intersection:** $\{(\mathrm{McP}), \Delta q\,\Delta p \ge \hbar/2\}$.
Cauchy--Schwarz appears in Algebraic Channel's operator framework; Fourier
analysis appears in Geometric Channel's wavefront framework. *Disjointness
verified.*

### The ontic reading: uncertainty as a kinematic projection of $x_4$-advance {#sec:ontic-uncertainty}

::: flushright
*"Standard reading (epistemic): the system would have sharp $(q, p)$
values were it not disturbed by measurement. Kinematic reading (ontic):
the system is being disturbed continuously by $x_4$-advance, whether or
not any observer is present."\
--- [@MG-Ontic-2026], introduction*
:::

The textbook tradition assigns the canonical commutator, the Heisenberg
inequality, and the spreading of free wavepackets a
measurement-disturbance interpretation --- Heisenberg's 1927 microscope
thought-experiment locates the inequality in the photon-mediated
momentum kick at the act of position measurement; Bohrian
complementarity generalises this to the limits of classical description
under measurement contexts. Both readings are *epistemic*: the four
facts are about the relation between observer and system. The May 8
ontic-derivation paper [@MG-Ontic-2026] establishes that under the
McGucken Principle the four facts are *ontic*: kinematic projections of
the universal $x_4$-advance through the suppression map $\sigma$,
present in every system whether or not any apparatus is involved. The
mechanism is summarised below.

::: {#def:suppression-map .definition}
**Definition 12.5** (Suppression map $\sigma$; Definition 4 of
[@MG-Ontic-2026]). Let $M_E$ be the four-dimensional real Euclidean
manifold with coordinates $(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4)$. The McGucken
constraint $\Phi_M := x_4 - ict$ vanishes precisely on the worldlines
satisfying the principle $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The *suppression map*
$$\sigma: M_E \to M_{1,3}, \qquad (x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4) \mapsto (x_1, x_2, x_3, t),$$
with $t = x_4/(ic) = -i\,x_4/c$, sends the real Euclidean line element
$d\ell^2 = dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2 + dx_4^2$ to the Lorentzian interval
$ds^2 = dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2 - c^2\,dt^2$ via
$dx_4^2 = (ic\,dt)^2 = -c^2\,dt^2$, and sends differential operators on
$M_E$ involving $\partial/\partial x_4$ to differential operators on
$M_{1,3}$ via the chain rule
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial t} = \dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}\cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial x_4} = ic\cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial x_4}.
\label{eq:sigma-chain-rule}$$ The suppression map is the technical
device that makes "the same $i$" a theorem rather than an analogy. Every
$i$ in non-relativistic quantum mechanics is the $\sigma$-chain-rule
factor for the corresponding $x_4$-derivative in the underlying real
construction on $M_E$.
:::

::: {#rmk:why-sigma .remark}
*Remark 12.6* (Why $\sigma$ is the central object of the ontic reading).
The Euclidean manifold $M_E$ carries no measurement structure;
observables, states, and apparatuses live on the Lorentzian arena
$M_{1,3}$ obtained as the constraint surface
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}). The suppression map $\sigma$ projects
from one to the other, sending $x_4$-derivatives (which act *ontically*,
at the level of the universal advance $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$) to
$t$-derivatives on the Lorentzian arena (which acquire an *epistemic*
reading whenever they appear in measurement-disturbance accounts). The
chain rule
[\[eq:sigma-chain-rule\]](#eq:sigma-chain-rule){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:sigma-chain-rule"} is the algebraic device that lets us
state: *every $i$ on the Lorentzian arena is the image, through
$\sigma$, of an $x_4$-derivative on the Euclidean manifold*. The factor
$ic$ in $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the universal projection
coefficient.
:::

::: {#thm:ontic-commutator .theorem}
**Theorem 12.7** (Kinematic commutator; Theorem 8 of [@MG-Ontic-2026]).
*The canonical commutator $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ at any event
$t_0$ is the differential limit, through the suppression map $\sigma$,
of the non-vanishing $x_4$-advance $\Delta x_4 = ic\,\Delta t$
accumulated over the interval $[t_0, t_0 + \Delta t]$ for
$\Delta t > 0$. In particular, the commutator is non-zero for ontic
reasons: $\Delta x_4 = ic\,\Delta t \ne 0$ for every $\Delta t > 0$,
with the action quantum $\hbar$ accumulating at one full unit per
Compton period $T_C = h/(mc^2)$ for rest-mass-$m$ matter.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof follows the structure of [@MG-Ontic-2026], Theorem 9
(Persistence at $\Delta t \to 0$), with six steps anchoring
the canonical commutator's algebraic form $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$
to $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ through the suppression map $\sigma$.

**Step 1: $\Delta x_4 \neq 0$ for every $\Delta t > 0$.** By the
principle $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at every event of $M_{G}$
(clauses (i), (v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}), the integral over a lab-time interval
$[t_0, t_0 + \Delta t]$ along a worldline gives
$$\Delta x_4 \;=\; \int_{t_0}^{t_0 + \Delta t}\frac{dx_4}{dt'}\,dt' \;=\; \int_{t_0}^{t_0 + \Delta t} ic\,dt' \;=\; ic\,\Delta t.$$
For every $\Delta t > 0$, $\Delta x_4 = ic\,\Delta t \neq 0$. The
$x_{4}$-advance is ongoing at every event, with the rate $ic$ supplying
both the magnitude $c\,\Delta t$ (the modulus of $\Delta x_4$) and the
perpendicularity marker $i$ (which signals the orthogonality of $x_4$ to
the spatial three). Clause (iii) (monotonicity) ensures the integral
curve is strictly increasing in $t$, so $\Delta x_4$ does not vanish by
cancellation.

**Step 2: Compton-period accumulation rate from the rest-frame
oscillation.** By Theorem [5.1](#thm:QMT5){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT5"} (rest-mass phase factor, derived from
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at the source event), the rest-frame matter
wavefunction carries the Compton-frequency phase factor
$$\psi_{\mathrm{rest}}(\tau) \;=\; \psi_0\,\exp\!\bigl(-i\,\omega_C\,\tau\bigr), \qquad \omega_C \;=\; \frac{mc^2}{\hbar},$$
where the angular frequency $\omega_C$ is the rate of phase accumulation
per unit proper time along the worldline. The Compton period is
$$T_C \;:=\; \frac{2\pi}{\omega_C} \;=\; \frac{2\pi\hbar}{mc^2} \;=\; \frac{h}{mc^2},$$
where $h = 2\pi\hbar$ is the Planck constant. By
Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"} (action
quantum per Sphere cycle), one full revolution of the rest-mass phase
factor (period $T_C$) accumulates phase $2\pi$, equivalently one quantum
of action $\hbar$ per radian; the natural unit of action accumulated by
the $x_{4}$-advance over one Compton period is $h$ (per cycle) or
$\hbar$ (per radian).

**Step 3: Action-rate identification.** The rate of action accumulation
per unit lab time, from the rest-frame Compton oscillation, is
$$\frac{dS}{dt}\Big|_{\mathrm{Compton}} \;=\; \frac{\hbar}{T_C/(2\pi)} \;=\; \frac{\hbar\,\omega_C}{2\pi}\cdot 2\pi \;=\; \hbar\,\omega_C \;=\; mc^2,$$
which is the rest-energy rate. Over a finite interval $\Delta t$, the
accumulated rest-frame action is
$\Delta S_{\mathrm{rest}} = -mc^2\,\Delta t$ (the rest-frame Lagrangian
$L_{\mathrm{rest}} = -mc^2$ for a free particle, integrated). The
accumulated phase is
$\Delta\theta = \Delta S/\hbar = -\omega_C\,\Delta t$, with one full
radian per $\hbar$ of action.

**Step 4: Differential form of the action accumulation at the
conjugate-pair plane.** The accumulated $x_{4}$-advance
$\Delta x_4 = ic\,\Delta t$ couples to spatial momentum via the de
Broglie relation derived from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ + Lorentz boost
on $M_{G}$ (Theorem [2.1](#thm:QMT2){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT2"}, Geometric Channel): the boost converts the rest-frame
$x_{4}$-oscillation into a moving-frame spatial wave with wavevector
$\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{p}/\hbar$. The position--momentum conjugate-pair
structure on the moving-frame spatial slice inherits the action quantum
$\hbar$ from the rest-frame Compton oscillation; this is the content of Theorem [10.1](#thm:QMT10){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT10"} (canonical commutator
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$, derived as a theorem of
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via Stone's theorem on the McGucken-derived
translation group).

The differential form at the conjugate-pair plane is therefore
$$[\hat{q},\, \hat{p}] \;=\; i\hbar\,\mathbf{1},$$ with the factor $i$
inherited from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the suppression-map chain
rule $\partial_t = ic\,\partial_{x_4}$
(Definition [12.5](#def:suppression-map){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:suppression-map"}), and the factor $\hbar$ inherited from
the action quantum per Compton cycle
(Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}). The
McGucken-Principle interpretation: the canonical commutator is the
differential signature of the ontological $x_{4}$-advance projected onto
the $(\hat{q}, \hat{p})$ plane through the suppression map $\sigma$.

**Step 5: Non-vanishing of the commutator forced by Stone-derived
$\hat{p}$.** The position--momentum commutator is non-zero for
reasons independent of the algebraic-value calculation of
Step 4. Suppose for contradiction $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = 0$. The strongly
continuous unitary translation group $\hat T_a = \exp(-ia\hat{p}/\hbar)$
has $\hat{p}$ as Stone-generator (QA2, Stone's theorem applied to the
spatial-translation invariance of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). By the
standard commutator-exponential identity, if $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = 0$
then $[\hat{q}, \hat T_a] = 0$ for all $a \in \mathbb{R}$.

But by the action of $\hat T_a$ on the position-representation
wavefunction (Lemma [2.2](#lem:phat-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-generator"}, $\hat T_a\psi(q) = \psi(q - a)$):
$$(\hat{q}\,\hat T_a\,\psi)(q) \;=\; q\,(\hat T_a\psi)(q) \;=\; q\,\psi(q - a),$$
$$(\hat T_a\,\hat{q}\,\psi)(q) \;=\; (\hat{q}\psi)(q - a) \;=\; (q - a)\,\psi(q - a).$$
Subtracting:
$$([\hat{q},\, \hat T_a]\psi)(q) \;=\; q\,\psi(q-a) - (q-a)\,\psi(q-a) \;=\; a\,\psi(q-a) \;=\; a\,(\hat T_a\psi)(q),$$
i.e., $[\hat{q}, \hat T_a] = a\,\hat T_a$ as an operator identity (not
zero for $a \neq 0$). This contradicts the supposition
$[\hat{q}, \hat T_a] = 0$.

Therefore $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] \neq 0$ on the
spatial-translation-invariant structure of $M_{G}$. The specific value
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ is fixed by Step 4 (the McGucken-anchored
action quantum and perpendicularity marker); Step 5 establishes that no
deformation of the dynamics can yield a vanishing commutator without
breaking the spatial-translation invariance of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

**Step 6: McGucken anchoring --- the chain.** The complete
chain from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ to the canonical
commutator is:

-   $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at every event $\;\Longrightarrow\;$
    non-vanishing $x_{4}$-advance $\Delta x_4 = ic\,\Delta t \neq 0$ for
    every $\Delta t > 0$ (Step 1);

-   Rest-frame Compton oscillation
    (Theorem [5.1](#thm:QMT5){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT5"}) $\;\Longrightarrow\;$ Compton-period
    $T_C = h/(mc^2)$ with action quantum $\hbar$ per radian
    (Steps 2--3);

-   Suppression-map chain rule
    (Definition [12.5](#def:suppression-map){reference-type="ref"
    reference="def:suppression-map"}, $\partial_t = ic\,\partial_{x_4}$)
    $\;\Longrightarrow\;$ the factor $i$ in the commutator inherits from
    the McGucken-Principle perpendicularity marker $i$ in
    $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$;

-   Stone's theorem on the spatial-translation invariance of
    $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (QA1+QA2) $\;\Longrightarrow\;$ the
    commutator is forced to be non-zero (Step 5);

-   The perpendicularity marker and the action quantum combined at the
    conjugate-pair plane $\;\Longrightarrow\;$ the specific value
    $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar\,\mathbf{1}$ (Step 4). Theorem [10.1](#thm:QMT10){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT10"} reaches the same value along both channels;
    the present theorem obtains it from the $x_{4}$-advance directly and
    agrees with it.

The canonical commutator is a kinematic theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ --- the differential signature of the
ontological $x_{4}$-advance projected through $\sigma$ onto every
conjugate-pair plane. The shift from the epistemic reading
(the commutator constrains simultaneous measurement) to the ontic
reading (the commutator is the differential form of $x_{4}$-advance)
follows: the commutator's non-zero value is forced by the principle's
content at every event, independent of measurement. ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:ontic-commutator-machinery .remark}
*Remark 12.8* (McGucken machinery used in the kinematic commutator
theorem). Every step is forced by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ alone.

**McGucken machinery used.** (1) $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via its
differential statement $dx_4 = ic\,dt$ giving Claim (i); (2)
Theorem [5.1](#thm:QMT5){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT5"}
(rest-mass phase factor) giving the Compton-period accumulation rate of
Claim (ii); (3) suppression map $\sigma$
(Definition [12.5](#def:suppression-map){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:suppression-map"}) supplying the chain-rule conversion of
$x_4$-derivatives to $t$-derivatives; (4) Algebraic Channel axioms QA1
(translation invariance) and QA2 (Stone packaging) closing Claim (iv).

**No external machinery is essential.** The Frobenius-rigidity
invocation in Claim (iv) is the same application as in
Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}: the algebraic uniqueness of $i$ on the
two-dimensional perpendicular extension is forced by $J^2 = -1$, with
Frobenius's 1878 classification confirming by abstract analysis.
:::

::: {#thm:ontic-dispersion .theorem}
**Theorem 12.9** (Kinematic dispersion; Theorem 14 of [@MG-Ontic-2026]).
*For a free-particle minimum-uncertainty Gaussian wavepacket initially
at $t = 0$ with position width $\sigma_q(0)$, the temporal evolution of
the width is
$$\sigma_q(t) = \sqrt{\sigma_q(0)^2 + \biggl(\frac{\hbar\,t}{2m\,\sigma_q(0)}\biggr)^{\!2}}.
\label{eq:gaussian-spread}$$ The spreading is identified as the
spatial-slice projection of $x_4$-advance over $[0, t]$ via the
suppression map $\sigma$: the wavepacket spreads at the speed of light
$c$ scaled by its dimensionless Compton-wavelength compactness
$\sigma_q(0)/\ell_C$, with $\ell_C = \hbar/(mc)$ the Compton wavelength
of the rest-mass-$m$ matter.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has six steps establishing the Gaussian
wavepacket spreading as a kinematic consequence of $x_{4}$-advance, with
the algebraic dynamics (Heisenberg-picture evolution) and the geometric
content (Compton-wavelength scaling) both anchored to
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

**Step 1: Heisenberg-picture equations of motion from $x_{4}$-advance.**
For a free particle with Hamiltonian $\hat{H}= \hat{p}^2/(2m)$
(Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT7"},
derived as a theorem of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ along both Algebraic Channel
via Stone's theorem and Geometric Channel via iterated McGucken-Sphere Huygens
propagation), the Heisenberg-picture operators evolve via
$$\frac{d\hat{q}}{dt} \;=\; \frac{i}{\hbar}[\hat{H},\, \hat{q}], \qquad \frac{d\hat{p}}{dt} \;=\; \frac{i}{\hbar}[\hat{H},\, \hat{p}].$$
The factor $i/\hbar$ is the McGucken-anchored conversion from commutator
to time-derivative: the $i$ is the perpendicularity marker of
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}); the $\hbar$ is the action quantum per
McGucken-Sphere cycle (Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:62"}).

Compute the two commutators using
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar\,\mathbf{1}$
(Theorem [12.7](#thm:ontic-commutator){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:ontic-commutator"}, the kinematic commutator derived from
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$) and the Leibniz rule for commutators
$[A, BC] = [A,B]C + B[A,C]$: $$\begin{aligned}
&\;=\; \tfrac{1}{2m}\,[\hat{p}^2,\, \hat{q}] \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{2m}\,[\hat{q},\, \hat{p}^2] \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{2m}\,\bigl([\hat{q},\hat{p}]\,\hat{p}+ \hat{p}\,[\hat{q},\hat{p}]\bigr) \\
  &\;=\; -\tfrac{1}{2m}\,(i\hbar\,\hat{p}+ \hat{p}\,i\hbar) \;=\; -\tfrac{2i\hbar}{2m}\,\hat{p}\;=\; -\tfrac{i\hbar}{m}\,\hat{p},
\end{aligned}$$ using that $i\hbar\,\mathbf{1}$ commutes with $\hat{p}$.
Substituting into the Heisenberg equation:
$$\frac{d\hat{q}}{dt} \;=\; \frac{i}{\hbar}\,\Bigl(-\frac{i\hbar}{m}\,\hat{p}\Bigr) \;=\; \frac{-i^2\,\hbar}{\hbar\,m}\,\hat{p}\;=\; \frac{\hat{p}}{m},$$
using $-i^2 = 1$ (the squaring rule of the perpendicularity marker, same
algebraic content as $dx_4^2 = -c^2 dt^2$ from
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}).

Similarly $[\hat{H}, \hat{p}] = \tfrac{1}{2m}[\hat{p}^2, \hat{p}] = 0$
(any operator commutes with its own polynomial), so $d\hat{p}/dt = 0$.

**Step 2: Operator solutions.** Integrating the Heisenberg equations of
motion:
$$\hat{p}(t) \;=\; \hat{p}(0), \qquad \hat{q}(t) \;=\; \hat{q}(0) + \frac{\hat{p}(0)\,t}{m}.$$
The momentum is conserved (consistent with spatial-translation
invariance of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$); the position evolves linearly
in $t$ --- the operator-level analogue of classical ballistic motion.
Dispersion appears at the level of state statistics, not at the operator
level.

**Step 3: Variance evolution with explicit cross-term.** In a Gaussian
state with $\langle\hat{q}(0)\rangle = \langle\hat{p}(0)\rangle = 0$,
the second moment is
$$\sigma_q(t)^2 \;=\; \langle\hat{q}(t)^2\rangle \;=\; \Bigl\langle\Bigl(\hat{q}(0) + \frac{\hat{p}(0)\,t}{m}\Bigr)^{\!2}\Bigr\rangle \;=\; \langle\hat{q}(0)^2\rangle + \frac{t}{m}\,\langle\hat{q}(0)\hat{p}(0) + \hat{p}(0)\hat{q}(0)\rangle + \frac{t^2}{m^2}\,\langle\hat{p}(0)^2\rangle,$$
where the cross-term symmetrises $\hat{q}\hat{p}$ and $\hat{p}\hat{q}$
because the squared sum expands as
$\hat{q}^2 + \hat{q}\hat{p}+ \hat{p}\hat{q}+ \hat{p}^2$ (the operators
do not commute, so the cross terms are kept ordered). The middle term
equals $\frac{t}{m}\langle\{\hat{q}(0), \hat{p}(0)\}\rangle$ with
$\{A, B\} = AB + BA$ the anticommutator.

*Vanishing of the cross-term for the symmetric Gaussian initial state.*
For the minimum-uncertainty Gaussian wavepacket (the
Cauchy--Schwarz-saturating Gaussian state, characterized by
$\delta\hat{p}\,\psi_0 = -i\alpha\,\delta\hat{q}\,\psi_0$ for some
$\alpha > 0$, equivalently a real Gaussian in the position basis), the
symmetric covariance vanishes:
$$\langle\{\hat{q}(0),\, \hat{p}(0)\}\rangle \;=\; 0.$$ Proof: in the
position representation
$\psi_0(q) = (2\pi\sigma_q^2)^{-1/4}\,e^{-q^2/(4\sigma_q^2)}$, compute
$$\langle\hat{q}\hat{p}\rangle \;=\; \int q\,\psi_0^*(q)\,(-i\hbar\partial_q)\psi_0(q)\,dq \;=\; -i\hbar\int q\,\psi_0(q)\,\partial_q\psi_0(q)\,dq,$$
(using $\psi_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ so $\psi_0^* = \psi_0$). With
$\partial_q\psi_0(q) = -q/(2\sigma_q^2)\,\psi_0(q)$:
$$\langle\hat{q}\hat{p}\rangle \;=\; -i\hbar\int q\cdot\Bigl(-\frac{q}{2\sigma_q^2}\Bigr)\,\psi_0(q)^2\,dq \;=\; \frac{i\hbar}{2\sigma_q^2}\int q^2\,\psi_0^2\,dq \;=\; \frac{i\hbar}{2\sigma_q^2}\cdot\sigma_q^2 \;=\; \frac{i\hbar}{2}.$$
Similarly $\langle\hat{p}\hat{q}\rangle = -i\hbar/2$ (by Hermitian
conjugation:
$\langle\hat{p}\hat{q}\rangle = \overline{\langle\hat{q}\hat{p}\rangle}^* = \overline{i\hbar/2} = -i\hbar/2$
using $\hat{q}, \hat{p}$ self-adjoint). Therefore
$$\langle\{\hat{q},\,\hat{p}\}\rangle \;=\; \langle\hat{q}\hat{p}\rangle + \langle\hat{p}\hat{q}\rangle \;=\; \frac{i\hbar}{2} + \Bigl(-\frac{i\hbar}{2}\Bigr) \;=\; 0,$$
as claimed. The cross-term in the variance evolution vanishes, leaving
$$\sigma_q(t)^2 \;=\; \sigma_q(0)^2 + \frac{t^2}{m^2}\,\sigma_p(0)^2.$$

**Step 4: Saturation of the Heisenberg bound.** For a Gaussian state
saturating the Heisenberg bound (the minimum-uncertainty wavepacket,
Theorem [12.1](#thm:QMT12){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT12"}):
$$\sigma_q(0)\,\sigma_p(0) \;=\; \frac{\hbar}{2}, \qquad \text{hence} \quad \sigma_p(0) \;=\; \frac{\hbar}{2\,\sigma_q(0)}.$$
Substituting into the variance evolution of Step 3:
$$\sigma_q(t)^2 \;=\; \sigma_q(0)^2 + \frac{t^2}{m^2}\cdot\frac{\hbar^2}{4\,\sigma_q(0)^2} \;=\; \sigma_q(0)^2 + \biggl(\frac{\hbar\,t}{2m\,\sigma_q(0)}\biggr)^{\!2}.$$
Taking the square root yields
equation [\[eq:gaussian-spread\]](#eq:gaussian-spread){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:gaussian-spread"}.

**Step 5: Kinematic interpretation via the Compton wavelength.** Rewrite
the spreading-rate prefactor by introducing the McGucken-anchored
Compton wavelength $\ell_C := \hbar/(mc)$
(Theorem [5.1](#thm:QMT5){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT5"},
the rest-frame oscillation wavelength of the McGucken-Sphere matter
wavefunction):
$$\frac{\hbar}{2m\,\sigma_q(0)} \;=\; \frac{\hbar/(mc)\cdot c}{2\,\sigma_q(0)} \;=\; \frac{\ell_C\cdot c}{2\,\sigma_q(0)} \;=\; \frac{c}{2\,(\sigma_q(0)/\ell_C)}.$$
The geometric reading: the McGucken-Principle $x_{4}$-advance proceeds
at rate $c$ from every event of the wavepacket's worldline (clause (i)
of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, with magnitude $c$); the dimensionless
wavepacket compactness $\sigma_q(0)/\ell_C$ measures the initial
position-width in units of the Compton wavelength; the spreading rate of
the wavepacket is the speed-of-light advance rate divided by twice the
dimensionless compactness. The factor $2$ in the denominator is the same
Cauchy--Schwarz factor that produces the $\hbar/2$ on the right-hand
side of the Heisenberg bound
(Theorem [12.1](#thm:QMT12){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT12"}).

**Step 6: Geometric Channel reading and McGucken anchoring.** The wavepacket
spreading is the spatial-slice projection through the suppression map
$\sigma$ (Definition [12.5](#def:suppression-map){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:suppression-map"}) of the universal $x_{4}$-advance
during the interval $[0, t]$. The geometric content traces to
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at three points:

-   The rate $c$ in the spreading-rate prefactor traces to the magnitude
    of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (clause (i)): the $x_{4}$-coordinate
    advances at rate $c$ at every event.

-   The Compton wavelength $\ell_C = \hbar/(mc)$ traces to the
    rest-frame Compton oscillation
    (Theorem [5.1](#thm:QMT5){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT5"}): the rest-frame matter wavefunction
    oscillates at frequency $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ with wavelength
    $c/\omega_C = \hbar/(mc) = \ell_C$ along $x_{4}$.

-   The factor $\hbar$ traces to the action quantum per Sphere cycle
    (Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}).

The wavepacket spreads in the spatial slice because the underlying 4D
McGucken Sphere wavefront has radius $c\,t$ in $x_{4}$-direction by
lab-time $t$; projecting through $\sigma$ onto the spatial slice gives a
spatial-position-uncertainty $\sigma_q(t)$ with the explicit form
derived in Step 4. The Schrödinger equation derivation
(Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT7"})
recovers this kinematic fact algebraically via the Heisenberg evolution
equations of Step 1; the McGucken-Sphere geometric content of Steps 5--6
supplies the reason for the algebraic result. The textbook
tradition's framing of wavepacket spreading as a calculational result of
the Schrödinger equation is consistent with the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework's
geometric framing --- both routes derive the same dispersion formula,
with the geometric route exposing the $x_{4}$-advance origin and the
algebraic route exposing the Heisenberg-picture evolution mechanism. ◻
:::

::: {#thm:ontic-time-energy .theorem}
**Theorem 12.10** (Time--energy uncertainty as a kinematic theorem;
Theorem 16 of [@MG-Ontic-2026]). *For any system with non-zero rest mass
$m$ and any covariant observable $\hat A$ that does not commute with the
Hamiltonian $\hat{H}$, the energy spread $\Delta E := \Delta H$ and the
characteristic time
$$\Delta t_A := \frac{\Delta A}{|d\langle\hat A\rangle/dt|}$$ over which
$\langle\hat A\rangle$ shifts by one standard deviation satisfy
$$\Delta E\cdot \Delta t_A \ge \hbar/2.
\label{eq:time-energy-uncertainty}$$ The factor $i$ entering the
Heisenberg evolution and the factor $\hbar$ multiplying it are the
*same* $i$ and $\hbar$ that enter $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and
Theorem [12.7](#thm:ontic-commutator){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:ontic-commutator"}, transported through the suppression
map $\sigma$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has six steps establishing the time-energy
uncertainty relation as a kinematic theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$,
with the Heisenberg evolution and the Cauchy--Schwarz bound both
McGucken-anchored.

**Step 1: Heisenberg evolution equation derived step-by-step from
Stone.** The time-evolution unitary group is
$$\hat{U}(t) \;=\; \exp\!\bigl(-i\hat{H}\,t/\hbar\bigr),$$ generated by
the Hamiltonian $\hat{H}$ via Stone's theorem
(Theorem [3.6](#thm:stone){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:stone"})
applied to the time-translation invariance of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(clause (i) of Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, derived as
Lemma [7.2](#lem:time-translation-unitary){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:time-translation-unitary"} of
Chapter [7](#ch:schrodinger){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:schrodinger"}). The Heisenberg-picture observable for a
Hermitian $\hat A$ without explicit time-dependence is
$$\hat A(t) \;:=\; \hat{U}^\dagger(t)\,\hat A\,\hat{U}(t),$$ i.e.,
$\hat A$ in the Heisenberg picture is the operator at time $t$ obtained
by conjugating the Schrödinger-picture $\hat A$ by the time-evolution
unitary.

Differentiate $\hat A(t)$ with respect to $t$ using the product rule.
From Stone's theorem,
$$\frac{d\hat{U}}{dt} \;=\; -\frac{i}{\hbar}\,\hat{H}\,\hat{U}, \qquad \frac{d\hat{U}^\dagger}{dt} \;=\; +\frac{i}{\hbar}\,\hat{U}^\dagger\,\hat{H},$$
where the second identity uses self-adjointness of $\hat{H}$ (so
$\hat{H}^\dagger = \hat{H}$) and the Hermitian-conjugate of the first.
Applying the product rule to
$\hat A(t) = \hat{U}^\dagger\hat A\,\hat{U}$:
$$\frac{d\hat A(t)}{dt} \;=\; \frac{d\hat{U}^\dagger}{dt}\,\hat A\,\hat{U}\,+\, \hat{U}^\dagger\,\hat A\,\frac{d\hat{U}}{dt} \;=\; \frac{i}{\hbar}\,\hat{U}^\dagger\,\hat{H}\,\hat A\,\hat{U}\,-\, \frac{i}{\hbar}\,\hat{U}^\dagger\,\hat A\,\hat{H}\,\hat{U}.$$
Factor:
$$\frac{d\hat A(t)}{dt} \;=\; \frac{i}{\hbar}\,\hat{U}^\dagger\,(\hat{H}\,\hat A - \hat A\,\hat{H})\,\hat{U}\;=\; \frac{i}{\hbar}\,\hat{U}^\dagger\,[\hat{H},\, \hat A]\,\hat{U}\;=\; \frac{i}{\hbar}\,[\hat{H}(t),\, \hat A(t)].$$
At $t = 0$, $\hat{U}(0) = \mathbf{1}$, so $\hat A(0) = \hat A$ and the
equation reads
$$\frac{d\hat A}{dt}\Big|_{t = 0} \;=\; \frac{i}{\hbar}\,[\hat{H},\, \hat A].$$
Taking expectation in the state $\lvert \psi \rangle$:
$$\frac{d\langle\hat A\rangle}{dt} \;=\; \frac{i}{\hbar}\,\langle\psi,\,[\hat{H},\,\hat A]\,\psi\rangle \;=\; \frac{i}{\hbar}\,\langle[\hat{H},\,\hat A]\rangle.$$
The factor $i/\hbar$ is McGucken-anchored: the $i$ is the
perpendicularity marker of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}), transported through the suppression map
$\sigma$ to the time-derivative via the chain rule
$\partial_t = ic\,\partial_{x_4}$
(Definition [12.5](#def:suppression-map){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:suppression-map"}); the $\hbar$ is the action quantum per
McGucken-Sphere cycle (Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:62"}).

**Step 2: Apply Robertson--Schrödinger to $(\hat{H}, \hat A)$.** The
Robertson inequality (Theorem [12.1](#thm:QMT12){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT12"}, derived in the master proof above via
Cauchy--Schwarz on the McGucken-derived Hilbert space) applied to the
pair of self-adjoint observables $(\hat{H}, \hat A)$ gives
$$\Delta H \cdot \Delta A \;\geq\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,|\langle[\hat{H},\,\hat A]\rangle|.$$
Substituting the expression for the commutator's expectation value from
Step 1:
$$|\langle[\hat{H},\,\hat A]\rangle| \;=\; \hbar\cdot\bigl|d\langle\hat A\rangle/dt\bigr|,$$
since
$d\langle\hat A\rangle/dt = (i/\hbar)\langle[\hat{H}, \hat A]\rangle$
implies
$\langle[\hat{H}, \hat A]\rangle = (\hbar/i)\,d\langle\hat A\rangle/dt = -i\hbar\,d\langle\hat A\rangle/dt$,
and taking modulus:
$|\langle[\hat{H}, \hat A]\rangle| = \hbar|d\langle\hat A\rangle/dt|$
(using $|{-i}| = 1$). Therefore
$$\Delta H \cdot \Delta A \;\geq\; \frac{\hbar}{2}\cdot\biggl|\frac{d\langle\hat A\rangle}{dt}\biggr|.$$

**Step 3: Rearrange to time-energy form.** Divide both sides by
$|d\langle\hat A\rangle/dt|$, which is non-zero by hypothesis (since
$\hat A$ does not commute with $\hat{H}$, Step 1 gives a non-zero RHS
for $d\langle\hat A\rangle/dt$ in generic states):
$$\Delta H \cdot \frac{\Delta A}{|d\langle\hat A\rangle/dt|} \;\geq\; \frac{\hbar}{2}.$$
Using the definition
$\Delta t_A := \Delta A/|d\langle\hat A\rangle/dt|$:
$$\Delta H \cdot \Delta t_A \;\geq\; \frac{\hbar}{2}.$$ Identifying
$\Delta E := \Delta H$ (the energy spread of the state) yields the
time-energy uncertainty
relation [\[eq:time-energy-uncertainty\]](#eq:time-energy-uncertainty){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:time-energy-uncertainty"}.

**Step 4: Pauli's obstruction circumvented, not contradicted.** Pauli's
1933 theorem (commented in the original Handbuch contribution) excludes
the existence of a self-adjoint time operator $\hat T$ conjugate to a
Hamiltonian $\hat{H}$ that is bounded below: there is no self-adjoint
operator $\hat T$ on $\mathcal{H}$ satisfying
$[\hat T, \hat{H}] = i\hbar\,\mathbf{1}$ for $\hat{H}$ with the standard
discrete-spectrum-bounded-below structure of physical Hamiltonians. The
derivation in Steps 1--3 introduces no such operator $\hat T$: the
quantity $\Delta t_A$ is defined as a ratio of two well-defined
quantities --- the spread $\Delta A$ of the observable $\hat A$ and the
rate $|d\langle\hat A\rangle/dt|$ of its expectation-value evolution.
Neither is the dispersion of a putative time operator. The time-energy
uncertainty relation is therefore a statement about characteristic
timescales of physical observables under unitary evolution, equivalent
to Mandelstam--Tamm 1945; Pauli's obstruction applies to a different
operator-pair conjugacy framing and does not constrain the present
derivation.

**Step 5: McGucken anchoring --- both $i$ and $\hbar$ trace to
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.** The proof uses two McGucken-derived
constants:

-   The $i$ in the Heisenberg evolution equation
    $d\hat A/dt = (i/\hbar)[\hat{H}, \hat A]$ is the suppression-map
    chain-rule factor: the $\partial/\partial t$ on the Lorentzian arena
    $M_{1,3}$ traces, via $\partial_t = ic\,\partial_{x_4}$ (the chain
    rule of Definition [12.5](#def:suppression-map){reference-type="ref"
    reference="def:suppression-map"}), to the underlying
    $\partial/\partial x_4$ on the Euclidean manifold $M_E$; the
    McGucken-Principle $i$ in $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ supplies the
    perpendicularity factor in the conversion
    (Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:twelve-i"} case 1).

-   The $\hbar$ in $(i/\hbar)$ and in the right-hand side $\hbar/2$ of
    the inequality is the action quantum per Sphere cycle
    (Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}),
    equivalently the action per Compton-period oscillation
    $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ derived from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at the
    source event (Theorem [5.1](#thm:QMT5){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT5"}).

Both constants entering the time-energy uncertainty relation are
shadows of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The uncertainty
inequality is the algebraic-symmetry projection of the universal
$x_{4}$-expansion at rate $ic$ onto the $(\hat A, \hat{H})$
conjugate-pair structure of any system with non-trivial
$[\hat{H}, \hat A]$.

**Step 6: Algebraic Channel characterisation and complementary Geometric Channel
reading.** The derivation uses three ingredients, all from the Algebraic Channel
algebraic-symmetry side: (i) Stone's theorem on the time-translation
unitary group (QA2, applied to the time-translation invariance of
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$); (ii) the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality on the
Hilbert-space inner product
(Theorem [3.2](#thm:cauchy-schwarz){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:cauchy-schwarz"}, an elementary fact on pre-Hilbert
spaces); (iii) the Robertson--Schrödinger inequality for non-commuting
self-adjoint observables
(Theorem [12.1](#thm:QMT12){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT12"},
derived from Cauchy--Schwarz and the symmetric/antisymmetric
decomposition). No McGucken-Sphere geometric wavefront analysis appears
in the algebraic chain; the proof is Algebraic Channel.

The complementary Geometric Channel reading is supplied by
Remark [12.11](#rmk:epistemic-to-ontic){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:epistemic-to-ontic"}: the time-energy uncertainty is the
geometric projection through $\sigma$ of the universal $x_{4}$-advance
into the energy-conjugate-time plane of every quantum system, with the
$x_{4}$-advance at rate $ic$ supplying both the perpendicularity marker
$i$ and the rate $c$ that generates the Compton-frequency oscillation
$\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$. The two channels (algebraic-symmetry and
geometric-propagation) reach the same inequality through derivationally
disjoint chains, each anchored to $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:epistemic-to-ontic .remark}
*Remark 12.11* (The shift: epistemic to ontic, and what it
means empirically). The standard reading of the four facts (canonical
commutator, Heisenberg uncertainty, wavepacket spreading, time--energy
uncertainty) locates them in measurement disturbance: *the system would
have sharp $(q, p)$ values were it not disturbed by measurement*. The
McGucken ontic reading locates them in $x_4$-advance: *the system is
being disturbed continuously by $x_4$-advance, whether or not any
observer is present*.

The empirical content of the contrast is sharp. The microscope reading
predicts that sufficiently gentle measurements --- low-momentum probes,
weak couplings, indirect inferences --- could in principle evade the
trade-off; experiments over a century show that they do not. The
complementarity reading predicts that unobserved systems have no
determinate joint $(q, p)$ values to constrain; the kinematic reading
predicts that the inequality applies regardless. The vacuum saturation
case is the clearest discriminator: the harmonic-oscillator ground state
attains $\sigma_q\,\sigma_p = \hbar/2$ exactly, with no apparatus
present, and the microscope reading has no explanation for why an
undisturbed, unmeasured ground state saturates the bound. The kinematic
reading explains this directly: the ground-state saturation is the
projection through $\sigma$
(Definition [12.5](#def:suppression-map){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:suppression-map"}) of the universal $x_4$-advance at rate
$ic$ into the optimally compact wavepacket configuration on the McGucken
Sphere; Theorem [12.9](#thm:ontic-dispersion){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:ontic-dispersion"} gives the spread of that wavepacket as
$c$ scaled by the Compton-wavelength compactness $\sigma_q(0)/\ell_C$,
with no apparatus.

The displacement has empirical content beyond the interpretive level.
The kinematic reading predicts that the four facts hold in unobserved
systems, in unprobed channels of quantum-non-demolition measurements, in
vacuum fluctuations, and during free-evolution intervals; the empirical
record (squeezed-light below the standard quantum limit [@Wu1986],
trapped-ion ground-state cooling at Heisenberg saturation
[@Wineland2003], the Compton-coupling residual diffusion of [@Syn-2026])
is consistent with the ontic reading and underdetermined by the
epistemic reading. Under the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, the four facts of QM
are kinematic projections of the universal expansion
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at the Compton-frequency rate
$\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ into every conjugate-pair plane of every quantum
system: the canonical commutator is the differential signature of the
$x_{4}$-advance at the spatial $(\hat{q}, \hat{p})$-plane
(Theorem [12.7](#thm:ontic-commutator){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:ontic-commutator"}), the Heisenberg uncertainty
inequality is the Cauchy--Schwarz expression of that signature
(Theorem [12.1](#thm:QMT12){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT12"}), the wavepacket dispersion is the spatial-slice
projection of the 4D Sphere wavefront radius $c\,t$ at coordinate time
$t$ (Theorem [12.9](#thm:ontic-dispersion){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:ontic-dispersion"}), and the time-energy uncertainty
inequality is the conjugate-pair instance of the same signature on the
$(\hat{H}, \hat A)$-plane
(Theorem [12.10](#thm:ontic-time-energy){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:ontic-time-energy"}). Each of the four facts traces to
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ through a named theorem, with the
perpendicularity marker $i$ supplied uniformly by the McGucken-Principle
$i$ via the suppression-map chain rule and the action quantum $\hbar$
supplied uniformly by Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:62"} (action per Sphere cycle).
:::

### The universal non-closure quantum: $\hbar$ across foundational physics {#sec:universal-non-closure}

The canonical commutator $[\hat{q}_i, \hat{p}_j] = i\hbar\delta_{ij}$
(Chapter [10](#ch:ccr){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:ccr"}) and the
Robertson uncertainty bound $\sigma_q\sigma_p \geq \hbar/2$
(Theorem [12.1](#thm:QMT12){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT12"})
above are not isolated occurrences of $\hbar$. The McGucken framework's
reading of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ with action quantum $\hbar$ per
radian of the Compton-frequency oscillation of $x_4$-advance
(Theorem [9.35](#thm:c-hbar-twin){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:c-hbar-twin"} of
Chapter [9](#ch:hilbert-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:hilbert-theorem"}) supplies a single physical mechanism by
which *any closed loop in physics that involves a round-trip through
$x_{4}$ cannot close more tightly than the action quantum $\hbar$*. This
minimum-non-closure principle is the upstream physical content of nine
independently-celebrated results across foundational physics, each
treated historically as a separate empirical fact requiring its own
derivation. The present section establishes the unification as
Theorem [12.12](#thm:universal-non-closure){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:universal-non-closure"} below.

::: {#thm:universal-non-closure .theorem}
**Theorem 12.12** (Universal non-closure quantum of $x_{4}$-involving
rotations; [@MG-Pointwise-2026] Theorem 12.11). *Let $R$ denote any
physical operation involving rotation through the perpendicular
$x_{4}$-direction of the McGucken constraint surface $M_{1,3}$ ---
including (but not limited to): a quantum-mechanical operator action
involving $x_{4}$-phase via the operator $i$; a closed loop in phase
space; a closed loop in parameter space for adiabatic transport; a
closed spatial loop around a region of gauge curvature; a closed orbit
traversing classical turning points; a composition of non-parallel
Lorentz boosts; or any other process whose round-trip closure depends on
the integrated $x_{4}$-content along the trajectory. Then the round-trip
non-closure of $R$ is bounded below by the action quantum $\hbar$
supplied by Theorem [9.35](#thm:c-hbar-twin){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:c-hbar-twin"}:
$$\mathrm{non\text{-}closure}(R) \;\geq\; \hbar \times \kappa(R),$$
where $\kappa(R)$ is a topological coefficient determined by the
operation's structure (ranging from $1/2$ for the Robertson uncertainty
bound, the Bohr--Sommerfeld--Maslov correction, the spin-1/2 $4\pi$
closure relative to $2\pi$, and the Dirac monopole minimum quantization;
through $1$ for the infinitesimal canonical-commutator case; up to large
integers determined by winding number or Chern number for
global-topology cases). The universal lower bound $\hbar$ across all
instances is the action quantum carried by one Compton-frequency
oscillation of $x_{4}$-advance; any round-trip involving $x_{4}$ cannot
resolve a phase difference finer than this quantum because
$x_{4}$-advance occurs in discrete units of $\hbar$ per oscillation.*

**Nine canonical instances unified.* The following nine
independently-celebrated results are all instances of this
universal non-closure principle, with the same $\hbar$ in each:*

1.  **Canonical commutator* [@HeisenbergBornJordan1925]:
    $[\hat{q}_i, \hat{p}_j] = i\hbar\delta_{ij}$. The infinitesimal-loop
    non-closure of $(\hat{q}, \hat{p})$-rotation, with non-closure
    quantum $\hbar$. The position $\hat{q}$ is in $x_1 x_2 x_3$; the
    momentum $\hat{p}$ accesses $x_{4}$; the round-trip in the
    $(\hat{q}, \hat{p})$-plane around an infinitesimal parallelogram
    does not close because $\hat{q}$ and $\hat{p}$ access orthogonal
    level directions of the four-dimensional structure.
    Coefficient $\kappa = 1$.*

2.  **Heisenberg uncertainty principle* [@Heisenberg1927]:
    $\sigma_q\sigma_p \geq \hbar/2$. The statistical version of (N1):
    the minimum product of standard deviations is exactly half the
    non-closure quantum, with the $1/2$ supplied by Cauchy--Schwarz on
    the commutator's $i\hbar$ [@Robertson1929]. Coefficient
    $\kappa = 1/2$.*

3.  **Berry geometric phase* [@Berry1984]:
    $\gamma_B = \oint_C \mathbf{A}\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell$. The global
    non-closure of an adiabatic loop in parameter space. The phase
    $\gamma_B$ is the surface integral of the Berry curvature; in the
    McGucken reading, the adiabatic loop in parameter space corresponds
    to a closed loop of $x_{4}$-phase-content traversals, with the
    non-zero $\gamma_B$ being the accumulated $x_{4}$-content the loop
    carries. Coefficient $\kappa$ determined by the loop's winding
    number on the parameter-space fiber bundle.*

4.  **Spin-1/2 $4\pi$ closure* ($SU(2)$ double cover of $SO(3)$;
    Rauch--Werner--Colella--Overhauser 1975
    [@RauchWernerColellaOverhauser1975], Werner et al. 1975
    [@WernerEtAl1975]). A spin-1/2 particle rotated by $2\pi$ in
    physical space picks up phase $\exp(i\pi) = -1$, requiring a full
    $4\pi$ rotation for closure. The "extra $2\pi$" is exactly the
    half-quantum of $x_{4}$-rotation that a spin-1/2 particle carries:
    its angular momentum is in units of $\hbar/2$, and the rotation by
    $2\pi$ gives action $S = \pi\hbar$, half the $2\pi\hbar$ that would
    give full closure. Coefficient $\kappa = 1/2$.*

5.  **Bohr--Sommerfeld + Maslov $\tfrac{1}{2}$-quantum correction*
    [@Maslov1965; @Arnold1967]: $\oint p\,dq = (n + \mu/4)h$, where
    $\mu$ is the Maslov index counting caustic / turning-point
    traversals. At each classical turning point, the particle reverses
    direction in $x_1 x_2 x_3$, which requires a rotation through the
    perpendicular $x_{4}$-direction; each such turning-point traversal
    contributes one quarter-quantum of action $\hbar$ to the round-trip,
    with the cumulative Maslov correction being the total non-closure of
    all turning-point rotations. Coefficient $\kappa = 1/4$ per turning
    point.*

6.  **Aharonov--Bohm phase* [@AharonovBohm1959; @TonomuraEtAl1986]:
    $\exp(ie\Phi/\hbar)$. The closed-loop phase of a charged particle
    around a region of confined magnetic flux $\Phi$, with the field
    zero along the trajectory. The phase is $e\Phi/\hbar$ in units of
    the action quantum; the elementary magnetic flux quantum is $h/e$.
    The $U(1)$ gauge fiber is geometrically the $x_{4}$-phase circle
    (the perpendicular direction whose advance carries the $\hbar$
    quantum); the closed spatial loop in the $(x_1, x_2)$ plane around
    the flux tube is a failed round-trip in the full $(x_1, x_2, x_{4})$
    structure because the gauge bundle's curvature (the magnetic flux
    $\Phi$) makes the loop pick up $x_{4}$-phase that cannot be removed.
    Coefficient $\kappa =$ winding number around the flux tube.*

7.  **Dirac magnetic monopole quantization* [@Dirac1931]:
    $eg = (n/2)\hbar c$. The minimum monopole charge $eg = (1/2)\hbar c$
    is set by single-valuedness of the wavefunction around the Dirac
    string. The string is a singular $x_{4}$-phase line in the McGucken
    reading; the round-trip around it accumulates phase in units of
    $\hbar/2$. Reformulated as fiber-bundle topology by Wu--Yang (1975)
    [@WuYang1975]. Coefficient $\kappa = 1/2$ minimum.*

8.  **Wigner rotation from non-parallel boost composition*
    [@Wigner1939; @Thomas1927]. Two non-parallel Lorentz boosts do not
    compose to a single Lorentz boost; they produce a boost plus a
    residual rotation. Boosts are rotations involving $x_{4}$ (by the
    boost-as-$x_{4}$-rotation content of Step 1 of
    Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}); two non-parallel boosts compose to
    a boost plus a residual rotation because boost-composition in a
    curved (hyperbolic) velocity space does not close. The curvature of
    velocity space is geometrically the same as the Berry curvature of
    (N3): both descend from $x_{4}$-involving rotations of the
    four-dimensional structure. The classical-relativistic non-closure
    (Wigner) and the quantum-adiabatic non-closure (Berry) are the same
    kind of geometric content at different levels of the chain.*

9.  **Path-integral interference* [@Feynman1948]:
    $\exp(iS[\gamma]/\hbar)$. The phase a quantum particle accumulates
    along a path $\gamma$ is the action $S[\gamma]$ divided by the
    action quantum $\hbar$. The interference between two distinct paths
    is $\exp(i(S[\gamma_1] - S[\gamma_2])/\hbar)$; the action difference
    is the integrated non-closure of the loop $\gamma_1$ followed by
    $\gamma_2$ reversed. Every quantum interference effect ---
    double-slit fringes, neutron interferometry, atom interferometry,
    photon interferometry --- is the empirical record of "rotation into
    $x_{4}$ along path A and along path B does not agree on the return,"
    with the disagreement being the action difference between the two
    paths in units of $\hbar$. The universal carrier $\exp(iS/\hbar)$
    has the $i$ marking $x_{4}$-perpendicularity and the $\hbar$ marking
    the action quantum per oscillation of $x_{4}$-advance --- the twin
    constants of Theorem [9.35](#thm:c-hbar-twin){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:c-hbar-twin"}.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). Each item is established by an existing theorem of the present
textbook, an existing theorem of the corpus, or a standard result of
foundational physics, with the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework supplying the upstream
reading.

**(N1) Canonical commutator.**
$[\hat{q}_i, \hat{p}_j] = i\hbar\delta_{ij}$ is Theorem QM T10
(Chapter [10](#ch:ccr){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:ccr"}), with
the operator-level reading as the algebraic statement of
$x_1 x_2 x_3 \perp x_{4}$. The non-closure quantum is $i\hbar$, with $i$
the perpendicularity marker
(Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}) and $\hbar$ the action quantum per
radian of the Compton-frequency oscillation of $x_{4}$-advance
(Theorem [9.35](#thm:c-hbar-twin){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:c-hbar-twin"}). Coefficient $\kappa = 1$. ✓

**(N2) Heisenberg uncertainty principle.**
$\sigma_q\sigma_p \geq \hbar/2$ is
Theorem [12.1](#thm:QMT12){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT12"},
with the $1/2$ supplied by the Cauchy--Schwarz step on the canonical
commutator's $i\hbar$ (Robertson 1929). The factor $i$ is absent on the
right-hand side because $\sigma_q\sigma_p$ is a real-valued product of
real-valued standard deviations. The $\hbar$ is the same action quantum
as (N1). Coefficient $\kappa = 1/2$. ✓

**(N3) Berry geometric phase.**
$\gamma_B = \oint_C \mathbf{A}\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell$ is established by
Berry (1984) [@Berry1984] and Simon (1983) [@Simon1983], with the
holonomy formulation on principal $U(1)$ bundles over parameter space.
The Berry phase is the surface integral of the Berry curvature (the
field-strength of the connection $\mathbf{A}$ on the parameter-space
fiber bundle). In the McGucken reading, the adiabatic loop corresponds
to a closed loop of $x_{4}$-phase-content traversals, with the
accumulated $x_{4}$-content being the Berry phase. Wilczek and Zee
(1984) [@WilczekZee1984] extended to non-Abelian gauge structures. The
$\hbar$ is the same as (N1) and (N2). ✓

**(N4) Spin-1/2 $4\pi$ closure.** The $SU(2) \to SO(3)$ double cover is
a standard mathematical fact. The empirical confirmation that spin-1/2
requires $4\pi$ rotation (not $2\pi$) for full closure is the
Rauch--Werner--Colella--Overhauser 1975 neutron-interferometry
experiment [@RauchWernerColellaOverhauser1975] and the Werner et
al. 1975 experiment [@WernerEtAl1975]. The McGucken reading: a spin-1/2
particle's $x_{4}$-content is half the standard quantum, so its
round-trip in $2\pi$ picks up only half the standard $2\pi\hbar$ action
that would give full closure. The "extra $2\pi$" required is the same
$\hbar$ at half-quantum level. ✓

**(N5) Bohr--Sommerfeld + Maslov rule.** $\oint p\,dq = (n + \mu/4)h$ is
established by Bohr (1913) and Sommerfeld (1916) for the integer-$n$
form, with the Maslov-index correction $\mu/4$ by Maslov (1965)
[@Maslov1965] and Arnold (1967) [@Arnold1967]. The McGucken reading:
each classical turning-point traversal reverses the particle's direction
in $x_1 x_2 x_3$, which requires a rotation through $x_{4}$. Each such
rotation contributes one quarter-quantum of action $\hbar$ to the
round-trip; the cumulative Maslov correction $\mu/4$ is the total
non-closure of all turning-point rotations along the closed orbit. ✓

**(N6) Aharonov--Bohm phase.** $\exp(ie\Phi/\hbar)$ is established by
Aharonov--Bohm (1959) [@AharonovBohm1959], confirmed empirically by
Tonomura et al. (1986) [@TonomuraEtAl1986], and shown to be a
gauge-theoretic non-closure by Wu--Yang (1975) [@WuYang1975]. The
McGucken reading: the $U(1)$ gauge fiber is geometrically the
$x_{4}$-phase circle; a closed spatial loop around a region of gauge
curvature (magnetic flux $\Phi$) accumulates $x_{4}$-phase that cannot
be removed by deforming the loop within the field-free region. The
elementary flux quantum $h/e$ corresponds to one full round-trip of
$x_{4}$-phase circulation. ✓

**(N7) Dirac monopole quantization.** $eg = (n/2)\hbar c$ is established
by Dirac (1931) [@Dirac1931] and reformulated as fiber-bundle topology
by Wu--Yang (1975, 1976) [@WuYang1975]. The McGucken reading: the Dirac
string is a singular $x_{4}$-phase line; the round-trip around it
accumulates phase in units of $\hbar/2$, with single-valuedness
requiring this be an integer multiple of $2\pi$. The minimum monopole
charge $eg = (1/2)\hbar c$ is the minimum non-closure the global
geometry of the $x_{4}$-phase bundle tolerates. The $\hbar/2$ quantum is
the same as in (N2) and (N4). ✓

**(N8) Wigner rotation.** The Wigner rotation from non-parallel boost
composition is established by Wigner (1939) [@Wigner1939], with the
Thomas precession application by Thomas (1927) [@Thomas1927]. The
McGucken reading: boosts are rotations involving $x_{4}$ (the Lorentz
arena is generated by $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the embedding
$\iota: (t, \mathbf{x}) \mapsto (\mathbf{x}, ict)$ in
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}); two non-parallel boosts compose to a
boost plus a residual rotation because boost-composition in hyperbolic
velocity space does not close. The curvature of velocity space is
geometrically the same as the Berry curvature of (N3) at a different
level of the chain. Thomas precession in atomic spectra (the factor of $1/2$
in the spin-orbit coupling) is the empirical record of the Wigner
rotation's non-closure across the periodic motion of an electron in a
Coulomb field. ✓

**(N9) Path-integral interference.** $\exp(iS[\gamma]/\hbar)$ is
established by Feynman (1948) [@Feynman1948], with the McGucken-internal
derivation given by the Geometric Channel path-integral construction
(Chapter [4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:foundations"}, Geometric Channel axioms, and
Chapter [9](#ch:hilbert-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:hilbert-theorem"}). The McGucken reading: the
path-integral phase is the integrated $x_{4}$-phase along the path, with
$i$ the perpendicularity marker for $x_{4}$ and $\hbar$ the action
quantum per radian of the Compton-frequency oscillation of $x_{4}$-advance. Every
quantum interference effect is the empirical record of integrated
$x_{4}$-phase non-closure between distinct paths. ✓

**Common upstream principle.** The nine items share their non-closure
quantum $\hbar$ because all nine involve rotations of, or phase-content
along, $x_{4}= ict$, and $x_{4}$-advance occurs in discrete quanta of
$\hbar$ per radian of the Compton-frequency oscillation
(Theorem [9.35](#thm:c-hbar-twin){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:c-hbar-twin"}). The universal lower bound $\hbar$ across
all nine instances is the empirical content of the action-quantization
clause of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, measured nine different ways.
$\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:nine-threads-never-unified .remark}
*Remark 12.13* (Historical context: nine separate threads, never
unified). The history of the nine results in
Theorem [12.12](#thm:universal-non-closure){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:universal-non-closure"} is the history of nine separate
threads, with partial unifications among subsets but no overall
connection to the canonical commutator and to a common upstream physical
principle. The closest a prior program came to a comprehensive
unification was the combined **Yang--Wu (1975)** +
**Berry--Simon--Wilczek--Zee (1983--1984)** corpus, which mathematically
unified gauge-theoretic non-closures (items N3, N6, N7) plus
adiabatic-quantum non-closures (N3) through fiber-bundle holonomy on
principal $U(1)$ bundles. **Souriau--Kostant (1970)** geometric
quantization unified Bohr--Sommerfeld--Maslov (N5), Dirac monopole
quantization (N7), and magnetic flux quantization via the
prequantization integrality condition on symplectic 2-forms. But
geometric quantization treated $\hbar$ as the input to the
framework, not as a derived quantity of an upstream physical principle.
None of these unifications connected to the canonical commutator (N1),
the uncertainty bound (N2), the spin-1/2 $4\pi$ closure (N4), or the
Wigner rotation (N8). The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework supplies the missing
physical content: $i$ and $\hbar$ are twin properties of one geometric
flow (Theorem [9.35](#thm:c-hbar-twin){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:c-hbar-twin"}), and every non-closure that involves
$x_{4}$ inherits the $i\hbar$ structure as its algebraic signature.
:::

::: {#rmk:nine-instances-one-content .remark}
*Remark 12.14* (Architectural significance: nine instances measured nine
ways of one physical content). The architectural significance of
Theorem [12.12](#thm:universal-non-closure){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:universal-non-closure"} is that the empirical
universality of $\hbar$ across the nine independently-celebrated results
is the empirical content of
Theorem [9.35](#thm:c-hbar-twin){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:c-hbar-twin"} itself, measured nine different ways. Every
interferometer (path-integral interference N9, Aharonov--Bohm N6), every
monopole-search experiment (Dirac monopole N7), every neutron-spin
rotation (spin-1/2 $4\pi$ closure N4), every adiabatic quantum transport
(Berry phase N3), every semiclassical Bohr--Sommerfeld orbit (Maslov
correction N5), every relativistic Thomas precession measurement (Wigner
rotation N8), every position-momentum precision measurement (canonical
commutator N1, uncertainty bound N2), and every quantum interference
experiment is, in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, a measurement of the same
physical quantity --- the action carried by one cycle of $x_{4}$-advance
--- instantiated at the level of the chain appropriate to the experimental
setup. The agreement of all these measurements on the same numerical
value of $\hbar = 1.054571817 \times 10^{-34}$ J$\cdot$s has the
reading of the same empirical content measured by different
probes, with the role of nine independent empirical coincidences
replaced by the role of nine level instantiations of one
upstream physical fact. The framework's prediction is that
the universal non-closure quantum will continue to emerge in any future
foundational physics experiment that involves rotation through $x_{4}$.
:::

### Empirical anchor

-   Single-slit electron diffraction: the diffraction pattern's width is
    the manifestation of $\Delta x \cdot \Delta p_y \ge \hbar/2$ at the
    slit.

-   Squeezed light (Wu et al. 1986): one quadrature is reduced below the
    standard quantum limit at the cost of increasing the conjugate
    quadrature.

-   Trapped-ion ground-state cooling (Wineland Nobel 2012):
    position-momentum uncertainty in the trap ground state saturates the
    Heisenberg bound for a Gaussian wavepacket.

## QM T13: The CHSH Inequality and the Tsirelson Bound $2\sqrt{2}$ {#ch:tsirelson}

> *The McGucken Principle.* The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality.
> Every result below descends from that expansion.


*Recall.* the McGucken Principle ($\mathrm{McP}$:
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$) asserts that the fourth spacetime dimension
$x_4$ expands at the velocity of light $c$, carrying the
perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguishes it from the spatial
three. Throughout this chapter, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ refers to this
principle and to the five-clause content (i)--(v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: (i) *invariance* --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content; (ii) *spherical symmetry* --- the
expansion is isotropic in the spatial three, with the set of events
reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a 2-sphere of radius
$c\tau$; (iii) *monotonicity* --- the integral curve is strictly
monotonically increasing in $t$, fixing the arrow of $x_4$-advance; (iv)
*Lorentz consistency* --- the structure is $SO^+(1,3)$-invariant on
$M_{G}$; (v) *global validity* --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at
every event of $M_{G}$. The integrated kinematic shadow
$x_4 = ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is the kinematic shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the central fact.

The CHSH inequality and its quantum-mechanical violation up to the
Tsirelson bound $2\sqrt{2}$ is the empirical signature of quantum
nonlocality. The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework derives both---the classical-local
upper bound 2, and the quantum-mechanical upper bound $2\sqrt{2}$---as
theorems of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

### Statement

::: {#thm:QMT13 .theorem}
**Theorem 13.1** (QM T13: CHSH/Tsirelson, = Theorem 72 (Algebraic Channel) and
Theorem 95 (Geometric Channel) of [@Syn-2026]). *For any local hidden-variable
theory, the CHSH correlation function satisfies
$$|\langle CHSH\rangle| = |E(a,b) + E(a,b') + E(a',b) - E(a',b')| \le 2,$$
where $E(a,b) = \langle A(a)B(b)\rangle$ is the correlation of
dichotomic measurements at settings $a, b$. Quantum mechanics permits
$$|\langle CHSH\rangle|_{\text{QM}} \le 2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.828,$$ the
Tsirelson bound, saturated by maximally entangled singlet states at
optimal measurement settings.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). We prove the classical bound (CHSH) and the quantum bound
(Tsirelson) separately, then exhibit explicit saturation by the singlet
state at optimal settings. The proof uses the McGucken-derived Hilbert
space $\mathcal{H}$
(Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}) and the tensor-product structure
$\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B$ for independent subsystems (from
Stone--von Neumann uniqueness packaging of QA4); the operator-norm
bounds are elementary functional analysis on any Hilbert space.

**Classical CHSH bound $|\langle CHSH\rangle| \leq 2$.** In a local
hidden-variable theory, the measurement outcomes
$A(a, \lambda), B(b, \lambda) \in \{-1, +1\}$ are deterministic
functions of hidden variables $\lambda$ and the local measurement
setting only: $A(a, \lambda)$ depends on $a$ but not on $b$, and
$B(b, \lambda)$ depends on $b$ but not on $a$. The CHSH combination
evaluated at a fixed $\lambda$ is
$$A(a,\lambda)B(b,\lambda) + A(a,\lambda)B(b',\lambda) + A(a',\lambda)B(b,\lambda) - A(a',\lambda)B(b',\lambda).$$
Factor by $A$-prefix:
$$= A(a, \lambda)\bigl[B(b, \lambda) + B(b', \lambda)\bigr] + A(a', \lambda)\bigl[B(b, \lambda) - B(b', \lambda)\bigr].$$
Since $B(b, \lambda), B(b', \lambda) \in \{-1, +1\}$, the pair
$\bigl(B(b, \lambda) + B(b', \lambda),\; B(b, \lambda) - B(b', \lambda)\bigr)$
takes exactly one of two values: either $(\pm 2, 0)$ when
$B(b, \lambda) = B(b', \lambda)$, or $(0, \pm 2)$ when
$B(b, \lambda) = -B(b', \lambda)$. In either case, one of the two
brackets is zero and the other has magnitude $2$. Combined with
$|A(a, \lambda)| = |A(a', \lambda)| = 1$, the entire combination has
magnitude $2$ at every $\lambda$. Averaging over the hidden-variable
distribution preserves the bound:
$$|\langle CHSH\rangle| \;=\; \biggl|\int \bigl[A(a,\lambda)B(b,\lambda) + A(a,\lambda)B(b',\lambda) + A(a',\lambda)B(b,\lambda) - A(a',\lambda)B(b',\lambda)\bigr]\,d\mu(\lambda)\biggr| \;\leq\; 2.$$
This is the CHSH classical-local bound (Clauser--Horne--Shimony--Holt
1969).

**Quantum Tsirelson bound
$|\langle CHSH\rangle|_{\mathrm{QM}} \leq 2\sqrt 2$.** Let
$\hat A, \hat A', \hat B, \hat B'$ be self-adjoint operators on the
tensor-product Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B$ with
eigenvalues in $\{-1, +1\}$ (dichotomic observables). The operators
$\hat A, \hat A'$ act on the $A$-factor (with eigenvalues $\pm 1$ for
Alice's two measurement settings), and $\hat B, \hat B'$ act on the
$B$-factor. The locality assumption is the tensor-product structure:
each $\hat A_i = \hat A_i^{(\mathrm{loc})} \otimes \mathbf{1}_B$ acts
only on the $A$-factor, and each
$\hat B_j = \mathbf{1}_A \otimes \hat B_j^{(\mathrm{loc})}$ acts only on
the $B$-factor. Consequently
$$[\hat A_i,\, \hat B_j] \;=\; 0 \qquad \forall\, i \in \{\text{unprimed},\,\text{primed}\}_A,\; j \in \{\text{unprimed},\,\text{primed}\}_B,$$
since operators acting on independent tensor factors commute
(Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Vol. I, §II.4, on the tensor-product
Hilbert-space construction).

Define the *CHSH operator*
$$\hat S \;:=\; \hat A\,\hat B + \hat A\,\hat B' + \hat A'\,\hat B - \hat A'\,\hat B'.$$

**Self-adjointness of $\hat S$.** Each term $\hat A_i\hat B_j$ is the
product of two commuting self-adjoint operators
$[\hat A_i, \hat B_j] = 0$; the product of two commuting self-adjoint
operators is self-adjoint, since
$(\hat A_i\hat B_j)^* = \hat B_j^*\,\hat A_i^* = \hat B_j\,\hat A_i = \hat A_i\,\hat B_j$
using commutativity in the last step. The CHSH operator $\hat S$ is a
real linear combination of four self-adjoint operators, hence
self-adjoint.

**Step 1: CHSH-squared identity by full expansion.** Using
$\hat A^2 = \hat A'^2 = \hat B^2 = \hat B'^2 = \mathbf{1}$ (a
self-adjoint operator with eigenvalues $\pm 1$ satisfies
$\hat T^2 = \mathbf{1}$ on its eigenspaces, hence everywhere by spectral
decomposition; Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Vol. I, Theorem VII.3) and
the locality $[\hat A_i, \hat B_j] = 0$, expand
$\hat S^2 = (\hat A\hat B + \hat A\hat B' + \hat A'\hat B - \hat A'\hat B')^2$
term by term. The expansion has $4\times 4 = 16$ products, grouped into
four classes.

*Class (a) Diagonal squares* (four products, one from each term
squared):
$$(\hat A\hat B)^2,\; (\hat A\hat B')^2,\; (\hat A'\hat B)^2,\; (-\hat A'\hat B')^2.$$
For the first: using $[\hat A, \hat B] = 0$,
$(\hat A\hat B)^2 = \hat A\hat B\hat A\hat B = \hat A^2\hat B^2 = \mathbf{1}\cdot\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}$.
The other three give $\mathbf{1}$ by identical computation. Class (a)
total: $4\,\mathbf{1}$.

*Class (b) Same-$A$ cross terms* (four products with matching
unprimed-$A$ or matching primed-$A$):
$$\underbrace{(\hat A\hat B)(\hat A\hat B') + (\hat A\hat B')(\hat A\hat B)}_{\text{same-}\hat A\text{ pair}} \,+\, \underbrace{(\hat A'\hat B)(-\hat A'\hat B') + (-\hat A'\hat B')(\hat A'\hat B)}_{\text{same-}\hat A'\text{ pair}}.$$
For the same-$\hat A$ pair:
$(\hat A\hat B)(\hat A\hat B') = \hat A\hat B\hat A\hat B' = \hat A^2\hat B\hat B' = \hat B\hat B'$
using $[\hat A, \hat B] = 0$ in the middle step; similarly
$(\hat A\hat B')(\hat A\hat B) = \hat B'\hat B$. Sum:
$\hat B\hat B' + \hat B'\hat B = \{\hat B, \hat B'\}$ (anticommutator).

For the same-$\hat A'$ pair:
$(\hat A'\hat B)(-\hat A'\hat B') = -\hat A'\hat B\hat A'\hat B' = -\hat A'^2\hat B\hat B' = -\hat B\hat B'$;
$(-\hat A'\hat B')(\hat A'\hat B) = -\hat A'\hat B'\hat A'\hat B = -\hat A'^2\hat B'\hat B = -\hat B'\hat B$.
Sum: $-\hat B\hat B' - \hat B'\hat B = -\{\hat B, \hat B'\}$.

Class (b) total: $\{\hat B, \hat B'\} - \{\hat B, \hat B'\} = 0$.

*Class (c) Same-$B$ cross terms* (four products with matching
unprimed-$B$ or matching primed-$B$):
$$\underbrace{(\hat A\hat B)(\hat A'\hat B) + (\hat A'\hat B)(\hat A\hat B)}_{\text{same-}\hat B\text{ pair}} \,+\, \underbrace{(\hat A\hat B')(-\hat A'\hat B') + (-\hat A'\hat B')(\hat A\hat B')}_{\text{same-}\hat B'\text{ pair}}.$$
For the same-$\hat B$ pair:
$(\hat A\hat B)(\hat A'\hat B) = \hat A\hat A'\hat B^2 = \hat A\hat A'$
using $[\hat A', \hat B] = 0$; similarly
$(\hat A'\hat B)(\hat A\hat B) = \hat A'\hat A$. Sum:
$\hat A\hat A' + \hat A'\hat A = \{\hat A, \hat A'\}$.

For the same-$\hat B'$ pair:
$(\hat A\hat B')(-\hat A'\hat B') = -\hat A\hat A'\hat B'^2 = -\hat A\hat A'$;
$(-\hat A'\hat B')(\hat A\hat B') = -\hat A'\hat A\hat B'^2 = -\hat A'\hat A$.
Sum: $-\hat A\hat A' - \hat A'\hat A = -\{\hat A, \hat A'\}$.

Class (c) total: $\{\hat A, \hat A'\} - \{\hat A, \hat A'\} = 0$.

*Class (d) Cross terms with different $A$ and different $B$* (four
remaining products):
$$(\hat A\hat B)(-\hat A'\hat B') + (-\hat A'\hat B')(\hat A\hat B) + (\hat A\hat B')(\hat A'\hat B) + (\hat A'\hat B)(\hat A\hat B').$$
Using locality $[\hat A_i, \hat B_j] = 0$ to reorder the $A$- and
$B$-factors: $$\begin{aligned}
  (\hat A\hat B)(-\hat A'\hat B') &= -\hat A\hat A'\hat B\hat B', \\
  (-\hat A'\hat B')(\hat A\hat B) &= -\hat A'\hat A\hat B'\hat B, \\
  (\hat A\hat B')(\hat A'\hat B) &= \hat A\hat A'\hat B'\hat B, \\
  (\hat A'\hat B)(\hat A\hat B') &= \hat A'\hat A\hat B\hat B'.
\end{aligned}$$ Group by $A$-prefix. The $\hat A\hat A'$-terms (first
and third) sum to
$-\hat A\hat A'\hat B\hat B' + \hat A\hat A'\hat B'\hat B = -\hat A\hat A'(\hat B\hat B' - \hat B'\hat B) = -\hat A\hat A'\,[\hat B, \hat B']$.
The $\hat A'\hat A$-terms (second and fourth) sum to
$-\hat A'\hat A\hat B'\hat B + \hat A'\hat A\hat B\hat B' = +\hat A'\hat A(\hat B\hat B' - \hat B'\hat B) = +\hat A'\hat A\,[\hat B, \hat B']$.

Class (d) total:
$(-\hat A\hat A' + \hat A'\hat A)\,[\hat B, \hat B'] = -(\hat A\hat A' - \hat A'\hat A)\,[\hat B, \hat B'] = -[\hat A, \hat A']\,[\hat B, \hat B']$.

*Total $\hat S^2$:* Summing classes (a) through (d):
$$\hat S^2 \;=\; 4\,\mathbf{1} + 0 + 0 + \bigl(-[\hat A, \hat A']\,[\hat B, \hat B']\bigr) \;=\; 4\,\mathbf{1} \,-\, [\hat A, \hat A']\,[\hat B, \hat B'].
  \label{eq:CHSH-squared-identity}$$ This is the CHSH-squared identity,
derived by full term-by-term expansion using only
$\hat T^2 = \mathbf{1}$ (dichotomic) and locality
$[\hat A_i, \hat B_j] = 0$ (tensor-product structure).

**Step 2: Operator-norm bound on $\hat S^2$.**

*Step 2a: Norm of dichotomic operators.* For a self-adjoint operator
$\hat T$ with eigenvalues in $\{-1, +1\}$, the operator norm equals the
spectral radius (Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Vol. I, Theorem VI.6,
$\|\hat T\| = \sup\{|\lambda| : \lambda \in \sigma(\hat T)\}$ for
self-adjoint $\hat T$), so
$\|\hat A\| = \|\hat A'\| = \|\hat B\| = \|\hat B'\| = 1$.

*Step 2b: Commutator-norm bound.* By the triangle inequality and
submultiplicativity of the operator norm:
$$\|[\hat A,\hat A']\| \;=\; \|\hat A\hat A' - \hat A'\hat A\| \;\leq\; \|\hat A\hat A'\| + \|\hat A'\hat A\| \;\leq\; \|\hat A\|\,\|\hat A'\| + \|\hat A'\|\,\|\hat A\| \;=\; 1 + 1 \;=\; 2.$$
The same argument gives $\|[\hat B,\hat B']\| \leq 2$.

*Step 2c: Bound on the product of commutators.* By submultiplicativity
once more:
$$\|[\hat A,\hat A']\,[\hat B,\hat B']\| \;\leq\; \|[\hat A,\hat A']\| \cdot \|[\hat B,\hat B']\| \;\leq\; 2 \cdot 2 \;=\; 4.$$

*Step 2d: Bound on $\hat S^2$.* From identity
[\[eq:CHSH-squared-identity\]](#eq:CHSH-squared-identity){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:CHSH-squared-identity"} and the triangle inequality:
$$\|\hat S^2\| \;=\; \|4\,\mathbf{1} - [\hat A,\hat A']\,[\hat B,\hat B']\| \;\leq\; \|4\,\mathbf{1}\| + \|[\hat A,\hat A']\,[\hat B,\hat B']\| \;\leq\; 4 + 4 \;=\; 8,$$
using $\|4\,\mathbf{1}\| = 4$ (the operator norm of $\lambda\mathbf{1}$
is $|\lambda|$).

*Step 2e: Bound on $\hat S$ via the $C^*$-identity.* The CHSH operator
$\hat S$ is self-adjoint (verified above). For self-adjoint $\hat S$,
the $C^*$-algebra identity $\|\hat T^*\hat T\| = \|\hat T\|^2$ applied
with $\hat T = \hat S$ gives
$\|\hat S^2\| = \|\hat S^*\hat S\| = \|\hat S\|^2$ (Reed--Simon
[@ReedSimon1980] Vol. I, the $C^*$-property of
$\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$). Therefore
$$\|\hat S\| \;=\; \sqrt{\|\hat S^2\|} \;\leq\; \sqrt 8 \;=\; 2\sqrt 2.$$

**Step 3: From operator norm to expectation value.** For any normalized
state $\lvert \psi  \rangle\in \mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B$
($\|\psi\| = 1$), the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality on
$\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B$
(Theorem [3.2](#thm:cauchy-schwarz){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:cauchy-schwarz"}) gives
$$|\langle\psi,\, \hat S\,\psi\rangle| \;\leq\; \|\psi\|\cdot\|\hat S\,\psi\| \;\leq\; \|\hat S\|\cdot\|\psi\|^2 \;=\; \|\hat S\| \;\leq\; 2\sqrt 2,$$
using $\|\hat S\psi\| \leq \|\hat S\|\,\|\psi\|$ from the definition of
the operator norm. Therefore
$|\langle CHSH\rangle|_{\mathrm{QM}} \leq 2\sqrt 2$ for every normalized
state.

**Step 4: Explicit saturation by the singlet at optimal settings.** By
the Geometric Channel derivation in
§[13.3](#ssec:T13-channelB){reference-type="ref"
reference="ssec:T13-channelB"} below, the singlet state
$\lvert \Psi^- \rangle = (\lvert \uparrow\downarrow \rangle - \lvert \downarrow\uparrow \rangle)/\sqrt 2$
on the McGucken-Sphere two-spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ system has
spin-correlation function
$$E_{\mathrm{singlet}}(\hat a, \hat b) \;=\; \langle\Psi^-,\, (\vec\sigma_A\!\cdot\!\hat a) \otimes (\vec\sigma_B\!\cdot\!\hat b)\,\Psi^-\rangle \;=\; -\hat a\cdot\hat b.$$
Choose measurement directions in the $xz$-plane of the McGucken Sphere:
$$\hat a \;=\; \hat z, \qquad \hat a' \;=\; \hat x, \qquad \hat b \;=\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}(\hat z + \hat x), \qquad \hat b' \;=\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}(\hat z - \hat x).$$
Direct computation of the four correlations: $$\begin{aligned}
  E(\hat a, \hat b) &\;=\; -\hat z\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}(\hat z + \hat x) \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\,(1 + 0) \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}, \\
  E(\hat a, \hat b') &\;=\; -\hat z\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}(\hat z - \hat x) \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\,(1 - 0) \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}, \\
  E(\hat a', \hat b) &\;=\; -\hat x\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}(\hat z + \hat x) \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\,(0 + 1) \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}, \\
  E(\hat a', \hat b') &\;=\; -\hat x\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}(\hat z - \hat x) \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\,(0 - 1) \;=\; +\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}.
\end{aligned}$$ Substituting into the CHSH combination:
$$\langle CHSH\rangle_{\mathrm{singlet}} \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2} - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2} - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2} - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2} \;=\; -\frac{4}{\sqrt 2} \;=\; -2\sqrt 2.$$
Hence $|\langle CHSH\rangle_{\mathrm{singlet}}| = 2\sqrt 2$, saturating
the Tsirelson bound established in Step 3.

**Geometric Channel reading.** The geometric content of the Tsirelson bound is
the saturation of four inner products of unit vectors on a great circle
of the McGucken Sphere $S^2$; the same algebraic bound $2\sqrt 2$
follows directly from Cauchy--Schwarz applied to the inner-product
structure on $\mathbb{R}^3$ (Step B-3 of
§[13.3](#ssec:T13-channelB){reference-type="ref"
reference="ssec:T13-channelB"} below). Geometric Channel and Algebraic Channel reach the
bound through derivationally disjoint chains. $\square$ ◻
:::

### Geometric Channel derivation (QB7 --- Sphere $SO(3)$-Haar correlation) {#ssec:T13-channelB}

::: channelb
*Geometric Channel Derivation 13.4* (Tsirelson from Sphere singlet correlation
$+$ explicit saturation). **Step B-1 (Singlet correlation as Sphere
inner product).** The McGucken Sphere $S^2$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (ii), spherical symmetry of the
