$x_{4}$-expansion) carries the standard $SO(3)$-action by rotations. The
double cover $SU(2) \to SO(3)$ acts on the two-qubit Hilbert space
$\mathbb{C}^2 \otimes \mathbb{C}^2$ via the diagonal representation
$U \otimes U$ for $U \in SU(2)$.

*$SU(2)$-invariance of the singlet.* The singlet state
$$\lvert \Psi^- \rangle \;:=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\bigl(\lvert \uparrow\downarrow \rangle - \lvert \downarrow\uparrow \rangle\bigr) \;\in\; \mathbb{C}^2 \otimes \mathbb{C}^2$$
is $SU(2)$-invariant under the diagonal action: for any $U \in SU(2)$,
$$(U \otimes U)\lvert \Psi^- \rangle \;=\; \det(U)\,\lvert \Psi^- \rangle \;=\; \lvert \Psi^- \rangle,$$
using $\det U = 1$ for $U \in SU(2)$. (Proof: in the standard basis
$\{\lvert \uparrow \rangle, \lvert \downarrow \rangle\}$, the singlet is
the unique antisymmetric two-tensor up to scalar, equal to
$\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\,\varepsilon_{ij}\lvert i \rangle\otimes\lvert j \rangle$
with $\varepsilon_{ij}$ the antisymmetric epsilon-symbol; this is the
standard $SU(2)$-invariant (Cohen-Tannoudji [@CT2019] Ch. X §B, on the
addition of two spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ angular momenta and the
singlet/triplet decomposition).) Consequently the singlet correlation
function
$E_{\mathrm{singlet}}(\hat a, \hat b) = \langle\Psi^-,\, (\vec\sigma_A\cdot\hat a) \otimes (\vec\sigma_B\cdot\hat b)\,\Psi^-\rangle$
depends only on the $SO(3)$-invariant quantity $\hat a \cdot \hat b$.

We compute $E_{\mathrm{singlet}}$ explicitly using the Pauli matrices.

*Pauli action on the standard basis.* The Pauli matrices
$\vec\sigma = (\sigma^x, \sigma^y, \sigma^z)$ act on $\mathbb{C}^2$ via
$$\sigma^x\lvert \uparrow \rangle = \lvert \downarrow \rangle, \quad \sigma^x\lvert \downarrow \rangle = \lvert \uparrow \rangle; \quad \sigma^y\lvert \uparrow \rangle = i\lvert \downarrow \rangle, \quad \sigma^y\lvert \downarrow \rangle = -i\lvert \uparrow \rangle; \quad \sigma^z\lvert \uparrow \rangle = +\lvert \uparrow \rangle, \quad \sigma^z\lvert \downarrow \rangle = -\lvert \downarrow \rangle.$$

*Coordinate choice via $SO(3)$-invariance.* By the $SU(2)$-invariance of
the singlet established above, rotate to a frame where $\hat a = \hat z$
and $\hat b$ lies in the $xz$-plane:
$$\hat a \;=\; (0, 0, 1), \qquad \hat b \;=\; (\sin\theta, 0, \cos\theta), \qquad \theta \;=\; \theta_{ab} \;\in\; [0, \pi].$$
Then $\vec\sigma_A\cdot\hat a = \sigma^z_A$ and
$\vec\sigma_B\cdot\hat b = \sin\theta\,\sigma^x_B + \cos\theta\,\sigma^z_B$.

*Action of $\sigma^z_A$ on $\lvert \Psi^- \rangle$.* Apply $\sigma^z$ to
the $A$-qubit of each term:
$$\sigma^z_A\,\lvert \Psi^- \rangle \;=\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\bigl(\sigma^z\lvert \uparrow \rangle\otimes\lvert \downarrow \rangle - \sigma^z\lvert \downarrow \rangle\otimes\lvert \uparrow \rangle\bigr) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\bigl(\lvert \uparrow\downarrow \rangle + \lvert \downarrow\uparrow \rangle\bigr).$$
(Note: the second term picks up a sign flip from
$\sigma^z\lvert \downarrow \rangle = -\lvert \downarrow \rangle$, then
another from the minus sign in the singlet, giving the net
$+\lvert \downarrow\uparrow \rangle$.)

*Action of $\sigma^x_B$ on $\lvert \Psi^- \rangle$.*
$$\sigma^x_B\,\lvert \Psi^- \rangle \;=\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\bigl(\lvert \uparrow \rangle\otimes\sigma^x\lvert \downarrow \rangle - \lvert \downarrow \rangle\otimes\sigma^x\lvert \uparrow \rangle\bigr) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\bigl(\lvert \uparrow\uparrow \rangle - \lvert \downarrow\downarrow \rangle\bigr).$$

*Action of $\sigma^z_B$ on $\lvert \Psi^- \rangle$.*
$$\sigma^z_B\,\lvert \Psi^- \rangle \;=\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\bigl(\lvert \uparrow \rangle\otimes\sigma^z\lvert \downarrow \rangle - \lvert \downarrow \rangle\otimes\sigma^z\lvert \uparrow \rangle\bigr) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\bigl(-\lvert \uparrow\downarrow \rangle - \lvert \downarrow\uparrow \rangle\bigr).$$

*Composite actions $\sigma^z_A\sigma^x_B$ and $\sigma^z_A\sigma^z_B$.*
Using the explicit forms above: $$\begin{aligned}
  \sigma^z_A\sigma^x_B\,\lvert \Psi^- \rangle \;&=\; \sigma^z_A\,\Bigl[\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\bigl(\lvert \uparrow\uparrow \rangle - \lvert \downarrow\downarrow \rangle\bigr)\Bigr] \;=\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\bigl(+\lvert \uparrow\uparrow \rangle - (-\lvert \downarrow\downarrow \rangle)\bigr) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\bigl(\lvert \uparrow\uparrow \rangle + \lvert \downarrow\downarrow \rangle\bigr), \\
  \sigma^z_A\sigma^z_B\,\lvert \Psi^- \rangle \;&=\; \sigma^z_A\,\Bigl[\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\bigl(-\lvert \uparrow\downarrow \rangle - \lvert \downarrow\uparrow \rangle\bigr)\Bigr] \;=\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\bigl(-\lvert \uparrow\downarrow \rangle + \lvert \downarrow\uparrow \rangle\bigr) \;=\; -\lvert \Psi^- \rangle.
\end{aligned}$$

*Composite action $(\sigma^z_A)(\vec\sigma_B\cdot\hat b)$.* By
linearity:
$$(\sigma^z_A)(\vec\sigma_B\cdot\hat b)\,\lvert \Psi^- \rangle \;=\; \sin\theta\,(\sigma^z_A\sigma^x_B)\lvert \Psi^- \rangle + \cos\theta\,(\sigma^z_A\sigma^z_B)\lvert \Psi^- \rangle \;=\; \tfrac{\sin\theta}{\sqrt 2}\bigl(\lvert \uparrow\uparrow \rangle + \lvert \downarrow\downarrow \rangle\bigr) \,-\, \cos\theta\,\lvert \Psi^- \rangle.$$

*Inner product with $\lvert \Psi^- \rangle$.* Take the inner product
$\langle\Psi^-,\, \cdot\,\rangle$ of the result. The singlet
$\lvert \Psi^- \rangle$ has support on
$\{\lvert \uparrow\downarrow \rangle, \lvert \downarrow\uparrow \rangle\}$,
while
$\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}(\lvert \uparrow\uparrow \rangle + \lvert \downarrow\downarrow \rangle)$
has support on the orthogonal subspace
$\{\lvert \uparrow\uparrow \rangle, \lvert \downarrow\downarrow \rangle\}$.
Since the four basis states
$\{\lvert \uparrow\uparrow \rangle, \lvert \uparrow\downarrow \rangle, \lvert \downarrow\uparrow \rangle, \lvert \downarrow\downarrow \rangle\}$
are mutually orthonormal in $\mathbb{C}^2 \otimes \mathbb{C}^2$, the
inner product of the singlet with the symmetric-triplet term vanishes:
$$\langle\Psi^-,\, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}(\lvert \uparrow\uparrow \rangle + \lvert \downarrow\downarrow \rangle)\rangle \;=\; 0.$$
The contribution to the inner product comes only from the second
summand:
$$\langle\Psi^-,\, -\cos\theta\,\lvert \Psi^- \rangle\rangle \;=\; -\cos\theta\,\langle\Psi^-,\, \Psi^-\rangle \;=\; -\cos\theta,$$
using $\langle\Psi^-, \Psi^-\rangle = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + 1) = 1$
(normalization). Therefore
$$E_{\mathrm{singlet}}(\hat a, \hat b) \;=\; -\cos\theta_{ab} \;=\; -\hat a\cdot\hat b,
  \label{eq:singlet-correlation-derived}$$ the negative inner product of
unit vectors on the McGucken Sphere $S^2$, with the negative sign
reflecting the antisymmetric character of the singlet under particle
exchange.

**Step B-2 (Explicit saturation at optimal settings).** Choose the
measurement directions in a single plane (say the $xz$-plane of the
McGucken Sphere): $$\begin{aligned}
\hat{a} &= \hat{z}, & \hat{a}' &= \hat{x}, \\
\hat{b} &= (\hat{z}+\hat{x})/\sqrt{2}, & \hat{b}' &= (\hat{z}-\hat{x})/\sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}$$ Compute each of the four singlet correlations using
[\[eq:singlet-correlation-derived\]](#eq:singlet-correlation-derived){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:singlet-correlation-derived"}: $$\begin{aligned}
E(\hat{a}, \hat{b}) &= -\hat{z}\cdot(\hat{z}+\hat{x})/\sqrt{2} = -1/\sqrt{2}, \\
E(\hat{a}, \hat{b}') &= -\hat{z}\cdot(\hat{z}-\hat{x})/\sqrt{2} = -1/\sqrt{2}, \\
E(\hat{a}', \hat{b}) &= -\hat{x}\cdot(\hat{z}+\hat{x})/\sqrt{2} = -1/\sqrt{2}, \\
E(\hat{a}', \hat{b}') &= -\hat{x}\cdot(\hat{z}-\hat{x})/\sqrt{2} = +1/\sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}$$ Substituting into the CHSH combination:
$$\begin{aligned}
\langle CHSH\rangle &= E(\hat{a},\hat{b}) + E(\hat{a},\hat{b}') + E(\hat{a}',\hat{b}) - E(\hat{a}',\hat{b}') \\
&= -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = -\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} = -2\sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}$$ Hence $|\langle CHSH\rangle| = 2\sqrt{2}$, the Tsirelson
bound is *saturated* by the singlet at these optimal measurement
settings.

**Step B-3 (Tsirelson upper bound from Cauchy--Schwarz on $S^2$).** For
arbitrary unit vectors
$\hat a, \hat a', \hat b, \hat b' \in S^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$, we
derive the Tsirelson upper bound by elementary Euclidean geometry on the
McGucken Sphere.

*Sub-step B-3a: Algebraic regrouping.* Using
equation [\[eq:singlet-correlation-derived\]](#eq:singlet-correlation-derived){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:singlet-correlation-derived"} for the singlet correlation,
$$\langle CHSH\rangle \;=\; E(\hat a,\hat b) + E(\hat a,\hat b') + E(\hat a',\hat b) - E(\hat a',\hat b') \;=\; -\hat a\cdot\hat b - \hat a\cdot\hat b' - \hat a'\cdot\hat b + \hat a'\cdot\hat b'.$$
Regroup by $\hat a$- and $\hat a'$-prefix:
$$|\langle CHSH\rangle| \;=\; |\hat a\cdot(\hat b + \hat b') + \hat a'\cdot(\hat b - \hat b')|,$$
where we absorbed the overall minus sign into the absolute value
(irrelevant for the modulus bound).

*Sub-step B-3b: Cauchy--Schwarz on $\mathbb{R}^3$.* By the triangle
inequality on $\mathbb{R}$:
$$|\hat a\cdot(\hat b + \hat b') + \hat a'\cdot(\hat b - \hat b')| \;\leq\; |\hat a\cdot(\hat b + \hat b')| + |\hat a'\cdot(\hat b - \hat b')|.$$
By Cauchy--Schwarz applied to inner products of vectors in
$\mathbb{R}^3$ (Theorem [3.2](#thm:cauchy-schwarz){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:cauchy-schwarz"} restricted to the finite-dimensional
Hilbert space $\mathbb{R}^3$):
$$|\hat a\cdot(\hat b + \hat b')| \;\leq\; \|\hat a\|\cdot\|\hat b + \hat b'\| \;=\; \|\hat b + \hat b'\|, \qquad |\hat a'\cdot(\hat b - \hat b')| \;\leq\; \|\hat a'\|\cdot\|\hat b - \hat b'\| \;=\; \|\hat b - \hat b'\|,$$
using $\|\hat a\| = \|\hat a'\| = 1$ (unit vectors on the McGucken
Sphere). Therefore
$$|\langle CHSH\rangle| \;\leq\; \|\hat b + \hat b'\| + \|\hat b - \hat b'\|.$$

*Sub-step B-3c: Perpendicularity of the sum and difference.* The vectors
$\hat b + \hat b'$ and $\hat b - \hat b'$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are
orthogonal:
$$(\hat b + \hat b') \cdot (\hat b - \hat b') \;=\; \|\hat b\|^2 - \|\hat b'\|^2 \;=\; 1 - 1 \;=\; 0,$$
using $\|\hat b\| = \|\hat b'\| = 1$. The squared lengths are
$$\|\hat b \pm \hat b'\|^2 \;=\; \|\hat b\|^2 \pm 2\,\hat b\cdot\hat b' + \|\hat b'\|^2 \;=\; 1 \pm 2\,\hat b\cdot\hat b' + 1 \;=\; 2\,(1 \pm \hat b\cdot\hat b').$$
Setting $x := \hat b\cdot\hat b' \in [-1, 1]$ (the inner product of two
unit vectors lies in this interval):
$$\|\hat b + \hat b'\| \;=\; \sqrt{2(1 + x)}, \qquad \|\hat b - \hat b'\| \;=\; \sqrt{2(1 - x)}.$$

*Sub-step B-3d: Maximization via calculus.* Define
$$f(x) \;:=\; \sqrt{2(1+x)} + \sqrt{2(1-x)}, \qquad x \in [-1, 1].$$ We
find the maximum of $f$ on the closed interval $[-1, 1]$.

*Endpoint values.* $f(-1) = 0 + \sqrt 4 = 2$ and
$f(1) = \sqrt 4 + 0 = 2$.

*Critical points.* Differentiate $f$ on the open interval $(-1, 1)$:
$$f'(x) \;=\; \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2(1+x)}} - \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2(1-x)}} \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2(1+x)}} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2(1-x)}}.$$
Setting $f'(x) = 0$ requires $\sqrt{2(1+x)} = \sqrt{2(1-x)}$,
equivalently $1 + x = 1 - x$, i.e., $x = 0$. This is the unique critical
point in $(-1, 1)$. The value is
$$f(0) \;=\; \sqrt 2 + \sqrt 2 \;=\; 2\sqrt 2 \;\approx\; 2.828.$$

*Verification of maximum.* Second derivative on $(-1, 1)$:
$$f''(x) \;=\; -\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{[2(1+x)]^{3/2}}\cdot 2 - \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{[2(1-x)]^{3/2}}\cdot 2 \;=\; -\frac{2}{[2(1+x)]^{3/2}} - \frac{2}{[2(1-x)]^{3/2}} \;<\; 0$$
for all $x \in (-1, 1)$, so $f$ is concave on $(-1, 1)$. Combined with
$f(0) = 2\sqrt 2 > 2 = f(\pm 1)$, the maximum of $f$ on $[-1, 1]$ is
attained at the interior critical point $x = 0$, i.e., at
$\hat b \cdot \hat b' = 0$ (perpendicular measurement directions).

*Sub-step B-3e: Conclusion.*
$$|\langle CHSH\rangle| \;\leq\; \|\hat b + \hat b'\| + \|\hat b - \hat b'\| \;=\; f(\hat b\cdot\hat b') \;\leq\; \max_{x \in [-1, 1]} f(x) \;=\; f(0) \;=\; 2\sqrt 2.$$
The Tsirelson bound is saturated when (i) Cauchy--Schwarz is saturated,
i.e., $\hat a \parallel (\hat b + \hat b')/\|\hat b + \hat b'\|$ and
$\hat a' \parallel (\hat b - \hat b')/\|\hat b - \hat b'\|$, and (ii)
$\hat b \perp \hat b'$. Both conditions hold at the explicit settings of
Step B-2: with $\hat b = (\hat z + \hat x)/\sqrt 2$ and
$\hat b' = (\hat z - \hat x)/\sqrt 2$, we have
$\hat b \cdot \hat b' = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 - 1) = 0$ (perpendicular),
$\hat b + \hat b' = \sqrt 2\,\hat z$ (aligned with $\hat a = \hat z$),
and $\hat b - \hat b' = \sqrt 2\,\hat x$ (aligned with
$\hat a' = \hat x$). The Sphere-Haar Geometric Channel derivation therefore
exhibits the Tsirelson bound and its explicit saturation, using only
elementary Euclidean geometry on the McGucken Sphere $S^2$ and
Cauchy--Schwarz on $\mathbb{R}^3$. $\square$
:::

### Algebraic Channel derivation (QA3 nonlocality via operator-norm bound)

::: channela
*Algebraic Channel Derivation 13.2* (Tsirelson bound from operator-algebraic
Cauchy--Schwarz on CHSH-squared). The Algebraic Channel derivation proceeds in
five explicit steps, each anchored to the McGucken-derived Hilbert space
and operator algebra where applicable.

**Step CA-1: McGucken-derived inputs.** The proof uses three inputs:

1.  The Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3\mathbf{x})$
    for a single subsystem and the tensor-product Hilbert space
    $\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B$ for two independent subsystems
    (Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}, derived from
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the rank-$2$ Minkowski metric of
    Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}; the tensor-product structure for
    spacelike-separated subsystems descends from Stone--von Neumann
    uniqueness applied to the joint observable algebra, QA4).

2.  The locality condition: for $\hat A_i$ acting on $\mathcal{H}_A$ and
    $\hat B_j$ acting on $\mathcal{H}_B$ at spacelike-separated spatial
    regions, $[\hat A_i, \hat B_j] = 0$. This is the tensor-product
    factorisation of operators on $\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B$:
    $\hat A_i = \hat A_i^{(\mathrm{loc})} \otimes \mathbf{1}_B$,
    $\hat B_j = \mathbf{1}_A \otimes \hat B_j^{(\mathrm{loc})}$, with
    commutativity following from
    $\hat A_i \hat B_j = \hat A_i^{(\mathrm{loc})} \otimes \hat B_j^{(\mathrm{loc})} = \hat B_j \hat A_i$
    (Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Vol. I, §II.4).

3.  Elementary operator-norm submultiplicativity and the $C^*$-identity
    $\|\hat T^*\hat T\| = \|\hat T\|^2$ on $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$
    (Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Vol. I, Theorem VI.6 on the spectral
    radius for self-adjoint operators).

**Step CA-2: Dichotomic operator algebra.** Let $\hat A, \hat A'$ be
self-adjoint operators on $\mathcal{H}_A$ with eigenvalues in
$\{-1, +1\}$, and $\hat B, \hat B'$ analogous operators on
$\mathcal{H}_B$. The dichotomic condition implies
$$\hat A^2 \;=\; \hat A'^2 \;=\; \hat B^2 \;=\; \hat B'^2 \;=\; \mathbf{1},$$
by spectral decomposition: a self-adjoint operator $\hat T$ with
eigenvalues $\lambda \in \{-1, +1\}$ satisfies
$\hat T = \hat P_+ - \hat P_-$ with $\hat P_{\pm}$ the projections onto
the $\pm 1$ eigenspaces; squaring gives
$\hat T^2 = \hat P_+^2 - \hat P_+\hat P_- - \hat P_-\hat P_+ + \hat P_-^2 = \hat P_+ + \hat P_- = \mathbf{1}$
(using $\hat P_\pm^2 = \hat P_\pm$ and
$\hat P_+\hat P_- = \hat P_-\hat P_+ = 0$ for orthogonal projections).

Define the CHSH operator
$$\hat S \;:=\; \hat A\,\hat B + \hat A\,\hat B' + \hat A'\,\hat B - \hat A'\,\hat B'.$$
Each term $\hat A_i\hat B_j$ is the product of two commuting
self-adjoint operators, hence self-adjoint:
$(\hat A_i\hat B_j)^* = \hat B_j^*\hat A_i^* = \hat B_j\hat A_i = \hat A_i\hat B_j$
(using locality $[\hat A_i, \hat B_j] = 0$ in the last step). The CHSH
operator $\hat S$ is a real linear combination of four self-adjoint
operators, hence self-adjoint.

**Step CA-3: CHSH-squared identity by full expansion.** Expanding
$\hat S^2 = (\hat A\hat B + \hat A\hat B' + \hat A'\hat B - \hat A'\hat B')^2$
gives $4 \times 4 = 16$ products, grouped into four classes:

*Class (i) Diagonal squares* (four products):
$$(\hat A\hat B)^2 + (\hat A\hat B')^2 + (\hat A'\hat B)^2 + (-\hat A'\hat B')^2 \;=\; 4\,\mathbf{1},$$
each squaring to $\mathbf{1}$ via
$(\hat A_i\hat B_j)^2 = \hat A_i\hat B_j\hat A_i\hat B_j = \hat A_i^2\hat B_j^2 = \mathbf{1}\cdot\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}$
using locality to commute the inner $\hat B_j$ past $\hat A_i$.

*Class (ii) Same-$A$ cross terms* (four products): $$\begin{aligned}
  (\hat A\hat B)(\hat A\hat B') + (\hat A\hat B')(\hat A\hat B) &\;=\; \hat A^2\hat B\hat B' + \hat A^2\hat B'\hat B \;=\; \hat B\hat B' + \hat B'\hat B \;=\; \{\hat B,\hat B'\}, \\
  (\hat A'\hat B)(-\hat A'\hat B') + (-\hat A'\hat B')(\hat A'\hat B) &\;=\; -\hat A'^2\hat B\hat B' - \hat A'^2\hat B'\hat B \;=\; -\{\hat B,\hat B'\}.
\end{aligned}$$ Class (ii) total:
$\{\hat B,\hat B'\} - \{\hat B,\hat B'\} = 0$. The same-$A$/same-$A'$
contributions cancel exactly because the two summands have opposite
signs.

*Class (iii) Same-$B$ cross terms* (four products): $$\begin{aligned}
  (\hat A\hat B)(\hat A'\hat B) + (\hat A'\hat B)(\hat A\hat B) &\;=\; \hat A\hat A'\hat B^2 + \hat A'\hat A\hat B^2 \;=\; \{\hat A,\hat A'\}, \\
  (\hat A\hat B')(-\hat A'\hat B') + (-\hat A'\hat B')(\hat A\hat B') &\;=\; -\hat A\hat A'\hat B'^2 - \hat A'\hat A\hat B'^2 \;=\; -\{\hat A,\hat A'\}.
\end{aligned}$$ Class (iii) total:
$\{\hat A,\hat A'\} - \{\hat A,\hat A'\} = 0$. The same-$B$/same-$B'$
contributions cancel for the same reason.

*Class (iv) Cross terms with different $A$ and different $B$* (four
products): $$\begin{aligned}
  (\hat A\hat B)(-\hat A'\hat B') + (-\hat A'\hat B')(\hat A\hat B) + (\hat A\hat B')(\hat A'\hat B) + (\hat A'\hat B)(\hat A\hat B').
\end{aligned}$$ Use locality $[\hat A_i, \hat B_j] = 0$ to reorder all
$A$-factors to the left and $B$-factors to the right: $$\begin{aligned}
  (\hat A\hat B)(-\hat A'\hat B') &\;=\; -\hat A\hat A'\hat B\hat B', \\
  (-\hat A'\hat B')(\hat A\hat B) &\;=\; -\hat A'\hat A\hat B'\hat B, \\
  (\hat A\hat B')(\hat A'\hat B) &\;=\; \hat A\hat A'\hat B'\hat B, \\
  (\hat A'\hat B)(\hat A\hat B') &\;=\; \hat A'\hat A\hat B\hat B'.
\end{aligned}$$ Group by $A$-prefix:
$$\underbrace{\bigl[-\hat A\hat A'\hat B\hat B' + \hat A\hat A'\hat B'\hat B\bigr]}_{\hat A\hat A'\text{-terms}} \,+\, \underbrace{\bigl[-\hat A'\hat A\hat B'\hat B + \hat A'\hat A\hat B\hat B'\bigr]}_{\hat A'\hat A\text{-terms}} \;=\; -\hat A\hat A'\,[\hat B,\hat B'] + \hat A'\hat A\,[\hat B,\hat B'],$$
where $[\hat B, \hat B'] = \hat B\hat B' - \hat B'\hat B$. Factor the
common $[\hat B, \hat B']$:
$$=\; (\hat A'\hat A - \hat A\hat A')\,[\hat B,\hat B'] \;=\; -[\hat A,\hat A']\,[\hat B,\hat B'].$$
Class (iv) total: $-[\hat A,\hat A'][\hat B,\hat B']$.

*Sum of classes (i) through (iv).*
$$\hat S^2 \;=\; 4\,\mathbf{1} + 0 + 0 + \bigl(-[\hat A,\hat A'][\hat B,\hat B']\bigr) \;=\; 4\,\mathbf{1} \,-\, [\hat A,\hat A']\,[\hat B,\hat B'].
  \label{eq:CHSH-squared-channelA}$$ This is the CHSH-squared identity,
derived by full term-by-term expansion from the dichotomic condition
$\hat T^2 = \mathbf{1}$ and the locality $[\hat A_i, \hat B_j] = 0$
alone.

**Step CA-4: Operator-norm bound on $\hat S$.**

*Sub-step CA-4a: Norm of dichotomic operators.* For a self-adjoint
operator $\hat T$ with eigenvalues in $\{-1, +1\}$, the operator norm
equals the spectral radius (Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Vol. I,
Theorem VI.6), so
$\|\hat A\| = \|\hat A'\| = \|\hat B\| = \|\hat B'\| = 1$.

*Sub-step CA-4b: Commutator-norm bound.* By the triangle inequality on
the operator norm:
$$\|[\hat A,\hat A']\| \;=\; \|\hat A\hat A' - \hat A'\hat A\| \;\leq\; \|\hat A\hat A'\| + \|\hat A'\hat A\|.$$
By submultiplicativity ($\|\hat S\hat T\| \leq \|\hat S\|\,\|\hat T\|$
on $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$):
$$\|\hat A\hat A'\| + \|\hat A'\hat A\| \;\leq\; \|\hat A\|\,\|\hat A'\| + \|\hat A'\|\,\|\hat A\| \;=\; 1\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 1 \;=\; 2.$$
Hence $\|[\hat A, \hat A']\| \leq 2$. Identical argument:
$\|[\hat B, \hat B']\| \leq 2$.

*Sub-step CA-4c: Bound on the product of commutators.* By
submultiplicativity again:
$$\|[\hat A,\hat A']\,[\hat B,\hat B']\| \;\leq\; \|[\hat A,\hat A']\|\cdot\|[\hat B,\hat B']\| \;\leq\; 2\cdot 2 \;=\; 4.$$

*Sub-step CA-4d: Bound on $\hat S^2$.* From the identity
[\[eq:CHSH-squared-channelA\]](#eq:CHSH-squared-channelA){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:CHSH-squared-channelA"} and the triangle inequality:
$$\|\hat S^2\| \;=\; \|4\,\mathbf{1} - [\hat A,\hat A']\,[\hat B,\hat B']\| \;\leq\; \|4\,\mathbf{1}\| + \|[\hat A,\hat A']\,[\hat B,\hat B']\| \;\leq\; 4 + 4 \;=\; 8,$$
using $\|\lambda\mathbf{1}\| = |\lambda|$.

*Sub-step CA-4e: Bound on $\hat S$ via the $C^*$-identity.* The CHSH
operator $\hat S$ is self-adjoint (Step CA-2); for self-adjoint
$\hat T$, the $C^*$-identity gives
$\|\hat T^2\| = \|\hat T^*\hat T\| = \|\hat T\|^2$ (Reed--Simon
[@ReedSimon1980] Vol. I, the $C^*$-property of
$\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$). Therefore
$$\|\hat S\|^2 \;=\; \|\hat S^2\| \;\leq\; 8, \qquad \text{hence} \qquad \|\hat S\| \;\leq\; \sqrt 8 \;=\; 2\sqrt 2.$$

**Step CA-5: Expectation-value bound via Cauchy--Schwarz.** For any
normalized state
$\lvert \psi  \rangle\in \mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B$
($\|\psi\| = 1$):
$$|\langle\psi,\, \hat S\,\psi\rangle| \;\overset{\text{C-S}}{\leq}\; \|\psi\|\,\|\hat S\psi\| \;\overset{\text{op. norm}}{\leq}\; \|\hat S\|\,\|\psi\|^2 \;=\; \|\hat S\| \;\leq\; 2\sqrt 2,$$
where the first inequality is Cauchy--Schwarz on
$\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B$
(Theorem [3.2](#thm:cauchy-schwarz){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:cauchy-schwarz"}) and the second is the definition of the
operator norm $\|\hat S\| = \sup_{\|\psi\|=1}\|\hat S\psi\|$. The
Tsirelson bound $|\langle CHSH\rangle_{\mathrm{QM}}| \leq 2\sqrt 2$
holds for every normalized state on
$\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B$. $\square$
:::

::: {#rmk:tsirelson-channelA-machinery .remark}
*Remark 13.3* (McGucken machinery used in the Algebraic Channel Tsirelson
proof). Every step is forced by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ alone, with no
external postulate essential.

**McGucken machinery used.** (1) The tensor-product Hilbert space
$\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B$ as a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (the joint observable algebra is the Stone--von
Neumann unique irreducible representation on the joint system, Algebraic Channel
axiom QA4); (2) the locality assumption
$[\hat A \otimes \mathbb{1}, \mathbb{1}\otimes \hat B] = 0$, which is
itself the statement that spacelike-separated regions of $M_{G}$ have
non-overlapping spatial slices
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}); (3) the operator-norm inequalities on
$\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B$, which are elementary
linear-algebra facts (operator-norm submultiplicativity, the spectral
characterisation $\|\hat T\| = \sqrt{\|\hat T^\dagger \hat T\|}$ for
self-adjoint $\hat T$); (4) the CHSH-squared algebraic identity
$\hat S^2 = 4\mathbb{1}- [\hat A, \hat A'][\hat B, \hat B']$, a direct
algebraic consequence of the eigenvalue-$\pm 1$ constraint and the
locality assumption.

**No external machinery is essential.** The Tsirelson--Cirel'son
original derivation (1980) used the same algebraic argument; the
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework's added value is establishing the operator algebra
itself as a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

**Geometric Channel saturation and upper bound.** The Geometric Channel proof below
(Sphere singlet correlation $E(a, b) = -\hat a\cdot\hat b$ with explicit
saturation at
$(\hat z, \hat x, (\hat z+\hat x)/\sqrt{2}, (\hat z-\hat x)/\sqrt{2})$
giving $\langle CHSH\rangle = -2\sqrt{2}$) supplies the geometric
content; the McGucken No-Signaling Theorem
(Theorem [17.32](#thm:mcgucken-no-signaling){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:mcgucken-no-signaling"},
Chapter [17](#ch:nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:nonlocality"}) supplies the mutual calibration with
marginal flatness.
:::

### Disjointness audit {#disjointness-audit-11}

**Geometric Channel:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, singlet $SO(3)$-Haar
correlation, $-\hat{a}\cdot\hat{b}$ inner-product structure,
Cauchy--Schwarz on inner products on $S^2$.

**Algebraic Channel:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, dichotomic operator algebra,
locality $[\hat{A}, \hat{B}] = 0$, operator-norm bounds,
$\hat{S}^2 = 4 - [\hat{A},\hat{A}'][\hat{B},\hat{B}']$ identity.

**Intersection:**
$\{(\mathrm{McP}), |\langle CHSH\rangle|_{\text{QM}} \le 2\sqrt{2}\}$.
*Disjointness verified.*

### Empirical anchor

-   Aspect, Dalibard, Roger 1982 [@Aspect1982]: first
    space-like-separated Bell-inequality test,
    $\langle CHSH\rangle_{\text{meas}} = 2.697 \pm 0.015$, violating the
    classical bound of 2 by $\sim 40$ standard deviations.

-   Hensen et al. 2015 [@Hensen2015]: first loophole-free Bell test
    using NV (nitrogen--vacancy)-center spins separated by 1.3 km;
    $\langle CHSH\rangle_{\text{meas}} = 2.42 \pm 0.20$, closing both
    detection and locality loopholes simultaneously.

-   BIG Bell Test 2018 [@BigBellTest2018]: Bell test using
    human-generated randomness, closing the freedom-of-choice loophole.

The Tsirelson bound is saturated by experiment within statistical and
systematic uncertainties.

## QM T14: The Four Major Dualities {#ch:dualities}

> *The McGucken Principle.* The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality.
> Every result below descends from that expansion.


*Recall.* the McGucken Principle ($\mathrm{McP}$:
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$) asserts that the fourth spacetime dimension
$x_4$ expands at the velocity of light $c$, carrying the
perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguishes it from the spatial
three. Throughout this chapter, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ refers to this
principle and to the five-clause content (i)--(v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: (i) *invariance* --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content; (ii) *spherical symmetry* --- the
expansion is isotropic in the spatial three, with the set of events
reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a 2-sphere of radius
$c\tau$; (iii) *monotonicity* --- the integral curve is strictly
monotonically increasing in $t$, fixing the arrow of $x_4$-advance; (iv)
*Lorentz consistency* --- the structure is $SO^+(1,3)$-invariant on
$M_{G}$; (v) *global validity* --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at
every event of $M_{G}$. The integrated kinematic shadow
$x_4 = ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is the kinematic shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the central fact.

### Statement

::: {#thm:QMT14 .theorem}
**Theorem 14.1** (QM T14: Four Major Dualities, = Theorem 73 (Algebraic Channel)
and Theorem 96 (Geometric Channel) of [@Syn-2026]). *The four major dualities of
quantum mechanics --- wave--particle duality, position--momentum
(Fourier) duality, time--energy duality, matter--antimatter duality ---
are four readings of the same McGucken Sphere $S_p$ generated
by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at every event $p \in M_{G}$. Each duality
pair corresponds to a specific mathematical conjugation on the Hilbert
space $\mathcal{H}$ whose geometric origin is a precise feature of $S_p$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The proof has seven steps. Each of the four
dualities is exhibited as a pair of complementary readings of the same
underlying McGucken Sphere $S_p$ generated by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
at every event $p \in M_{G}$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i)--(v), with the integrated kinematic shadow
$x_{4}= ict$ as the kinematic shadow per
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}). Steps 1--4 establish each duality
in turn with explicit Hilbert-space conjugation. Step 5 records the
synthesis. Step 6 verifies the global validity of the four-duality
structure across $M_{G}$. Step 7 closes with the McGucken anchoring.

**Step 1: Wave--particle duality as apex/wavefront reading of $S_p$.**
By Definition [4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:sphere"} of
Chapter [4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:foundations"}, the McGucken Sphere $S_p$ at source event
$p \in M_{G}$ consists of:

-   the *apex* --- the source event $p = (\mathbf{x}_p, t_p)$ itself, a
    single spacetime point where the Sphere is sourced;

-   the *wavefront* --- the 2-sphere
    $M^{+}_{p}(t) = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 : |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_p| = c(t - t_p)\}$
    at lab time $t > t_p$, propagating outward at rate $c$ by
    Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
    reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (ii) (spherical symmetry of
    $x_{4}$-expansion).

By Lemma [6.6](#lem:sphere-apex-wavefront){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:sphere-apex-wavefront"}, both readings coexist on the
same Sphere: the apex reading concentrates the wavefunction at the
source event (particle locus), and the wavefront reading distributes the
wavefunction over the 2-sphere of radius $c(t - t_p)$ (wave extension).
The explicit Hilbert-space realisation is the spherical-wave amplitude
$\psi(\mathbf{x}, t) = f(r - ct)/r$ with
$r = |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_p|$
(Lemma [1.5](#lem:spherical-wave-kinematics){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:spherical-wave-kinematics"}), which simultaneously
exhibits:

-   particle-localization: the source-region $r \to 0$ singularity
    (delta-function-like apex);

-   wave-extension: the $r > 0$ wavefront propagating outward at rate
    $c$ with $\Box\psi = 0$ off the source locus.

By Theorem [6.1](#thm:QMT6){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT6"}
(Wave--Particle Duality), the position eigenbasis
$\{\lvert \mathbf \rangle{x}\}$ and momentum eigenbasis
$\{\lvert \mathbf \rangle{p}\}$ are Fourier-conjugate complete bases for
$\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$
(Lemma [6.2](#lem:position-localized){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:position-localized"} for the position-localized states,
Lemma [6.3](#lem:momentum-planewave){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:momentum-planewave"} for the momentum-plane-wave states):
each $\psi \in \mathcal{H}$ admits both representations
$\psi(\mathbf{x}) = \braket{\mathbf{x}|\psi}$ (position-localized) and
$\tilde\psi(\mathbf{p}) = \braket{\mathbf{p}|\psi}$
(momentum-plane-wave) via the Fourier transform of
Lemma [6.4](#lem:fourier-conjugate){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:fourier-conjugate"}. Wave--particle duality has the
reading of the apex/wavefront decomposition of $S_p$
generated by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

**Step 2: Position--momentum duality as Fourier-conjugate readings of
$M^{+}_{p}(t)$.** By Theorem [10.1](#thm:QMT10){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT10"} (Canonical Commutation Relation), the position
operator $\hat{q}^j$ and momentum operator $\hat{p}_k$ on $\mathcal{H}$
satisfy
$$[\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k] \;=\; i\hbar\,\delta^j_k\,\mathbf{1}, \qquad j, k = 1, 2, 3.$$
The operators are Fourier-conjugate self-adjoint generators: $\hat{q}$
generates spatial-momentum translation (eigenvalue $\mathbf{x}$ on
$\lvert \mathbf \rangle{x}$), and $\hat{p}$ generates phase
multiplication (eigenvalue $\mathbf{p}$ on $\lvert \mathbf \rangle{p}$),
with the position/momentum representations connected by Fourier
transform (Lemma [6.4](#lem:fourier-conjugate){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:fourier-conjugate"}). On the McGucken Sphere wavefront
$M^{+}_{p}(t)$, the position operator is the spatial coordinate
$\mathbf{x}$ on the 2-sphere of radius $c(t-t_p)$ centred at
$\mathbf{x}_p$, and the momentum operator $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\nabla$ acts
on plane-wave eigenfunctions $e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}}$ with
eigenvalue $\hbar\mathbf{k}$. The Fourier-conjugate structure descends
from the McGucken-Sphere construction: the wavefront sphere of radius
$r$ centred at $\mathbf{x}_p$ admits a plane-wave expansion
$$\psi(\mathbf{x}, t) \;=\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi\hbar)^{3/2}}\,\tilde\psi(\mathbf{k}, t)\,e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}/\hbar}$$
on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ (Fourier completeness via Plancherel-Parseval,
Lemma [6.4](#lem:fourier-conjugate){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:fourier-conjugate"}), with the conjugate pair
$(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{k})$ Fourier-dual. Position-on-wavefront and
wavevector-of-wavefront have the reading of Fourier-conjugate
operators on the McGucken-Sphere wavefront, with the conjugation forced
by the $SO(3)$-isotropy of the wavefront from
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (ii). The Hilbert-space conjugation is
the canonical commutator $[\hat{q}^j, \hat{p}_k] = i\hbar\delta^j_k$,
derived in Algebraic Channel
(Lemma [\[lem:QMT10-channelA-proof\]](#lem:QMT10-channelA-proof){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT10-channelA-proof"}) and Geometric Channel (geometric
construction in Chapter [10](#ch:ccr){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:ccr"}) from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via Stone's theorem
applied to translation invariance.

**Step 3: Time--energy duality as apex-time / phase-rate reading of
$S_p$.** By Theorem [3.1](#thm:QMT3){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT3"} (Planck--Einstein, $E = \hbar\omega$), time and
energy are conjugate variables generated by
$\hat{H}= i\hbar\,\partial_t$ via Stone's theorem applied to
time-translation invariance of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Lemma [7.3](#lem:hamiltonian-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:hamiltonian-generator"}, with time-translation invariance
forced by Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (i)). On the McGucken Sphere $S_p$:

-   *time* corresponds to the apex proper-time advance --- the worldline
    parameter $\tau$ along which the integrated $x_{4}= ict$ accumulates
    by Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
    reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"};

-   *energy* corresponds to the rate of Sphere phase cycling
    $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$
    (Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT4"}, the Compton oscillation frequency) at which
    the rest-frame wavefunction
    $\psi_{\mathrm{rest}}(\tau) = \psi_0 e^{-i\omega_C\tau}$ advances.

Apex proper-time advance and Sphere phase-cycling rate are conjugate
readings of $S_p$ generated by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The
Hilbert-space realisation is the time-energy commutator relation
$[\hat{H}, t]$ acting on wavefunctions via $i\hbar\partial_t$, with the
$\Delta t\cdot\Delta E \ge \hbar/2$ uncertainty interpreted as a
relation between lifetimes of energy eigenstates and energy spread.

*Caveat:* the parameter $t$ in standard QM has the role of a coordinate
label rather than a self-adjoint operator on $\mathcal{H}$, since the
Pauli objection forbids a self-adjoint time operator with
$[\hat T, \hat{H}] = i\hbar$ on a Hilbert space with $\hat{H}$ bounded
below (Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Vol. I, §X.5: if $\hat T$ were
self-adjoint with $[\hat T, \hat{H}] = i\hbar$, then $\hat{H}$ would
have spectrum on all of $\mathbb{R}$ by the Stone--von Neumann theorem,
contradicting boundedness from below). The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework treats $t$
operationally as the coordinate parameter along the worldline, and the
time-energy uncertainty is the standard Mandelshtam--Tamm formulation
$\Delta t \cdot \Delta E \ge \hbar/2$ where $\Delta t$ is the
characteristic timescale of an observable's change rather than the
spread of a time-eigenvalue.

**Step 4: Matter--antimatter duality as $\pm ic$ branch reading of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.** By
Theorem [9.1](#thm:QMT9){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT9"}
(Dirac equation, Geometric Channel and Algebraic Channel), the Dirac equation
$(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - mc/\hbar)\psi = 0$ on $M_{G}$ admits both
positive-energy ($E > 0$) and negative-energy ($E < 0$) solutions, which
in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework
(Remark [9.16](#rmk:dirac-antimatter){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:dirac-antimatter"}) correspond directly to the
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= +ic$ and $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= -ic$ branches of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$:

-   the matter branch ($+ic$): the Sphere expands at rate $+ic$ along
    the worldline, with $x_4(t) = +ict$ being the mere integrated kinematic shadow of $\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = +ic$. This
    branch is selected by
    Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
    reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iii) (monotonicity) for the
    matter sector, with the matter orientation condition (M) of
    Definition [9.6](#def:matter-orientation-M){reference-type="ref"
    reference="def:matter-orientation-M"}
    (Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:dirac"})
    requiring $\Psi = \Psi_0\exp(+I\cdot kx_4)$ with $k = mc/\hbar > 0$.

-   the antimatter branch ($-ic$): the Sphere expands at rate $-ic$
    along the antimatter worldline, with $x_4(t) = -ict$. This branch is
    the antimatter orientation condition $\overline{\mathrm{M}}$ of
    Definition [9.6](#def:matter-orientation-M){reference-type="ref"
    reference="def:matter-orientation-M"},
    $\Psi = \Psi_0\exp(-I\cdot kx_4)$ with $k > 0$.

The two branches are exchanged by CPT
(Lemma [9.12](#lem:CPT-as-4D-inversion){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:CPT-as-4D-inversion"}: full 4D coordinate inversion
$\mathrm{CPT}: \Psi \mapsto I\Psi I^{-1} = -\Psi$ up to phase, the
algebraic content of branch exchange). The Hilbert-space conjugation is
the charge-conjugation operator $C = i\gamma^2\gamma^0$
(Lemma [9.11](#lem:charge-conjugation-component){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:charge-conjugation-component"}), implementing the
$x_{4}$-reversal at the matrix level. Matter--antimatter duality has the
reading of the $\pm ic$-sign branch structure of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at every event $p$.

**Step 5: Synthesis --- four dualities as four readings of one Sphere.**
The four dualities established in Steps 1--4 are four complementary
readings of the same underlying McGucken Sphere $S_p$:
$$\begin{array}{lll}
  \text{Step 1 (wave/particle):} & \text{apex vs.\ wavefront} & \text{(spatial structure)} \\
  \text{Step 2 (position/momentum):} & \text{position-on-wavefront vs.\ wavevector-of-wavefront} & \text{(Fourier conjugation)} \\
  \text{Step 3 (time/energy):} & \text{apex proper-time vs.\ phase-cycling rate} & \text{(Stone-generator conjugation)} \\
  \text{Step 4 (matter/antimatter):} & \text{$+ic$ expansion vs.\ $-ic$ expansion} & \text{($\pm i$ branch sign)}
  \end{array}$$ Each duality is a pair of complementary readings of the
Sphere extracted by a specific Hilbert-space conjugation (Fourier
transform, Stone generator, charge conjugation). The four dualities
share the same geometric origin: the decomposition of $S_p$ generated by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ carries these four complementary readings simultaneously, and each Hilbert-space conjugation extracts the
corresponding pair. The unification has the reading of the
McGucken-Sphere geometry: each duality pair corresponds to a precise
mathematical conjugation on the Hilbert space
(Theorems [6.1](#thm:QMT6){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT6"},
[10.1](#thm:QMT10){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT10"},
[3.1](#thm:QMT3){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT3"},
[9.1](#thm:QMT9){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT9"}) whose
geometric origin is a specific feature of $S_p$.

**Step 6: Global validity of the four-duality structure on $M_{G}$.** By
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (v) (global validity:
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event of $M_{G}$), the same McGucken Sphere $S_p$ exists at every event
$p \in M_{G}$. Consequently, the four-duality structure of Steps 1--4
holds globally: every event $p \in M_{G}$ sources its own Sphere $S_p$
admitting the four readings, and the global wavefunction
$\psi$ on $M_{G}$ is a superposition of contributions from every source
event (Huygens iteration,
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (ii) extended via QB1, QB2 of
Chapter [1](#ch:wave-equation){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:wave-equation"}). The four dualities are global features
of the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ derived from the global structure of
$M_{G}$.

**Step 7: McGucken anchoring.** The four dualities trace to
four distinct features of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$:

-   Wave--particle: the Sphere has both an apex (the source event $p$)
    and a wavefront (the 2-sphere at radius $c(t-t_p)$), supplied by
    Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
    reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (i) (invariance: the principle
    holds at $p$) and clause (ii) (spherical symmetry of
    $x_{4}$-expansion);

-   Position--momentum: the spatial 3-translation invariance of
    $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ supplies the momentum operator via Stone's
    theorem (Lemma [2.2](#lem:phat-generator){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:phat-generator"}), with the Fourier conjugation
    forced by the $SO(3)$-isotropy of the wavefront;

-   Time--energy: the temporal 1-translation invariance of
    $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ supplies the Hamiltonian via Stone's
    theorem
    (Lemma [7.3](#lem:hamiltonian-generator){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:hamiltonian-generator"}), with the Compton
    oscillation rate $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ as the phase-cycling rate
    of the rest-frame Sphere;

-   Matter--antimatter: the $\pm i$ sign of the perpendicularity marker
    in $dx_4/dt = \pm ic$ supplies the matter--antimatter branch
    structure, with CPT exchanging the two branches.

The four dualities are the four readings of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at the Sphere level, made manifest in the
Hilbert space via the four corresponding conjugations. $\square$ ◻
:::

### Geometric Channel reading (geometric wavefront / Sphere structure)

::: channelb
*Geometric Channel Derivation 14.3* (Four dualities as Sphere readings).

1.  *Wave--Particle:* Sphere apex (particle) vs. Sphere wavefront
    (wave); both readings of $S_p$.

2.  *Position--Momentum:* Sphere position-on-wavefront vs. Sphere
    wavevector-of-wavefront; conjugate via the Sphere's spatial-Fourier
    structure.

3.  *Time--Energy:* Sphere apex proper-time advance vs. Sphere
    phase-cycling rate; conjugate via the Compton-coupling relation
    $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$.

4.  *Matter--Antimatter:* Sphere expansion at rate $+ic$ (matter branch)
    vs. Sphere expansion at rate $-ic$ (antimatter branch); both
    branches of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (the $\pm i$ sign).

Each duality is the reading multiplicity of $S_p$. ◻
:::

### Algebraic Channel reading (operator-algebraic / Stone--von Neumann)

::: channela
*Algebraic Channel Derivation 14.2* (Four dualities as operator-pair
conjugations).

1.  *Wave--Particle:* $\hat{q}$-eigenstates (particle-localized) and
    $\hat{p}$-eigenstates (plane waves), conjugate under Fourier
    (Theorem [6.1](#thm:QMT6){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT6"}).

2.  *Position--Momentum:* $\hat{q}$ and $\hat{p}$ with
    $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$, the canonical commutator
    (Theorem [10.5](#thm:QMT10-channelA){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT10-channelA"}).

3.  *Time--Energy:* time-translation generator $\hat{H}$
    (Theorem [3.1](#thm:QMT3){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT3"}), with the $\Delta t\,\Delta E \ge \hbar/2$
    relation parallel to position--momentum, with the subtlety that $t$
    enters as a coordinate label on $\mathcal{H}$ rather than a
    self-adjoint operator (Pauli objection, Step 3 of the master proof).

4.  *Matter--Antimatter:* positive- and negative-energy solutions of the
    Dirac equation, conjugate under CPT
    (Theorem [21.1](#thm:QMT21){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT21"} below).

Each pair is the operator-algebraic shadow of a feature of
the McGucken Sphere. ◻
:::


### Disjointness audit {#sec:QMT14-disjointness}

The two readings above reach the same four duality pairs through
machinery with empty intersection. The audit is stated in the same form
as the audits of QM T1--T13 and T15--T21.

| Duality pair | Geometric Channel machinery | Algebraic Channel machinery | Shared machinery |
|:-------------|:----------------------------|:----------------------------|:-----------------|
| Wave--particle | Sphere apex / wavefront readings of $S_p$ (Lemma 6.6, apex-wavefront duality; QB1) | $\hat q$- and $\hat p$-eigenstates conjugate under Fourier (Theorem 6.1) | None |
| Position--momentum | Position on the wavefront vs. wavevector of the wavefront, via the Sphere's spatial-Fourier structure (QB1 + clause (ii)) | $[\hat q, \hat p] = i\hbar$ via Stone and Stone--von Neumann (Theorem 10.5) | None |
| Time--energy | Apex proper-time advance vs. Sphere phase-cycling rate, via $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ (QB4) | Stone generator $\hat H = i\hbar\,\partial_t$ on the time-translation group (Theorem 3.1) | None |
| Matter--antimatter | Sphere expansion at $+ic$ and at $-ic$ as the two branches of the principle (C1 directional) | Positive- and negative-energy Dirac solutions conjugate under CPT (Theorem 21.1) | None |

The Geometric Channel column uses Sphere generation, the apex/wavefront
duality, the Compton phase rate, and the $\pm ic$ branch structure. The
Algebraic Channel column uses Fourier conjugation on $\mathcal{H}$,
Stone's theorem, Stone--von Neumann uniqueness, and CPT on Dirac
spinors. No entry appears in both columns, so the intersection of
intermediate machinery is $\{(\mathrm{McP})\}$ --- the McGucken
Principle itself --- together with the four duality pairs that are the
common output.

**Common source.** Both columns descend from
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}. C5 generates $S_p$ at every event, giving
the apex and wavefront readings that the Geometric column reads
directly; C2 supplies the perpendicularity marker whose Hilbert-space
image is the Fourier conjugation and the commutator that the Algebraic
column reads; C1 directional supplies the $\pm ic$ branch pair; C4
extends the structure to every event of $M_{G}$, which is Step 6 of the
master proof. The four dualities are therefore four readings of one
Sphere, reached twice.

**Scope of the two columns.** The entries above are readings rather than
independent derivations of new content: QM T14 collects four results
that Chapters 6, 10, 3 and 21 derive, and exhibits them as four
projections of a single Sphere. The disjointness recorded here is the
disjointness of the two readings, and the derivational disjointness of
the four underlying results is audited in those chapters.

### Empirical anchor

The four dualities are tested by:

-   double-slit experiments (wave--particle, Davisson--Germer
    [@Davisson1927] onwards);

-   Heisenberg uncertainty saturation by Gaussian wavepackets
    (position--momentum);

-   time-energy uncertainty in unstable particle lifetimes
    ($\Delta E \cdot \tau \ge \hbar/2$);

-   the discovery of the positron (Anderson 1932) and subsequent
    antiparticle physics (matter--antimatter).

## QM T15: The Feynman Path Integral {#ch:path-integral}

> *The McGucken Principle.* The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality.
> Every result below descends from that expansion.


*Recall.* the McGucken Principle ($\mathrm{McP}$:
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$) asserts that the fourth spacetime dimension
$x_4$ expands at the velocity of light $c$, carrying the
perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguishes it from the spatial
three. Throughout this chapter, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ refers to this
principle and to the five-clause content (i)--(v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: (i) *invariance* --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content; (ii) *spherical symmetry* --- the
expansion is isotropic in the spatial three, with the set of events
reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a 2-sphere of radius
$c\tau$; (iii) *monotonicity* --- the integral curve is strictly
monotonically increasing in $t$, fixing the arrow of $x_4$-advance; (iv)
*Lorentz consistency* --- the structure is $SO^+(1,3)$-invariant on
$M_{G}$; (v) *global validity* --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at
every event of $M_{G}$. The integrated kinematic shadow
$x_4 = ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is the kinematic shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the central fact.

### Statement

::: {#thm:QMT15 .theorem}
**Theorem 15.1** (QM T15: Feynman path integral, = Theorem 74 (Algebraic
Channel) and Theorem 97 (Geometric Channel) of [@Syn-2026]). *The propagator
$K(x_B, t_B; x_A, t_A) = \langle x_B | \hat{U}(t_B - t_A) | x_A\rangle$
admits the path-integral representation
$$K(x_B, t_B; x_A, t_A) = \int \mathcal{D}[\gamma]\,\exp\!\left(\frac{i}{\hbar}S[\gamma]\right),
\label{eq:Feynman-PI}$$ summed over all continuous paths
$\gamma: [t_A, t_B] \to \mathbb{R}^3$ from $\gamma(t_A) = x_A$ to
$\gamma(t_B) = x_B$, with $S[\gamma] = \int_{t_A}^{t_B} L\,dt$ the
classical action.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). We prove the path-integral representation along Algebraic Channel
(Trotter decomposition of $\hat{U}$) and Geometric Channel (iterated
McGucken-Sphere Huygens construction); the two are disjoint. Eight explicit steps establish the full result: four for
Algebraic Channel (Trotter algebra) and four for Geometric Channel (iterated Sphere
Huygens), both descending from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}).

**Step 1 (Algebraic Channel): Trotter product formula from time-translation
invariance.** By Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (i) (invariance of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ across events of $M_{G}$), time-translation
acts as a one-parameter group; by QA2 (Stone's theorem applied via
Lemma [7.3](#lem:hamiltonian-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:hamiltonian-generator"}), the time-evolution operator is
$\hat{U}(t) = \exp(-it\hat{H}/\hbar)$ with Hamiltonian
$\hat{H}= -\hbar^2\nabla^2/(2m) + V(\mathbf{x}) =: \hat T + \hat V$
(kinetic + potential, Lemmas [7.4](#lem:H-free){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:H-free"}--[7.5](#lem:H-potential){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:H-potential"}). Slice the time interval into $N$ short
steps of duration $\varepsilon = (t_B - t_A)/N$. The Trotter product
formula (Trotter [@Trotter1959]; Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Theorem
VIII.31) gives, for self-adjoint $\hat T, \hat V$ with appropriate
boundedness conditions:
$$\exp(-it\hat{H}/\hbar) = \lim_{N\to\infty}[\exp(-i\varepsilon\hat T/\hbar)\,\exp(-i\varepsilon\hat V/\hbar)]^N.$$

**Step 2 (Algebraic Channel): Insert position completeness.** Insert complete
sets of position eigenstates
$\mathbf{1} = \int d^3\mathbf{x}_k\,\lvert \mathbf{x}_k \rangle\langle \mathbf{x}_k \rvert$
between each pair of factors of the Trotter product:
$$\langle \mathbf{x}_B | \hat{U}| \mathbf{x}_A\rangle = \lim_{N\to\infty}\int\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}d^3\mathbf{x}_k\,\prod_{k=1}^{N}\langle\mathbf{x}_k|e^{-i\varepsilon\hat T/\hbar}e^{-i\varepsilon\hat V/\hbar}|\mathbf{x}_{k-1}\rangle,$$
with $\mathbf{x}_0 := \mathbf{x}_A, \mathbf{x}_N := \mathbf{x}_B$.

**Step 3 (Algebraic Channel): Matrix elements from the Gaussian short-time
kernel.** The kinetic-energy matrix element evaluates by Fourier
transform:
$$\langle\mathbf{x}_k|e^{-i\varepsilon\hat T/\hbar}|\mathbf{x}_{k-1}\rangle = \left(\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}\right)^{3/2}\,\exp\!\left[\frac{im(\mathbf{x}_k - \mathbf{x}_{k-1})^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\right].$$
This is the free-particle short-time kernel of
Lemma [7.10](#lem:gaussian-normalization){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:gaussian-normalization"}, evaluated for
$\hat T = -\hbar^2\nabla^2/(2m)$ via the standard Fresnel-integral
identity. The potential factor is diagonal in position:
$\langle\mathbf{x}_{k-1}|e^{-i\varepsilon\hat V/\hbar}|\mathbf{x}_{k-1}\rangle = e^{-i\varepsilon V(\mathbf{x}_{k-1})/\hbar}$.

**Step 4 (Algebraic Channel): Combine into action exponent and pass to
continuum.** Substituting the matrix elements:
$$\langle\mathbf{x}_B|\hat{U}|\mathbf{x}_A\rangle = \lim_{N\to\infty}\int\prod_k d^3\mathbf{x}_k\,(\mathcal{N}_\varepsilon)^N\,\exp\!\left[\frac{i\varepsilon}{\hbar}\sum_{k=1}^N\left(\frac{m(\mathbf{x}_k - \mathbf{x}_{k-1})^2}{2\varepsilon^2} - V(\mathbf{x}_{k-1})\right)\right].$$
The exponent is
$i\varepsilon\sum_k[\tfrac{1}{2}m\dot{\mathbf{x}}_k^2 - V]/\hbar$. In
the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$, this converges to
$(i/\hbar)\int_{t_A}^{t_B} L(\mathbf{x}, \dot{\mathbf{x}})\,dt = (i/\hbar)S[\gamma]$
where $L = \tfrac{1}{2}m\dot{\mathbf{x}}^2 - V$ is the classical
Lagrangian. The integration $\int\prod_k d^3\mathbf{x}_k$ becomes the
formal path integral $\int\mathcal{D}[\gamma]$ over continuous paths
$\gamma$ from $\mathbf{x}_A$ to $\mathbf{x}_B$. Therefore
$K(\mathbf{x}_B, t_B; \mathbf{x}_A, t_A) = \int\mathcal{D}[\gamma]\,\exp(iS[\gamma]/\hbar)$,
the Feynman path integral
[\[eq:Feynman-PI\]](#eq:Feynman-PI){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:Feynman-PI"}. The factor $i$ in $iS/\hbar$ traces (via the
$i$ in $\hat T = -\hbar^2\nabla^2/(2m)$'s Stone-generator origin and the
$i$ in $\exp(-i\varepsilon\hat{H}/\hbar)$) back to the $i$ in
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}).

**Step 5 (Geometric Channel): McGucken Sphere at every event.** By
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (v) (global validity),
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event $p \in M_{G}$; by clause
(ii) (spherical symmetry), the $x_{4}$-expansion at every event produces
a McGucken Sphere $S_p = M^{+}_{p}(t)$
(Lemma [7.7](#lem:sphere-and-huygens){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:sphere-and-huygens"}). This is QB1: the geometric
primitive of Geometric Channel is the Sphere sourced at every event by
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

**Step 6 (Geometric Channel): Iterated Huygens generates the path space.** By
Proposition [4.11](#prop:iter){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:iter"} (iterated composition of Spheres), every
wavefront point is a Huygens-secondary source:
$M^{+}_{p}(t_2) = \bigcup_{q \in M^{+}_{p}(t_1)}M^{+}_{q}(t_2 - t_1)$.
Iterating at $N \to \infty$ short times $\varepsilon = (t_B - t_A)/N$,
the set of paths from $(\mathbf{x}_A, t_A)$ to $(\mathbf{x}_B, t_B)$ is
generated by successive secondary-wavelet picks: each
$\mathbf{x}_k \in M^{+}_{\mathbf{x}_{k-1}}(\varepsilon)$, with the
continuum limit giving the space of all continuous paths $\gamma$. This
is QB3.

**Step 7 (Geometric Channel): Each path carries Compton phase
$e^{iS[\gamma]/\hbar}$.** By
Lemma [7.8](#lem:compton-phase-wavelet){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:compton-phase-wavelet"}, the phase accumulated along the
straight-line wavelet path from $\mathbf{x}_{k-1}$ to $\mathbf{x}_k$ in
time $\varepsilon$ is the classical action
$\Delta S = \varepsilon L(\mathbf{x}, \dot{\mathbf{x}})$ divided by
$\hbar$. Summing over the $N$ wavelet segments and passing to the
continuum:
$$\sum_{k=1}^N \varepsilon L_k/\hbar \;\longrightarrow\; (1/\hbar)\int_{t_A}^{t_B} L\,dt = S[\gamma]/\hbar.$$
Each path carries Compton phase $e^{iS[\gamma]/\hbar}$, with the factor
$i$ being the perpendicularity marker of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}, case 2 of the twelve-fold catalogue: the
path-integral phase factor). This is QB4.

**Step 8 (Geometric Channel): Sum over paths and disjointness.** By QB5, the
propagator is the sum over paths of these phase contributions:
$$K(\mathbf{x}_B, t_B; \mathbf{x}_A, t_A) = \int\mathcal{D}[\gamma]\,e^{iS[\gamma]/\hbar}.$$
The iterated-Sphere construction generates the path integral directly
from the geometric content of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; no Trotter
decomposition, no operator slicing, no spectral theorem. The Feynman
path integral is the natural representation of quantum dynamics in the
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework; the operator formulation of Steps 1--4 (Algebraic Channel)
is its algebraic shadow. The disjointness of Geometric and Algebraic Channels is: Stone's theorem and Trotter product enter Algebraic Channel but not
Geometric Channel; Postulate clauses (ii)+(v) and iterated Huygens
(Proposition [4.11](#prop:iter){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:iter"}) enter Geometric Channel but not Algebraic Channel. The two
channels share only $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and the final equation
[\[eq:Feynman-PI\]](#eq:Feynman-PI){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:Feynman-PI"}. $\square$ ◻
:::

### Geometric Channel derivation (QB1--QB5 --- natural setting of the path integral)

::: channelb
*Geometric Channel Derivation 15.3* (Feynman path integral as the natural
Sphere-Huygens representation). This is the natural setting of the path
integral in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework. By QB1--QB5, the propagator is
constructed directly:

1.  QB1: every event sources a McGucken Sphere;

2.  QB2: every wavefront point is a Huygens-secondary source;

3.  QB3: the set of paths from $(x_A, t_A)$ to $(x_B, t_B)$ is generated
    by iterated secondary-wavelet picks;

4.  QB4: each path carries Compton phase $e^{iS[\gamma]/\hbar}$;

5.  QB5: the propagator is the sum over paths of these phase
    contributions:
    $$K = \int\mathcal{D}[\gamma]\,e^{iS[\gamma]/\hbar}.$$

No Trotter decomposition, no operator slicing---the iterated Sphere
construction generates the path integral directly from the geometry of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The Feynman path integral is the natural
representation of quantum dynamics in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework; the
operator formulation is its algebraic shadow. ◻
:::

### Algebraic Channel derivation (QA2 plus Trotter decomposition)

::: channela
*Algebraic Channel Derivation 15.2* (Feynman path integral from Trotter
decomposition of $\hat{U}$). By QA2 (Stone's theorem), the
time-evolution operator is $\hat{U}(t) = \exp(-it\hat{H}/\hbar)$ with
Hamiltonian $\hat{H}= -\hbar^2\nabla^2/(2m) + V(x) =: \hat{T} + \hat{V}$
(kinetic + potential).

Slice the time interval into $N$ short steps of duration
$\varepsilon = (t_B - t_A)/N$. The Trotter product formula (Trotter 1959
[@Trotter1959]; Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] VIII.8) states that, for
self-adjoint $\hat{T}, \hat{V}$,
$$\exp(-it\hat{H}/\hbar) = \lim_{N\to\infty}\,[\exp(-i\varepsilon\hat{T}/\hbar)\,\exp(-i\varepsilon\hat{V}/\hbar)]^N.$$
Inserting complete sets of position eigenstates
$\mathbb{1}= \int dx_k\,\lvert x_k \rangle\!\langle x_k \rvert$ between
each pair of factors:
$$\langle x_B|\hat{U}(t)|x_A\rangle = \lim_{N\to\infty}\int\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}dx_k\,\prod_{k=1}^{N}\langle x_k|\exp(-i\varepsilon\hat{T}/\hbar)\,\exp(-i\varepsilon\hat{V}/\hbar)|x_{k-1}\rangle.$$
The matrix elements evaluate to (for free particle):
$$\langle x_k|\exp(-i\varepsilon\hat{T}/\hbar)|x_{k-1}\rangle = \left(\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}\right)^{3/2}\exp\!\left(\frac{im(x_k - x_{k-1})^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\right).$$
The potential factor is diagonal:
$\exp(-i\varepsilon V(x_{k-1})/\hbar)$. Combining:
$$\langle x_B|\hat{U}|x_A\rangle = \lim_{N\to\infty}\int\prod_k dx_k\,\prod_k \mathcal{N}_\varepsilon\,\exp\!\left(\frac{i\varepsilon}{\hbar}\sum_k\left[\frac{m(x_k - x_{k-1})^2}{2\varepsilon^2} - V(x_{k-1})\right]\right).$$
The exponent is
$i\varepsilon\sum_k[\tfrac{1}{2}m\dot{x}_k^2 - V] / \hbar \to (i/\hbar)\int L\,dt = (i/\hbar)S[\gamma]$
as $\varepsilon \to 0$. The integral over the intermediate positions
$x_k$ becomes the integral over paths $\gamma$. ◻
:::

### Disjointness audit {#disjointness-audit-12}

**Geometric Channel:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, McGucken Sphere, Huygens
iteration, Compton phase along proper time, Sphere-based path-integral
representation.

**Algebraic Channel:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, Stone's theorem, Trotter
product formula, operator-matrix elements between position eigenstates,
$\varepsilon \to 0$ limit to classical action.

**Intersection:**
$\{(\mathrm{McP}), K = \int\mathcal{D}[\gamma]\,e^{iS[\gamma]/\hbar}\}$.
*Disjointness verified.*

### Action as the measure of $x_4$-advance {#sec:action-as-x4-advance}

The dual-channel derivation of
Theorem [15.1](#thm:QMT15){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT15"}
establishes the path integral
$K = \int\mathcal{D}[\gamma]\,e^{iS[\gamma]/\hbar}$ both algebraically
(Trotter decomposition) and geometrically (iterated Huygens on the
McGucken Sphere). The geometric route supplies an explicit physical reading of what the action $S[\gamma]$ measures: it is the integrated
advance of the system through the expanding fourth dimension along the
path $\gamma$ [@MG-PathIntegral-2026].

::: {#rmk:action-as-x4-advance .remark}
*Remark 15.4* (Action as integrated $x_4$-advance;
[@MG-PathIntegral-2026] §6.1). The free-particle action
$S[\gamma] = -mc^2\int_\gamma d\tau$ is, in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, the
integrated advance of the particle through $x_4$ along the worldline
$\gamma$, weighted by the rest mass $-mc^2$ (the coupling of matter to
$x_4$ at the Compton frequency,
Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT4"}).
The proper-time element $d\tau$ measures the local $x_4$-advance per
coordinate-time tick, via the kinematic identity
$$d\tau^2 \;=\; dt^2\bigl(1 - |\mathbf{v}|^2/c^2\bigr),$$ where
$\mathbf{v} = d\mathbf{x}/dt$ is the three-velocity along $\gamma$. The
factor $\sqrt{1 - |\mathbf{v}|^2/c^2}$ has the geometric content: of the
full $x_4$-expansion budget $c$ available at every event (clause (i) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}), the fraction not spent on 3D motion at
velocity $\mathbf{v}$ is the fraction that advances the particle's
worldline through $x_4$. Equivalently, the four-speed identity
$u^\mu u_\mu = -c^2$ (a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the
Minkowski metric, Theorem 4 of [@Syn-2026]) is the algebraic statement
that the four-velocity has fixed magnitude $c$, with the budget
distributed between the temporal/$x_4$ component and the spatial
components according to the worldline's tangent direction.

The reading is:

1.  *Straighter paths advance more directly through $x_4$.* A timelike
    geodesic ($\mathbf{v}$ small or constant along the path) spends most
    of its four-velocity budget on $x_4$-advance and accumulates the
    maximal $\int d\tau$ between fixed endpoints. The action
    $S = -mc^2\int d\tau$ is at extremum (maximally negative, since
    $\int d\tau$ is maximally positive) for the geodesic.

2.  *Bent paths "waste" $x_4$-advance on spatial motion.* A worldline
    that takes a longer 3D route between fixed endpoints, or zig-zags
    spatially while progressing in $t$, spends more of its four-velocity
    budget on spatial $\mathbf{v}$-components and less on $x_4$-advance.
    The proper-time integral $\int d\tau$ along such paths is smaller;
    the action $S = -mc^2\int d\tau$ is less extreme.

3.  *The classical path is the path of stationary $x_4$-advance.* The
    principle of stationary action $\delta S[\gamma] = 0$
    (Euler--Lagrange equation) is, in this reading, the statement that
    the classical worldline is the path along which the integrated
    $x_4$-advance is stationary under small variations. This is the
    principle of least action re-read as a principle of stationary
    $x_4$-flow.

4.  *Each path's quantum phase records its $x_4$-history.* The path's
    contribution to the propagator is $e^{iS[\gamma]/\hbar}$, with the
    phase $S[\gamma]/\hbar$ proportional to the integrated $x_4$-advance
    along $\gamma$. The phase is therefore a record of how the path has
    ridden the expanding fourth dimension: how the path's accumulated
    $x_4$-advance compares, in detail, to the $x_4$-advance of all
    neighbouring paths. Paths with nearby $x_4$-histories interfere
    constructively (small phase difference); paths with very different
    $x_4$-histories interfere destructively (large phase difference
    modulo $2\pi$).

The physical mechanism is unified across the four manifestations: (a)
the McGucken Sphere is the locus of all next-step $x_4$-advance
positions reachable from the current event; (b) successive
Sphere-Huygens steps generate the space of all continuous paths
$\gamma$; (c) each path's quantum phase $e^{iS[\gamma]/\hbar}$ encodes
its integrated $x_4$-advance; (d) the classical limit
(Theorem [15.1](#thm:QMT15){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT15"}
stationary-phase, $S \gg \hbar$) selects the path of stationary
$x_4$-advance as the unique surviving worldline. The macroscopic world
is the interference pattern of the expanding fourth dimension, in which
only those histories that "surf" $x_4$ in stationarity survive.
:::

### Worked example: the free-particle propagator and its $i$ in the prefactor {#sec:free-particle-propagator-worked-example}

::: {#prop:free-particle-propagator .proposition}
**Proposition 15.5** (Free-particle propagator and its $i$-prefactor
from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; [@MG-PathIntegral-2026] §5.2). *The
free-particle propagator in one spatial dimension is
$$K(x_B, t_B; x_A, t_A) \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar T}}\,\exp\!\left(\frac{im(x_B - x_A)^2}{2\hbar T}\right), \qquad T := t_B - t_A.
\label{eq:free-particle-propagator}$$ The factor $i$ in the prefactor
$\sqrt{m/(2\pi i\hbar T)}$, which ensures that the propagator oscillates
rather than decays, is the same $i$ as in the McGucken Principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ --- the perpendicularity marker of $x_4$'s
orthogonality to the three spatial dimensions.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has six steps.

**Step 1: Time-slicing setup.** Divide $[t_A, t_B]$ into $N$ equal
intervals of duration $\varepsilon = T/N$. By
Theorem [15.1](#thm:QMT15){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT15"}
(Geometric Channel), the time-sliced propagator is the integral over
intermediate positions of products of short-time kernels:
$$K(x_B, t_B; x_A, t_A) \;=\; \lim_{N\to\infty}\int\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}dx_k\,\prod_{k=1}^{N}K_\varepsilon(x_k, x_{k-1}),$$
with $x_0 = x_A$, $x_N = x_B$, and the short-time kernel
$$K_\varepsilon(x_k, x_{k-1}) \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}}\,\exp\!\left(\frac{im(x_k - x_{k-1})^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\right),$$
the free-particle short-time kernel of the McGucken-Sphere Huygens
construction
(Lemma [7.8](#lem:compton-phase-wavelet){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:compton-phase-wavelet"}; rigorously derived from the
four-speed constraint of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} in
Proposition [15.6](#prop:short-time-kernel-four-speed){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:short-time-kernel-four-speed"} below).

**Step 2: Evaluate the Gaussian composition explicitly.** The two-step
composition is the convolution of two short-time kernels:
$$(K_\varepsilon * K_\varepsilon)(x_2, x_0) \;:=\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx_1\,K_\varepsilon(x_2, x_1)\,K_\varepsilon(x_1, x_0).$$
Substituting the short-time kernel:
$$(K_\varepsilon * K_\varepsilon)(x_2, x_0) \;=\; \frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx_1\,\exp\!\left[\frac{im}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\bigl((x_2 - x_1)^2 + (x_1 - x_0)^2\bigr)\right].$$
Complete the square in $x_1$: expand the quadratic
$$(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (x_1 - x_0)^2 \;=\; 2x_1^2 - 2x_1(x_0 + x_2) + x_0^2 + x_2^2 \;=\; 2\Bigl(x_1 - \frac{x_0 + x_2}{2}\Bigr)^2 + \frac{(x_2 - x_0)^2}{2},$$
using the algebraic identity $2u^2 - 2uv = 2(u - v/2)^2 - v^2/2$ with
$u = x_1$ and $v = x_0 + x_2$, then adding
$x_0^2 + x_2^2 = ((x_0+x_2)^2 + (x_2-x_0)^2)/2$ and simplifying. The
integral over $x_1$ is a shifted Fresnel-Gaussian integral with
quadratic coefficient $\alpha = im/(\hbar\varepsilon)$:
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx_1\,\exp\!\bigl(\alpha(x_1 - x_*)^2\bigr) \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{-\alpha}} \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{-\pi\hbar\varepsilon}{im}} \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{i\pi\hbar\varepsilon}{m}},$$
by the standard Fresnel-integral identity (analytic continuation of
$\int dx\,e^{-\beta x^2} = \sqrt{\pi/\beta}$ from real-positive $\beta$
to imaginary $\beta$; see Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Vol. II, §X.10
for the Fresnel-integral definition and convergence in the
distributional sense). Substituting back: $$\begin{aligned}
  (K_\varepsilon * K_\varepsilon)(x_2, x_0) &\;=\; \frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}\cdot\sqrt{\frac{i\pi\hbar\varepsilon}{m}}\cdot\exp\!\left(\frac{im(x_2 - x_0)^2}{4\hbar\varepsilon}\right) \\
  &\;=\; \sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}\cdot\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}\cdot\frac{i\pi\hbar\varepsilon}{m}}\cdot\exp\!\left(\frac{im(x_2 - x_0)^2}{2\hbar(2\varepsilon)}\right) \\
  &\;=\; \sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar(2\varepsilon)}}\,\exp\!\left(\frac{im(x_2 - x_0)^2}{2\hbar(2\varepsilon)}\right),
\end{aligned}$$ using the algebraic simplification
$(1/(2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon))^2 \cdot (i\pi\hbar\varepsilon/m) \cdot m = m/(4\pi^2 i^2 \hbar^2 \varepsilon^2)\cdot i\pi\hbar\varepsilon = m/(2\pi i \hbar (2\varepsilon))$
(cancelling factors of 2, $\pi$, $i$, $\hbar$, $\varepsilon$, $m$). The
exponent's denominator changes from $2\hbar\varepsilon$ in the
single-step kernel to $2\hbar(2\varepsilon)$ in the two-step
composition, reflecting the doubled time interval. The composition law
of Gaussian free-particle kernels is therefore: convolution of two
short-time kernels of width $\varepsilon$ produces a kernel of width
$2\varepsilon$ with the same functional form.

**Step 3: Iterate to $N$ steps.** By induction on the composition law of
Step 2, $N$ successive compositions produce the $N$-step kernel:
$$K_T(x_B, x_A) \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar(N\varepsilon)}}\,\exp\!\left(\frac{im(x_B - x_A)^2}{2\hbar(N\varepsilon)}\right) \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar T}}\,\exp\!\left(\frac{im(x_B - x_A)^2}{2\hbar T}\right),$$
since $N\varepsilon = T$. The induction hypothesis:
$K_{n\varepsilon}(x_n, x_0) = \sqrt{m/(2\pi i\hbar n\varepsilon)}\,\exp(im(x_n - x_0)^2/(2\hbar n\varepsilon))$.
The inductive step:
$K_{(n+1)\varepsilon}(x_{n+1}, x_0) = \int dx_n\,K_\varepsilon(x_{n+1}, x_n)\,K_{n\varepsilon}(x_n, x_0)$,
evaluated by the same Fresnel-Gaussian-integration argument of Step 2
with parameters $\alpha_1 = im/(\hbar\varepsilon)$ and
$\alpha_2 = im/(\hbar n\varepsilon)$ on the two quadratic factors,
yielding the closed-form
$\sqrt{m/(2\pi i\hbar(n+1)\varepsilon)}\exp(im(x_{n+1}-x_0)^2/(2\hbar(n+1)\varepsilon))$.
In the $N \to \infty$ limit ($\varepsilon \to 0$), the
discrete-sum-over-paths becomes the continuous Feynman path integral,
and the closed-form expression
[\[eq:free-particle-propagator\]](#eq:free-particle-propagator){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:free-particle-propagator"} is its evaluation for the free
particle.

**Step 4: Identify the $i$ in the prefactor.** The factor $i$ in
$\sqrt{m/(2\pi i\hbar T)}$ originates from the $i$ in the short-time
kernel $K_\varepsilon$ of Step 1. The short-time kernel is, by
Lemma [7.8](#lem:compton-phase-wavelet){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:compton-phase-wavelet"}, the McGucken-Sphere Huygens
wavelet amplitude with phase $e^{iS_\varepsilon/\hbar}$, where
$S_\varepsilon = m(x_k - x_{k-1})^2/(2\varepsilon)$ is the free-particle
action over the short straight-line segment. The phase
$S_\varepsilon/\hbar$ is dimensionally action-divided-by-action and
carries the perpendicularity marker $i$ from the McGucken Principle
through the Compton-frequency coupling
(Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT4"},
Geometric Channel) and from there into the Gaussian integral normalization.
Performing the Fresnel-Gaussian integral
$\int dx\,\exp(i\alpha x^2) = \sqrt{i\pi/\alpha}$ (the
imaginary-coefficient continuation of the standard Gaussian; see Step 2)
propagates the $i$ from the phase into the normalization, producing the
$\sqrt{1/i}$ factor that appears in the prefactor.

**Step 5: Trace the prefactor $i$ to $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.** The $i$
in the Gaussian-prefactor $\sqrt{m/(2\pi i\hbar T)}$ has the reading of an algebraic consequence of the $i$ in the path-integral
phase $e^{iS/\hbar}$. The $i$ in the phase is, by the Geometric Channel
derivation of Theorem [15.1](#thm:QMT15){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT15"} (specifically
Lemma [7.8](#lem:compton-phase-wavelet){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:compton-phase-wavelet"} and the Wick-rotation chapter,
Chapter [\[sec:mcgucken-wick-rotation-introduction\]](#sec:mcgucken-wick-rotation-introduction){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:mcgucken-wick-rotation-introduction"}), the same $i$ as in $x_4 = ict$ --- the
integrated kinematic shadow of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The chain of
dependences is:
$$\text{prefactor } i \;\longleftarrow\; \text{Gaussian normalization} \;\longleftarrow\; \text{path-integral phase } e^{iS/\hbar} \;\longleftarrow\; x_4 = ict \;\longleftarrow\; \tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic.$$
The $i$ in the prefactor has the reading of the same $i$ as
in the principle: the Fresnel-Gaussian integration extracts the $i$ from
the exponent's phase into the prefactor's normalization via the
analytic-continuation identity $\sqrt{i\pi/\alpha}$, with the
essential $i$ in $\alpha = im/(\hbar\varepsilon)$ tracing through the
chain above to the perpendicularity marker $i$ in
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}, case 2: the path-integral phase factor).

**Step 6: The propagator oscillates rather than decays.** The factor $i$
in the prefactor, combined with the $i$ in the exponent, makes the
propagator complex-oscillatory rather than real-decaying:
$K(x_B, t_B; x_A, t_A)$ has magnitude $\sqrt{m/(2\pi\hbar T)}$ and phase
$\arg = -\pi/4 + m(x_B - x_A)^2/(2\hbar T)$. The wavefunction
$\psi(x_B, t_B) = \int dx_A\,K\,\psi(x_A, t_A)$ propagates as an
oscillating wave packet, with the characteristic spreading and
interference of quantum dynamics. Without the $i$ in the principle ---
equivalently, with $x_4 = c\tau$ (Euclidean) replacing $x_4 = ict$
(Minkowski) --- the propagator would be real-decaying
$\sqrt{m/(2\pi\hbar T)}\,\exp(-m(x_B - x_A)^2/(2\hbar T))$, the
heat-equation Green's function: classical diffusion in place of quantum
oscillation. The Wick rotation $t \to -i\tau$ converts one into the
other
(Chapter [\[sec:mcgucken-wick-rotation-introduction\]](#sec:mcgucken-wick-rotation-introduction){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:mcgucken-wick-rotation-introduction"}). The same $i$ that distinguishes quantum
oscillation from classical diffusion in the free-particle propagator
distinguishes the Minkowski form $x_4 = ict$ from the Euclidean form
$x_4 = c\tau$ in the McGucken Principle. $\square$ ◻
:::

### The short-time kernel from the four-speed constraint: the Lagrangian as a derived consequence {#sec:short-time-kernel-from-four-speed}

The free-particle propagator derivation of
§[15.6](#sec:free-particle-propagator-worked-example){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:free-particle-propagator-worked-example"} takes the
short-time kernel $K_\varepsilon(x_k, x_{k-1})$ as the starting point of
the time-slicing argument. The April 23, 2026 Feynman-diagrams paper
[@MG-FeynmanDiagrams-2026] establishes a complementary derivation in
which the short-time kernel itself is derived directly from the
four-speed constraint of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, without assuming the non-relativistic
Lagrangian. The Lagrangian $L = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ then emerges as a
consequence of the derivation rather than as an input.

::: {#prop:short-time-kernel-four-speed .proposition}
**Proposition 15.6** (Short-time free-particle kernel from the
four-speed constraint; [@MG-FeynmanDiagrams-2026] §III.5). *Under
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, the short-time free-particle kernel
$K_\varepsilon(x_{k+1}, x_k)$ is derived directly from the four-speed
constraint $|d\mathbf{x}/dt|^2 + |dx_4/dt|^2 = c^2$ (a consequence of
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} and
Lemma [4.2](#lem:four-velocity-budget){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:four-velocity-budget"}, with the McGucken-derived
Minkowski metric on $M_{G}$ supplying the constraint surface
$u^\mu u_\mu = -c^2$), producing
$$K_\varepsilon(x_{k+1}, x_k) \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}}\,\exp\!\left(\frac{im(x_{k+1} - x_k)^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\right)$$
without assuming any classical Lagrangian. The non-relativistic
Lagrangian $L_{\mathrm{cl}} = \tfrac{1}{2}m|\mathbf{v}|^2$ has the
reading of a derived consequence of the four-speed
constraint, arising from the $x_{4}$-phase accumulation of the McGucken
Sphere wavelet.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has five steps establishing the short-time kernel and
the emergent Lagrangian.

**Step 1: $x_{4}$-advance over a short interval, derived from the
McGucken Minkowski metric.** The McGucken-derived Minkowski arena
$M_{G}$ has metric $\eta_{\mu\nu}$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}, descending from $dx_4 = ic\,dt$). The
four-velocity of a worldline parameterised by proper time $\tau$ is
$u^\mu = dx^\mu/d\tau$, and by
Lemma [4.2](#lem:four-velocity-budget){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:four-velocity-budget"} it satisfies the master equation
$$u^\mu u_\mu \;=\; -c^2,$$ the four-speed constraint on $M_{G}$.
Converting to coordinate-time parameterisation $t$ along a worldline
with three-velocity $\mathbf{v} = d\mathbf{x}/dt$: the relation
$d\tau = dt\sqrt{1 - |\mathbf{v}|^2/c^2}$ (the standard
proper-time-to-coordinate-time identity, derived from
$ds^2 = -c^2 d\tau^2 = -c^2 dt^2 + |d\mathbf{x}|^2$ on $M_{G}$) gives
the $x_{4}$-rate
$$\frac{dx_4}{dt} \;=\; ic\,\frac{d\tau}{dt}\,\frac{1}{d\tau/dt} \;=\; ic\,\sqrt{1 - |\mathbf{v}|^2/c^2}$$
in coordinate time (taking the $+ic$ root by
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iii) monotonicity along the matter
branch). Verification:
$|dx_4/dt|^2 = |ic|^2\,(1-|\mathbf{v}|^2/c^2) = c^2 - |\mathbf{v}|^2$,
hence
$$|d\mathbf{x}/dt|^2 + |dx_4/dt|^2 \;=\; |\mathbf{v}|^2 + (c^2 - |\mathbf{v}|^2) \;=\; c^2,$$
the coordinate-time four-speed constraint. The accumulated
$x_{4}$-advance over a short coordinate-time interval $\varepsilon$ is
therefore
$$\Delta x_4 \;=\; ic\,\varepsilon\,\sqrt{1 - |\mathbf{v}|^2/c^2}, \qquad \text{with } \mathbf{v} := (x_{k+1} - x_k)/\varepsilon.$$
