**Step 2: Non-relativistic expansion.** In the non-relativistic regime
$|\mathbf{v}| \ll c$, Taylor-expand the square root to first order in
$|\mathbf{v}|^2/c^2$:
$$\sqrt{1 - |\mathbf{v}|^2/c^2} \;=\; 1 - \frac{|\mathbf{v}|^2}{2c^2} + O\!\left(\frac{|\mathbf{v}|^4}{c^4}\right),$$
hence
$$\Delta x_4 \;\approx\; ic\,\varepsilon\,\left(1 - \frac{|\mathbf{v}|^2}{2c^2}\right) \;=\; ic\varepsilon - \frac{i\varepsilon}{2c}|\mathbf{v}|^2.$$
The first term $ic\varepsilon$ is the rest-frame $x_{4}$-advance
(constant across all paths from $x_k$ to $x_{k+1}$); the second term
$-(i\varepsilon/2c)|\mathbf{v}|^2 = -(i/2mc)\cdot m|\mathbf{v}|^2\varepsilon$
is the velocity-dependent correction proportional to the
non-relativistic kinetic energy $\tfrac{1}{2}m|\mathbf{v}|^2$.

**Step 3: $x_{4}$-phase accumulation at the Compton frequency.** By
Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT4"}
(Compton-frequency phase accumulation), the matter wavefunction
accumulates an $x_{4}$-phase $\theta = \omega_C\tau$ at the Compton
angular frequency $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$, where $\tau = |\Delta x_4|/c$
is the proper-time advance ($|\Delta x_4| = c\,d\tau$ from
$\Delta x_4 = ic\,d\tau$ on the matter branch). Equivalently, the phase
per unit $|\Delta x_4|$ is
$d\theta/d|\Delta x_4| = \omega_C/c = mc/\hbar$, and the phase factor
accumulated over the interval is $\exp(i\,mc\,|\Delta x_4|/\hbar)$.
Substituting $|\Delta x_4|$ from Step 2 (using
$|\Delta x_4| = c\varepsilon\sqrt{1-|\mathbf{v}|^2/c^2} \approx c\varepsilon - \varepsilon|\mathbf{v}|^2/(2c)$):
$$\begin{aligned}
  \exp\!\left(i\,\frac{mc}{\hbar}\,|\Delta x_4|\right) &\;=\; \exp\!\left(i\,\frac{mc}{\hbar}\cdot c\varepsilon\right) \cdot \exp\!\left(-i\,\frac{mc}{\hbar}\cdot \frac{\varepsilon|\mathbf{v}|^2}{2c}\right) \\
  &\;=\; \exp(imc^2\varepsilon/\hbar)\cdot\exp\!\left(\frac{im|\mathbf{v}|^2\varepsilon}{2\hbar}\right).
\end{aligned}$$ The first factor $\exp(imc^2\varepsilon/\hbar)$ is the
constant rest-frame phase (the same value for all paths from $x_k$ to
$x_{k+1}$); the second factor is the velocity-dependent phase that
contributes to interference between paths.

**Step 4: Constant phase absorbed into normalization (gauge-invariance
argument).** The constant rest-frame phase factor
$\exp(imc^2\varepsilon/\hbar)$ multiplies every path from $x_k$ to
$x_{k+1}$ by the same amount and contributes only to the overall phase
of the kernel, not to any relative phases between paths. By the global
$U(1)$ gauge invariance of the wavefunction
(Theorem [16.1](#thm:QMT16){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT16"};
see also
Remark [15.7](#rmk:global-phase-absorption){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:global-phase-absorption"} below for the gauge-invariance
justification), this constant overall phase has the role of a
gauge-choice freedom that can be absorbed into the normalization of
$K_\varepsilon$ without affecting any observable. The path-dependent
contribution is the second factor
$\exp(im|\mathbf{v}|^2\varepsilon/(2\hbar))$, which in terms of the
spatial displacement $x_{k+1} - x_k = \mathbf{v}\varepsilon$ becomes
$$\exp\!\left(\frac{im|\mathbf{v}|^2\varepsilon}{2\hbar}\right) \;=\; \exp\!\left(\frac{im(x_{k+1} - x_k)^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\right),$$
using $|\mathbf{v}|^2\varepsilon = (x_{k+1} - x_k)^2/\varepsilon$.

**Step 5: Normalization by unitarity gives the
$\sqrt{m/(2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon)}$ prefactor.** The short-time kernel
must satisfy the unitarity condition: in the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$,
the kernel approaches the resolution of the identity in position space,
$$K_\varepsilon(x_{k+1}, x_k) \;\xrightarrow{\varepsilon \to 0}\; \delta(x_{k+1} - x_k).$$
The unnormalized phase-only kernel
$\exp(im(x_{k+1}-x_k)^2/(2\hbar\varepsilon))$ is a complex Gaussian
peaked at $x_{k+1} = x_k$ with imaginary variance
$\sigma^2 = i\hbar\varepsilon/m$. The standard Gaussian-delta-function
identity (analytic continuation): the family
$$G_\sigma(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$$
satisfies $\lim_{\sigma^2 \to 0^+}G_\sigma(x) = \delta(x)$ for
real-positive $\sigma^2$. Analytically continuing to imaginary
$\sigma^2 = i\hbar\varepsilon/m$ (the Fresnel-Gaussian limit, taking
$\varepsilon \to 0^+$):
$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon/m}}\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x_{k+1}-x_k)^2}{2(i\hbar\varepsilon/m)}\right) \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}}\,\exp\!\left(\frac{im(x_{k+1}-x_k)^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\right),$$
using $-1/(2\cdot i) = i/2$. This gives the normalized short-time kernel
$$K_\varepsilon(x_{k+1}, x_k) \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar\varepsilon}}\,\exp\!\left(\frac{im(x_{k+1} - x_k)^2}{2\hbar\varepsilon}\right),$$
exactly the standard free-particle short-time kernel of
§[15.6](#sec:free-particle-propagator-worked-example){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:free-particle-propagator-worked-example"} Step 1,
satisfying $K_\varepsilon \to \delta(x_{k+1} - x_k)$ as
$\varepsilon \to 0$.

The non-relativistic Lagrangian
$L_{\mathrm{cl}} = \tfrac{1}{2}m|\mathbf{v}|^2$ has the reading of an *emergent* consequence of the four-speed constraint:
identifying the exponent with $iS/\hbar = i\int L\,dt/\hbar$ at the
leading-order non-relativistic expansion gives
$S = \tfrac{1}{2}m|\mathbf{v}|^2\varepsilon$, i.e.,
$L = \tfrac{1}{2}m|\mathbf{v}|^2$. The Lagrangian arises from the
McGucken-Sphere $x_{4}$-phase accumulation at the Compton frequency,
with the non-relativistic kinetic-energy form
$\tfrac{1}{2}m|\mathbf{v}|^2$ being the leading-order correction to the
rest-frame phase $mc^2\varepsilon$ in the expansion of the relativistic
phase $mc\,|\Delta x_4|$ in powers of $|\mathbf{v}|/c$. The derivation runs from
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} (McGucken Principle) $\to$
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} (Minkowski metric on $M_{G}$) $\to$
Lemma [4.2](#lem:four-velocity-budget){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:four-velocity-budget"} (four-speed constraint
$u^\mu u_\mu = -c^2$) $\to$
Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT4"}
(Compton-frequency phase accumulation) $\to$ short-time kernel +
Lagrangian. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:global-phase-absorption .remark}
*Remark 15.7* (The global-phase absorption as a $U(1)$ gauge-invariance
step; [@MG-FeynmanDiagrams-2026] Remark III.1). The step of absorbing
the constant rest-frame phase $\exp(imc^2\varepsilon/\hbar)$ into the
normalization of $K_\varepsilon$ (Step 4 of
Proposition [15.6](#prop:short-time-kernel-four-speed){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:short-time-kernel-four-speed"}) has the reading of a gauge-invariance step, justified by the global $U(1)$
symmetry of the matter wavefunction established as a theorem of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} in
Theorem [16.1](#thm:QMT16){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT16"}.

Under the global $U(1)$ phase transformation $\psi \to e^{i\alpha}\psi$
(constant $\alpha$), every observable is unchanged: $|\psi|^2$ is
invariant because $|e^{i\alpha}|^2 = 1$; expectation values
$\langle\psi|\hat O|\psi\rangle$ are invariant because phases cancel
between bra and ket; interference patterns depend on relative phase
differences between paths, and a common overall phase added to every
path factors out of the interference integral. This is the global $U(1)$
symmetry that produces conservation of electric charge via Noether's
theorem (Theorem [16.1](#thm:QMT16){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT16"}). The constant phase
$\exp(imc^2\varepsilon/\hbar)$ accumulated per time step from the
rest-mass $x_{4}$-advance is precisely such a global phase: it
multiplies every path from $x_k$ to $x_{k+1}$ by the same amount and
contributes only to the overall phase of $K$, with no contribution to
relative phases between paths. Absorbing it into the normalization has
the reading of a gauge choice equivalent to choosing the
origin of the action scale.

Within the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework this has an elegant corollary. The $i$ in
$x_4 = ict$ generates a rotational structure in the complex plane
(multiplication by $i$ is rotation by $90^\circ$), and global $U(1)$
gauge transformations are rotations in this same plane. The gauge
freedom of quantum mechanics has the reading of a direct
consequence of the perpendicular character of $x_{4}$
(Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}): the same mechanism that supplies the
propagator's complex structure (the $i$ in the phase $e^{iS/\hbar}$)
supplies the gauge freedom to absorb constant $x_{4}$-phase
contributions into normalization. The Step 4 absorption has the
reading of a feature of the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework descending
directly from the $U(1)$ rotational structure of $x_4 = ict$.
:::

### Empirical anchor

The Feynman path integral underlies all of modern quantum field theory
and is therefore empirically tested at every accelerator: Feynman
diagrams (Chapter [23](#ch:feynman-diagrams){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:feynman-diagrams"}) are the perturbative expansion of the
path integral. Direct confirmations include:

-   the Aharonov--Bohm effect (predicted from the path-integral phase
    shift along paths around a flux line; observed by Chambers 1960 and
    Tonomura et al. 1986);

-   Berry phase phenomena (interpreted as the holonomy of paths in
    parameter space);

-   the consistency of perturbative QED (quantum electrodynamics), QCD
    (quantum chromodynamics), and electroweak calculations with
    experimental cross-sections at all energies measured.

## QM T16: Gauge Invariance and Minimal Coupling {#ch:gauge}

> *The McGucken Principle.* The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality.
> Every result below descends from that expansion.


*Recall.* the McGucken Principle ($\mathrm{McP}$:
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$) asserts that the fourth spacetime dimension
$x_4$ expands at the velocity of light $c$, carrying the
perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguishes it from the spatial
three. Throughout this chapter, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ refers to this
principle and to the five-clause content (i)--(v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: (i) *invariance* --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content; (ii) *spherical symmetry* --- the
expansion is isotropic in the spatial three, with the set of events
reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a 2-sphere of radius
$c\tau$; (iii) *monotonicity* --- the integral curve is strictly
monotonically increasing in $t$, fixing the arrow of $x_4$-advance; (iv)
*Lorentz consistency* --- the structure is $SO^+(1,3)$-invariant on
$M_{G}$; (v) *global validity* --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at
every event of $M_{G}$. The integrated kinematic shadow
$x_4 = ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is the kinematic shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the central fact.

### Statement

::: {#thm:QMT16 .theorem}
**Theorem 16.1** (QM T16: Gauge Invariance, = Theorem 75 (Algebraic Channel) and
Theorem 98 (Geometric Channel) of [@Syn-2026]). *The wavefunction $\psi$ is
determined only up to a global phase $\psi \to e^{i\alpha}\psi$,
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ ($U(1)$ global gauge symmetry). Promoting
$\alpha$ to a spacetime-dependent function $\alpha(x)$ ($U(1)$ local
gauge symmetry) requires the introduction of a four-vector gauge field
$A_\mu$ via the covariant derivative
$$D_\mu = \partial_\mu + \frac{iq}{\hbar}A_\mu,
\label{eq:covd}$$ which is minimally coupled to the matter wavefunction
by the substitution $\partial_\mu \to D_\mu$ in the wave equation. The
conserved Noether current associated with the global $U(1)$ symmetry is
$$j^\mu = \frac{i\hbar}{2m}(\psi^*\,\partial^\mu\psi - \psi\,\partial^\mu\psi^*).
\label{eq:Noether-U1}$$*
:::

### Geometric Channel derivation: Sphere $U(1)$-bundle and connection

::: {#lem:QMT16-sphere-bundle .lemma}
**Lemma 16.5** (The McGucken Sphere carries a $U(1)$-bundle structure).
*By QB1, every event sources a McGucken Sphere with a $U(1)$ phase
fibre: at each spatial point on the wavefront $M^{+}_{p}(t)$, the
wavefunction value is a complex amplitude
$\psi(\mathbf{x}, t) \in \mathbb{C}$, whose phase lives on
$U(1) = \{e^{i\theta} : \theta \in \mathbb{R}\}/(\theta \sim \theta + 2\pi)$.
The Sphere is therefore a $U(1)$-bundle over $M_{G}$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **Step 1: Wavefunction takes values in $\mathbb{C}$.** By
Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}, the matter wavefunction
$\psi: M_{G}\to \mathbb{C}$ takes complex values at every spacetime
point. The complex structure of the target $\mathbb{C}$ is forced by the
principle's perpendicularity marker via the McGucken-Hilbert-space
construction (Chapter [9](#ch:hilbert-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:hilbert-theorem"}).

**Step 2: Polar decomposition of $\mathbb{C}$.** Any $\mathbb{C}$-value
$\psi(\mathbf{x}, t) \in \mathbb{C}$ admits the unique polar
decomposition
$$\psi(\mathbf{x}, t) = |\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)|\cdot e^{i\arg\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)},$$
where the magnitude $|\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)| \in [0, \infty)$ is the
Born-rule density (real-valued, observable as probability density) and
the phase
$\arg\psi(\mathbf{x}, t) \in \mathbb{R}/(2\pi\mathbb{Z}) \cong U(1)$ is
the phase angle (unobservable individually; only relative phases between
paths produce observable interference effects).

**Step 3: Phase lives on $U(1)$.** The unit circle
$U(1) = \{z \in \mathbb{C}: |z| = 1\} = \{e^{i\theta} : \theta \in \mathbb{R}\}/(\theta \sim \theta + 2\pi)$
is a one-dimensional compact Lie group. The phase
$e^{i\arg\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)}$ is an element of $U(1)$ at each spacetime
point. The assignment
$$(\mathbf{x}, t) \mapsto e^{i\arg\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)} \in U(1)$$ is a
smooth section of the trivial $U(1)$-bundle over $M_{G}$ in any local
gauge choice. (Gauge transformations of $\psi$ by
$\psi \to e^{i\alpha(\mathbf{x}, t)}\psi$ shift the phase section by
$\alpha$ but preserve the bundle structure.)

**Step 4: Sphere inherits the bundle structure.** Each McGucken Sphere
$S_p$ carries the wavefunction $\psi$ at every point of its wavefront
$M^{+}_{p}(t)$. The polar decomposition of Step 2 gives the magnitude
(intensity of the Sphere at that wavefront point) and the phase
(orientation of the wavefunction in the $U(1)$ fibre). The Sphere
construction therefore inherits the $U(1)$-bundle structure: each $S_p$
is a wavefront with $U(1)$-fibre at every spatial point on the
wavefront.

**Step 5: Geometric Channel characterisation.** The derivation uses only the
McGucken-Sphere construction (QB1), the complex structure of the
wavefunction (forced by
Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"} via $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$), and the
polar decomposition of $\mathbb{C}$. No Stone's theorem, no Noether's
theorem, no minimal-coupling prescription appears; the proof is Geometric
Channel (geometric-propagation), derivationally disjoint from the Algebraic Channel
Noether-current route of
Lemma [16.2](#lem:QMT16-noether){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-noether"}. ◻
:::

::: {#lem:QMT16-channelB-proof .lemma}
**Lemma 16.6** (Geometric Channel proof of QM T16). *The minimal-coupling
covariant derivative [\[eq:covd\]](#eq:covd){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:covd"} arises geometrically as the $U(1)$-bundle
connection on the McGucken-Sphere structure.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has six steps establishing the
McGucken-Sphere $U(1)$-bundle connection as the geometric origin of the
minimal-coupling covariant derivative.

**Step 1: Path-integral phase needs a connection.** By
Theorem [15.1](#thm:QMT15){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT15"}
(Feynman path integral, Geometric Channel), each path $\gamma$ from $(x_A, t_A)$
to $(x_B, t_B)$ carries a phase $e^{iS[\gamma]/\hbar}$, with the
path-integral propagator computed as
$K = \int\mathcal{D}[\gamma]\,e^{iS[\gamma]/\hbar}$. The overall phase
of $\psi$ is unobservable (only relative phases between paths matter for
interference, as in the global-$U(1)$ symmetry of
Lemma [16.2](#lem:QMT16-noether){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-noether"}). Locally, the choice of phase reference
is arbitrary at each event; globally, the choice must be made coherently
along any path on $M_{G}$ so that the relative phases between
intersecting paths are well-defined. The mathematical structure
prescribing a coherent choice of phase along a path on a principal
$G$-bundle is a *connection*; for the McGucken-Sphere $U(1)$-bundle of
Lemma [16.5](#lem:QMT16-sphere-bundle){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-sphere-bundle"}, the relevant connection is a
$\mathfrak{u}(1)$-valued one-form on the base manifold $M_{G}$.

**Step 2: Connection one-form and covariant derivative on the
$U(1)$-bundle.** On a principal $U(1)$-bundle $P \to M$ with structure
group $U(1)$ and Lie algebra $\mathfrak{u}(1) = i\mathbb{R}$ (the
imaginary axis, viewed as the tangent space to $U(1)$ at the identity),
a connection one-form $\omega \in \Omega^1(P, \mathfrak{u}(1))$ pulls
back via a local section $\sigma: U \to P$ to a $\mathfrak{u}(1)$-valued
one-form $\sigma^*\omega$ on the open set $U \subset M$. Writing
$\sigma^*\omega = (iq/\hbar)A_\mu\,dx^\mu$ with $A_\mu$ a real-valued
one-form (the gauge potential) and $iq/\hbar$ the conversion factor from
real-valued $A_\mu$ to $\mathfrak{u}(1)$-valued $\omega$ (with $q$ the
matter field's charge label and $\hbar$ the action quantum), the
covariant derivative of a section $\psi$ of the associated complex-line
bundle $P \times_{U(1)} \mathbb{C}$ in local coordinates is
$$D_\mu\psi \;=\; \partial_\mu\psi + \frac{iq}{\hbar}\,A_\mu\,\psi,$$
the standard formula for the bundle connection acting on a charge-$q$
section (Kobayashi--Nomizu [@KobayashiNomizu1963] Vol. I, §II.1;
Nakahara [@Nakahara2003] §10.3). The factor $iq/\hbar$ has three
roles: (a) the $i$ is the perpendicularity marker of
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"} case 10: the $U(1)$ gauge phase) supplied
through the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{u}(1) = i\mathbb{R}$; (b) the $q$ is
the matter field's charge label specifying the $U(1)$-representation
under which the section transforms; (c) the $\hbar^{-1}$ is the inverse
action quantum (Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:62"}) supplying the dimensional factor that makes
$qA_\mu/\hbar$ a phase per unit displacement.

**Step 3: Parallel transport along a path.** Given a path
$\gamma: [0, 1] \to M_{G}$ with $\gamma(0) = x_A$, $\gamma(1) = x_B$,
parallel transport of a section $\psi$ along $\gamma$ is determined by
the differential equation $D_{\dot\gamma}\psi = 0$ along the path,
equivalently
$\dot\gamma^\mu\bigl(\partial_\mu\psi + (iq/\hbar)A_\mu\psi\bigr) = 0$.
Solving along the path:
$\psi(\gamma(s)) = \psi(\gamma(0))\cdot\exp\bigl(-(iq/\hbar)\int_0^s A_\mu\dot\gamma^\mu\,ds'\bigr)$,
with the path-ordered exponential reducing to an ordinary exponential
since $U(1)$ is abelian. The accumulated holonomy along the closed loop
$\gamma$ (when $\gamma(0) = \gamma(1)$) is the line integral
$$\mathrm{hol}(\gamma) \;=\; \exp\!\left(-\frac{iq}{\hbar}\oint_\gamma A_\mu\,dx^\mu\right),$$
the parallel-transport holonomy of the $U(1)$-bundle along the loop.

**Step 4: Gauge transformation as bundle automorphism.** A local change
of gauge $\psi(x) \to e^{i\alpha(x)}\psi(x)$ is a bundle automorphism
--- a smooth section of the gauge group bundle that acts fibrewise by
$U(1)$ rotation. Under this automorphism, the section transforms as
$\psi \to e^{i\alpha}\psi$ and the connection one-form transforms by the
standard gauge-transformation rule for principal-bundle connections
(Kobayashi--Nomizu [@KobayashiNomizu1963] Vol. I, §II.1.3):
$$A_\mu \;\to\; A_\mu - \frac{\hbar}{q}\,\partial_\mu\alpha.$$ Direct
verification of covariance: substituting into $D_\mu$, $$\begin{aligned}
  D_\mu(e^{i\alpha}\psi) \;&=\; \partial_\mu(e^{i\alpha}\psi) + \frac{iq}{\hbar}\Bigl(A_\mu - \frac{\hbar}{q}\partial_\mu\alpha\Bigr)e^{i\alpha}\psi \\
  &=\; e^{i\alpha}(\partial_\mu\psi + i\partial_\mu\alpha\cdot\psi) + \frac{iq}{\hbar}A_\mu e^{i\alpha}\psi - i\partial_\mu\alpha\cdot e^{i\alpha}\psi \\
  &=\; e^{i\alpha}\Bigl(\partial_\mu\psi + \frac{iq}{\hbar}A_\mu\psi\Bigr) \;=\; e^{i\alpha}\,D_\mu\psi.
\end{aligned}$$ The covariant derivative transforms covariantly under
the bundle automorphism, exactly as in
Lemma [16.3](#lem:QMT16-local-promotion){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-local-promotion"} Step 4.

**Step 5: Curvature as field strength.** The curvature of the connection
one-form $\omega = (iq/\hbar)A_\mu\,dx^\mu$ is the two-form
$\Omega = d\omega + \omega \wedge \omega$. Since $U(1)$ is abelian, the
wedge term $\omega \wedge \omega = 0$ (a $\mathfrak{u}(1)$-valued
one-form wedged with itself vanishes by antisymmetry combined with
$\mathfrak{u}(1)$'s one-dimensionality), so $\Omega = d\omega$. In local
coordinates,
$$\Omega \;=\; \frac{iq}{\hbar}\,(\partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu)\,dx^\mu \wedge dx^\nu \;=\; \frac{iq}{\hbar}\,F_{\mu\nu}\,dx^\mu \wedge dx^\nu,$$
with $F_{\mu\nu} := \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu$ the
electromagnetic field strength. The factor $iq/\hbar$ is absorbed by the
convention that identifies the connection curvature with $F$ up to this
overall normalisation. The first Chern class of the bundle is the
integral of $F/(2\pi\hbar/q)$ over a closed 2-surface, an integer-valued
topological invariant by Chern--Weil theory; this is the subject of
Theorem [16.8](#thm:monopole-bundle-triviality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:monopole-bundle-triviality"} below.

**Step 6: Geometric Channel characterisation and McGucken anchoring.** The
Geometric Channel route reaches the same minimal-coupling prescription as
Algebraic Channel by way of $U(1)$-bundle geometry rather than Noether-current
analysis: Geometric Channel starts from the McGucken Sphere $U(1)$-bundle
(Lemma [16.5](#lem:QMT16-sphere-bundle){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-sphere-bundle"}, established from the
complex-valued matter wavefunction's polar decomposition, with the
complex structure descending from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the
McGucken-Hilbert-space construction of
Chapter [9](#ch:hilbert-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:hilbert-theorem"}), introduces a connection on this
bundle, and reads off the covariant derivative as the connection's
action on bundle sections. No Lagrangian, no Noether's theorem, no
minimal-coupling prescription is invoked at the geometric level; the
proof is Geometric Channel, derivationally disjoint from the Algebraic Channel
Noether-current route of
Lemma [16.4](#lem:QMT16-channelA-proof){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-channelA-proof"}. The Aharonov--Bohm effect
(Aharonov, Bohm 1959 [@AharonovBohm1959]) is the empirical manifestation
of the Geometric Channel holonomy (Step 3): a charged particle traversing a
region with $F_{\mu\nu} = 0$ but $A_\mu \ne 0$ acquires a phase shift
$-(q/\hbar)\oint A_\mu dx^\mu$ equal to the bundle holonomy along the
closed loop, observable in interference experiments even though the
local field strength vanishes along the particle's trajectory.
$\square$ ◻
:::

::: proof
*Proof of Theorem [16.1](#thm:QMT16){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT16"}.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The theorem asserts the $U(1)$ gauge invariance
of the matter wavefunction and the minimal-coupling covariant derivative
$D_\mu = \partial_\mu + (iq/\hbar)A_\mu$ with conserved Noether current
$j^\mu$. We establish this along both channels and verify their
derivational disjointness.

**Step 1: Algebraic Channel derivation
(Lemma [16.4](#lem:QMT16-channelA-proof){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-channelA-proof"}).** The matter Lagrangian
$\mathcal{L}(\psi, \partial_\mu\psi)$ has a global $U(1)$ symmetry:
$\psi \to e^{i\alpha}\psi$ for constant $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. By
Noether's theorem (Lemma [16.2](#lem:QMT16-noether){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-noether"}), the associated conserved current is
$$j^\mu = \frac{iq}{\hbar}(\psi^*\partial^\mu\psi - \psi\partial^\mu\psi^*), \qquad \partial_\mu j^\mu = 0.$$
Promoting the global $U(1)$ to a local symmetry $\alpha \to \alpha(x)$
requires introducing a gauge field $A_\mu$ with inhomogeneous
transformation $A_\mu \to A_\mu - (\hbar/q)\partial_\mu\alpha$, and
replacing $\partial_\mu$ by the covariant derivative
$D_\mu = \partial_\mu + (iq/\hbar)A_\mu$
(Lemma [16.3](#lem:QMT16-local-promotion){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-local-promotion"}: explicit cancellation of the
$\partial_\mu\alpha$ term in
$D_\mu(e^{i\alpha}\psi) = e^{i\alpha}D_\mu\psi$). The gauge field
acquires its own kinetic term $-\tfrac{1}{4}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$, with
Maxwell's equations as Euler-Lagrange consequences. The Algebraic Channel route:
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ matter Lagrangian $\to$ global $U(1)$ $\to$
Noether current $\to$ local-promotion requirement $\to$ minimal-coupling
covariant derivative.

**Step 2: Geometric Channel derivation
(Lemma [16.6](#lem:QMT16-channelB-proof){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-channelB-proof"}).** The McGucken Sphere wavefront
has, at every event $p$, a complex-phase degree of freedom --- the
perpendicularity marker $i$ in $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ generates a
$U(1)$-phase rotation on the wavefront amplitude. Globally, the McGucken
Sphere is a $U(1)$-bundle over $M_{G}$: the base is the McGucken Space,
the fibre is the $U(1)$-phase of the wavefront amplitude at each event.
A connection on this bundle is a 1-form $A_\mu$ on $M_{G}$ taking values
in the $U(1)$-Lie algebra. Parallel transport of the wavefront amplitude
along a path $\gamma$ in $M_{G}$ is governed by the covariant derivative
$D_\mu = \partial_\mu + (iq/\hbar)A_\mu$, which appears as the
connection's action on bundle sections. The Geometric Channel route:
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ $\to$ Sphere as $U(1)$-bundle $\to$ fibre phase
$\to$ connection $A_\mu$ $\to$ covariant derivative.

**Step 3: Derivational disjointness of the two channels.** Algebraic Channel uses
the matter Lagrangian, global $U(1)$ symmetry, Noether's theorem, the
local-promotion construction with explicit cancellation of the
obstruction term, and the gauge-field kinetic term. Geometric Channel uses the
McGucken-Sphere $U(1)$-bundle structure, the connection on the bundle,
and parallel transport of bundle sections. The intermediate machinery is
disjoint:

-   Lagrangian formalism, Noether's theorem, and local-promotion
    construction appear in Algebraic Channel, not in Geometric Channel;

-   $U(1)$-bundle structure, connection, and parallel transport appear
    in Geometric Channel, not in Algebraic Channel.

The two channels share only $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, the final
covariant derivative $D_\mu = \partial_\mu + (iq/\hbar)A_\mu$, and the
conservation $\partial_\mu j^\mu = 0$.

**Step 4: McGucken anchoring of the gauge structure.** The $U(1)$-bundle
structure of the McGucken Sphere descends from the principle's
perpendicularity-marker $i$ in $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: the $i$ is the
complex-phase rotation that generates the $U(1)$ fibre at every event.
The factor $iq/\hbar$ in the covariant derivative has the $i$ as a
chain-rule image of the McGucken-Principle $i$
(Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"} case 10: $U(1)$ gauge phase), the $\hbar$ as
action per Sphere cycle (Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:62"}), and the $q$ as the $U(1)$-charge label on the
matter representation. All three constants descend from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

**Step 5: Physical content and extension to non-abelian gauge.** The
$U(1)$ gauge invariance is the basis of quantum
electrodynamics (QED): the gauge field $A_\mu$ is the photon field, with
Maxwell equations as the Euler-Lagrange equations of the gauge kinetic
term. Extending to non-abelian gauge groups ($SU(2)$ weak, $SU(3)$
strong) follows the same pattern with the McGucken-Sphere
extended to higher-rank bundles; the Standard Model gauge group
$SU(3) \times SU(2) \times U(1)$ is derivable along this McGucken-bundle
programme (cf. [@MG-SM-2026]). The Aharonov-Bohm effect (Aharonov-Bohm
1959) is the empirical confirmation that the gauge potential $A_\mu$ ---
not just its curl $F_{\mu\nu}$ --- has observable consequences: a
charged particle traversing a region with $\mathbf{B} = 0$ but
$\mathbf{A} \ne 0$ acquires a phase shift proportional to
$\oint A\cdot d\ell$, exactly as predicted by the McGucken Sphere
bundle's parallel transport. ◻
:::

### Algebraic Channel derivation: Noether plus gauge promotion

::: {#lem:QMT16-noether .lemma}
**Lemma 16.2** (Noether current of global $U(1)$ symmetry). *Global
$U(1)$ phase invariance of the matter Lagrangian (QA7) yields the
conserved current
$j^\mu = (i\hbar/2m)(\psi^*\partial^\mu\psi - \psi\,\partial^\mu\psi^*)$
with $\partial_\mu j^\mu = 0$ on solutions of the Klein--Gordon
equation.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has four steps establishing the Noether
current and verifying its conservation.

**Step 1: $U(1)$ invariance forced by McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework.** By
Theorem [5.1](#thm:QMT5){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT5"}
(rest-mass phase factor), the matter wavefunction has the form
$\psi = A\,e^{-imc^2\tau/\hbar}\cdot(\text{spatial profile})$ with the
overall phase unobservable: the Born-rule density $|\psi|^2$
(Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"}) is invariant under
$\psi \to e^{i\alpha}\psi$ for any constant $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$.
This global $U(1)$ symmetry has the reading of a consequence
of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}): the integrated kinematic shadow $x_4 = ict$
(Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}, the kinematic shadow of the
dynamical principle) enters $\psi$ only through
$\exp(\text{linear in }x_4) = \exp(\text{linear in }t)$, with the
absolute origin of the $x_4$-phase undetermined by
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i)--(v) (only $dx_4/dt = ic$ is
determined, with the additive constant in the integrated $x_4$
undetermined).

**Step 2: Klein--Gordon Lagrangian and its variation.** The relativistic
Klein--Gordon Lagrangian for the matter wavefunction
$\psi: M_{G}\to \mathbb{C}$ is
$$\mathcal{L} \;=\; \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\,\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\psi^*\,\partial_\nu\psi - \frac{1}{2}mc^2\,|\psi|^2,$$
where $\eta^{\mu\nu}$ is the McGucken-derived Minkowski metric in
signature $(-,+,+,+)$
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}). Under the global $U(1)$ phase rotation
$\psi \to e^{i\alpha}\psi$ with constant $\alpha$, every term in
$\mathcal{L}$ is invariant:
$|\psi|^2 \to |e^{i\alpha}\psi|^2 = |\psi|^2$, and
$\partial_\mu\psi^*\partial_\nu\psi \to (e^{-i\alpha}\partial_\mu\psi^*)(e^{i\alpha}\partial_\nu\psi) = \partial_\mu\psi^*\partial_\nu\psi$
(the phase cancels because $\alpha$ is constant, so
$\partial_\mu(e^{\pm i\alpha}\psi) = e^{\pm i\alpha}\partial_\mu\psi$
with no extra term).

**Step 3: Apply Noether's first theorem.** For a continuous symmetry
generated by the infinitesimal transformation
$\delta\psi = i\alpha\psi$, $\delta\psi^* = -i\alpha\psi^*$, Noether's
first theorem (Noether 1918 [@Noether1918]) gives the conserved current
$$j^\mu \;=\; \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial(\partial_\mu\psi)}\,\delta\psi + \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial(\partial_\mu\psi^*)}\,\delta\psi^*,$$
after absorbing the parameter $\alpha$ into the current's overall
normalisation. Computing the partial derivatives of $\mathcal{L}$:
$$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial(\partial_\mu\psi)} \;=\; \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\,\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\nu\psi^* \;=\; \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\,\partial^\mu\psi^*, \qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial(\partial_\mu\psi^*)} \;=\; \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\,\partial^\mu\psi.$$
Substituting $\delta\psi = i\alpha\psi$, $\delta\psi^* = -i\alpha\psi^*$
and dividing out the $\alpha$:
$$j^\mu \;=\; \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\bigl(\partial^\mu\psi^*\cdot i\psi + \partial^\mu\psi\cdot(-i\psi^*)\bigr) \;=\; \frac{i\hbar^2}{2m}\bigl(\psi\,\partial^\mu\psi^* - \psi^*\,\partial^\mu\psi\bigr).$$
Multiplying by an overall minus sign (an admissible normalisation
choice, since the conservation law is preserved):
$$j^\mu \;=\; \frac{i\hbar^2}{2m}\bigl(\psi^*\,\partial^\mu\psi - \psi\,\partial^\mu\psi^*\bigr).$$
The standard convention used in the theorem statement
[\[eq:Noether-U1\]](#eq:Noether-U1){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:Noether-U1"} absorbs one factor of $\hbar$ into the
normalisation of the current (equivalently, rescales the global-$U(1)$
generator by $\hbar^{-1}$), giving
$$j^\mu \;=\; \frac{i\hbar}{2m}\bigl(\psi^*\,\partial^\mu\psi - \psi\,\partial^\mu\psi^*\bigr),$$
matching [\[eq:Noether-U1\]](#eq:Noether-U1){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:Noether-U1"}.

**Step 4: Verify conservation $\partial_\mu j^\mu = 0$ on Klein--Gordon
solutions.** Compute the four-divergence directly: $$\begin{aligned}
  \partial_\mu j^\mu \;&=\; \frac{i\hbar}{2m}\,\partial_\mu\bigl(\psi^*\,\partial^\mu\psi - \psi\,\partial^\mu\psi^*\bigr) \\
  &=\; \frac{i\hbar}{2m}\bigl(\partial_\mu\psi^*\,\partial^\mu\psi + \psi^*\,\Box\psi - \partial_\mu\psi\,\partial^\mu\psi^* - \psi\,\Box\psi^*\bigr),
\end{aligned}$$ where $\Box := \eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu$ is
the d'Alembertian. The first and third terms cancel exactly:
$\partial_\mu\psi^*\partial^\mu\psi = \partial_\mu\psi\partial^\mu\psi^*$
(both are real-valued scalars equal to each other). The remaining terms
vanish when $\psi$ satisfies the Klein--Gordon equation
$\Box\psi = (mc/\hbar)^2\psi$
(Theorem [8.1](#thm:QMT8){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT8"}):
substituting,
$$\psi^*\,\Box\psi - \psi\,\Box\psi^* \;=\; \psi^*\,(mc/\hbar)^2\psi - \psi\,(mc/\hbar)^2\psi^* \;=\; 0,$$
since the mass-squared coefficient is real and
$\psi^*\psi = \psi\psi^*$. Therefore $$\partial_\mu j^\mu \;=\; 0$$ on
Klein--Gordon solutions, establishing the conservation of $j^\mu$
on-shell. This is the standard on-shell content of Noether's first
theorem. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#lem:QMT16-local-promotion .lemma}
**Lemma 16.3** (Local-$U(1)$ promotion forces the covariant derivative).
*Promoting global $U(1)$ to local $U(1)$ by $\alpha \to \alpha(x)$
(spacetime-dependent phase) requires introducing a gauge field $A_\mu$
transforming as $A_\mu \to A_\mu - (\hbar/q)\partial_\mu\alpha$, and
replacing $\partial_\mu \to D_\mu = \partial_\mu + (iq/\hbar)A_\mu$ to
restore covariance.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has six steps establishing the
covariant-derivative formalism as forced by local $U(1)$ gauge
invariance.

**Step 1: Compute the obstruction under local $U(1)$.** Under the local
$U(1)$ phase rotation $\psi \to e^{i\alpha(x)}\psi$ with
$\alpha = \alpha(x)$ spacetime-dependent, the partial derivative
acquires an extra term via the product rule:
$$\partial_\mu(e^{i\alpha(x)}\psi) = e^{i\alpha(x)}(\partial_\mu\psi + i\,\partial_\mu\alpha(x)\cdot\psi).$$
The Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}(\psi, \partial_\mu\psi)$ is no longer
invariant under the local transformation: the extra term
$i\partial_\mu\alpha\cdot\psi$ contaminates the kinetic term
$\partial_\mu\psi^*\partial^\mu\psi$, producing cross-terms
$i\partial_\mu\alpha\cdot\psi^*\partial^\mu\psi$ that fail to cancel.

**Step 2: Introduce the gauge field $A_\mu$.** Postulate a four-vector
gauge field $A_\mu(x)$ on $M_{G}$ with the inhomogeneous transformation
law $$A_\mu \to A_\mu - \frac{\hbar}{q}\,\partial_\mu\alpha(x),$$ where
$q$ is the charge of the matter field and $\hbar$ the action quantum
(both McGucken-derived: $\hbar$ via
Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}, $q$ via
the $U(1)$ representation structure). The gauge field absorbs the
contamination from local $\alpha(x)$.

**Step 3: Define the covariant derivative.** Define the gauge-covariant
derivative
$$D_\mu\psi := \partial_\mu\psi + \frac{iq}{\hbar}A_\mu\psi.$$ The
minimal-coupling prescription replaces $\partial_\mu$ by $D_\mu$
throughout the Lagrangian.

**Step 4: Verify covariant transformation.** Compute
$D_\mu(e^{i\alpha(x)}\psi)$: $$\begin{aligned}
D_\mu(e^{i\alpha}\psi) &= \partial_\mu(e^{i\alpha}\psi) + \frac{iq}{\hbar}\left(A_\mu - \frac{\hbar}{q}\partial_\mu\alpha\right)(e^{i\alpha}\psi) \\
&= e^{i\alpha}(\partial_\mu\psi + i\,\partial_\mu\alpha\cdot\psi) + \frac{iq}{\hbar}A_\mu\,e^{i\alpha}\psi - i\,\partial_\mu\alpha\cdot e^{i\alpha}\psi \\
&= e^{i\alpha}\partial_\mu\psi + \frac{iq}{\hbar}A_\mu\,e^{i\alpha}\psi \\
&= e^{i\alpha}\left(\partial_\mu\psi + \frac{iq}{\hbar}A_\mu\psi\right) = e^{i\alpha}\,D_\mu\psi.
\end{aligned}$$ The cross-term $i\partial_\mu\alpha\cdot\psi$ from Step
1 is exactly cancelled by the gauge-field's inhomogeneous
transformation. The covariant derivative transforms covariantly:
$D_\mu(e^{i\alpha(x)}\psi) = e^{i\alpha(x)}D_\mu\psi$.

**Step 5: Lagrangian invariance and kinetic term for $A_\mu$.** The
Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}(\psi, D_\mu\psi)$ built by substituting
$\partial_\mu \to D_\mu$ is now invariant under local $U(1)$: the
kinetic term $|D_\mu\psi|^2$ transforms as
$|D_\mu(e^{i\alpha}\psi)|^2 = |e^{i\alpha}D_\mu\psi|^2 = |D_\mu\psi|^2$.
The gauge field $A_\mu$ requires its own kinetic term, which must itself
be gauge-invariant. The Maxwell field strength
$$F_{\mu\nu} := \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu$$ is
gauge-invariant by construction: under
$A_\mu \to A_\mu - (\hbar/q)\partial_\mu\alpha$, the change in
$F_{\mu\nu}$ is
$-(\hbar/q)(\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\alpha - \partial_\nu\partial_\mu\alpha) = 0$
by symmetry of mixed partials. The gauge-field Lagrangian is therefore
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gauge}} = -\frac{1}{4}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu},$$
whose Euler-Lagrange equations are Maxwell's equations.

**Step 6: McGucken anchoring.** The local $U(1)$ promotion is forced by
the fact that the McGucken-Sphere wavefront's $U(1)$-phase is
a local quantity at every wavefront point: the perpendicularity-marker
$i$ in $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is a local complex-phase rotation that
varies smoothly across the wavefront. Promoting the global rigidity to
local flexibility (independent phase rotation at each event) is the
natural McGucken-anchored move; the gauge field $A_\mu$ is the
connection on the $U(1)$-bundle over $M_{G}$ that makes the local
rotation consistent across events. The factor $iq/\hbar$ in $D_\mu$ has
the $i$ as a case-2 chain-rule image of the McGucken-Principle $i$
(Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}), the $\hbar$ as the action quantum per Sphere
cycle (Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}),
and the $q$ as the $U(1)$-charge label on the matter representation. All
three constants in the gauge-coupling factor descend from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. ◻
:::

::: {#lem:QMT16-channelA-proof .lemma}
**Lemma 16.4** (Algebraic Channel proof of QM T16). *The covariant derivative
[\[eq:covd\]](#eq:covd){reference-type="eqref" reference="eq:covd"} and
conserved Noether current
[\[eq:Noether-U1\]](#eq:Noether-U1){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:Noether-U1"} follow from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via
Lemmas [16.2](#lem:QMT16-noether){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-noether"}
and [16.3](#lem:QMT16-local-promotion){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-local-promotion"}.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **Step 1: Apply
Lemma [16.2](#lem:QMT16-noether){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-noether"} for global $U(1)$.** The McGucken matter
wavefunction $\psi: M_{G}\to \mathbb{C}$ has global $U(1)$ phase
freedom: under $\psi \mapsto e^{i\alpha}\psi$ for constant
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$, the Lagrangian density
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{matter}}(\psi, \partial_\mu\psi)$ is invariant
(the phase cancels in $|\psi|^2$ terms, and partial derivatives commute
with the constant phase since $\alpha$ is independent of $x$). By
Noether's first theorem
(Lemma [16.2](#lem:QMT16-noether){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-noether"}, four-step proof: $U(1)$ invariance from
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, Klein--Gordon Lagrangian invariance under constant
phase, Noether-current formula applied to $\delta\psi = i\alpha\psi$,
on-shell conservation via Klein--Gordon equation), this global symmetry
generates the conserved probability current
$$j^\mu \;=\; \frac{i\hbar}{2m}\bigl(\psi^*\,\partial^\mu\psi - \psi\,\partial^\mu\psi^*\bigr),$$
satisfying $\partial_\mu j^\mu = 0$ on Klein--Gordon solutions
(Lemma [16.2](#lem:QMT16-noether){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-noether"} Step 4). This is the probability
four-current of
equation [\[eq:Noether-U1\]](#eq:Noether-U1){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:Noether-U1"}. The corresponding electromagnetic
four-current is $j_{\mathrm{EM}}^\mu = q\,j^\mu$ (multiplication by the
matter field's charge $q$), which sources the Maxwell field strength in
Step 4 below.

**Step 2: Apply
Lemma [16.3](#lem:QMT16-local-promotion){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-local-promotion"} for local $U(1)$.** Promoting the
global $U(1)$ to a local gauge symmetry,
$\psi \mapsto e^{i\alpha(\mathbf{x}, t)}\psi$ with spacetime-dependent
phase $\alpha$, breaks naive Lagrangian invariance because
$\partial_\mu\psi$ no longer transforms covariantly:
$\partial_\mu(e^{i\alpha}\psi) = e^{i\alpha}(\partial_\mu\psi + i(\partial_\mu\alpha)\psi)$,
with the additional $i(\partial_\mu\alpha)\psi$ term breaking
invariance. By
Lemma [16.3](#lem:QMT16-local-promotion){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-local-promotion"} (six-step proof: identify the
obstruction $i\partial_\mu\alpha$, introduce gauge field $A_\mu$ with
inhomogeneous transformation, define covariant derivative
$D_\mu = \partial_\mu + iqA_\mu/\hbar$, verify
$D_\mu(e^{i\alpha}\psi) = e^{i\alpha}D_\mu\psi$ covariance, add Maxwell
kinetic term, anchor in McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework), restoring local-$U(1)$
invariance forces:
$$D_\mu \;:=\; \partial_\mu + \frac{iq}{\hbar}\,A_\mu, \qquad A_\mu \;\mapsto\; A_\mu - \frac{\hbar}{q}\,\partial_\mu\alpha.$$
This is the covariant derivative
[\[eq:covd\]](#eq:covd){reference-type="eqref" reference="eq:covd"} and
the gauge transformation of $A_\mu$, with $q$ the matter field's charge.

**Step 3: Gauge-invariant kinetic term for $A_\mu$.** The gauge field
$A_\mu$ requires its own dynamical term, gauge-invariant by
construction. The unique second-order Lorentz-invariant gauge-invariant
term is
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gauge}} \;=\; -\frac{1}{4}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}, \qquad F_{\mu\nu} \;:=\; \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu,$$
with $F_{\mu\nu}$ invariant under
$A_\mu \mapsto A_\mu - (\hbar/q)\partial_\mu\alpha$: the change in
$F_{\mu\nu}$ is
$-(\hbar/q)(\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\alpha - \partial_\nu\partial_\mu\alpha) = 0$
by symmetry of mixed partials, equivalently the closed-form identity
$d(d\alpha) = 0$.

**Step 4: Maxwell's equations as Euler--Lagrange consequences.** Varying
the full Lagrangian
$\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{matter}}(\psi, D_\mu\psi) + \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gauge}}$
with respect to $A_\mu$ gives the inhomogeneous Maxwell equation
$\partial_\nu F^{\nu\mu} = j_{\mathrm{EM}}^\mu = q\,j^\mu$ (the
electromagnetic four-current of Step 1 sources the field strength).
Varying with respect to $\psi$ gives the gauge-covariant matter equation
(Schrödinger/Klein--Gordon/Dirac, depending on the matter content) with
$\partial_\mu \to D_\mu$. The homogeneous Maxwell equation
$\partial_{[\mu}F_{\nu\rho]} = 0$ is the Bianchi identity, automatic
from $F = dA$.

**Step 5: Algebraic Channel characterisation.** The derivation uses Noether's
theorem (algebraic symmetry, supplying the conserved current from global
$U(1)$ invariance) and the minimal-coupling prescription (algebraic
gauge-covariance enforcement, supplying the covariant derivative from
local $U(1)$ promotion). No Sphere-geometric machinery is invoked at the
algebraic level; the proof is Algebraic Channel, derivationally disjoint from the
Geometric Channel route via the $U(1)$-bundle on the Sphere
(Lemma [16.5](#lem:QMT16-sphere-bundle){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-sphere-bundle"} below). $\square$ ◻
:::

### Vector coupling forced by condition (M): the right-multiplication argument {#sec:vector-coupling-from-M}

The covariant derivative construction of
Lemma [16.3](#lem:QMT16-local-promotion){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-local-promotion"} produces the gauge-coupled Dirac
Lagrangian. The next question --- addressed by [@MG-QED-2026]
§IV.4 --- is whether this construction produces the standard QED vector
coupling $-e A_\mu \bar\psi\gamma^\mu\psi$ or the alternative
axial-vector coupling $-e A_\mu \bar\psi\gamma^\mu\gamma^5\psi$. The
answer is non-trivial: a naive left-multiplication ansatz produces
axial-vector coupling, which is wrong. The correct right-multiplication
structure dictated by condition (M) from
Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:dirac"}
produces the standard vector coupling. This subsection makes the
distinction rigorous.

::: {#prop:vector-coupling-from-M .proposition}
**Proposition 16.7** (Vector coupling derived from condition (M);
[@MG-QED-2026] §IV.4). *Let the McGucken-coupled Dirac Lagrangian be
obtained from Theorem [9.1](#thm:QMT9){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT9"} by minimal coupling via
$\partial_\mu \to D_\mu = \partial_\mu + ieA_\mu I$ in the
geometric-algebra formulation, with
$I = \gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3$ the Clifford pseudoscalar and $e$
the electron charge. Let the local phase rotation be implemented by
right-multiplication consistent with the matter orientation condition
(M) of Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:dirac"}:
$$\Psi(x, x_4) \;\longrightarrow\; \Psi(x, x_4) \cdot e^{i\alpha(x) I}\big|_{\mathrm{right}}.$$
Then the induced interaction term in the matrix-spinor formulation is
the standard QED vector coupling
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{int}} \;=\; -e\,\bar\psi\,\gamma^\mu\,\psi\,A_\mu,$$
not the axial-vector coupling
$-e\,\bar\psi\,\gamma^\mu\gamma^5\,\psi\,A_\mu$ that would arise from a
left-multiplication ansatz.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has six steps establishing that condition
(M)'s right-multiplication structure forces vector coupling.

**Step 1: The Clifford-algebraic facts.** In $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$ with
metric signature $(-, +, +, +)$, the pseudoscalar
$I = \gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3$ satisfies
(Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:dirac"},
Lemma [9.10](#lem:gamma4-equals-igamma0){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:gamma4-equals-igamma0"} and surrounding lemmas):

-   $I^2 = -1$ (the pseudoscalar squares to $-1$ in $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$);

-   $\gamma^\mu I = -I\gamma^\mu$ (anticommutation with vectors);

-   $I$ commutes with all even-grade elements (scalars, bivectors, the
    pseudoscalar itself).

**Step 2: The naive left-multiplication ansatz produces axial-vector
coupling.** Suppose the local rotation acts by *left-multiplication*:
$\Psi \to e^{i\alpha I}\Psi$. The covariant derivative
$D_\mu = \partial_\mu + ieA_\mu I$ acting through the Dirac kinetic term
gives the interaction: $$\begin{aligned}
i\gamma^\mu D_\mu\Psi \;&=\; i\gamma^\mu(\partial_\mu + ieA_\mu I)\Psi \\
&=\; i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\Psi + ieA_\mu\,i\gamma^\mu I\,\Psi \\
&=\; i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\Psi - eA_\mu\,\gamma^\mu I\,\Psi,
\end{aligned}$$ where the second $i$ combined with $\gamma^\mu I$
produces the explicit sign. The interaction is therefore
$-eA_\mu\bar\Psi\gamma^\mu I\Psi$. Using the Weyl-basis identity
$I = i\gamma^5$ (direct computation from
$I = \gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3$ in the Weyl basis gives
$i\gamma^5$ with $\gamma^5 := i\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3$ in
standard conventions), this becomes
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{int,naive}} \;=\; -eA_\mu\,\bar\Psi\,\gamma^\mu\,(i\gamma^5)\,\Psi \;=\; -ieA_\mu\,\bar\Psi\,\gamma^\mu\gamma^5\,\Psi.$$
This is the *axial-vector* current $\bar\psi\gamma^\mu\gamma^5\psi$
coupled to $A_\mu$, not the vector current $\bar\psi\gamma^\mu\psi$.
Standard QED couples $A_\mu$ to the vector current; the naive
left-multiplication ansatz produces a different theory. This would be a
serious problem if the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework forced left-multiplication.

**Step 3: Condition (M) forces right-multiplication.** By
Definition [9.6](#def:matter-orientation-M){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:matter-orientation-M"}
(Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:dirac"}), the
matter orientation condition is
$$\Psi(x, x_4) \;=\; \Psi_0(x)\cdot\exp(+I\cdot k_C x_4)$$ with
right-multiplication of the $x_4$-rotor onto $\Psi_0(x)$. By
Theorem [9.8](#thm:single-sided-preservation-QMT9){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:single-sided-preservation-QMT9"} (Single-Sided
Preservation), this right-multiplication structure is the *unique*
algebraic action of the $x_4$-rotor on $\Psi$ that preserves (M) under
all bivector generators of the Lorentz group; left-action or sandwich
action of $x_4$-involving bivectors fails to preserve (M). The local
$U(1)$ phase rotation that is consistent with condition (M) must
therefore act by right-multiplication on $\Psi$, not
left-multiplication:
$$\Psi(x, x_4) \;\longrightarrow\; \Psi(x, x_4) \cdot e^{i\alpha(x) I}\big|_{\mathrm{right}}.$$
The matter orientation condition (M) is the input that
selects right-multiplication over left-multiplication. The condition (M)
has the reading of the algebraic shadow of the
single-sided-preservation theorem from the Dirac chapter
(Theorem [9.8](#thm:single-sided-preservation-QMT9){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:single-sided-preservation-QMT9"}): the
right-multiplication structure of $e^{i\alpha I}$ on $\Psi$ has the role
of a forced consequence of the half-angle preservation of condition (M)
under all bivector generators of the Lorentz group, rather than a free
choice of convention.

**Step 4: Right-multiplication translates to pure-phase
left-multiplication on matrix spinors.** Using the Doran--Lasenby
correspondence (Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:dirac"}, §[9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:dirac"} relating geometric-algebra multivectors to matrix
spinors), a Dirac matrix spinor $\psi_{\mathrm{matrix}}$ corresponds to
the geometric-algebra multivector $\Psi$ via
$\psi_{\mathrm{matrix}} = \Psi \cdot \xi_0$ where $\xi_0$ is a fixed
reference spinor in $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$. Under right-multiplication of
$\Psi$ by $e^{i\alpha I}$,
$$\Psi \;\longrightarrow\; \Psi\,e^{i\alpha I}, \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{matrix}} \;=\; \Psi\cdot\xi_0 \;\longrightarrow\; \Psi\,e^{i\alpha I}\cdot\xi_0 \;=\; \Psi\cdot(e^{i\alpha I}\,\xi_0).$$
The reference spinor $\xi_0$ is chosen such that $I\xi_0 = i\xi_0$ in
the matrix representation (which is consistent with $I = i\gamma^5$ and
the chirality structure of $\xi_0$ in the standard conventions).
Therefore
$e^{i\alpha I}\xi_0 = e^{i\alpha\cdot i}\xi_0 = e^{i^2\alpha}\xi_0$, but
with the algebraic absorption: $\xi_0$'s position absorbs the
pseudoscalar into a pure complex phase. The net effect on the matrix
spinor is
$$\psi_{\mathrm{matrix}} \;\longrightarrow\; e^{i\alpha(x)}\,\psi_{\mathrm{matrix}},$$
a *pure complex phase rotation on the matrix spinor*, with no $\gamma^5$
appearing. This is the central translation step: right-multiplication by
$e^{i\alpha I}$ in the geometric algebra is left-multiplication by the
pure phase $e^{i\alpha}$ on the matrix spinor.

**Step 5: The covariant derivative in matrix form gives vector
coupling.** With the pure-phase rotation $\psi \to e^{i\alpha(x)}\psi$
on matrix spinors, the standard QED covariant derivative is
$$D_\mu\psi \;=\; (\partial_\mu + ieA_\mu)\,\psi$$ with *no* $\gamma^5$
in the gauge term, transforming covariantly under the local $U(1)$ phase
rotation. The induced interaction in the Dirac Lagrangian is
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{int}} \;=\; \bar\psi(i\gamma^\mu D_\mu)\psi - \bar\psi(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu)\psi \;=\; -eA_\mu\,\bar\psi\,\gamma^\mu\,\psi.$$
This is the standard QED vector coupling. The factor $\gamma^5$ that
appeared in the naive left-multiplication ansatz of Step 2 does *not*
appear here, because the matrix-spinor phase rotation is a pure phase
with no pseudoscalar admixture.

**Step 6: Why this matters at the level of derivation.** The vector-coupling structure
of standard QED has the reading of a forced consequence of
the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework via condition (M) and
Theorem [9.8](#thm:single-sided-preservation-QMT9){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:single-sided-preservation-QMT9"}. A reader who suspected
the LTD framework was a loose reinterpretation of standard QED might
worry that the coupling form is freely choosable; the rigorous
derivation of Steps 1--5 shows that condition (M) pins down the coupling
to vectorial. The axial-vector current $\bar\psi\gamma^\mu\gamma^5\psi$
exists as a legitimate operator in the theory --- the same operator that
couples to the weak interaction $SU(2)_L$ in the Standard Model --- but
its coupling to the electromagnetic gauge field $A_\mu$ vanishes by the
right-multiplication structure of condition (M). The electromagnetic
current is vectorial because $A_\mu$ has the geometric reading of a
connection on the right-multiplication $x_4$-orientation bundle; the
weak charged current is $V - A$ because the weak gauge field has the
geometric reading of a connection on a different geometric structure
(transverse-to-$x_4$ rotations, sketched in [@MG-QED-2026] §IV.4 closing
paragraph). The LTD framework distinguishes the two by their distinct
underlying geometric structures, consistent with the empirical Standard
Model: pure $V$ for electromagnetism, $V - A$ for the weak charged
current. $\square$ ◻
:::

### Magnetic monopole absence as a rigorous bundle-triviality theorem {#sec:monopole-bundle-triviality}

The $U(1)$-bundle structure of the McGucken Sphere is established in
Lemma [16.5](#lem:QMT16-sphere-bundle){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-sphere-bundle"}. The next question is
the *topological class* of this bundle. A non-trivial $U(1)$-bundle with
first Chern class $c_1(P) \ne 0$ would correspond to the existence of
magnetic monopoles --- point sources for the magnetic field with
non-zero magnetic charge $\int_{S^2}F/(2\pi) = g \ne 0$ on a 2-sphere
surrounding the monopole. The McGucken Principle's global directionality
$dx_4/dt = +ic$ provides a argument that the bundle is
trivial and monopoles are forbidden. We make this argument rigorous via
the standard fiber-bundle topology equivalence of triviality and global
section.

::: {#thm:monopole-bundle-triviality .theorem}
**Theorem 16.8** (Triviality of the $x_4$-orientation $U(1)$-bundle and
absence of magnetic monopoles; [@MG-QED-2026] §VIII.3). *The principal
$U(1)$-bundle $P \to M_{G}$ whose connection one-form is $A_\mu\,dx^\mu$
admits a globally defined continuous section --- namely the section
provided by the McGucken Principle's globally defined direction
$dx_4/dt = +ic$. Consequently:*

1.  *$P$ is trivial: $P \cong M_{G}\times U(1)$ as a principal
    $U(1)$-bundle.*

2.  *The first Chern class vanishes:
    $c_1(P) = 0 \in H^2(M_{G}, \mathbb{Z})$.*

3.  *No magnetic monopoles exist: the integral of $F/(2\pi)$ over any
    closed 2-surface $\Sigma \subset M_{G}$ vanishes,
    $$\int_\Sigma \frac{F}{2\pi} \;=\; 0,$$ forbidding any point source
    of magnetic charge $g \ne 0$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has five steps invoking the standard
equivalence of bundle triviality and existence of a global section, with
the McGucken Principle providing the required global section.

**Step 1: Standard fiber-bundle theorem (global section
$\Leftrightarrow$ trivial).** For a principal $G$-bundle $P \to M$ with
structure group $G$ a Lie group, the standard theorem of fiber-bundle
topology (Kobayashi--Nomizu [@KobayashiNomizu1963] Volume I Proposition
I.5.4; Nakahara [@Nakahara2003] §9.2) states that $P$ is trivial (i.e.,
isomorphic to the product bundle $M \times G$) if and only if $P$ admits
a continuous global section $\sigma: M \to P$ with
$\pi \circ \sigma = \mathrm{id}_M$, where $\pi$ is the bundle
projection. The equivalence is constructive: given a global section, the
trivialization $P \cong M \times G$ is constructed by
$(\sigma(x), g) \leftrightarrow p$ where $p \in P_x$ is determined by
$p = \sigma(x) \cdot g$ via the right $G$-action. Conversely, the
trivialization gives a canonical section $\sigma(x) = (x, e)$ with
$e \in G$ the identity.

**Step 2: McGucken Principle provides a global section.** The McGucken
Principle $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ specifies (clause (i) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}) a uniform $x_4$-expansion rate $c$ at every
event of $M_{G}$, with the direction $+i$ (rather than $-i$) fixed
globally. By clause (v) (global validity), the principle holds at every
event without exception. The $U(1)$-fibre at each event is the circle of
possible $x_4$-orientation phases in the 2D plane perpendicular to the
$x_4$-expansion direction. The McGucken Principle's globally fixed $+i$
direction picks out a specific reference phase angle in this 2D plane at
every event:
$$\sigma(x) \;:=\; \text{the } x_4\text{-orientation phase whose argument is } 0 \text{ in the direction of } dx_4/dt = +ic.$$
This assignment is continuous (indeed, constant) across all of $M_{G}$
because the expansion direction is uniformly $+ic$ everywhere. The
assignment is well-defined as a section of $P$: at each $x \in M_{G}$,
$\sigma(x)$ is the bundle element corresponding to the reference phase,
with the fiber action of $U(1)$ providing all other phase choices via
$\sigma(x)\cdot e^{i\theta}$ for $\theta \in [0, 2\pi)$.

**Step 3: Triviality of the bundle.** By the standard fiber-bundle
theorem of Step 1, the existence of the continuous global section
$\sigma$ of Step 2 establishes that $P$ is trivial:
$$P \;\cong\; M_{G}\times U(1)$$ as a principal $U(1)$-bundle. The
trivialization is given by
$(x, e^{i\theta}) \leftrightarrow \sigma(x)\cdot e^{i\theta}$.

**Step 4: Vanishing of the first Chern class.** For a trivial principal
$U(1)$-bundle, the first Chern class vanishes:
$$c_1(P) \;=\; 0 \in H^2(M_{G}, \mathbb{Z}).$$ This is the standard
result of characteristic-class theory (Nakahara [@Nakahara2003] §11.4):
the Chern class measures the topological obstruction to bundle
triviality, and a trivial bundle has zero Chern class by definition.
Algebraically, the connection one-form on a trivial bundle is globally
defined as a pure $\mathbb{R}$-valued (rather than only
locally-$\mathbb{R}$-valued) one-form, so the curvature two-form
$F = dA$ is exact globally, and its integral over any closed 2-surface
vanishes by Stokes' theorem:
$$\int_\Sigma F \;=\; \int_\Sigma dA \;=\; \int_{\partial\Sigma} A \;=\; 0$$
since $\partial\Sigma = \emptyset$ for a closed surface.

**Step 5: No monopoles exist.** A magnetic monopole at a point
$p \in M_{G}$ would correspond to a $U(1)$-bundle defined over
$M_{G}\setminus \{p\}$ with first Chern class on a small 2-sphere
$S^2_\varepsilon$ surrounding $p$ equal to the (Dirac-quantized)
magnetic charge:
$$\int_{S^2_\varepsilon} \frac{F}{2\pi} \;=\; g \ne 0.$$ By Step 4, the
McGucken-derived $U(1)$-bundle on $M_{G}$ has $c_1(P) = 0$, so the
integral of $F/(2\pi)$ over any closed 2-surface in $M_{G}$ is zero. In
particular, no point $p \in M_{G}$ can support a magnetic monopole,
because doing so would require the bundle's first Chern class on a
2-sphere surrounding $p$ to be non-zero, contradicting the bundle
triviality established in Step 3. Magnetic monopoles are therefore
forbidden in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework at the geometric level of bundle
triviality, with the absence reading as a consequence of the
globally defined $+ic$ direction of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ rather than
an experimental suppression to be circumvented at higher energies.

**Geometric content of the absence of monopoles.** A spacetime region
containing a magnetic monopole would require the $x_4$-expansion
direction to be *topologically twisted* over some neighborhood of the
monopole, in such a way that the $x_4$-orientation reference direction
cannot be continuously assigned. But the McGucken Principle
$dx_4/dt = +ic$ specifies that the expansion direction is uniformly
$+ic$ at every event with no possibility of twist (clauses (i), (iv),
(v) of Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: invariance, Lorentz consistency, global
validity). A monopole would therefore require the McGucken Principle to
fail at the monopole's location --- which is impossible by clause (v). A
single observed magnetic monopole anywhere in the universe would refute
the McGucken Principle. The current experimental status (null results
across all monopole searches since Dirac's 1931 proposal [@Dirac1931],
including MoEDAL at the LHC, MACRO and IceCube, and cosmic-ray and
matter searches) is consistent with the prediction but does not uniquely
confirm it; many theories predict suppressed monopole densities. What
distinguishes the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework is that the prediction is
*absolute*: not suppressed, but forbidden. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:monopole-vs-gut .remark}
*Remark 16.9* (Contrast with grand-unified theories). In grand-unified
theories (Georgi--Glashow $SU(5)$, Pati--Salam, $SO(10)$, $E_6$),
magnetic monopoles arise from the symmetry-breaking structure of the
unified group down to $U(1)_{\mathrm{EM}}$ via the 't Hooft--Polyakov
mechanism. A GUT with non-trivial second homotopy group
$\pi_2(G/H) \ne 0$ predicts monopole solitons with masses near the GUT
scale ($\sim 10^{15}$--$10^{16}$ GeV), well above current experimental
reach; the non-observation of GUT monopoles does not (yet) falsify GUTs.
The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework has distinct content: monopoles are
forbidden at the foundational level by the bundle-triviality theorem of
Theorem [16.8](#thm:monopole-bundle-triviality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:monopole-bundle-triviality"}, with the bundle's
$c_1(P) = 0$ as a geometric consequence of the globally defined $+ic$
direction rather than a high-mass-scale suppression. A single monopole
observation would refute the McGucken Principle directly --- the bundle
could not be trivial, the global section could not exist, and the
principle's globally fixed $+ic$ direction would fail. This has the role
of a stronger and more falsifiable prediction than the GUT prediction.
:::

### Why $U(1)$ specifically, and why the photon is massless {#sec:u1-uniqueness-and-photon-masslessness}

::: {#rmk:why-u1 .remark}
*Remark 16.10* (Why the gauge group is $U(1)$ rather than another Lie
group; [@MG-QED-2026] §VIII.1). The gauge group of QED has emerged as
$U(1)$ rather than $SU(2)$, $SU(3)$, or another Lie group. The reason is: the $x_4$-orientation at each event of $M_{G}$ is
characterized by a *single complex phase*, parameterized by an angle
$\alpha \in [0, 2\pi)$ in the 2D plane perpendicular to the
$x_4$-expansion direction. The group of possible choices of reference
phase is the circle $S^1 = U(1)$, the symmetry group of complex phase
rotations on a one-dimensional complex line. Gauge invariance is the
statement that physics is invariant under reparametrization of this
circle at each event, which is precisely local $U(1)$ invariance.

Other gauge groups arise in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework when different
geometric structures are promoted to local symmetries
(cf. [@MG-QED-2026] §X.3, §X.4). The weak gauge group $SU(2)_L$ arises
from the $\mathrm{Spin}(4) = SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R$ rotation structure
of Euclidean 4-space, with $SU(2)_L$ as the transverse-to-$x_4$
rotations and $SU(2)_R$ identified with the gravitational sector; the
strong gauge group $SU(3)$ arises from the three spatial dimensions as a
natural triplet. The full Standard Model gauge group
$SU(3)_c \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$ emerges from these distinct
geometric structures, each promoted to local symmetry via its own bundle
structure. For the $x_4$-orientation alone --- the structure that gives
rise to electromagnetism --- the group is uniquely $U(1)$, because the
orientation is a complex phase, and complex phases have $U(1)$ symmetry.
The gauge group has the reading of a derived consequence of
the geometric structure being made locally invariant: each geometric
structure on $M_{G}$ supplies its own bundle and hence its own gauge
group via the geometric construction of
Lemma [16.6](#lem:QMT16-channelB-proof){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-channelB-proof"}.
:::

::: {#rmk:photon-masslessness .remark}
*Remark 16.11* (Photon masslessness from gauge invariance and from
geometric structure; [@MG-QED-2026] §VIII.2). The photon is the quantum
of the gauge field $A_\mu$. A photon mass term in the Lagrangian would
be $-\tfrac{1}{2}m_\gamma^2 A_\mu A^\mu$, but this term is not invariant
under the gauge transformation
$A_\mu \to A_\mu - (\hbar/q)\partial_\mu\alpha$:
$$-\tfrac{1}{2}m_\gamma^2(A_\mu - (\hbar/q)\partial_\mu\alpha)(A^\mu - (\hbar/q)\partial^\mu\alpha) \;\ne\; -\tfrac{1}{2}m_\gamma^2 A_\mu A^\mu.$$
Local $U(1)$ gauge invariance therefore *forbids* a photon mass: the
photon has exactly zero mass at the gauge-invariant Lagrangian level,
with no approximate-mass slack admissible without breaking local $U(1)$
invariance. This is the standard QED argument.

In the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, the photon-masslessness has a direct
*geometric* content beyond the algebraic gauge-invariance argument. A
photon mass would mean the photon has a rest frame, i.e., a
Compton-frequency standing-wave structure in $x_4$ at rate
$\omega_C = m_\gamma c^2/\hbar$ (by
Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT4"}
applied to a massive photon). But the photon is, by the
Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:dirac"}
characterization, a *pure $x_4$-oscillation without standing-wave
component*: the photon's worldline is null, with its entire share of the expansion spent on spatial motion --- $v_{x_4} = \sqrt{c^{2} - v^{2}} = 0$ at $v = c$ (Definition [4.2B](#def:x4-share){reference-type="ref" reference="def:x4-share"}) --- so that $X_{4}$ does not accumulate along the worldline and no proper time elapses. The photon has no rest frame in which a standing wave could be defined. The condition for a Compton-frequency
standing wave to form requires the particle's worldline to be timelike
(proper time elapses, the rest-mass phase $e^{-imc^2\tau/\hbar}$
accumulates); for a null worldline, no proper time elapses and no
standing wave can form. The masslessness of the photon and the
masslessness of the gauge field are two faces of the same McGucken fact:
a particle that rides the McGucken Sphere directly (null worldline)
cannot have a Compton-frequency standing wave (timelike requirement),
and cannot have a mass.

The three faces of the photon's masslessness --- algebraic (gauge
invariance forbids the mass term), geometric (pure $x_4$-oscillation has
no rest frame) (no Compton-frequency standing wave) ---
are equivalent in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework. Breaking one breaks the
others: a massive photon would require non-gauge-invariance, a rest
frame, and a Compton standing-wave structure simultaneously, all of
which are forbidden by the geometry of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
together. Current experimental bounds give $m_\gamma < 10^{-27}$ eV
(from Coulomb's law at large distances and astrophysical magnetic-field
measurements); the McGucken prediction is exactly zero, consistent with
all current measurements.
:::

### Disjointness audit {#disjointness-audit-13}

**Geometric Channel:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, McGucken Sphere as
$U(1)$-bundle base, fiber phase, connection on the bundle.

**Algebraic Channel:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, global $U(1)$ phase symmetry,
Noether's theorem, local-promotion requirement, covariant derivative
construction.

**Intersection:**
$\{(\mathrm{McP}), D_\mu = \partial_\mu + iqA_\mu/\hbar, j^\mu \text{ conserved}\}$.
*Disjointness verified.*

### Empirical anchor

-   Maxwell's equations follow from $U(1)$ minimal coupling with
    $\mathcal{L}_{\text{gauge}} = -\tfrac{1}{4}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$
    (Maxwell 1865 [@Maxwell1865]); confirmed in classical
    electrodynamics since.

-   The Aharonov--Bohm effect (Aharonov, Bohm 1959 [@AharonovBohm1959],
    observed Chambers 1960; Tonomura 1986): the gauge field $A_\mu$ has
    physical effects on the matter wavefunction even in regions where
    $F_{\mu\nu} = 0$, confirming that the connection (not the field
    strength) is the fundamental object.

-   The extension to non-Abelian gauge groups ($SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$
    electroweak, $SU(3)_c$ QCD (quantum chromodynamics)) underlies the
    entire Standard Model.

## QM T17: Quantum Nonlocality {#ch:nonlocality}

> *The McGucken Principle.* The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality.
> Every result below descends from that expansion.


*Recall.* the McGucken Principle ($\mathrm{McP}$:
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$) asserts that the fourth spacetime dimension
$x_4$ expands at the velocity of light $c$, carrying the
perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguishes it from the spatial
three. Throughout this chapter, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ refers to this
principle and to the five-clause content (i)--(v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: (i) *invariance* --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content; (ii) *spherical symmetry* --- the
expansion is isotropic in the spatial three, with the set of events
reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a 2-sphere of radius
$c\tau$; (iii) *monotonicity* --- the integral curve is strictly
monotonically increasing in $t$, fixing the arrow of $x_4$-advance; (iv)
*Lorentz consistency* --- the structure is $SO^+(1,3)$-invariant on
$M_{G}$; (v) *global validity* --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at
every event of $M_{G}$. The integrated kinematic shadow
$x_4 = ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is the kinematic shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the central fact.

### Statement

::: {#thm:QMT17 .theorem}
**Theorem 17.1** (QM T17: Nonlocality, = Theorem 76 (Algebraic Channel) and
Theorem 99 (Geometric Channel) of [@Syn-2026]). *Quantum mechanics violates
Bell-type local-hidden-variable inequalities (e.g. CHSH
(Clauser--Horne--Shimony--Holt inequality),
Theorem [13.1](#thm:QMT13){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT13"}),
with correlations between spatially separated measurements that exceed
any local explanation. The violation does not permit superluminal
signaling (the no-signaling theorem), but it does establish that the
correlations cannot be reproduced by any local theory.*
:::

### Geometric Channel derivation (QB1 --- joint Sphere wavefront from common past)

::: channelb
*Geometric Channel Derivation 17.3* (Nonlocality from joint McGucken-Sphere
wavefront from common past event). By QB1, when two entangled particles
are emitted from a common source event $p_0$, they share a joint
McGucken-Sphere structure: both particles' wavefronts $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$
propagate outward from the same source event, with the entanglement
correlations imprinted at emission.

The correlations measured at later events $p_A, p_B$ (Alice's and Bob's
detection events) are determined by the joint Sphere structure inherited
from $p_0$. The correlations are not transmitted at the moment of
measurement; they were imprinted at the source. The Geometric Channel reading
therefore exhibits the apparent "spooky action at a distance" as a
consequence of the wavefront's memory of its source: the
correlations are real, but they are not transmitted faster than light
because the imprint occurred at the source, propagated at $c$ along the
wavefronts to both detectors, and was registered when the measurements
were performed.

This is the geometric content of nonlocality in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework:
*the correlations are local in the sense that they were established at
the source and carried outward at $c$ on the McGucken Sphere; they are
nonlocal in the sense that the joint wavefront cannot be factored into
independent local descriptions of the two particles.* ◻
:::

### Algebraic Channel derivation (QA3, QA4 --- tensor product + non-commutativity)

::: channela
*Algebraic Channel Derivation 17.2* (Nonlocality from tensor-product Hilbert
space + non-commuting observables). By QA1+QA4 (Stone--von Neumann
uniqueness on the joint observable algebra), the Hilbert space of two
independent subsystems is the tensor product
$\mathcal{H}_{AB} = \mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B$. Bob's operator
$\hat{B} \otimes \mathbb{1}_A$ commutes trivially with Alice's
$\hat{A} \otimes \mathbb{1}_B$, ensuring spacelike separated
measurements commute (no-signaling).

However, the joint state $\lvert \Psi \rangle_{AB} \in \mathcal{H}_{AB}$
need not be a product
$\lvert \psi \rangle_A \otimes \lvert \phi \rangle_B$. For entangled
states (singlet, GHZ (Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger), W, etc.), the
joint state is non-factorizable, and the correlations of measurements on
$A$ and $B$ exceed the local-hidden-variable bound. The Algebraic Channel
derivation of the Tsirelson bound (Algebraic Channel of
Theorem [13.1](#thm:QMT13){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT13"})
gives the explicit quantum-mechanical maximum of $2\sqrt{2}$ for these
correlations.

The no-signaling theorem is the statement that the marginal probability
distribution at Alice's end is independent of Bob's measurement choice:
$\operatorname{tr}_B[\hat{A}\,\rho_{AB}] = \operatorname{tr}_B[\hat{A}\,(\mathbb{1}_A \otimes \hat{M}_B)\rho_{AB}(\mathbb{1}_A \otimes \hat{M}_B^\dagger)]$
for any Bob-measurement $\hat{M}_B$. This follows from the commutativity
$[\hat{A} \otimes \mathbb{1}_B, \mathbb{1}_A \otimes \hat{M}_B] = 0$. ◻
:::

### The Two Laws of Nonlocality and the six-fold geometric identity {#sec:two-laws-six-fold}

::: flushright
*"All quantum nonlocality begins in locality."\
--- [@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026], title*
:::

The Geometric Channel derivation above identified the geometric source of
nonlocality as the shared wavefront $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ emerging from a
common past event $p_0$. The April 17, 2026 paper
[@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026] sharpens this into two formal Laws
governing the origin and growth of nonlocality, and establishes a
*six-fold geometric identity* of the expanding wavefront across six
independent mathematical frameworks. The Laws and the identity together
constitute the canonical foundation on which the McGucken No-Signaling
Theorem of §[17.5](#sec:no-signaling){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:no-signaling"} below sits.

#### The First and Second McGucken Laws of Nonlocality {#the-first-and-second-mcgucken-laws-of-nonlocality .unnumbered}

::: {#thm:first-law-nonlocality .theorem}
**Theorem 17.4** (First McGucken Law of Nonlocality;
[@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026] §2.1). *Two quantum systems can exhibit
nonlocal correlations (entanglement) only if they have shared a common
local origin, or if each has interacted locally with members of a system
that itself shared a common local origin. *Equivalently:* only systems
of particles with intersecting light spheres --- with each light sphere
having originated from each respective particle --- can ever be
entangled. The property of entanglement between particles is limited by
the velocity of light, even though the nonlocal influences found in
entanglement are instantaneous.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The proof has six steps establishing that
entanglement requires a common local origin or a locally-originated
mediating chain. The First Law descends from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, the physical, geometric fact that the fourth
dimension expands at the velocity of light in a spherically symmetric
manner, with $x_4 = ict$ the integrated kinematic shadow per
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}): the joint McGucken-Sphere wavefront
from a common source event $p_0$ is the unique structure on which
non-classical correlations can supervene, and the wavefront's growth is
bounded by the speed of light $c$.

**Step 1: McGucken-Sphere structure at every event.** By the McGucken
Principle (Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i) invariance, (ii) spherical
symmetry, and (v) global validity), every event $p \in M_{G}$ is the
source of an expanding McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{p}(t)$ of radius
$c(t - t_p)$ centred at $\mathbf{x}_p$
(Definition [4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:sphere"},
Theorem [4.6](#thm:mcp-to-lorentzian){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:mcp-to-lorentzian"}). The Sphere is the geometric locus
of $x_{4}$-coherent wavefronts originating from $p$.

**Step 2: Entanglement as shared wavefront identity.** By the Geometric Channel
reading of nonlocality
(Lemma [18.5](#lem:QMT18-joint-wavefront){reference-type="ref"
