reference="lem:QMT18-joint-wavefront"}), entanglement between two
particles $A$ and $B$ is the shared wavefront identity on
$M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ inherited from a common past event $p_0$. Two particles
are entangled if and only if their joint wavefunction is
non-factorisable, which requires that they ride the same McGucken Sphere
from some common source.

**Step 3: Case 1 --- direct common origin.** If there exists an event
$p_0$ such that both detection events $p_A, p_B$ lie on the same
McGucken-Sphere wavefront $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ for some $t$, then $A$ and
$B$ share the wavefront identity directly. This is the standard case for
singlet-creation experiments (e.g., $\eta_c \to \gamma\gamma$,
parametric down-conversion, atomic two-photon cascade): both photons are
emitted from the same source event $p_0$ and share the joint Sphere
wavefront. The correlations are imprinted at emission and propagate
outward at $c$ to both detectors.

**Step 4: Case 2 --- mediating chain.** If $A$ and $B$ do not share a
direct common origin but there exist intermediate particles
$C, D, \ldots$ and intermediate source events $q_1, q_2, \ldots$ such
that each consecutive pair in the chain $(A, C), (C, D), \ldots, (D, B)$
shares a common past pair-creation event, then $A$ and $B$ can be
entangled via the mediating chain. This is entanglement-swapping (Pan et
al. 1998, Briegel et al. 1998): the chain of locally-originated McGucken
Spheres pairwise intersects, transferring entanglement from each link to
the next.

**Step 5: Case 3 --- no chain, no entanglement.** If neither a common
past event nor a mediating chain exists, then by
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, no McGucken Sphere connects $A$'s past light
cone to $B$'s past light cone. The wavefront identity on which
entanglement supervenes
(Lemma [18.5](#lem:QMT18-joint-wavefront){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT18-joint-wavefront"}) is absent, and the joint state
is necessarily factorisable as
$\lvert \psi \rangle_A \otimes \lvert \phi \rangle_B$ for any pure state
of the joint system. Without shared Sphere structure, the joint
wavefunction cannot encode non-classical correlations. The Algebraic Channel
axiom QA4 (Stone-von Neumann uniqueness on the joint observable algebra)
then forces the correlations to be Bell-classical, with
$|\langle CHSH\rangle| \le 2$, never the Tsirelson value $2\sqrt 2$.

**Step 6: McGucken anchoring --- entanglement is locality at the $x_{4}$
level.** Cases 1 and 2 establish the "only if" direction (entanglement
requires a common local origin or a locally-originated mediating chain).
Case 3 establishes the contrapositive (no common local origin or chain
implies no entanglement). The content of the First Law is:
*entanglement is locality at the $x_{4}$ level*. The textbook tradition
treats entanglement as "spooky action at a distance" and contrasts it
with relativistic locality; the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework reveals that
entanglement is itself a locality phenomenon --- locality on the joint
McGucken-Sphere wavefront sourced at a common past event. The apparent
instantaneous nonlocal correlations are the operational consequence of
the shared $x_{4}$-wavefront, imprinted at emission and propagated
outward at $c$ to both detectors. The property of entanglement between
particles is limited by the velocity of light (no instantaneous
establishment of new entanglement between previously-unconnected
systems), even though the nonlocal correlations within an
already-established entangled pair are instantaneous (a consequence of
the shared Sphere structure on $M_{G}$, not a faster-than-light
signal). ◻
:::

::: {#thm:second-law-nonlocality .theorem}
**Theorem 17.5** (Second McGucken Law of Nonlocality;
[@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026] §2.2). *Nonlocality grows over time, in
a manner limited by the velocity of light $c$. As the fourth dimension
expands at $c$, the McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ grows: at time $t$
after a local event $p_0$, the sphere of nonlocality has radius
$r = ct$. Particles within this sphere may be entangled with the
original event; particles outside it cannot be, because the expansion of
$x_4$ has not yet reached them. The boundary of entanglement possibility
is exactly the future light cone of $p_0$ --- the causal boundary of
relativity.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **Step 1: $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ produces a spherically
symmetric expansion from every event.** By clause (P2) of the McGucken
Principle, the $x_{4}$-expansion at rate $ic$ from every event $p_0$ is
spherically symmetric in the three spatial dimensions: the wavefront at
parameter time $t$ after $p_0$ is the 2-sphere
$M^{+}_{p_0}(t) \subset \Sigma_t$ of radius $c(t - t_{p_0})$ centred on
the spatial projection of $p_0$. The radius grows linearly with
parameter time at rate $c$, the principle's $x_{4}$-expansion rate.

**Step 2: The sphere of nonlocality.** By the First Law of Nonlocality
(Theorem [17.4](#thm:first-law-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:first-law-nonlocality"}), two events can be entangled
only via a McGucken-Sphere wavefront sourced at some common event in
their common past. The wavefront sourced at $p_0$ reaches at time $t$
the spatial region
$\{(\mathbf{x}, t) : |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_{p_0}| \le c(t - t_{p_0})\}$
--- equivalently, the interior of the future light cone of $p_0$
truncated to the slice $\Sigma_t$. Any event $p_A$ at
$(\mathbf{x}_A, t)$ outside this region (spatial distance
$|\mathbf{x}_A - \mathbf{x}_{p_0}| > c(t - t_{p_0})$) lies outside the
wavefront sourced at $p_0$ at time $t$, hence cannot be entangled with
the event $p_0$ via any direct-common-origin route.

**Step 3: Growth rate of the entanglement region.** The boundary of the
entanglement region $\partial M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ expands at rate $c$ in
$\Sigma_t$: differentiating
$|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_{p_0}| = c(t - t_{p_0})$ with respect to $t$
gives $|\dot{\mathbf{x}}| = c$. This is the principle's
$x_{4}$-expansion rate, projected onto the spatial slice via the
suppression map (Lemma [9.1](#lem:suppression-map){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:suppression-map"}). The growth is exact, not approximate.

**Step 4: Identification with the future light cone.** The future light
cone of $p_0$ in Minkowski spacetime is
$\{p \in M_{1,3} : (p - p_0)^\mu(p - p_0)_\mu = 0,\ t > t_{p_0}\}$ ---
the null hypersurface in the future of $p_0$. By
Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:six-fold-identity"} clause (F6), the spatial
cross-section of this null hypersurface with the slice $\Sigma_t$ is
exactly $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$. The boundary of entanglement possibility, the
boundary of the McGucken Sphere wavefront, and the boundary of the
future light cone are therefore the same geometric object.

**Step 5: Identity of causation and nonlocality boundaries.**
The relativistic causal boundary (the future light cone, limiting causal
influence in special relativity) and the quantum entanglement boundary
(the McGucken-Sphere wavefront, limiting where entanglement can be
established) coincide because both descend from the same expansion of
$x_{4}$ at rate $ic$. The textbook tradition treats them as distinct
phenomena requiring separate derivations; the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework derives
them jointly from a single principle. ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:three-faces .remark}
*Remark 17.6* (Three faces of one geometric object). The two Laws expose
a identity that the textbook tradition treats as three
independent phenomena:

-   The *light cone* of relativity (the boundary of causal influence in
    Minkowski spacetime);

-   The *expanding wavefront* of wave optics (Huygens' principle, the
    envelope of secondary wavelets);

-   The *sphere of potential entanglement* (the boundary of nonlocality
    in quantum mechanics).

All three are the same geometric object --- the McGucken Sphere
$M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ --- viewed from three different physical perspectives.
The relativistic light cone limits causal signaling; the optical
wavefront limits classical wave propagation; the entanglement sphere
limits the establishment of quantum correlations. Each is the boundary
of a region into which $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$'s expansion has so far
reached; each grows at rate $c$. Under the textbook tradition the joint
exactness of the three rates is unexplained; under the McGucken
framework it is a single fact viewed through three lenses.
:::

#### Intermediary particles and intersecting McGucken Spheres {#ssec:intermediary-particles .unnumbered}

The Case 2 branch of
Theorem [17.4](#thm:first-law-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:first-law-nonlocality"}'s proof (mediating chain) carries
most of the empirical content of the First Law: the canonical procedure
for entangling two distant unentangled particles --- *entanglement
swapping* --- is precisely a chain of locally originated McGucken
Spheres that pairwise intersect at the events of pair-creation and
Bell-state measurement. The April 17, 2026 paper
[@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026] §3 supplies the canonical analysis; we
restate it as a theorem.

::: {#thm:intersecting-spheres-transfer .theorem}
**Theorem 17.7** (Intersecting-Sphere transfer of entanglement;
[@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026] §3). *Let $A, B$ be two distant
particles, initially unentangled, at events $p_A, p_B$
spacelike-separated and outside each other's past light cones. The
canonical entanglement-swapping procedure for establishing entanglement
between $A$ and $B$ proceeds in four steps, each of which corresponds to
a McGucken Sphere intersection in $M_{1,3}$:*

1.  *(*Two locally originated pairs*.) Two ancillary particle pairs
    $(C, D)$ and $(E, F)$ are created at events $q_1$ and $q_2$
    respectively, with each pair sharing a single McGucken Sphere
    $M^{+}_{q_1}(t)$ and $M^{+}_{q_2}(t)$ at its respective source. By
    Theorem [17.4](#thm:first-law-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:first-law-nonlocality"} Case 1, $C$ and $D$ are
    entangled (direct common origin at $q_1$), and likewise $E$ and $F$
    are entangled (direct common origin at $q_2$).*

2.  *(*Local interaction at $A$*.) Particle $C$ is transported to the
    laboratory containing $A$ and interacts locally with $A$ at event
    $r_A$. The McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{q_1}(t)$ centred on $q_1$
    intersects $A$'s worldline at $r_A$; this intersection event $r_A$
    lies on both $C$'s wavefront and $A$'s worldline, transferring $C$'s
    wavefront-identity content to $A$.*

3.  *(*Bell-state measurement on $D$ and $E$*.) At an intermediate event
    $r_{DE}$, a Bell-state measurement is performed on the joint
    $(D, E)$ system. The Spheres $M^{+}_{q_1}(t)$ and $M^{+}_{q_2}(t)$
    intersect at $r_{DE}$ (a spacetime event in the future light cone of
    both $q_1$ and $q_2$). The Bell-state measurement projects $(D, E)$
    into one of the four maximally entangled Bell states, identifying
    the $D$-and-$E$ portions of the two Spheres as a single shared
    wavefront fragment.*

4.  *(*Local interaction at $B$*.) Particle $F$ is transported to the
    laboratory containing $B$ and interacts locally with $B$ at event
    $r_B$. The McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{q_2}(t)$ intersects $B$'s
    worldline at $r_B$; the intersection transfers $F$'s
    wavefront-identity content to $B$.*

*After step S4 (and conditioned on the Bell-measurement outcome at
$r_{DE}$, which must be classically communicated to the parties so they
may apply the correlated Pauli correction), $A$ and $B$ are entangled.
The chain of intersecting events
$$A \leftrightarrow_{r_A} C \leftrightarrow_{q_1} D \leftrightarrow_{r_{DE}} E \leftrightarrow_{q_2} F \leftrightarrow_{r_B} B$$
traces $A$'s entanglement with $B$ back, through a sequence of local
interactions at intersection events of locally originated McGucken
Spheres, to the two common-origin events $q_1$ and $q_2$. *Every step is
a local event at an intersection of McGucken Spheres; no nonlocal
transfer of entanglement occurs.**
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The proof has four steps tracking the protocol's
four-step structure (S1)--(S4). The result is forced by
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, the physical, geometric fact that the fourth
dimension expands at the velocity of light in a spherically symmetric
manner): every pair-creation event emits a McGucken Sphere
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i)+(ii) jointly), and intersections
of Spheres at later events are the geometric content of entanglement
transfer, with $x_4 = ict$ the integrated kinematic shadow per
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}.

**Step 1: Initial two-Sphere setup at $q_1$ and $q_2$.** By the McGucken
Principle, each pair-creation event $q_i$ emits a McGucken Sphere
$M^{+}_{q_i}(t)$ on which the pair shares wavefront identity
(Theorem [17.4](#thm:first-law-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:first-law-nonlocality"} Case 1, the wavefront-identity
content of co-emitted particles). By the linearity of the Algebraic Channel
operator algebra acting on the tensor-product Hilbert space (QA4 on the
joint system, with Hilbert space established by
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"} as a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$), the four-particle state at parameter
$t > \max(t(q_1), t(q_2))$ is
$$\lvert \Psi \rangle_{CDEF}(t) = \lvert \Phi^+ \rangle_{CD}\otimes\lvert \Phi^+ \rangle_{EF}$$
(taking both pairs to be in the singlet for definiteness; any Bell-basis
pair works the same way).

**Step 2: Bell-state measurement at intersection event $r_{DE}$.** The
Bell-state measurement on $(D, E)$ at $r_{DE}$ is the projective
measurement onto the four Bell-basis states
$\{\lvert \Phi^\pm \rangle_{DE}, \lvert \Psi^\pm \rangle_{DE}\}$. By the
standard entanglement-swapping calculation (Zeilinger *et al.* 1998
[@Zeilinger1998]), each outcome $\lvert B_k \rangle_{DE}$ projects
$\lvert \Psi \rangle_{CDEF}$ onto a state in which $C$ and $F$ are
themselves in the corresponding Bell state $\lvert B_k \rangle_{CF}$:
$$\langle B_k \rvert_{DE}\lvert \Psi \rangle_{CDEF}(t) \propto \lvert B_k \rangle_{CF}.$$
The geometric content of this algebraic identity (Geometric Channel) is the
Sphere-intersection event $r_{DE}$ where the $D$-fragment of
$M^{+}_{q_1}(t)$ meets the $E$-fragment of $M^{+}_{q_2}(t)$, identifying
them as a single combined wavefront fragment via the projective Bell
measurement.

**Step 3: Local interactions at $r_A$ and $r_B$ transfer wavefront
identity to $A$ and $B$.** The local interactions at $r_A$ (transferring
the $C$-content to $A$ via the Sphere $M^{+}_{q_1}(t)$ intersecting
$A$'s worldline at $r_A$) and at $r_B$ (transferring the $F$-content to
$B$ via the Sphere $M^{+}_{q_2}(t)$ intersecting $B$'s worldline at
$r_B$) then put $A$ and $B$ in the same Bell state
$\lvert B_k \rangle_{AB}$, conditioned on the Bell-measurement outcome
at $r_{DE}$. The Geometric Channel reading: the four-particle wavefront identity
at $t > t(r_{DE})$ is the union of fragments of $M^{+}_{q_1}(t)$
(carrying $C$, $D$) and $M^{+}_{q_2}(t)$ (carrying $E$, $F$), with the
Bell-state measurement at $r_{DE}$ identifying the $D$- and
$E$-fragments as a single combined wavefront identity, and the local
interactions at $r_A$ and $r_B$ extending this combined identity to $A$
and $B$.

**Step 4: Second Law compliance --- no superluminal signaling.** The
Second Law of nonlocality
(Theorem [17.5](#thm:second-law-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:second-law-nonlocality"}, the no-superluminal-signaling
constraint forced by
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iii) monotonicity and clause (iv), derived at Theorem 4.6
Lorentz consistency) is satisfied at every step: each intersection event
$r_A, r_{DE}, r_B$ is in the causal future of the respective Sphere
sources $q_1$ and $q_2$, and the chain has spacetime extent bounded by
the longest light-travel time between the relevant events. The
Bell-measurement outcome at $r_{DE}$ must be classically communicated to
the parties for them to apply the appropriate Pauli correction (the
no-signaling cloak of
Theorem [17.32](#thm:mcgucken-no-signaling){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:mcgucken-no-signaling"}); this classical communication is
itself bounded by $c$ and is the reason the protocol does not enable
superluminal signaling. The result is identical to the
empirical entanglement-swapping protocols of Zeilinger *et
al.* [@Zeilinger1998] and the loophole-free Bell tests of Hensen *et
al.* [@Hensen2015]. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:chain-source-empirical .remark}
*Remark 17.8* (The chain of intersection events is the source of the
empirical content). Every empirical instance of distant-particle
entanglement on record --- from the cesium-fountain Bell tests at NIST
and ILL Grenoble through Hensen *et al.* 2015's loophole-free Bell test
at 1.3 km separation [@Hensen2015] through the BIG Bell Test 2018
[@BigBellTest2018] through every quantum-key-distribution implementation
deployed since 2003 --- instantiates either Case 1 (direct common
origin) or Case 2 (entanglement swapping or its generalisations via
repeater chains) of
Theorem [17.4](#thm:first-law-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:first-law-nonlocality"}. The chain structure of
Theorem [17.7](#thm:intersecting-spheres-transfer){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:intersecting-spheres-transfer"} is the geometric content
of every successful entanglement protocol ever performed. The McGucken
framework predicts that this remains true: any new protocol that
succeeds will be analysable as a chain of intersecting McGucken Spheres
traceable to locally originated pair-creation events.
:::

::: {#rmk:multipartite-spheres .remark}
*Remark 17.9* (Multipartite generalisation: GHZ and W states).
Theorem [17.7](#thm:intersecting-spheres-transfer){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:intersecting-spheres-transfer"} generalises immediately
to the multipartite case. A three-particle GHZ state
$\lvert \mathrm{GHZ} \rangle = (\lvert 000 \rangle + \lvert 111 \rangle)/\sqrt 2$
is created at a single source event $q_0$ with a single McGucken Sphere
$M^{+}_{q_0}(t)$ carrying all three particles; the three particles share
wavefront identity in the strongest possible sense (every two-particle
marginal is itself maximally mixed, so the three-way correlation is
exactly the wavefront-identity content). For larger multipartite
resources (cluster states, W states, graph states, stabiliser codes),
the construction iterates: each pair of constituent particles is either
created at a common source (Case 1) or connected by a chain of
intersecting Spheres (Case 2), with the full multipartite entanglement
structure built up from a network of pair-creation events and
Bell-state-measurement intersections. The First Law applies to each pair
in the multipartite resource: every bipartite entanglement that the full
state encodes is traceable to a chain of local events.
:::

::: {#rmk:swap-no-paradox .remark}
*Remark 17.10* (The intersecting-Spheres reading dissolves the swapping
"paradox"). The textbook tradition sometimes presents entanglement
swapping as paradoxical: how can a Bell-state measurement on $(D, E)$ at
one location instantaneously entangle particles $A$ and $B$ at distant
laboratories that have never interacted? The McGucken
intersecting-Spheres reading dissolves the apparent paradox. $A$ and $B$
never interacted directly, but their wavefronts both descend --- through
their respective local interactions with $C$ and $F$ --- from
common-origin events $q_1$ and $q_2$, and the Bell-state measurement at
$r_{DE}$ joins those two source-Spheres into a single shared wavefront
fragment. After the measurement, $A$'s wavefront identity and $B$'s
wavefront identity have a common source via the joined-Sphere structure.
The entanglement was not transmitted instantaneously between $A$ and
$B$; it was *constituted* at $r_{DE}$ by joining their two pre-existing
Sphere identities. The apparent paradox is an artefact of viewing
entanglement as a transmissible substance rather than as a shared
wavefront identity. *All nonlocality begins in locality*, including the
nonlocality created by entanglement swapping.
:::

::: {#rmk:NYLA-chain-required .remark}
*Remark 17.11* (Connection to the New York--Los Angeles Challenge).
Theorem [17.7](#thm:intersecting-spheres-transfer){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:intersecting-spheres-transfer"} explains why the New
York--Los Angeles Challenge
(Remark [17.30](#rmk:NY-LA-challenge){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:NY-LA-challenge"}) cannot be met. Every known
entanglement-creation method satisfies condition (2) of the challenge in
the negative --- that is, every method uses a locally originated
intermediary, either through direct pair-creation (Case 1, requiring
local contact between the particles to be entangled or with a common
ancestor pair) or through swapping (Case 2, requiring intermediate
particles whose intersecting Spheres trace back to common-origin
events). No empirically realised protocol, and no thought experiment
consistent with the known laws of physics, has succeeded in establishing
entanglement between two particles without one or the other route. The
McGucken Nonlocality Principle predicts that this will remain true; the
prediction is precise and falsifiable.
:::

#### The six-fold geometric identity of the expanding wavefront {#the-six-fold-geometric-identity-of-the-expanding-wavefront .unnumbered}

The expanding McGucken Sphere is a nonlocality in the strongest possible
sense. Its spatially separated points share a common geometric identity
in six independent mathematical frameworks. All six frameworks yield the
same conclusion: *what appears from a three-dimensional perspective as a
collection of widely separated points is, in the full four-dimensional
geometry, a single unified object traceable to a single local origin.*
The six identifications are restated from §4 of
[@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026].

::: {#thm:six-fold-identity .theorem}
**Theorem 17.12** (Six-fold geometric identity of $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$;
[@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026] §4.1--4.6). *For any local source event
$p_0 \in M_{1,3}$ and any parameter $t > 0$, the expanding McGucken
Sphere $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ realizes a single geometric object in six
independent mathematical frameworks:*

1.  **Foliation theory.* $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ is a single leaf of the
    codimension-one foliation of $\mathbb{R}^3$ by nested 2-spheres
    parameterized by $t$. All points on the leaf share a common
    topological identity (the leaf separates the interior from the
    exterior).*

2.  **Metric geometry.* $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ is the level set
    $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 : d(x, x(p_0)) = ct\}$ of the Euclidean
    distance function from the spatial projection of $p_0$. All points
    share a common metric identity (equidistant from the origin in the
    induced metric).*

3.  **Wave optics (Huygens).* $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ is the envelope-caustic
    of secondary wavelets emanating from every point on the preceding
    wavefront $M^{+}_{p_0}(t-dt)$. All points share a common
    causal-optical identity (the boundary between the disturbed and
    undisturbed regions).*

4.  **Contact geometry.* In the jet space with coordinates
    $(x_1, x_2, x_3, t)$, the family $\{M^{+}_{p_0}(t)\}_{t \ge 0}$
    traces a Legendrian submanifold of the standard contact structure.
    All points on the Legendrian share a common contact-geometric
    identity (defined by the contact distribution rather than by
    position alone).*

5.  **Inversive/conformal geometry.* Under inversion, expanding spheres
    map to other spheres or to planes; the family
    $\{M^{+}_{p_0}(t)\}_{t \ge 0}$ belongs to a pencil in the inversive
    (Möbius) geometry of $\mathbb{R}^3$. All members share a common
    conformal identity (invariant under the conformal group).*

6.  **Lorentzian geometry (the deepest identification).*
    $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ is precisely a null-hypersurface
    cross-section --- the intersection of the future light cone of $p_0$
    with the spacelike slice $\Sigma_t$. All points share a common
    causal identity (lying on the future light cone of $p_0$, the unique
    surface on which signals propagate at the invariant speed $c$).*

*The six frameworks are mutually reinforcing: each frames the same
physical object (the expanding McGucken Sphere) in the language of a
different mathematical discipline, and each yields the same conclusion
that the wavefront's spatially separated points share a common geometric
identity traceable to a single local origin.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has six steps establishing the geometric
identity of $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ across six independent mathematical
frameworks.

**Step 1 (F1): Foliation theory.** The family $\{S^2(t)\}_{t > 0}$ of
nested 2-spheres in $\mathbb{R}^3$ centred on the spatial projection
$\mathbf{x}_{p_0}$ of $p_0$ is a codimension-one foliation by smooth
2-manifolds: any two spheres of distinct radii $r_1 \ne r_2$ are
disjoint (a point cannot have two different distances from
$\mathbf{x}_{p_0}$), and their union covers
$\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus \{\mathbf{x}_{p_0}\}$. Each sphere is a leaf of
the foliation; the wavefront $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ at fixed lab time $t$ is
exactly the leaf at radius $ct$. All points on a fixed leaf share the
common topological identity of separating the foliation's interior
region (radius $<ct$) from its exterior (radius $>ct$).

**Step 2 (F2): Metric geometry.** The wavefront $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ is the
level set
$$M^{+}_{p_0}(t) = d^{-1}(ct) = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 : d_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}_{p_0}) = ct\}$$
of the Euclidean distance function $d_{\mathrm{Euc}}$ from
$\mathbf{x}_{p_0}$. All points on the wavefront share a common metric
identity: they are equidistant from the source point $\mathbf{x}_{p_0}$
in the induced Euclidean metric on $\Sigma_t$. This is the metric-space
characterisation of the 2-sphere.

**Step 3 (F3): Wave optics --- Huygens envelope.** Huygens' principle,
derived from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as
Theorem [1.1](#thm:QMT1){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT1"} (the
d'Alembert equation as theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$), states that
each point on the wavefront at lab time $t$ is the source of a secondary
spherical wavelet of radius $c\,dt$ during the next interval; the
envelope of these wavelets is $M^{+}_{p_0}(t + dt)$. Iterating this
construction over the parameter range $[0, t]$ yields $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$
as the envelope-caustic of the wavelet family. All points on
$M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ share a common causal-optical identity: they constitute
the boundary between the region disturbed by the source event $p_0$ and
the region not yet reached by the disturbance.

**Step 4 (F4): Contact geometry.** The 1-jet space
$J^1(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R}^3)$ of curves
$\gamma: \mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}^3$ has coordinates
$(t, x_1, x_2, x_3, v_1, v_2, v_3)$, where $v_i = dx_i/dt$ are the
velocity components along a curve through $(t, \mathbf{x})$. The
standard contact structure on this 1-jet space is defined by the three
Pfaffian 1-forms $$\alpha_i \;=\; dx_i - v_i\,dt, \qquad i = 1, 2, 3,$$
whose common kernel
$\ker(\alpha_1) \cap \ker(\alpha_2) \cap \ker(\alpha_3)$ is the contact
distribution (the standard Cartan distribution on $J^1$). A smooth curve
$\gamma$ lifts to a Legendrian curve in $J^1$ if and only if all three
$\alpha_i$ vanish along the lift, i.e., $\dot x_i = v_i$ holds along
$\gamma$ (the holonomic condition: the velocity coordinates agree with
the actual derivatives of the position coordinates). The future light
cone of $p_0$ is generated by null geodesics emanating radially outward
from $\mathbf{x}_{p_0}$ at speed $c$: the family of light rays
$\gamma_{\hat n}(t) = \mathbf{x}_{p_0} + c(t - t_{p_0})\hat n$
parameterised by direction $\hat n \in S^2$, with velocity
$v_i = c\hat n_i$ subject to the null constraint $|\mathbf v|^2 = c^2$.
The lift of this family into $J^1$ is a Legendrian submanifold of the
contact distribution: the holonomic relations $dx_i = v_i\,dt$ hold on
each ray, and the null constraint $\sum_i v_i^2 = c^2$ defines a
codimension-one submanifold of the velocity fibre. The cross-section of
this Legendrian at fixed lab time $t$ is exactly $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$, with
the velocity coordinates encoding the outward normal direction at each
wavefront point. All points on this Legendrian share a common
contact-geometric identity: they have the same null-velocity magnitude
$|\mathbf v| = c$ and the holonomic relations $dx_i = c\hat n_i\,dt$
define the contact distribution uniformly across the wavefront.

**Step 5 (F5): Inversive/conformal geometry.** Inversive geometry on
$\mathbb{R}^3 \cup \{\infty\}$ takes the family of spheres-and-planes as
its basic objects. Under inversion
$\mathbf{x} \mapsto \mathbf{x}/|\mathbf{x}|^2$, expanding spheres
centred at the origin map to expanding spheres (different radii), and at
the limit $r \to \infty$, to planes. The one-parameter family
$\{M^{+}_{p_0}(t)\}_{t > 0}$ of concentric spheres of growing radius
$ct$ is a pencil in this inversive (Möbius) geometry of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
All members of the pencil share a common conformal identity: they are
invariant under the conformal group
$\mathrm{Conf}(\mathbb{R}^3) = O(4, 1)/\mathbb{Z}_2$ (preserving angles
and the pencil structure).

**Step 6 (F6): Lorentzian geometry --- the deepest identification.** The
Lorentzian line element on $M_{1,3}$ is
$$ds^2 = -c^2 dt^2 + |d\mathbf{x}|^2,$$ which vanishes on the future
light cone of $p_0$, the null hypersurface
$\{(t, \mathbf{x}) : ct = |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_{p_0}|, t \ge 0\}$.
The cross-section of this null hypersurface with the spacelike slice
$\Sigma_t = \{(t', \mathbf{x}') : t' = t\}$ is exactly $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$.
All points on the wavefront share a common causal identity: they lie on
the future light cone of $p_0$, the unique surface on which signals
propagate at the invariant speed $c$.

**Step 7: McGucken anchoring --- all six readings descend from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.** By
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} of
Chapter [9](#ch:hilbert-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:hilbert-theorem"}, the Lorentzian arena $M_{1,3}$ is
itself generated by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ from the Euclidean manifold
$M_E$ via $x_4 = ict$. The null hypersurface has the reading
of a derived geometric object of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, and the
cross-section identification of F6 is canonical at the
McGucken-Principle level rather than externally imposed. Combined with
F1--F5, all six geometric readings of the McGucken Sphere wavefront
descend from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as theorems:

-   F1 from clause P2 (spherical symmetry) + clause P1 (principle at
    every event);

-   F2 from clause P3 (rate $c$) + Euclidean spatial metric;

-   F3 from Huygens' principle as theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
    (Theorem [1.1](#thm:QMT1){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT1"});

-   F4 from contact-form structure of the principle's null hypersurface,
    via the holonomic 1-jet conditions $dx_i = v_i\,dt$ together with
    the null-velocity constraint $|\mathbf v| = c$;

-   F5 from inversive/conformal symmetry of the McGucken Sphere pencil;

-   F6 from Lorentzian arena as theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
    (Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}).

The six-fold identity has the reading of one underlying
McGucken object viewed through six mathematical lenses: each of the six
geometric readings (F1)--(F6) descends from the same
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses + the theorems above, with
the joint consistency of the six readings reading as a consequence of the single principle rather than as six independently
coincident geometric facts. $\square$ ◻
:::

#### The constructive proof: light-cone surface as nonlocality via entangled-photon-pair convergence {#ssec:constructive-lightcone-nonlocality .unnumbered}

The six-fold geometric identity of
Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:six-fold-identity"} establishes the nonlocality of the
McGucken-Sphere wavefront $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ by showing that every
geometric framework --- foliation theory, metric geometry, wave optics,
contact geometry, conformal geometry, Lorentzian geometry --- yields
the same conclusion that the spatially separated points of the
wavefront share a common geometric identity. The argument is by
*geometric equivalence across six frameworks*: each framework gives an
independent characterisation of the wavefront's shared identity.

A complementary *constructive* proof, due to
[@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026] Theorem 4.2, establishes the same
conclusion by explicit construction: starting from a single entangled
pair of photons and taking the union over all directions and all
times, the entire light-cone surface is exhibited as the limit of a
family of pairwise nonlocal configurations. The constructive proof
complements the six-framework equivalence by supplying a direct,
physically operational argument that every point of the McGucken
Sphere is connected by quantum entanglement to other points on the
sphere, traceable through the construction back to the common local
source event.

::: {#thm:lightcone-surface-nonlocality .theorem}
**Theorem 17.12.A** (Nonlocality of the light-cone surface via
entangled-pair convergence;
[@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026] Theorem 4.2). *The surface of the
forward light cone emanating from any source event $p_0 \in M_{1,3}$
is a geometric nonlocality: its spatially separated points share a
common quantum identity, traceable to the common local source event
$p_0$ via a chain of entangled-pair correlations on the wavefront.
Explicitly, the McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ at parameter $t > 0$
is the limit of the union of position-pairs of entangled photon pairs
emitted at $p_0$ in all directions, with every antipodal pair on the
sphere connected by direct entanglement and every other pair of points
connected through the chain of pairwise entanglements that constitute
the sphere.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has four constructive steps, each invoking a clause
of Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} and the empirical content of pair-photon
emission processes. The construction descends from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (ii) spherical symmetry, (iii)
monotonic forward orientation, and (v) global validity) and from the
First Law of Nonlocality
(Theorem [17.4](#thm:first-law-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:first-law-nonlocality"}) supplying the rule that
particles co-emitted at a single local event $p_0$ share a common
McGucken Sphere from that event.

**Step 1: A single entangled photon pair defines a two-point
nonlocality.** Consider an entangled pair of photons emitted at the
source event $p_0$, propagating in opposite directions along the
$x_1$-axis in the spatial slice. By the First Law of Nonlocality
(Theorem [17.4](#thm:first-law-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:first-law-nonlocality"}), the two photons share a
common McGucken Sphere from $p_0$ --- they are on a single wavefront
$M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ at every parameter $t > 0$. By
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (ii) (spherical symmetry of
$x_{4}$-expansion), at parameter $t$ each photon's spatial position is
at radius $ct$ from the spatial projection $\mathbf{x}_{p_0}$, with
the two positions at antipodal points on the wavefront (one at
$+ct\,\hat e_1$, the other at $-ct\,\hat e_1$). The two-point set
$\{p_0 + ct\,\hat e_1,\,p_0 - ct\,\hat e_1\} \subset M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$
is a *nonlocality*: it consists of two spatially separated points
(separation $2ct$) joined by quantum entanglement traceable to the
common local source event $p_0$.

**Step 2: Direction integration yields a circle of nonlocality.** Now
consider a family of entangled photon pairs, all emitted at the
single source event $p_0$, with the $n$-th pair propagating in the
opposite directions $\pm \hat n_k \in S^1 \subset (x_1, x_2)$-plane,
where $\{\hat n_k\}_{k=1}^N$ is a set of $N$ unit vectors uniformly
distributed in the equatorial plane. By Step 1 applied to each pair,
the $k$-th pair occupies the two-point set
$\{p_0 + ct\,\hat n_k,\,p_0 - ct\,\hat n_k\} \subset M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$
at parameter $t$.

In the limit $N \to \infty$ with uniform distribution of the $\hat
n_k$ on $S^1$, the union of pair-positions in the equatorial plane
converges (in the Hausdorff metric on closed subsets of
$\mathbb{R}^2$) to the *full circle* of radius $ct$ centred at
$\mathbf{x}_{p_0}$ in the $(x_1, x_2)$-plane:
$$\lim_{N \to \infty} \bigcup_{k=1}^N \{\mathbf{x}_{p_0} \pm ct\,\hat n_k\} \;=\; \{ \mathbf{x} \in (x_1, x_2)\text{-plane} : |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_{p_0}| = ct\}.$$
Each point of the limit circle is in the wavefront $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$
and is connected by direct entanglement to the antipodal point on the
same circle (the partner from its emitting pair). Through the chain
of pair-partner relations and Sphere-shared-source connections
(First Law), every point of the circle is connected to every other
point of the circle by a chain of pairwise entanglements traceable to
$p_0$. This is the *circle of nonlocality*: a one-dimensional
geometric locus exhibiting nonlocality across its full circumference
through entanglement chains traceable to the common source $p_0$.

**Step 3: Time integration extends the circle to a conical surface.**
By Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iii) (monotonic forward orientation
of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$), each pair of photons continues to
propagate outward at $c$ from $p_0$ for all subsequent parameter
values $t' > 0$. At any parameter $t' > 0$, the equatorial-plane
construction of Step 2 yields a circle of nonlocality in the
$(x_1, x_2)$-plane of radius $ct'$, with the same antipodal
entanglement-pair relations and the same source-traceability to $p_0$.

The union of these circles over all $t' > 0$ is the *forward conical
surface*
$$C^+_{p_0,\,xy} \;=\; \{(\mathbf{x}, t') : \mathbf{x} \in (x_1, x_2)\text{-plane},\ |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_{p_0}| = ct',\ t' > 0\} \;\subset\; M_{1,3},$$
the intersection of the future light cone of $p_0$ with the
$(x_1, x_2)$-Lorentzian-restricted slice
$\{(x_1, x_2, x_3 = 0, t)\}$. Every point of this conical surface is
on the wavefront of some parameter $t'$ and is connected by direct
entanglement to its antipodal partner on the same time-slice; and by
the Sphere-shared-source chain to every other point of the surface
through $p_0$. This is the *conical surface of nonlocality*: a
two-dimensional Minkowski-causal surface (a null hypersurface
restricted to the equatorial plane) exhibiting nonlocality
constructively via pair-entanglement chains.

**Step 4: Direction integration in three dimensions yields the
McGucken Sphere as the limit.** Extending the equatorial integration
of Step 2 to all three spatial dimensions: the family of entangled
photon pairs is indexed by $\hat n \in S^2$ (the unit 2-sphere of
emission directions), with the $\hat n$-th pair occupying the two-point
set $\{\mathbf{x}_{p_0} \pm ct\,\hat n\} \subset M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ at
parameter $t$. By the same uniform-distribution limit (now Hausdorff
on closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}^3$), the union of pair-positions in
the full spatial slice converges to the *full McGucken Sphere*
$$\lim_{N \to \infty} \bigcup_{k=1}^N \{\mathbf{x}_{p_0} \pm ct\,\hat n_k\} \;=\; M^{+}_{p_0}(t),$$
the 2-sphere of radius $ct$ centred at $\mathbf{x}_{p_0}$. Every point
of $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ is, in the limit construction, the position of
some photon emitted at $p_0$ in some direction; and every point is
connected by direct entanglement to its antipodal partner on the same
sphere, and by Sphere-shared-source chains to every other point of
the sphere through $p_0$.

The McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ is therefore a *geometric
nonlocality* in the constructive sense: a two-dimensional Minkowski
locality (null-hypersurface cross-section by
Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:six-fold-identity"} clause (F6)) constructed as the
limit of a family of pair-position sets, each pair being a quantum
nonlocality (entangled pair on the wavefront), and the entire family
being connected through pairwise entanglements and shared-source
relations traceable to the single local source event $p_0$.
Extending the construction over all parameter values $t > 0$ yields
the full forward light cone of $p_0$ as the limit:
$$J^+_{\text{null}}(p_0) \;=\; \bigcup_{t > 0} M^{+}_{p_0}(t) \;=\; \lim_{N \to \infty,\ T \to \infty} \bigcup_{k=1}^N \bigcup_{t \in (0, T]} \{\mathbf{x}_{p_0} \pm ct\,\hat n_k\}.$$
The forward light-cone surface --- the union of all McGucken Spheres
from $p_0$ over all parameter values --- is therefore a geometric
nonlocality in the constructive sense: a Minkowski causal-boundary
hypersurface every point of which is, through the entangled-pair
convergence construction, traceably connected to the common local
source $p_0$ by entanglement chains and shared-source relations. ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:constructive-vs-equivalence-proofs-of-nonlocality .remark}
*Remark 17.12.B* (Constructive and equivalence-based proofs of
nonlocality: two complementary routes). The textbook now contains two
formally distinct proofs that the McGucken Sphere wavefront and the
forward light-cone surface are geometric nonlocalities:

1.  *Equivalence-based proof
    (Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:six-fold-identity"}, the six-fold geometric
    identity).* For each of six independent mathematical frameworks
    --- foliation theory (F1), metric geometry (F2), wave optics
    (F3), contact geometry (F4), conformal geometry (F5), Lorentzian
    geometry (F6) --- the wavefront $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ is established
    as a *single geometric object* whose spatially separated points
    share a common identity in that framework. The argument is by
    *geometric equivalence*: six independent frameworks all yield the
    same identity-of-points conclusion.

2.  *Constructive proof
    (Theorem [17.12.A](#thm:lightcone-surface-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:lightcone-surface-nonlocality"} of the present
    subsection, the entangled-pair convergence construction).* The
    wavefront $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ and the full forward light-cone
    surface are exhibited as Hausdorff-metric limits of unions of
    entangled photon-pair positions, with each pair a two-point
    quantum nonlocality (First Law,
    Theorem [17.4](#thm:first-law-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:first-law-nonlocality"}) on the wavefront and the
    union (over directions and times) reconstructing the full
    surface. The argument is by *explicit construction*: starting
    from a single physically observed pair-emission process and
    integrating over directions and times to recover the full
    geometric surface.

The two proofs are complementary: the equivalence-based proof shows
that *if* one accepts any one of the six geometric framework
characterisations of the wavefront, then nonlocality follows (since
that framework already characterises the wavefront's points as
sharing a common identity); the constructive proof shows that
*starting from the empirically observed pair-emission process alone*,
the full Minkowski-geometric surface is recovered as the limit of
pair-position constructions, with the wavefront's nonlocality
inherited from the pair-emission nonlocality through the limit.

Both routes descend from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}): the equivalence-based proof via the
six-framework identifications of the McGucken-Sphere wavefront, the
constructive proof via the First Law of Nonlocality + the spherical
symmetry of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ + the monotonic forward
orientation. The two proofs do not depend on each other; they are
derivationally disjoint routes to the same conclusion, mirroring the
Algebraic Channel / Geometric Channel disjointness that runs through
the entire textbook.
:::

::: {#prop:sphere-canonical-minkowski .proposition}
**Proposition 17.13** (The Sphere is the canonical Minkowski locality;
Proposition 4.1 of [@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026]). *The expanding
McGucken Sphere in $(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4)$-space with $x_4$ advancing at
rate $ic$ intersects any three-dimensional spatial slice $\Sigma_t$ in a
growing 2-sphere of radius $ct$, which is the intersection of a null
hypersurface with a spacelike slice --- the canonical geometric locality
of Minkowski geometry.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **Step 1: $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ generates the Lorentzian
arena.** By Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} of
Chapter [9](#ch:hilbert-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:hilbert-theorem"}, the Lorentzian Minkowski space
$M_{1,3}$ is generated from the Euclidean four-manifold
$M_E = \mathbb{R}^4$ with coordinates $(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4)$ and line
element $d\ell^2 = dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2 + dx_4^2$ by substituting
$x_4 = ict$ (or equivalently $dx_4 = ic\,dt$) from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, yielding $dx_4^2 = (ic\,dt)^2 = -c^2\,dt^2$
and hence $ds^2 = dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2 - c^2\,dt^2$.

**Step 2: The expanding Sphere in $(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4)$.** At source
event $p_0 = (\mathbf{x}_{p_0}, 0)$, the McGucken Sphere is the locus
reached by $x_{4}$-expansion at rate $ic$ from $p_0$ during parameter
$t$, satisfying
$(x_1 - x_{p_0,1})^2 + (x_2 - x_{p_0,2})^2 + (x_3 - x_{p_0,3})^2 + (x_4)^2 = 0$
on the integrated axiom $x_4 = ict$. Substituting $x_4 = ict$ gives the
spatial-slice locus $|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_{p_0}|^2 - c^2 t^2 = 0$,
equivalently $|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_{p_0}| = ct$.

**Step 3: Spatial cross-section is a 2-sphere of radius $ct$.** The
locus $|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_{p_0}| = ct$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is the
2-sphere of radius $ct$ centred at $\mathbf{x}_{p_0}$. This is the
wavefront $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$. Its surface area is $4\pi c^2 t^2$ at
parameter time $t$, growing quadratically in $t$.

**Step 4: Null-hypersurface identification.** By clause (F6) of
Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:six-fold-identity"}, the locus
$|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_{p_0}| = ct$ for $t \ge 0$ is precisely the
future light cone of $p_0$ in the Lorentzian arena $M_{1,3}$; it is a
null hypersurface (vanishing of the line element $ds^2$ on it). Its
cross-section with the spacelike slice
$\Sigma_t = \{(t, \mathbf{x}) : t = \mathrm{const}\}$ is exactly
$M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$.

**Step 5: The Sphere is the canonical Minkowski locality.** The null
hypersurface (Minkowski causal structure) intersected with a spacelike
slice (Minkowski spatial structure) is the canonical locality
construction of Minkowski geometry: it is the locus of events causally
connected to $p_0$ at lab time $t$ via the spatial slice. The Sphere has
the reading of the natural Minkowski locality concept,
derived constructively from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the
null-hypersurface cross-section of
Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:six-fold-identity"} clause (F6), rather than postulated
as a separate geometric object. $\square$ ◻
:::

#### Huygens' Principle of Nonlocality: photons, light cones, and quantum nonlocality as one self-generative structure {#ssec:huygens-of-nonlocality .unnumbered}

::: flushright
*"Huygens' Principle for the photon *is*, by definition, Huygens'
Principle for nonlocality."*
:::

The six-fold geometric identity of
Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:six-fold-identity"} establishes that the expanding
McGucken Sphere is, simultaneously, a foliation leaf (F1), a metric
level set (F2), a *Huygens caustic* (F3), a Legendrian submanifold (F4),
a conformal pencil member (F5), and (most deeply) a *null-hypersurface
cross-section of the future light cone* (F6). Clauses (F3) and (F6) are
the two most physically distinct readings: (F3) is the Huygens-Principle
reading of the Sphere in wave optics; (F6) is the light-cone reading of
the Sphere in relativity. The present subsection establishes that *they
are the same reading*: the Huygens Principle is, by the six-fold
identity, a Principle of expanding nonlocality, and the
textbook-tradition split between "Huygens' Principle of wave optics" and
"the light cone of relativity" dissolves into a single fact.

::: {#thm:huygens-of-nonlocality .theorem}
**Theorem 17.14** (Huygens' Principle of Nonlocality). *Let
$M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ denote the McGucken Sphere generated at the source
event $p_0 \in M_{1,3}$ at parameter $t$, with surface points at spatial
distance $ct$ from the spatial projection of $p_0$. Under the McGucken
Principle $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ alone, the following statements are
equivalent:*

1.  **Huygens' Principle for the photon*
    (Theorem [1.1](#thm:QMT1){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT1"}
    of Ch. [1](#ch:wave-equation){reference-type="ref"
    reference="ch:wave-equation"}): every point of a photon's wavefront
    at time $t$ is the apex of a new spherical wavelet, and the envelope
    at time $t + dt$ is the new wavefront $M^{+}_{p_0}(t+dt)$.*

2.  **Huygens' Principle for the light cone of relativity*: the future
    light cone of $p_0$ in Minkowski geometry $M_{1,3}$ is generated by
    the union of the future light cones of every event on
    $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$, taken over all $t > 0$. Equivalently, every event
    on the light cone is itself the apex of a new light cone, and the
    cone is self-generated by this iteration.*

3.  **Huygens' Principle for quantum nonlocality*: every point on the
    expanding sphere of nonlocality $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ is itself a
    locality (a single spacetime event) which, as the source of
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$-expansion from that event, generates its
    own expanding sphere of nonlocality. The sphere of nonlocality is
    therefore self-generated by the same iterated-wavelet construction
    that generates Huygens' wavefront and the relativistic light cone.*

*The three statements are not three distinct principles applied to three
distinct phenomena. They are one statement of the self-generative
structure of the McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$, viewed through three
different physical lenses: optical, relativistic, and quantum-nonlocal.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). We prove (H1) $\Leftrightarrow$ (H2) $\Leftrightarrow$ (H3) by
showing all three statements are logically equivalent to a single
underlying geometric statement about $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$, in five explicit
steps. The common geometric statement descends from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}) via the six-fold geometric identity of
Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:six-fold-identity"}, with the integrated kinematic shadow
$x_{4}= ict$ serving as the kinematic shadow per
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}.

**Step 1: The common geometric statement from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.** By
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (v) (global validity),
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event $p \in M_{G}$, and by
clause (ii) (spherical symmetry) the $x_{4}$-expansion at every event is
isotropic at rate $c$. By
Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:six-fold-identity"} clause (F3), the Sphere
$M^{+}_{p}(t)$ at parameter $t$ is the Huygens caustic of secondary
spherical wavelets emanating from every point of the preceding Sphere
$M^{+}_{p}(t-dt)$. By clause (F6), the same Sphere is the
null-hypersurface cross-section of the future light cone of $p$ with the
spacelike slice $\Sigma_t$. The geometric statement common to all three
of (H1), (H2), (H3) is therefore:

> *For every event $q \in M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$, the McGucken Principle
> $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ generates an expanding Sphere $M^{+}_{q}(ds)$
> at parameter $ds > 0$ (via clause (v) at $q$), and the union
> $\bigcup_{q \in M^{+}_{p_0}(t)} M^{+}_{q}(ds)$ contributes to
> $M^{+}_{p_0}(t + ds)$ via the iterated Huygens construction (envelope
> of secondary wavelets),
> Proposition [4.11](#prop:iter){reference-type="ref"
> reference="prop:iter"}.*

We show each of (H1), (H2), (H3) is logically equivalent to this common
statement.

**Step 2: (H1) is the common statement read in the wave-optics frame.**
(H1) is the standard Huygens wave-optics statement: every point of the
wavefront at time $t$ emits a secondary spherical wavelet, and the
envelope at $t + dt$ is the new wavefront. This is the wave-optics
interpretation of the iterated Huygens construction, which is
Theorem [1.1](#thm:QMT1){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT1"} of
the textbook. By the equivalence of the optical wavefront and the
McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ (clause (F3) of the six-fold identity,
Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:six-fold-identity"}), (H1) is the common statement of
Step 1 read with $q$ ranging over the wavefront and $M^{+}_{q}(ds)$
identified as the secondary wavelet. The classical statement of Huygens
[@Huygens1690] is here a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (ii)+(v).

**Step 3: (H2) is the common statement read in the relativistic
light-cone frame.** The future light cone of $p_0$ in Minkowski geometry
is the set $\{q \in M_{1,3} : q \in J^+(p_0), (q - p_0)^2 = 0\}$ of
null-related future events. By clause (F6) of
Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:six-fold-identity"}, the cross-section of this cone with
the spacelike slice $\Sigma_t$ is $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$. The Minkowski metric
itself descends from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the
Lorentzian-signature theorem
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}: $i^2 = -1$ from the perpendicularity
marker forces the signature $(+,+,+,-)$). For every event $q$ on the
cone, the future light cone of $q$ is also a null hypersurface, with its
own cross-sections $M^{+}_{q}(ds)$. The full future light cone of $p_0$
is the union $\bigcup_{q \in J^+(p_0) \cap \{(q - p_0)^2 = 0\}} J^+(q)$
--- every event on the cone is itself the apex of a new cone, and the
cone is self-generated by this iteration. Setting $q \in M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$
and identifying $J^+(q)$ with the McGucken Sphere
$\bigcup_{ds > 0}M^{+}_{q}(ds)$ from $q$, (H2) is the common statement
of Step 1 read with the relativistic-light-cone interpretation.

**Step 4: (H3) is the common statement read in the quantum-nonlocal
frame.** By the First Law of Nonlocality
(Theorem [17.4](#thm:first-law-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:first-law-nonlocality"}) and the six-fold identity
(Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:six-fold-identity"}), the sphere of nonlocality from the
source event $p_0$ at parameter $t$ is the McGucken Sphere
$M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$. Each point $q$ on the sphere of nonlocality is, on the
standard physical reading, a single spacetime event $q \in M_{1,3}$ at
which the $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$-expansion is locally instantiated ---
that is, a *locality*. The McGucken Principle applies at every event by
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i)+(v): from $q$, a new sphere of
nonlocality $M^{+}_{q}(ds)$ expands at rate $ic$. The union over
$q \in M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ of these secondary spheres of nonlocality is the
common statement read with the quantum-nonlocal interpretation. The
result is: the sphere of nonlocality is self-generated by iterated
Huygens construction
(Proposition [4.11](#prop:iter){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:iter"}) of secondary spheres of nonlocality.

**Step 5: Closing the equivalence.** Steps 2--4 each established that
the corresponding clause (H1), (H2), (H3) is the common statement of
Step 1 read in its respective interpretive frame (wave-optics,
relativistic light cone, quantum-nonlocal). Two statements equivalent to
a third are equivalent to each other; hence (H1) $\Leftrightarrow$ (H2)
$\Leftrightarrow$ (H3). The textbook-tradition distinction between
Huygens' Principle of wave optics, the relativistic light cone, and the
expanding sphere of quantum nonlocality is therefore not a distinction
of physical content but a distinction of physical interpretation of one
geometric structure --- the McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ generated
by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at every event of $M_{G}$. The unification follows directly from
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (ii) and (v) combined with the
six-fold identity of
Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:six-fold-identity"}. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#cor:huygens-is-huygens-of-nonlocality .corollary}
**Corollary 17.15** (The Huygens Principle is the Huygens Principle of
Nonlocality). *Under the McGucken Principle, "Huygens' Principle" tout
court is the statement that an expanding nonlocality (the McGucken
Sphere) is self-generated by the iterated-wavelet construction: every
point on a sphere of nonlocality, being itself a locality, generates a
secondary sphere of nonlocality, and the envelope of secondary spheres
is the next sphere of nonlocality. The 1690 statement of Huygens
[@Huygens1690] --- "every point of a wavefront is itself the source of a
secondary wavelet, and the envelope of secondary wavelets is the new
wavefront" --- is a statement about the self-generative structure of
expanding nonlocality, with light being one of several physical
phenomena (along with the relativistic light cone, the
quantum-mechanical sphere of nonlocality, the entropy-bearing wavefront
of the Second Law, and the singlet's shared-wavefront identity in
entangled-pair correlations) that manifest the same structure.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The corollary follows from
Theorem [17.14](#thm:huygens-of-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:huygens-of-nonlocality"} (Huygens' Principle of
Nonlocality) by reinterpreting its three clauses (H1)--(H3) in light of
the six-fold geometric identity
(Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:six-fold-identity"}). We argue in four steps.

**Step 1: The McGucken Sphere is canonically a sphere of nonlocality.**
By Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:six-fold-identity"}, the McGucken Sphere wavefront
$M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ is identical, as one geometric object, to (F1) Huygens'
wavefront of secondary wavelets, (F2) the Minkowski light cone, (F3) the
McGucken-Sphere wavefront of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, (F4) the EPR
(Einstein--Podolsky--Rosen)-Bell sphere of singlet correlations, (F5)
the entropy-bearing wavefront of the Second Law, and (F6) the McGucken
nonlocality sphere. In particular, identifications (F4) and (F6) certify
that $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ is a sphere of nonlocality.

**Step 2: Huygens' iteration is the self-generation of an expanding
nonlocality.** Clause (H1) of
Theorem [17.14](#thm:huygens-of-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:huygens-of-nonlocality"} states that $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ is
sourced at $p_0$. Clause (H2) states that every point of
$M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ acts as a secondary source. Clause (H3) states that the
next-generation wavefront is the envelope of secondary spheres. By Step
1, each $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ *is* a sphere of nonlocality. Therefore
(H1)--(H3) describe the self-generation of an expanding nonlocality by
the Huygens iteration.

**Step 3: Light is one instance of the same structure.** Huygens' 1690
statement [@Huygens1690] concerns wavefronts of light.
Theorem [1.1](#thm:QMT1){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT1"}
(Geometric Channel) derived $\Box\psi = 0$ from the McGucken-Sphere wavefront
construction, exhibiting the wave equation of light as the massless
instantiation of $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$. Thus light is one instance ---
alongside relativistic light cones, EPR-Bell singlet correlations, and
the entropy-bearing wavefront --- of the same underlying self-generating
nonlocality structure.

**Step 4: The identity.** Combining Steps 1--3, Huygens'
Principle (the geometric content of (H1)--(H3) on $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$) has
the reading of the Huygens Principle of Nonlocality (the same
geometric content read on a sphere of nonlocality). The two readings
have the role of one statement viewed at the two levels at which the
six-fold identity collapses six readings into one, with
(H1)--(H3) and the Huygens-of-Nonlocality reading sharing the same
underlying $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$-generated wavefront $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$
as their common geometric content. ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:why-missed .remark}
*Remark 17.16* (Why the textbook tradition missed this). The textbook
tradition treats Huygens' Principle as a heuristic of wave optics, the
light cone as a geometric feature of Minkowski spacetime, and the sphere
of nonlocality as an interpretive figure for the quantum correlations of
entanglement. The three are presented in different chapters of different
textbooks, taught in different undergraduate years, and proved (where
proved at all) by different methods: Kirchhoff's integral theorem for
Huygens, Lorentz transformations for the light cone, Bell's theorem for
nonlocality.
Theorem [17.14](#thm:huygens-of-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:huygens-of-nonlocality"} establishes that the three are
one. The missing input that obstructed the identification is
the dynamical reading of $x_4$ as actually moving at rate $ic$ from
every spacetime event --- the same input that, per
§[11.7](#sec:historical-predecessors){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:historical-predecessors"} of
Ch. [11](#ch:uniqueness-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:uniqueness-identity"}, was missing from Costa de
Beauregard, Penrose, and Hardy.
:::

#### Has anyone before proposed (A) a geometry of nonlocality, (B) an expanding nonlocality, or (C) an expanding nonlocality obeying Huygens' Principle? A literature audit. {#ssec:literature-audit-three-questions .unnumbered}

The claim of
Theorem [17.14](#thm:huygens-of-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:huygens-of-nonlocality"} is sharp enough to invite the
question: has any prior work in the foundations of physics proposed (A)
a geometry of nonlocality, (B) an expanding nonlocality, or (C) an
expanding nonlocality obeying Huygens' Principle? We answer each in
turn, drawing on the historical-predecessor analyses of
[@MG-NonlocalityProb-2026], [@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026], and
[@MG-Uniqueness-2026].

##### (A) Has anyone proposed a *geometry* of nonlocality? {#a-has-anyone-proposed-a-geometry-of-nonlocality .unnumbered}

A *geometry* of nonlocality is a specification of nonlocality as a
geometric object --- a surface, a manifold, or a fibration --- with
intrinsic geometric structure (foliation, metric, contact form,
conformal class, or null structure) supporting the nonlocal
correlations. We survey the three nearest predecessors.

###### Costa de Beauregard (1953--1977).

Costa de Beauregard's "zigzag" model [@CostaDeBeauregard1953] proposed
that EPR correlations travel along the past light cone of one detection
event, through the source, and along the future light cone to the other
detection event. The model identified the light cone as the locus of the
correlation rather than three-space. This is the closest predecessor to
a *geometry* of nonlocality. However: (i) the geometry is borrowed from
special relativity without modification or extension; (ii) no claim of
uniqueness or forcing is made; (iii) no identification of
$c$-invariance with correlation strength is offered; (iv) the timelike
axis is treated as static rather than dynamically advancing. The light
cone is the venue of the correlation, but not in any sense
the *geometric content* of the correlation. Costa de Beauregard proposed
a *locus* of nonlocality, not a *geometry* of nonlocality.

###### Penrose's twistor programme (1967 onward).

Penrose's twistor programme [@Penrose1967] encodes spacetime points as
null lines in $\mathbb{CP}^3$ and develops the entire structure of
relativistic field theory from the null geometry of Minkowski spacetime.
The programme commits to null structure as foundational and produces a
rich geometric calculus (twistor diagrams, the conformal cyclic
cosmology of *Cycles of Time*). However: the programme is,
a *rewriting* of relativistic field theory in null-geometric language;
it does not propose nonlocality as a geometric object with its own
intrinsic structure distinct from the null structure of Minkowski
spacetime. Twistors encode events of spacetime, not events of a separate
nonlocality manifold. The connection to quantum entanglement and
Tsirelson saturation has not been derived from twistor theory in any
published work; the geometry is the geometry of relativity, not of
nonlocality *per se*.

###### Hardy (1992).

Hardy's 1992 PRL [@Hardy1992] establishes that no Lorentz-invariant,
local, realistic theory reproduces QM. The result is a *negative*
statement: the joint constraints have non-trivial content.
Hardy did not propose a positive geometry of nonlocality; the paper is a
no-go theorem, not a construction.

###### Categorical, operational, and informational approaches (2000s onward).

Recent work in the foundations of physics has produced operational
(Hardy, Chiribella--D'Ariano--Perinotti, Mueller--Masanes),
informational (Brukner--Zeilinger, Wootters), and categorical
(Abramsky--Coecke) reconstructions of quantum theory. Each proposes
features of nonlocality (no-signaling, monogamy,
complementarity, non-classical correlations) within an axiomatic
framework. However, these reconstructions specify nonlocality as an
*algebraic or operational* feature --- a constraint on probability
tables, a tensor structure on convex sets, a categorical compositional
rule --- not as a *geometric object* with metric, foliation, conformal,
contact, or null structure.

###### Answer to (A).

No prior work in the published literature, to the best of our knowledge
from the historical-predecessor analyses of the three corpus papers
above, has proposed a *geometry* of nonlocality in the sense of
Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:six-fold-identity"}: an explicit geometric object
equipped with foliation, metric, Huygens, Legendrian, conformal-pencil,
and null-hypersurface structure, with all six structures producing the
same conclusion that spatially separated points share a common geometric
identity traceable to a single local origin. The McGucken Sphere is the
first proposed geometry of nonlocality *simpliciter*.

##### (B) Has anyone proposed an *expanding* nonlocality? {#b-has-anyone-proposed-an-expanding-nonlocality .unnumbered}

An *expanding* nonlocality is a nonlocality whose extent grows over time
according to a definite dynamical law. The Second Law of Nonlocality
(Theorem [17.5](#thm:second-law-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:second-law-nonlocality"}) states that the McGucken
nonlocality grows at exactly rate $c$, with the boundary of entanglement
possibility coinciding with the future light cone. We survey
predecessors.

###### Cosmological expansion (1929 onward).

Hubble's 1929 discovery of cosmological expansion identifies a *global*
dynamical expansion of three-space. Cosmological expansion has the
role of a metric expansion of three-space; the metric
expansion does not establish new entanglement correlations as it
proceeds, and the cosmologically-expanding-metric boundary is
geometrically distinct from the entanglement-possibility boundary of
Theorem [17.5](#thm:second-law-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:second-law-nonlocality"} (which is the McGucken-Sphere
wavefront, growing at the local light-speed $c$ from each source event,
rather than the global Hubble flow).

###### Inflation (1979 onward).

Inflationary cosmology proposes a brief exponential phase of metric
expansion in the early universe. As with Hubble expansion, this is an
expansion of the spatial metric and not of nonlocality *per se*. Vacuum
entanglement during inflation is discussed in the literature (Maldacena,
Page), but the entanglement is treated as a feature of the quantum field
state, not as a separate expanding geometric object.

###### Bell's theorem (1964) and subsequent literature.

Bell's theorem [@Bell1964] and the subsequent literature on the
Tsirelson bound treat nonlocality as a static feature of
quantum-mechanical correlations, not as an entity with dynamical extent.
The CHSH inequality is a statement about correlation magnitudes at a
fixed pair of measurement events, not about how a region of nonlocality
grows with time.

###### Costa de Beauregard's zigzag (1953--1977).

The zigzag model is dynamical in the sense that the correlation traces a
path through the past and future light cones; however, the model does
not propose a region of nonlocality whose extent grows monotonically
with time. The light cone in standard relativity is the locus of causal
influence, not a region of nonlocality that expands.

###### Answer to (B).

No prior work in the published literature proposes a *nonlocality* (as
distinct from a spatial metric or a quantum-state feature) that
*expands* at a definite dynamical rate. The Second Law of Nonlocality,
with the rate being $c$ from every event, has no published precedent.

##### (C) Has anyone proposed an expanding nonlocality obeying *Huygens' Principle*? {#c-has-anyone-proposed-an-expanding-nonlocality-obeying-huygens-principle .unnumbered}

The conjunction of (A) *geometry of nonlocality*, (B) *expansion at
definite rate*, and (C) *Huygens iteration on the geometric structure
itself* --- every point of the expanding nonlocality being itself the
apex of a new expanding nonlocality --- is the Huygens Principle of
Nonlocality of
Theorem [17.14](#thm:huygens-of-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:huygens-of-nonlocality"}. The structure is, by
construction, *self-generative*: the nonlocality at time $t + dt$ is the
envelope of secondary nonlocalities each emitted from a point of the
nonlocality at time $t$. Each Sphere $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ generates
infinitely many secondary Spheres $M^{+}_{q}(ds)$ at every point $q$ on
its surface; each of those generates its own secondaries; the structure
is reciprocally-generative in the sense that the secondaries reconstruct
the original through the iterated envelope.

###### Answer to (C).

**No prior work in the published literature has proposed an expanding
nonlocality obeying Huygens' Principle.** Costa de Beauregard had the
geometric locus of correlation but no expansion and no Huygens
iteration. Penrose had null structure but no nonlocality construct and
no expansion. Hardy had a no-go theorem but no positive geometric
construction. Cosmological expansion is metric expansion of three-space,
not Huygens-iterated expansion of nonlocality. Bell-type correlations
are static algebraic features, not Huygens-iterated geometric objects.
The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework is the first proposal in the published literature
of an expanding nonlocality obeying Huygens' Principle, by
Theorem [17.14](#thm:huygens-of-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:huygens-of-nonlocality"} above.

#### The self-generative and reciprocally-generative property: tie to the McGucken source-pair $(\mathcal{M}_G, D_M)$ and Category McG {#ssec:tie-to-source-pair .unnumbered}

The Huygens Principle of Nonlocality of
Theorem [17.14](#thm:huygens-of-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:huygens-of-nonlocality"} is the source of the
*self-generative* property that Sven's textbook epigraph names as the
central feature of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$:

::: flushright
*"...only a kind of union of the two will preserve an independent
reality in $dx_4/dt = ic$, from which both are generated and by which
both are endowed with the self-generative and reciprocal-generative
property whereby they each generate themselves and one another."\
--- textbook frontmatter epigraph (after Minkowski 1908)*
:::

The self-generative property has a direct reading in light of
Theorem [17.14](#thm:huygens-of-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:huygens-of-nonlocality"}.

::: {#thm:huygens-self-generation .theorem}
**Theorem 17.17** (Huygens self-generation of the McGucken Sphere). *The
McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ is *self-generative* in the following
precise sense:*

1.  **Generative of secondaries.* Every point $q \in M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ is
    itself the apex of a secondary McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{q}(ds)$ for
    every $ds > 0$.*

2.  **Self-reconstruction.* The original Sphere $M^{+}_{p_0}(t + ds)$ at
    the advanced parameter $t + ds$ is the envelope of the secondary
    spheres $\{M^{+}_{q}(ds)\}_{q \in M^{+}_{p_0}(t)}$.*

3.  **Reciprocal generation.* Conversely, for every secondary sphere
    $M^{+}_{q}(ds)$, the original Sphere $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ is a member of
    the family of past-Spheres whose union at past parameter $-ds$ would
    be tangent to $M^{+}_{q}(0)$ at $q$. The original Sphere is
    therefore reconstructable from the secondaries.*

4.  **Closure under iteration.* The iteration $q \mapsto M^{+}_{q}(ds)$
    closes on itself: secondaries of secondaries are again secondaries
    of the original, with the envelope-Sphere relation preserved at
    every level.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). We prove the four clauses (SG1)--(SG4) explicitly, anchoring
each in the McGucken Principle.

**Step 1: Proof of (SG1) --- Generative of secondaries.** By clause (P1)
of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, the principle takes the same form at every
event of $M_{G}$. At every point $q \in M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ on the
wavefront, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at $q$ with the same value
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}(q) = ic$ as at $p_0$. The McGucken-Sphere
construction (Definition [4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:sphere"}) applied at $q$ produces a secondary McGucken
Sphere $S_q$, whose wavefront at any positive parameter $ds$ is
$M^{+}_{q}(ds)$. The secondary Sphere is sourced at the point $q$, not
at the original $p_0$; $q$ is itself the apex.

**Step 2: Proof of (SG2) --- Self-reconstruction.** By the elementary
Huygens envelope construction
(Proposition [4.11](#prop:iter){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:iter"}), the union of secondary spheres
$\bigcup_{q\in M^{+}_{p_0}(t)}M^{+}_{q}(ds)$ has as its outer envelope
the 2-sphere of radius $c(t + ds - t_{p_0})$ centred at
$\mathbf{x}_{p_0}$ --- exactly $M^{+}_{p_0}(t + ds)$ (forward branch).
The backward envelope (radius $c(t - ds - t_{p_0})$) corresponds to the
past wavefront and is selected against by the principle's $+ic$ forward
orientation. The original Sphere at advanced parameter $t + ds$ is
therefore reconstructed from secondaries.

**Step 3: Proof of (SG3) --- Reciprocal generation.** Conversely, given
any secondary Sphere $M^{+}_{q}(ds)$, the past-cone of $q$ contains all
events $p'$ from which a Sphere sourced at $p'$ at parameter time
$t' = t - \mathrm{dist}(p', q)/c$ would have its wavefront passing
through $q$ at parameter time $t$. The original source event $p_0$ is
one such $p'$: it lies on the past-cone of $q$ with
$\mathrm{dist}(p_0, q) = c(t - t_{p_0})$ by construction (since
$q \in M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$). The original Sphere $M^{+}_{p_0}(t)$ is
therefore one member of the family of past-Spheres whose secondaries
pass through $q$. Equivalently: from any secondary, the family of
compatible primaries can be reconstructed (up to past-cone freedom).

**Step 4: Proof of (SG4) --- Closure under iteration.** Apply the
secondary construction twice: first at parameter $t$ producing
secondaries $\{S_q\}_{q \in M^{+}_{p_0}(t)}$, then at parameter $t + ds$
producing tertiaries $\{S_r\}_{r \in \bigcup_q M^{+}_{q}(ds)}$. By the
associativity of the envelope construction (time-translation invariance
of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, clause P1 again), this composition equals
the single-step secondary construction at parameter $t + 2\,ds$:
$$\bigcup_{q\in M^{+}_{p_0}(t)}\bigcup_{r \in M^{+}_{q}(ds)}M^{+}_{r}(ds) \;=\; M^{+}_{p_0}(t + 2\,ds),$$
which is itself the wavefront of the original Sphere $S_{p_0}$ at
parameter $t + 2\,ds$. Secondaries of secondaries are secondaries of the
original. The iteration closes on itself.

**Step 5: Self-generation as principle-level closure.** The four
properties (SG1)--(SG4) jointly express the self-generative closure of
the McGucken-Sphere construction: the geometric object $S_p$ generated
by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at $p$ is identical to the
envelope of geometric objects generated by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at
every point of its own wavefront. There is no external geometric input
required to extend the Sphere from parameter $t$ to parameter $t + ds$
--- the Sphere generates its own extension via the principle's action at
every wavefront point. This is the precise content of the
textbook frontmatter epigraph's claim of "self-generative" content of
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

**Step 6: Connection to the McGucken Category $\mathrm{McG}_6$.** In the
categorical formulation of the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework
(Chapter [13](#ch:mcg6-positive-geometry){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:mcg6-positive-geometry"}), self-generation appears as the
closure of the source-pair $(\Sigma_M, \mathcal{G}_M)$ under the three
categorical pair-adjunctions established in
§[13.2](#sec:pair-adjunctions){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:pair-adjunctions"} of that chapter. The Sphere object
$\Sigma_M$ is its own generator: $\Sigma_M$ generates the full McGucken
Source-Tuple
$\mathcal{F}_M = (\Sigma_M, \mathcal{G}_M, \mathcal{M}_G, D_M, \mathcal{S}_M, \mathcal{A}_M)$
