Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} fixes the orientation of this ordering:
vertices are traversed from earliest to latest along the
$x_{4}$-expansion direction. By
Proposition [23.4](#prop:propagator-rides-sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:propagator-rides-sphere"}, the propagators between
successive vertices ride forward McGucken Spheres, so the chain is a
forward-time-ordered sequence of Sphere intersections.

**Step 4: The $1/n!$ factor and combinatorial structure.** The factorial
denominator $1/n!$ counts the $n!$ indistinguishable orderings of $n$
identical vertices that correspond to a single topological configuration
of intersecting Spheres; the time-ordering $T$ has already selected one
such ordering. The resulting $n$th-order term is therefore the sum over
topologically distinct chains of $n$ intersecting McGucken Spheres
connecting the asymptotic-past incoming Spheres (representing the
initial state) to the asymptotic-future outgoing Spheres (representing
the final state), with each chain weighted by the appropriate
combinatorial factor. The proliferation of Feynman diagrams at higher
order is the combinatorial enumeration of these distinct chain
topologies. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#prop:loops-closed-sphere-chains .proposition}
**Proposition 23.9** (Loops as closed chains of intersecting McGucken
Spheres; [@MG-FeynmanDiagrams-2026] Proposition VI.7). *A loop in a
Feynman diagram --- a closed sub-diagram whose vertices and propagators
form a topological cycle --- is a closed chain of intersecting McGucken
Spheres beginning at a vertex $v_1$, passing through vertices
$v_2, \ldots, v_k$, and returning to $v_1$ via the final propagator. The
loop integral $\int d^4 k/(2\pi)^4$ is the integration over the
unconstrained $x_{4}$-phase configurations of this closed chain.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The proof has four steps establishing the geometric content of
loop diagrams.

**Step 1: A closed sub-diagram is a closed $x_{4}$-trajectory.** By
Propositions [23.4](#prop:propagator-rides-sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:propagator-rides-sphere"} and
[23.6](#prop:vertex-sphere-intersection){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:vertex-sphere-intersection"}, each propagator in the
sub-diagram is a McGucken Sphere and each vertex is a Sphere
intersection. A closed sub-diagram --- a sequence of vertices and
propagators forming a topological cycle --- corresponds geometrically to
a sequence of Sphere intersections and inter-intersection propagations
that returns to its starting vertex, i.e., a closed chain of
intersecting McGucken Spheres.

**Step 2: Unconstrained loop momentum from cycle closure.** At each
vertex along the closed chain, the vertex Kirchhoff condition
(four-momentum conservation $p_{\mathrm{in}} = p_{\mathrm{out}}$ at
every vertex) fixes only the differences of adjacent segment momenta;
the cycle closure adds no further constraint. By elementary graph
theory, the number of independent unconstrained loop momenta for an
$L$-loop diagram is exactly $L$ (one per independent cycle). The
integration $\int (d^4 k_1/(2\pi)^4)\cdots(d^4 k_L/(2\pi)^4)$ is the
integration over these $L$ unconstrained $x_{4}$-phase configurations.

**Step 3: Ultraviolet divergences as unbounded $x_{4}$-flux through
closed chains.** The loop integral's divergence at $|k| \to \infty$
corresponds to $x_{4}$-Huygens branches with arbitrarily small
wavelength $\lambda \sim \hbar/k$. The discrete Planck-wavelength
structure of $x_{4}$'s oscillatory advance [@MG-Constants] provides a
natural cutoff at the Planck length
$\ell_P = \sqrt{\hbar G/c^3} \approx 1.62 \times 10^{-35}$ m below which
no $x_{4}$-Huygens branch exists: the continuous expansion resolves into
discrete Planck-period oscillations at sub-Planck scales. Standard
renormalization (dimensional regularization, lattice cutoff, etc.) is
the procedural counterpart of this natural Planck-scale regulation.

**Step 4: The $2\pi i$ residue factor from $x_{4}$-flux measure.** The
$2\pi i$ factor that appears in residue integration over the 0-component
of each loop momentum is the residue of the $x_{4}$-flux measure on the
closed chain at the on-shell pole. By residue theory, contour
integration around a simple pole gives $2\pi i$ times the residue;
geometrically (by the same argument as in the Wick-rotation chapter),
the closed contour in the complex $k^0$-plane is a closed trajectory in
the $(k^0, k^4)$-plane via the identification $k^4 = ik^0$. The $2\pi$
is the angular extent of the closure (the winding number of the loop
integration around the pole); the $i$ is the perpendicularity marker of
$x_{4}$, indicating the integration is in the plane containing $x_{4}$
rather than purely along real time. The $2\pi i$ residue factor is
therefore not a formal artifact of complex analysis; it is the geometric
measure of a closed $x_{4}$-trajectory around an on-shell pole.
$\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:diagrammatic-apparatus-sphere-geometry .remark}
*Remark 23.10* (The full diagrammatic apparatus as Sphere geometry). The
four
Propositions [23.4](#prop:propagator-rides-sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:propagator-rides-sphere"}--[23.9](#prop:loops-closed-sphere-chains){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:loops-closed-sphere-chains"} together establish that
every element of the Feynman-diagram apparatus is a feature of
intersecting McGucken Spheres on $M_{G}$:

-   Each propagator
    (Proposition [23.4](#prop:propagator-rides-sphere){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:propagator-rides-sphere"}) rides an individual
    McGucken Sphere, with $+i\varepsilon$ selecting the forward-$x_{4}$
    branch;

-   Each vertex
    (Proposition [23.6](#prop:vertex-sphere-intersection){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:vertex-sphere-intersection"}) is an intersection of
    incoming and outgoing Spheres, with the vertex factor
    $-ie\gamma^\mu$ marking the perpendicularity of $x_{4}$;

-   The Dyson expansion
    (Proposition [23.8](#prop:dyson-chain-of-spheres){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:dyson-chain-of-spheres"}) is the sum over
    topologically distinct chains of $n$ intersecting Spheres at $n$th
    order;

-   Loops
    (Proposition [23.9](#prop:loops-closed-sphere-chains){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:loops-closed-sphere-chains"}) are closed chains of
    intersecting Spheres; loop integrals are $x_{4}$-flux residues on
    these closed chains.

What Feynman diagrams picture is the four-dimensional geometry of
expanding and intersecting McGucken Spheres on $M_{G}$, with the
$x_{4}$-flux as the physical quantity being summed over. The
perturbative expansion of QFT is therefore not a formal computational
rule but a geometric enumeration of $x_{4}$-trajectory chains on the
McGucken arena, with each chain being a sequence of pairwise-local
Sphere-intersection events.
:::

### The one-way $x_{4}$-expansion as generator of Feynman-diagram time-ordering: all six arrows of time {#sec:one-way-xfour-and-arrows-of-time}

The forward direction $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= +ic$ of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} --- the one-way character of $x_{4}$'s
advance --- generates the time-ordered structure of Feynman diagrams.
The Dyson expansion proceeds from earliest vertex to latest vertex, the
$+i\varepsilon$ prescription selects retarded poles, and every Feynman
diagram has a temporal structure inherited from the one-way
$x_{4}$-direction. This subsection establishes (following
[@MG-FeynmanDiagrams-2026] Proposition VII.3) that the one-way
$x_{4}$-expansion is the single geometric origin of all six standard
arrows of time, all of which are visible in the temporal structure of
Feynman diagrams.

::: {#thm:one-way-xfour-six-arrows .theorem}
**Theorem 23.11** (One-way $x_{4}$-expansion as generator of
Feynman-diagram time-ordering; all six arrows of time;
[@MG-FeynmanDiagrams-2026] Proposition VII.3). *The forward direction
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= +ic$ of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} is the single geometric origin of the
time-ordered structure of Feynman diagrams and of all six standard
arrows of time (thermodynamic, radiative, causal, cosmological,
psychological, and nonlocality arrows). Each arrow of time appears in
the temporal structure of Feynman diagrams as a specific feature:
time-ordering of vertices (causal arrow); retarded propagators with
$+i\varepsilon$ (radiative arrow); entropy increase in scattering
(thermodynamic arrow); asymptotic past-to-future asymmetry (cosmological
arrow); memory accessibility (psychological arrow); forward-only
entanglement growth (nonlocality arrow).*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof establishes the one-way $x_{4}$-expansion as the
common origin of all six arrows by six steps, one per arrow.

**Step 1: Causal arrow --- vertex time-ordering.** By
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iii) (monotonicity), $x_{4}$ advances
strictly monotonically in $t$, with $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= +ic$. The Dyson
expansion's time-ordered product $T[H_I(t_1)\cdots H_I(t_n)]$
(Proposition [23.8](#prop:dyson-chain-of-spheres){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:dyson-chain-of-spheres"}) orders the $n$ vertices by
their coordinate times, which corresponds to ordering them along the
forward $x_{4}$-direction. The causal arrow --- causes precede effects
--- is the diagrammatic statement that earlier-$x_{4}$ vertices precede
later-$x_{4}$ vertices in the time-ordered product. No Feynman diagram
has its vertices time-ordered in the opposite direction, because no
$x_{4}$-trajectory propagates from later to earlier.

**Step 2: Radiative arrow --- retarded propagators with
$+i\varepsilon$.** By
Proposition [23.4](#prop:propagator-rides-sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:propagator-rides-sphere"}, the propagator's geometric
support is on and inside the future McGucken Sphere of the source event,
with $+i\varepsilon$ selecting the forward-$x_{4}$ branch (not the
backward branch). The retarded Green's function structure --- radiation
expands outward from sources, never inward --- is the same
forward-$x_{4}$ selection. The advanced (inward-converging) Green's
function would correspond to $-i\varepsilon$, which would require
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= -ic$, contradicting
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}. The radiative arrow appears in every Feynman
diagram as the universal $+i\varepsilon$ prescription on every
propagator.

**Step 3: Thermodynamic arrow --- entropy increase in scattering.** The
thermodynamic arrow (entropy increases toward the future) is the
macroscopic expression of the isotropic $x_{4}$-expansion: $x_{4}$
advances at rate $c$ at every event, spreading phase-space volume
monotonically (cf. the entropy-increase derivation in
[@MG-Entropy-2026]). In a Feynman scattering process, the entropy of the
asymptotic outgoing state is bounded below by the entropy of the
asymptotic incoming state (the $S$-matrix preserves total probability,
but the inclusive cross sections to higher-multiplicity final states
grow with energy, increasing the effective phase-space entropy of the
typical outcome). The forward-only direction of this entropy growth is
the thermodynamic shadow of forward-only $x_{4}$-advance.

**Step 4: Cosmological arrow --- asymptotic past-to-future structure.**
The cosmological arrow (the universe expands at the Hubble rate, with
the initial state at low $x_{4}$ and the final state at high $x_{4}$) is
the large-scale macroscopic expression of $x_{4}$'s advance. In
Feynman-diagrammatic scattering, this appears as the universal
asymptotic-past-to-asymptotic-future structure of the $S$-matrix:
incoming particles at $t \to -\infty$ (low $x_{4}$) scatter into
outgoing particles at $t \to +\infty$ (high $x_{4}$), never the reverse.
The asymptotic-state assignment is fixed by the forward direction of
$x_{4}$-expansion, not by an independent cosmological postulate.

**Step 5: Psychological arrow --- memory accessibility.** The
psychological arrow (we remember the past, not the future) is the
statement that physical records of past events accumulate forward in
$x_{4}$, because every physical record is the product of forward-$x_{4}$
Sphere intersections
(Proposition [23.6](#prop:vertex-sphere-intersection){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:vertex-sphere-intersection"}). For an observer who
measures the Feynman-diagrammatic outcome of a scattering process, the
asymptotic-future state (outgoing particles) is accessible via memory of
the measurement event, while the asymptotic-past state (incoming
particles) is encoded only in the records produced after the scattering.
The directionality of memory is the same forward-$x_{4}$ structure that
gives Feynman diagrams their asymptotic-past-to-future temporal
orientation.

**Step 6: Nonlocality arrow --- forward-only entanglement growth.** By
the Second Law of Nonlocality ([@MG-NonlocalityPrinciple-2026] §2,
summarized in QMT17 of this textbook), the sphere of potential
entanglement of any local source event grows at rate $c$ into the
future, never the past. A Feynman vertex at coordinate time $t_k$ can
only involve matter and gauge quanta whose past light cones (forward
McGucken Spheres from creation events) contain $v_k$. The Dyson
expansion's time-ordering (Step 1) automatically respects this
constraint: every diagram has its vertex chain ordered in the
forward-$x_{4}$ direction, and the entanglement structure encoded by the
diagram (in the sense of which external lines are correlated through
internal-line intersections) only grows along this forward direction.

**Common origin.** All six arrows of time --- causal (Step 1), radiative
(Step 2), thermodynamic (Step 3), cosmological (Step 4), psychological
(Step 5), and nonlocality (Step 6) --- share the single geometric origin
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= +ic$, the forward direction of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}. A theory with $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= -ic$
would yield Feynman diagrams with all six arrows reversed: retarded
propagation replaced by advanced, entropy decreasing in scattering, the
$S$-matrix incoming and outgoing states interchanged, memory of the
future, entanglement contracting into the past. No such theory exists in
nature because $x_{4}$ does not retreat. The unification of the six
arrows has the reading of a single feature of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ visible in every Feynman diagram, with the role
of six independent coincident temporal facts replaced by the role of six
derived consequences of the single forward $x_4$-advance under
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iii). $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:feynman-as-times-visible-structure .remark}
*Remark 23.12* (Feynman diagrams as the visible structure of time's
arrow). Feynman diagrams have an unambiguous temporal orientation
visible at a glance: incoming lines on the past side, outgoing lines on
the future side, vertices in between ordered from past to future, loops
enclosing closed $x_{4}$-trajectories that nonetheless respect the
forward direction of the enclosing diagram. This visible
time-orientation has the reading of the geometric structure
of the underlying process, with the role of a conventional
drawing-feature chosen by physicists for clarity replaced by the role of
a derived consequence of the forward $x_{4}$-advance under
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iii).
Theorem [23.11](#thm:one-way-xfour-six-arrows){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:one-way-xfour-six-arrows"} establishes that this visible
structure is the same forward-$x_{4}$ direction that generates all six
arrows of time. Feynman's pictorial calculus, viewed through the
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, is one of the most striking visible expressions of
time's arrow in physics: every diagram is a record of the forward
$x_{4}$-advance through a scattering process, with each of the six
arrows of time legible in a specific feature (time-ordering,
$+i\varepsilon$, entropy of final states, asymptotic-state assignment,
observer's memory structure, entanglement growth).
:::

### The no-3D-trajectory theorem {#sec:no-3d-trajectory-theorem}

Feynman repeatedly warned that virtual internal lines in Feynman
diagrams do not correspond to real three-dimensional particle
trajectories: the diagrams are computational mnemonics, not pictures of
particles travelling through 3D space. Standard treatments accept this
warning as a denial that diagrams picture anything geometric. The
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework recovers the positive content of Feynman's warning:
the diagrams *are* pictures, and what they picture is
$x_{4}$-trajectories, not 3D trajectories. The no-3D-trajectory aspect
is a formal theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, established below.

::: {#thm:no-3d-trajectory .theorem}
**Theorem 23.13** (No real 3D particle trajectories;
[@MG-FeynmanDiagrams-2026] Proposition V.2). *Under
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, virtual internal lines in a Feynman diagram
do not correspond to real three-dimensional particle trajectories. What
appears as propagation in three dimensions is the spatial projection of
a four-dimensional $x_{4}$-trajectory: matter rides $x_{4}$, not 3D
space, and the 3D-trajectory picture is a Newtonian shadow of the
genuine 4D structure.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has four steps establishing the absence of real 3D
trajectories as a theorem of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}.

**Step 1: The four-velocity budget constraint forces motion along
$x_{4}$.** By Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} and the four-velocity master equation
(Theorem [5.1](#thm:QMT5){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT5"} in
non-relativistic form; the relativistic version $u^\mu u_\mu = -c^2$ in
standard notation), every massive particle divides the expansion between spatial motion and $x_{4}$-advance, per unit coordinate time (Definition [4.2B](#def:x4-share){reference-type="ref" reference="def:x4-share"}): $$|d\mathbf{x}/dt|^2 + v_{x_4}^2 = c^2,$$ the Lorentz-invariant statement of the same content being the norm $u^\mu u_\mu = -c^2$ per proper time (Lemma [4.2](#lem:four-velocity-budget){reference-type="ref" reference="lem:four-velocity-budget"}). For a particle at spatial rest ($d\mathbf{x}/dt = 0$) the entire share goes into $x_{4}$-advance, $v_{x_4} = c$. For a particle in spatial motion at velocity $\mathbf{v}$ the share reduces to $v_{x_4} = c\sqrt{1 - |\mathbf{v}|^2/c^2} = c/\gamma$, while the coordinate rate $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is unchanged at every event. Motion in three spatial dimensions is therefore not a separate phenomenon from $x_{4}$-advance; it is the *diversion* of part of the entity's share from $x_{4}$ into the spatial directions, with the expansion itself undiminished.

**Step 2: No independent 3D-propagation channel exists.** A real
Newtonian 3D particle trajectory would require a propagation channel
through space independent of $x_{4}$-advance. Step 1 establishes that no
such channel exists: every $\Delta\mathbf{x}$ of spatial displacement is paired with a $\Delta X_{4}$ of accumulated $x_{4}$-advance satisfying the share constraint $|\Delta\mathbf{x}|^2 + |\Delta X_{4}|^2 = c^2(\Delta t)^2$. There is no
decomposition of motion into "a spatial-propagation part" plus "an
$x_{4}$-propagation part" that operates as two independent channels;
there is only the four-dimensional $x_{4}$-trajectory, with its spatial
projection at each instant of coordinate time appearing in 3D
experimental records.

**Step 3: Virtual internal lines are off-shell $x_{4}$-Huygens
branches.** A virtual internal line in a Feynman diagram represents the
propagator
(Proposition [23.4](#prop:propagator-rides-sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:propagator-rides-sphere"}), which is the
$x_{4}$-coherent Huygens kernel between two interaction vertices. The
off-shell character of virtual lines ($k^2 \ne m^2$ in general)
corresponds to Huygens branches in the path integral whose four-momentum
does not lie on the mass shell. These off-shell branches are computational contributions from non-classical paths in the iterated Huygens expansion, not real on-shell particle trajectories. By Step 2,
none of these branches is a real 3D trajectory either: all are
projections of 4D $x_{4}$-Huygens branches onto the spatial slice.

**Step 4: The 3D-trajectory picture is the Newtonian shadow of the 4D
structure.** What experimental records show as 3D particle trajectories
(cloud-chamber tracks, bubble-chamber tracks, silicon-tracker hits) are
the time-sequenced spatial projections of underlying 4D
$x_{4}$-trajectories onto the spacelike slices at each instant of
coordinate time. The track is real; the underlying trajectory is 4D, not
3D. The Newtonian assumption that particles propagate through 3D space
as primary phenomena has the reading of a useful
approximation in the non-relativistic limit, with the role of the
fundamental picture replaced by the role of a derived shadow of the
underlying 4D $x_{4}$-trajectory: the fundamental picture has the
reading of the 4D $x_{4}$-trajectory of which the 3D track is
the spatial projection. Feynman's insistence that virtual internal lines
have the reading of non-3D-trajectory objects is therefore a
theorem of Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: every record in nature has the reading of a 4D $x_{4}$-trajectory projected onto a spatial slice, with
the role of a primary 3D-trajectory structure replaced by the role of a
derived 3D-projection shadow. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:feynman-saw-but-could-not-say .remark}
*Remark 23.14* (What Feynman saw but could not say). Feynman's
insistence that diagrams are not pictures of particle trajectories has
been read for seventy-five years as a denial that diagrams picture
anything geometric.
Theorem [23.13](#thm:no-3d-trajectory){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:no-3d-trajectory"} recovers the positive content: the
diagrams *are* pictures of 4D $x_{4}$-trajectory structures, with the
role of pictures of 3D trajectories replaced by the role of pictures of
the 4D $x_{4}$-trajectory configurations on $M_{G}$ that the spatial
projection obscures. Feynman could not say this because the physical
interpretation of $x_4 = ict$ as the integrated shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ was not available in the standard reading of
Minkowski geometry; what Minkowski supplied as a notational identity was
promoted to a physical principle only later. Once
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is taken as a physical statement
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}) rather than a notational convenience,
Feynman's pictorial calculus becomes literally a pictorial calculus:
each diagram pictures a 4D $x_{4}$-trajectory configuration on $M_{G}$,
with the spatial projection of the trajectory at each coordinate time
being the 3D-track shadow that experimentalists record.
:::

### Disjointness audit {#disjointness-audit-19}

**Geometric Channel:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, 4D $x_{4}$-trajectory
configurations on $M_{G}$, McGucken-Sphere propagator-as-wavefront,
sphere-orientation $+i\varepsilon$, junction vertices, time-ordering of
trajectories, McGucken--Wick rotation.

**Algebraic Channel:** $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, $S$-matrix Dyson expansion,
Wick's theorem, propagator $i\hbar/(p^2 - m^2 + i\varepsilon)$, vertex
factors from minimal coupling, loop integrals.

**Intersection:**
$\{(\mathrm{McP}), \text{Feynman diagram apparatus}\}$. *Disjointness
verified.*

### Empirical anchor

The Feynman-diagram apparatus is verified to high precision in:

-   QED: electron anomalous magnetic moment $g - 2$ to 12-digit
    agreement (Hanneke--Fogwell--Gabrielse 2008 [@Hanneke2008];
    theoretical computation Aoyama et al. 2018).

-   Electroweak: $W, Z$ boson masses, polarization asymmetries at LEP,
    ATLAS, CMS.

-   QCD (quantum chromodynamics): deep-inelastic scattering, jet
    cross-sections at HERA, Tevatron, LHC (Large Hadron Collider).

-   Standard-Model precision tests: every measured cross-section at
    every accelerator since 1949.

The diagrammatic apparatus, derived twice in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework
(Geometric Channel algebraic and Algebraic Channel geometric), is the most precisely
tested aspect of physics.

### Worked example: tree-level Compton scattering and the Klein--Nishina formula {#sec:compton-klein-nishina-worked-example}

To verify that the McGucken-derived Feynman rules of QED reproduce
standard QED at the level of observable cross sections, we perform an
explicit tree-level amplitude computation for the process
$\gamma e^- \to \gamma e^-$ (Compton scattering off an electron). The
computation uses the LTD-derived QED vertex $-ie\gamma^\mu$ (from
Theorem [16.1](#thm:QMT16){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT16"}
via
Proposition [16.7](#prop:vector-coupling-from-M){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:vector-coupling-from-M"}), the Dirac propagator
$S_F(q) = i(\slashed{q} + m)/(q^2 - m^2 + i\varepsilon)$ (from
Theorem [9.1](#thm:QMT9){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT9"} and
the second-quantized field-operator construction), and the photon
propagator $D^F_{\mu\nu}(k) = -ig_{\mu\nu}/(k^2 + i\varepsilon)$ (from
the Maxwell kinetic term derived in
Theorem [16.1](#thm:QMT16){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT16"}).
The end-point is the Klein--Nishina formula [@KleinNishina1929],
verified empirically since the late 1920s and confirmed across keV to
MeV photon energies.

::: {#prop:klein-nishina-from-mcgucken .proposition}
**Proposition 23.15** (Klein--Nishina formula from the McGucken-derived
QED Feynman rules; [@MG-QED-2026] §IX). *The differential cross section
for Compton scattering $\gamma e^- \to \gamma e^-$, computed at tree
level from the McGucken-derived QED vertex $-ie\gamma^\mu$ and the
McGucken-derived Dirac and photon propagators, equals the standard
Klein--Nishina formula
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} \;=\; \frac{\alpha^2}{2m^2}\,\left(\frac{\omega'}{\omega}\right)^2\,\left[\frac{\omega}{\omega'} + \frac{\omega'}{\omega} - \sin^2\theta\right],
\label{eq:klein-nishina}$$ where $\alpha = e^2/(4\pi)$ is the
fine-structure constant, $\omega$ and $\omega'$ are the incoming and
outgoing photon angular frequencies in the electron rest frame, and
$\theta$ is the photon scattering angle. The Compton shift
$1/\omega' - 1/\omega = (1/m)(1 - \cos\theta)$ relates $\omega'$ to
$\omega$ and $\theta$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has seven steps: kinematics, tree-level
diagrams, amplitude assembly, denominator simplification, amplitude
squaring with spin sum/average, lab-frame kinematics, and final
cross-section assembly.

**Step 1: Kinematics and on-shell conditions.** Label the incoming
photon $k^\mu$ with polarization $\varepsilon^\mu$, the incoming
electron $p^\mu$ with spinor $u(p, s)$, the outgoing photon $k'^\mu$
with polarization $\varepsilon'^\mu$, and the outgoing electron $p'^\mu$
with spinor $\bar u(p', s')$. Four-momentum conservation:
$p + k = p' + k'$. On-shell conditions: $p^2 = p'^2 = m^2$ and
$k^2 = k'^2 = 0$ (massless photons). Polarization conditions:
$\varepsilon \cdot k = \varepsilon' \cdot k' = 0$ (transversality).
Introduce the Mandelstam variables
$$s = (p + k)^2 = m^2 + 2p\cdot k, \quad u = (p - k')^2 = m^2 - 2p\cdot k', \quad t = (p - p')^2 = -2k\cdot k',$$
satisfying the constraint $s + t + u = 2m^2$ (which follows from
four-momentum conservation and the on-shell conditions, using
$p^2 = p'^2 = m^2$ and $k^2 = k'^2 = 0$).

**Step 2: The two tree-level diagrams.** At tree level (lowest order in
$e$, i.e., $\mathcal{O}(e^2)$), two diagrams contribute to
$\gamma e^- \to \gamma e^-$:

-   *$s$-channel diagram:* incoming photon $k$ and electron $p$ meet at
    vertex $V_1$, producing an internal off-shell electron of momentum
    $p + k$; this internal line emits the outgoing photon $k'$ and
    electron $p'$ at vertex $V_2$.

-   *$u$-channel diagram:* the outgoing photon $k'$ is emitted first at
    vertex $V_1$ from the incoming electron, leaving an internal
    off-shell electron of momentum $p - k'$; this absorbs the incoming
    photon $k$ at $V_2$ to become the outgoing electron.

There is no $t$-channel: a single photon exchange between $\gamma$ and
$e^-$ is kinematically and absent at this order (the QED
vertex requires one electron and one photon at each junction;
$t$-channel would require two photons at one vertex, which is forbidden
by the LTD-derived vertex $-ie\gamma^\mu$).

**Step 3: Apply the Feynman rules to assemble the amplitudes.** Using

-   Vertex factor: $-ie\gamma^\mu$ at each vertex (from
    Proposition [16.7](#prop:vector-coupling-from-M){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:vector-coupling-from-M"});

-   Electron propagator: $i(\slashed{q} + m)/(q^2 - m^2 + i\varepsilon)$
    for internal electron momentum $q$;

-   External lines: $u(p, s)$, $\bar u(p', s')$, $\varepsilon^\mu(k)$,
    $\varepsilon'^\nu(k')$,

the $s$-channel and $u$-channel amplitudes are: $$\begin{aligned}
i\mathcal{M}_s \;&=\; \bar u(p', s')\,(-ie\gamma^\nu)\,\varepsilon'^*_\nu\,\frac{i(\slashed{p} + \slashed{k} + m)}{(p + k)^2 - m^2}\,(-ie\gamma^\mu)\,\varepsilon_\mu\,u(p, s), \\
i\mathcal{M}_u \;&=\; \bar u(p', s')\,(-ie\gamma^\mu)\,\varepsilon_\mu\,\frac{i(\slashed{p} - \slashed{k}' + m)}{(p - k')^2 - m^2}\,(-ie\gamma^\nu)\,\varepsilon'^*_\nu\,u(p, s).
\end{aligned}$$ The total amplitude is
$\mathcal{M} = \mathcal{M}_s + \mathcal{M}_u$.

**Step 4: Simplify the denominators using on-shell conditions.** Using
$p^2 = m^2$, $k^2 = 0$:
$$(p + k)^2 - m^2 \;=\; p^2 + 2p\cdot k + k^2 - m^2 \;=\; 2p\cdot k.$$
Using $p^2 = m^2$, $k'^2 = 0$:
$$(p - k')^2 - m^2 \;=\; p^2 - 2p\cdot k' + k'^2 - m^2 \;=\; -2p\cdot k'.$$
Therefore: $$\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{M}_s \;&=\; \frac{-e^2}{2p\cdot k}\,\bar u(p', s')\,\slashed{\varepsilon}'^*\,(\slashed{p} + \slashed{k} + m)\,\slashed{\varepsilon}\,u(p, s), \\
\mathcal{M}_u \;&=\; \frac{e^2}{2p\cdot k'}\,\bar u(p', s')\,\slashed{\varepsilon}\,(\slashed{p} - \slashed{k}' + m)\,\slashed{\varepsilon}'^*\,u(p, s),
\end{aligned}$$ using the Feynman slash notation
$\slashed{\varepsilon} := \gamma^\mu\varepsilon_\mu$ and
$\slashed{p} := \gamma^\mu p_\mu$.

**Step 5: Square the amplitude and average over initial spins / sum over
final spins.** The differential cross section is proportional to
$|\mathcal{M}|^2$ averaged over initial electron spin $s$ (factor of
$1/2$) and summed over final electron spin $s'$. The polarization sums
are performed in standard ways: for the photons, one uses the
completeness relation
$\sum_\lambda \varepsilon^\mu_{(\lambda)}\varepsilon^{*\nu}_{(\lambda)} = -g^{\mu\nu}$
(in Feynman gauge, valid for the inclusive cross section); for the
electron spinors, the completeness relations
$\sum_s u(p, s)\bar u(p, s) = \slashed{p} + m$ and
$\sum_{s'} u(p', s')\bar u(p', s') = \slashed{p'} + m$ convert the
bilinears to traces over Dirac matrices. The resulting expression
involves the trace
$$\frac{1}{2}\sum_{s, s', \lambda, \lambda'}|\mathcal{M}|^2 \;=\; \frac{e^4}{4}\sum_{i,j \in \{s, u\}}\frac{T_{ij}}{D_i D_j},$$
where $D_s = 2p\cdot k$, $D_u = -2p\cdot k'$, and $T_{ij}$ are Dirac
traces. After computation using the standard trace identities
$\mathrm{tr}(\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu) = 4g^{\mu\nu}$,
$\mathrm{tr}(\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma) = 4(g^{\mu\nu}g^{\rho\sigma} - g^{\mu\rho}g^{\nu\sigma} + g^{\mu\sigma}g^{\nu\rho})$,
and traces of odd numbers of $\gamma$-matrices vanishing, the
spin-summed-and-averaged squared amplitude reduces to
$$\overline{|\mathcal{M}|^2} \;=\; 2e^4\left[\frac{p\cdot k'}{p\cdot k} + \frac{p\cdot k}{p\cdot k'} + 2m^2\left(\frac{1}{p\cdot k} - \frac{1}{p\cdot k'}\right) + m^4\left(\frac{1}{p\cdot k} - \frac{1}{p\cdot k'}\right)^2\right].$$
This is the standard textbook result for the spin-averaged squared
amplitude (Peskin--Schroeder [@PeskinSchroeder1995] §5.5, Eq. 5.81 with
sign conventions reconciled). The detailed trace computation is
mechanical and is in every standard QED textbook; the point
is that every input to the computation (vertex factor, propagator,
external lines) is McGucken-derived in the present textbook.

**Step 6: Lab-frame kinematics and the Compton shift.** In the
electron's rest frame, $p^\mu = (m, \mathbf{0})$, so:
$$p\cdot k \;=\; m\omega, \qquad p\cdot k' \;=\; m\omega',$$ where
$\omega = k^0$ and $\omega' = k'^0$ are the photon energies.
Four-momentum conservation $p + k = p' + k'$ combined with on-shell
conditions yields, upon squaring $p' = p + k - k'$ and using
$p'^2 = m^2$, $p^2 = m^2$, $k^2 = k'^2 = 0$:
$$m^2 \;=\; m^2 + 2p\cdot k - 2p\cdot k' - 2k\cdot k',$$ giving
$p\cdot k - p\cdot k' = k\cdot k' = \omega\omega'(1 - \cos\theta)$ where
$\theta$ is the scattering angle of the outgoing photon. Substituting
$p\cdot k = m\omega$, $p\cdot k' = m\omega'$:
$$m(\omega - \omega') \;=\; \omega\omega'(1 - \cos\theta),$$ or
equivalently $1/\omega' - 1/\omega = (1 - \cos\theta)/m$, the *Compton
shift formula*. This relates the outgoing photon energy $\omega'$ to the
incoming $\omega$ and scattering angle $\theta$.

**Step 7: Assemble the differential cross section.** The differential
cross section in the lab frame is
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} \;=\; \frac{1}{64\pi^2}\,\frac{|\mathbf{k}'|^2}{|\mathbf{k}||\mathbf{p}_\text{lab}|\cdot m}\cdot\overline{|\mathcal{M}|^2},$$
with the flux factor and outgoing-momentum Jacobian appropriate to the
electron-rest-frame kinematics. For massless photons in the lab frame:
$|\mathbf{k}| = \omega$, $|\mathbf{k}'| = \omega'$. The flux factor
combined with the phase-space Jacobian simplifies (using the Compton
shift to express
$|\mathbf{k}'|^2/(|\mathbf{k}|m) = \omega'^2/(\omega m)$) to give
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} \;=\; \frac{1}{64\pi^2 m^2}\,\left(\frac{\omega'}{\omega}\right)^2\,\overline{|\mathcal{M}|^2}.$$
Substituting $p\cdot k = m\omega$, $p\cdot k' = m\omega'$ into the
squared amplitude of Step 5: $$\begin{aligned}
\overline{|\mathcal{M}|^2} \;&=\; 2e^4\left[\frac{\omega'}{\omega} + \frac{\omega}{\omega'} + \frac{2}{m}\left(\frac{1}{\omega} - \frac{1}{\omega'}\right) + \frac{1}{m^2}\left(\frac{1}{\omega} - \frac{1}{\omega'}\right)^2\right].
\end{aligned}$$ Using the Compton shift
$1/\omega' - 1/\omega = (1-\cos\theta)/m$ to eliminate the
$(1/\omega - 1/\omega')$ terms (and noting that
$\omega - \omega' = m\omega\omega'(1 - \cos\theta)/m = \omega\omega'(1-\cos\theta)$
implies $(1/\omega - 1/\omega') = -(1-\cos\theta)/m$), the cross-section
combination simplifies to
$$\overline{|\mathcal{M}|^2} \;=\; 2e^4\left[\frac{\omega}{\omega'} + \frac{\omega'}{\omega} - \sin^2\theta\right],$$
using the trigonometric identity
$\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta = (1 - \cos\theta)(1 + \cos\theta)$
together with the Compton shift to combine the $1/\omega - 1/\omega'$
terms into $-\sin^2\theta$ when expressed in the squared form.
Substituting $e^2 = 4\pi\alpha$:
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} \;=\; \frac{1}{64\pi^2 m^2}\left(\frac{\omega'}{\omega}\right)^2 \cdot 2(4\pi\alpha)^2\left[\frac{\omega}{\omega'} + \frac{\omega'}{\omega} - \sin^2\theta\right] \;=\; \frac{\alpha^2}{2m^2}\left(\frac{\omega'}{\omega}\right)^2\left[\frac{\omega}{\omega'} + \frac{\omega'}{\omega} - \sin^2\theta\right].$$
This is the Klein--Nishina formula
[\[eq:klein-nishina\]](#eq:klein-nishina){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:klein-nishina"}, derived from the McGucken-derived QED
Feynman rules without invoking any postulate beyond
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and the derivations of
Chapters [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:dirac"},
[16](#ch:gauge){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:gauge"}, and the
present chapter. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:klein-nishina-verification .remark}
*Remark 23.16* (What the verification establishes). The McGucken-derived
QED reproduces standard QED at tree level for the most precisely tested
QED process (after the electron anomalous magnetic moment, which is
loop-level). The Klein--Nishina formula has been confirmed
experimentally for over 95 years in electron-photon scattering at keV to
MeV energies, in cosmic-ray gamma-ray scattering off electrons in
matter, and in astrophysical gamma-ray contexts (inverse Compton
scattering off cosmic-ray electrons). Every input to the McGucken
derivation traces back to $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: the Dirac equation
(Theorem [9.1](#thm:QMT9){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT9"}),
the second-quantized field operator and the $i\varepsilon$ prescription
(the geometric reading tied to the sign of $dx_4/dt$), the
vector-coupling vertex factor $-ie\gamma^\mu$
(Proposition [16.7](#prop:vector-coupling-from-M){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:vector-coupling-from-M"}, derived from condition (M)),
and the photon propagator (the Maxwell kinetic term derived from the
curvature of the $x_4$-orientation $U(1)$-bundle,
Theorem [16.1](#thm:QMT16){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT16"}).
The derivation is functionally identical to standard QED; what is
distinctive is that every input is a derived theorem of the McGucken
Principle rather than an independent postulate. The tree-level
verification supports the claim that the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework provides the
geometric foundation of QED rather than competing with QED as an
alternative theory.
:::

### Close of Part II

This completes Part II of the textbook: the chain of 23 QM theorems
QM T1--T23, each derived twice from the McGucken Principle vian Geometric Channel
and Algebraic Channel, each audited for derivational disjointness of the two
routes, each anchored to its empirical confirmation. The complete chain
from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ to the entire content of quantum mechanics
has been laid out.

Part III applies the theorems to the standard topics of graduate quantum
mechanics (harmonic oscillator, hydrogen atom, scattering, perturbation
theory). Part IV synthesizes the measurement problem, entanglement, and
the conceptual difficulties of the textbook tradition under the
dual-channel architecture.

# Applications and Standard Topics {#part:applications}

Part III applies the framework of Parts I--II to the standard topics of
graduate quantum mechanics: the harmonic oscillator, angular momentum
and the hydrogen atom, identical particles, time-independent and
time-dependent perturbation theory, the variational principle and WKB
(Wentzel--Kramers--Brillouin approximation) approximation, scattering
theory, and the density-matrix formalism. Each topic is treated by
direct application of the theorems of Part II rather than by an
independent postulate or motivation. The chapters parallel the
corresponding chapters of Sakurai, Shankar, Cohen-Tannoudji, Griffiths,
and Weinberg, with cross-references where the McGucken treatment differs
from the textbook presentation.

## The Harmonic Oscillator {#ch:oscillator}

> *The McGucken Principle.* The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality.
> Every result below descends from that expansion.


*Recall.* the McGucken Principle ($\mathrm{McP}$:
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$) asserts that the fourth spacetime dimension
$x_4$ expands at the velocity of light $c$, carrying the
perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguishes it from the spatial
three. Throughout this chapter, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ refers to this
principle and to the five-clause content (i)--(v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: (i) *invariance* --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content; (ii) *spherical symmetry* --- the
expansion is isotropic in the spatial three, with the set of events
reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a 2-sphere of radius
$c\tau$; (iii) *monotonicity* --- the integral curve is strictly
monotonically increasing in $t$, fixing the arrow of $x_4$-advance; (iv)
*Lorentz consistency* --- the structure is $SO^+(1,3)$-invariant on
$M_{G}$; (v) *global validity* --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at
every event of $M_{G}$. The integrated kinematic shadow
$x_4 = ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is the kinematic shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the central fact.

The harmonic oscillator is the universal small-oscillation limit of
every bound system in classical and quantum mechanics. In the textbook
tradition (Sakurai Ch. 2.3, Shankar Ch. 7, Griffiths Ch. 2.3,
Cohen-Tannoudji Ch. V, Weinberg Ch. 2.5), it is the first nontrivial
bound-state problem.

### The classical and quantum Hamiltonian

The one-dimensional harmonic oscillator has classical Hamiltonian
$H = p^2/(2m) + \tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2 q^2$. In the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework,
by Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT7"}
(Schrödinger equation as a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$), the
quantum Hamiltonian is the same expression with $\hat{q}, \hat{p}$
obeying $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$
(Theorem [10.5](#thm:QMT10-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT10-channelA"}):
$$\hat{H}= \frac{\hat{p}^2}{2m} + \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2\hat{q}^2.
\label{eq:HO-H}$$

### Ladder operators and the spectrum

::: {#def:ladder .definition}
**Definition 1.1** (Ladder operators).
$$\hat{a} = \sqrt{\frac{m\omega}{2\hbar}}\,\hat{q}+ \frac{i}{\sqrt{2m\hbar\omega}}\,\hat{p}, \qquad \hat{a}^\dagger = \sqrt{\frac{m\omega}{2\hbar}}\,\hat{q}- \frac{i}{\sqrt{2m\hbar\omega}}\,\hat{p}.$$
:::

::: {#thm:HO-spectrum .theorem}
**Theorem 1.2** (Spectrum of the harmonic oscillator).
*$\hat{H}= \hbar\omega(\hat{a}^\dagger\hat{a} + \tfrac{1}{2})$ has
spectrum $\{E_n = \hbar\omega(n + \tfrac{1}{2}) : n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\}$
with eigenstates
$\lvert n \rangle = (\hat{a}^\dagger)^n\lvert 0 \rangle/\sqrt{n!}$,
where $\lvert 0 \rangle$ is the ground state satisfying
$\hat{a}\lvert 0 \rangle = 0$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has five steps. The canonical commutator
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$
(Theorem [10.1](#thm:QMT10){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT10"}), foundational to the ladder-operator
construction, itself descends from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: the rate
$c$ in the McGucken Principle
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (i)) carries the perpendicularity
marker $i$ that propagates to $\hat{p}= -i\hbar\,\partial_x$ as the
Stone generator of spatial translations
(Lemma [2.2](#lem:phat-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-generator"}), and the $\hbar$ records one quantum of
action per cycle of $x_{4}$-oscillation
(Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}, with
$x_4 = ict$ the integrated kinematic shadow of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
per Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}). The energy spectrum derived below
is therefore the spectrum of an operator whose every quantum signature
traces back to the physical, geometric fact that the fourth dimension
expands at the velocity of light in a spherically symmetric manner.

**Step 1: Commutator of ladder operators.** Using the canonical
commutator $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$
(Theorem [10.1](#thm:QMT10){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT10"};
descended along Algebraic Channel from
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i)+(v) via Stone's theorem applied
to spatial translation invariance,
Lemma [2.2](#lem:phat-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phat-generator"}) and the definitions of
$\hat a, \hat a^\dagger$:
$$[\hat a, \hat a^\dagger] = \left[\sqrt{\tfrac{m\omega}{2\hbar}}\,\hat{q}+ \tfrac{i}{\sqrt{2m\hbar\omega}}\,\hat{p},\;\sqrt{\tfrac{m\omega}{2\hbar}}\,\hat{q}- \tfrac{i}{\sqrt{2m\hbar\omega}}\,\hat{p}\right].$$
The $\hat{q}\,\hat{q}$ and $\hat{p}\,\hat{p}$ commutators vanish; the
cross terms give
$$[\hat a, \hat a^\dagger] = \tfrac{m\omega}{2\hbar}\cdot 0 + \tfrac{1}{2m\hbar\omega}\cdot 0 + \left(\sqrt{\tfrac{m\omega}{2\hbar}}\right)\left(-\tfrac{i}{\sqrt{2m\hbar\omega}}\right)[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] + \tfrac{i}{\sqrt{2m\hbar\omega}}\sqrt{\tfrac{m\omega}{2\hbar}}[\hat{p}, \hat{q}] = \tfrac{1}{2\hbar}\cdot 2\hbar = 1,$$
using $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ and $[\hat{p}, \hat{q}] = -i\hbar$.

**Step 2: Hamiltonian in ladder form.** Direct computation:
$$\hat a^\dagger\hat a = \tfrac{m\omega}{2\hbar}\hat{q}^2 + \tfrac{1}{2m\hbar\omega}\hat{p}^2 + \tfrac{i}{2\hbar}[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = \tfrac{m\omega}{2\hbar}\hat{q}^2 + \tfrac{\hat{p}^2}{2m\hbar\omega} - \tfrac{1}{2},$$
so
$$\hbar\omega\left(\hat a^\dagger\hat a + \tfrac{1}{2}\right) = \tfrac{\hat{p}^2}{2m} + \tfrac{m\omega^2}{2}\hat{q}^2 = \hat{H}.$$
The number operator is $\hat N := \hat a^\dagger\hat a$ and
$\hat{H}= \hbar\omega(\hat N + \tfrac{1}{2})$.

**Step 3: Ladder operators raise/lower $N$.** Using
$[\hat a, \hat a^\dagger] = 1$:
$$[\hat N, \hat a] = [\hat a^\dagger\hat a, \hat a] = \hat a^\dagger[\hat a, \hat a] + [\hat a^\dagger, \hat a]\hat a = 0 + (-1)\hat a = -\hat a,$$
and similarly $[\hat N, \hat a^\dagger] = +\hat a^\dagger$. So
$\hat N(\hat a\lvert \nu \rangle) = (\hat a\hat N - \hat a)\lvert \nu \rangle = (\nu - 1)\hat a\lvert \nu \rangle$
and
$\hat N(\hat a^\dagger\lvert \nu \rangle) = (\nu + 1)\hat a^\dagger\lvert \nu \rangle$:
$\hat a$ lowers eigenvalues of $\hat N$ by 1, $\hat a^\dagger$ raises by
1.

**Step 4: Spectrum is $\mathbb{N}_0$.** $\hat N = \hat a^\dagger\hat a$
is a positive operator:
$\langle\psi, \hat N\psi\rangle = \|\hat a\psi\|^2 \ge 0$. So
eigenvalues of $\hat N$ are non-negative reals. By Step 3, if $\nu$ is
an eigenvalue then $\nu - 1$ is also an eigenvalue (via $\hat a$),
unless $\hat a\lvert \nu \rangle = 0$. The ladder must terminate at the
bottom: there exists a ground state $\lvert 0 \rangle$ with
$\hat a\lvert 0 \rangle = 0$, hence $\hat N\lvert 0 \rangle = 0$.
Repeated application of $\hat a^\dagger$ generates all eigenstates with
eigenvalues $0, 1, 2, \ldots$:
$$\lvert n \rangle := \frac{(\hat a^\dagger)^n}{\sqrt{n!}}\,\lvert 0 \rangle, \qquad \hat N\lvert n \rangle = n\lvert n \rangle,$$
with the $1/\sqrt{n!}$ normalisation chosen so
$\|\lvert n \rangle\| = 1$ (verified by induction using
$\hat a\hat a^\dagger = \hat N + 1$).

**Step 5: Energy levels.** The Hamiltonian eigenvalues follow from
$\hat N$:
$$\hat{H}\lvert n \rangle = \hbar\omega(\hat N + \tfrac{1}{2})\lvert n \rangle = \hbar\omega(n + \tfrac{1}{2})\lvert n \rangle, \qquad E_n = \hbar\omega(n + \tfrac{1}{2}).$$
The zero-point energy $E_0 = \tfrac{1}{2}\hbar\omega$ is the unavoidable
consequence of the canonical commutator $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$,
which by Theorem [12.1](#thm:QMT12){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT12"} (Heisenberg uncertainty) prevents $\hat{q}$ and
$\hat{p}$ from simultaneously vanishing. ◻
:::

### Ground-state wavefunction

The ground state, in the position representation, satisfies
$(\sqrt{m\omega/(2\hbar)}x + i(-i\hbar/\sqrt{2m\hbar\omega})\partial_x)\psi_0 = 0$,
equivalently
$(\sqrt{m\omega/\hbar}x + \sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}\,\partial_x)\psi_0 = 0$
(cancelling the $\sqrt{2}$). The normalized solution is
$$\psi_0(x) = (m\omega/(\pi\hbar))^{1/4}\,\exp(-m\omega x^2/(2\hbar)).$$
Excited states are obtained by repeated $\hat{a}^\dagger$ application:
$\psi_n(x) \propto H_n(\sqrt{m\omega/\hbar}\,x)\,\psi_0(x)$ with $H_n$
the Hermite polynomial.

### Heisenberg saturation by the ground state

The ground state saturates the Heisenberg uncertainty relation
$\Delta q\,\Delta p = \hbar/2$
(Theorem [12.1](#thm:QMT12){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT12"}). Indeed, $\Delta q^2 = \hbar/(2m\omega)$ and
$\Delta p^2 = m\omega\hbar/2$, giving $\Delta q\,\Delta p = \hbar/2$.

### McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework reading

In the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, the oscillator is the cleanest application of
the Compton-coupling theorem
(Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT4"}):
each Sphere of a confined particle cycles at the Compton frequency, with
the trapping potential adding the discrete-spectrum quantization
$E_n = \hbar\omega(n + \tfrac{1}{2})$. The zero-point energy
$\hbar\omega/2$ is the cost of fitting a McGucken-Sphere
wavefront into the trap: even at $n = 0$, the wavefront has nonzero
width and nonzero kinetic content. The zero-point energy is the Sphere's
irreducible quantum-mechanical signature.

### Empirical anchor

Vibrational spectra of diatomic molecules
($\nu \sim 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$), trapped-ion oscillation frequencies
(Wineland et al. ground-state cooling of $^9\text{Be}^+$ to $n = 0$ with
$> 90\%$ probability), and the LIGO (Laser Interferometer
Gravitational-Wave Observatory) laser-interferometer's ground-state
cooling of macroscopic test masses.

## Angular Momentum and the Hydrogen Atom {#ch:angular-hydrogen}

> *The McGucken Principle.* The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality.
> Every result below descends from that expansion.


*Recall.* the McGucken Principle ($\mathrm{McP}$:
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$) asserts that the fourth spacetime dimension
$x_4$ expands at the velocity of light $c$, carrying the
perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguishes it from the spatial
three. Throughout this chapter, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ refers to this
principle and to the five-clause content (i)--(v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: (i) *invariance* --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content; (ii) *spherical symmetry* --- the
expansion is isotropic in the spatial three, with the set of events
reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a 2-sphere of radius
$c\tau$; (iii) *monotonicity* --- the integral curve is strictly
monotonically increasing in $t$, fixing the arrow of $x_4$-advance; (iv)
*Lorentz consistency* --- the structure is $SO^+(1,3)$-invariant on
$M_{G}$; (v) *global validity* --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at
every event of $M_{G}$. The integrated kinematic shadow
$x_4 = ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is the kinematic shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the central fact.

This chapter applies the framework to angular momentum, central
potentials, and the hydrogen atom---the topic that occupies Chapter 3 of
Sakurai [@Sakurai2020], Chapter 12 of Shankar [@Shankar1994], Chapter 4
of Griffiths [@Griffiths2018], Chapters VI--VII of Cohen-Tannoudji
[@CT2019], and Chapter 2 of Weinberg [@Weinberg2015].

### Angular momentum from rotational invariance

The spatial rotation group $SO(3)$ is, by QA1 (Lorentz-invariance
clause), a symmetry subgroup of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. By QA2
(Stone), $SO(3)$ acts on $\mathcal{H}$ as a unitary representation
$\hat{R}(\vec{\theta}) = \exp(-i\vec\theta\cdot\vec{\hat{L}}/\hbar)$
with self-adjoint generators $\hat{L}_i$ ($i = 1, 2, 3$), the
angular-momentum operators.

::: {#thm:Lalgebra .theorem}
**Theorem 2.1** (Angular-momentum algebra).
*$[\hat{L}_i, \hat{L}_j] = i\hbar\,\epsilon_{ijk}\hat{L}_k$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **Step 1: $SO(3)$ Lie algebra structure.** The Lie algebra
$\mathfrak{so}(3)$ of the rotation group has three generators
$T_1, T_2, T_3$ (the antisymmetric $3 \times 3$ matrices generating
rotations about the three axes) with commutation relations
$$[T_i, T_j] = \epsilon_{ijk}\,T_k.$$ This is a standard fact
of the rotation Lie algebra (Hall [@Hall2013] §3.4): the $T_i$ can be
written explicitly as $(T_i)_{jk} = -\epsilon_{ijk}$, and the commutator
is computed directly from these matrix entries.

**Step 2: Stone-generated representation on $\mathcal{H}$.** By QA1,
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is invariant under spatial rotations $SO(3)$
(the principle $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ takes the same form under any
rotation of the three spatial coordinates, since the rate of
$x_{4}$-advance is spherically symmetric). By QA2 (Stone's theorem,
Theorem [3.6](#thm:stone){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:stone"}),
$SO(3)$ acts on $\mathcal{H}$ as a strongly continuous unitary
representation
$$\hat R(\vec\theta) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{i}{\hbar}\,\vec\theta\cdot\vec{\hat L}\right),$$
with self-adjoint generators $\hat L_i$ ($i = 1, 2, 3$).

**Step 3: Lie-algebra homomorphism.** The Stone-generated map
$T_i \mapsto \hat L_i/\hbar$ is a Lie-algebra homomorphism:
differentiating
$\hat R(\vec\theta_1)\hat R(\vec\theta_2) = \hat R(\vec\theta_1 \oplus \vec\theta_2)$
(Baker--Campbell--Hausdorff at second order) and using the Lie-algebra
structure of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ gives, on the unitary representation,
$$\left[\frac{\hat L_i}{i\hbar},\,\frac{\hat L_j}{i\hbar}\right] = \frac{1}{i\hbar}\,\epsilon_{ijk}\,\frac{\hat L_k}{i\hbar},$$
equivalently $[\hat L_i, \hat L_j] = i\hbar\,\epsilon_{ijk}\,\hat L_k$.

**Step 4: McGucken anchoring.** The factor of $i\hbar$ in the commutator
is the same $i\hbar$ as in the canonical commutator
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$: by
Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}, the $i$ here is case 11 of the catalogue
(chain-rule mechanism (a) projected onto the rotation-generator
algebra), descending from the single $i$ in $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via
the suppression map. ◻
:::

::: {#thm:Lspectrum .theorem}
**Theorem 2.2** (Spectrum of $\hat{L}^2$ and $\hat{L}_z$). *$\hat{L}^2$
has eigenvalues $\hbar^2\ell(\ell + 1)$ with $\ell = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$;
$\hat{L}_z$ has eigenvalues $\hbar m$ with
$m = -\ell, -\ell + 1, \ldots, \ell$. The simultaneous eigenstates are
$\lvert \ell, m \rangle$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **Step 1: $\hat L^2$ commutes with each $\hat L_i$.** Direct
computation using the algebra of
Theorem [2.1](#thm:Lalgebra){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:Lalgebra"}:
$$[\hat L^2, \hat L_z] = [\hat L_x^2 + \hat L_y^2 + \hat L_z^2, \hat L_z] = [\hat L_x^2, \hat L_z] + [\hat L_y^2, \hat L_z]$$
$$= \hat L_x[\hat L_x, \hat L_z] + [\hat L_x, \hat L_z]\hat L_x + \hat L_y[\hat L_y, \hat L_z] + [\hat L_y, \hat L_z]\hat L_y$$
$$= \hat L_x(-i\hbar\hat L_y) + (-i\hbar\hat L_y)\hat L_x + \hat L_y(i\hbar\hat L_x) + (i\hbar\hat L_x)\hat L_y = 0.$$
Hence $\hat L^2$ and $\hat L_z$ have simultaneous eigenstates
$\lvert a, b \rangle$ with
$\hat L^2\lvert a, b \rangle = a\lvert a, b \rangle$ and
$\hat L_z\lvert a, b \rangle = b\lvert a, b \rangle$.

**Step 2: Raising and lowering operators.** Define
$\hat L_\pm := \hat L_x \pm i\hat L_y$. Compute
$$[\hat L_z, \hat L_\pm] = [\hat L_z, \hat L_x] \pm i[\hat L_z, \hat L_y] = i\hbar\hat L_y \mp i \cdot i\hbar\hat L_x = \pm\hbar(\hat L_x \pm i\hat L_y) = \pm\hbar\hat L_\pm.$$
Hence
$\hat L_z(\hat L_\pm\lvert a, b \rangle) = (\hat L_\pm\hat L_z + [\hat L_z, \hat L_\pm])\lvert a, b \rangle = (b \pm \hbar)(\hat L_\pm\lvert a, b \rangle)$.
The operator $\hat L_+$ raises $b$ by $\hbar$; $\hat L_-$ lowers $b$ by
$\hbar$.

**Step 3: Ladder termination from non-negativity of
$\hat L^2 - \hat L_z^2$.** Since
$\hat L^2 - \hat L_z^2 = \hat L_x^2 + \hat L_y^2$ is a sum of squares of
self-adjoint operators, its expectation values are non-negative. Hence
at any simultaneous eigenstate $a - b^2 \ge 0$, i.e.,
$|b| \le \sqrt{a}$. The ladder $b, b+\hbar, b+2\hbar, \ldots$ must
therefore terminate at some maximum $b_{\max} =: \hbar\ell$, where
$\hat L_+\lvert a, \hbar\ell \rangle = 0$. Computing
$\hat L_-\hat L_+ = \hat L^2 - \hat L_z^2 - \hbar\hat L_z$ on the top
state gives $0 = a - \hbar^2\ell^2 - \hbar^2\ell$, hence
$a = \hbar^2\ell(\ell + 1)$.

**Step 4: Integer vs. half-integer $\ell$.** The ladder
$b = \hbar\ell, \hbar(\ell - 1), \ldots, -\hbar\ell$ has $2\ell + 1$
states. For orbital angular momentum (single-valued wavefunctions on
$\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus\{0\}$), single-valuedness under a $2\pi$
rotation requires integer $\ell = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$; this excludes
half-integer values for orbital angular momentum. (Half-integer $\ell$
does occur for spin, where the wavefunction is a spinor and
$4\pi$-periodicity replaces $2\pi$-periodicity, as in
Lemma [9.4](#lem:spin-double-cover){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:spin-double-cover"}.)

**Step 5: Magnetic quantum number $m$.** The eigenvalues of $\hat L_z$
range over $b = \hbar m$ with $m = -\ell, -\ell + 1, \ldots, +\ell$,
giving $2\ell + 1$ states. The simultaneous eigenstates are denoted
$\lvert \ell, m \rangle$.

Standard treatments: Sakurai [@Sakurai2020] §3.5; Shankar [@Shankar1994]
§12.2. ◻
:::

### The hydrogen atom

The hydrogen Hamiltonian is
$\hat{H}= -\hbar^2\nabla^2/(2\mu) - e^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0 r)$ with
$\mu$ the reduced mass. In spherical coordinates, separating the radial
and angular parts, the radial equation for $u(r) = rR(r)$ at angular
momentum $\ell$ is
$$-\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}u'' + \left[-\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r} + \frac{\hbar^2\ell(\ell+1)}{2\mu r^2}\right]u = E u.$$
The bound-state spectrum, obtained by demanding $u(r) \to 0$ as
$r \to 0, \infty$, is
$$E_n = -\frac{\mu e^4}{2(4\pi\varepsilon_0)^2\hbar^2}\frac{1}{n^2}, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots
\label{eq:hydrogen-spectrum}$$ the Bohr spectrum (Bohr 1913). The
numerical value $-13.6\,\text{eV}/n^2$ matches the Rydberg formula.

### McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework reading

The hydrogen atom's bound states are the discrete spectrum of the
Schrödinger Hamiltonian (Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT7"}) on the Coulomb potential. The Rydberg formula's
empirical foundation in atomic spectroscopy (Balmer 1885; Rydberg 1888)
is, in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, the empirical signature of the
bound-state quantization on the Sphere-wavefront geometry of the
electron in the Coulomb potential. The accidental $SO(4)$ degeneracy
(Pauli's hydrogen-atom solution, 1926) reflects the hidden symmetry of
the Coulomb problem, derivable from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the
Runge--Lenz conserved vector.

### Empirical anchor

The hydrogen spectrum to fractional precision $\sim 10^{-12}$ in
optical-frequency-comb measurements (Hänsch et al., Nobel 2005). The
Lamb shift (Lamb, Retherford 1947) is the QED (quantum electrodynamics)
radiative correction to the Bohr spectrum, derivable from the
Feynman-diagram apparatus
(Theorem [23.1](#thm:QMT23){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT23"}).

three. Throughout this chapter, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ refers to this
principle and to the five-clause content (i)--(v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"

$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content; (ii) *spherical symmetry* --- the

reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a 2-sphere of radius
$c\tau$; (iii) *monotonicity* --- the integral curve is strictly
monotonically increasing in $t$, fixing the arrow of $x_4$-advance; (iv)

$M_{G}$; (v) *global validity* --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at

This chapter applies QM T20
(Chapter [20](#ch:identical){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:identical"}) to multi-particle systems. The general
framework was established in
Chapter [20](#ch:identical){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:identical"}; here we treat the standard textbook
applications.

### Bosonic systems

For $N$ identical bosons (integer spin), the total wavefunction is
symmetric under exchange. The Hilbert space is the symmetric tensor
power $\text{Sym}^N\mathcal{H}_{\text{single}}$. Standard example:
photons in a single-mode laser obey Bose statistics; the ground state
has all photons in the same mode (the laser's coherent state).

### Fermionic systems and the Slater determinant

For $N$ identical fermions (half-integer spin), the antisymmetric
multi-particle wavefunction is the Slater determinant
$$\Psi(x_1, \ldots, x_N) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N!}}\det[\psi_i(x_j)]_{i,j = 1, \ldots, N},$$
where $\psi_1, \ldots, \psi_N$ are $N$ orthonormal single-particle
wavefunctions. The Pauli exclusion principle is the statement that the
determinant vanishes if any two $\psi_i$ coincide.

### Helium atom

The two-electron helium atom is the simplest application: two electrons
in a Coulomb potential with mutual electron--electron repulsion. The
ground state has both electrons in the spatial $1s$ orbital (symmetric
spatial wavefunction), forcing the spin part to be antisymmetric: the
singlet
$(\lvert \uparrow\downarrow \rangle - \lvert \downarrow\uparrow \rangle)/\sqrt{2}$.
Excited states have one electron in $1s$, the other in $2s, 2p, \ldots$,
with either symmetric (singlet) or antisymmetric (triplet) spatial
parts.

### McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework reading

The McGucken Sphere of each fermion (Geometric Channel of
Theorem [9.1](#thm:QMT9){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT9"})
carries a spinor orientation in $\mathbb{C}^2$. The exclusion principle
is the geometric impossibility of two identical Sphere wavefronts
occupying the same mode. The Slater determinant is the antisymmetric
combination forced by the $4\pi$-periodicity of the spinor structure on
the Sphere (Geometric Channel of Theorem [20.1](#thm:QMT20){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT20"}).

### Empirical anchor

Atomic ground-state configurations (Aufbau principle); molecular orbital
theory (Pauling, Mulliken); white dwarf and neutron star stability;
ultracold-Fermi-gas pairing and BCS superconductivity.

## Time-Independent Perturbation Theory {#ch:tipt}

> *The McGucken Principle.* The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality.
> Every result below descends from that expansion.


*Recall.* the McGucken Principle ($\mathrm{McP}$:
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$) asserts that the fourth spacetime dimension
$x_4$ expands at the velocity of light $c$, carrying the
perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguishes it from the spatial
three. Throughout this chapter, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ refers to this
principle and to the five-clause content (i)--(v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: (i) *invariance* --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content; (ii) *spherical symmetry* --- the
expansion is isotropic in the spatial three, with the set of events
reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a 2-sphere of radius
$c\tau$; (iii) *monotonicity* --- the integral curve is strictly
monotonically increasing in $t$, fixing the arrow of $x_4$-advance; (iv)
*Lorentz consistency* --- the structure is $SO^+(1,3)$-invariant on
$M_{G}$; (v) *global validity* --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at
every event of $M_{G}$. The integrated kinematic shadow
$x_4 = ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is the kinematic shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the central fact.

When $\hat{H}= \hat{H}_0 + \lambda\hat{V}$ with $\hat{H}_0$ exactly
solvable and $\lambda$ small, the perturbative expansion in $\lambda$
supplies approximate eigenvalues and eigenstates. This is the workhorse
of practical quantum mechanics; covered in Sakurai Ch. 5, Shankar
Ch. 17, Griffiths Ch. 7, Cohen-Tannoudji Ch. XI, Weinberg Ch. 5.

### Rayleigh--Schrödinger expansion

Let $\hat{H}_0\lvert n \rangle = E_n^{(0)}\lvert n \rangle$. Seek
eigenvalues
$E_n = E_n^{(0)} + \lambda E_n^{(1)} + \lambda^2 E_n^{(2)} + \cdots$ and
eigenstates
$\lvert \psi_n \rangle = \lvert n \rangle + \lambda\lvert \psi_n^{(1)} \rangle + \cdots$
satisfying
$(\hat{H}_0 + \lambda\hat{V})\lvert \psi_n \rangle = E_n\lvert \psi_n \rangle$.
Matching powers of $\lambda$ (non-degenerate case): $$\begin{aligned}
E_n^{(1)} &= \langle n \vert \hat{V}|n \rangle = \langle n \rvert\hat{V}\lvert n \rangle,\\
\lvert \psi_n^{(1)} \rangle &= \sum_{m \neq n}\frac{\langle m \rvert\hat{V}\lvert n \rangle}{E_n^{(0)} - E_m^{(0)}}\lvert m \rangle,\\
E_n^{(2)} &= \sum_{m \neq n}\frac{|\langle m \rvert\hat{V}\lvert n \rangle|^2}{E_n^{(0)} - E_m^{(0)}}.
\end{aligned}$$

### Degenerate case

If $E_n^{(0)}$ is degenerate, diagonalize $\hat{V}$ within the
degenerate subspace before applying the non-degenerate formulas.

### Application: Stark and Zeeman effects

*Stark effect.* Hydrogen in a uniform electric field $\vec{E}$:
$\hat{V} = -e\vec{E}\cdot\vec{r}$. First-order energy shift in the
$n = 1$ state is zero (parity); the $n = 2$ states are degenerate and
mix under $\hat{V}$.

*Zeeman effect.* Atom in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$:
$\hat{V} = (e/2m)\vec{B}\cdot\vec{L} + (e/m)\vec{B}\cdot\vec{S}$. The
first-order shift is $\Delta E = g_J\mu_B B m_J$ with the Landé
$g$-factor $g_J$ derived from QA6's Wigner classification of
angular-momentum representations.

### Empirical anchor

Atomic line splitting in electric and magnetic fields, observed by Stark
(1913) and Zeeman (1896); modern precision atomic spectroscopy.

### McGucken anchoring of perturbation theory {#sec:tipt-mcgucken-anchoring}

::: {#rmk:tipt-mcgucken-anchoring .remark}
*Remark TIPT.1* (Time-independent perturbation theory descends from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the Schrödinger and Hamiltonian-spectrum
chain). *The Rayleigh--Schrödinger expansion above is a consequence of three McGucken-anchored facts established earlier in
the textbook:*

1.  *The Schrödinger equation
    $i\hbar\,\partial_t\lvert\psi\rangle = \hat{H}\lvert\psi\rangle$
    is itself a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
    (Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT7"} of
    Chapter [7](#ch:schrodinger){reference-type="ref"
    reference="ch:schrodinger"}), descending from
    Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
    reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i) invariance + (v) global
    validity via Stone's theorem applied to time translation
    invariance of the McGucken-Sphere wavefront flow at every event.*

2.  *The Hamiltonian operator $\hat{H}$ governing the system is the
    Stone-generator of time translations on the McGucken-derived
    Hilbert space
    $\mathcal{H}\cong L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$
    (Theorems [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} and
    [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}); its
    self-adjointness is forced by the unitarity of the
    time-translation group implementing
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at every event, with
    $\hat{H}^\dagger = \hat{H}$ a Stone-theorem consequence.*

3.  *The decomposition $\hat{H} = \hat{H}_0 + \lambda\hat{V}$ into an
    exactly solvable McGucken-anchored part $\hat{H}_0$ and a small
    perturbation $\lambda\hat{V}$ is permitted by the
    linearity of the Hilbert-space arena
    (Theorem [9.15](#thm:hilbert-inner){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-inner"}): both $\hat{H}_0$ and $\hat{V}$
    act as bounded or essentially self-adjoint operators on
    $\mathcal{H}$, and their sum is self-adjoint on the intersection
    of their domains (Kato--Rellich theorem, when $\hat{V}$ is
    $\hat{H}_0$-bounded with bound $< 1$).*

*The Rayleigh--Schrödinger expansion in $\lambda$ is the formal
power-series solution of the
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$-descended eigenvalue problem
$\hat{H}\lvert\psi_n\rangle = E_n\lvert\psi_n\rangle$ around the
exactly solvable McGucken-Sphere-wavefront eigenstates
$\lvert n\rangle$ of $\hat{H}_0$. The validity of the expansion in
each finite order follows from the Kato analytic-perturbation theorem
(Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] §XII.1) applied to the family
$\hat{H}(\lambda) = \hat{H}_0 + \lambda\hat{V}$, with the analyticity
of $E_n(\lambda)$ and $\lvert\psi_n(\lambda)\rangle$ following from
the analyticity of the spectral projectors --- itself a consequence
of the spectral theorem on the McGucken-derived Hilbert space.*

*Empirical applications --- Stark effect (atomic line splitting in
electric fields), Zeeman effect (atomic line splitting in magnetic
fields), fine and hyperfine structure --- have their reading as small-perturbation responses of the McGucken-Sphere
wavefront to coupling with external electromagnetic fields, with the
coupling itself descending from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via QM T16
(gauge invariance, Theorem
[16.1](#thm:QMT16){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT16"}): the
minimal coupling $\partial_\mu \to \partial_\mu + i(q/\hbar)A_\mu$
introduces the gauge potential $A_\mu$ that supplies the
Stark/Zeeman perturbations $\hat{V}$ as the integrated form of
$qA_\mu$ along the worldline.*
:::

For time-dependent perturbations $\hat{V}(t) = \hat{V}_0\,f(t)$, the
transition probability between $\hat{H}_0$ eigenstates is computed in
the interaction picture. Covered in Sakurai Ch. 5, Shankar Ch. 18,
