Piron--Solèr 1964/1995, Hardy 2001, Chiribella--D'Ariano--Perinotti
2011, Masanes--Galley--Müller 2019, and the twenty other programs
surveyed in §6.2 of [@MG-Pointwise-2026]) operate as upstream postulates
that do not appear in the theorems they entail. The
pointwise-instantiation property is what makes the mutual generativity
of general relativity and quantum mechanics possible
(Theorems [9.24](#thm:pointwise-constitutivity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:pointwise-constitutivity"} and
[9.28](#thm:mutual-recoverability){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:mutual-recoverability"} above, with
Theorem [9.31](#thm:hilbert-minkowski-one-object){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-minkowski-one-object"} as the deepest single
corollary): because the principle is present at every point of every
structure of both theories, the principle is recoverable
from either side and generates the other.
:::

::: {#rmk:pointwise-vs-ancestry .remark}
*Remark 9.27* (Pointwise constitutivity versus upstream ancestry). The
distinction between pointwise constitutivity and upstream ancestry is
essential. In ordinary derivation, the upstream
foundation is ancestral: the downstream structure inherits its existence
from the upstream but is not, in its own formal handling, dependent on
the upstream's local presence. Hilbert space, treated as a Dirac--von
Neumann postulate, has no upstream ancestor at all: it is itself the
primitive. Hilbert space, treated as a downstream of the
chain of theorems in the ordinary-derivation sense, would have
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as an ancestor but would not require the
ancestor to be present at every event of the spatial slice on which the
inner product is computed. The joint reading is stronger: the
principle is required to be present at every event, and the value of
$\psi(\mathbf{x})$ at every spatial slice point is a local reading of
the principle's content at the source events that contribute to
$\mathbf{x}$. The principle remains the constitutive content of $\mathcal{H}$ at every
spatial-slice point.
:::

#### Reciprocal generation through the chain of theorems {#ssec:reciprocal-generation}

::: {#thm:mutual-recoverability .theorem}
**Theorem 9.28** (Mutual recoverability of levels of the chain through
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as common waypoint). *The four levels of the
chain of theorems of
Definition [9.22](#def:cogenerative-chain){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:cogenerative-chain"} are mutually recoverable through
the principle $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as common waypoint. Specifically,
for any two levels $L_j$ and $L_k$ of the chain of theorems
($j, k \in \{1,2,3,4\}$, $j \neq k$), there is a derivation from $L_j$
through $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ to $L_k$, and conversely from $L_k$
through $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ to $L_j$. The structures are reciprocally accessible through the principle as the shared waypoint of all paths between them.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof exploits the pointwise constitutivity of
Theorem [9.24](#thm:pointwise-constitutivity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:pointwise-constitutivity"}: $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is
the local content of every level. To recover $L_j$ from $L_k$, we
exploit the principle's presence in $L_k$, read off the principle at
every event of $L_k$, and then re-derive $L_j$ from the principle
through the arrow $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic \to L_j$. We verify
three representative cases.

**Recovering $\mathcal{M}_G$ from $\mathcal{H}$.** Given the Hilbert
space $\mathcal{H}$ of quantum mechanics, with its inner product
$\langle\phi|\psi\rangle = \int\phi^*\psi\,d^3x$ on spatial slices, the
principle $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is recovered as follows. The complex
character of $\psi$ is read off as the algebraic content of the local
amplitude at every event; the perpendicularity of $x_4$ to the spatial
three is read off as the geometric content of the complex structure; the
rate $c$ of $x_4$-advance is read off as the velocity content of the
integrated $x_4 = ict$ coordinate; the action quantum $\hbar$ is read
off as the action per radian of the Compton-frequency oscillation of $x_4$-advance. The
principle is thereby reconstructed from the Hilbert-space data. The
moving four-manifold $\mathcal{M}_G$ is then re-derived from the
principle as the locus on which $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every
event. The recovery is unique: no other physical principle is compatible
with the complex separable Hilbert space of standard quantum mechanics
plus the Lorentzian background of special relativity and the action
quantum of Planck.

**Recovering $M_{1,3}$ from $\mathcal{V}$.** Given the complex amplitude
space $\mathcal{V}$, with the rule that each $\psi \in \mathcal{V}$
takes values in $\mathbb{C}$, the Lorentzian arena $M_{1,3}$ is
recovered as follows. The complex structure of $\mathbb{C}$ is read off
as the algebraic content of the perpendicularity of $x_4$; the squaring
rule $i^2 = -1$ is read off as the algebraic shadow of $(ic)^2 = -c^2$;
the Lorentzian signature $(-,+,+,+)$ is reconstructed from the squaring
rule plus the principle's velocity content. The recovery is unique.

**Recovering $\mathcal{H}$ from $M_{1,3}$.** The forward chain of theorems arrow
$M_{1,3} \to \mathcal{V} \to \mathcal{H}$ delivers $\mathcal{H}$ from
$M_{1,3}$ through the slice projection plus the forward--conjugate
$x_4$-overlap. This is the standard direction of the chain of theorems
(Theorems [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}--[9.17](#thm:hilbert-complete){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complete"}).

By symmetry of the construction, any two levels $L_j$ and $L_k$ are
mutually recoverable through the principle as common waypoint:
$L_j \to \tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic \to L_k$ and
$L_k \to \tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic \to L_j$ are both valid derivation
paths. ◻
:::

::: {#cor:sibling-cogeneration .corollary}
**Corollary 9.29** (Sibling joint derivation: $\mathcal{H}$ and Born rule
derived together from a common pre-Hilbert parent). *The Hilbert space
$\mathcal{H}$ and the Born rule $P = |\psi|^2$ are siblings derived together from a common pre-Hilbert parent: the *rank-2 sesquilinear pairing on complex amplitudes over
$M_{1,3}$*. Specifically, the pairing
$\langle\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\rangle: \mathcal{V} \times \mathcal{V} \to \mathbb{C}$
defined by $\langle\phi, \psi\rangle = \int\phi^*\psi\,d^3x$ on the
spatial slice is the common parent; the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ is
generated from the pairing by completion
(Theorem [9.17](#thm:hilbert-complete){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complete"}); the Born rule $P = |\psi|^2$ is
generated from the pairing on the diagonal $\phi = \psi$ as
$\langle\psi,\psi\rangle = \int|\psi|^2 d^3x$ with probabilistic
interpretation. The pairing is itself as jointly derived read from $M_{1,3}$
(the integration domain and the metric for $d^3x$), from $\mathcal{V}$
(the complex amplitudes being paired), and from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(the forward--conjugate $x_4$-overlap that the pairing geometrically
realises). $\mathcal{H}$ and Born are siblings of the same parent,
neither derived from the other.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The standard derivation of the Born rule from the Hilbert
space, in the Dirac--von Neumann tradition, treats the Born rule as a
downstream postulate added to the Hilbert-space framework after the fact
(DvN-3, on which see
§[9.11.6](#ssec:DvN-corollaries){reference-type="ref"
reference="ssec:DvN-corollaries"} below). The joint reading
treats both as siblings: the rank-2 sesquilinear pairing on
$\mathcal{V}$ is the common parent, with the Hilbert space generated by
the pairing's completion and the Born rule generated by the pairing's
diagonal restriction. The two generations operate from the same pairing,
in two distinct manners: completion generates a
topological-vector-space structure (the Cauchy completion of
$\mathcal{V}$ under the pairing's induced norm), while diagonal
restriction generates a real non-negative scalar (the squared magnitude
$|\psi|^2 = \langle\psi,\psi\rangle/\int 1\,d^3x$ on the unit-normalised
diagonal). The two generations are co-equal: neither is upstream of the
other. ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:sibling-inversion .remark}
*Remark 9.30* (Sibling joint derivation as a inversion of
textbook QM). The sibling joint derivation of $\mathcal{H}$ and the Born
rule is a inversion of the textbook treatment. The Dirac--von
Neumann tradition postulates $\mathcal{H}$ first and the Born rule
second, with the Born rule appearing as DvN-3 added to the $\mathcal{H}$
framework of DvN-1 and DvN-2. In the textbook view, $\mathcal{H}$ is
parent and Born is child. The joint reading: the rank-2
sesquilinear pairing on $\mathcal{V}$ is parent; both $\mathcal{H}$ and
Born are children, generated by two distinct operations on the common
parent (completion for $\mathcal{H}$, diagonal restriction for Born).
The joint reading explains a feature that the textbook treatment
leaves mysterious: *why* $\mathcal{H}$ and Born are compatible at all.
In the textbook view, the compatibility is built into the postulates:
$\mathcal{H}$ is postulated, then Born is postulated to take values
consistent with the inner-product structure of $\mathcal{H}$. In the
joint view, the compatibility is automatic: $\mathcal{H}$ and
Born are both generated from the same pairing, and their compatibility
is the compatibility of two operations on a common parent.
:::

#### The Hilbert space and the Minkowski manifold as one geometric object at two levels of the chain {#ssec:hilbert-minkowski-one-object}

The pointwise-constitutivity property
(Theorem [9.24](#thm:pointwise-constitutivity){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:pointwise-constitutivity"}) and the mutual recoverability
property
(Theorem [9.28](#thm:mutual-recoverability){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:mutual-recoverability"}) above have a deepest single
corollary, established as Theorem 10.6 of [@MG-Pointwise-2026]: the
spacetime manifold $M_{1,3}$ of special relativity and the Hilbert space
$\mathcal{H}$ of quantum mechanics are the same geometric object at two
levels of the chain of representation. $M_{1,3}$ is the point-set /
manifold-level rendering of the constraint surface where
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds locally; $\mathcal{H}$ is the
function-space-level rendering of the same constraint surface. The
Lorentzian metric of $M_{1,3}$ becomes the sesquilinear inner product of
$\mathcal{H}$ by the standard $L^2$ construction, with the rank-2
character of the metric
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}) surviving as the rank-2 sesquilinear
character of the inner product
(Lemma [9.13](#lem:bilinearity-rank2){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:bilinearity-rank2"}). The perpendicular fourth dimension
$x_{4}= ict$ survives as the wavefunction's complex character
(Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}). The spatial points of $M_{1,3}$ are
in canonical bijection with the position-eigenstate basis of
$\mathcal{H}$.

::: {#thm:hilbert-minkowski-one-object .theorem}
**Theorem 9.31** (The Hilbert space and the Minkowski manifold as one
geometric object at two levels of the chain; [@MG-Pointwise-2026] Theorem
10.6). *The Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ of quantum mechanics and the
Minkowski spacetime manifold $M_{1,3}$ of special relativity are the
same geometric object at two levels of the chain of representation. The
relationship admits the explicit form
$$\mathcal{H}\;\cong\; L^2(M_{1,3}, \eta_{\mu\nu})$$ under the standard
$L^2$-functional construction on a pseudo-Riemannian manifold. Three
identifications make the identity explicit:*

1.  **Canonical $L^2$-functional construction.* For the
    pseudo-Riemannian manifold $(M_{1,3}, \eta_{\mu\nu})$ with Minkowski
    metric $\eta = \mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(-1, +1, +1, +1)$, the
    canonical $L^2$ construction supplies a complex Hilbert space
    $L^2(M_{1,3}, \eta) = \{ f: M_{1,3} \to \mathbb{C}\mid \int |f|^2 \sqrt{|\eta|}\,d^4x < \infty \}$
    with sesquilinear inner product
    $\langle\phi, \psi\rangle_{L^2} = \int \phi^*\psi\,\sqrt{|\eta|}\,d^4x$.
    The spatial-slice restriction (integration over the spatial slice
    $\mathbb{R}^3$ at fixed parameter time $t$, with measure $d^3x$)
    yields the non-relativistic Schrödinger-picture Hilbert space
    $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3x)$ of
    Theorem [9.17](#thm:hilbert-complete){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-complete"}.*

2.  **Canonical bijection of spacetime points and position-eigenstate
    basis.* The point-set of $M_{1,3}$ at parameter time $t$ and the
    position-eigenstate basis of $\mathcal{H}$ at parameter time $t$ are
    in canonical bijection. For each spatial point
    $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ on the spatial slice at time $t$, the
    position eigenstate $$\lvert x_0 \rangle \;:=\; \delta^3(x - x_0)$$
    is the (rigged-Hilbert-space) eigenvector of the position operator
    $\hat{q}_i$ with eigenvalue $(x_0)_i$. The map
    $x_0 \leftrightarrow \lvert x_0 \rangle$ is a bijection between the
    spatial points of $M_{1,3}$ at time $t$ and the position-basis of
    $\mathcal{H}$ at time $t$. The position eigenstates form a complete
    (rigged-Hilbert-space) basis:
    $\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} \lvert x \rangle\langle x \rvert\,d^3x = \mathbb{1}$
    on $\mathcal{H}$, and an orthonormal one in the distributional
    sense: $\langle x_0 \rvert\lvert x_1 \rangle = \delta^3(x_0 - x_1)$.
    At the most concrete level, the manifold $M_{1,3}$ at time $t$ and
    the position-basis of $\mathcal{H}$ at time $t$ are the same set of
    objects, with the manifold giving the geometric/distance content and
    $\mathcal{H}$ giving the algebraic/inner-product content.*

3.  **Feature-by-feature correspondence.* Every feature of $\mathcal{H}$ that the Dirac--von Neumann tradition
    treated as an independent axiomatic input is a function-space-level
    rendering of a geometric feature of $M_{1,3}$ that the McGucken
    Principle supplies at the manifold level. (i) The complex character
    of $\psi$ (DvN-1 demands $\mathcal{H}$ over $\mathbb{C}$) is the
    algebraic record of $x_4$-perpendicularity
    (Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}). (ii) The rank-2 sesquilinear
    inner product (DvN-1 demands a positive-definite Hermitian form) is
    the $L^2$-rendering of the rank-2 Lorentzian metric
    (Lemma [9.13](#lem:bilinearity-rank2){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:bilinearity-rank2"}). (iii) The non-commutative
    operator algebra $[\hat{q}_i, \hat{p}_j] = i\hbar\delta_{ij}$
    (DvN-2) is the operator-level statement of the geometric
    perpendicularity $x_1 x_2 x_3 \perp x_{4}$. (iv) The unitary time
    evolution (DvN-5) is $x_{4}$-flux conservation between slices
    (Theorem [9.15](#thm:hilbert-inner){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-inner"} and Remark on conservation of
    $x_{4}$-flux).*

*There is no separate Hilbert space "where quantum mechanics lives"
connected by postulated bridges to a separate spacetime "where
relativity lives"; there is one geometric structure rendered at two
levels of the chain, with the McGucken Principle pointwise instantiated in
both.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has three steps, one per clause.

**Step 1: Clause (O1) --- the canonical $L^2$ construction.** For any
pseudo-Riemannian manifold $(X, g_{\mu\nu})$, the standard
$L^2$-functional construction supplies a complex Hilbert space
$L^2(X, g)$ uniquely determined up to natural isomorphism. The complex
character of $L^2(X, g)$ comes from the complex-valuedness of the
functions $f: X \to \mathbb{C}$, not from any additional algebraic
input. The sesquilinear inner product structure (conjugate-linear in the
first slot, linear in the second) is forced by the requirement that
$\langle\psi, \psi\rangle \geq 0$ be real-valued and equal to
$\|\psi\|^2$ for any $\psi$. Applying the $L^2$ construction to
$(M_{1,3}, \eta_{\mu\nu})$ supplies the four-dimensional Hilbert space
$L^2(M_{1,3}, \eta_{\mu\nu})$; restricting to the spatial slice
$\mathbb{R}^3$ at fixed parameter time $t$ with measure $d^3x$ yields
exactly the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3x)$
constructed in
Theorem [9.17](#thm:hilbert-complete){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complete"}. The structures are identical: the
spatial-slice $L^2$ rendering of $M_{1,3}$ is the non-relativistic
Schrödinger-picture Hilbert space.

**Step 2: Clause (O2) --- the canonical bijection.** For each spatial
point $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ on the spatial slice at parameter time $t$,
the position eigenstate
$\lvert x_0 \rangle := \delta^3(\mathbf{x} - x_0)$ is the
(rigged-Hilbert-space) eigenvector of the position operator $\hat{q}_i$
with eigenvalue $(x_0)_i$:
$\hat{q}_i \lvert x_0 \rangle = (x_0)_i \lvert x_0 \rangle$. The map
$x_0 \mapsto \lvert x_0 \rangle$ is well-defined (each spatial point
determines a unique delta function), injective (distinct spatial points
give distinct delta functions, since
$\delta^3(\mathbf{x} - x_0) = \delta^3(\mathbf{x} - x_1)$ as
distributions implies $x_0 = x_1$), and surjective onto the
position-basis (every position eigenstate is a delta function at some
spatial point). The completeness relation
$\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} \lvert x \rangle\langle x \rvert\,d^3x = \mathbb{1}$
and the distributional orthonormality
$\langle x_0 \rvert\lvert x_1 \rangle = \delta^3(x_0 - x_1)$ are
standard rigged-Hilbert-space facts (Gelfand--Vilenkin 1964
[@GelfandVilenkin1964], Bohm 1978 [@Bohm1978]). The delta-function inner
product reproduces, in distributional form, the spatial-distance content
of the Minkowski metric: two distinct spatial points have zero overlap
(the metric distance is non-zero), and a point with itself has unit
overlap (the metric distance is zero). The Hilbert-space inner product
of position eigenstates is the function-space rendering of the Minkowski
metric's behavior on spatial points.

**Step 3: Clause (O3) --- the feature-by-feature
correspondence.** We verify each of the four sub-claims (i)--(iv).

*(i) Complex character.* The complex-valuedness of
$\psi \in \mathcal{H}$ is forced by
Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"} (Complex amplitudes), which establishes
that the wavefunction's algebra is $\mathbb{C}$ by the slice-projection
content of $x_{4}= ict$ on $M_{1,3}$: the imaginary unit $i$ in the
algebra of $\mathcal{H}$ is the perpendicularity marker for $x_{4}$'s
orthogonality to $x_1 x_2 x_3$, which is a feature of
$M_{1,3}$ via the integrated kinematic shadow of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}).

*(ii) Rank-2 sesquilinear inner product.* The bilinearity of the inner
product on $\mathcal{H}$ in $(\phi^*, \psi)$ is forced by
Lemma [9.13](#lem:bilinearity-rank2){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:bilinearity-rank2"} (Bilinearity from rank-2 Minkowski
metric): the rank-2 character of the Lorentzian metric $\eta_{\mu\nu}$
on $M_{1,3}$ survives, under the $L^2$-functional construction, as the
rank-2 sesquilinear character of the inner product
$\langle\phi, \psi\rangle = \int\phi^*\psi\,d^3x$ on $\mathcal{H}$. The
rank-2 character of the metric is itself a consequence of
$(ic)^2 = -c^2$ in $x_{4}= ict$
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}), the integrated kinematic shadow of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

*(iii) Canonical commutator.* The non-commutativity
$[\hat{q}_i, \hat{p}_j] = i\hbar\delta_{ij}$ is the operator-level
statement of the geometric perpendicularity $x_1 x_2 x_3 \perp x_{4}$ on
$M_{1,3}$: the position operators $\hat{q}_i$ act in the spatial three
$x_1 x_2 x_3$ as multiplication operators, and the momentum operators
$\hat{p}_i = -i\hbar\,\partial/\partial x_i$ are the spatial gradient
operators, with the imaginary unit $i$ being the same perpendicularity
marker from $x_{4}= ict$. The non-commutativity records the
perpendicularity at the operator-algebra level (§5 of
[@MG-Pointwise-2026]; see also Proposition 12.10 of the same paper for
the explicit position-in-$x_1 x_2 x_3$ versus momentum-in-$x_{4}$
reading of the canonical commutator).

*(iv) Unitary time evolution.* The unitary evolution operator
$U(t) = \exp(-i\hat{H}t/\hbar)$ generated by the Hamiltonian $\hat{H}$
on $\mathcal{H}$ is the $L^2$-rendering of $x_{4}$-flux conservation
between successive spatial slices of $M_{1,3}$
(Theorem [9.15](#thm:hilbert-inner){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-inner"}, with the conservation-of-$x_{4}$-flux
remark). The unitary preservation of the inner product
$\langle\psi(t), \psi(t)\rangle = \langle\psi(0), \psi(0)\rangle$ across
$t$ is the function-space-level expression of the geometric fact that
the $x_{4}$-advance between successive spatial slices preserves the
total amplitude flux through each slice.

All three clauses verified. The Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ and the
Minkowski manifold $M_{1,3}$ are the same geometric object at two
levels of the chain of representation, with the manifold-level rendering
supplying the geometric/distance content and the function-space
rendering supplying the algebraic/inner-product content. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:two-worlds-dissolved .remark}
*Remark 9.32* (The two-worlds framing dissolved). The orthodox reading
of quantum mechanics treats $\mathcal{H}$ as an abstract complex vector
space whose connection to physical spacetime is supplied externally ---
wavefunctions introduced as "amplitudes" without geometric content, the
inner product introduced as "physically meaningful overlap" without
explanation, the complex numbers appearing because "QM requires them"
without further account, the operator algebra postulated rather than
derived. The mystery of "why is quantum mechanics in a Hilbert space"
was never resolved in the prior tradition because $\mathcal{H}$ was
treated as a separate mathematical universe from the spacetime in which
it acts. The reading of
Theorem [9.31](#thm:hilbert-minkowski-one-object){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-minkowski-one-object"} is the resolution: there
is no separate Hilbert space "where quantum mechanics lives." There is
one geometric structure --- the constraint surface $M_{1,3}$ where
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds locally --- and the Hilbert space is
$M_{1,3}$ in its function-valued representation. The "two-worlds"
framing of QM-vs-relativity that every century-long program
for QM struggled with (Mackey 1963, Piron 1964, Solèr 1995, Hardy 2001,
Chiribella--D'Ariano--Perinotti 2011, Masanes--Galley--Müller 2019, and
twenty other programs surveyed in §6.2 of [@MG-Pointwise-2026]) is
dissolved in one move. Every prior attempt tried to derive the
Hilbert-space structure from axioms internal to $\mathcal{H}$, missing
that $\mathcal{H}$ is $M_{1,3}$ in its function-valued representation,
with structure forced by the geometric content of the manifold under
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. This is the reason that no prior
program succeeded: the arena was misidentified as separate, when in fact
it has the role of a function-space rendering of the same constraint
surface that special relativity's manifold renders point-set-wise.
:::

::: {#prop:infinite-dim-as-x4-radii .proposition}
**Proposition 9.33** (Infinite-dimensionality of $\mathcal{H}$ as the
continuum of McGucken-Sphere radii; [@MG-Pointwise-2026] Proposition
10.7). *The infinite-dimensionality of the Hilbert space
$\mathcal{H}= L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3x)$
(Theorem [9.17](#thm:hilbert-complete){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complete"}) admits a manifold-level geometric
source under the chain of theorems: it is the level
expression of the continuum of perpendicular $x_{4}$-radii from McGucken
Spheres at every event of $M_{1,3}$. Specifically:*

1.  **McGucken-Sphere structure at every event.* At every spacetime
    event $E \in M_{1,3}$, the McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{E}(t)$ at
    parameter time $t$
    (Definition [4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref"
    reference="def:sphere"} of
    Chapter [4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref"
    reference="ch:foundations"}) is a 2-sphere of radius $c(t - t_E)$ in
    the spatial slice, with each point $P \in M^{+}_{E}(t)$
    corresponding to one outward-pointing $x_{4}$-radius from $E$ along
    the line $EP$. Each radius is in a perpendicular direction (the
    $i$-marker for $x_{4}$-perpendicularity attaches to it, via
    Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}), with the radial geometric content
    being one specific $x_{4}$-direction at $E$ along which the active
    expansion at rate $ic$ is proceeding.*

2.  **Continuum of $x_{4}$-radii per event.* The cardinality of the set
    $\{x_{4}\text{-radii emanating from } E\}$ is the cardinality of the
    2-sphere $M^{+}_{E}(t)$, which is $2^{\aleph_0}$ for any
    $E \in M_{1,3}$. Every event in $M_{1,3}$ has a continuum of
    perpendicular $x_{4}$-radii. The radii are not finite-dimensional:
    the 2-sphere is not a discrete set; the radii form a continuous
    manifold of directions at each event.*

3.  **Wavefunction as path-integral sum over arriving $x_{4}$-radii.*
    The McGucken wavefunction at spatial point $x$ at parameter time $t$
    (the path-integral kernel of
    Chapter [4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref"
    reference="ch:foundations"}) is the sum
    $$\psi(x, t) \;=\; \sum_\gamma \exp\!\bigl(iS[\gamma]/\hbar\bigr)$$
    over all paths $\gamma$ from past events to $x$. In the McGucken
    reading, each path $\gamma$ corresponds to one specific
    $x_{4}$-radius from some past event $E$ to $x$ --- equivalently, one
    specific direction on the McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{E}(t)$ that
    arrives at $x$ at parameter time $t$. The path-integral sum is the
    sum over all $x_{4}$-radii from past events arriving at $x$ at time
    $t$. The $i$ in $\exp(iS[\gamma]/\hbar)$ is the perpendicularity
    marker for each contributing $x_{4}$-radius; the action
    $S[\gamma]/\hbar$ supplies the phase per radius normalised by the
    action quantum.*

4.  **The "4 vs $\infty$" dimensional contrast dissolved.* The
    cardinality counts are now: *4* counts the spacetime dimensions of
    $M_{1,3}$ at the manifold level (three spatial $x_1 x_2 x_3$ plus
    one perpendicular $x_{4}$); *$2^{\aleph_0}$* counts the
    perpendicular $x_{4}$-radii from McGucken Spheres at the
    function-space level (one per spatial point on the slice times one
    per direction on the 2-sphere from each past event). The two counts
    are at two different levels of the chain of the same geometric structure,
    with no fundamental dimensional contrast between $M_{1,3}$ and
    $\mathcal{H}$.*

5.  **Continuous spectra of position and momentum forced.* The
    continuous spectra of position and momentum (Dirac 1930
    [@Dirac1930], von Neumann 1932 [@vonNeumann1932], treated for a
    century as primitives of the kinematical formalism) are
    correspondingly forced: position has a continuum of values because
    the McGucken-Sphere wavefront has a continuum of arrival points on
    the spatial slice; momentum has a continuum of values because the
    McGucken Sphere at every event has a continuum of directions.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). We verify each clause.

**Clause (I1).** By Definition [4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:sphere"}, at every event $E \in M_{1,3}$ the McGucken
Sphere $M^{+}_{E}(t)$ is the 2-sphere of radius $c(t - t_E)$ in the
spatial slice at parameter time $t$, centered at the spatial projection
of $E$. Each point $P \in M^{+}_{E}(t)$ lies on a null geodesic from $E$
to $P$ (since $|P - x_E|/(t - t_E) = c$); the radial line from $E$ to
$P$ has its temporal-direction content along $x_{4}$ at rate $ic$
(Lemma [4.7](#lem:reverse-reading-equivalence){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:reverse-reading-equivalence"} expressed at $E$) and its
spatial-direction content along $\hat n_P := (P - x_E)/|P - x_E|$. The
radius from $E$ to $P$ is therefore a specific outward-pointing
$x_{4}$-direction at $E$, marked by the $i$-marker for
$x_{4}$-perpendicularity
(Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}). ✓

**Clause (I2).** The 2-sphere $M^{+}_{E}(t)$ is a compact 2-manifold of
cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$ (the cardinality of the continuum in two
parameters $\theta, \phi$ on a compact 2-manifold). Therefore the
cardinality of $x_{4}$-radii emanating from $E$ is $2^{\aleph_0}$, the
cardinality of the continuum. ✓

**Clause (I3).** By the path-integral construction of the wavefunction
(the Geometric Channel reading of the chain of theorems, with the path-integral kernel as
the explicit form of $\psi$ on $M_{1,3}$), the wavefunction at $(x, t)$
is the sum over all paths $\gamma$ from past events to $(x, t)$,
weighted by the action phase $\exp(iS[\gamma]/\hbar)$. Each path
$\gamma$ has a unique starting event $E_\gamma$ and arrives at $(x, t)$;
the spatial direction at $E_\gamma$ pointing toward $x$ is one specific
direction on the McGucken Sphere $M^{+}_{E_\gamma}(t)$. The
path-integral sum is therefore the sum over all $x_{4}$-radii from past
events arriving at $(x, t)$. The $i$ in the phase
$\exp(iS[\gamma]/\hbar)$ is the perpendicularity marker for each
contributing $x_{4}$-radius
(Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}); the action $S[\gamma]/\hbar$ supplies
the phase per radius normalised by the action quantum $\hbar$
(Theorem [9.35](#thm:c-hbar-twin){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:c-hbar-twin"} below). ✓

**Clause (I4).** By
Theorem [9.31](#thm:hilbert-minkowski-one-object){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-minkowski-one-object"}, $\mathcal{H}$ and
$M_{1,3}$ are the same geometric object at two levels of the chain. The
spacetime-dimension count of $M_{1,3}$ is 4 (three spatial plus one
$x_{4}$); the basis-dimension count of $\mathcal{H}$ at parameter time
$t$ is $2^{\aleph_0}$ (continuum, by the canonical bijection of clause
(O2) of
Theorem [9.31](#thm:hilbert-minkowski-one-object){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-minkowski-one-object"}, with each spatial point
in the slice corresponding to one position eigenstate, and each position
eigenstate being the convergence-locus of a continuum of $x_{4}$-radii
from past events per clause (I3)). The "4 vs $\infty$" framing that the
orthodox tradition treated as a fundamental dimensional contrast between
$M_{1,3}$ and $\mathcal{H}$ is the same geometric structure counted at
two levels of the chain, with the spacetime-dimension count at the manifold
level and the cardinality of the position basis at the function-space
level. No fundamental dimensional contrast exists between $M_{1,3}$ and
$\mathcal{H}$: they are the same geometric object. ✓

**Clause (I5).** The position operator $\hat{q}$ on $\mathcal{H}$ has
continuous spectrum $\mathbb{R}^3$, with the position eigenstates
$\lvert x_0 \rangle$ in canonical bijection with the spatial points of
$M_{1,3}$ at time $t$ (clause (O2) of
Theorem [9.31](#thm:hilbert-minkowski-one-object){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-minkowski-one-object"}). The continuum of
position eigenvalues is therefore the continuum of spatial points on the
slice, with each spatial point being the convergence-locus of a
continuum of arriving $x_{4}$-radii per clause (I3). The momentum
operator $\hat{p}$ has continuous spectrum $\mathbb{R}^3$, with the
momentum eigenstates being the Fourier transforms of position
eigenstates and the continuum of momentum eigenvalues corresponding to
the continuum of directions on each McGucken Sphere from each past
event. Both continuous spectra are forced by the underlying continuum
structure of the McGucken-Sphere radii at every event of $M_{1,3}$. ✓

All five clauses verified. The infinite-dimensionality of $\mathcal{H}$
is the level expression of the continuum of perpendicular
$x_{4}$-radii from McGucken Spheres at every event of $M_{1,3}$, with
the orthodox "infinite-dimensional Hilbert space" framing resolving into
"continuum of McGucken-Sphere radii at the function-space level of the
same geometric structure that $M_{1,3}$ renders at the manifold level."
$\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:wheeler-grade-simplicity-infinite-dim .remark}
*Remark 9.34* (The Wheeler-grade simplicity of the infinite-dimensional
content). The orthodox tradition treated the infinite-dimensionality of
$\mathcal{H}$ as an abstract algebraic feature of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$
with no manifold-level geometric source: "$L^2$ is what it is" (Dirac
1930 [@Dirac1930], von Neumann 1932 [@vonNeumann1932], Reed--Simon
1972--1980 [@ReedSimon1980]), followed by a chain of definitions without
any geometric primitive to anchor the "infinite."
Proposition [9.33](#prop:infinite-dim-as-x4-radii){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:infinite-dim-as-x4-radii"} supplies a manifold-level
source for the cardinality: each event of $M_{1,3}$ carries a McGucken
Sphere with a continuum of perpendicular $x_{4}$-radii; each radius is
one specific direction along which the active $x_{4}$-expansion at rate
$ic$ is proceeding; the wavefunction at any spatial point is the
path-integral sum over all $x_{4}$-radii from past events arriving at
that point; the position basis of $\mathcal{H}$ labels the
convergence-loci of these radii on the spatial slice. The
infinite-dimensionality of $\mathcal{H}$ is the level expression
of this manifold-level continuum --- a Wheeler-grade simple geometric
quantity (the continuum of perpendicular $x_{4}$-radii from McGucken
Spheres at every spacetime event) made level explicit at the
function-space level of the same geometric structure that $M_{1,3}$
renders at the manifold level. The simplicity is the geometric primitive
of perpendicular $x_{4}$-radii at every event; the orthodox cardinality
is the level shadow.
:::

#### $c$ and $\hbar$ as twin constants of one geometric flow {#ssec:c-and-hbar-twin}

::: {#thm:c-hbar-twin .theorem}
**Theorem 9.35** ($c$ and $\hbar$ as twin properties of the one
geometric flow $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). *The two fundamental constants
$c$ and $\hbar$ of quantum mechanics are twin properties of the single
geometric flow $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: $c$ is the rate of
$x_4$-advance per unit time, and $\hbar$ is the action per
radian of the Compton-frequency oscillation of $x_4$-advance. The two constants are properties of one principle, and every appearance of $i\hbar$
in standard quantum mechanics has both factors traced to that principle:
the factor $i$ from the perpendicularity of $x_4$ to the spatial three
(the perpendicularity selection of $\mathbb{C}$ on the one perpendicular axis,
Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}), and the factor $\hbar$ from the
action-quantization of $x_4$-advance per radian of the Compton-frequency oscillation.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). **The two constants are read off one wavefront.** The McGucken
Principle has the physical content
(Remark [4.2](#rmk:substantive-content-of-principle){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:substantive-content-of-principle"} of
Chapter [4](#ch:foundations){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:foundations"}) that $x_4$ advances as a
spherically-symmetric wavefront at velocity $c$ from every event of
$M_{G}$. A wavefront at $c$ carries wavelength, frequency, phase, and
therefore action: wavelength $\lambda$ (supported by the spectral
content of the advance, with $\ell_P$ as minimum), frequency
$\nu = c/\lambda$ (supported by the same content, with
$\omega_P = 1/t_P$ as maximum), phase $\varphi$ rotating at angular rate
$\omega$ on the 2-sphere $M^{+}_{p}(t)$, and action $\hbar$ per
oscillatory cycle at the Planck frequency. The two constants are read
directly off this single physical content: $c$ is the rate at which the
wavefront advances; $\hbar$ is the action it carries per oscillatory
cycle at the Planck frequency. The two are therefore properties of one
geometric flow, with the role of two independent empirical inputs
replaced by the role of two readings of one wavefront advance.

**Formal statement.** The McGucken Principle in its full statement
[@MG-Cogeneration-2026; @MG-Hilbert-2026] contains two
physical-geometric facts about the $x_4$-flow: (a) the velocity content
$|dx_4/dt| = c$, asserting that $x_4$ advances at the velocity of light;
(b) the action quantization content, asserting that each oscillatory
step of the $x_4$-advance at the Planck frequency $\omega_P = 1/t_P$
(with $t_P$ the Planck time) carries action $\hbar$. The two facts
together determine the principle's two constants:
$$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic, \qquad S_{\text{per Planck oscillation}} = \hbar.$$
The first fact gives $c$ as the rate of $x_4$-advance; the second fact
gives $\hbar$ as the action per oscillation. Both are properties of the
same geometric flow --- the same spherically-symmetric wavefront at $c$
whose wavelength, frequency, phase, and action are present in the
physical content of the principle.

The standard appearances of $i\hbar$ in quantum mechanics each have both
factors traced:

-   *Canonical commutator* $[\hat{q},\hat{p}] = i\hbar$: the $i$ from
    the perpendicularity of $x_4$
    (Theorem [9.10](#thm:hilbert-complex){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-complex"}, the perpendicularity selection of
    $\mathbb{C}$); the $\hbar$ from the action-quantization of
    $x_4$-advance [@MG-Cogeneration-2026], Theorem 5.1.

-   *Schrödinger equation* $i\hbar\partial_t\psi = \hat{H}\psi$: the
    $i\hbar$ on the left encoding the principle's twin constants in the
    time-evolution generator. The $i$ supplies the unitary phase
    rotation of $\psi$ under time translation; the $\hbar$ supplies the
    action scale at which the rotation occurs.

-   *Heisenberg uncertainty* $\sigma_x\sigma_p \geq \hbar/2$: the
    $\hbar$ from action quantization; the $1/2$ from Cauchy--Schwarz on
    the derived commutator and derived Hilbert space (Robertson's
    general uncertainty bound). The factor $i$ is absent on the
    right-hand side because $\sigma_x\sigma_p$ is a real-valued product
    of real-valued standard deviations.

-   *Feynman path integral weight* $e^{iS/\hbar}$: the $i$ from the
    perpendicularity (the complex structure on the amplitude space); the
    $\hbar$ from action quantization (the normalisation of the action to
    the principle's action quantum).

Every $i\hbar$ in quantum mechanics is the joint signature of the
principle's twin constants. The Dirac--von Neumann tradition treated $c$
and $\hbar$ as separately measured empirical inputs; the joint
reading derives both from the single principle. ◻
:::

::: {#cor:i-and-hbar-distinct-origins .corollary}
**Corollary 9.36** (The $i$ and the $\hbar$ have distinct geometric
origins in the principle). *The factor $i$ in $i\hbar$ has its origin in
the *perpendicularity content* of the principle: $x_4$ is perpendicular
to the spatial three, with the perpendicularity marker $i$ entering as
the algebraic shadow of $(ic)^2 = -c^2$ in the Minkowski signature
(§[9.3](#sec:hilbert-step1){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:hilbert-step1"}, Axis 1 of the McGucken-Wick rotation
section in Chapter [1](#ch:diagnosis){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:diagnosis"}). The factor $\hbar$ in $i\hbar$ has its
origin in the *action-quantization content* of the principle: each
Compton-frequency oscillation of the $x_4$-advance carries action
$h$, i.e. $\hbar$ per radian. The two contents are independent properties of the same
geometric flow: removing the perpendicularity (treating $x_4$ as a
fourth spatial axis) eliminates the $i$ while preserving the $\hbar$;
removing the action-quantization (treating $x_4$ as a smooth flow
without discrete oscillatory steps) eliminates the $\hbar$ while
preserving the $i$. The Dirac--von Neumann tradition's joint treatment
of $i$ and $\hbar$ as a single empirical parameter $i\hbar$ obscured
this distinction; the joint reading restores it. ◻*
:::

#### The Dirac--von Neumann axioms DvN-1 through DvN-6 as corollaries of the chain of theorems {#ssec:DvN-corollaries}

The Dirac--von Neumann axiomatization [@vonNeumann1932] is stated at
varying granularity across the literature. The minimal formulation carries three statements
--- observables as self-adjoint operators, states as rays, expectation
values as inner products --- and omits both the projection postulate and
the composite-system postulate; textbook presentations commonly carry
four or five. The enumeration used here is the maximal list, DvN-1
through DvN-6, chosen so that every statement the orthodox tradition
treats as postulational appears somewhere in the chain of theorems: states are unit vectors in a
complex separable Hilbert space (DvN-1); observables are self-adjoint
operators on that space (DvN-2); measurement outcomes occur with
Born-rule probabilities (DvN-3); upon measurement, the state projects
onto the eigenspace of the observed value (DvN-4); unobserved evolution
is unitary by the Schrödinger equation (DvN-5); composite systems live
on the tensor product of the component Hilbert spaces (DvN-6). The
chain of theorems reveals these statements as *corollaries* of
upstream theorems already proved in the chain of theorems, not as postulates on equal footing with $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

::: {#cor:DvN-1 .corollary}
**Corollary 9.37** (DvN-1: states as unit vectors in a complex separable
Hilbert space). *The DvN-1 axiom (states are unit vectors in
$\mathcal{H}$, with $\mathcal{H}$ a complex separable Hilbert space) is
a corollary of
Theorem [9.17](#thm:hilbert-complete){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complete"} together with the unit-norm
convention. The complete separable complex Hilbert-space structure
$\mathcal{H}\cong L^2(M_{1,3}, d\mu_M)$ is forced by the chain of theorems, with
the unit-norm convention $\langle\psi|\psi\rangle = 1$ a
probability-conservation normalisation following from the Born rule
(Corollary [9.29](#cor:sibling-cogeneration){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor:sibling-cogeneration"}). DvN-1 is therefore not
foundational; it is downstream of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ through the
four-level chain of theorems. ◻*
:::

::: proof
*Proof of Corollary [9.37](#cor:DvN-1){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor:DvN-1"}.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). By
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"},
$\mathcal{H} \cong L^2(M_{1,3}, d\mu_M)$ is the Cauchy completion
of the pre-Hilbert space of complex-valued square-integrable
amplitudes over the McGucken-derived Lorentzian spacetime. The
McGucken wavefunction $\psi$ is a point in this space.

*Normalization.* The Born probability density
(Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"}) is $P = |\psi|^2$, and the
requirement that total probability sum to unity gives
$\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} |\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)|^2 d^3 x = 1$,
the statement that $\psi$ is a *unit* vector in $\mathcal{H}$ with
respect to the McGucken-derived inner product.

*Phase invariance.* By requirement (R3) in the Born derivation
(Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"} Step 3), the Born density is
invariant under global phase $\psi \to e^{i\alpha}\psi$ for all
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Geometrically, this is the universality
of $x_4$-expansion from every event: a homogeneous shift of the
$x_4$-origin is unobservable. Two unit vectors differing by an
overall phase therefore represent the same physical state. The set
of physical states is the projective Hilbert space
$\mathbb{P}\mathcal{H} = (\mathcal{H} \setminus \{0\})/\sim$
where $\psi \sim e^{i\alpha}\psi$ for any
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ — i.e., the set of *rays* in $\mathcal{H}$.

*Density operators.* For statistical mixtures, the natural extension
is to convex combinations of pure-state projectors:
$\rho = \sum_i p_i |\psi_i\rangle\langle\psi_i|$ with
$p_i \ge 0$ and $\sum_i p_i = 1$. This forces
$\operatorname{tr}(\rho) = 1$, $\rho \ge 0$, and
$\rho = \rho^\dagger$ as automatic consequences of the
convex-combination structure on the derived $\mathcal{H}$.

*Separability.* The McGucken-derived $\mathcal{H}$ is
$L^2(M_{1,3}, d\mu_M)$, separable because $M_{1,3}$ as a constraint
surface in $E_4$ carries a $\sigma$-finite measure $\Sigma_M$
inherited from Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the
proper-time measure. $L^2$ spaces of separable measure spaces are
separable Hilbert spaces by the Riesz--Fischer theorem and the
existence of countable dense subsets in $L^2$. ◻
:::

::: {#cor:DvN-2 .corollary}
**Corollary 9.38** (DvN-2: observables as self-adjoint operators). *The
DvN-2 axiom (observables are self-adjoint operators on $\mathcal{H}$) is
a corollary of the $x_4$-flux conservation theorem of
[@MG-Cogeneration-2026] (Theorem 9.2) together with Stone's theorem. The
$x_4$-flux conservation gives the unitarity of the one-parameter
time-translation group; Stone's theorem identifies the self-adjoint
generators of the unitary group with the observables; the spectral
theorem on self-adjoint operators gives the eigenvalue-eigenspace
structure that supplies measurement outcomes. DvN-2 is therefore not
foundational; it is the operator-theoretic content of the principle's
unitary $x_4$-flow. ◻*
:::

::: proof
*Proof of Corollary [9.38](#cor:DvN-2){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor:DvN-2"}.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). An observable $\hat{A}$ on $\mathcal{H}$
represents a measurable physical quantity. Two requirements force
self-adjointness.

*Real-valued spectrum.* Physical measurements yield real numbers.
The expectation value
$\langle\hat{A}\rangle = \langle\psi|\hat{A}|\psi\rangle$
must be real for every $\psi \in \mathcal{H}$. The standard
linear-algebraic fact is that
$\langle\psi|\hat{A}|\psi\rangle \in \mathbb{R}$ for all
$\psi$ if and only if $\hat{A}$ is self-adjoint:
$\hat{A} = \hat{A}^\dagger$. The spectral theorem on a complex
separable Hilbert space then guarantees that the spectrum of a
self-adjoint $\hat{A}$ is a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, and $\hat{A}$
admits a spectral decomposition
$\hat{A} = \int \lambda\, dP_\lambda$. The points in its
spectrum are the possible measurement outcomes.

*Generation of unitary evolution.* By
Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT7"}, time evolution on the McGucken-derived
$\mathcal{H}$ preserves the Born inner product — equivalently, it
preserves the $x_4$-flux
$\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} |\psi|^2 d^3 x$. Stone's theorem on
one-parameter unitary groups then forces the generator of the
evolution to be self-adjoint: if $U(t) = e^{-i\hat{A}t/\hbar}$ is
unitary for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$, then $\hat{A}$ is
self-adjoint. Hence the Hamiltonian $\hat{H}$ and, by extension,
all observables that generate one-parameter unitary subgroups of
the symmetry group of $\mathcal{H}$ are self-adjoint.

The conjunction of the two arguments — real-valued spectra from
measurement, self-adjoint generators from unitarity — fixes the
observable status as self-adjoint operators on the derived
$\mathcal{H}$. ◻
:::

::: {#cor:DvN-3 .corollary}
**Corollary 9.39** (DvN-3: the Born rule). *The DvN-3 axiom (measurement
of observable $\hat{A}$ in eigenstate $\lvert a \rangle$ yields outcome
$a$ with probability $|\langle a|\psi\rangle|^2$) is a corollary of the
Born-rule theorem (§[11](#ch:born){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:born"},
Theorem [10.24](#thm:SG-Born-rule){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:SG-Born-rule"} on the spin-$1/2$ case;
[@MG-Cogeneration-2026] Theorem 7.2 on the general case). The Born rule
is generated from the rank-2 sesquilinear pairing on the diagonal
(Corollary [9.29](#cor:sibling-cogeneration){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor:sibling-cogeneration"}); the diagonal restriction
supplies the squared-magnitude probability density. DvN-3 is therefore
not a postulate but the theorem for the
probabilistic interpretation. ◻*
:::

::: proof
*Proof of Corollary [9.39](#cor:DvN-3){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor:DvN-3"}.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). By
Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"}, the unique probability density on
the McGucken-derived Hilbert space satisfying reality (R1),
non-negativity (R2), phase invariance (R3), and bilinearity in
$(\psi, \psi^*)$ (R4) is $P = |\psi|^2$. The position-basis
statement is $\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} |\psi(\mathbf{x})|^2 d^3 x = 1$
over the spatial slice.

For an arbitrary observable $\hat{A}$ with eigenbasis
$\{|a_n\rangle\}$, expand $\psi$ in this basis:
$$|\psi\rangle = \sum_n c_n |a_n\rangle, \quad c_n = \langle a_n|\psi\rangle.$$
The probability of the system being found in the $a_n$-eigenstate
is the squared modulus of $c_n$ by the same uniqueness argument as
Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"} applied in the $|a_n\rangle$ basis
rather than the position basis. The Born requirements
(R1)--(R4) are basis-independent: reality, non-negativity, phase
invariance, and bilinearity in $(\psi, \psi^*)$ hold in any
orthonormal basis of the McGucken-derived $\mathcal{H}$. Hence the
unique density on the $|a_n\rangle$-coefficient $c_n$ is
$|c_n|^2$, giving
$$P(a_n) = |c_n|^2 = |\langle a_n|\psi\rangle|^2.$$
For density operators, the same argument applied to the convex
combination $\rho = \sum_i p_i |\psi_i\rangle\langle\psi_i|$
gives
$$P(a_n) = \sum_i p_i |\langle a_n|\psi_i\rangle|^2 = \langle a_n|\rho|a_n\rangle = \operatorname{tr}(P_n \rho).$$
The Born rule in arbitrary-observable form is therefore
Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"} re-expressed in eigenvector-basis
language by basis-independence of the (R1)--(R4) Born requirements;
the rank-2 sesquilinear pairing inherited from
$(ict)^2 = -c^2 t^2$
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}) supplies the bilinearity; the Haar
measure on the McGucken Sphere supplies the squared-modulus density
structure. No new derivational content. ◻
:::

::: {#cor:DvN-4 .corollary}
**Corollary 9.40** (DvN-4: projection (collapse) on measurement). *The
DvN-4 axiom (upon measurement of $\hat{A}$ yielding outcome $a$, the
state projects to $\lvert a \rangle\langle a \rvert\psi/\|\ldots\|$) is
a corollary of the geometric incidence theorem for forward and conjugate
$x_4$-expansions at the apparatus
(§[10.6](#sec:apparent-collapse){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:apparent-collapse"}, Proposition V.1;
[@MG-Cogeneration-2026] Theorem 7.4). The four-dimensional McGucken
Sphere's intersection with the three-dimensional apparatus slice
produces the apparent projection; the projection is the geometric
three-dimensional reading of the four-dimensional content
(Remark [10.33](#rmk:SG-4D-3D){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:SG-4D-3D"} of the Stern--Gerlach section). DvN-4 is
therefore not foundational; the "collapse" is the geometric registration
content of the principle at the apparatus event. ◻*
:::

::: proof
*Proof of Corollary [9.40](#cor:DvN-4){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor:DvN-4"}.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). By
Lemma [9.14](#lem:born-as-x4-overlap){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:born-as-x4-overlap"} (Born density as Sphere
overlap), measurement in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework is the geometric
incidence of the forward $x_4$-expansion of $\psi$ (carrying phase
from $x_4 = ict$) and the conjugate $x_4$-expansion (carrying phase
from $x_4^* = -ict$) at a localized absorber — the apparatus,
which exists at a definite $x_4$-coordinate by prior decoherence.
The probability of detection is the overlap $\psi^* \psi$ at the
apparatus's localized position.

The collapse postulate is the geometric statement that *after* the
meeting of the two expansions at a specific event $B$, the system
is localized at the eigenvalue of $\hat{A}$ corresponding to $B$'s
eigenspace. This is the geometric fact that the meeting of forward
and conjugate expansions happens at *one event*, not at all events
simultaneously. The forward expansion that meets the apparatus is
the component of the superposition whose eigenvalue matches the
apparatus's measurement basis; the other components do not meet
the apparatus at this event.

Formally: write
$|\psi\rangle = \sum_n c_n |a_n\rangle$. The post-measurement
state, conditioned on outcome $a_n$, is the component
$|a_n\rangle$ of $\psi$ that geometrically overlapped with the
apparatus at the detection event. Re-normalizing, the conditional
state is
$$|\psi'\rangle = \frac{P_n |\psi\rangle}{\|P_n |\psi\rangle\|} = \frac{c_n |a_n\rangle}{|c_n|} = e^{i \arg c_n} |a_n\rangle,$$
which represents the same ray as $|a_n\rangle$ up to phase
(Corollary [9.37](#cor:DvN-1){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor:DvN-1"}). Hence the post-measurement state *is*
$|a_n\rangle$ as a physical state.

The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework's geometric reading supplies the *mechanism*
(two-expansion incidence) for what standard QM leaves as a brute
postulate (collapse). It is not a hidden-variable theory:
single-outcome probabilities remain governed by the Born rule
(Corollary [9.39](#cor:DvN-3){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor:DvN-3"}), but the *conditional state* after
measurement is the geometric statement that the meeting of forward
and conjugate expansions happens at one specific event with one
specific eigenvalue. There is no "collapse dynamics" because there
is no second dynamical law — only the geometric fact of where the
two expansions overlap. ◻
:::

::: {#cor:DvN-5 .corollary}
**Corollary 9.41** (DvN-5: unitary Schrödinger evolution). *The DvN-5
axiom (unobserved evolution is unitary by
$i\hbar\partial_t\lvert \psi \rangle = \hat{H}\lvert \psi \rangle$) is a
corollary of the Schrödinger-equation derivation in
[@MG-Cogeneration-2026] (Theorems 9.1, 9.2): the equation is the unique
first-order linear evolution along $x_4$ generated by the McGucken
source operator, with the $i\hbar$ on the left encoding the
perpendicularity-and-action-quantization structure of $x_4$-advance
(Theorem [9.35](#thm:c-hbar-twin){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:c-hbar-twin"} above). DvN-5 is therefore not
foundational; it is the temporal-evolution content of the principle's
unitary $x_4$-flow. ◻*
:::

::: proof
*Proof of Corollary [9.41](#cor:DvN-5){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor:DvN-5"}.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). By
Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT7"} the Schrödinger equation
$i\hbar\,\partial_t \psi = \hat{H}\psi$ is the unique
first-order linear evolution along $x_4$ generated by the McGucken
source operator on the derived Hilbert space, with both factors of
$i\hbar$ on the left descending from the McGucken Principle's twin
constants ($i$ from perpendicularity of $x_4$, $\hbar$ from
action quantization of $x_4$-advance). The unitarity-conservation
content of
Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT7"} (the unitary evolution preserves the inner
product) gives the unitarity of the evolution operator.

The evolution operator solving
$i\hbar\,\partial_t \psi = \hat{H}\psi$ with initial condition
$\psi(0)$ is $\psi(t) = U(t)\psi(0)$ where
$$U(t) = \exp(-i\hat{H}t/\hbar).$$
By inner-product preservation,
$\langle U(t)\psi | U(t)\varphi \rangle = \langle\psi|\varphi\rangle$
for all $\psi, \varphi \in \mathcal{H}$ and all
$t \in \mathbb{R}$. An inner-product-preserving bijection of a
Hilbert space is unitary by definition; equivalently,
$U^\dagger U = U U^\dagger = I$. By Stone's theorem, every
one-parameter unitary group $U(t)$ on a complex Hilbert space is of
the form $U(t) = e^{-i\hat{A}t/\hbar}$ for a unique self-adjoint
generator $\hat{A}$, and conversely every self-adjoint $\hat{A}$
generates such a group. Taking $\hat{A} = \hat{H}$ recovers the
standard Schrödinger dynamics. ◻
:::

::: {#cor:DvN-6 .corollary}
**Corollary 9.42** (DvN-6: composite-system tensor product). *The DvN-6
axiom (composite system of two subsystems $A$ and $B$ has Hilbert space
$\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B$) is a corollary of
Theorem [9.17](#thm:hilbert-complete){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-complete"} applied to product measure spaces,
together with the Fubini--Tonelli theorem for the integration of the
product inner product. The universality of $x_4$-expansion from
independent events (the principle holds at every event of
$\mathcal{M}_G$, and two independent source events $p_A, p_B$ generate
two independent McGucken Spheres $\Sigma_M(p_A, t), \Sigma_M(p_B, t)$
whose product is the joint Sphere
$\Sigma_M(p_A, t) \otimes \Sigma_M(p_B, t)$ on the joint manifold
$\mathcal{M}_G \times \mathcal{M}_G$) supplies the tensor-product
structure at the level of joint amplitudes; the $L^2$ completion on the
product measure gives the tensor-product Hilbert space at the level of
the joint inner product. DvN-6 is therefore not foundational; it is the
joint-event content of the principle's pointwise $x_4$-flow. ◻*
:::

::: proof
*Proof of Corollary [9.42](#cor:DvN-6){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor:DvN-6"}.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). By
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}, each subsystem's Hilbert space
is the $L^2$ completion of complex amplitudes over its constraint
surface:
$\mathcal{H}_A = L^2(M_{1,3}^{(A)}, d\mu_M^{(A)})$,
$\mathcal{H}_B = L^2(M_{1,3}^{(B)}, d\mu_M^{(B)})$. The constraint
surface of the composite system is the Cartesian product
$M_{1,3}^{(A)} \times M_{1,3}^{(B)}$ — each subsystem carrying its
own copy of $x_4$-expansion from its own events. The natural
measure on the product is the product measure
$d\mu_M^{(A)} \otimes d\mu_M^{(B)}$.

The Fubini--Tonelli theorem then gives
$$L^2(M_{1,3}^{(A)} \times M_{1,3}^{(B)}, d\mu_M^{(A)} \otimes d\mu_M^{(B)}) \cong L^2(M_{1,3}^{(A)}, d\mu_M^{(A)}) \otimes L^2(M_{1,3}^{(B)}, d\mu_M^{(B)}) = \mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B.$$
The tensor-product structure is therefore an immediate corollary of
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"} applied to product measure
spaces. The Fubini--Tonelli theorem is standard real analysis; the
only physical input is that two independent subsystems carry two
independent constraint surfaces, which is the statement that
$x_4$-expansion from event $E_A$ is independent of $x_4$-expansion
from event $E_B$ — the universality clause of
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$ applied to two events. ◻
:::

#### The architectural inversion {#ssec:architectural-inversion}

::: {#thm:architectural-inversion .theorem}
**Theorem 9.43** (The architectural inversion: from postulated Hilbert
space to derived Hilbert space). *The chain of theorems of
Definition [9.22](#def:cogenerative-chain){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:cogenerative-chain"} accomplishes an architectural
inversion of the Dirac--von Neumann foundation of quantum mechanics.
Where the Dirac--von Neumann tradition treated $\mathcal{H}$ as the
primitive and derived everything else as theorems on
$\mathcal{H}$, the chain of theorems treats $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
as the primitive and derives $\mathcal{H}$ together with
the Born rule, the canonical commutator, the Heisenberg uncertainty, the
Schrödinger equation, and the Dirac--von Neumann axioms DvN-1 through DvN-6 as chain of theorems
outputs. The inversion has three significant features.*

***(i) The arena is derived.** The complex separable Hilbert space
$\mathcal{H}$ of standard quantum mechanics is the level-4 output of the
chain of theorems
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic \to \mathcal{M}_G \to M_{1,3} \to \mathcal{V} \to \mathcal{H}$.
Eleven prior derivation programmes catalogued in [@MG-Cogeneration-2026]
(von Neumann 1932, Dirac 1930, Mackey 1963, Piron--Solèr 1964/1995,
Jordan--von Neumann--Wigner 1934, Hardy 2001,
Chiribella--D'Ariano--Perinotti 2010s, Abramsky--Coecke, Stueckelberg
1960, Adler 1995/2004, Renou et al. 2021) postulated $\mathcal{H}$ as
the primitive; the chain of theorems is the first
programme to derive $\mathcal{H}$ from a physical principle.*

***(ii) Both constants are derived.** The two fundamental
constants $c$ and $\hbar$ of quantum mechanics are twin properties of the single geometric flow
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.35](#thm:c-hbar-twin){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:c-hbar-twin"}). The principle is a two-constant statement
about a single flow, not two independent constants supplied externally.*

***(iii) The textbook axioms are corollaries.** The DvN-1--DvN-6
Dirac--von Neumann axioms are corollaries of upstream theorems in the chain of theorems
(Corollaries [9.37](#cor:DvN-1){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor:DvN-1"}--[9.42](#cor:DvN-6){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor:DvN-6"}). The orthodox foundation of quantum mechanics is
itself the output of the McGucken chain of theorems.*

*The combined architectural inversion: where standard quantum mechanics
has six postulates (DvN-1 through DvN-6) plus two empirical
constants ($c$, $\hbar$) plus one arena ($\mathcal{H}$),
the chain of theorems has one principle
($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$), with all six postulates, both constants, and
the arena being downstream theorems.*
:::

::: {#rmk:why-DvN-works .remark}
*Remark 9.44* (The joint reading and the question of why the
Dirac--von Neumann axioms "work"). A natural question raised by the
architectural inversion of
Theorem [9.43](#thm:architectural-inversion){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:architectural-inversion"} is: why did the Dirac--von
Neumann axioms, treated as postulates rather than
corollaries, produce a theory that agrees with experiment to
extraordinary precision? The joint reading supplies the
answer: the Dirac--von Neumann axioms are the theorems
of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, so they agree with experiment for the same
reason the theorems agree with experiment --- because the
principle from which they descend is the correct physical principle of
the foundational level. The Dirac--von Neumann tradition succeeded
empirically because it correctly catalogued the theorems (even
without recognising them as outputs); it failed because it
treated the outputs as foundational rather than as downstream
consequences. The joint reading does not invalidate the
Dirac--von Neumann tradition; it explains why the tradition succeeded
and supplies the deeper principle that the tradition did
not identify.

::: {#rmk:why-no-prior-cogen .remark}
*Remark 9.45* (Why no prior programme could accomplish this). The
joint derivation paper [@MG-Cogeneration-2026] (§12) catalogues seven
reasons that no prior programme in the foundations of quantum
mechanics could have accomplished the chain of theorems derivation:
(i) the block universe took the dynamics out of $x_4$, fixing the fourth
dimension as a static spatial-like axis and eliminating the possibility
of an $x_4$-flow at the velocity of light; (ii) the factor of $i$ was
treated as a formal mathematical convenience rather than a geometric
perpendicularity marker, so the connection between $i$ and $x_4$ was not
visible; (iii) quantum mechanics and relativity were treated as separate
theories with separate structures, so the principle that
generates both was not sought; (iv) the interpretation industry kept
everyone inside Hilbert space, treating the Hilbert space as the arena
within which interpretive choices are made rather than as a downstream
object to be derived; (v) the path required Wheeler's question ("Why the
quantum?"), and the question was rarely posed as a question about
deriving the quantum from a deeper principle; (vi) the simplicity was
the giveaway --- the principle is so simple
($dx_4/dt = ic$) that the foundational tradition, conditioned to expect
complex axiom systems at the foundational level, did not look for a
single principle of this form; (vii) the non-Markovian alternative (the
Barandes stochastic-quantum correspondence) did not see that
Markovianity holds on the right manifold ($\mathcal{M}_G$, the moving
four-manifold) rather than on the standard four-dimensional Lorentzian
spacetime, so it did not recognise that the apparent non-Markovianity of
standard quantum mechanics dissolves under the principle's pointwise
constitutive content. The seven reasons combine to explain why the
chain of theorems was not derived before the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework: the
foundational tradition was blocked from seeing the
principle.
:::

### The robustness of empirically-anchored derivation chains {#sec:robustness}

The chain of theorems developed in the preceding sections has a
property that distinguishes it from purely mathematical
derivations and that warrants explicit articulation. The derivation
chains are both deductively connected and empirically anchored at every
essential theorem. This dual character is the source of
the framework's robustness, and it warrants a section of its own because
the criterion of robustness it embodies is the criterion by which the
great results of physics and mathematics have been judged
for two and a half millennia.

#### Mathematical proofs versus mathematical-physics proofs

A purely mathematical proof is a deductive sequence: axiom $\to$ lemma
$\to \cdots \to$ theorem. Each step depends on the previous steps for
its truth. If a step fails, every downstream consequence fails along
with it. Wiles' proof of Fermat's Last Theorem either holds or it does
not; a gap at any step collapses the proof until repaired.

A mathematical-physics proof is different. The theorems it
produces are not only deductive consequences of axioms --- they are also
statements about empirically observed features of the physical world
that exist independent of any particular derivation. The Lorentzian
metric of Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} is both a deductive consequence of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and the empirically validated metric of
special relativity, confirmed by every accelerator experiment, every GPS
timing correction, every Michelson--Morley-class test since 1905. The
Hilbert space of
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"} (the result of the four-step chain of theorems
$\mathcal{M}_G \to M_{1,3} \to \mathcal{V} \to \mathcal{H}$) is a
deductive output of the chain of theorems and the empirically
validated arena where every quantum experiment since 1925 has been
correctly described. The Born rule of
Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"} is both a unique consequence of (R1)--(R4) and the empirically confirmed measurement statistic of every quantum experiment performed in the past century, with relative
precision better than $10^{-9}$ in the cleanest atomic-clock tests. The
canonical commutation relation of
Theorem [10.1](#thm:QMT10){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT10"}
is what every laboratory implementation of position and momentum
measurement obeys. The uncertainty principle of
Theorem [12.1](#thm:QMT12){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT12"}
is the bound saturated by every Gaussian state ever prepared. The
Schrödinger equation of Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT7"} is the dynamics that fits hydrogen spectra,
harmonic-oscillator level spacings, tunnelling rates, and every other
non-relativistic quantum observation.

Each theorem in the chain is therefore subject to two independent
constraints. It must follow deductively from its proof. It must also
match the empirical fact it asserts. A mathematical-physics derivation
succeeds only when both constraints are satisfied --- the deductive
chain holds, and the theorems it produces are the theorems the universe
actually exhibits.

#### The chains as structures with redundant load paths

The chain of theorems combines this empirical anchoring with a second
property: every essential conclusion has multiple
derivationally disjoint derivation routes from the upstream principle.
This is the dual-channel architecture established throughout Part II of
the present textbook and developed in detail in the companion paper
[@MG-QM-2026], with the Convergent Overdetermination Lemma of
[@MG-Cogeneration-2026] establishing that the canonical commutator
$[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ is derivable through two disjoint intermediate routes --- the Hamiltonian route (Algebraic Channel:
Noether on $x_4$-translation invariance $\to$ Stone's theorem $\to$
Stone--von Neumann uniqueness) and the Lagrangian route (Geometric Channel:
Huygens-wavefront propagation $\to$ path summation $\to$
action-quantization phase derivative). Geometric Channel and Algebraic Channel share no
intermediate machinery between the principle and the conclusion. The
same dual-channel structure applies to the Born rule (Algebraic Channel: rank-2
sesquilinear pairing from the Minkowski metric,
Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"}; Geometric Channel: geometric overlap of forward
and conjugate $x_4$-expansions at the apparatus event,
Lemma [9.14](#lem:born-as-x4-overlap){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:born-as-x4-overlap"}) and to the Hilbert space (the
$L^2$-completion of $x_4$-projections,
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}, has both an
inner-product-completion realisation and a path-integral-overlap
realisation).

The metaphor of a chain --- one thread, one weakest link --- does not
fit. The metaphor of a cable --- many threads, fails when all threads
cut --- fits better but still understates the structure. The accurate
metaphor is a structure with redundant load paths and verified ground
anchors at every joint: a truss in which every joint is independently
bolted to bedrock, and in which the load between joints can redistribute
through multiple struts. Cutting individual struts does not collapse the
structure because the load redistributes; verifying each joint can be
done independently of the others because each joint has its own ground
anchor.

#### The robustness property

Three properties combine to produce the robustness of the
framework.

**(i) Empirical anchoring at every theorem.** Each essential theorem
of the
chain of theorems --- Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} (Lorentzian metric),
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"} (Hilbert space),
Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"} (Born rule),
Theorem [10.1](#thm:QMT10){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT10"}
(canonical commutator), Theorem [12.1](#thm:QMT12){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT12"} (uncertainty principle),
Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT7"}
(Schrödinger equation) --- corresponds to an empirically established
feature of the physical world, validated independently of any derivation
by a century of experiments.

**(ii) Multiple disjoint derivation routes.** Every essential conclusion has at least two independent derivations from
the upstream principle, sharing no intermediate machinery (the Geometric Channel
/ Algebraic Channel architecture developed throughout Part II, with the
Convergent Overdetermination Lemma of [@MG-Cogeneration-2026] making the
disjointness explicit).

**(iii) Multi-domain support for the upstream principle.** The McGucken
Principle $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is anchored by the QM derivations of
the present textbook and by independent derivations across the McGucken
corpus: the general-relativity derivation showing that
$(ict)^2 = -c^2 t^2$ gives the Lorentzian signature, that
$x_4$-curvature in the presence of stress-energy gives Einstein's field
equations, and that the Schwarzschild solution,
Friedmann--Lemaître--Robertson--Walker cosmology, and the Hawking $1/4$
factor for black-hole entropy all descend from the principle
(Chapter [[ch:mcgucken-GR]](#ch:mcgucken-GR){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:mcgucken-GR"});
the thermodynamics derivation showing that the twenty-three theorems of
classical thermodynamics --- Carnot, Kelvin, Clausius, the Second Law
itself --- descend from $x_4$-expansion structure; and the QM
derivations of Part II. The principle has empirical anchoring through every domain it generates.

Combined, these three properties produce a derivation structure that
fails in a fundamentally different way than a single-thread mathematical
proof. A break at any one node --- a gap in the deductive content of any
one theorem --- has bounded consequences:

-   The empirical fact at that node does not disappear from physics. The
    fact is independently established by observation; the derivation
    explains why the observed fact is what we see, but the fact's
    existence does not depend on the explanation's correctness.

-   The other nodes of the chain of theorems do not lose their derivability. The
    break is local. The bilinearity argument of
    Lemma [9.13](#lem:bilinearity-rank2){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:bilinearity-rank2"} can be repaired without
    rebuilding Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} or
    Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}, because the
    Lorentzian-signature lemma holds independently and the Hilbert-space
    theorem has its own derivation route from the joint derivation
    architecture.

-   The conclusion at the broken node can still be reached through the
    parallel channel. If Algebraic Channel's route to the canonical commutator
    developed a gap, Geometric Channel's path-integral route is still intact.
    The conclusion is overdetermined.

-   The upstream principle $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is not destabilised.
    It is supported by GR and thermodynamics independently of the
    specific QM theorem whose derivation has a local issue.

In a purely mathematical chain, a single break is fatal. In an
empirically-anchored chain with redundant load paths, a single break is
local and repairable, with the surrounding structure remaining standing
while repair occurs.

#### Stated for the record

The chain of theorems has been audited multiple times across the
development of the present textbook and the companion derivation papers.
No essential theorem has exhibited a gap. The chain holds at every
step. The empirical anchoring at every node, the dual-channel
architecture supplying parallel derivation routes, and the multi-domain
support for $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ combine to give a derivation
structure that is --- by the criterion that mature physical theories are
robust to local errors while remaining empirically faithful --- what a
result should look like.

What hostile scrutiny can do is identify whether a specific theorem
fails to be derivable from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at all --- whether
all the parallel routes to that theorem simultaneously fail. That is a
meaningful question. What hostile scrutiny cannot do is destroy the
framework by finding a single deductive gap, because the framework's
empirical content is anchored independently and the width of
the chains absorbs local breaks. This is the property that
mature physical theories share --- Newtonian mechanics, Maxwell's
electrodynamics, special and general relativity, the Standard Model.
Each of these theories has been refined, corrected, and rederived in
many ways without losing its empirical content, because each is multiply
anchored to observation rather than dependent on a single deductive
thread. The chain of theorems developed here exhibits the same
property at the derivation level.

### The heritage of simple foundational principles: Euclid, Newton, Hilbert, Einstein, Dirac, Wheeler {#sec:heritage-simple-principles}

The chain of theorems exhibited in the preceding sections derives the
full edifice of non-relativistic quantum mechanics --- the Hilbert
space, the canonical commutator, the Born rule, the uncertainty
principle, the Schrödinger equation, the Dirac--von Neumann axioms DvN-1 through DvN-6
as corollaries --- from a single physical principle,
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The form of the derivation --- one principle,
deductive chain of theorems, theorems agreeing with experiment, no superfluous
postulates --- is the form that the great results of
physics and mathematics have taken since antiquity. This section places
the chain of theorems in the lineage of programmes that
share its form, from Euclid in the third century BCE to
Wheeler in the late twentieth century, and articulates the spirit of the
fathers of science, physics, and philosophy that the framework
consciously serves.

#### Euclid (c. 300 BCE): the founding gesture of axiomatic deduction

Euclid's *Elements* established the founding gesture of all subsequent
mathematical and physical deduction: a small number of simple,
self-evident principles, set down at the start, from which the entire
structure of an empirically observed domain is deductively derived. The
*Elements* opens with twenty-three Definitions (the simplest being
Definition I.1, "A point is that which has no part"), five Postulates
(P1: a straight line can be drawn from any point to any other; P2: a
straight line can be extended indefinitely; P3: a circle can be
described with any centre and radius; P4: all right angles are equal;
P5: the parallel postulate), and five Common Notions (CN1: things equal
to the same thing are equal; CN2: equals added to equals give equals;
CN3: equals subtracted from equals give equals; CN4: things that
