coincide are equal; CN5: the whole is greater than the part). From this
list of thirty-three statements, Euclid derived 465 propositions across
thirteen books, covering plane geometry, solid geometry, number theory,
and what we would today call the foundations of irrational quantities.

The form is exact: small input, exhaustive output, with each
output statement traceable through a finite chain of deductive steps to
the input. The empirical anchoring is exact: every theorem
of Euclidean plane geometry is an empirically validated fact of
ruler-and-compass construction in Euclidean physical space (within the
regime of small curvatures where Euclidean geometry is empirically
accurate). The chain of theorems of the present textbook serves the
same form: one principle ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$), exhaustive output
(the structure of quantum mechanics together with that of special
relativity and the foundations of thermodynamics), with each chain of theorems
output empirically validated independently.

#### Newton (1687, 1726): the regulae philosophandi and the simplicity of Nature

Newton's *Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica*, in its third
edition of 1726, opens Book III with the *Regulae Philosophandi* --- the
Rules of Reasoning in Natural Philosophy --- which formalise the
methodological criteria by which a physical principle ought
to be judged. Newton's Rule I reads, in his Latin: *"Causas rerum
naturalium non plures admitti debere, quàm quæ & veræ sint & earum
phænomenis explicandis sufficiant. Dicunt utique philosophi: Natura
nihil agit frustra, & frustra sit per plura quod fieri potest per
pauciora. Natura enim simplex est & rerum causis superfluis non
luxuriat."* ("No more causes of natural things should be admitted than
are both true and sufficient to explain their phenomena. Philosophers
say: Nature does nothing in vain, and more is in vain when less will
serve. For Nature is simple, and does not luxuriate in superfluous
causes.")

Three essential principles of methodology in one paragraph: (a) only
true and sufficient causes are to be admitted, (b) parsimony is
constitutive of natural philosophy (less is to be preferred to more
where both suffice), and (c) the simplicity of Nature itself is the
metaphysical ground of the methodological preference for simplicity.
Newton's Rule II adds that the same effects are to be assigned the same
causes *quatenus fieri potest* (insofar as is possible), enforcing
universality: respiration in humans and animals, descent of stones in
Europe and America, light of fire and light of the sun, reflection of
light on the Earth and on the planets. Rule III enforces inductive
universality of qualities, and Rule IV the provisional acceptance of
inductive conclusions until refined or refuted.

The chain of theorems serves Newton's Rules directly. (a) Only one
principle --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ --- is admitted, the minimum
possible. (b) That principle is both true (empirically validated through
every domain it generates) and sufficient (the entire structure of QM,
GR, and the foundations of thermodynamics descend from it). (c) The
simplicity of the principle is the source of its derivational
power --- a complex axiom system at the foundational level would not
have admitted the chain of theorems structure, because the redundant
load paths and dual-channel disjointness require a principle whose content is geometric and singular rather than algebraic
and compound. Newton's metaphysical commitment that *Natura enim simplex
est* --- Nature is simple --- is the metaphysical commitment that the
chain of theorems embodies.

#### Hilbert (1899, 1900, 1918): the axiomatic method and the deepening of the foundations

David Hilbert's *Grundlagen der Geometrie* (1899) reconstructed Euclid's
geometric foundation with the standards of nineteenth-century
mathematical rigour, identifying twenty axioms in five groups
(incidence, order, congruence, parallels, continuity) and analysing
their independence, consistency, and completeness. Hilbert's
programmatic 1918 address *Axiomatisches Denken* ("Axiomatic Thinking")
articulated the methodology that the *Grundlagen* embodied: "By pushing
ahead to ever deeper layers of axioms in the sense explained above, we
also win ever-deeper insights into the essence of scientific thought
itself, and we become ever more conscious of the unity of our knowledge.
In the sign of the axiomatic method, mathematics is summoned to a
leading role in science."

Hilbert's procedure had three essential features. (a) The
foundational primitives are identified and stated explicitly, with no
covert assumptions. (b) The derivational chain from primitives to
theorems is made fully formal. (c) The foundational primitives are
themselves analysed for independence, consistency, and (where possible)
completeness, with the methodological goal of "deepening the
foundations" --- replacing a working axiom system with a deeper system
from which the working system descends as a theorem.

Hilbert's Sixth Problem (Paris, 1900) explicitly extended this programme
to physics: "the axiomatic treatment of those physical sciences in which
mathematics plays an important part, in the first rank of which are the
theory of probabilities and mechanics." The Sixth Problem stood open as
the foundational call to physicists for over a century. The joint
chain of theorems is the present textbook's response to Hilbert's Sixth Problem at
the quantum-mechanical tier: one physical principle
($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$), with the Dirac--von Neumann axioms DvN-1 through DvN-6
derived as corollaries (Corollaries 11.1--11.6 of the companion paper
[@MG-Cogeneration-2026] and the corresponding theorems of the present
textbook), and the arena $\mathcal{H}$ itself appearing as
a downstream theorem rather than as an input axiom. Hilbert's
procedure of "deepening the foundations" --- replacing a working axiom
system (the Dirac--von Neumann postulates) with a deeper system (the
McGucken Principle) from which the working system descends --- is what
the chain of theorems performs at the quantum-mechanical foundation.

#### Einstein (1933): simplicity as the supreme goal of theory

Albert Einstein's Herbert Spencer Lecture at Oxford on 10 June 1933, *On
the Method of Theoretical Physics*, contains the line that Einstein's
later *Reader's Digest*-era paraphrase ("everything should be made as
simple as possible, but not simpler") compresses: "It can scarcely be
denied that the supreme goal of all theory is to make the irreducible
basic elements as simple and as few as possible without having to
surrender the adequate representation of a single datum of experience."

Three essential criteria: (a) the supreme goal of theory is
simplicity, (b) the criterion is the minimisation of the
irreducible basic elements both in their internal complexity (*as simple
as possible*) and in their number (*as few as possible*), (c) the
constraint is that no datum of experience is surrendered --- empirical
adequacy is non-negotiable. The chain of theorems satisfies
Einstein's criteria exactly. The irreducible basic element is one
principle, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, internally as simple as a
first-order ordinary differential equation can be, and numerically
minimal (one principle, not five, not twenty, not the DvN-1--DvN-6
postulate list of Dirac--von Neumann quantum mechanics). The
empirical-adequacy constraint is met because every theorem
corresponds to an empirically validated feature of the physical world.

Einstein's metaphysical commitment, expressed across many sources (*God
always takes the simplest way*; *Out of clutter, find simplicity*; the
*Subtle is the Lord* epigraph of Abraham Pais's biography), is the
commitment that the chain of theorems embodies. The
simplicity is the form that a successful foundational theory
must take.

#### Dirac (1956, 1963): mathematical beauty as the mark of a fundamental theory

In 1956 at Moscow University, Paul Dirac was invited to write on the
blackboard a sentence summarising his philosophy of physics. He wrote:
*"A physical law must possess mathematical beauty."* In his 1963
*Scientific American* essay *The Evolution of the Physicist's Picture of
Nature*, Dirac developed the principle: "It seems to be one of the
fundamental features of nature that fundamental physical laws are
described in terms of a mathematical theory of great beauty and power."

Dirac's criterion of mathematical beauty has three operationally
identifiable components in his own usage: (a) economy of input (a beautiful theory derives much from little), (b) derivational unity of derivation (the deductive chain has a single architectural form
rather than a patchwork of disjoint constructions), and (c)
inevitability of conclusion (the theorems follow from the principles in
a way that, upon understanding, makes any alternative seem forced or ad
hoc). The chain of theorems satisfies all three: one principle
(economy), one architectural form (the chain of theorems
$\mathcal{M}_G \to M_{1,3} \to \mathcal{V} \to \mathcal{H}$, with the
dual-channel structure as its operational signature), and the
inevitability of each theorem from the principle (the Lorentzian
signature follows from squaring the integrated principle; the complex
amplitudes follow from the perpendicularity of $x_4$; the Hilbert space
follows from $L^2$-completion of $x_4$-projections; the Born rule
follows from the rank-2 character of the Minkowski metric; the canonical
commutator follows from Stone's theorem applied to the principle's
translation invariance; the Schrödinger equation follows from the
principle's master equation $u^\mu u_\mu = -c^2$ together with canonical
quantisation).

Dirac's famous claim in the same 1963 essay --- "it is more important to
have beauty in one's equations than to have them fit experiment" --- is
the rhetorically strongest version of a methodological position that, in
practice, both Dirac and the present textbook treat as a dual
constraint: beauty and empirical fit together, not one against the
other. The chain of theorems respects the dual constraint: it is
beautiful (one principle, exhaustive output) and it fits experiment
(every theorem empirically validated independently).

#### Wheeler (1989--1998): the simple geometric principle and "It from Bit"

John Archibald Wheeler --- Princeton mentor of the present author,
collaborator of Bohr on the original 1939 paper on nuclear fission, of
Feynman on the absorber theory and on path integrals, of Misner and
Thorne on *Gravitation* --- explicitly programmed for the kind of
derivational structure that the chain of theorems exhibits. In his
1989 essay *Information, Physics, Quantum: The Search for Links*,
Wheeler articulated the "It from Bit" programme: "every it --- every
particle, every field of force, even the spacetime continuum
itself --- derives its function, its meaning, its very existence
entirely --- even if in some contexts indirectly --- from the
apparatus-elicited answers to yes-or-no questions, binary choices,
bits." The metaphysical commitment --- that the deepest layer of
physical reality is a simple structure from which the
apparent "things" of the world are derived --- is the metaphysical
commitment of the chain of theorems. The McGucken Principle replaces
"It from Bit" (the deepest layer is information) with "It from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$" (the deepest layer is the active expansion of
the fourth dimension at the velocity of light), but the form of the
programme is Wheeler's.

Wheeler's earlier *A Journey into Gravity and Spacetime* (1990) built
the entire structure of general relativity from a single simple
geometric principle --- "the boundary of a boundary is zero" --- a
methodological gesture exactly parallel to the chain of theorems's
derivation of quantum mechanics from a single simple physical principle.
Wheeler's career-long position, recorded in his interviews and in the
*Geons, Black Holes, and Quantum Foam* autobiography (with Kenneth Ford,
1998), was that the foundational layer of physics is simple, that the
apparent complexity of the world is a downstream consequence of the
simplicity, and that the task of foundational physics is to
identify the simple principle and derive the world from it.

Wheeler's question *"Why the quantum?"*, posed to the present author at
Princeton in 1986 and repeated in many subsequent settings, is the
question the chain of theorems answers. The answer: the quantum is
because $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The Hilbert space is the spatial-slice
projection of the principle; the Born rule is the rank-2 sesquilinear
pairing of forward and conjugate $x_4$-expansions; the canonical
commutator is the Stone-theorem reading of the principle's translation
invariance; the Schrödinger equation is the quantised master equation
$u^\mu u_\mu = -c^2$ of the principle's four-vector form. The quantum is
what the active expansion of the fourth dimension looks like to
apparatus on the spatial slice.

#### The unbroken chain

The chain from Euclid's twenty-three Definitions, five Postulates, and
five Common Notions to the chain of theorems's one principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is unbroken. Each link in the chain represents
a programme of the same form: small input, exhaustive deductive output, empirical anchoring of every output unity of the derivational architecture, and the metaphysical
commitment that the simplicity of the input is what reveals
the unity of the empirically observed world.

Newton: *Natura enim simplex est*. Nature is simple. The metaphysical
commitment of all foundational physics.

Hilbert: *by pushing ahead to ever deeper layers of axioms...we win
ever-deeper insights into the essence of scientific thought itself, and
we become ever more conscious of the unity of our knowledge.* The
methodological programme of deepening the foundations.

Einstein: *the supreme goal of all theory is to make the irreducible
basic elements as simple and as few as possible without having to
surrender the adequate representation of a single datum of experience.*
The dual constraint of simplicity and empirical adequacy.

Dirac: *a physical law must possess mathematical beauty.* The criterion
of unity, economy, and inevitability.

Wheeler: *We can and will understand.* The conviction that the
foundational layer of physics is simple, knowable, and accessible to
deduction.

The present textbook serves this lineage. The chain of theorems
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic \to \mathcal{M}_G \to M_{1,3} \to \mathcal{V} \to \mathcal{H}$,
with the dual-channel structure of the QM theorems and the empirical
anchoring at every essential node, is the chain of theorems that Euclid's
axiomatic method, Newton's *regulae philosophandi*, Hilbert's deepening
of the foundations, Einstein's supreme-goal criterion, Dirac's
mathematical beauty, and Wheeler's question all collectively point
toward. The fathers of science, physics, and philosophy set the form;
the chain of theorems is the form fulfilled at the quantum-mechanical
foundation.

### Close: $\mathcal{H}$ before and after McGucken

Before McGucken: $\mathcal{H}$ was an axiom of quantum mechanics,
postulated at the foundation of every textbook, with no derivation from
physical principles.

After McGucken: $\mathcal{H}$ is a theorem of the single physical
principle $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The four formal
features --- Lorentzian arena, complex amplitudes, inner product,
completeness --- are each forced by the principle's own algebraic and
geometric content, with no external mathematical postulate essential.

## The Measurement Problem Resolved {#ch:measurement-resolved}

> *The McGucken Principle.* The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality.
> Every result below descends from that expansion.


*Recall.* the McGucken Principle ($\mathrm{McP}$:
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$) asserts that the fourth spacetime dimension
$x_4$ expands at the velocity of light $c$, carrying the
perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguishes it from the spatial
three. Throughout this chapter, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ refers to this
principle and to the five-clause content (i)--(v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: (i) *invariance* --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content; (ii) *spherical symmetry* --- the
expansion is isotropic in the spatial three, with the set of events
reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a 2-sphere of radius
$c\tau$; (iii) *monotonicity* --- the integral curve is strictly
monotonically increasing in $t$, fixing the arrow of $x_4$-advance; (iv)
*Lorentz consistency* --- the structure is $SO^+(1,3)$-invariant on
$M_{G}$; (v) *global validity* --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at
every event of $M_{G}$. The integrated kinematic shadow
$x_4 = ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is the kinematic shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the central fact.

::: flushright
*"The measurement problem is the central conceptual problem of quantum
mechanics, and any interpretation of quantum mechanics worthy of the
name must address it."\
--- Tim Maudlin, *Three Measurement Problems* (1995).*
:::

This chapter expands on Theorem [19.1](#thm:QMT19){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT19"} (Ch. [19](#ch:measurement){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:measurement"}) into a complete account of how the textbook
measurement problem is dissolved in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework. The chapter
parallels Griffiths' Afterword [@Griffiths2018] (the most candid
textbook treatment of foundations), Weinberg's Chapter 3 discussion of
interpretations [@Weinberg2015], and the Cohen-Tannoudji complement on
collapse [@CT2019], drawing the content from
[@MG-Measurement-2026].

### The textbook measurement problem in its strongest form

The textbook formulation has four ingredients:

1.  The Schrödinger equation
    $i\hbar\partial_t\lvert \psi \rangle = \hat{H}\lvert \psi \rangle$
    is unitary, deterministic, and time-reversible.

2.  The projection postulate
    $\lvert \psi \rangle \to \hat{P}_n\lvert \psi \rangle/\|\hat{P}_n\lvert \psi \rangle\|$
    on measurement is non-unitary, probabilistic, and irreversible.

3.  The two cannot both apply simultaneously to the same system: when
    does which one apply?

4.  The von Neumann "Heisenberg cut" between system and apparatus is not
    specified by the postulates.

Maudlin's 1995 paper [@Maudlin1995] distinguishes *three* distinct measurement problems: the Problem of Outcomes (the
Schrödinger--measurement trilemma); the Problem of Statistics (the
determinism--Born-rule trilemma); and the Problem of Effect (the
dynamics of possessed properties between successive measurements). The
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework dispositions of these three problems in full rigour
are given in Section [10.3](#sec:maudlin-resolved){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:maudlin-resolved"} below. [@MG-Measurement-2026] develops
an *extended* six-sub-problem taxonomy (P0)--(P5) that supplements
Maudlin's three with three further sub-problems made explicit in the
post-Maudlin literature --- the antecedent question of where
superposition itself comes from (P0), the preferred-basis problem (P3)
introduced by Zurek and others, and the nonlocality problem (P5) made
explicit by the EPR (Einstein--Podolsky--Rosen)--Bell literature:

-   *The superposition problem.* Where does the linear superposition
    principle (SP) come from? Standard formulations postulate it; the
    McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework demands a deeper account.

-   *The probability problem.* Where does the Born rule $P = |\psi|^2$
    come from?

-   *The collapse problem.* Why and how does the wavefunction collapse
    upon measurement?

-   *The preferred-basis problem.* Why does the observer see definite
    outcomes in some preferred basis (position, energy) rather than in
    arbitrary superpositions?

-   *The irreversibility problem.* Why is the apparent collapse
    irreversible given unitary microdynamics?

-   *The nonlocality problem.* How does the wavefunction at
    spacelike-separated points "know" about a measurement?

Maudlin's three problems map into this taxonomy as: Problem of Outcomes
$\leftrightarrow$ (P2); Problem of Statistics $\leftrightarrow$ (P1);
Problem of Effect $\leftrightarrow$ (P3) + (P4) combined. The (P0)--(P5)
taxonomy is therefore a refinement of Maudlin's, not a substitute for
it; Section [10.3](#sec:maudlin-resolved){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:maudlin-resolved"} below addresses Maudlin's three in his
own formulation, while the (P0)--(P5) accounting is recovered in
Section [10.10](#sec:absence-of-R-law){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:absence-of-R-law"}
(Proposition [10.39](#prop:no-separate-R){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:no-separate-R"}).

The textbook responses are familiar: Copenhagen (operationally specify
the cut), many-worlds (deny the projection, branch instead), Bohmian
mechanics (deny the wavefunction's completeness, add hidden variables),
GRW (modify the Schrödinger equation with spontaneous-collapse terms),
QBism (interpret probabilities as personal credences). Each addresses
one or two of Maudlin's three problems at the cost of introducing new
commitments. None resolves all three from a single deeper
principle, and none even attempts the broader (P0)--(P5) accounting.

### The dual-channel resolution at the highest level

The dual-channel architecture supplies the resolution as a theorem:

1.  The unitary Schrödinger evolution is the Algebraic Channel reading of
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via Stone's theorem
    (Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT7"}, Algebraic Channel). It governs the wavefunction on
    the 4D manifold $M_{G}$.

2.  The projection postulate is the Geometric Channel reading of registration: a
    3D-projection of the 4D McGucken Sphere at the registration event
    (Theorem [19.1](#thm:QMT19){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT19"}, Geometric Channel). It governs the operationally
    observed outcome on the 3D spatial slice at the measurement
    coordinate time.

3.  The two channels are the derivationally disjoint readings of
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
    (Theorem [4.27](#thm:disjointness){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:disjointness"}). The 4D side remains unitary; the
    3D-projection side is operationally irreversible because the
    information has been transferred to a macroscopic pointer.

4.  The Heisenberg cut is operationally specified by the device's
    coupling extent (a finite spatial scale determined by the
    experimental setup), not by an additional postulate.

::: {#cor:channel-asymmetry-measurement-problem .corollary}
**Corollary 10.1** (The channel asymmetry as the source of
the orthodox-tradition's measurement problem). *The orthodox-tradition
measurement problem --- the seventy-year debate about how to reconcile
Process 2 (Schrödinger unitary evolution: deterministic, continuous,
reversible) with Process 1 (measurement collapse: probabilistic,
discontinuous, irreversible) --- is diagnosed by the
channel asymmetry of
Theorem [1.5](#thm:channel-differential-response){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:channel-differential-response"}: Algebraic Channel is
Lorentzian-locked and does not admit the McGucken-Wick rotation as a
transport, while Geometric Channel is bi-signature and admits the rotation as
its internal signature-bridge. The dual-channel architecture of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, together with the channel asymmetry, supplies
the source of why both Process 1 and Process 2 are forced
content of the matter-dynamics tier, dissolving the orthodox-tradition's
incompatibility-puzzle into a single dual-reading structure of one
physical event.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The corollary is established in five steps, each
appealing to a result already proved in the present paper.

**Step 1 --- The two processes are two phases of one measurement event,
each phase admitting both channel readings.** By the von Neumann
diagnostic case of
§[1.10](#sec:two-faces-of-one-reality){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:two-faces-of-one-reality"}, between measurements the
matter-dynamics tier exhibits Process 2 (unitary Schrödinger evolution),
with Algebraic Channel supplying the Stone-theorem unitary group
$U(t) = e^{-i\hat{H}t/\hbar}$ on the operator-algebraic side and Geometric
Channel supplying the McGucken-Sphere expansion on $M_{G}$ on the
geometric-propagation side. At the measurement event, the
matter-dynamics tier exhibits Process 1 (projection and registration),
with Algebraic Channel's unitary group destroyed by the apparatus-performed
McGucken-Wick rotation into a projection operator
$\hat{P}_n = \lvert a_n \rangle\langle a_n \rvert$ and Geometric Channel's
four-dimensional Sphere transported from Lorentzian to Euclidean
signature, intersected with the three-dimensional apparatus slice,
giving the geometric three-dimensional localisation and the Born
probability $|\psi|^2$ on the slice. Both processes therefore have both
channel readings; the distinction between them is phase-aligned (during
evolution vs. at the measurement event), not channel-aligned.

**Step 2 --- Algebraic Channel's Lorentzian-locked status preserves Process 2's
unitary character between measurements and forces Process 1's projection
structure at the measurement event.** By
Theorem [1.5](#thm:channel-differential-response){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:channel-differential-response"}(A), Algebraic Channel is
destroyed by the McGucken-Wick rotation: the unitary group
$U(t) = e^{-i\hat{H}t/\hbar}$ becomes a non-invertible projection-like
operator under $\Wick$. Between measurements, when the apparatus does
not perform the rotation, Algebraic Channel's unitary group is intact and
supplies the reversible deterministic unitary evolution of Process 2. At
the measurement event, when the apparatus performs the rotation, Algebraic
Channel's group structure dissolves and supplies the irreversible projection
operator $\hat{P}_n$ of Process 1. The Lorentzian-locked status of
Algebraic Channel is therefore precisely what makes Process 2 reversible between
measurements and what makes Process 1 irreversible at the measurement
event: the rotation that the apparatus performs cannot be undone,
because applying $\Wick$ to Algebraic Channel destroys its invertibility.

**Step 3 --- Geometric Channel's bi-signature status supplies the geometric
content of Process 2 between measurements and Process 1 at the
measurement event.** By
Theorem [1.5](#thm:channel-differential-response){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:channel-differential-response"}(B), Geometric Channel is
transported by the McGucken-Wick rotation from Lorentzian to Euclidean
signature, with the iterated-Sphere geometric content preserved through
the signature change. Between measurements, Geometric Channel's
Lorentzian-signature content is the four-dimensional McGucken Sphere
expanding on $M_{G}$ from past source events --- the
geometric-propagation content of Process 2. At the measurement event,
the apparatus performs the rotation on Geometric Channel; the rotation
transports the four-dimensional Sphere into its Euclidean-signature
reading, where the path-integral phase factor $\exp(iS/\hbar)$ becomes
the real positive exponential $\exp(-S_E/\hbar)$, and the
modulus-squared $|\psi|^2$ emerges as the real positive Born density on
the three-dimensional apparatus slice. The $SO(3)$-Haar measure on the
McGucken-Sphere wavefront, weighted by $|\psi|^2$, supplies the Born
probability distribution for the registered outcome
(Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"}, Geometric Channel reading). Geometric Channel's
bi-signature status is therefore precisely what makes Process 1
probabilistic: the apparatus-performed rotation transports Geometric Channel
into its Euclidean reading, where the geometric content takes the form
of a real positive probability density.

**Step 4 --- The modulus operation $\lvert\cdot\rvert^2$ is the exact
boundary between Algebraic Channel's complex-unitary content and the
apparatus's real-outcome registration.** The transformation that takes
the complex amplitude $\psi \in \mathbb{C}$ to the real positive density
$|\psi|^2 \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ is the exteriorization of the
imaginary unit $i$ from the path-integral phase $\exp(iS/\hbar)$ onto
the coordinate axis of the Euclidean signature. This exteriorization is
unavailable to Algebraic Channel: removing the $i$ from the Stone
unitary $\exp(-i\hat{H}t/\hbar)$ converts it into the
propagation-evolution semigroup $\exp(-\tau\hat{H}/\hbar)$, which is no
longer a unitary representation of the time-translation group and
therefore no longer supplies Algebraic Channel's content. The exteriorization is
available to Geometric Channel: removing the $i$ from the path-integral phase
converts $\exp(iS/\hbar)$ into $\exp(-S_E/\hbar)$, which is a real
positive Boltzmann-type weight preserving the iterated-Sphere geometric
content under the signature change. The modulus operation is therefore
the precise location at which Algebraic Channel's derivational reach
ends and Geometric Channel's apparatus-registered content begins. Algebraic Channel
produces the complex-unitary skeleton of quantum mechanics (Hilbert
space, self-adjoint operators, canonical commutator, Schrödinger
evolution, uncertainty principle); Geometric Channel's Euclidean-signature
reading produces the probabilistic-irreversible-real-measure flesh (Born
density, measurement registration, strict Second Law, the arrow of
time). The Born rule's four requirements
(Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"}) sit precisely at this boundary:
requirement (R3) phase invariance is Algebraic Channel content (the universality
clause of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at every event); requirement (R4)
bilinearity is Geometric Channel content (the rank-2 character of the
McGucken-derived Minkowski metric forces the bilinear pairing of forward
and conjugate $x_4$-expansions); requirements (R1) reality and (R2)
non-negativity are imposed by the apparatus's three-dimensional-slice
registration, which is the apparatus-performed McGucken-Wick rotation
acting on Geometric Channel's content. The Born rule's $|\,\cdot\,|^2$ is
therefore not an Algebraic Channel theorem or a Geometric Channel theorem but the
boundary theorem at which Algebraic Channel's complex-unitary content
meets Geometric Channel's apparatus-registered real-outcome content via the
apparatus-performed McGucken-Wick rotation at the measurement event.

**Step 5 --- The orthodox-tradition's measurement problem is the
symptom of reading the matter-dynamics tier through Algebraic
Channel's content only without the dual-channel diagnostic.** The orthodox
tradition has empirical access to both Process 2 (laboratory unitary
Schrödinger evolution between measurements) and Process 1 (laboratory
measurement outcomes with Born-rule probabilities and irreversible
registration). Lacking the dual-channel architecture, the orthodox
tradition reads Algebraic Channel's content as "the dynamics"
(operator-algebraic, unitary, complex-valued, deterministic) and is
forced to introduce Geometric Channel's apparatus-registered content (real
positive Born density, irreversible projection, probabilistic outcomes)
either (a) as a separate axiom (Copenhagen Born-rule postulate and
projection postulate), (b) as an interpretation question (Everett
many-worlds branching, Bohmian guidance, QBist Dutch-book coherence),
(c) as a hidden physical process (Ghirardi-Rimini-Weber spontaneous
localization, Penrose-Diósi gravitational collapse), or (d) as a
statistical-environmental artifact (decoherence-only). None of these
readings supplies a source for why Process 1 exists at
all --- because Algebraic Channel alone, without the modulus operation that
exteriorizes the $i$, cannot produce a real positive measure. The
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework's diagnosis: Process 1 is the apparatus-performed
McGucken-Wick rotation acting on both channels jointly --- destroying
Algebraic Channel's unitary group structure (yielding the projection operator
$\hat{P}_n$) and transporting Geometric Channel from Lorentzian to Euclidean
signature (yielding the real positive Born density $|\psi|^2$ on the
apparatus slice). The measurement problem is the orthodox-tradition's
symptom of having empirical access to both channels'
apparatus-registered content without having the foundational diagnostic
that identifies the apparatus-performed rotation as a single physical
operation acting on both channels jointly. ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:modulus-boundary .remark}
*Remark 10.2* (The modulus boundary as the locator of the
measurement problem). The content of Step 4 of
Corollary [10.1](#cor:channel-asymmetry-measurement-problem){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor:channel-asymmetry-measurement-problem"} admits a sharper
statement worth recording separately. Quantum mechanics is fully
derivable through Algebraic Channel's content up to and not including the
modulus operation $|\,\cdot\,|^2$. Algebraic Channel produces the Hilbert space
(Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}), the self-adjoint operators
(QM T2--T9 generators via Stone's theorem), the canonical commutator
(Theorem [10.1](#thm:QMT10){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT10"}), the Schrödinger evolution
(Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT7"}),
the uncertainty principle
(Theorem [12.1](#thm:QMT12){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT12"}
as Robertson--Cauchy--Schwarz on the derived commutator), and the
unitarity of evolution
(the QM T9 unitarity theorem as conservation of $x_4$-flux). All of
these are Lorentzian-locked, complex-valued, deterministic, reversible.
They are the complex-unitary skeleton of quantum mechanics.

What Algebraic Channel cannot produce, is a real positive
probability measure. The transformation from $\psi \in \mathbb{C}$ to
$|\psi|^2 \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ requires the exteriorization of the
imaginary unit, which dissolves Algebraic Channel's defining unitary-group
structure (the Stone unitary becomes a non-invertible semigroup under
$\Wick$). Algebraic Channel is therefore Lorentzian-locked precisely because it
cannot perform that exteriorization while remaining itself. The modulus
operation is the exact boundary at which Algebraic Channel's
derivational capacity ends.

Every empirical content of quantum mechanics that requires real
numbers --- probabilities, measurement statistics, irreversibility, the
strict Second Law, the arrow of time, the existence of definite
measurement outcomes --- sits on the Geometric Channel side of the modulus
boundary, supplied by the apparatus-performed McGucken-Wick rotation on
Geometric Channel's geometric content. The orthodox-tradition's seventy-year
measurement-problem debate is the footprint of trying to
derive the real-outcome content of quantum mechanics from the
complex-unitary content alone, without recognizing that the modulus is
the channel-boundary at which apparatus-registered content emerges from
the apparatus-performed McGucken-Wick rotation on Geometric Channel's geometric
content. The dual-channel architecture names the boundary explicitly;
the orthodox tradition pushes against it from the complex-unitary side
without naming what lies beyond.
:::

The remainder of this chapter develops the resolution at the level of
six propositions, one per sub-problem (P0)--(P5), drawn from
[@MG-Measurement-2026], each with a self-contained proof. Before that,
Section [10.3](#sec:maudlin-resolved){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:maudlin-resolved"} below carries out the disposition of
Maudlin's own three problems in his own formulation, with full rigour,
to show that each is dissolved into a forced theorem of
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

### Maudlin's three measurement problems dissolved as theorems of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ {#sec:maudlin-resolved}

This section reproduces, in Maudlin's own formulation, the three
measurement problems of [@Maudlin1995], and disposes of each by
exhibiting which Proposition of [@MG-Measurement-2026] forces its
resolution. The general diagnosis is the following. Maudlin's
three problems each assume that the wavefunction lives on a single 3D
spatial-temporal manifold. The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework distinguishes two
levels: the four-dimensional wavefunction
$\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4)$ on the McGucken Space $\mathcal{M}_G$, and its
3D cross-section $\psi(\mathbf{x}, t) = \Psi(\mathbf{x}, ict)$ at the
McGucken-constraint locus. Each of Maudlin's three trilemmas resolves
once this two-level structure is recognised: the propositions Maudlin
requires to be jointly inconsistent live at distinct organisational
scales and can therefore be jointly true.

#### Maudlin's Problem 1: the Problem of Outcomes {#ssec:maudlin-problem-1}

::: {#thm:maudlin-trilemma-1 .theorem}
**Theorem 10.3** (Maudlin's Trilemma of Outcomes; [@Maudlin1995] §1).
*The following three claims are mutually inconsistent in standard
quantum mechanics:*

::: description
**Completeness.* The wavefunction of a system is complete: it specifies,
directly or indirectly, all the physical properties of the system.*

**Linearity.* The wavefunction always evolves in accord with a linear
dynamical equation (e.g. the Schrödinger equation).*

**Determinate outcomes.* Measurements of the spin of an electron always
(or at least usually) have determinate outcomes: at the end of the
measurement, the apparatus is either in a state which indicates spin up
(and not down) or spin down (and not up).*
:::
:::

::: proof
*Sketch of Maudlin's inconsistency argument.* The standard inconsistency
argument has six logical steps, which we reproduce in detail to make
explicit the assumption that the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework will dissolve (see
Theorem [10.4](#thm:maudlin-1-dissolved){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:maudlin-1-dissolved"} below). The argument concludes that
(1.A)+(1.B)+(1.C) are inconsistent under the standard reading; the
McGucken dissolution recognises that (1.A) and (1.B) hold at the 4D
level on $M_{G}$ while (1.C) holds at the 3D-cross-section reading, with
the distinction forced by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

**Step 1: Prepare an entangled state.** Consider an electron prepared in
an $x$-spin eigenstate
$$\lvert \psi_e \rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\bigl(\lvert \uparrow \rangle_z + \lvert \downarrow \rangle_z\bigr),$$
fed into an ideal Stern--Gerlach device measuring $z$-spin. The
apparatus's initial state is the ready state $\lvert m_0 \rangle_M$. The
joint Hilbert space is the tensor product
$\mathcal{H}_e \otimes \mathcal{H}_M$ established by
Lemma [10.4](#lem:stone-vonNeumann-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:stone-vonNeumann-uniqueness"} (Stone--von Neumann
uniqueness for the joint observable algebra).

**Step 2: Linear unitary evolution under (1.B).** Under linearity of the
dynamics (1.B), the joint initial state
$\lvert \psi_e \rangle \otimes \lvert m_0 \rangle_M$ evolves under the
unitary measurement-interaction operator $\hat U_{\mathrm{meas}}$ over
the measurement interaction time $\tau$ to the entangled superposition
$$\lvert \Psi(\tau) \rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\bigl(\lvert \uparrow \rangle_z \otimes \lvert + \rangle_M + \lvert \downarrow \rangle_z \otimes \lvert - \rangle_M\bigr),$$
where $\lvert + \rangle_M$ and $\lvert - \rangle_M$ are the apparatus
pointer states corresponding to spin-up and spin-down outcomes,
respectively. This is the standard von Neumann measurement scheme: the
unitary measurement interaction couples system spin to apparatus
pointer, creating an entangled superposition. The unitarity of
$\hat U_{\mathrm{meas}}$ descends from time-translation invariance of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via
Lemma [7.2](#lem:time-translation-unitary){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:time-translation-unitary"} and
Lemma [3.3](#lem:Hhat-generator){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:Hhat-generator"} (Stone's theorem applied to the
time-translation subgroup).

**Step 3: Completeness under (1.A).** Under completeness (1.A), the
wavefunction $\lvert \Psi(\tau) \rangle$ specifies all physical
properties of the apparatus. The apparatus's physical state is therefore
exactly the entangled superposition: there is no additional hidden
variable or physical descriptor beyond $\lvert \Psi(\tau) \rangle$.

**Step 4: Eigenlink.** Apply the Eigenlink principle (Maudlin
[@Maudlin1995]): a property is possessed iff the state lies in the
corresponding eigenspace. The apparatus's pointer state
$\lvert + \rangle_M$ corresponds to the eigenspace of the
pointer-position observable with eigenvalue $+$; similarly for
$\lvert - \rangle_M$. The joint state $\lvert \Psi(\tau) \rangle$ does
*not* lie in either eigenspace alone: it lies in the superposition. By
the Eigenlink, the apparatus possesses neither the property
$\lvert + \rangle_M$ nor the property $\lvert - \rangle_M$.

**Step 5: Contradiction with determinate outcomes (1.C).** However,
claim (1.C) asserts that measurements always have determinate outcomes:
at the end of the measurement, the apparatus is in state
$\lvert + \rangle_M$ (and not $\lvert - \rangle_M$) or state
$\lvert - \rangle_M$ (and not $\lvert + \rangle_M$). This contradicts
Step 4, which says the apparatus possesses neither.

**Step 6: The trilemma and the McGucken dissolution.** The three claims
(1.A), (1.B), (1.C) are therefore mutually inconsistent in standard
quantum mechanics. Each interpretation of QM must give up at least one
of the three: hidden-variable theories reject (1.A);
spontaneous-collapse theories reject (1.B); many-worlds theories reject
(1.C). *The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework rejects none.* The assumption
that the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework will dissolve is the implicit identification
of the wavefunction with a single 3D spatial-temporal object --- i.e.,
the assumption that $\lvert \Psi(\tau) \rangle$ in Step 2 lives at the
same organisational level as the determinate-outcome state in Step 5. By
Theorem [19.1](#thm:QMT19){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT19"}
(the 3D cross-section reading of the 4D McGucken Sphere) and
Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} (the 4D Lorentzian arena from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$), the McGucken framework distinguishes the 4D
wavefunction $\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4)$ on $M_{G}$ (where (1.A) and (1.B)
hold) from its 3D cross-section reading at the McGucken-constraint locus
$x_{4}= ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}, the integrated kinematic shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$) where (1.C) holds. This two-level structure is
the resolution: see
Theorem [10.4](#thm:maudlin-1-dissolved){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:maudlin-1-dissolved"} below. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#thm:maudlin-1-dissolved .theorem}
**Theorem 10.4** (Maudlin's Problem 1 dissolved as a theorem of
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). *Under the McGucken Principle, the three
claims (1.A), (1.B), (1.C) are jointly true once the wavefunction is
recognised to be the four-dimensional structure $\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4)$
on $\mathcal{M}_G$ rather than its 3D-cross-section reading
$\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)$. Specifically:*

-   *The 4D wavefunction $\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4)$ on $\mathcal{M}_G$ is
    complete in Maudlin's sense: it specifies all physical properties of
    the system.
    Proposition [10.17](#def:mcgucken-wavefunction){reference-type="ref"
    reference="def:mcgucken-wavefunction"} (Definition V.1) establishes
    $\Psi$ as the complex amplitude of the spherical $x_4$-wavefront
    $\Sigma_M(p_0, t)$ emanating from the source event, and
    Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"} (Hilbert Space as Theorem of
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$) establishes the Hilbert-space structure on
    $\Psi$.*

-   *The 4D wavefunction $\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4)$ evolves unitarily on
    $\mathcal{M}_G$ in accord with the linear McGucken operator
    $D_M = \partial_t + ic\,\partial_{x_4}$ (the operator that
    derives together with $\mathcal{M}_G$ with $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The
    unitarity is exact and never suspended: there is no separate
    non-linear $(R)$ dynamics.
    Proposition [10.19](#prop:apparent-collapse){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:apparent-collapse"} (Proposition V.1) records this
    explicitly: "the unitary evolution is exact; the apparent collapse
    is the observer's restricted access to the 3D cross-section."*

-   *The cross-section $\pi_{\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}}\Psi$ taken by an
    observer at spatial location $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ delivers a
    single determinate branch with the Born-rule probability $|c_k|^2$
    on $k$
    (Proposition [10.13](#prop:born-rule-geometric){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:born-rule-geometric"}, Proposition III.1). The
    apparatus reading is therefore determinate at each cross-section.*

*The trilemma dissolves because (1.A), (1.B), (1.C) live at distinct
organisational scales of the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework: (1.A) and (1.B) at the
4D level, (1.C) at the 3D-cross-section reading. Maudlin's argument
assumed all three claims lived at the same level; under that assumption
they are inconsistent. Under $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ they are jointly
true.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof; from
Propositions [10.13](#prop:born-rule-geometric){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:born-rule-geometric"}, [10.19](#prop:apparent-collapse){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:apparent-collapse"},
and [10.17](#def:mcgucken-wavefunction){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:mcgucken-wavefunction"}.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has six steps establishing the joint consistency of (1.A), (1.B), (1.C) under
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

**Step 1: Verification of (1.A) at the 4D level --- completeness.** The
McGucken wavefunction $\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4)$ is defined
(Definition [10.17](#def:mcgucken-wavefunction){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:mcgucken-wavefunction"}) as the complex amplitude carried
by the McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_M(p_0, t)$ on the 4D manifold $M_{G}$. By
Remark [10.18](#rmk:seven-ingredients){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:seven-ingredients"} (the seven ingredients of
the wavefunction), $\Psi$ encodes all physical properties of the system:

-   Phase structure (Compton-rate at rest,
    Theorem [5.1](#thm:QMT5){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT5"});

-   Amplitude (Sphere wavefront magnitude);

-   Multi-particle entanglement structure (joint Sphere from common
    source,
    Lemma [18.5](#lem:QMT18-joint-wavefront){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:QMT18-joint-wavefront"});

-   Matter-orientation phase $\exp(+ik_C x_4)$ vs. antimatter
    $\exp(-ik_C x_4)$;

-   Rest-mass content (Compton frequency labelling).

The 4D wavefunction is therefore complete in Maudlin's sense --- it
specifies all physical properties --- establishing claim (1.A).

**Step 2: Verification of (1.B) at the 4D level --- exact unitary
evolution.** The McGucken operator
$D_M = \partial_t + ic\,\partial_{x_4}$ acts linearly on $\Psi$. By
Stone's theorem (Theorem [3.6](#thm:stone){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:stone"}) applied to $D_M$, the operator generates a
strongly continuous one-parameter group of unitary transformations on
$M_{G}$. The unitary evolution
$$\Psi(\tau) = e^{-i\tau\hat H_M/\hbar}\Psi(0)$$ preserves the full
superposition structure on $M_{G}$ exactly; there is no separate
dynamical mechanism for $(R)$ at the 4D level. This is the categorical
content of Proposition [10.39](#prop:no-separate-R){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:no-separate-R"}: the standard $(U) + (R)$ dual-law
structure is replaced by $(U) + \dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, with $(R)$
derived as an appearance at the cross-section level. Claim (1.B) holds
at the 4D level.

**Step 3: Verification of (1.C) at the 3D-cross-section reading ---
determinate outcomes.** An observer at spatial location
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ accesses only the 3D cross-section
$\pi_{\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}}\Psi$ of the four-dimensional state at
the McGucken-constraint locus $x_4 = ict$. By
Proposition [10.13](#prop:born-rule-geometric){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:born-rule-geometric"} (Born rule from $SO(3)$-Haar
measure on the McGucken Sphere wavefront), the cross-section reading is
a single branch
$\lvert s_k \rangle\otimes\lvert A_k \rangle\otimes\lvert E_k \rangle$
with probability $|c_k|^2$. Each cross-section reading is therefore
determinate at the apparatus level: the observer registers a specific
outcome $k$. Claim (1.C) holds at the 3D-cross-section reading.

**Step 4: Joint consistency via two organisational scales.** Claims
(1.A), (1.B), (1.C) are jointly satisfied because they live at distinct
organisational scales of the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework:

-   (1.A) and (1.B) are claims about the 4D structure on $M_{G}$;

-   (1.C) is a claim about the 3D-cross-section reading
    $\pi_{\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}}\Psi$.

The two levels are related by the suppression-map projection
$\pi_{\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}}: \Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4) \to \psi(\mathbf{x}, t)$
at the McGucken-constraint locus, with the Born-rule weights $|c_k|^2$
being theorems of the $SO(3)$-equivariant geometry of the McGucken
Sphere cross-section. Maudlin's argument assumed all three claims lived
at the same level; under that assumption they are inconsistent, but
under $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ with its two-level structure they are
jointly true.

**Step 5: Diagnosis of the resolution.** The dissolution of
Maudlin's Problem 1 is therefore derivational rather than interpretive: it is
a forced consequence of the McGucken-Principle's two-level structure (4D
wavefunction + 3D cross-section reading via $\pi$). The standard 3D
wavefunction $\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)$ that Maudlin's argument treats as
primary is, in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, the 3D cross-section reading of
the underlying 4D object $\Psi$; the trilemma assumed (incorrectly) that
$\psi$ is the complete wavefunction, but in fact it is the spatial-slice
projection of $\Psi$ at fixed $t$.

**Step 6: McGucken anchoring of the two-level structure.** The two-level
structure of the framework is itself a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$:

-   The 4D manifold $M_{G}$ arises from the integrated kinematic shadow $x_4 = ict$
    of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
    (Theorem [4.6](#thm:mcp-to-lorentzian){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:mcp-to-lorentzian"});

-   The 3D-cross-section projection $\pi$ is the suppression map
    $\sigma$ at fixed $t$
    (Lemma [9.1](#lem:suppression-map){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:suppression-map"});

-   The Born probabilities $|c_k|^2$ at the cross-section level are the
    $SO(3)$-Haar measure on the McGucken Sphere wavefront
    (Theorem [17.28](#thm:geometric-to-quantum-probability){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:geometric-to-quantum-probability"}, derived from
    clause P2 of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ --- spherical symmetry of
    $x_{4}$-expansion).

The dissolution of Maudlin's Problem 1 is therefore not an ad-hoc
resolution but a forced consequence of the McGucken-Principle's
content. ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:maudlin-1-diagnosis .remark}
*Remark 10.5* (The diagnosis of Maudlin's Problem 1).
Maudlin's inconsistency argument requires the wavefunction to live at
one organisational scale on which (1.A), (1.B), and (1.C) must all hold
simultaneously. The framework $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ supplies an
additional organisational scale: the 4D structure $\mathcal{M}_G$ on
which (1.A) and (1.B) hold exactly, with (1.C) holding at the
cross-section reading $\pi_{\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}}\Psi$. The
dissolution is, not semantic: it is the geometric content of
the McGucken Principle that two organisational scales exist and that the
standard 3D wavefunction is a cross-section reading of a 4D object.
:::

#### Maudlin's Problem 2: the Problem of Statistics {#ssec:maudlin-problem-2}

::: {#thm:maudlin-trilemma-2 .theorem}
**Theorem 10.6** (Maudlin's Trilemma of Statistics; [@Maudlin1995] §2).
*The following three claims are mutually inconsistent in standard
quantum mechanics:*

::: description
**Completeness* (identical to 1.A).*

**Determinism.* The wavefunction always evolves in accord with a
deterministic dynamical equation (e.g. the Schrödinger equation).*

**Born statistics.* Measurement situations described by identical
initial wavefunctions sometimes have different outcomes, and the
probability of each possible outcome is given (at least approximately)
by Born's rule.*
:::
:::

::: proof
*Sketch of Maudlin's inconsistency argument.* **Step 1: Determinism plus
identical initial conditions yield identical evolutions.** Take two
systems prepared in identical initial wavefunctions $\psi_0$. By (2.B)
Determinism, both systems evolve under the same deterministic dynamical
equation (Schrödinger's equation, say):
$i\hbar\,\partial_t\psi = \hat{H}\psi$ with the same $\hat{H}$ for both
systems --- this is Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT7"} (the Schrödinger equation as a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The Cauchy problem for a deterministic linear
PDE has unique solutions given initial data (standard $L^2$-existence
theory, Reed--Simon [@ReedSimon1980] Vol. II, Theorem X.49), so both
systems produce the same final wavefunction $\psi(t)$ at every later
time $t$.

**Step 2: Completeness identifies wavefunction with physical state.** By
(2.A) Completeness, the wavefunction provides a complete specification
of the physical state: two systems with the same wavefunction at time
$t$ are physically identical in every respect, including the
configuration of any measurement apparatus interacting with them. This
is the textbook reading of completeness assumed by Bohr in his 1935
reply to EPR; the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework version
(Proposition [10.19](#prop:apparent-collapse){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:apparent-collapse"}) replaces the textbook
3D-wavefunction with the 4D wavefunction $\Psi$ on $M_{G}$.

**Step 3: Contradiction with statistical outcomes.** However, (2.C) Born
statistics (Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"}) asserts that two systems with identical
initial wavefunctions can have detectors registering *different*
outcomes (e.g., spin-up vs. spin-down in a Stern--Gerlach experiment),
with probabilities given by Born's rule. Different macroscopic detector
states are physically distinguishable. Steps 1--2 require physical
identity at every $t$; Step 3 requires physical distinguishability of
outcomes. The two are mutually inconsistent.

**Step 4: Reformulation of the trilemma.** Standard quantum mechanics
must therefore abandon at least one of the three:

-   Reject (2.A): hidden variables theories (Bohm, deBroglie-Bohm) ---
    wavefunction is not complete.

-   Reject (2.B): collapse theories (Ghirardi--Rimini--Weber, Penrose)
    --- evolution is not deterministic; spontaneous stochastic collapse
    occurs.

-   Reject (2.C): many-worlds (Everett) --- all outcomes occur in
    branching universes; "different outcomes" is reinterpreted as branch
    indexing.

See Maudlin [@Maudlin1995] §2 for the original analysis. The McGucken
framework dissolves the trilemma
(Theorem [10.7](#thm:maudlin-2-dissolved){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:maudlin-2-dissolved"}) by distinguishing the
deterministic 4D wavefunction evolution from the probabilistic
3D-cross-section reading: both (2.B) and (2.C) hold simultaneously when
applied to the correct level, the distinction being forced by
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} (with $x_4 = ict$ the integrated kinematic
shadow of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$,
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}). ◻
:::

::: {#thm:maudlin-2-dissolved .theorem}
**Theorem 10.7** (Maudlin's Problem 2 dissolved as a theorem of
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). *Under the McGucken Principle, the three
claims (2.A), (2.B), (2.C) are jointly true once the deterministic 4D
evolution is recognised to be distinct from the probabilistic
3D-cross-section reading. Specifically:*

-   *Same content as
    Theorem [10.4](#thm:maudlin-1-dissolved){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:maudlin-1-dissolved"}: $\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4)$ on
    $\mathcal{M}_G$ is complete.*

-   *$\Psi$ evolves deterministically under the linear McGucken operator
    $D_M$: two identical initial 4D wavefunctions evolve into identical
    final 4D wavefunctions, identical at every 4D event.*

-   *Two observers at distinct spatial locations
    $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ and $\mathbf{x}'_{\mathrm{obs}}$ take
    *distinct* 3D cross-sections of the same 4D state, with
    $SO(3)$-equivariant Born-rule probabilities $|c_k|^2$ given by
    Proposition [10.13](#prop:born-rule-geometric){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:born-rule-geometric"}. Different observers
    (different cross-sections) can therefore report different outcomes
    from the same 4D state --- with probabilities exactly as Born
    requires.*

*The trilemma dissolves because (2.A) and (2.B) are claims about the 4D
evolution while (2.C) is a claim about the statistical distribution of
3D-cross-section readings across observers (or across runs of the
experiment, the ensemble interpretation Maudlin had in mind).*
:::

::: proof
*Proof; from
Propositions [10.13](#prop:born-rule-geometric){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:born-rule-geometric"}
and [10.19](#prop:apparent-collapse){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:apparent-collapse"}.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof of (2.A), (2.B), (2.C)
being jointly true uses the two-level structure of the McGucken
framework: 4D wavefunction $\Psi$ on $M_{G}$ vs. 3D-cross-section
reading $\psi$ at the McGucken-constraint locus.

**Step 1: (2.A) at the 4D level.** As in the proof of
Theorem [10.4](#thm:maudlin-1-dissolved){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:maudlin-1-dissolved"}, the 4D wavefunction
$\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4)$ on $M_{G}$ is complete (Maudlin sense: specifies
all physical properties of the system). This is Proposition V.1 of
[@MG-Measurement-2026], recorded as
Proposition [10.19](#prop:apparent-collapse){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:apparent-collapse"}: "the unitary evolution is exact" on
the 4D manifold.

**Step 2: (2.B) at the 4D level --- deterministic evolution.** The 4D
wavefunction $\Psi$ evolves deterministically under the linear McGucken
operator $$D_M = \partial_t + ic\,\partial_{x_4},$$ which derives together with
$M_{G}$ together with $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. By Stone's theorem
(Theorem [3.6](#thm:stone){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:stone"}),
the operator $D_M$ on $\Psi$ generates a strongly continuous
one-parameter group of unitaries; two identical initial 4D wavefunctions
$\Psi_1(0) = \Psi_2(0)$ evolve into identical final 4D wavefunctions
$\Psi_1(\tau) = \Psi_2(\tau)$ at every event of $M_{G}$. Determinism at
the 4D level is therefore exact: same initial 4D state $\to$ same final
4D state.

**Step 3: (2.C) at the 3D-cross-section reading --- probabilistic
outcomes.** An observer at spatial location $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}$
takes the 3D cross-section $\pi_{\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}}\Psi$ of the
4D state at the registration event. Different observers at distinct
spatial locations
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}} \ne \mathbf{x}'_{\mathrm{obs}}$ take
*distinct* 3D cross-sections of the same 4D state. By
Proposition [10.13](#prop:born-rule-geometric){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:born-rule-geometric"} (Born rule derived geometrically
from $SO(3)$-Haar measure on the McGucken Sphere wavefront), the
cross-section reading at $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ registers branch
$k$ with probability $|c_k|^2$. The $SO(3)$-Haar measure on the McGucken
Sphere is equivariant --- the probability distribution transforms
covariantly under rotations of the observer's frame.

**Step 4: Distinct observers $\to$ distinct readings, same statistics.**
For two observers at
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}, \mathbf{x}'_{\mathrm{obs}}$:

-   Each takes a 3D cross-section of the same 4D wavefunction $\Psi$;

-   Each registers a single branch with Born probability $|c_k|^2$;

-   The two observers may register different branches (different $k$
    values), and across many runs of the experiment, the relative
    frequencies converge to the Born statistics.

The probabilistic content of (2.C) is therefore a statement about the
statistical distribution of 3D-cross-section readings across observers
(or across runs of the same experiment) --- not a statement about the 4D
wavefunction's evolution.

**Step 5: Joint consistency.** (2.A) and (2.B) are claims about the 4D
evolution: at this level, $\Psi$ is complete and deterministic. (2.C) is
a claim about the statistical distribution of 3D-cross-section readings:
at this level, outcomes are probabilistic with Born weights. The two
levels are not in tension because they describe distinct organisational
scales of the same physical structure. The trilemma assumed
(incorrectly) that both 4D evolution and 3D outcomes lived at the same
level; the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework distinguishes them via the projection
$\pi_{\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}}$ at the McGucken-constraint locus.

**Step 6: Origin in $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.** The two-level
structure (4D vs. 3D cross-section) and the Born statistics on the 3D
cross-section both descend from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$:

-   The 4D structure $M_{G}$ arises from the integrated kinematic shadow $x_4 = ict$
    of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$;

-   The 3D-cross-section projection $\pi$ is the suppression map
    $\sigma$ at fixed $t$
    (Lemma [9.1](#lem:suppression-map){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:suppression-map"});

-   The Born probabilities $|c_k|^2$ are the $SO(3)$-Haar measure on the
    McGucken Sphere wavefront
    (Theorem [17.28](#thm:geometric-to-quantum-probability){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:geometric-to-quantum-probability"}, derived from
    clause P2 of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ --- spherical symmetry of the
    $x_{4}$-expansion).

The dissolution of Maudlin's Problem 2 is therefore not an ad-hoc
resolution but a forced consequence of the McGucken Principle's
two-level structure. ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:why-no-prior-maudlin2 .remark}
*Remark 10.8* (Why no prior framework can dissolve Maudlin's Problem 2
this way). The dissolution of
Theorem [10.7](#thm:maudlin-2-dissolved){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:maudlin-2-dissolved"} requires three facts
that are simultaneously theorems of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$:

-   the existence of the 4D structure $\Psi$ on $\mathcal{M}_G$ on which
    (2.A) and (2.B) hold;

-   the 4D-to-3D projection $\pi_{\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}}$ at the
    McGucken-constraint locus, which separates the levels;

-   the $SO(3)$ Haar measure on the McGucken Sphere cross-section, which
    forces the Born weights.

No prior interpretation possesses all three: Copenhagen lacks the 4D
structure, many-worlds has the 4D structure (the universal wavefunction)
but not the $SO(3)$ Haar measure on cross-sections (the Born rule is
added or rationalised via decision theory), Bohmian mechanics has hidden
variables to break completeness but no 4D wavefunction, GRW modifies the
deterministic evolution (denies 2.B). The McGucken framework supplies
all three from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, hence the unique dissolution.
:::

#### Maudlin's Problem 3: the Problem of Effect {#ssec:maudlin-problem-3}

::: {#thm:maudlin-trilemma-3 .theorem}
**Theorem 10.9** (Maudlin's Problem 3 of Effect; [@Maudlin1995] §3). *A
theory of measurement that treats outcomes as revealing possessed
determinate properties of the measured system must specify the *effect*
of one measurement on the dynamics of properties that determine
subsequent measurement outcomes. If outcomes merely reveal properties
and the wavefunction evolves linearly, then the property attributions of
successive measurements are not connected by any dynamical mechanism,
and the statistical correlations between successive measurements
(e.g. repeated Stern--Gerlach with the same setting yielding the same
outcome) cannot be derived.*
:::

::: proof
*Sketch of Maudlin's inconsistency argument.* The standard inconsistency
argument has six logical steps, parallel to those of
Theorems [10.3](#thm:maudlin-trilemma-1){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:maudlin-trilemma-1"}
and [10.6](#thm:maudlin-trilemma-2){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:maudlin-trilemma-2"}. Maudlin's Problem 3 targets the
family of interpretations that posit determinate possessed properties
revealed by measurement (the modal family: Kochen, Dieks, Vermaas,
Healey, van Fraassen, Bub) while retaining linear unitary wavefunction
dynamics. The three claims are:

-   *Properties-revealed*: each measurement outcome reveals a
    determinate property already possessed by the measured system at the
    moment of measurement.

-   *Linear dynamics*: between measurements, the wavefunction evolves
    under the linear unitary Schrödinger equation, with no separate
    stochastic or collapse dynamics on the property attributions.

-   *Correlated successive outcomes*: empirically, successive
    measurements of the same observable on the same system in a short
    enough interval yield the same outcome (repeated Stern--Gerlach with
    fixed setting; repeated which-slit detection in interference; the
    projection-postulate phenomenology of Lüders).

The argument shows that (3.A)+(3.B)+(3.C) are not jointly tenable in the
standard reading; the McGucken dissolution
(Theorem [10.11](#thm:maudlin-3-dissolved){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:maudlin-3-dissolved"}) supplies the missing dynamical
mechanism explicitly.

**Step 1: First measurement entangles system with apparatus.** A first
measurement of observable $\hat O$ at time $t_1$ on system state
$\lvert \psi  \rangle= \sum_n c_n\lvert o_n \rangle$ produces, under the
unitary measurement interaction $\hat U_{\mathrm{meas}}$
(Lemma [19.2](#lem:QMT19-coupling){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT19-coupling"}), the entangled joint system--apparatus
state
$$\lvert \Psi \rangle(t_1) = \sum_n c_n\,\lvert o_n \rangle_{\mathrm{sys}}\otimes\lvert D_n \rangle_{\mathrm{dev}},$$
where $\lvert D_n \rangle_{\mathrm{dev}}$ are macroscopically
distinguishable pointer states. The unitarity of
$\hat U_{\mathrm{meas}}$ descends from time-translation invariance of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via
Lemma [7.2](#lem:time-translation-unitary){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:time-translation-unitary"}. Under (3.A), at time $t_1$
the system possesses some determinate property labelled by an outcome
$o_k$ revealed by the apparatus reading $D_k$.

**Step 2: Linear unitary evolution between measurements (3.B).** Between
$t_1$ and the second measurement at $t_2 > t_1$, the joint state evolves
under the linear unitary group
$\hat U(t_2 - t_1) = e^{-i(t_2 - t_1)\hat H/\hbar}$, with $\hat H$ the
joint Hamiltonian (system + apparatus + environment if any). Crucially,
under (3.B) this is the *only* dynamics applied: there is no separate
dynamical equation governing the possessed property attributions, no
collapse, no stochastic update beyond the unitary $\hat U(t_2 - t_1)$.
The joint wavefunction at $t_2$ is therefore
$$\lvert \Psi \rangle(t_2) = \hat U(t_2 - t_1)\,\lvert \Psi \rangle(t_1).$$

**Step 3: Second measurement.** A second measurement of the same
observable $\hat O$ at $t_2$ couples the system to a second apparatus
(or re-uses the first), producing a further entanglement with a second
pointer-state register. The empirical observation (3.C) is that the
second measurement reading equals the first reading with probability
$\to 1$ in the limit of short $(t_2 - t_1)$ and no intervening
Hamiltonian dynamics that would rotate $\lvert o_n \rangle$ out of the
$\hat O$-eigenbasis. This is the projection-postulate phenomenology,
codified in the Lüders rule, and confirmed experimentally over thousands
of repeat-measurement protocols.

**Step 4: Modal interpretations specify (3.A)+(3.B) without supplying a
dynamics of properties.** Under modal interpretations, the property
attribution $o_k \mapsto$ "system possessed property $o_k$ at $t_1$" is
layered onto the wavefunction without modifying $\hat U(t_2 - t_1)$. The
wavefunction continues to evolve linearly through $\hat U(t_2 - t_1)$
exactly as it would absent the measurement; only the interpretive
overlay (which outcome is "actual") is modified by the measurement. But
this interpretive overlay is dynamically inert: nothing in (3.A)+(3.B)
provides a rule for how the possessed-property attribution at $t_1$
relates to the possessed-property attribution at $t_2$.

**Step 5: The missing link.** For (3.C) to hold, there must be a
dynamical mechanism connecting the possessed-property attribution at
$t_1$ to the possessed-property attribution at $t_2$. Three possibilities exhaust the options under (3.A)+(3.B):

1.  The possessed-property attribution at $t_2$ is computed from the
    wavefunction $\lvert \Psi \rangle(t_2)$ alone (with no reference to
    the $t_1$ attribution). But the wavefunction
    $\lvert \Psi \rangle(t_2)$ still contains all terms
    $\sum_n c_n\ldots$ (linear unitary evolution preserves the
    superposition's branch structure), so the property attribution at
    $t_2$ would in general assign a different outcome than at $t_1$,
    contradicting (3.C).

2.  The possessed-property attribution at $t_2$ inherits from the $t_1$
    attribution by some non-wavefunction dynamical rule. But under (3.B)
    there is no such rule: the wavefunction is the only dynamical
    object, and (3.A) explicitly denies modifying it by the measurement.

3.  Some hidden additional variable (beyond the wavefunction) is updated
    by the measurement and propagated unitarily to $t_2$. But this is
    the hidden-variable strategy of (1.A) rejection in
    Theorem [10.3](#thm:maudlin-trilemma-1){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:maudlin-trilemma-1"}, which modal interpretations
    explicitly disavow (they treat the wavefunction together with modal
    interpretive rules as exhaustive).

None of the three options is available without giving up (3.A), (3.B),
or implicitly importing a hidden-variable structure beyond what modal
interpretations admit.

**Step 6: The trilemma and the McGucken dissolution.** The three claims
(3.A), (3.B), (3.C) are therefore not jointly tenable under modal
interpretations: a coherent specification of (3.A)+(3.B) does not derive
(3.C). [@Maudlin1995] §3 concludes that modal interpretations fail
Problem 3 because they offer no dynamical account of the correlation of
successive measurement outcomes. *The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework dissolves
Problem 3* by supplying the missing mechanism explicitly: by
Proposition [10.36](#prop:preferred-basis-compton){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:preferred-basis-compton"} (Compton-frequency decoherence
of the system--apparatus--environment composite, with rate
$\Gamma_{\mathrm{dec}} \approx \sum_i \omega_{C,i}\,g_{S,i}^2/\hbar$ for
$N \sim 10^{23}$ environmental constituents), the reduced density matrix
$\rho_S$ becomes diagonal in the measured-observable basis on
Planck-short timescales after the first measurement; by
Proposition [10.35](#prop:measurement-irreversibility){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:measurement-irreversibility"} ($x_{4}$-monotonicity from
clause P3 of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$), this diagonalisation is
irreversible on any observable timescale. The second measurement at
$t_2 > t_1$ then accesses the same diagonal form and yields the same
outcome with probability $\to 1$, recovering (3.C). The dynamics of
properties between measurements is therefore the Compton-decoherence +
$x_{4}$-monotonicity composite of
Proposition [10.35](#prop:measurement-irreversibility){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:measurement-irreversibility"} and
Proposition [10.36](#prop:preferred-basis-compton){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:preferred-basis-compton"}, explicit and
McGucken-derived; the gap that defeats modal interpretations is filled
by a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. See
Theorem [10.11](#thm:maudlin-3-dissolved){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:maudlin-3-dissolved"} below for the full dissolution.
$\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:maudlin-problem-3-diagnosis .remark}
*Remark 10.10* (Maudlin's diagnosis of Problem 3). Maudlin's third
problem is targeted specifically at modal interpretations (the family
including Kochen, Dieks, Vermaas, Healey, van Fraassen, Bub) that read
measurement outcomes as revealing possessed determinate properties
without modifying the wavefunction dynamics. The criticism is that such
interpretations leave the property dynamics underspecified: between
successive measurements, what governs the evolution of the possessed
properties? [@Maudlin1995] §3 concludes that modal interpretations fail
Problem 3 because they offer no answer.
:::

::: {#thm:maudlin-3-dissolved .theorem}
**Theorem 10.11** (Maudlin's Problem 3 dissolved as a theorem of
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). *Under the McGucken Principle, the dynamics
of possessed properties between successive measurements is the
Compton-frequency decoherence dynamics of
Proposition [10.36](#prop:preferred-basis-compton){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:preferred-basis-compton"} (Proposition VII.1) combined
with the $x_4$-monotonicity irreversibility of
Proposition [10.35](#prop:measurement-irreversibility){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:measurement-irreversibility"} (Proposition VI.1).
Successive measurement outcomes are correlated by a concrete physical
mechanism --- the system's entanglement with the apparatus and with the
environmental Compton-frequency degrees of freedom --- which makes the
second measurement a measurement of an already-determined property in
the relevant basis.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof; from
Propositions [10.35](#prop:measurement-irreversibility){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:measurement-irreversibility"}
and [10.36](#prop:preferred-basis-compton){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:preferred-basis-compton"}.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof establishes the
property dynamics between successive measurements via the
Compton-frequency decoherence + $x_{4}$-monotonicity mechanism in six
steps. The dynamics is forced by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, with $x_4 = ict$ the integrated kinematic
shadow per Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}): clause (iii) monotonicity supplies
the irreversibility of the diagonalisation, and the Compton-frequency
mechanism (Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT4"}, with each species coupling at its Compton
frequency $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ derived from the $x_{4}$-expansion
rate) supplies the decoherence.

**Step 1: First measurement entangles system with environment.** After
the first measurement of observable $\hat O$ at time $t_1$, the system
has been entangled (via the Stone-theorem coupling Hamiltonian,
Lemma [19.2](#lem:QMT19-coupling){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT19-coupling"}) with a macroscopic apparatus and
through it with the environmental degrees of freedom. The joint state is
$\lvert \Psi \rangle(t_1) = \sum_n c_n\lvert o_n \rangle_{\mathrm{sys}}\otimes\lvert D_n \rangle_{\mathrm{dev}}\otimes\lvert E_n \rangle_{\mathrm{env}}$,
with $N \sim 10^{23}$ environmental constituents oscillating at Compton
frequencies $\omega_{C,i} = m_i c^2/\hbar$ for each species $i$
(Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT4"},
the Compton coupling forced by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$).

**Step 2: Compton-frequency decoherence rate.** By
Proposition [10.36](#prop:preferred-basis-compton){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:preferred-basis-compton"} (Compton-coupling
preferred-basis mechanism, derived from
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i)+(ii) jointly), the effective
decoherence rate of the system's reduced density matrix is
$$\Gamma_{\mathrm{dec}} \approx \sum_{i=1}^N\frac{\omega_{C,i}\,g_{S,i}^2}{\hbar},$$
where $g_{S,i}$ is the coupling strength of the system to environmental
constituent $i$. For macroscopic environments with $N \sim 10^{23}$ and
Compton frequencies $\omega_C \sim 10^{20}$--$10^{24}$ rad/s, the rate
$\Gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}$ is enormous: off-diagonal terms of the reduced
density matrix $\rho_S$ in the position (or energy) basis decay to zero
on Planck-short timescales (Joos--Zeh [@JoosZeh1985] for the standard
decoherence-rate estimates; here re-derived as a McGucken-Compton
consequence).

**Step 3: Diagonalisation in the preferred basis.** The system's reduced
density matrix after the first measurement is diagonal in the position
basis (for spatial outcomes) or the energy basis (for stationary
states):
$$\rho_S(t \ge t_1) \approx \sum_n|c_n|^2\,\lvert o_n \rangle\langle o_n \rvert.$$
The off-diagonal terms $\rho_S(t)_{nm}$ for $n \ne m$ are exponentially
suppressed by $\exp(-\Gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}(t - t_1))$ and effectively
zero for any $t - t_1$ exceeding the decoherence time
$1/\Gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}$.

**Step 4: $x_{4}$-monotonicity makes diagonalisation irreversible.** By
Proposition [10.35](#prop:measurement-irreversibility){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:measurement-irreversibility"} ($x_{4}$-monotonicity from
clause P3 of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$), the diagonalisation is
irreversible on observational timescales. The reverse process
(reassembling the off-diagonal terms from the environment's Compton
oscillations into the system's reduced density matrix) requires
precisely coordinating $N \sim 10^{23}$ phase relationships across the
environment --- a process whose practical reversibility timescale
exceeds the age of the universe by many orders of magnitude (factors
involving the entropy of the apparatus and environment). The arrow of
$x_{4}$-advance therefore makes the diagonalisation a one-way process.

**Step 5: Second measurement and outcome correlation.** A second
measurement of the same observable $\hat O$ on the same system at a
later time $t_2 > t_1$ accesses the same diagonal reduced density matrix
