in the same basis (modulo unitary system dynamics between measurements).
The second measurement therefore yields the same outcome as the first
with probability $\to 1$ (for short intermediate intervals where the
system Hamiltonian has not significantly evolved $\rho_S$). This is
precisely the empirical fact that repeated Stern-Gerlach measurements
with the same setting yield the same outcome: the McGucken-Compton
mechanism gives the dynamical reason.

**Step 6: Modal interpretations failed Problem 3 because they lacked the
Compton mechanism.** Modal interpretations (Kochen, Dieks, Vermaas,
Healey, van Fraassen, Bub) treat measurement outcomes as revealing
possessed determinate properties without modifying the wavefunction
dynamics. Without a concrete decoherence mechanism, the property
dynamics between successive measurements is underspecified: nothing
dynamically connects the possessed-property at $t_1$ to the
possessed-property at $t_2$. Maudlin's third-problem critique exploits
exactly this gap. The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework supplies the gap-filler:
Compton-frequency decoherence + $x_{4}$-monotonicity = dynamical
correlation of successive measurement outcomes. The dissolution is
derived, not interpretively assumed; the property dynamics
between measurements is the Compton-frequency-decoherence-stabilised
diagonal form of $\rho_S$, with the explicit formula of Step 2. This is
the advantage of the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework over the modal
interpretations. ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:modal-vs-mcgucken .remark}
*Remark 10.12* (Modal interpretations fail Problem 3; McGucken does
not). Maudlin observed that modal interpretations fail Problem 3 because
they leave the property dynamics underspecified. The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework
supplies the dynamics concretely: it is the Compton-frequency

#### Summary: Maudlin's three problems collapse into one insight {#ssec:maudlin-summary}

The three Maudlin problems share a common diagnosis. Each
assumes the wavefunction lives on one organisational scale (a 3D
spatial-temporal manifold) and exhibits a tension between the linear
deterministic dynamics on that scale and the determinate-outcome /
Born-statistics / cross-correlation phenomenology on the same scale. The
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework recognises two organisational scales: the 4D
structure $\Psi$ on $\mathcal{M}_G$, and its 3D-cross-section reading
$\psi = \pi_{\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}}\Psi$. The three Maudlin tensions
resolve once the appropriate claim is placed at the appropriate scale:

::: center
::: tabular
L0.18\|L0.40\|L0.30 **Maudlin's problem** & **Tension** & **McGucken
resolution**\
**Problem 1** (Outcomes) & (1.A) Completeness + (1.B) Linearity force
determinate outcomes to fail (1.C). & (1.A) and (1.B) hold at the 4D
level; (1.C) holds at the 3D-cross-section reading.
Proposition [10.19](#prop:apparent-collapse){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:apparent-collapse"}.\
**Problem 2** (Statistics) & (2.A) + (2.B) force identical 4D evolution,
contradicting (2.C) Born-rule variability of outcomes. & (2.A) and (2.B)
hold at the 4D level; (2.C) holds across cross-section readings, with
$SO(3)$ Haar measure forcing the Born weights.
Proposition [10.13](#prop:born-rule-geometric){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:born-rule-geometric"}.\
**Problem 3** (Effect) & Dynamics of possessed properties between
measurements is underspecified. & Compton-frequency decoherence of
Proposition [10.36](#prop:preferred-basis-compton){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:preferred-basis-compton"} supplies the dynamics;
$x_4$-monotonicity of
Proposition [10.35](#prop:measurement-irreversibility){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:measurement-irreversibility"} supplies the
irreversibility; cross-species signature
$T_{\mathrm{dec},A}/T_{\mathrm{dec},B} = (m_B/m_A)^2$ is empirically
testable.\
:::
:::

The insight is one fact: *the wavefunction is a
four-dimensional geometric object on $\mathcal{M}_G$ whose
3D-cross-section reading at any spacetime event is the standard
quantum-mechanical wavefunction*. Maudlin's three problems become three
illustrations of the same insight, each dissolved by reading the
appropriate claim at the appropriate scale, with the resolution forced
by $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

### Proposition III.1: The Born rule as squared-amplitude geometry of $x_4$-wavefront cross-sections {#sec:born-rule-geometric}

::: {#prop:born-rule-geometric .proposition}
**Proposition 10.13** (The Born rule as theorem of
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; [@MG-Measurement-2026] Proposition III.1).
*The probability density of finding a quantum particle at spatial
position $\mathbf{x}$ at time $t$, given wavefunction
$\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)$, is
$$P(\mathbf{x}, t) \;=\; |\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)|^2,$$ as a forced
geometric consequence of three facts about $x_4$'s
spherically symmetric expansion: (i) the complex character of $\psi$ is
the perpendicularity marker of $x_4$ relative to the spatial three; (ii)
the squared exponent is the unique simple polynomial order producing a
positive-definite probability density that respects superposition and
gives correct interference patterns; (iii) the $SO(3)$ Haar measure on
the McGucken-wavefront cross-section forces the squared-amplitude form
on the angular distribution.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof; from [@MG-Measurement-2026] §III.1, three pieces.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof
proceeds in three pieces (each a Step), independently ruling
out alternatives to $|\psi|^2$ and jointly forcing the Born rule.

**Step 1 (Piece 1): Why $\psi$ is complex.** By
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, $x_4 = ict$, with the $i$ the perpendicularity
marker of $x_4$ relative to the spatial three. The wavefunction
$\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)$ is, by
Theorem [6.1](#thm:QMT6){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT6"}
(wave-particle duality as dual-channel reading), the 3D cross-section of
the four-dimensional McGucken-wavefront associated with the particle.
The four-dimensional object has both a spatial-three projection
(real-valued) and an $x_4$ projection (imaginary-valued), and the
complex amplitude $\psi = \mathrm{Re}\,\psi + i\,\mathrm{Im}\,\psi$
records both projections simultaneously. The complex structure of $\psi$
is therefore not a postulate; it is the algebraic expression of the
four-dimensional structure of the McGucken-wavefront, with $i$ tracking
the $x_4$-component. Real-valued wavefunctions exist as standing waves
but cannot account for the probability current
$\mathbf{j} = (\hbar/m)\,\mathrm{Im}(\psi^* \nabla\psi)$ or coherent
time-evolution.

**Step 2 (Piece 2): Why the exponent is 2 (not 1 or 3).** A probability
density derived from $\psi$ must satisfy four conditions:

-   (C1) Positivity: $P \ge 0$ at every spacetime point;

-   (C2) Normalisation: $\int P\,d^3x = 1$ for normalised $\psi$;

-   (C3) Superposition-respecting interference: cross-terms in
    $|\alpha\phi + \beta\chi|^2$ match observed double-slit patterns;

-   (C4) Lorentz-covariance as time-component of a four-current.

Consider the candidate exponents:

-   $P = |\psi|^1 = |\psi|$ violates (C3): for
    $\psi = \alpha\phi + \beta\chi$, $|\alpha\phi + \beta\chi|$ does not
    produce the cross-term $\cos\theta$ interference observed in
    double-slit, Mach--Zehnder, and matter-wave experiments;

-   $P = |\psi|^3$ violates (C2) for normalisable $\psi$ in 3D space
    without ad-hoc rescaling, and violates (C3) with the wrong
    cross-term functional form;

-   $P = \mathrm{Re}(\psi)$ alone violates (C1): $\psi$ may be purely
    imaginary, giving $\mathrm{Re}(\psi) = 0$ globally;

-   $P = \mathrm{Im}(\psi)$ alone is the symmetric problem;

-   $P = \mathrm{Re}(\psi)^2 + \mathrm{Im}(\psi)^2 = |\psi|^2$ satisfies
    all four: (C1) automatic; (C2) the $L^2$ normalisation condition;
    (C3) the cross-term $2\,\mathrm{Re}(\alpha^*\beta\,\phi^*\chi)$ in
    $|\alpha\phi + \beta\chi|^2$ is exactly the observed interference
    term; (C4) $\psi^*\psi$ is the time-component of the conserved
    Klein-Gordon current $j^\mu$;

-   $P = |\psi|^{2n}$ for $n > 1$ violates (C2) without ad-hoc rescaling
    and produces wrong higher-order correlations in interference.

The squared exponent is therefore *forced* by (C1)--(C4) combined with
observed interference. No other exponent works.

**Step 3 (Piece 3): $SO(3)$ Haar measure forces the squared form on
angular distributions.** The McGucken Sphere is a 2-sphere expanding at
speed $c$ from each spacetime event
(Definition [4.9](#def:sphere){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:sphere"}). Spherical symmetry of $x_4$'s expansion
(clause P2 of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$) forces $SO(3)$ invariance of the
angular distribution of the McGucken-wavefront cross-section. The unique
$SO(3)$-invariant measure on the 2-sphere is the $SO(3)$ Haar measure
$$d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}} = \sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi.$$ For a
wavefunction with angular structure
$\psi(r, \theta, \phi) = R(r) Y(\theta, \phi)$, the probability density
in solid angle is
$$P(\theta, \phi)\,d\Omega \propto |Y(\theta, \phi)|^2\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi.$$
The squared form $|Y|^2$ is forced by $SO(3)$-equivariance: any other
functional form (e.g. $|Y|$, $|Y|^3$, $\mathrm{Re}(Y)^2$) breaks
$SO(3)$-equivariance under change of polar axis, since complex
amplitudes $Y(\theta, \phi)$ acquire phases under $SO(3)$ rotation while
$|Y|^2$ is phase-invariant.

**Step 4: Combination of the three pieces.** Steps 1--3 together force
$P = |\psi|^2$:

-   Step 1 forces the complex wavefunction structure (from
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$'s perpendicularity marker);

-   Step 2 forces the squared exponent (from the four functional
    requirements C1--C4);

-   Step 3 forces the squared modulus on angular distributions (from
    $SO(3)$-Haar on the McGucken Sphere).

No other functional form $P[\psi]$ satisfies the joint constraints. The
three pieces jointly force $P = |\psi|^2$, the Born rule.

**Step 5: McGucken anchoring --- Born is forced by geometry
of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.** The Born rule is therefore not an
independent postulate of quantum mechanics but a forced theorem of the
McGucken Principle:

-   Complex wavefunction structure: from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$'s $i$
    (perpendicularity marker);

-   Squared exponent: from continuity-equation conservation under
    Schrödinger evolution (itself a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$,
    Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT7"})
    combined with C1--C4;

-   Squared modulus on angular distributions: from $SO(3)$-Haar
    uniqueness on the McGucken Sphere wavefront
    (Theorem [17.28](#thm:geometric-to-quantum-probability){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:geometric-to-quantum-probability"}, derived from
    clause P2 of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$).

**Step 6: Advantage over prior derivations.** The McGucken
derivation is the only Born-rule derivation that traces the rule to a
single underlying physical principle ($\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$) without
invoking auxiliary structure (Hilbert space, noncontextuality,
decision-theoretic axioms, Many-Worlds ontology, envariance hypothesis,
or infinite-repetition idealisation). Each prior derivation (Gleason
1957 [@Gleason1957], Deutsch-Wallace 1999/2012, Zurek 2003, Hartle 1968)
establishes Born conditional on additional structure; the McGucken
derivation is unconditional, supplying its auxiliary structure as
upstream theorems of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:born-rule-prior-comparisons .remark}
*Remark 10.14* (Comparison with prior Born-rule derivations;
[@MG-Measurement-2026] §III.2). The Born rule has been the subject of
multiple derivations from auxiliary axioms over ninety years. The
McGucken derivation differs from each:

-   *Gleason's theorem (1957)* [@Gleason1957]: derives Born from
    noncontextuality on Hilbert spaces of dimension $\geq 3$, but takes
    the Hilbert space and the noncontextuality assumption as starting
    points. The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework derives both: the Hilbert space
    follows from the linear superposition of McGucken-wavefronts
    (Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}), and noncontextuality follows
    from $SO(3)$ invariance of the cross-section (Piece 3 above).

-   *Decision-theoretic derivation (Deutsch 1999; Wallace 2012)*:
    derives Born within Many-Worlds from rationality axioms, but
    requires accepting (i) the equivalence of all branches as
    "real," (ii) specific rationality axioms (independence,
    transitivity, dominance), and (iii) the Many-Worlds ontology.

-   *Envariance (Zurek 2003)*: derives Born from environment-assisted
    invariance, but requires the assumption that the environment exists
    and is structured to produce envariance.

-   *Frequentist limits (Hartle 1968; Farhi--Goldstone--Gutmann 1989)*:
    derive Born from infinite-repetition limits, but require the
    infinite-repetition idealisation.

Each prior derivation establishes Born conditional on auxiliary
structure. The McGucken derivation is the only one that traces Born to a
single underlying physical principle ($\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$) without
invoking auxiliary structure.
:::

### Proposition IV.1: Superposition as geometric overlap of McGucken-Sphere wavefronts {#sec:superposition-geometric}

::: {#prop:superposition-geometric .proposition}
**Proposition 10.15** (Linear superposition as theorem of
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; [@MG-Measurement-2026] Proposition IV.1). *The
linear superposition principle of quantum mechanics --- that for any
normalised states $\lvert \psi \rangle, \lvert \phi \rangle$ and complex
coefficients $\alpha, \beta$ with $|\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1$ the
combination $\alpha\lvert \psi \rangle + \beta\lvert \phi \rangle$ is
also a physically realisable state --- is a forced consequence of three
facts about McGucken-Sphere wavefronts: (i) multiple
wavefronts emanating from distinct source events can coexist at a common
spacetime point, because $x_4$'s uniform advance does not select between
sources; (ii) the combination operation at a common field point is
forced to be linear addition with complex coefficients, by four
conditions $D_1$--$D_4$ on the combination operator (associativity,
commutativity, scaling, distributivity-with-phase); (iii) the
perpendicularity marker $i$ encodes relative phase between
contributions, since the mere integrated kinematic shadow $x_4 = ict$
descends from the dynamical principle $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ per
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof; from [@MG-Measurement-2026] §IV.1, three pieces.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has
three pieces, all anchored in McGucken-Sphere kinematics.

**Piece 1: Multi-wavefront coexistence at a common field point.** By
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (clause P1: principle applies at every event),
each spacetime source event $p_i$ initiates a McGucken-Sphere wavefront
$S_{p_i}$ expanding spherically at rate $c$. At a field point
$q = (\mathbf{x}_q, t_q)$ later in $x_{4}$-advance, the wavefront
$S_{p_i}$ passes through $q$ if and only if
$|q - p_i| = c(t_q - t_{p_i})$ (light-cone condition). For multiple
sources $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ satisfying this condition
simultaneously, all $n$ wavefronts are present at $q$ at the same
parameter time.

Crucially, the advance of $x_{4}$ at rate $ic$ is uniform across
sources: no source is preferentially selected by
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The coexistence of multiple wavefronts at a
common field point is therefore forced, not just allowed
--- it is the generic configuration whenever multiple emission events
lie on $q$'s past light cone.

**Piece 2: Combination operator is uniquely complex linear addition.**
At the field point $q$, the multiple wavefront contributions combine to
give a single physical amplitude $\psi_q$. Let $\oplus$ denote the
combination operator:
$\psi_q = \psi_1 \oplus \psi_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus \psi_n$. We require:

-   (D1) *Associativity:*
    $(\psi_1 \oplus \psi_2) \oplus \psi_3 = \psi_1 \oplus (\psi_2 \oplus \psi_3)$
    --- order of combination doesn't affect the result;

-   (D2) *Commutativity:* $\psi_1 \oplus \psi_2 = \psi_2 \oplus \psi_1$
    --- wavefronts are unordered;

-   (D3) *Scaling:*
    $(\lambda\psi_1) \oplus (\lambda\psi_2) = \lambda(\psi_1 \oplus \psi_2)$
    for real $\lambda$ --- uniform amplitude rescaling commutes with
    combination;

-   (D4) *Distributivity-with-phase:*
    $(e^{i\alpha}\psi_1) \oplus (e^{i\alpha}\psi_2) = e^{i\alpha}(\psi_1 \oplus \psi_2)$
    --- common phase factors out;

By the universal-algebra theorem on bilinear operations satisfying
(D1)--(D4) on a complex vector space, the unique operation is complex
linear addition: $\psi_1 \oplus \psi_2 = \psi_1 + \psi_2$ in the complex
amplitude space. Linear superposition with complex coefficients is
therefore forced by the four requirements.

**Piece 3: Relative phase encoded by the perpendicularity marker $i$.**
The relative phase between two wavefront contributions $\psi_1, \psi_2$
at a common field point $q$ is encoded by the principle's
perpendicularity marker $i$. Two source events $p_1, p_2$ at distinct
$x_{4}$-coordinates differ by $\Delta x_4 = ic\,\Delta t$; this
$x_{4}$-difference translates to a complex phase factor
$e^{i\Delta\phi}$ where $\Delta\phi = \omega\,\Delta t$ for plane-wave
modes (using Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:62"} action-per-Sphere-cycle).

The complex character of the phase is forced by the $i$ in
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: were the principle real-valued ($x_4 = ct$, no
$i$), the phase difference would be a real factor
$e^{c\,\Delta t/\hbar}$ producing exponential growth/decay, not bounded
oscillation. The McGucken-Principle $i$ ensures that wavefronts
interfere with bounded amplitudes, producing the standard
quantum-mechanical interference patterns observed in double-slit,
Mach--Zehnder, matter-wave, and many-particle experiments.

**Step 4: Combining the three pieces.** The three pieces force linear
superposition with complex coefficients on the wavefunction space:

-   Piece 1: multi-wavefront coexistence is forced by
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at every event;

-   Piece 2: the combination operator is uniquely complex linear
    addition by (D1)--(D4);

-   Piece 3: relative phases are complex, encoded by the
    McGucken-Principle $i$.

Together, these establish the linear superposition principle as a
theorem of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, not an independent postulate.

**Step 5: Geometric Channel characterisation.** The proof uses only
McGucken-Sphere kinematics (QB1, QB2: Sphere generation at every event,
Huygens iteration), the principle's perpendicularity marker $i$, and
universal-algebra constraints on the combination operator. No
Hilbert-space postulate, no Stone's theorem, no abstract linear-algebra
axiom is invoked at the level of the proof. The result is Geometric Channel
(geometric-propagation), establishing $(SP)$ as a
wavefront-superposition theorem.

**Step 6: Hilbert-space postulate $(Q_1)$ as theorem.** Combined with
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"} (Hilbert space as theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$), this proposition establishes that the
linear-superposition postulate $(Q_1)$ of the Dirac-von Neumann
formalism is fully derivable from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The McGucken
framework derives both $(Q_1)$ (superposition, this proposition) and
$(Q_3)$ (Born rule,
Proposition [10.13](#prop:born-rule-geometric){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:born-rule-geometric"}) from the single principle
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ --- the advantage over prior
frameworks that take both as primitive postulates. ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:linearity-not-postulate .remark}
*Remark 10.16* (The Hilbert-space postulate $(Q_1)$ as theorem). The
Hilbert-space postulate $(Q_1)$ of the Dirac--von Neumann
formalism --- that physical states form a complex separable Hilbert
space and physically realisable states are unit vectors in
$\mathcal{H}$ --- is in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework a theorem. Its linearity
is the algebraic consequence of
Proposition [10.15](#prop:superposition-geometric){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:superposition-geometric"}; the inner product,
completeness, and dimensionality follow from Theorems of
Ch. [9](#ch:hilbert-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:hilbert-theorem"} (Hilbert Space as Theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$,
Theorem [9.20](#thm:hilbert-as-theorem){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-as-theorem"}). The entire Hilbert-space machinery
descends as theorems from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.
:::

### Proposition V.1: Apparent collapse as 3D cross-section reading {#sec:apparent-collapse}

::: {#def:mcgucken-wavefunction .definition}
**Definition 10.17** (The McGucken wave function; [@MG-Measurement-2026]
Definition V.1). Let $p_0 = (\mathbf{x}_0, t_0)$ be a source event in
spacetime, and let $\Sigma_M(p_0, t)$ denote the McGucken Sphere --- the
spherical $x_4$-wavefront generated from $p_0$ by
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, expanding at the velocity of light $c$ over
the time interval $t - t_0$. The wave function $\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)$ at
the field point $\mathbf{x}$ is the complex amplitude carried by
$\Sigma_M(p_0, t)$ at the cross-section point $\mathbf{x}$, with the
complex character supplied by $i$ as the perpendicularity marker of
$x_4$ relative to the spatial axes, and the phase structure supplied by
the rate $c$ of $x_4$'s advance per unit time. The wave function is
therefore a physically real, four-dimensional, geometric object --- the
amplitude of a wavefront in physical space that propagates with $x_4$'s
expansion at the velocity of light --- with the standard 3D wave
function $\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)$ being the spatial-slice cross-section of
the underlying 4D structure $\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4)$ at the
McGucken-constraint locus $x_4 = ict$ (the mere integrated kinematic
shadow of the dynamical principle $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ per
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}).
:::

::: {#rmk:seven-ingredients .remark}
*Remark 10.18* (The seven ingredients of the wave function,
each derived). [@MG-Measurement-2026] §V.1.2 catalogues the seven
ingredients of $\psi$, each derived as a theorem of
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ rather than postulated:

1.  *Complex character of $\psi$:* the imaginary unit $i$ is the
    perpendicularity marker of $x_4$ (three-piece breakdown of Piece 1
    of
    Proposition [10.13](#prop:born-rule-geometric){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:born-rule-geometric"}).

2.  *Phase rate $\omega = E/\hbar$:* the de Broglie--Planck--Einstein
    relation, derived in Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT4"} from the rate $c$ of $x_4$-advance and the
    energy carried by the wavefront.

3.  *Wavefront propagation:* each source event generates a spherical
    wavefront expanding at $c$; Huygens' principle is a theorem of this
    structure
    (Theorem [17.14](#thm:huygens-of-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:huygens-of-nonlocality"}).

4.  *Linearity and superposition:* forced by
    Proposition [10.15](#prop:superposition-geometric){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:superposition-geometric"}.

5.  *Schrödinger equation:* the combination of phase advance, wavefront
    expansion at $c$, and superposition produces the wave equation; the
    non-relativistic limit produces Schrödinger.

6.  *Born rule:* the $SO(3)$ Haar measure on the spherical
    cross-section, $|\psi|^2$
    (Proposition [10.13](#prop:born-rule-geometric){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:born-rule-geometric"}).

7.  *Multi-particle entanglement structure:* tensor products of
    single-particle wavefront structure, with joint $x_4$-extended state
    encoding entanglement; configuration space is $N$ copies of
    $\mathcal{M}_G$ joined by McGucken Sphere structure.

Each step is a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The wave function in
the McGucken framework is specifically the complex amplitude of a
spherically-expanding $x_4$-wavefront, with every aspect of its
mathematical form being a derivation rather than a postulate.
:::

::: {#prop:apparent-collapse .proposition}
**Proposition 10.19** (Apparent collapse as 3D cross-section of 4D
unitary evolution; [@MG-Measurement-2026] Proposition V.1). *Let
$\lvert \Psi(t) \rangle = \sum_k c_k\,\lvert s_k \rangle \otimes \lvert A_k \rangle \otimes \lvert E_k \rangle$
be the unitarily evolved entangled system-apparatus-environment state at
coordinate time $t$, with system eigenstates $\lvert s_k \rangle$,
apparatus pointer states $\lvert A_k \rangle$, and environmental states
$\lvert E_k \rangle$. An observer at spatial location
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ accesses only the 3D cross-section
$\pi_{\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}}\lvert \Psi(t) \rangle$ of the
four-dimensional state. The cross-section reading is, by the Born rule
(Proposition [10.13](#prop:born-rule-geometric){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:born-rule-geometric"}), a single branch
$\lvert s_k \rangle \otimes \lvert A_k \rangle \otimes \lvert E_k \rangle$
with probability $|c_k|^2$. The apparent collapse is the observer's
restricted access to one branch of the unitarily evolved state.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has four steps: characterise the 4D state, define the
3D projection, apply the Born rule, identify the apparent collapse.

**Step 1: Unitary evolution preserves the full superposition on
$M_{G}$.** By Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT7"} (the Schrödinger equation as a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$) and
Lemma [7.2](#lem:time-translation-unitary){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:time-translation-unitary"} (time evolution is unitary),
the system-apparatus-environment state $\lvert \Psi(t) \rangle$ evolves
unitarily on the four-dimensional manifold $M_{G}$. The entangled
superposition
$\sum_k c_k\,\lvert s_k \rangle\otimes\lvert A_k \rangle\otimes\lvert E_k \rangle$
is preserved in full at every coordinate time $t$; no terms vanish, no
probabilities concentrate, no collapse occurs at the 4D level.

**Step 2: Observer access is restricted to a 3D cross-section.** An
observer at spatial location $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ accesses only
the spatial cross-section
$\Sigma_t \cap \{\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}\}$ of the 4D
state at coordinate time $t$. The projection operator
$\pi_{\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}}$ formalises this restriction: it maps
the full 4D wavefunction to its value at $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ on
the spatial slice $\Sigma_t$. This is a feature of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: $x_{4}$-advance is the principle, and the
spatial slice $\mathbb{R}^3$ is the sliced cross-section accessible to a
co-moving observer.

**Step 3: Born rule selects a single branch.** By
Theorem [19.1](#thm:QMT19){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT19"}
(Geometric Channel reading of measurement) and
Proposition [10.13](#prop:born-rule-geometric){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:born-rule-geometric"}, the 3D cross-section reading at
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ at coordinate time $t$ registers a single
branch
$\lvert s_k \rangle\otimes\lvert A_k \rangle\otimes\lvert E_k \rangle$
with probability $$\Pr(\text{branch } k) = |c_k|^2.$$ The Born rule is
the calibration of the cross-section intensity to outcome
probability (Theorem [11.1](#thm:QMT11-channelA){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT11-channelA"}); it does not invoke a separate collapse
dynamics.

**Step 4: Apparent collapse identification.** The "collapse of the
wavefunction" that observers report at the moment of measurement is the
operational manifestation of this restricted 3D access: the full 4D
state remains in superposition, but the observer's cross-section access
registers only one branch. The textbook framing of collapse as a
separate dynamical law (von Neumann's projection postulate) is
redundant in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework: the projection is the
kinematic consequence of $x_{4}$-sliced observer access. No additional
dynamical law is required to explain measurement outcomes. ◻
:::

### The Stern--Gerlach experiment as the canonical test of the dual-channel architecture {#sec:stern-gerlach-canonical-test}

::: flushright
*"Der experimentelle Nachweis der Richtungsquantelung im Magnetfeld"\
--- Gerlach & Stern, the founding empirical fact of spatial quantisation
in the magnetic field, Frankfurt am Main, 1922 [@Stern1922Gerlach]*
:::

The 1922 Stern--Gerlach experiment
[@Stern1922Gerlach; @FriedrichHerschbach2003] is the canonical worked
example for the framework's account of *how probability arises*, *what
measurement is*, and *why the McGucken Principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ supplies the explanation of both*. A
beam of silver atoms, prepared by evaporation from an oven and
collimated to a narrow forward velocity distribution, is passed through
an inhomogeneous magnetic field with a strong gradient $\partial_z B_z$
perpendicular to the beam direction; on a downstream screen the beam
splits into *exactly two spots*, never a continuum, with the spots
displaced along the gradient axis. The result is the founding empirical
fact of spatial quantisation, and it is, in the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, the
cleanest geometric demonstration that von Neumann's Process 1 and
Process 2 (§[1.10](#sec:two-faces-of-one-reality){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:two-faces-of-one-reality"}) are two faces of one physical
process and not two independent facts.

This section supplies the full McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework derivation of the
Stern--Gerlach result. We establish: (1) a precise definition of the
experimental setup as a four-dimensional geometric configuration on the
McGucken manifold $M_{G}$; (2) the spatial-separation theorem and its
symbolic verification; (3) the Born-rule probability assignment for the
two outcomes; (4) the identification of Process 1 with the
four-dimensional Sphere's three-dimensional registration at the detector
and Process 2 with the Sphere's four-dimensional propagation through the
apparatus; and (5) the dissolution of the textbook measurement problem
on this concrete case. Three corollaries (repeated-measurement
persistence, sequential-apparatus phenomenology, hidden-classical-spin
falsification) and three remarks complete the section.

#### Setup as a four-dimensional geometric configuration {#ssec:SG-setup}

::: {#def:SG-setup .definition}
**Definition 10.20** (Stern--Gerlach setup as a McGucken-manifold
configuration). The Stern--Gerlach experiment is defined by four
geometric ingredients on the McGucken manifold
$M_{G}= (\mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{R}, \eta)$ with metric signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ generated from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ by squaring
(§[1.11.1](#ssec:mcgucken-wick-five-axes){reference-type="ref"
reference="ssec:mcgucken-wick-five-axes"}, Axis 1):

1.  *Source region* $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$: a localised oven from
    which neutral silver atoms ($Z = 47$, ground configuration
    $[\text{Kr}]\,4d^{10}\,5s^1$, with a single unpaired $5s$ valence
    electron supplying total angular momentum $J = 1/2$ from pure spin,
    since $L = 0$) emerge with a forward-velocity distribution centred
    on $\mathbf{v}_y$ and with the spin orientation determined by the
    source preparation. The McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_M(p_0, t)$ generated
    at each emission event
    $p_0 = (\mathbf{x}_0, t_0) \in S \times \mathbb{R}$ carries the full
    complex-amplitude content of the atom's wavefunction
    (Definition [10.17](#def:mcgucken-wavefunction){reference-type="ref"
    reference="def:mcgucken-wavefunction"} of
    §[10.6](#sec:apparent-collapse){reference-type="ref"
    reference="sec:apparent-collapse"}).

2.  *Magnet region* $M \subset \mathbb{R}^3$: a region in which a strong
    inhomogeneous magnetic field $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})$ is established
    with the dominant component along $\hat{z}$ and a non-zero gradient
    $\partial_z B_z \neq 0$. The atom's magnetic moment
    $\bm{\mu} = -g_s \mu_B \mathbf{S}/\hbar$ couples to the field
    through the Pauli Hamiltonian
    $\hat{H}_{\text{int}} = -\bm{\mu} \cdot \mathbf{B}$.

3.  *Detector region* $D \subset \mathbb{R}^3$: a downstream screen on
    which atoms register at well-defined spatial positions, recording
    the post-traversal spatial distribution of the beam.

4.  *Traversal time* $T \in \mathbb{R}$: the elapsed time between exit
    from $S$ and arrival at $D$, equal to $L_{SD}/|\mathbf{v}_y|$ where
    $L_{SD}$ is the source--detector separation along the beam
    direction.

The four ingredients constitute a four-dimensional geometric
configuration on $M_{G}$ with the following feature: at every
event $p \in M_{G}$ along the atom's worldline, the McGucken Sphere
$\Sigma_M(p, t)$ is expanding at the velocity of light by
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, with the complex amplitude content (the
wavefunction) propagating with it.
:::

::: {#rmk:why-silver .remark}
*Remark 10.21* (Why silver). The choice of silver is non-accidental and is recorded in the 1922 papers
[@Stern1922Gerlach; @FriedrichHerschbach2003]. Silver's $5s^1$ valence
electron supplies $J = 1/2$ with $L = 0$, so the magnetic moment is pure
spin and the experiment probes the spin-$1/2$ structure directly. The
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework's reading: the silver atom's McGucken Sphere carries
spin-$1/2$ content because the underlying Dirac structure
(Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:dirac"})
requires $4\pi$ periodicity --- the McGucken Sphere expands at $c$ from
the source event, with the phase advance per Compton period
$\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ traversing a $4\pi$ rotation in $SU(2)$ rather
than the $2\pi$ rotation of $SO(3)$. The two-spot Stern--Gerlach pattern
is the experimental signature of this $4\pi$ periodicity: only two $S_z$
eigenvalues are present because the $SU(2)$ representation associated
with the silver atom's $x_4$-evolution has dimension two.
:::

#### The spatial-separation theorem {#ssec:SG-spatial-separation}

::: {#thm:SG-spatial-separation .theorem}
**Theorem 10.22** (Stern--Gerlach spatial separation; Geometric Channel and
Algebraic Channel derivations). *Under the setup of
Definition [10.20](#def:SG-setup){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:SG-setup"}, with traversal time $T$ and gradient
$\partial_z B_z$, a silver atom in spin eigenstate $S_z = +\hbar/2$ is
deflected along the $+\hat{z}$ axis by displacement
$z_\uparrow = +\tfrac{1}{4}\gamma\hbar(\partial_z B_z)T^2/m$, where
$\gamma = g_s\mu_B/\hbar$ is the gyromagnetic ratio. A silver atom in
spin eigenstate $S_z = -\hbar/2$ is deflected by displacement
$z_\downarrow = -\tfrac{1}{4}\gamma\hbar(\partial_z B_z)T^2/m$. The
total spatial separation between the two outcomes on the detector screen
is therefore
$$\Delta z \;=\; z_\uparrow - z_\downarrow \;=\; \frac{\gamma\hbar(\partial_z B_z)T^2}{2m},$$
with the two spots arising at $\pm\Delta z/2$ from the undeflected beam
axis. No intermediate spots, and no continuum of deflections, appear.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). *Algebraic Channel derivation.* The Pauli Hamiltonian in the field
gradient is
$\hat{H}_{\text{int}} = -\hat{\bm{\mu}}\cdot\mathbf{B} = -\gamma \hat{\mathbf{S}}\cdot\mathbf{B}$.
With $\mathbf{B} = B_z(z)\hat{z}$ to leading order in the gradient,
$\hat{H}_{\text{int}} = -\gamma B_z(z)\hat{S}_z$. The classical force on
the atom's centre of mass, derived from the Hamiltonian by Ehrenfest's
theorem
$\langle \hat{F}_z\rangle = -\langle\partial_z\hat{H}_{\text{int}}\rangle = \gamma\langle\hat{S}_z\rangle(\partial_z B_z)$,
supplies the Newtonian acceleration
$a_z = \gamma\langle\hat{S}_z\rangle(\partial_z B_z)/m$. For an atom
prepared in the $S_z = +\hbar/2$ eigenstate,
$\langle\hat{S}_z\rangle = +\hbar/2$ at all times in the absence of
competing precession (since the spin commutes with
$\hat{H}_{\text{int}}$ when the gradient is parallel to the spin axis).
The kinematic equation
$z_\uparrow(T) = \tfrac{1}{2}a_z T^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(\gamma\hbar(\partial_z B_z)/2m)T^2 = +\tfrac{1}{4}\gamma\hbar(\partial_z B_z)T^2/m$.
The analogous derivation for $S_z = -\hbar/2$ gives
$z_\downarrow(T) = -\tfrac{1}{4}\gamma\hbar(\partial_z B_z)T^2/m$. The
separation is
$\Delta z = z_\uparrow - z_\downarrow = \gamma\hbar(\partial_z B_z)T^2/(2m)$.
The only-two-spots feature follows from the spectrum of $\hat{S}_z$: by
QM T9 (Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:dirac"}, the Dirac equation and spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$), the
$5s^1$ silver atom has $\sigma(\hat{S}_z) = \{+\hbar/2, -\hbar/2\}$,
with no other eigenvalues; the discreteness of the spectrum is the
algebraic-symmetry content of Algebraic Channel's $SU(2)$ Lie algebra, with the
two eigenvalues corresponding to the two basis elements of the
spin-$1/2$ representation.

*Geometric Channel derivation.* The silver atom emerges from the source event
$p_0 \in S \times \mathbb{R}$ carrying a four-dimensional McGucken
Sphere $\Sigma_M(p_0, t)$ expanding at the velocity of light from $p_0$
by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The Sphere's spin content is the
$4\pi$-periodic Dirac structure
(Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:dirac"},
QM T9): the Sphere's expansion in $x_4$ encodes a phase advance at the
Compton rate $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$, and the $4\pi$ periodicity of the
silver atom's $SU(2)$ representation forces the spin content to split
into exactly two oppositely-oriented sub-spheres,
$\Sigma_M^{(\uparrow)}(p_0, t)$ and $\Sigma_M^{(\downarrow)}(p_0, t)$,
corresponding to the two $S_z$ eigenstates. In the magnet region $M$,
the inhomogeneous field gradient couples differentially to the two
sub-spheres through the Pauli term: the sub-sphere
$\Sigma_M^{(\uparrow)}$ acquires a $+\hat{z}$-directed centre-of-mass
impulse $\Delta p_z = \gamma(\hbar/2)(\partial_z B_z)T$, while
$\Sigma_M^{(\downarrow)}$ acquires the equal-and-opposite impulse
$-\gamma(\hbar/2)(\partial_z B_z)T$. The centre-of-mass positions of the
two sub-spheres at time $T$ are therefore separated by
$\Delta z = \gamma\hbar(\partial_z B_z)T^2/(2m)$, matching the Algebraic Channel
result. The two-and-only-two count of sub-spheres follows from the
geometric content of Geometric Channel's $SU(2)$ representation on the moving
four-manifold: the $4\pi$ periodicity of the Sphere's $x_4$-evolution
forces the spin-$1/2$ representation to be two-dimensional, with no
third sub-sphere available.

The two derivations converge on the same predictions
($\Delta z = \gamma\hbar(\partial_z B_z)T^2/(2m)$; two-spot pattern)
through derivationally disjoint chains: Algebraic Channel invokes the Pauli
Hamiltonian, Ehrenfest's theorem, and the $SU(2)$ Lie-algebra spectrum;
Geometric Channel invokes the iterated McGucken Sphere, the $4\pi$-periodic
Dirac structure, and the differential coupling of two sub-spheres to the
field gradient. Symbolic verification of the algebraic content is
supplied by
Lemma [10.23](#lem:SG-symbolic-separation){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:SG-symbolic-separation"} below. ◻
:::

::: {#lem:SG-symbolic-separation .lemma}
**Lemma 10.23** (Symbolic verification of the Stern--Gerlach
spatial-separation formula). *Direct symbolic computation in SymPy:*

-   *Spin-up trajectory:
    $z_\uparrow(t) = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\gamma\hbar/(2m)\bigr)(\partial_z B_z)\,t^2 = \tfrac{1}{4}\gamma\hbar(\partial_z B_z)t^2/m$.*

-   *Spin-down trajectory:
    $z_\downarrow(t) = -\tfrac{1}{4}\gamma\hbar(\partial_z B_z)t^2/m$.*

-   *Spatial separation at time $t$:
    $\Delta z(t) = z_\uparrow(t) - z_\downarrow(t) = \tfrac{1}{2}\gamma\hbar(\partial_z B_z)t^2/m$.*

*The separation is exact (no approximations), positive for
$\partial_z B_z > 0$, scales quadratically with traversal time, and is
proportional to $\gamma\hbar/m$. ◻*
:::

#### The Born-rule probability assignment {#ssec:SG-Born-rule}

The spatial-separation theorem
(Theorem [10.22](#thm:SG-spatial-separation){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:SG-spatial-separation"}) gives the deflection of a silver
atom *prepared in an $S_z$ eigenstate*. For an atom prepared in an
arbitrary spin orientation $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ at angle $\theta$ from the
apparatus $\hat{z}$-axis, the spin state is the superposition
$$\lvert +\hat{\mathbf{n}} \rangle \;=\; \cos(\theta/2)\lvert \uparrow \rangle_z \,+\, e^{i\varphi}\sin(\theta/2)\lvert \downarrow \rangle_z,$$
and the outcome at the detector is random, with probabilities supplied
by the Born rule. We derive the probability assignment as a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the framework's existing Born-rule chapter
(QM T11, Chapter [11](#ch:born){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:born"}) applied to the spin-1/2 case.

::: {#thm:SG-Born-rule .theorem}
**Theorem 10.24** (Stern--Gerlach Born-rule probability). *A silver atom
prepared in spin state $\lvert +\hat{\mathbf{n}} \rangle$ at angle
$\theta$ from the apparatus $\hat{z}$-axis, fed into a Stern--Gerlach
apparatus measuring $S_z$, produces the spin-up outcome (deflection
$+\Delta z/2$) with probability $P(\uparrow) = \cos^2(\theta/2)$ and the
spin-down outcome (deflection $-\Delta z/2$) with probability
$P(\downarrow) = \sin^2(\theta/2)$. The total probability
$P(\uparrow) + P(\downarrow) = 1$, and the probability assignment is
independent of the azimuthal phase $\varphi$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). *Algebraic Channel derivation.* The standard Born-rule projection gives
$P(\uparrow) = |\langle\uparrow|+\hat{\mathbf{n}}\rangle|^2 = |\cos(\theta/2)|^2 = \cos^2(\theta/2)$
and
$P(\downarrow) = |\langle\downarrow|+\hat{\mathbf{n}}\rangle|^2 = |e^{i\varphi}\sin(\theta/2)|^2 = \sin^2(\theta/2)$.
The squaring is forced by the Algebraic Channel derivation of Born from the
bilinearity of the inner product on $\mathcal{H}$ plus the requirement
of phase invariance (Chapter [11](#ch:born){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:born"}, Algebraic Channel subsection); the perpendicularity of
$x_4$ to the spatial three (Axis 1 of
§[1.11.1](#ssec:mcgucken-wick-five-axes){reference-type="ref"
reference="ssec:mcgucken-wick-five-axes"}) forces the wavefunction to be
complex, and the unique phase-invariant real non-negative scalar is
$|\psi|^2$
(Lemma [10.25](#lem:phase-invariant-scalar){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phase-invariant-scalar"} below).

*Geometric Channel derivation.* The silver atom's McGucken Sphere
$\Sigma_M(p_0, t)$ is, by
Theorem [10.22](#thm:SG-spatial-separation){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:SG-spatial-separation"}, split into two
oppositely-oriented sub-spheres $\Sigma_M^{(\uparrow)}$ and
$\Sigma_M^{(\downarrow)}$. For an atom prepared in
$\lvert +\hat{\mathbf{n}} \rangle$, the source-event amplitude content
of the two sub-spheres is $\cos(\theta/2)$ for $\Sigma_M^{(\uparrow)}$
and $e^{i\varphi}\sin(\theta/2)$ for $\Sigma_M^{(\downarrow)}$. The
probability that the atom registers at the upper spot on the detector
is, by the $SO(3)$-Haar Geometric Channel derivation of Born
(Chapter [11](#ch:born){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:born"},
Geometric Channel subsection), the squared magnitude of the upper sub-sphere's
source amplitude integrated over the geometric cross-section at the
detector:
$P(\uparrow) = |\cos(\theta/2)|^2\int d\Omega_{SO(3)} = \cos^2(\theta/2)$,
with the $SO(3)$-Haar measure normalised so the integral over a single
sub-sphere's solid-angle content is unity. The analogous computation
gives $P(\downarrow) = \sin^2(\theta/2)$. The total
$P(\uparrow) + P(\downarrow) = \cos^2(\theta/2) + \sin^2(\theta/2) = 1$
by the Pythagorean identity. The $\varphi$-independence follows from the
phase invariance of the squared magnitude.

The two derivations converge on the same probability assignment through
derivationally disjoint chains, giving the convergent-overdetermination
signature of §[1.9](#sec:remarkable-feature){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:remarkable-feature"} for the Born rule applied to
spin-1/2. ◻
:::

::: {#lem:phase-invariant-scalar .lemma}
**Lemma 10.25** ($|\psi|^2$ as the unique phase-invariant real
non-negative scalar of a complex amplitude). *Let $\psi = a + ib$ with
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ be the complex amplitude content of a McGucken
Sphere at a spatial-slice cross-section. Under the phase rotation
$\psi \mapsto \psi e^{i\varphi}$, the real-valued bilinear scalar
functions of $(a,b)$ that are non-negative and phase-invariant form a
one-parameter family parameterised by an overall normalisation constant;
the unique phase-invariant real non-negative scalar with unit
normalisation is $|\psi|^2 = a^2 + b^2$. The real part
$\mathrm{Re}(\psi) = a$ and the imaginary part $\mathrm{Im}(\psi) = b$
are *not* phase-invariant: under $\psi \mapsto \psi e^{i\varphi}$,
$\mathrm{Re}(\psi) \mapsto a\cos\varphi - b\sin\varphi$ and
$\mathrm{Im}(\psi) \mapsto a\sin\varphi + b\cos\varphi$. Direct symbolic
verification:
$|\psi e^{i\varphi}|^2 = (\psi e^{i\varphi})^*(\psi e^{i\varphi}) = \psi^*\psi = |\psi|^2$.
◻*
:::

::: {#cor:SG-Born-angles .corollary}
**Corollary 10.26** (Born probabilities at canonical angles). *The
Born-rule probabilities at four canonical angles are: (i) $\theta = 0$
(eigenstate $\lvert \uparrow \rangle_z$): $P(\uparrow) = 1$,
$P(\downarrow) = 0$ --- deterministic upper-spot deflection. (ii)
$\theta = \pi/2$ (eigenstate of $\hat{S}_x$ or $\hat{S}_y$, "unbiased"
atom): $P(\uparrow) = P(\downarrow) = 1/2$ --- maximally indeterminate,
50/50 statistics. (iii) $\theta = \pi$ (eigenstate
$\lvert \downarrow \rangle_z$): $P(\uparrow) = 0$,
$P(\downarrow) = 1$ --- deterministic lower-spot deflection. (iv)
$\theta = \pi/3$: $P(\uparrow) = 3/4$,
$P(\downarrow) = 1/4$ --- asymmetric statistics governed by the angular
geometry. These four canonical cases match the empirical predictions of
standard quantum mechanics and have been verified to high precision in
modern Stern--Gerlach-style experiments on a variety of atomic and
molecular species. ◻*
:::

#### Process 1 and Process 2 on the Stern--Gerlach apparatus {#ssec:SG-process-1-2}

The two-process identification of
§[1.10](#sec:two-faces-of-one-reality){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:two-faces-of-one-reality"}
(Remark [1.3](#rmk:vonneumann-architecture-1932){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:vonneumann-architecture-1932"}) is exemplified on the
Stern--Gerlach setup in geometric detail.

::: {#thm:SG-process-1-2 .theorem}
**Theorem 10.27** (Process 1 / Process 2 identification on
Stern--Gerlach). *The two von Neumann processes operate on the
Stern--Gerlach silver atom as follows:*

-   **Process 2 during traversal* ($p_0 \to D$): The atom's McGucken
    Sphere $\Sigma_M(p_0, t)$ propagates continuously and reversibly
    through the source-to-detector trajectory, with the unitary
    $x_4$-evolution $U(t) = e^{-i\hat{H}t/\hbar}$ governing the Sphere's
    phase and the two sub-spheres $\Sigma_M^{(\uparrow)}$ and
    $\Sigma_M^{(\downarrow)}$ propagating side-by-side, each picking up
    the differential spatial impulse derived in
    Theorem [10.22](#thm:SG-spatial-separation){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:SG-spatial-separation"}. The process is continuous,
    deterministic, reversible (the trajectory could in principle be
    reversed by reversing the field gradient direction and the initial
    velocity), and four-dimensional (the Sphere is an object on $M_{G}$
    with three spatial dimensions plus the moving $x_4$).*

-   **Process 1 at the detector* ($D$): The atom's McGucken Sphere
    intersects the detector region $D \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ on a single
    three-dimensional spatial slice; the four-dimensional Sphere content
    is localised at the apparatus-intersection event by the geometric
    incidence of the Sphere with the apparatus's three-dimensional
    registration surface. The localisation is the geometric content of
    Process 1: the four-dimensional content of $\Sigma_M(p_0, T)$,
    distributed over the entire sphere of radius $cT$ around $p_0$, is
    registered at a single point of the detector. The process is
    discontinuous (the Sphere's three-dimensional projection on the
    detector slice is a single point), indeterministic (the Born-rule
    probabilities of
    Theorem [10.24](#thm:SG-Born-rule){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:SG-Born-rule"} govern which spot the atom registers
    at), irreversible (the localisation is not reversible by any local
    apparatus operation), and three-dimensional (the registration is on
    a single spatial slice).*

*The two processes are the two faces of the McGucken Sphere's
four-dimensional / three-dimensional duality: Process 2 is the
four-dimensional content of the Sphere on $M_{G}$, Process 1 is the
three-dimensional registration of that content at the detector slice.
Both processes are theorems of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: Process 2 from
the principle's geometric content (the Sphere's expansion at the
velocity of light), Process 1 from the principle's three-dimensional
projection at the detector locus (the Sphere's intersection with the
apparatus's spatial slice).*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The identification follows directly from the
differential-response theorem
(Theorem [1.5](#thm:channel-differential-response){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:channel-differential-response"}) applied to the
Stern--Gerlach configuration. Algebraic Channel's unitary group
$U(t) = e^{-i\hat{H}t/\hbar}$ is the operational content of Process 2
during traversal; under the McGucken-Wick rotation, Algebraic Channel's group
structure dissolves to a semigroup, and the discontinuous projection
operator
$\hat{P}_\uparrow = \lvert \uparrow \rangle\langle \uparrow \rvert$ at
the detector is a non-invertible projector representing the geometric
three-dimensional localisation. Geometric Channel's iterated McGucken Sphere
derivation is transported by the Wick rotation through its signature
change, with the Sphere geometry preserved; the four-dimensional Sphere
is the operational content of Process 2 (its expansion on $M_{G}$), and
the three-dimensional localisation at the detector is the operational
content of Process 1 (the Sphere's intersection with the apparatus
slice). The differential response of the two channels to the Wick
rotation gives the distinction between the two processes:
irreversible-discontinuous-indeterministic at the apparatus (Process 1)
vs. reversible-continuous-deterministic during traversal (Process 2).
Both processes are derivations from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, with the
apparent "collapse" being the geometric three-dimensional reading of the
four-dimensional Sphere on the detector slice (Proposition V.1 of
§[10.6](#sec:apparent-collapse){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:apparent-collapse"}). ◻
:::

::: {#thm:SG-measurement-event .theorem}
**Theorem 10.28** (The measurement event as McGucken-Sphere--detector
intersection). *A measurement event in the Stern--Gerlach setup is the
geometric intersection of the silver atom's McGucken Sphere
$\Sigma_M(p_0, T)$ with the detector region $D \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ on
the spatial slice at time $t = T$. The intersection is a single point of
$D$ (the registration locus), selected from the two-spot support of the
post-traversal Sphere by the geometric incidence of the Sphere with the
apparatus's microscopic registration mechanism (e.g., a fluorescent
silver atom striking a photographic plate at one of two displacements
$\pm\Delta z/2$). The selection is probabilistic in the Born-rule sense
(Theorem [10.24](#thm:SG-Born-rule){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:SG-Born-rule"}) because the apparatus's microscopic
registration mechanism samples the Sphere's complex amplitude content
with weight $|\psi|^2$ at each candidate registration locus, by the
unique phase-invariance of the squared magnitude
(Lemma [10.25](#lem:phase-invariant-scalar){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:phase-invariant-scalar"}). The selection is irreversible
because the apparatus's registration mechanism (the photographic plate's
chemical change, the photomultiplier's electronic chain of theorems, or any
analogous macroscopic-amplification process) is a thermodynamic process
with positive entropy production, by the second law applied to the
apparatus. The selection is discontinuous because the Sphere's
two-sub-sphere structure
(Theorem [10.22](#thm:SG-spatial-separation){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:SG-spatial-separation"}) has support only at the two
spots $\pm\Delta z/2$, not at intermediate displacements.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The geometric content of the intersection is supplied by
Definition [10.17](#def:mcgucken-wavefunction){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:mcgucken-wavefunction"} (the McGucken wavefunction as
cross-section of the four-dimensional Sphere). The probabilistic weight
is supplied by the Born-rule chapter (QM T11,
Chapter [11](#ch:born){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:born"})
applied to the spin-1/2 case. The irreversibility is supplied by the
thermodynamic content of the apparatus's macroscopic-amplification
process, which is independent of the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework and follows from
the standard second law of thermodynamics; the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework
supplies the reason for the apparent collapse (the
four-dimensional Sphere's three-dimensional registration) but does not
modify the thermodynamic irreversibility of the amplification step. The
discontinuity follows from the two-eigenvalue spectrum of $\hat{S}_z$
for the spin-1/2 silver atom, which by
Theorem [10.22](#thm:SG-spatial-separation){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:SG-spatial-separation"} gives only two candidate
registration loci on the detector. ◻
:::

#### Three corollaries on the dissolution of the textbook measurement problem {#ssec:SG-corollaries}

::: {#cor:SG-repeated .corollary}
**Corollary 10.29** (Repeated Stern--Gerlach with the same setting
yields the same outcome). *Let an atom be prepared in spin state
$\lvert +\hat{\mathbf{n}} \rangle$ and fed through a first
Stern--Gerlach apparatus measuring $\hat{S}_z$, registering at the upper
spot with probability $\cos^2(\theta/2)$. Suppose the registration is
upper. The post-registration state of the atom (its surviving McGucken
Sphere content after the apparatus interaction) is
$\lvert \uparrow \rangle_z$, since the three-dimensional registration at
the upper spot has selected the upper sub-sphere $\Sigma_M^{(\uparrow)}$
from the pre-traversal superposition. Feeding this atom into a second
Stern--Gerlach apparatus also measuring $\hat{S}_z$ (with the same
gradient direction): the atom is now in the $S_z = +\hbar/2$ eigenstate,
so by Theorem [10.24](#thm:SG-Born-rule){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:SG-Born-rule"} at $\theta = 0$, the registration
probability at the second apparatus is $P(\uparrow) = 1$,
$P(\downarrow) = 0$. The outcome is deterministic and identical to the
first measurement. The empirical fact of repeated-measurement
persistence (Maudlin's Problem 3 in its strongest form) is dissolved on
the Stern--Gerlach case by the geometric content of
Theorem [10.28](#thm:SG-measurement-event){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:SG-measurement-event"}: the apparatus's first
registration selected $\Sigma_M^{(\uparrow)}$, and the surviving Sphere
is now an $S_z = +\hbar/2$ eigenstate Sphere, which registers at the
upper spot deterministically. ◻*
:::

::: {#cor:SG-sequential .corollary}
**Corollary 10.30** (Sequential Stern--Gerlach with different settings
reproduces standard quantum mechanics). *Let an atom be prepared in the
$S_z = +\hbar/2$ eigenstate, fed through an $\hat{S}_x$ apparatus, then
through an $\hat{S}_z$ apparatus. The first apparatus measures
$\hat{S}_x$ on the $\lvert \uparrow \rangle_z$ state: at
$\theta = \pi/2$, the registration probabilities are
$P(+\hat{x}) = P(-\hat{x}) = 1/2$. Suppose the registration is
$+\hat{x}$; the post-registration state is
$\lvert +\hat{x} \rangle = (\lvert \uparrow \rangle_z + \lvert \downarrow \rangle_z)/\sqrt{2}$.
The second apparatus measures $\hat{S}_z$ on this state: the
registration probabilities are $P(\uparrow) = P(\downarrow) = 1/2$. The
atom does *not* retain its original $S_z = +\hbar/2$ value, because the
$\hat{S}_x$ measurement at the first apparatus selected an $S_x$
eigenstate Sphere that is a superposition of $S_z$ eigenstates. The
sequential-apparatus phenomenology is the standard textbook result,
reproduced as a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the geometric
content of
Theorem [10.28](#thm:SG-measurement-event){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:SG-measurement-event"}. ◻*
:::

::: {#cor:SG-falsifies-classical-spin .corollary}
**Corollary 10.31** (The Stern--Gerlach result falsifies
hidden-classical-spin interpretations). *Suppose, contrary to the
McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework reading, that the silver atom possesses a hidden
classical magnetic moment vector $\bm{\mu}_{\text{cl}}$ at every spatial
direction $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$, with the direction $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$
being a determinate but unknown property of the atom. Then the
deflection of the atom in the Stern--Gerlach apparatus would be
proportional to
$\bm{\mu}_{\text{cl}}\cdot\hat{z} = |\bm{\mu}_{\text{cl}}|\cos\alpha$
where $\alpha$ is the angle between the hidden direction and the
apparatus axis. Averaged over a beam of atoms with isotropically
distributed hidden directions, the deflection distribution would be
continuous and symmetric, with the maximum density at zero deflection
(the bulk of $\cos\alpha$-weighted directions). The empirical
Stern--Gerlach result --- two discrete spots at $\pm\Delta z/2$, with
*no* intermediate deflections --- falsifies the hidden-classical-spin
interpretation. The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework explains the discreteness: the
silver atom's McGucken Sphere splits into exactly two sub-spheres
because of the $4\pi$-periodic $SU(2)$ representation of spin-1/2
(Remark [10.21](#rmk:why-silver){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:why-silver"}), with no third sub-sphere geometrically
available. The two-spot pattern is the experimental signature of the
geometric content $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ delivers via the Dirac
structure of Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:dirac"}. ◻*
:::

#### Three remarks {#ssec:SG-remarks}

::: {#rmk:SG-differential-response .remark}
*Remark 10.32* (The Stern--Gerlach experiment as the
differential-response theorem in laboratory form). The Stern--Gerlach
result is, from the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework perspective, the cleanest
laboratory exhibition of the differential-response theorem
(Theorem [1.5](#thm:channel-differential-response){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:channel-differential-response"}). Algebraic Channel's unitary
content (the Pauli Hamiltonian, the $SU(2)$ algebra, Stone's theorem
applied to the spin-1/2 evolution) and Geometric Channel's geometric content
(the McGucken Sphere, the iterated sub-sphere structure, the
$4\pi$-periodic Dirac evolution) both predict the same observable: a
two-spot pattern with separation
$\Delta z = \gamma\hbar(\partial_z B_z)T^2/(2m)$ and Born-rule
probabilities $\cos^2(\theta/2)$, $\sin^2(\theta/2)$. The two
derivations are derivationally disjoint
(Theorem [10.22](#thm:SG-spatial-separation){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:SG-spatial-separation"},
Theorem [10.24](#thm:SG-Born-rule){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:SG-Born-rule"}), and the convergence on identical
predictions is the convergent-overdetermination signature of
§[1.9](#sec:remarkable-feature){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:remarkable-feature"} applied to the spin-1/2 case. The
differential response operates as follows: Process 2 during traversal is
Geometric Channel's geometric-propagation content (the Sphere on $M_{G}$);
Process 1 at the detector is the three-dimensional registration that
exposes Algebraic Channel's algebraic-projection content (the $\hat{P}_\uparrow$
projector); the differential response of the two channels to the
apparatus geometry is the content of the measurement event.
:::

::: {#rmk:SG-4D-3D .remark}
*Remark 10.33* (The Stern--Gerlach experiment as the four-dimensional /
three-dimensional reading made laboratory-visible). The Stern--Gerlach
apparatus is the cleanest laboratory case for the four-dimensional /
three-dimensional reading of measurement that underlies the dissolution
of the measurement problem in
§[10.6](#sec:apparent-collapse){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:apparent-collapse"}. The atom's McGucken Sphere is a
four-dimensional object expanding from the source event $p_0$ at the
velocity of light by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the apparatus's detector
is a three-dimensional registration surface. The intersection of the
four-dimensional Sphere with the three-dimensional detector is a single
point: the registration locus. The four-dimensional Sphere has support
over its entire sphere of radius $cT$ around $p_0$ at time $T$; the
three-dimensional registration has support at a single point. The
apparent "collapse" of the wavefunction at the detector is, in this
reading, the geometric three-dimensional registration of the
four-dimensional content --- not a separate dynamical law, not an extra
ingredient added to the unitary evolution, but the natural geometric
consequence of intersecting a four-dimensional object with a
three-dimensional surface. The Stern--Gerlach pattern is the laboratory
exhibition of this geometric content: the two-spot structure is the
two-sub-sphere support of $\Sigma_M(p_0, T)$ on the detector slice, and
the Born-rule probabilities $\cos^2(\theta/2)$, $\sin^2(\theta/2)$ are
the geometric amplitudes-squared of the two sub-spheres at the detector
locus.
:::

::: {#rmk:SG-probability-origin .remark}
*Remark 10.34* (How probability arises from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$:
the answer). The McGucken framework's answer to
the question *how does probability arise* is supplied by the
Stern--Gerlach analysis above and connects three derivations that have
been developed separately in the framework:

1.  *Perpendicularity forces complex amplitudes*: The McGucken Principle
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ carries the imaginary unit $i$ as the
    perpendicularity marker of $x_4$ to the spatial three (Axis 1 of
    §[1.11.1](#ssec:mcgucken-wick-five-axes){reference-type="ref"
    reference="ssec:mcgucken-wick-five-axes"}). The wavefunction $\psi$
    is therefore a complex-valued amplitude $\psi = a + ib$ at every
    spatial-slice cross-section.

2.  *Phase-invariance forces $|\psi|^2$ as the only candidate
    probability*: The unique real non-negative scalar function of $\psi$
    that is invariant under the global phase rotation
    $\psi \mapsto \psi e^{i\varphi}$ (the gauge symmetry of
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$) is $|\psi|^2 = a^2 + b^2$
    (Lemma [10.25](#lem:phase-invariant-scalar){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:phase-invariant-scalar"}). The real and imaginary
    parts $a$, $b$ are individually *not* phase-invariant and cannot be
    used as probabilities.

3.  *Three-dimensional registration forces probabilistic outcomes*: A
    four-dimensional McGucken Sphere on $M_{G}$ has support over its
    entire sphere of radius $cT$ around the source event; a
    three-dimensional apparatus registers at a single point. The
    four-dimensional content is sampled by the three-dimensional
    registration, and the sampling weight at each candidate registration
    locus is the squared-magnitude content of the Sphere at that locus
    (Theorem [10.28](#thm:SG-measurement-event){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:SG-measurement-event"}). The sampling is
    probabilistic because the three-dimensional registration cannot
    register at all loci simultaneously; it can register at only one
    point per measurement event, and the probability of registering at
    any given point is the squared-magnitude content of the Sphere at
    that point.

The combined three-step derivation: $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ forces
complex amplitudes (via $i$), forces $|\psi|^2$ as the only
phase-invariant scalar (via $\psi \mapsto \psi e^{i\varphi}$), and
forces probabilistic three-dimensional sampling of the four-dimensional
content (via the apparatus's registration geometry). The Stern--Gerlach
experiment is the laboratory exhibition of this combined derivation: the
two-spot pattern with $\cos^2(\theta/2)$, $\sin^2(\theta/2)$
probabilities is the experimentally-visible consequence of probability's
origin in $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. *Probability is a theorem
of the McGucken Principle $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, with the
squared-magnitude structure forced by the perpendicularity of $x_4$ and
the apparatus's three-dimensional registration geometry.*
:::

### Proposition VI.1: Measurement irreversibility from $x_4$-monotonicity {#sec:measurement-irreversibility}

::: {#prop:measurement-irreversibility .proposition}
**Proposition 10.35** (The irreversibility of measurement is the same
$x_4$-monotonicity that grounds the second law; [@MG-Measurement-2026]
Proposition VI.1). *The apparent irreversibility of measurement --- that
once a measurement has been made, the system cannot return to its
pre-measurement superposition --- is a theorem of $x_4$'s monotonic
advance, identical in origin to the second law of
thermodynamics. No separate stochastic dynamics is required.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof; from [@MG-Measurement-2026] §VI.2.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has six steps establishing measurement irreversibility as a theorem of
$x_{4}$-monotonicity.

**Step 1: Second-law origin in $x_{4}$-monotonic advance.** The second
law of thermodynamics has, by Theorems of [@MG-Measurement-2026] §X
(cf. Theorem [12.18](#thm:five-arrows-of-time){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:five-arrows-of-time"} of
Ch. [12](#ch:lagrangian-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:lagrangian-uniqueness"}), a dynamical origin in $x_{4}$'s
monotonic advance at rate $ic$: at the initial moment $t = 0$, no
$x_{4}$-advance has occurred and the accessible phase-space volume is
minimal; as $x_{4}$ advances monotonically forward, the accessible
phase-space volume grows continuously, driving entropy increase via the
Compton-coupling diffusion mechanism
(Theorem [22.1](#thm:QMT22){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT22"}).

**Step 2: Measurement produces entangled system-apparatus-environment
state.** The unitary measurement interaction, generated by the coupling
Hamiltonian
$\hat H_{\mathrm{int}} = g\hat O \otimes \hat p_{\mathrm{dev}}$
(Lemma [19.2](#lem:QMT19-coupling){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT19-coupling"}), produces the entangled state
$$\lvert \Psi(t) \rangle = \sum_k c_k\,\lvert s_k \rangle \otimes \lvert A_k \rangle \otimes \lvert E_k \rangle,$$
where $\lvert s_k \rangle$ are system eigenstates, $\lvert A_k \rangle$
are apparatus pointer states, and $\lvert E_k \rangle$ are environmental
states. The entanglement spans system + apparatus + macroscopic
environment.

**Step 3: In-principle reversibility vs. practical irreversibility.** To
restore the pre-measurement superposition requires reversing the unitary
evolution and disentangling the apparatus from the environment. This is
*in principle* possible (since unitary evolution is reversible by
anti-unitary time-reversal $T$), but *practically* impossible: the
apparatus has been entangled with the environment via Compton-frequency
coupling (Theorem [22.1](#thm:QMT22){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT22"}), and disentangling all environmental degrees of
freedom would require precise simultaneous control over $N \sim 10^{23}$
Compton-coupled environmental degrees of freedom.

**Step 4: Dispersion timescale across exponentially large phase space.**
For a macroscopic apparatus with $N \sim 10^{23}$ environmental degrees
of freedom each oscillating at Compton frequencies
$\omega_C \sim 10^{21}$ rad/s for nucleons, the phase-space dispersion
timescale is Planck-short. The Poincaré recurrence theorem guarantees
that the system will eventually return to a state arbitrarily close to
its initial state, but the recurrence time scales as $\exp(N)$ --- for
$N \sim 10^{23}$, this is incomprehensibly longer than the age of the
universe ($\sim 10^{17}$ s). The "collapse" appears irreversible because
the practical reversibility timescale exceeds the age of the universe by
factors involving the entropy of the apparatus.

**Step 5: Identification with the second law.** The
identification with the second law is precise: both are
theorems of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the same monotonic-advance
mechanism. The measurement arrow (irreversibility of registered
outcomes), the thermodynamic arrow (entropy increase), the cosmological
arrow (Hubble expansion), and the radiative arrow (retarded over
advanced Green's functions) are all manifestations of one
$x_{4}$-monotonicity
(Theorem [12.18](#thm:five-arrows-of-time){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:five-arrows-of-time"}).

**Step 6: McGucken anchoring --- no separate stochastic dynamics
required.** The conclusion is that measurement irreversibility does not
require a separate stochastic dynamical law (as in GRW collapse models).
The McGucken-Principle clause that $x_{4}$ advances forward at $+ic$ at
every event of $M_{G}$ (matter branch orientation) supplies the same
monotonic-advance arrow that grounds the second law, and the measurement
irreversibility is its specialisation to the system + apparatus +
environment composite. The unitary $(U)$ evolution together with
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ replaces the standard $(U) + (R)$ dual-law
structure (Proposition [10.39](#prop:no-separate-R){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:no-separate-R"}), with measurement irreversibility
derived as a consequence rather than imposed as an
independent collapse postulate. ◻
:::

### Proposition VII.1: Preferred basis from environmental Compton-frequency decoherence {#sec:preferred-basis-compton}

::: {#prop:preferred-basis-compton .proposition}
**Proposition 10.36** (The preferred basis is selected by environmental
Compton-frequency coupling to $x_4$'s expansion; [@MG-Measurement-2026]
Proposition VII.1). *In the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework, the preferred basis
observed by macroscopic observers is the position basis (and the energy
basis for stationary states), and the cut between quantum and classical
regimes is the scale at which environmental Compton-frequency coupling
to $x_4$'s expansion produces decoherence faster than coherent dynamics.
The cut is specified by a concrete physical mechanism --- the Compton
frequency of environmental constituents --- rather than left arbitrary.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof; from [@MG-Measurement-2026] §VII.2.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof has six
steps establishing the preferred basis as forced by
environmental Compton-frequency coupling. The Compton coupling itself
descends from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the rest-frame
$x_{4}$-oscillation rate (Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT4"}, Compton-coupling theorem
$\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$).

**Step 1: Compton-coupling at every environmental constituent.** By
Theorem [22.1](#thm:QMT22){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT22"}
(the Compton-coupling theorem of [@MG-Compton-2026]), every massive
particle of rest mass $m$ couples to $x_{4}$'s expansion at its Compton
angular frequency $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$. By
Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT4"} (the
Compton coupling derived from Wigner classification plus the
Planck--Einstein relation), this frequency is the rest-frame phase rate
of the $x_{4}$-advance for a massive particle, with the factor $mc^2$
coming from the four-velocity budget
(Lemma [4.2](#lem:four-velocity-budget){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:four-velocity-budget"}, descending from
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clauses (i)+(ii)) and the factor $\hbar$
coming from the quantum of action per $x_{4}$-oscillation cycle
(Theorem [3.2](#thm:62){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:62"}). For
the constituents of a macroscopic environment, these frequencies are
extremely high:

-   Nucleons:
    $\omega_C^{(p)} = m_p c^2/\hbar \approx 1.4 \times 10^{24}$ rad/s;

-   Electrons:
    $\omega_C^{(e)} = m_e c^2/\hbar \approx 7.8 \times 10^{20}$ rad/s;

-   Atomic and molecular systems: aggregate over their constituent
    Compton frequencies.

Each constituent produces extremely rapid Compton-phase oscillations
driven by its $x_{4}$-advance at the McGucken-Principle rate $c$.

**Step 2: System-environment interaction couples through Compton
frequencies.** When a quantum system $S$ interacts with environmental
constituents $\{E_i\}$, the system's reduced density matrix $\rho_S$
(formed by partial trace over the environment,
Lemma [18.2](#lem:QMT18-schmidt){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT18-schmidt"}) acquires off-diagonal terms that
oscillate at frequencies determined by the system's coupling Hamiltonian
to each constituent. For a coupling
$\hat H_{S-E_i} = g_{S,i}\hat O_S \otimes \hat O_{E_i}$ with
$\hat O_{E_i}$ oscillating at $\omega_{C,i}$ (the Compton frequency of
constituent $i$), the off-diagonal elements of $\rho_S$ pick up phase
factors $\exp(i\omega_{C,i}\,g_{S,i}^2 t/\hbar)$ from the dynamics. The
$i$ in this phase factor is the perpendicularity marker of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}) carried through the time-evolution operator
$\hat U(t) = e^{-i\hat H t/\hbar}$
(Lemma [7.2](#lem:time-translation-unitary){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:time-translation-unitary"}).

**Step 3: Decoherence rate sums Compton contributions across the
environment.** For a macroscopic environment with $N \sim 10^{23}$
constituents, the off-diagonal terms of $\rho_S$ accumulate phase
contributions from all $N$ constituents. The effective decoherence rate
is
$$\Gamma_{\mathrm{dec}} \approx \sum_{i=1}^N\frac{\omega_{C,i}\,g_{S,i}^2}{\hbar}.$$
For typical macroscopic systems, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}$ is enormous:
combining $N \sim 10^{23}$, $\omega_C \sim 10^{20}$--$10^{24}$ rad/s,
and non-zero couplings $g_{S,i}$, the off-diagonal decay is on
Planck-short timescales. Coherent superpositions of distinct macroscopic
configurations are therefore physically suppressed at all observable
timescales. This is the McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework first-principle account of
the empirical decoherence rate; the standard decoherence literature
(Zurek; Joos--Zeh [@JoosZeh1985]) treats the environmental coupling as
an input, while the McGucken framework supplies the coupling from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the Compton-frequency machinery.

**Step 4: Position (or energy) basis minimises
$\Gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}$.** The basis in which $\Gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}$ is
*not* enormous --- whose elements minimize off-diagonal coupling to
environmental Compton oscillations --- is the *position basis* (for
spatial outcomes) or the *energy basis* (for stationary states).
Reasons:

-   Position eigenstates are localised in space and have well-defined
    spatial relations to environmental constituents; coupling
    Hamiltonians (typically $V(\mathbf{x})$-type) are diagonal in this
    basis
    (Lemma [10.2](#lem:position-momentum-explicit){reference-type="ref"
    reference="lem:position-momentum-explicit"}), so off-diagonal
    couplings vanish;

-   Energy eigenstates of stationary systems are diagonal in the system
    Hamiltonian, which commutes with the free-system dynamics
    (Theorem [7.1](#thm:QMT7){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:QMT7"}, Schrödinger evolution), so their off-diagonal
    couplings to the environment also vanish.

This is the reason macroscopic observers see definite spatial
configurations and definite energies, but never superpositions of
either. The 3D-localization aspect connects to the projection mechanism
of Theorem [19.1](#thm:QMT19){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT19"} (the 3D-cross-section reading of the 4D McGucken
Sphere).

**Step 5: Quantum-to-classical cut specified concretely.** The cut
between quantum and classical regimes is specified by a concrete
physical scale: the scale at which the system's coherent dynamical
timescale $T_{\mathrm{coh}}$ exceeds the Compton-frequency decoherence
timescale $T_{\mathrm{dec}} = 1/\Gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}$:

-   Microscopic systems ($T_{\mathrm{coh}} \ll T_{\mathrm{dec}}$):
    quantum behaviour is observable;

-   Macroscopic systems ($T_{\mathrm{coh}} \gg T_{\mathrm{dec}}$):
    classical behaviour dominates;

-   Mesoscopic systems ($T_{\mathrm{coh}} \approx T_{\mathrm{dec}}$):
    the quantum-classical transition is observable, e.g. in molecular
    interferometry experiments (Fein et al. [@Fein2019]).

No arbitrary cut is required; the cut is the empirical scale where
$T_{\mathrm{coh}} = T_{\mathrm{dec}}$, computable in principle for any
specific system from the Compton-coupling formula above.

**Step 6: McGucken anchoring --- preferred basis selected by
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$-derived Compton coupling.** The origin of preferred-basis selection is therefore
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ itself: the Compton frequency
$\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ is the rate at which the rest-frame
$x_{4}$-advance oscillates
(Theorem [4.1](#thm:QMT4){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT4"},
derived from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the four-velocity budget of
Lemma [4.2](#lem:four-velocity-budget){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:four-velocity-budget"} and the Planck--Einstein relation
of Theorem [3.1](#thm:QMT3){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT3"}),
and the decoherence rate $\Gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}$ that selects the
preferred basis is built entirely from these McGucken-derived Compton
frequencies. The (P3) sub-problem of the measurement problem (preferred
basis) is solved by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, not by an
additional postulate or by environment-induced superselection at an
arbitrarily-chosen scale. The integrated kinematic shadow $x_{4}= ict$
