### Historical Predecessors {#sec:historical-predecessors}

Three lines of thought in the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries
got close to the identity claim of
Theorem [11.11](#thm:identity-lorentz-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:identity-lorentz-nonlocality"} without arriving at it.
[@MG-Uniqueness-2026] §10 supplies the diagnosis of why each
fell short. We summarise.

#### Costa de Beauregard (1953--1977): The cone carries the correlation

Olivier Costa de Beauregard, in a series of papers beginning in 1953
[@CostaDeBeauregard1953], argued that EPR (Einstein--Podolsky--Rosen)
correlations are mediated through the light-cone structure itself, not
through faster-than-light signals in three-space. His "zigzag" model
proposed that the correlation between spatially separated entangled
particles travels along the past light cone of one detection event,
through the source, and along the future light cone to the other
detection event.

*What Costa de Beauregard had:* the intuition that the light
cone, not three-space, is where quantum nonlocality lives. He explicitly
identified the cone as the locus of the correlation rather than treating
nonlocality as a faster-than-light spatial signal.

*What he did not have:* (i) any uniqueness argument that the cone
configuration is forced; (ii) any identification of $c$-invariance with
the correlation strength; (iii) any dynamical reading of the timelike
axis as actually moving; (iv) any formal theorem connecting the cone's
geometric properties to the Tsirelson bound. He was working within
standard Minkowski geometry to interpret EPR. The intuition was sharp;
the formal apparatus to make the identity claim was not available.

#### Penrose (1967 onward): null structure as fundamental

Roger Penrose, beginning with the 1967 introduction of twistors
[@Penrose1967] and continuing through five decades of work culminating
in *The Road to Reality* and the conformal cyclic cosmology of *Cycles
of Time*, has maintained that the null structure of spacetime --- the
light-cone structure --- is more fundamental than the metric and that
quantum mechanics must descend from this null structure.

*What Penrose had:* the commitment that null structure is
foundational. Twistor theory makes this precise by encoding spacetime
points as null lines in $\mathbb{CP}^3$, and the entire programme of
twistor diagrams attempts to derive QM amplitudes from the null
geometry.

*What he did not have:* the dynamical reading of $x_4$ as actually
moving at rate $ic$. The Penrose programme treats null structure as a
static feature of Minkowski geometry; without the dynamical advance of
$x_4$, the connection to the Tsirelson saturation cannot be derived.
Twistors encode null lines algebraically but do not supply the
$SO(3)$-Haar mechanism that gives the singlet correlation.

#### Hardy (1992): the closest formal result

Lucien Hardy, in a 1992 *Physical Review Letters* paper [@Hardy1992],
established the closest formal result in the published literature to the
Identity Theorem. Hardy proved that no Lorentz-invariant, local,
realistic theory can reproduce the predictions of quantum
mechanics --- the strongest statement to date that the joint demands of
Lorentz invariance and quantum nonlocality have non-trivial content.

*What Hardy had:* a rigorous formal proof that Lorentz invariance plus
locality plus realism fails to reproduce QM, with explicit construction
of the failure mode (the "Hardy paradox"). The result demonstrated that
$c$-invariance and Bell-violation are not logically
independent --- there is content in their conjunction.

*What he did not have:* the result runs the opposite direction from the
Identity Theorem. Hardy treated Lorentz invariance, locality, and
realism as three independent constraints and showed they cannot be
jointly satisfied alongside QM predictions; the paper is a no-go theorem
for a particular conjunction of postulates. The Identity Theorem of the
present chapter makes the affirmative identity claim --- that
$c$-invariance and Tsirelson saturation are two readings of one
geometric fact --- which is the stronger statement: not
"these three things conflict" but "these two things are the same thing."

#### Why the identity claim required the dynamical $x_4$

The recurring pattern across the three predecessors is that each
captured a piece without arriving at the identity. Costa de
Beauregard had the cone-as-locus-of-correlation; Penrose had the
null-structure-as-fundamental; Hardy had the formal proof that the joint
constraints have non-trivial structure. None of them had the dynamical
reading of the fourth dimension as actually moving at $ic$.

This is the reason the identity claim has not been published
before. Without $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as a dynamical principle, the
most one can do is observe that the Lorentz-invariant cone and the
Tsirelson-saturating shared sphere are facts that coexist consistently
(the no-signaling theorem stitching them at the operational level). With
the dynamical principle, the two have the reading of two
channel-projections of one underlying fact, with the role of two
coexisting-but-distinct facts to be operationally reconciled replaced by
the role of two readings of the same $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$-generated
sphere-surface $x_{4}$-locality, and the Identity Theorem becomes
provable.

### Implications for the unification of quantum mechanics and relativity {#sec:qm-gr-unification}

The Identity Theorem closes the loop on the central goal of
twentieth-century theoretical physics: *the unification of quantum
mechanics and relativity*. The standard approach to this goal has been
to construct a quantum theory of gravity that quantises the metric
tensor, on the assumption that the path to unification leads through the
imposition of quantum structure on classical general relativity. This
approach has run for ninety years without producing an empirically
distinguishable, mathematically complete, predictive quantum theory of
gravity.

The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework supplies an alternative path. Both quantum
mechanics and relativity descend from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as
theorems:

-   *The entire content of quantum mechanics* (23 QM theorems QM T1--T23
    of Part II, all derived from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via dual
    channels);

-   *The Lorentzian arena of relativity*
    (Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:hilbert-arena"} of
    Chapter [9](#ch:hilbert-theorem){reference-type="ref"
    reference="ch:hilbert-theorem"}, in which $M_{1,3}$ is generated
    from $M_E$ by substituting $x_4 = ict$);

-   *The metric structure* (induced by the Lorentzian line element
    derived from $dx_4 = ic\,dt$ squared);

-   *The light cone* (the future light cone of $p$ is the McGucken
    Sphere $M^{+}_{p}(t)$ by
    Theorem [17.12](#thm:six-fold-identity){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:six-fold-identity"} clause (F6), the
    null-hypersurface cross-section);

-   *Lorentz invariance of $c$*
    (Theorem [11.11](#thm:identity-lorentz-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:identity-lorentz-nonlocality"} clause (i), via
    Algebraic Channel);

-   *Quantum nonlocality saturating Tsirelson*
    (Theorem [11.11](#thm:identity-lorentz-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:identity-lorentz-nonlocality"} clause (ii), via
    Geometric Channel);

-   *General relativity* (the gravitational Einstein equations as
    theorems of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ via the curvature of the
    spatial-slice geometry induced by the principle's expansion on a
    non-flat background --- Theorem 23 of Part II of the synthesis paper
    [@Syn-2026]).

The unification is therefore  rather than constructive: not
"quantise gravity" but "recognise that quantum mechanics and gravity are
two readings of the same deeper geometric fact." The Identity Theorem
makes this explicit at the level of the most quantitative testable
predictions of the two domains (Tsirelson saturation and
$c$-invariance).

::: remark
*Remark 11.13* (The dx$_4$/dt = ic statement of unification). The
unification statement reduces to a single line:
$$\boxed{\ \dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic\ \implies\ \text{both quantum mechanics and relativity}.\ }$$
The fourth dimension advances spherically symmetrically at $c$ from
every spacetime event. This single fact, read through Algebraic Channel,
produces Lorentz invariance and the relativistic structure of spacetime.
Read through Geometric Channel, it produces the entire content of quantum
mechanics, including the saturation of Tsirelson at $2\sqrt 2$. The two
are two readings of one principle.
:::

### Close: one principle, two channels, one universe

The import of this chapter, with the rest of the textbook
taken as background, is the following. Twentieth-century physics was
built on two pillars: relativity, which placed Lorentz invariance and
the light cone at the foundation of spacetime; and quantum mechanics,
which placed nonlocality, probability, and the Tsirelson bound at the
foundation of matter. The two were thought to coexist in tension, with
the no-signaling theorem as the operational bridge that prevented
outright contradiction.

The McGucken $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ framework shows that this tension is an artefact of
incomplete description. *Sphere-surface $x_4$-locality* is the deeper
geometric fact of which Lorentz invariance and Tsirelson saturation are
two readings. Algebraic Channel's algebraic-symmetry reading produces the
relativistic content; Geometric Channel's geometric-propagation reading produces
the quantum content. The two are one.

The First McGucken Law of Nonlocality
(Theorem [17.4](#thm:first-law-nonlocality){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:first-law-nonlocality"}) is, in this light, a forced
theorem of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, with the role of an interpretive
principle layered onto quantum mechanics replaced by the role of a
derived consequence at the McGucken-Principle level. The
light cone of relativity and the McGucken Sphere of quantum nonlocality
are the same surface in spacetime; nonlocality is locality at the level
of $x_4$; the propagation of $x_4$-locality from event to event at rate
$c$ is the Geometric Channel mechanism by which spatially separated systems
remain correlated through their shared past Sphere intersection.

::: flushright
*"Quantum nonlocality and Lorentz invariance of the light cone are not
two empirical facts but two readings of one geometric fact."\
--- [@MG-Uniqueness-2026], Identity Theorem closing statement.*
:::

## The Unique McGucken Lagrangian: Four-Sector Uniqueness from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ {#ch:lagrangian-uniqueness}

> *The McGucken Principle.* The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension $x_4$ is expanding at the velocity of light: $dx_4/dt = ic$, with $x_4 = ict$, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action $h$ and whose volume defines a nonlocality.
> Every result below descends from that expansion.


*Recall.* the McGucken Principle ($\mathrm{McP}$:
$\tfrac{dx_4}{dt} = ic$) asserts that the fourth spacetime dimension
$x_4$ expands at the velocity of light $c$, carrying the
perpendicularity marker $i$ that distinguishes it from the spatial
three. Throughout this chapter, $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ refers to this
principle and to the five-clause content (i)--(v) of
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}: (i) *invariance* --- the rate
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event with the same value,
independent of matter content; (ii) *spherical symmetry* --- the
expansion is isotropic in the spatial three, with the set of events
reachable from $p$ in proper time $\tau$ being a 2-sphere of radius
$c\tau$; (iii) *monotonicity* --- the integral curve is strictly
monotonically increasing in $t$, fixing the arrow of $x_4$-advance; (iv)
*Lorentz consistency* --- the structure is $SO^+(1,3)$-invariant on
$M_{G}$; (v) *global validity* --- $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at
every event of $M_{G}$. The integrated kinematic shadow
$x_4 = ict$ (Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) is the kinematic shadow of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$; the dynamical principle
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ is the central fact.

::: flushright
*"The McGucken Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{McG}}$ is the first
Lagrangian in the 282-year history of Lagrangian physics whose complete
four-sector form --- free-particle kinetic, Dirac matter, Yang--Mills
gauge, Einstein--Hilbert gravitational --- is forced by a single
geometric principle."\
--- [@MG-Lagrangian-2026], Abstract*
:::

The preceding chapters of Part IV resolved the measurement problem
(Ch. [19](#ch:measurement){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:measurement"}) and exhibited entanglement as the
joint-Sphere wavefront
(Ch. [\[ch:entanglement\]](#ch:entanglement){reference-type="ref"
reference="ch:entanglement"}). The present chapter establishes
the result that closes the Lagrangian programme of
theoretical physics: *the entire least-action functional of
physics --- free particle, Dirac matter, Yang--Mills gauge, and
Einstein--Hilbert gravity --- is forced by $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
alone*, with no independent postulates added beyond minimal consistency
requirements at each sector.

The strategy follows the April 23, 2026 paper [@MG-Lagrangian-2026].
Each of the four sectors of the standard Lagrangian of theoretical
physics is shown to be the *unique* Lorentz-invariant first-order local
action consistent with $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, given a single
additional symmetry requirement (reparametrization invariance for the
free-particle sector; spinor first-order field equations for the matter
sector; local gauge invariance for the gauge sector; diffeomorphism
invariance for the gravitational sector). The four uniqueness
subtheorems combine into the four-fold uniqueness theorem, Theorem VI.1
of the paper.

### The McGucken Lagrangian {#sec:mcgucken-lagrangian-form}

The composite Lagrangian assembled from the four sectors is: $$\boxed{\,
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{McG}} \;=\; \underbrace{-mc\,\sqrt{-\partial_\mu x_4 \,\partial^\mu x_4}}_{\text{free-particle kinetic}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\bar\psi\,(i\gamma^\mu D_\mu - m)\,\psi}_{\text{Dirac matter}}
\;-\; \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{4}\,F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}}_{\text{Yang--Mills gauge}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\frac{c^4}{16\pi G}\,R[g]}_{\text{Einstein--Hilbert gravity}}\,,
\label{eq:lagrangian-mcg}
}$$ subject to the constraint
$\partial_\mu x_4\,\partial^\mu x_4 = -c^2$ (the integrated kinematic
shadow of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ as a covariant statement) and the
matter orientation condition
$$\Psi(x, x_4) = \Psi_0(x) \cdot \exp(+I \cdot k_C\,x_4), \qquad k_C = mc/\hbar > 0,
\label{eq:matter-orientation}$$ where $I$ is the Clifford pseudoscalar
of spacetime algebra and $k_C$ is the species' Compton wavenumber. The
positive sign of $k_C$ selects matter; antimatter is described by the
opposite sign [@MG-Lagrangian-2026], §V.1.

::: {#rmk:free-particle-form .remark}
*Remark 12.1* (The form
$-mc\sqrt{-\partial_\mu x_4 \partial^\mu x_4} = -mc|dx_4|$). The
free-particle term has three equivalent expressions, each making a
different physical content explicit:
$$S_{\mathrm{free}}[\gamma] \;=\; -mc \int_\gamma \sqrt{-\eta_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu \dot x^\nu}\,d\lambda \;=\; -mc \int_\gamma |dx_4| \;=\; -mc^2 \int_\gamma d\tau.$$
The first expression is the Lorentz-scalar reparametrization-invariant
integrand. The second expression is the accumulated magnitude of $x_4$'s
advance along the worldline --- the geometric reading. The third
expression, $-mc^2\int d\tau$, is the standard textbook free-particle
action in proper time. The three are equal under the constraint
$\partial_\mu x_4 \partial^\mu x_4 = -c^2$ and the standard
identification $|dx_4| = c\,d\tau$ along a timelike worldline. The
McGucken reading of the free-particle action is therefore not a new
formula but a new identification of what the formula *is*: it is the
accumulated $x_4$-advance, with the proper-time integral being its
kinematic shadow under $x_4 = ict$.
:::

### The Four-Fold Uniqueness Theorem {#sec:four-fold-uniqueness}

The central technical result of [@MG-Lagrangian-2026] consolidates the
four sector-by-sector uniqueness proofs into one theorem.

::: {#thm:four-fold-uniqueness .theorem}
**Theorem 12.2** (The Unique McGucken Lagrangian, after
[@MG-Lagrangian-2026]). *The McGucken Lagrangian
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{McG}}$ of
equation [\[eq:lagrangian-mcg\]](#eq:lagrangian-mcg){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:lagrangian-mcg"}, subject to the constraint
$\partial_\mu x_4\,\partial^\mu x_4 = -c^2$ and the matter orientation
condition [\[eq:matter-orientation\]](#eq:matter-orientation){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:matter-orientation"}, is the unique Lorentz-invariant,
reparametrization-invariant, first-order local Lagrangian consistent
with the McGucken Principle $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. Each sector is
forced by a specific uniqueness subtheorem:*

1.  **Free-particle kinetic term* forced by
    Proposition [12.4](#prop:free-particle-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:free-particle-uniqueness"} (full proof in
    §[12.3](#sec:free-particle-proof){reference-type="ref"
    reference="sec:free-particle-proof"} below);*

2.  **Dirac matter sector* forced by
    Proposition [12.6](#prop:dirac-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:dirac-uniqueness"} (full proof now given in
    §[12.4](#sec:dirac-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
    reference="sec:dirac-uniqueness"} below, drawing on [@MG-Dirac-2026]
    §§II--IV and IX read in full);*

3.  **Yang--Mills gauge sector* forced by
    Proposition [12.11](#prop:gauge-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:gauge-uniqueness"} (full proof now given in
    §[12.5](#sec:gauge-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
    reference="sec:gauge-uniqueness"} below, drawing on [@MG-SM-2026]
    Theorems 10 and 11 read in full);*

4.  **Einstein--Hilbert gravitational sector* forced by
    Proposition [12.14](#prop:gravity-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:gravity-uniqueness"} via the Schuller closure
    theorem (full proof now given in
    §[12.6](#sec:gravity-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
    reference="sec:gravity-uniqueness"} below, drawing on [@MG-SM-2026]
    Theorem 12 read in full, with the ADM (Arnowitt--Deser--Misner 3+1
    formulation) foliation from [@MG-GR-2026] §II.2 read in full and
    developed in Ch. [14](#ch:mcgucken-GR){reference-type="ref"
    reference="ch:mcgucken-GR"}).*

*Each uniqueness subtheorem reduces to $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ combined
with a single minimal consistency requirement: Lorentz invariance for
(a) and (b); local gauge invariance for (c); diffeomorphism invariance
for (d). No additional free choices are made at any step.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof of Theorem [12.2](#thm:four-fold-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:four-fold-uniqueness"}, umbrella structure.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The theorem
assembles four sector-uniqueness propositions into a single Lagrangian.
We give the overview here; the four sub-proofs follow in
§§[12.3](#sec:free-particle-proof){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:free-particle-proof"},
[12.4](#sec:dirac-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:dirac-uniqueness"},
[12.5](#sec:gauge-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:gauge-uniqueness"},
[12.6](#sec:gravity-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:gravity-uniqueness"} below.

**Step 1: Sector decomposition is forced by the four-fold structure of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.** The McGucken Principle
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ at every event of $M_{G}$ admits four
distinct couplings whose simultaneous presence is
consistent with the principle's clauses (P1)--(P5): (a) the principle's
own kinematic action on a worldline (free-particle kinetic); (b) the
matter wavefunction's coupling to $x_{4}$-orientation (Dirac); (c) the
internal-fibre $U(1)$-bundle of phase-rotation symmetry (Yang--Mills);
(d) the spacetime-metric coupling that maintains the principle's
universal rate $|\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}| = c$ under arbitrary
diffeomorphisms (Einstein--Hilbert). No other sector arises from
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ within the Lorentz-, gauge-, and
diffeomorphism-invariant first-order local class.

**Step 2: Free-particle sector ---
Proposition [12.4](#prop:free-particle-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:free-particle-uniqueness"}.** The free-particle kinetic
Lagrangian
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{free}} = -mc\sqrt{-\partial_\mu x_4\,\partial^\mu x_4}$
is the unique reparametrization-invariant first-order local Lagrangian
whose Euler--Lagrange equation enforces the constraint
$\partial_\mu x_4\,\partial^\mu x_4 = -c^2$ (the integrated kinematic shadow of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, with $x_4 = ict$ the kinematic shadow per
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}).
Proposition [12.4](#prop:free-particle-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:free-particle-uniqueness"}
(§[12.3](#sec:free-particle-proof){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:free-particle-proof"}) derives this by exhausting the
alternatives (polynomial, exponential, logarithmic kinetic terms) and
showing each either violates reparametrization invariance, fails to
enforce the constraint, or introduces dimensional inconsistency.

**Step 3: Dirac matter sector ---
Proposition [12.6](#prop:dirac-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:dirac-uniqueness"}.** The Dirac matter Lagrangian
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Dirac}} = \bar\psi(i\gamma^\mu D_\mu - m)\psi$ is
the unique first-order Lorentz-covariant matter Lagrangian whose
Euler--Lagrange equation is the Dirac equation
$(i\gamma^\mu D_\mu - m)\psi = 0$, with the Clifford-algebraic content
$\{\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu\} = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}\mathbf{1}$ forced by
squaring to Klein--Gordon
(Lemma [9.2](#lem:clifford-existence){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:clifford-existence"},
Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:dirac"}).
Proposition [12.6](#prop:dirac-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:dirac-uniqueness"}
(§[12.4](#sec:dirac-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:dirac-uniqueness"}) derives this by combining the
Klein--Gordon-squaring requirement with the matter orientation condition
(M) of
equation [\[eq:matter-orientation\]](#eq:matter-orientation){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:matter-orientation"} and the Single-Sided Preservation
Theorem [12.8](#thm:single-sided-preservation){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:single-sided-preservation"} (the half-angle spinor
transformation forced by preservation of (M) across the full bivector
group).

**Step 4: Yang--Mills gauge sector ---
Proposition [12.11](#prop:gauge-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:gauge-uniqueness"}.** The Yang--Mills gauge Lagrangian
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{YM}} = -\tfrac{1}{4}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ is the
unique local-gauge-invariant, Lorentz-invariant, first-order
quadratic-in-$F$ Lagrangian for the gauge field $A_\mu$ whose
Euler--Lagrange equation reproduces the (sourced or sourceless)
Maxwell/Yang--Mills equations.
Proposition [12.11](#prop:gauge-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:gauge-uniqueness"}
(§[12.5](#sec:gauge-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:gauge-uniqueness"}) derives this by combining local
$U(1)$ gauge invariance
(Theorem [12.12](#thm:local-U1-gauge){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:local-U1-gauge"}, the $x_{4}$-phase indeterminacy
theorem) with the requirement that the gauge Lagrangian be quadratic in
$F$ (forced by linearity of the Maxwell--Yang--Mills equations) and
Lorentz-invariant (forced by the Lorentz-tensor structure of
$F_{\mu\nu}$). The $-\tfrac{1}{4}$ normalisation is fixed by
canonical-momentum and energy-density conventions.

**Step 5: Einstein--Hilbert gravitational sector ---
Proposition [12.14](#prop:gravity-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:gravity-uniqueness"}.** The Einstein--Hilbert
gravitational Lagrangian
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{EH}} = (c^4/16\pi G)\,R[g]$ is the unique
diffeomorphism-invariant, second-order-in-derivatives local Lagrangian
for the metric $g_{\mu\nu}$ whose Euler--Lagrange equation is the
Einstein field equation $G_{\mu\nu} = (8\pi G/c^4)\,T_{\mu\nu}$.
Proposition [12.14](#prop:gravity-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:gravity-uniqueness"}
(§[12.6](#sec:gravity-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:gravity-uniqueness"}) derives this via the Schuller
closure theorem (Schuller--Wohlfarth, 2007 onwards): given a Lorentzian
arena descended from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}) and the requirement that the
gravitational equations be second-order in the metric (no higher
derivatives) with diffeomorphism invariance, the unique allowed
Lagrangian density is a linear combination of $R[g]$ and a
cosmological-constant term $\Lambda\sqrt{-g}$; the cosmological-constant
coefficient is empirically constrained but does not affect the
uniqueness of $R[g]$ as the kinetic gravitational term.

**Step 6: No fifth sector.** The four sectors (a)--(d) exhaust the
allowed couplings from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ within the
Lorentz-, gauge-, and diffeomorphism-invariant first-order local class.
Any candidate fifth sector would either (i) violate one of the three
invariances and is therefore excluded by the
Lorentz/gauge/diffeomorphism requirements; (ii) introduce a primitive beyond $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ and the seven McGucken
primitives (cf. the No-Seventh-Primitive theorem of
[@No-Seventh-Primitive-2026]); or (iii) reduce to a linear combination
of the existing four sectors, contributing no new content.
The combined Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{McG}}$ is therefore the
unique Lagrangian consistent with the four invariance requirements and
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, with each sector forced by its dedicated
uniqueness subtheorem and no additional free choices.
$\square$ ◻
:::

### Proposition IV.1: Uniqueness of the Free-Particle Action {#sec:free-particle-proof}

::: {#prop:free-particle-uniqueness .proposition}
**Proposition 12.4** (Uniqueness of the free-particle action;
[@MG-Lagrangian-2026], §IV). *Let $\gamma$ be a timelike worldline in
Minkowski spacetime, and let $S[\gamma]$ be a real scalar functional of
$\gamma$ satisfying the following five conditions:*

1.  **Poincaré invariance* --- $S[\gamma]$ is invariant under the full
    Poincaré group (Lorentz transformations plus translations), so that
    no spacetime point is preferred;*

2.  **reparametrization invariance* --- $S[\gamma]$ depends on $\gamma$
    only through its image as a curve in $\mathcal{M}$, not on the
    choice of parameter $\lambda$;*

3.  **locality* --- $S[\gamma] = \int_\gamma F(x^\mu, \dot x^\mu)\,d\lambda$
    for some local function $F$;*

4.  **first-order derivatives only* --- $F$ depends on $\dot x^\mu$ but
    not on $\ddot x^\mu$ or higher derivatives;*

5.  **dimensional consistency* --- $S$ has units of action.*

*Under (C1)--(C5), the unique (up to overall multiplicative constant and
additive total-derivative terms) functional $S[\gamma]$ is
$$S[\gamma] \;=\; -mc \int_\gamma \sqrt{-\eta_{\mu\nu}\,\dot x^\mu \dot x^\nu}\,d\lambda \;=\; -mc \int_\gamma |dx_4| \;=\; -mc^2 \int_\gamma d\tau,$$
with $m$ a constant of dimension mass. No other functional of the
worldline satisfies all five conditions.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof; from [@MG-Lagrangian-2026] §IV.1.* The proof has six steps. The free-particle action $S = -mc^2\int d\tau$ is a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, the physical, geometric fact that the fourth
dimension expands at the velocity of light in a spherically symmetric
manner): the proper time $\tau$ is the integrated $x_{4}$-advance along
the worldline, $|\Delta x_4| = c\tau$
(Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}, $x_4 = ict$ as the kinematic shadow
of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$), and the action is proportional to the
accumulated $x_{4}$-advance. The five conditions (C1)--(C5) plus the
McGucken-Principle constraint force the action functional uniquely. By
(C3), $S[\gamma] = \int F(x, \dot x)\,d\lambda$ for some local $F$.

**Step 1: Reparametrization invariance forces degree-one homogeneity in
$\dot x$.** By (C2), $F$ must be homogeneous of degree one in
$\dot x^\mu$: $F(x, \alpha\dot x) = \alpha F(x, \dot x)$ for
$\alpha > 0$. Consider a reparametrization
$\lambda \to \lambda'(\lambda)$ with $d\lambda' = \alpha\,d\lambda$ for
constant $\alpha > 0$. The velocity in the new parameter is
$\dot x_{\mathrm{new}} = dx/d\lambda' = \dot x/\alpha$, and the measure
transforms as $d\lambda = d\lambda'/\alpha$. The integrand transforms as
$F(x, \dot x)\,d\lambda = F(x, \alpha\,\dot x_{\mathrm{new}})\,(d\lambda'/\alpha)$.
Reparametrization invariance requires this to equal
$F(x, \dot x_{\mathrm{new}})\,d\lambda'$, so
$F(x, \alpha\,\dot x_{\mathrm{new}}) = \alpha\,F(x, \dot x_{\mathrm{new}})$.

**Step 2: Lorentz invariance forces the two-term form.** By (C1) and
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iv), derived at Theorem 4.6 (Lorentz consistency: the
structure is $SO^+(1,3)$-invariant on $M_{G}$), $F$ must be a Lorentz
scalar built from $\dot x^\mu$ and $\eta_{\mu\nu}$. The most general
such $F$ that is homogeneous of degree one in $\dot x$ is
$$F(x, \dot x) = A(x)\sqrt{-\eta_{\mu\nu}\,\dot x^\mu \dot x^\nu} + B_\mu(x)\,\dot x^\mu,$$
where $A(x)$ is a Lorentz scalar and $B_\mu(x)$ is a Lorentz covector.
The first term, proportional to $\sqrt{-\dot x \cdot \dot x}$, is
homogeneous of degree one and Lorentz-invariant (Naber [@Naber2012]
§1.3, the standard Lorentz-invariant arc-length functional on Minkowski
space). The second term, proportional to $\dot x^\mu$ contracted with a
covector, is also homogeneous of degree one. *Exhaustiveness:* any other
degree-one scalar built from $\dot x$ with $\eta$-contractions must be
an odd power of $\dot x \cdot \dot x$, but only the half-power case is
degree one (giving the first term); degree-one-in-$\dot x$ scalars with
external covector structure must contract $\dot x$ against a rank-one
object (giving the second term).

**Step 3: Locality and first-order condition force $A$ and $B_\mu$ to be
$\dot x$-independent.** By (C4) (no higher-order derivatives) and (C3)
(locality), neither $A(x)$ nor $B_\mu(x)$ can depend on $\dot x^\mu$.

**Step 4: The free-particle condition eliminates $B_\mu$.** For a free
particle --- by hypothesis, no external fields couple to it --- the
$B_\mu(x)\dot x^\mu$ term must either vanish or reduce to a boundary
term. A nonzero field strength
$F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu B_\nu - \partial_\nu B_\mu$ would produce,
under variation, the Euler--Lagrange equation
$d/d\lambda(\partial F/\partial \dot x^\mu) - \partial F/\partial x^\mu = 0$,
containing the term $F_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\nu$. This is the Lorentz force on
a unit-charge particle in external electromagnetic potential
$A_\mu = B_\mu$ (the same coupling that emerges in QM T16 via
local-$U(1)$ promotion of the global phase symmetry,
Theorem [16.1](#thm:QMT16){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT16"}
and Lemma [16.3](#lem:QMT16-local-promotion){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-local-promotion"}). The free-particle assumption
therefore forces $F_{\mu\nu} = 0$, i.e. $B_\mu$ is closed. By the
Poincaré lemma on the contractible Minkowski manifold
(Misner--Thorne--Wheeler [@MTW1973] §4.5, the standard Poincaré lemma on
Minkowski $M_{G}$), a closed covector is exact:
$B_\mu = \partial_\mu \varphi$ for some scalar $\varphi$. The
contribution to $S$ is
$\int \partial_\mu \varphi \cdot \dot x^\mu\,d\lambda = \int d\varphi/d\lambda\,d\lambda = \varphi(\text{end}) - \varphi(\text{start})$,
a pure boundary term, which can be dropped without affecting the
Euler--Lagrange equations.

**Step 5: Translation invariance forces $A$ to be $x$-independent.** By
the translation-invariance piece of (C1) and
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (v) (global validity:
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ holds at every event of $M_{G}$, so no event is preferred), $A(x)$ cannot depend on
$x^\mu$: any $x$-dependent $A(x)$ would distinguish some spacetime point
as the origin. Hence $A$ is a constant.

**Step 6: Dimensional consistency fixes the form of $A$, with the
velocity scale supplied by the McGucken Principle.** By (C5), $A$ must
have units of action divided by time times velocity --- that is, units
of mass $\times$ velocity. Writing $A = -mc$ with $m$ a constant of
dimension mass and $c$ the velocity of $x_4$-expansion
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (i), the rate $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
supplying the universal velocity scale; Einstein [@Einstein1905E] §3 for
the historical identification of $c$ as the universal velocity in
special relativity), we obtain
$$F(x, \dot x) = -mc\,\sqrt{-\eta_{\mu\nu}\,\dot x^\mu \dot x^\nu}.$$
The sign convention $A = -mc$ (rather than $+mc$) is chosen so that the
variational principle $\delta S = 0$ for timelike worldlines extremises
proper time, with extremals being geodesics of the Minkowski metric. The
five conditions therefore determine $S[\gamma]$ uniquely up to overall
normalisation (the choice of $m$) and additive boundary terms (the
eliminated $B_\mu$ contribution). The result
$S = -mc^2\int d\tau = -mc\int|dx_4|$ is the action read directly as the
$x_{4}$-advance accumulated along the worldline
(Remark [12.5](#rmk:free-particle-as-x4-advance){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:free-particle-as-x4-advance"} below), establishing that
the relativistic free-particle action is identical to the
McGucken-Principle $x_{4}$-advance functional. $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:free-particle-as-x4-advance .remark}
*Remark 12.5* (The free-particle action as $x_4$-advance). The result
$S_{\mathrm{free}} = -mc\int_\gamma|dx_4|$ has a direct physical
reading: the action is proportional to the magnitude of $x_4$'s
accumulated advance along the worldline. By the McGucken Principle,
$x_4$ advances at rate $ic$ from every event; the integrated advance
along the worldline $\gamma$ is the proper time $\int d\tau$, and the
action is $-mc^2\int d\tau$ --- the textbook free-particle action. The
Lorentz-invariant statement $\sqrt{-\eta_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu}$,
the $x_4$-geometric statement $|dx_4|$, and the proper-time statement
$c\,d\tau$ are three projections of one fact: the worldline's
accumulated $x_4$-advance.
:::

### Proposition V.1: Uniqueness of the Dirac Matter Sector {#sec:dirac-uniqueness}

::: {#prop:dirac-uniqueness .proposition}
**Proposition 12.6** (Uniqueness of the Dirac matter Lagrangian;
[@MG-Lagrangian-2026], §V and [@MG-Dirac-2026], §§II--IV and IX). *Under
the matter orientation
condition [\[eq:matter-orientation\]](#eq:matter-orientation){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:matter-orientation"} of the McGucken Principle, the Dirac
Lagrangian
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Dirac}} \;=\; \bar\psi\,(i\gamma^\mu \partial_\mu - m)\,\psi$$
is the unique first-order Lorentz-invariant Lagrangian on
Clifford-algebra fields satisfying:*

1.  *$\mathcal{L}$ is a Lorentz scalar built from
    $\psi, \bar\psi, \partial_\mu \psi, \partial_\mu \bar\psi$, the
    Minkowski metric $\eta_{\mu\nu}$, and the Dirac matrices
    $\gamma^\mu$ satisfying
    $\{\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu\} = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}$;*

2.  *$\mathcal{L}$ is linear in first derivatives of $\psi$ and
    $\bar\psi$ (first-order field equations);*

3.  *the resulting field equations reproduce the Klein--Gordon
    mass-shell dispersion $E^2 = p^2 c^2 + m^2 c^4$;*

4.  *$\mathcal{L}$ reduces, on-shell in the classical limit, to the
    free-particle action $-mc^2\int d\tau$ of
    Proposition [12.4](#prop:free-particle-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
    reference="prop:free-particle-uniqueness"}.*

*The Clifford algebra $\{\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu\} = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}$ is
itself a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$: the Minkowski signature
$\eta = \mathrm{diag}(+, +, +, -)$ comes from $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$,
and the Clifford algebra is the minimal algebra supporting first-order
Lorentz-covariant spinor fields on this signature.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof; from [@MG-Dirac-2026] §§II--IV and IX.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). The proof proceeds in
four steps, each tracing to $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.

**Step 1: The Minkowski signature from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.** The
McGucken Principle $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ integrates to $x_4 = ict$.
The Euclidean-form infinitesimal interval
$ds^2 = dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2 + dx_4^2$ on the four real coordinates
becomes, after substituting $dx_4^2 = (ic\,dt)^2 = -c^2\,dt^2$:
$$ds^2 \;=\; dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2 - c^2\,dt^2,$$ which is the
Minkowski interval with signature $\eta = \mathrm{diag}(+, +, +, -)$.
The Lorentzian signature is not imposed; it emerges directly from the
$i$ in $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ [@MG-Dirac-2026] §II.1.

**Step 2: The Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$ from the signature.**
Any first-order wave operator that squares to the Klein--Gordon operator
on the Minkowski signature must satisfy the Clifford algebra
$\{\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu\} = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}\,\mathbf{1}$. This is the
algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$. Its minimal faithful representation is
four-dimensional, and the objects on which it acts are Dirac spinors
[@MG-Dirac-2026] §II.3. Therefore condition (D1) reduces to the
Minkowski-signature theorem of Step 1 combined with the algebraic
requirement that the kinetic operator square to Klein--Gordon.

**Step 3: First-order in all four coordinates from coequal treatment.**
The McGucken Principle treats $x_4$ on the same footing as
$x_1, x_2, x_3$: the four coordinates of spacetime are coequal partners
in the geometry. The wave operator for matter must therefore be
first-order in all four spacetime derivatives,
$i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu$, with $\mu$ running over $\{0, 1, 2, 3\}$, not
first-order in three spatial derivatives and second-order in time (the
Klein--Gordon route). This forces condition (D2) [@MG-Dirac-2026] §IX.

**Step 4: The Compton-frequency mass term from the matter orientation
condition.** The matter orientation
condition [\[eq:matter-orientation\]](#eq:matter-orientation){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:matter-orientation"},
$\Psi(x, x_4) = \Psi_0(x) \cdot \exp(+I \cdot k_C\,x_4)$ with
$k_C = mc/\hbar > 0$, makes the $x_4$-dependence of $\Psi$ a standing
oscillation at the Compton frequency $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$. The
Klein--Gordon dispersion $E^2 = p^2 c^2 + m^2 c^4$ of condition (D3) is
the eigenvalue equation for $i\hbar\,\partial_t$ on a wavefunction with
$x_4$-phase $\exp(I\,k_C\,x_4)$: the eigenvalue is
$\hbar\,\omega_C = mc^2$ in the rest frame, and
$\sqrt{p^2 c^2 + m^2 c^4}$ in a moving frame. The mass term $m$ in
$(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - m)\psi = 0$ is the Compton-frequency
wavenumber $k_C$ rendered as a parameter of the matter field
[@MG-Dirac-2026] §II.2 and §IX.1.

The four steps assemble: Steps 1+2+3 force the kinetic operator
$i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu$ acting on a four-component Dirac spinor; Step
4 forces the mass term $-m\psi$ as the Compton-frequency content of the
matter orientation condition; condition (D4) (classical-limit
correspondence) fixes the overall normalization. The unique first-order
Lorentz-covariant Lagrangian on Clifford-algebra fields satisfying
(D1)--(D4) is therefore
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Dirac}} \;=\; \bar\psi(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - m)\psi,$$
which is the Dirac Lagrangian. ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:spin-half-theorem .remark}
*Remark 12.7* (Spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ as a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). A deeper content of
[@MG-Dirac-2026] §IV is that the characteristic spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$
double cover $SU(2) \to SO(3)$ --- traditionally attributed to abstract
representation theory of the Lorentz group --- is itself a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$. The mechanism is the matter orientation
condition (M), which selects right-multiplication of $\Psi$ by the
$x_4$-rotor $\exp(+I \cdot k_C\,x_4)$ and thereby breaks the symmetry
between left-action and sandwich-action of bivector generators on
$\Psi$. The Theorem of Single-Sided Preservation
(Theorem [12.8](#thm:single-sided-preservation){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:single-sided-preservation"} below) establishes that
left-action $\Psi \to R\Psi$ uniquely preserves the orientation
constraint (M); the half-angle in $R = \exp(\theta/2 \cdot e_P)$ is
therefore not a representation-theoretic accident but a geometric
necessity, with spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ as its forced consequence.
:::

::: {#thm:single-sided-preservation .theorem}
**Theorem 12.8** (Single-Sided Preservation, the geometric origin of
spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$; [@MG-Dirac-2026] Theorem IV.3). *Let $\Psi$ satisfy
the matter orientation
condition [\[eq:matter-orientation\]](#eq:matter-orientation){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:matter-orientation"}, and let
$R = \exp(\theta/2 \cdot e_P)$ be a rotor generated by a spatial
bivector $e_P \in \{e_{12}, e_{23}, e_{31}\}$. Then:*

1.  **Left-action* $\Psi \to R\Psi$ preserves the orientation condition
    (M): $R\Psi$ satisfies (M) with rest-frame amplitude
    $\Psi_0' = R\Psi_0$ and the same Compton wavenumber $k_C$.*

2.  **Sandwich action* $\Psi \to R^{-1}\Psi R$ does *not* preserve (M)
    in general: for $x_4$-involving bivectors, $R^{-1}\Psi R$ partially
    converts $\exp(+I \cdot k_C\,x_4)$ into a mixture containing
    $\exp(-I \cdot k_C\,x_4)$ --- i.e. it partially converts matter into
    antimatter.*

*Single-sided action is therefore the *unique* transformation that
preserves the matter orientation constraint across all bivector
generators needed to describe Lorentz transformations. Matter fields
must transform under bivector generators by single-sided action only:
$\Psi \to \exp(\theta/2 \cdot e_P)\,\Psi$. The half-angle in the spinor
transformation is therefore the geometric content of the theorem that
single-sided transformation is the unique action on matter fields
preserving (M).*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Everything below descends from the physical expansion of $x_{4}$ at the velocity of light, in a spherically symmetric manner, from every event of $M_{G}$ ($\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). This theorem is the same statement as
Theorem [9.8](#thm:single-sided-preservation-QMT9){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:single-sided-preservation-QMT9"} of
Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:dirac"}, where
it is proved in full detail across six steps. We summarise
the essential argument here and refer to the master proof of
Theorem [9.8](#thm:single-sided-preservation-QMT9){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:single-sided-preservation-QMT9"} for full detail.

**Step 1: Spatial bivectors commute with the pseudoscalar.** For a
spatial bivector $e_P \in \{e_{12}, e_{23}, e_{31}\}$ and the
pseudoscalar $I = \gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3$ of the Clifford
algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$ associated to the McGucken-derived Minkowski
signature (Lemma [9.3](#lem:clifford-minimal-rep){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:clifford-minimal-rep"} of
Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:dirac"}),
direct computation gives $[e_P, I] = 0$. The reason: $e_P$ contains two
$\gamma$-factors, and moving $e_P$ past $I$ requires two
anticommutations, giving overall sign $(-1)^2 = +1$. Consequently the
spatial rotor $R = \exp(\theta/2\cdot e_P)$ also commutes with the
matter-orientation phase factor $\exp(+I\cdot k_C\,x_4)$.

**Step 2: Left-action preserves (M) --- claim (a).** Since the spatial
rotor $R$ depends only on spatial coordinates and commutes with
$\exp(+I\cdot k_C\,x_4)$ by Step 1,
$$R\Psi \;=\; R\cdot\Psi_0\cdot\exp(+I\cdot k_C\,x_4) \;=\; (R\Psi_0)\cdot\exp(+I\cdot k_C\,x_4),$$
which satisfies (M) with new rest-frame amplitude $\Psi_0' = R\Psi_0$
and unchanged Compton wavenumber $k_C$. This establishes claim (a).

**Step 3: $x_{4}$-involving bivectors do not commute with $I$.** Lorentz
boosts in the McGucken-derived Minkowski arena
(Theorem [9.2](#thm:hilbert-arena){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:hilbert-arena"}) are generated by $x_{4}$-involving
bivectors $e_{i4}$ ($i = 1, 2, 3$). For these, the commutator with $I$
is non-zero: $e_{i4}$ contains $\gamma^i$ and $\gamma^4 = i\gamma^0$
(Lemma [9.10](#lem:gamma4-equals-igamma0){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:gamma4-equals-igamma0"} of
Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:dirac"}), and
explicit Clifford-algebra computation gives
$[e_{i4}, I] = 2\,e_{i4}\cdot I_\perp \ne 0$, where $I_\perp$ denotes
the pseudoscalar's projection onto the bivector's orthogonal complement.
Therefore the boost rotor $R = \exp(\phi/2\cdot e_{i4})$ does not
commute with $\exp(+I\cdot k_C\,x_4)$.

**Step 4: Sandwich-action fails (M) for $x_{4}$-involving bivectors ---
claim (b).** For $R = \exp(\phi/2\cdot e_{i4})$, the sandwich action
transports the rotor through the pseudoscalar exponent:
$$R^{-1}\Psi R \;=\; (R^{-1}\Psi_0\,R)\cdot\exp\!\bigl(+\,R^{-1}IR\cdot k_C\,x_4\bigr).$$
By Step 3, $R^{-1}IR \ne I$ in general. Explicit computation gives
$$R^{-1}IR \;=\; \cos(\phi)\cdot I + \sin(\phi)\cdot J,$$ for some
bivector $J$ orthogonal to $I$ in the Clifford algebra. The transformed
multivector therefore decomposes as a mixture
$$\Psi^{\mathrm{sandwich}} \;=\; (R^{-1}\Psi_0 R)\cdot\bigl[\cos(\phi)\exp(+I\cdot k_C\,x_4) + \sin(\phi)\exp(+J\cdot k_C\,x_4)\bigr],$$
which is a partial conversion of matter ($+I$-orientation) into
antimatter ($-I$-orientation when $\cos(\phi) < 0$, i.e. for
$|\phi| > \pi/2$). The matter orientation condition (M) is broken under
sandwich-action for any non-zero boost generator. This establishes claim
(b).

**Step 5: Single-sided left-action is unique.** Steps 2 and 4 together
establish that left-action preserves (M) across the full bivector group
(spatial *and* $x_{4}$-involving generators of the Lorentz algebra),
while sandwich-action fails (M) for $x_{4}$-involving generators. Since
matter must transform consistently under all Lorentz generators
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iv), derived at Theorem 4.6 Lorentz consistency),
single-sided left-action is the unique transformation preserving (M).

**Step 6: Half-angle forced by single-sided action.** The exponent of
$R = \exp(\theta/2\cdot e_P)$ acts directly on $\Psi$ under single-sided
action (without the doubling that would arise from sandwich action).
Using $e_P^2 = -1$ for spatial bivectors, a $2\pi$ rotation gives
$R(2\pi) = \exp(\pi e_P) = -\mathbf{1}$, so matter acquires a sign-flip
under rotation by $2\pi$; only a $4\pi$ rotation recovers the identity.
This is the $4\pi$-periodicity of spinors (Hestenes [@Hestenes1966-STA],
the spacetime-algebra reading), derived as a forced theorem of (M)
rather than a postulated property. The result is consistent with the
standard double-cover $\mathrm{Spin}(1,3) \to SO^+(1,3)$
(Lemma [9.4](#lem:spin-double-cover){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:spin-double-cover"} of
Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:dirac"};
Penrose--Rindler [@PenroseRindler1984]): matter spinors are sections of
the double cover, with the lift forced by the $x_{4}$-orientation
constraint (M) descending from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ (with
$x_4 = ict$ the integrated kinematic shadow per
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}).

The full six-step argument with explicit Clifford-algebra computations
appears in the proof of
Theorem [9.8](#thm:single-sided-preservation-QMT9){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:single-sided-preservation-QMT9"} of
Chapter [9](#ch:dirac){reference-type="ref" reference="ch:dirac"}; the
present proof reproduces the argument for completeness.
$\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:antimatter-cpt-geometric .remark}
*Remark 12.9* (Antimatter and CPT as geometric consequences of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$). [@MG-Dirac-2026] §§VII--VIII establishes two
further results forced by $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$:

-   *Antimatter as right-action.* The corresponding orientation
    condition for antimatter is
    $\Psi(x, x_4) = \Psi_0(x) \cdot \exp(-I \cdot k_C\,x_4)$ with the
    same $k_C > 0$. Antimatter is therefore motion *against*
    $x_4$-expansion. The standard charge-conjugation operator
    $C = i\gamma^2\gamma^0$ acting as $\psi \to C\gamma^0\psi^*$ is
    shown to be identical, at the component level via the Doran--Lasenby
    correspondence, to the geometric operation
    $\Psi \to \Psi \cdot \gamma_2\gamma_1$: both produce
    $(0, -1, 0, 1)^\top \cdot e^{+iEt/\hbar}$, the rest-frame spin-up
    positron, from the spin-up electron
    $(1, 0, 1, 0)^\top \cdot e^{-iEt/\hbar}$ [@MG-Dirac-2026] §VIII.7.

-   *CPT as 4D geometric inversion.* The CPT theorem becomes the
    geometric statement that full 4D coordinate reversal preserves the
    $x_4$-dynamics. CPT is therefore not a separately-proved theorem
    requiring Lorentz invariance and locality as independent axioms; it
    is automatic 4D inversion symmetry of $\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
    [@MG-Dirac-2026] §VIII.9.

The microscopic $T$-violation observed in kaon and $B$-meson decays and
the macroscopic thermodynamic arrow of time are accordingly not separate
phenomena but the same geometric fact ($\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= +ic$, not
$-ic$) manifesting at different scales [@MG-Dirac-2026] §X.4, consistent
with Theorem [12.18](#thm:five-arrows-of-time){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:five-arrows-of-time"} of the present chapter.
:::

::: {#rmk:closing-chain-dirac .remark}
*Remark 12.10* (Closing the chain: from $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ to
spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ Dirac matter). With
Theorem [12.8](#thm:single-sided-preservation){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:single-sided-preservation"} and
Remark [12.9](#rmk:antimatter-cpt-geometric){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:antimatter-cpt-geometric"}, the chain
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic \Rightarrow \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Dirac}}$
closes:
$$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic \;\Longrightarrow\; \eta = \mathrm{diag}(+,+,+,-) \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathrm{Cl}(1,3) \;\Longrightarrow\; (\text{M}) \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{spin-}\tfrac{1}{2} \;\Longrightarrow\; (i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - m)\psi = 0.$$
Every distinctive feature of the Dirac equation --- Clifford algebra,
four-component spinors, spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$, $SU(2)$ double cover, two
Weyl chiralities, mass as Compton-frequency coupling, antimatter, charge
conjugation $C$, and CPT --- is derived from the single principle
$\dfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$.
Proposition [12.6](#prop:dirac-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:dirac-uniqueness"} is therefore no longer cited at the
level of statement only; the full proof chain is given above, with the
four-step kinetic-Lagrangian derivation in the main proof body and the
spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ / antimatter / CPT content in
Theorem [12.8](#thm:single-sided-preservation){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:single-sided-preservation"} and
Remark [12.9](#rmk:antimatter-cpt-geometric){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:antimatter-cpt-geometric"}.
:::

### Proposition VI.2: Uniqueness of the Yang--Mills Gauge Sector {#sec:gauge-uniqueness}

::: {#prop:gauge-uniqueness .proposition}
**Proposition 12.11** (Uniqueness of the Yang--Mills gauge Lagrangian;
[@MG-Lagrangian-2026], §VI and [@MG-SM-2026], Theorems 10--11). *For any
compact Lie group $G$, the Yang--Mills Lagrangian
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gauge}} \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{4}\,F_{\mu\nu}^a F^{a\,\mu\nu}, \qquad D_\mu = \partial_\mu - i g\,A_\mu^a T^a,$$
with field strength
$F_{\mu\nu}^a = \partial_\mu A_\nu^a - \partial_\nu A_\mu^a + g\,f^{abc}A_\mu^b A_\nu^c$,
is the unique gauge-invariant Lagrangian for the gauge group $G$
satisfying:*

1.  *local gauge invariance under $G$ --- which is itself derived from
    the local $x_4$-phase indeterminacy implied by
    $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ per
    Theorem [12.12](#thm:local-U1-gauge){reference-type="ref"
    reference="thm:local-U1-gauge"} below ([@MG-SM-2026] Theorem 5);*

2.  *Lorentz invariance;*

3.  *locality (polynomial in fields and first derivatives only);*

4.  *correct mass dimension $\leq 4$ for a four-dimensional kinetic
    Lagrangian (renormalisability).*

*The specific Standard Model gauge group
$G = U(1)_Y \times SU(2)_L \times SU(3)_c$ is an empirical input per
[@MG-Lagrangian-2026] (and [@MG-SM-2026], §XV.1); but *given* any
compact Lie group $G$, the form of the kinetic Lagrangian is
forced by
Proposition [12.11](#prop:gauge-uniqueness){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:gauge-uniqueness"}.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof; from [@MG-SM-2026] Theorems 10 and 11.* The proof has four
steps, following the template of Theorems 10 and 11 of the
source paper. The Yang--Mills gauge sector is forced by
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, the physical, geometric fact that the fourth
dimension expands at the velocity of light in a spherically symmetric
manner): the global $U(1)$ matter-phase symmetry
(Theorem [16.1](#thm:QMT16){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT16"})
extended to internal non-abelian symmetries via the matter orientation
condition
(Definition [9.6](#def:matter-orientation-M){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:matter-orientation-M"}, encoding the $+ic$-branch
selection of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ per
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iii) monotonicity) forces the
gauge-connection machinery, with the Yang--Mills Lagrangian fixed
uniquely by mass-dimension and Lorentz-invariance.

**Step 1: Non-abelian gauge connection (Theorem 10).** Let $G$ be a
compact Lie group with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ spanned by generators
$T^a$ satisfying $[T^a, T^b] = i f^{abc} T^c$. Assume matter fields
$\psi(x)$ transform in a unitary representation $R$ of $G$: under global
$U = \exp(i\alpha^a T^a)$ with constant $\alpha^a$, $\psi \to U\psi$
(the non-abelian generalisation of the global $U(1)$ symmetry of
Theorem [12.12](#thm:local-U1-gauge){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:local-U1-gauge"}, with the origin in
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (i)+(v) being the same: $x_{4}$-phase
indeterminacy at every event of $M_{G}$, with $x_4 = ict$ the integrated
kinematic shadow per
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}). Demand invariance under local
transformations $\psi(x) \to U(x)\psi(x)$,
$U(x) = \exp(i\alpha^a(x) T^a)$, while preserving first-order derivative
structure. The covariant derivative takes the form
$D_\mu = \partial_\mu - i g A_\mu(x)$, where $A_\mu(x) = A_\mu^a(x) T^a$
is a Lie-algebra-valued one-form. The requirement that $D_\mu \psi$
transforms covariantly --- $(D_\mu \psi)' = U(x)\,D_\mu \psi$ ---
uniquely fixes the gauge field transformation law:
$$A_\mu' = U A_\mu U^{-1} + (i/g)\,U\,\partial_\mu U^{-1}.$$

**Step 2: Derive the transformation law.** To derive this, expand
$D_\mu' \psi' = \partial_\mu(U\psi) - i g A_\mu' U \psi = (\partial_\mu U)\psi + U \partial_\mu \psi - i g A_\mu' U \psi$,
and equate to $U(D_\mu \psi) = U \partial_\mu \psi - i g U A_\mu \psi$.
Rearranging gives $(\partial_\mu U) - i g A_\mu' U = -i g U A_\mu$,
hence the transformation law upon right-multiplication by $U^{-1}$. The
curvature of the connection is the field strength
$$F_{\mu\nu} = (i/g)[D_\mu, D_\nu] = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu + i g [A_\mu, A_\nu],$$
which transforms covariantly as $F_{\mu\nu}' = U F_{\mu\nu} U^{-1}$
since $D_\mu' = U D_\mu U^{-1}$. The factor of $i$ in
$F_{\mu\nu} = (i/g)[D_\mu, D_\nu]$ is the non-abelian generalisation of
case 6 of the twelve canonical $i$-insertions
(Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}), tracking the local-phase-gradient image of
the McGucken-Principle $i$ into the non-abelian connection.

**Step 3: Yang--Mills Lagrangian invariance and dimensional analysis
(Theorem 11 setup).** Assume the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ admits an
invariant non-degenerate bilinear form $\mathrm{Tr}(\cdot\,\cdot)$
(e.g. the trace in the fundamental representation, suitably normalised).
The pure gauge-field Lagrangian must be: (a) local; (b)
Lorentz-invariant by
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (iv), derived at Theorem 4.6 (Lorentz consistency of the
structure on $M_{G}$); (c) invariant under local $G$ transformations;
(d) polynomial of mass dimension $\leq 4$ (condition (G4)). By (a)+(c),
any gauge-invariant scalar must be built from $F_{\mu\nu}$ contracted
using an invariant trace. By the invariance of the trace,
$\mathrm{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu}' F'^{\mu\nu}) = \mathrm{Tr}(U F_{\mu\nu} U^{-1} U F^{\mu\nu} U^{-1}) = \mathrm{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu} F^{\mu\nu})$.

**Step 4: Uniqueness of the Yang--Mills form.** Since $[A_\mu] = 1$ and
$[F_{\mu\nu}] = 2$, the term $\mathrm{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu})$ has
mass dimension 4 --- the maximum allowed by (G4). Terms with more
factors of $F$ (e.g. $\mathrm{Tr}(F^2)^2$, $\mathrm{Tr}(F^3)$) have
dimension $\geq 6$ and violate (G4) without unsuppressed coefficients.
The parity-odd term
$\mathrm{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu}\tilde F^{\mu\nu}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\mathrm{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu} F_{\rho\sigma})$
is a total derivative in four dimensions and does not affect equations
of motion (Weinberg [@Weinberg1995-QFT] §23.5, the standard
total-derivative argument for the $\theta$-term). The unique candidate
is therefore
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{YM}} \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{4}\,\mathrm{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu} F^{\mu\nu}),$$
with the factor $-\tfrac{1}{4}$ fixed by comparison with the Abelian
limit ($\mathrm{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}) \to F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$) and
the Maxwell Lagrangian of Theorem 7 of the source paper (the same
Maxwell sector derived in
Theorem [16.1](#thm:QMT16){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT16"}
of this textbook as the abelian special case of local-$U(1)$ gauge
invariance). In component form,
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{YM}} = -\tfrac{1}{4}F_{\mu\nu}^a F^{a\,\mu\nu}$.
$\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#thm:local-U1-gauge .theorem}
**Theorem 12.12** (Local $U(1)$ gauge invariance from $x_4$-phase
indeterminacy; [@MG-SM-2026] Theorem 5). *Let $\psi(x)$ be a matter
field with global $U(1)$ symmetry (the McGucken matter orientation
condition [\[eq:matter-orientation\]](#eq:matter-orientation){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:matter-orientation"} of
§[12.1](#sec:mcgucken-lagrangian-form){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:mcgucken-lagrangian-form"} establishes this $U(1)$ as the
$x_4$-phase symmetry). Suppose:*

1.  *$\psi(x)$ has a global $U(1)$ symmetry $\psi \to e^{iq\Lambda}\psi$
    (Theorem 4 of [@MG-SM-2026], the local-shift version of
    $x_4 \to x_4 + 2\pi/k_C$);*

2.  *One demands invariance under local phase rotations
    $\psi(x) \to e^{iq\Lambda(x)}\psi(x)$ for arbitrary smooth
    $\Lambda(x, t)$;*

3.  *The kinetic term must remain first-order in derivatives of $\psi$.*

*Under (E1)--(E3), local gauge invariance is achievable if and only if
the ordinary derivative $\partial_\mu$ is replaced by the covariant
derivative $D_\mu = \partial_\mu - i q A_\mu$, where $A_\mu$ transforms
as $A_\mu \to A_\mu + \partial_\mu \Lambda$. The transformation law is
the unique one consistent with (E2)--(E3).*
:::

::: proof
*Proof; from [@MG-SM-2026] Theorem 5.* The proof has five steps. Local $U(1)$ gauge invariance is a theorem of
$\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, the physical, geometric fact that the fourth
dimension expands at the velocity of light in a spherically symmetric
manner): the integrated kinematic shadow $x_4 = ict$
(Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}, the kinematic shadow of the
dynamical principle) enters the matter wavefunction only through
$\exp(+I \cdot k_C\,x_4)$, where the absolute origin of the
$x_{4}$-phase is undetermined; promoting the constant shift to a local
shift forces the gauge-field machinery below.

**Step 1: Ordinary derivative breaks local invariance.** Under the local
$U(1)$ transformation $\psi'(x) = e^{iq\Lambda(x)}\psi(x)$ with
spacetime-dependent phase $\Lambda(x)$, the ordinary derivative
transforms by the product rule:
$$\partial_\mu\psi'(x) = \partial_\mu(e^{iq\Lambda}\psi) = e^{iq\Lambda}\,\partial_\mu\psi + e^{iq\Lambda}\cdot iq\,(\partial_\mu\Lambda)\,\psi = e^{iq\Lambda}(\partial_\mu + iq\,\partial_\mu\Lambda)\psi.$$
The extra term $iq\,(\partial_\mu\Lambda)\psi$ is the obstruction to
local-invariance: the Lagrangian terms involving $\partial_\mu\psi$
(typically the kinetic term and current-coupling terms) fail to be
invariant. The $i$ in the obstruction is case 6 of the twelve canonical
$i$-insertions (Theorem [9.21](#thm:twelve-i){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:twelve-i"}, the local-phase-gradient image of the
McGucken-Principle $i$).

**Step 2: Introduce the covariant derivative.** Define
$D_\mu\psi := (\partial_\mu - iqA_\mu)\psi$, where $A_\mu$ is a new
gauge field with its own transformation rule (to be determined). Demand
that $D_\mu\psi$ transforms covariantly:
$$(D_\mu\psi)'(x) = e^{iq\Lambda(x)}D_\mu\psi(x).$$ This requirement is
forced by (E2)--(E3): the kinetic term must remain first-order in
derivatives and must be locally invariant under the local $U(1)$
transformation. The covariant derivative is the same construction as in
Theorem [16.1](#thm:QMT16){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:QMT16"}
(gauge invariance as a theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$, via
Lemma [16.3](#lem:QMT16-local-promotion){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem:QMT16-local-promotion"}).

**Step 3: Solve for the gauge-field transformation rule.** Expand the
left-hand side of the covariance condition:
$$(D_\mu\psi)'(x) = (\partial_\mu - iqA_\mu'(x))(e^{iq\Lambda}\psi) = e^{iq\Lambda}(\partial_\mu + iq\partial_\mu\Lambda - iqA_\mu')\psi.$$
Setting this equal to
$e^{iq\Lambda}D_\mu\psi = e^{iq\Lambda}(\partial_\mu - iqA_\mu)\psi$ and
cancelling the common factor:
$$\partial_\mu + iq\partial_\mu\Lambda - iqA_\mu' = \partial_\mu - iqA_\mu.$$
Subtracting $\partial_\mu$ and dividing by $iq$:
$$A_\mu' = A_\mu + \partial_\mu\Lambda.$$ This is the gauge-field
transformation rule.

**Step 4: Uniqueness.** The transformation rule
$A_\mu \mapsto A_\mu + \partial_\mu\Lambda$ is uniquely determined by
the requirement (E2) (local-$U(1)$ invariance) combined with (E3)
(first-order-in-derivative kinetic term). Any other transformation rule
would either fail to cancel the obstruction term $iq\partial_\mu\Lambda$
from Step 1, or would introduce higher-derivative dependence into the
covariant derivative. The uniqueness is the standard one of abelian
gauge theory (Weinberg [@Weinberg1995-QFT] §8.1, restated here as a
derivation from the $x_{4}$-phase indeterminacy).

**Step 5: McGucken anchoring.** The deeper fact
(Remark [12.13](#rmk:local-gauge-from-x4){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:local-gauge-from-x4"} below) is that the local-$U(1)$
symmetry of the matter field traces to the $x_{4}$-phase indeterminacy
of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$
(Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"}, with the integrated $x_4 = ict$ entering
$\psi$ only through $\exp(+I \cdot k_C x_4)$ per
Remark [4.3](#rmk:integrated-shadow){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk:integrated-shadow"}) via the matter orientation condition
(Definition [9.6](#def:matter-orientation-M){reference-type="ref"
reference="def:matter-orientation-M"}). The phase $\exp(ik_C x_4)$ in
the matter wavefunction is invariant under constant shifts
$x_4 \to x_4 + 2\pi/k_C$; promoting the constant shift to a local shift
$x_4 \to x_4 + \alpha(x)/k_C$ generates the local-$U(1)$ gauge
invariance of $\psi$. The gauge field $A_\mu$ is the geometric necessity
of making the local phase symmetry of $x_{4}$'s expansion consistent
across spacetime --- the connection parallel-transporting the phase of
$x_{4}$ between different spacetime points. The result is the same as Theorem [16.1](#thm:QMT16){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:QMT16"}: gauge invariance is a forced consequence of the
McGucken Principle $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ combined with
Postulate [4.1](#postulate:mcp){reference-type="ref"
reference="postulate:mcp"} clause (v) (global validity, with the gauge
field supplying the inter-event consistency required by the local
promotion). $\square$ ◻
:::

::: {#rmk:local-gauge-from-x4 .remark}
*Remark 12.13* (Local gauge invariance from $x_4$-phase indeterminacy).
The deeper fact established by
Theorem [12.12](#thm:local-U1-gauge){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:local-U1-gauge"} is that local gauge invariance is a
theorem of $\tfrac{dx_{4}}{dt}= ic$ per [@MG-SM-2026] Theorem 5. The
matter orientation
condition [\[eq:matter-orientation\]](#eq:matter-orientation){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq:matter-orientation"} introduces a phase
$\exp(+I \cdot k_C\,x_4)$ that is invariant under a constant shift
$x_4 \to x_4 + 2\pi/k_C$. If the constant shift is promoted to a local
shift $x_4 \to x_4 + \alpha(x)/k_C$, the invariance becomes the local
$U(1)$ gauge invariance of the matter field. The gauge field $A_\mu$ is
the geometric necessity of making the local phase symmetry of $x_4$'s
expansion consistent across spacetime --- the connection
parallel-transports the phase of $x_4$ between different spacetime
points ([@MG-SM-2026] Remark following Theorem 5). Extending to
